Title:
Disease Prediction using Machine Learning

Problem Statement:
Hospitals have a lot of data and doctors are very busy. Machine learning can help predict diseases so patients get better.

Objectives:
1. To predict diseases.
2. To use machine learning.
3. To help hospitals.

Methodology:
I will collect some data and use machine learning algorithms in Python to classify the diseases. Then I will check if it works.

Scope:
This project will be used by all hospitals and clinics everywhere to predict any kind of disease.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A system that predicts diseases.
2. Happy patients and doctors.

Title:
Deep Learning for Finance Images

Problem Statement:
Finance is important and there are many pictures and charts. Deep learning is very powerful and can look at images to help banks.

Objectives:
1. To use deep learning.
2. To look at finance images.
3. To make banks better.

Methodology:
I will use a neural network and computer vision to study the images. I will train the model and see the results using Python.

Scope:
The system works for the whole finance industry and any image related to money.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A deep learning model.
2. Better decisions for banks.

Title:
NLP System for Factories

Problem Statement:
Factories produce a lot of reports and text. Natural language processing is a trending technology that can read text and understand it for manufacturing.

Objectives:
1. To apply NLP.
2. To read factory text.
3. To improve manufacturing.

Methodology:
I plan to use NLP and some libraries to process the text. The system will analyse the words and give output. I will do testing at the end.

Scope:
It can handle all types of documents from any factory in the world.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An NLP tool.
2. Faster factory work.

Title:
A Recommender System for Public Safety Alerts

Problem Statement:
Residents in a city receive many safety notices, but most are generic and not relevant to where a person lives or what they care about. People may ignore alerts that do not seem to apply to them, which is a problem during emergencies.

Objectives:
1. To build a recommender system that suggests relevant safety alerts to users.
2. To use user location and past behaviour as inputs.
3. To evaluate whether users find the recommendations useful.

Methodology:
The project will use collaborative filtering to recommend alerts based on similar users. User data such as location and clicked alerts will be stored in a database. The recommendations will be shown in a simple web interface, and a small survey will be used to check satisfaction.

Scope:
The system focuses on one city and a limited set of alert categories such as flood, fire and crime. It will not handle real-time emergency dispatch.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working recommender prototype for safety alerts.
2. A report on user satisfaction from the survey.

Timeline:
The project will run for two semesters, with development in the first and testing in the second.

Title:
Speech Recognition for Energy Plant Operators

Problem Statement:
Operators in energy plants often have their hands busy and cannot type commands or notes. A speech recognition system could let them log readings and issue commands by voice, reducing errors and saving time.

Objectives:
1. To develop a speech recognition module for plant commands.
2. To recognise a set of common operator phrases.
3. To test recognition accuracy in a noisy environment.

Methodology:
The system will use an existing speech recognition library to convert voice to text. A small vocabulary of commands will be defined. Audio samples will be recorded and the accuracy measured by comparing output text to the spoken command.

Scope:
The project covers English commands only and a fixed vocabulary of about thirty phrases. It will not control real plant equipment for safety reasons.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A prototype voice command recogniser.
2. Accuracy results across quiet and noisy conditions.

Timeline:
Eight months total: requirements and data collection first, then development and testing.

Title:
Network Intrusion Detection for Small Businesses

Problem Statement:
Small businesses usually cannot afford expensive security appliances and lack IT staff. As a result, network attacks often go unnoticed until damage is done. A lightweight intrusion detection tool could help these businesses spot suspicious traffic.

Objectives:
1. To build an intrusion detection system suitable for small business networks.
2. To detect common attack patterns such as port scans and brute-force attempts.
3. To present alerts in a simple dashboard.

Methodology:
Network traffic will be captured and features extracted. A machine learning classifier will be trained on a public dataset to label traffic as normal or malicious. Detected events will be shown on a web dashboard. Detection will be evaluated using accuracy and false-positive rate.

Scope:
The tool targets small office networks with limited traffic. It focuses on a few well-known attack types and does not provide automatic blocking.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A prototype intrusion detection tool with a dashboard.
2. Evaluation results showing detection accuracy and false positives.

Timeline:
Two semesters, with data preparation and model training in the first and dashboard plus testing in the second.

Title:
A Web Application Security Scanner for Agriculture Platforms

Problem Statement:
Many agriculture marketplaces and farm management websites are built quickly with little attention to security. Common flaws like SQL injection and cross-site scripting can expose farmer and buyer data. A simple scanner could help small developers find these issues.

Objectives:
1. To develop a web vulnerability scanner for common flaws.
2. To detect SQL injection and cross-site scripting points.
3. To generate a readable report of findings.

Methodology:
The scanner will crawl a target site to find input fields, then send test payloads to check for injection and scripting vulnerabilities. Results will be compiled into a report. The tool will be tested against a deliberately vulnerable demo site such as DVWA.

Scope:
The scanner covers two vulnerability types on small agriculture web apps. It will not test authentication bypass or perform exploitation beyond detection.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working scanner that detects two vulnerability classes.
2. A sample report from testing on a vulnerable demo site.

Timeline:
The work spans two semesters, with crawler and payload logic first, then reporting and testing.

Title:
Static and Dynamic Malware Analysis for Transportation Control Systems

Problem Statement:
Transportation systems such as traffic controllers and fleet management servers increasingly run on standard operating systems, making them targets for malware. Analysts need a way to quickly characterise suspicious binaries found in these environments, but combining static and dynamic analysis is often manual and slow.

Objectives:
1. To build a pipeline that runs both static and dynamic analysis on submitted binaries.
2. To extract indicators such as imported APIs, strings, and runtime behaviour in a sandbox.
3. To classify samples as likely benign or malicious based on extracted features.

Methodology:
Static analysis will use tools like PEfile and YARA rules to extract headers, imports and string patterns. Dynamic analysis will run samples inside a Cuckoo-style sandbox virtual machine to log API calls and network activity. Extracted features will feed a Random Forest classifier trained on a labelled malware dataset. Evaluation will use accuracy, precision and recall against a held-out test set.

Scope:
The project targets Windows PE binaries relevant to transportation back-office systems. It will not analyse firmware or mobile malware, and sandboxing is limited to a single VM image.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An analysis pipeline producing per-sample feature reports.
2. A classifier with reported accuracy and recall on test data.

Timeline:
Semester one: static analysis and sandbox setup. Semester two: classifier, evaluation and reporting.

Title:
A Responsive Web Platform for Community Sustainability Reporting

Problem Statement:
Communities running sustainability initiatives such as recycling drives and tree planting struggle to track and share progress. Information is scattered across spreadsheets and chat groups, making it hard to see overall impact or keep volunteers engaged.

Objectives:
1. To develop a responsive web platform where communities log sustainability activities.
2. To visualise aggregate metrics such as waste recycled and trees planted.
3. To support multiple user roles including organisers and volunteers.

Methodology:
The platform will be built with React on the front end and a Node.js and PostgreSQL back end. Activity data will be entered through forms and aggregated into dashboards using a charting library. Role-based access will separate organiser and volunteer permissions. Usability will be evaluated with a small group of users using the System Usability Scale.

Scope:
The platform covers activity logging and reporting for community groups. It will not include financial donations or integration with government databases.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A responsive web application with role-based dashboards.
2. Usability results from a pilot with real community users.

Timeline:
Eight months: design and core CRUD first, dashboards and usability testing second.

Title:
A Progressive Web App for Last-Mile Logistics Tracking

Problem Statement:
Small logistics operators often rely on phone calls and paper to manage last-mile deliveries, leading to lost parcels and poor visibility for customers. A lightweight app that works on low-end devices and unstable connections could improve tracking without costly hardware.

Objectives:
1. To build a progressive web app for drivers and dispatchers to manage deliveries.
2. To support offline use with later synchronisation when connectivity returns.
3. To let customers track parcel status through a shared link.

Methodology:
The PWA will use service workers and IndexedDB to cache data and queue updates while offline. The back end will expose a REST API built with Express, syncing delivery status to a database. Push notifications will inform customers of status changes. Functionality will be tested under simulated offline conditions and on a mid-range Android browser.

Scope:
The app focuses on delivery status tracking and offline sync. It excludes route optimisation, payments, and integration with national postal carriers.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An installable PWA with offline-capable delivery tracking.
2. Test results confirming correct sync after connectivity loss.

Timeline:
Two semesters: API and core PWA first, offline sync and notifications second.

Title:
A Cross-Platform Mobile App for E-Government Service Requests

Problem Statement:
Citizens often need to visit multiple government offices or websites to submit simple requests such as reporting a broken streetlight or applying for a permit. The process is fragmented and unclear, especially for less tech-savvy users. A single mobile app could streamline common municipal requests.

Objectives:
1. To develop a cross-platform mobile app for submitting and tracking municipal service requests.
2. To provide categorised request forms with photo and location attachment.
3. To let users view the status of their submitted requests.

Methodology:
The app will be built with Flutter to target both Android and iOS from one codebase. A Firebase back end will store requests and statuses, with authentication for citizens. GPS and the camera will be used to attach context to reports. Acceptance testing will follow defined user scenarios, and feedback will be gathered from a small test group.

Scope:
The app covers a fixed set of common request types for one municipality. It will not handle payments or connect to live internal government systems.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A cross-platform app for submitting and tracking requests.
2. Acceptance test results across the defined scenarios.

Timeline:
Eight months split into design, core development, and testing phases.

Title:
An Android Native App for Personalised Exam Revision

Problem Statement:
Students preparing for exams often lack a structured way to review weak topics, relying on rereading notes without focus. Existing apps are generic and do not adapt to what a student gets wrong. A native Android app could schedule revision based on quiz performance.

Objectives:
1. To build a native Android app that delivers topic-based quizzes.
2. To track per-topic performance and recommend what to revise next.
3. To use spaced repetition to schedule reviews of weak topics.

Methodology:
The app will be developed in Kotlin using Android Jetpack components and a local Room database for offline storage. Quiz results per topic will drive a simple spaced-repetition scheduler based on the SM-2 algorithm. The app will be evaluated through a two-week trial with students, measuring quiz score improvement and collecting feedback.

Scope:
The app targets a few subjects with a preloaded question bank. It will not include teacher dashboards, cloud sync, or content authoring tools.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A native Android revision app with spaced repetition.
2. Trial results comparing scores before and after use.

Timeline:
Semester one for design and core features; semester two for scheduling logic and the student trial.

Title:
An IoT Sensor Network for In-Store Retail Analytics

Problem Statement:
Physical retail stores have limited insight into how customers move and where they spend time, unlike online shops that track every click. Expensive camera systems raise privacy concerns. A low-cost IoT sensor network could estimate footfall and dwell time in store zones without identifying individuals.

Objectives:
1. To build an IoT sensor network that counts foot traffic across store zones.
2. To estimate dwell time per zone using sensor data.
3. To present footfall and dwell metrics on a dashboard.

Methodology:
ESP32 microcontrollers with passive infrared and Wi-Fi probe sensors will be placed in zones to detect presence. Data will be sent over MQTT to a Raspberry Pi broker, then stored in a database. A web dashboard will aggregate counts and estimated dwell times. The estimates will be validated against manual counts during test sessions.

Scope:
The system covers anonymous footfall and dwell estimation in a small store layout. It will not perform facial recognition or individual customer tracking.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working sensor network reporting zone-level footfall.
2. Validation results comparing sensor counts to manual counts.

Timeline:
Two semesters: hardware and data pipeline first, dashboard and validation second.

Title:
An Energy-Aware Smart Home Automation Hub for Smart-City Demand Response

Problem Statement:
As cities introduce time-of-use electricity pricing and demand-response programs, individual homes lack an easy way to shift appliance usage to off-peak periods. Existing smart-home hubs automate convenience but rarely optimise for grid signals, leaving potential savings and grid relief unrealised.

Objectives:
1. To build a smart-home hub that schedules deferrable appliances based on time-of-use tariffs and demand-response signals.
2. To predict short-term household load using historical consumption.
3. To evaluate cost savings and peak reduction against an always-on baseline.

Methodology:
The hub will run on a Raspberry Pi using Home Assistant for device control over Zigbee and MQTT. A scheduling module will defer flexible loads such as water heating and EV charging into off-peak windows, driven by a published tariff and a simulated demand-response event feed. Short-term load forecasting will use a gradient-boosted regression model on a public household consumption dataset. Evaluation compares cost and peak demand under the optimised schedule versus an unscheduled baseline over a simulated month.

Scope:
The project covers scheduling of a defined set of deferrable appliances and load forecasting. It will not implement two-way grid settlement or real utility integration; demand-response events are simulated.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A functioning automation hub with tariff-aware scheduling.
2. Quantified cost and peak-demand savings versus the baseline.

Timeline:
Month 1-2 setup and device integration; 3-5 scheduling and forecasting; 6-7 evaluation; 8 reporting.

Title:
Edge-Based Crowd and Queue Estimation for Tourism Attractions

Problem Statement:
Popular tourist attractions suffer from unpredictable crowding, frustrating visitors and straining staff. Cloud-based video analytics for crowd estimation is costly and raises privacy and bandwidth concerns when streaming footage off-site. Processing at the edge could give near-real-time crowd estimates without sending raw video to the cloud.

Objectives:
1. To deploy an edge device that estimates crowd density and queue length from a camera feed locally.
2. To run a lightweight detection model on the edge within latency constraints.
3. To compare edge inference accuracy and latency against a cloud baseline.

Methodology:
A Jetson Nano will run a quantised YOLO-based person detector to count people in defined regions, computing density and queue length without exporting frames. Only aggregate counts are sent to a small dashboard. The model will be optimised with TensorRT and INT8 quantisation. Evaluation measures detection accuracy on a public crowd dataset plus latency and throughput on the edge device, compared to running the unquantised model on a cloud GPU.

Scope:
The project covers single-camera crowd and queue estimation at the edge. It excludes multi-camera tracking, re-identification across cameras, and storage of personal imagery.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An edge crowd-estimation prototype with a live dashboard.
2. An accuracy-versus-latency comparison of edge and cloud inference.

Timeline:
Two semesters: model and edge optimisation first, deployment and comparative evaluation second.

Title:
A Cloud-Native Microservices Backend for a Social Media Feed

Problem Statement:
Monolithic social platforms struggle to scale individual features independently; a spike in messaging can degrade the entire app. Microservices promise independent scaling, but students rarely study the operational trade-offs such as inter-service latency and data consistency in a realistic setup.

Objectives:
1. To design a cloud-native microservices backend for core social-feed features (posts, follow, timeline).
2. To deploy the services on Kubernetes with independent scaling.
3. To measure latency and throughput under load compared to a monolithic baseline.

Methodology:
Services will be built in Spring Boot, containerised with Docker, and orchestrated on a local Kubernetes cluster (Minikube). Inter-service communication uses REST and an event broker (Kafka) for timeline fan-out. Each service owns its database (PostgreSQL or Redis) following the database-per-service pattern. Load testing with k6 will compare p95 latency and throughput between the microservices version and an equivalent monolith under increasing concurrent users.

Scope:
The project covers three core services plus an API gateway. It excludes media storage, recommendation algorithms, and production-grade multi-region deployment.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A deployed microservices backend with autoscaling on Kubernetes.
2. A latency and throughput comparison against a monolithic implementation.

Timeline:
Months 1-3 service implementation; 4-5 Kubernetes and event broker; 6-7 load testing; 8 analysis and write-up.

Title:
A CI/CD Pipeline with Automated Quality Gates for a Healthcare Web Service

Problem Statement:
Healthcare software demands reliability, yet many small development teams deploy manually, risking regressions and slow releases. Without automated testing and security gates in the delivery pipeline, defects can reach patient-facing systems. A reproducible CI/CD pipeline with quality gates could shorten release cycles while enforcing standards.

Objectives:
1. To build a CI/CD pipeline that automatically tests, scans, and deploys a sample healthcare web service.
2. To enforce quality gates for code coverage and known vulnerabilities before deployment.
3. To measure the effect on lead time and deployment failure rate using DORA metrics.

Methodology:
The pipeline will use GitHub Actions to run unit and integration tests, enforce a coverage threshold via JaCoCo, and run dependency and container scanning with Trivy. Passing builds are deployed to a staging environment on Docker, with infrastructure defined as code using Docker Compose. The four DORA metrics (lead time, deployment frequency, change failure rate, time to restore) will be tracked across a series of simulated changes, including deliberately introduced failing changes to test the gates.

Scope:
The project covers the pipeline and quality gates for one representative service. It excludes production deployment to real clinical systems and full HIPAA-style compliance auditing.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working CI/CD pipeline with enforced quality gates.
2. DORA-metric results before and after introducing the gates.

Timeline:
Semester one: service and base pipeline. Semester two: quality gates, metrics collection, and evaluation.

Title:
A Big-Data Analytics Pipeline for Detecting Anomalous Financial Transactions

Problem Statement:
Financial institutions process millions of transactions and must flag anomalies that may indicate fraud, but batch reports arrive too late and naive thresholds miss subtle patterns. A scalable streaming analytics pipeline could surface anomalies closer to real time while handling high volume.

Objectives:
1. To build a streaming big-data pipeline that ingests and processes transaction events.
2. To detect anomalous transactions using an unsupervised model on streamed features.
3. To evaluate detection quality and processing throughput at increasing event rates.

Methodology:
Transactions from a public dataset will be replayed into Apache Kafka to simulate a live stream. Apache Spark Structured Streaming will compute rolling features (per-account velocity, amount deviation) and apply an Isolation Forest model to score anomalies, writing flagged events to a store for review. Detection will be evaluated with precision-recall against labelled fraud cases, and scalability measured by throughput and latency as ingestion rate rises. A baseline of static rule thresholds is included for comparison.

Scope:
The pipeline covers ingestion, feature computation, and anomaly scoring on a single-node cluster. It excludes case-management workflows and real bank-system integration.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working streaming pipeline with anomaly scoring.
2. Precision-recall and throughput results versus the rule-based baseline.

Timeline:
Months 1-2 ingestion and dataset prep; 3-5 streaming features and model; 6-7 evaluation; 8 reporting.

Title:
A Self-Service Business Intelligence Dashboard for Manufacturing OEE with Automated Root-Cause Hints

Problem Statement:
Manufacturing plants track Overall Equipment Effectiveness (OEE) but typically through static daily reports that tell managers what dropped without indicating why. Existing BI tools require analysts to manually drill into availability, performance, and quality losses. Line supervisors, who act on the data, lack a self-service view that both visualises OEE and surfaces likely loss drivers, slowing corrective action.

Objectives:
1. To design a self-service BI dashboard that computes and visualises OEE and its three component losses from machine event logs within one shift of latency.
2. To implement an automated root-cause hint module that ranks the top contributing loss reasons per machine using association-rule mining on downtime codes.
3. To evaluate dashboard usability with supervisors (SUS) and validate hint relevance against expert-labelled incidents (precision@3).

Methodology:
A star-schema warehouse in PostgreSQL will model machine events, downtime reasons, and production counts; a dbt transformation layer computes availability, performance, and quality to derive OEE. The dashboard is built in a Metabase/Apache Superset stack with drill-down by line, shift, and machine. The root-cause module applies FP-Growth association-rule mining over downtime-code sequences to rank likely loss drivers, refreshed via a scheduled job. Evaluation uses a public manufacturing dataset plus a synthetic event generator; usability is measured with SUS across five supervisor personas, and hint quality via precision@3 and recall against expert labels, benchmarked against a frequency-only baseline.

Scope:
Included: OEE computation, interactive drill-down, and ranked root-cause hints for discrete-manufacturing lines. Excluded: predictive maintenance, automated control actions, real-time sub-second streaming, and integration with proprietary PLC firmware. Scope is one plant model with up to ten machines.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A deployed self-service OEE dashboard with sub-shift refresh and drill-down.
2. An evaluation report: SUS usability score plus precision@3/recall for root-cause hints versus a frequency baseline.

Timeline:
M1-2 warehouse and dbt OEE model; M3-4 dashboard and drill-down; M5-6 association-rule hint module; M7 evaluation and benchmarking; M8 thesis write-up.

Title:
Short-Term Forecasting of Emergency Incident Volume for Public-Safety Resource Allocation

Problem Statement:
Emergency dispatch centres must staff and position resources ahead of demand, yet many still rely on simple historical averages that ignore weather, events, and temporal patterns. Under- or over-staffing raises response times or wastes budget. A rigorously evaluated short-term forecast of incident volume per district could inform shift planning, but it must beat naive baselines to justify adoption.

Objectives:
1. To build hourly incident-volume forecasts per city district for a 24-hour horizon using historical calls plus weather and calendar features.
2. To compare classical, gradient-boosting, and deep sequence models against seasonal-naive and ARIMA baselines under a unified protocol.
3. To quantify forecast value via expected staffing error and to assess calibration of prediction intervals.

Methodology:
Using a public emergency-calls dataset joined with hourly weather and holiday calendars, features include lagged volumes, rolling means, hour-of-week, and weather variables. Models compared: seasonal-naive and ARIMA baselines, an XGBoost regressor, and an LSTM, all tuned with time-series (rolling-origin) cross-validation to prevent leakage. Point accuracy is measured with MAE and sMAPE per district; probabilistic forecasts are evaluated with pinball loss and prediction-interval coverage. Statistical significance of differences uses the Diebold-Mariano test. A staffing-cost proxy translates errors into over/under-staffing hours.

Scope:
Included: district-level hourly forecasting, the named models, and the evaluation protocol on one city's open data. Excluded: individual-incident severity prediction, live CAD-system integration, geospatial routing, and any personally identifiable data.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A reproducible forecasting pipeline with the four model families and rolling-origin evaluation.
2. A comparative report ranking models by MAE/sMAPE, pinball loss, interval coverage, and staffing-error proxy, with significance testing.

Timeline:
M1 data assembly and EDA; M2-3 baselines and feature engineering; M4-5 XGBoost and LSTM with CV; M6 probabilistic evaluation; M7 significance and staffing analysis; M8 write-up.

Title:
Blockchain Smart Contracts for Smart City

Problem Statement:
Smart cities have a lot of data and problems. Blockchain is a new technology that can help. People need a better system.

Objectives:
1. Make a blockchain
2. Use smart contracts
3. Help the smart city

Methodology:
I will use blockchain and smart contracts. I will code it and test it. Some research will be done online.

Scope:
This is for all smart cities everywhere and will be used by the government and everyone.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A blockchain system
2. Smart city improvement

Title:
AR App for Tourism

Problem Statement:
Tourists do not know where to go. An augmented reality app is cool and can show them things. Tourism is important for the economy.

Objectives:
1. Build an AR app
2. Show tourist places
3. Make tourism better

Methodology:
I will make an AR app using a phone. It will point at things and show information. I will test it with some users.

Scope:
The app is for tourists in any country and any city.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An AR tourism app
2. Happy tourists

Title:
VR Training Simulation for Social Media

Problem Statement:
Social media is everywhere and people use it wrong. VR is immersive. We can train people using VR so they are better.

Objectives:
1. Create VR simulation
2. Train social media users
3. Improve behaviour

Methodology:
I will build a VR simulation and put people in it to train them. VR headsets will be used. Then I check if they learned.

Scope:
For all social media users globally.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A VR training system
2. Better social media users

Title:
A 2D Game to Teach Children About Healthy Eating

Problem Statement:
Many children do not understand which foods are healthy, and traditional health classes can feel boring. A simple game might make learning about nutrition more fun and memorable for young students.

Objectives:
1. Develop a 2D game where the player sorts healthy and unhealthy foods.
2. Add levels and a scoring system to keep children engaged.
3. Test whether children enjoy the game.

Methodology:
The game will be built in Unity using C# for a desktop platform. Sprites and a simple level system will be created. After building, a small group of children will play it and give feedback through a short survey.

Scope:
The game focuses on basic nutrition for primary school children and will have around five levels. It will not cover detailed dietary science or run on mobile.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A playable 2D nutrition game.
2. Feedback showing whether children found it fun.

Timeline:
The project will take about 14 weeks, with design, building, and testing phases.

Title:
A Serious Game for Teaching Personal Budgeting

Problem Statement:
Young adults often struggle to manage money because budgeting is rarely taught in an engaging way. A game-based approach could let users practise spending decisions in a safe environment before doing it in real life.

Objectives:
1. Build a serious game where the player manages a monthly budget.
2. Include events like bills and unexpected expenses.
3. See if players understand budgeting better after playing.

Methodology:
The game will be made with Unity and C#. Players start with a salary and must pay expenses while saving. A pre-test and post-test quiz will check if their budgeting knowledge improved after a play session.

Scope:
The game targets college students and covers simple monthly budgeting only. It will not include investing, loans, or tax calculations.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working budgeting game.
2. Quiz results comparing before and after play.

Timeline:
Roughly one semester, split into planning, development, and evaluation.

Title:
A Maintenance Logging System for Factory Equipment

Problem Statement:
In small manufacturing plants, machine maintenance is often recorded on paper, making it hard to track when a machine was last serviced. This can lead to missed maintenance and unexpected breakdowns on the factory floor.

Objectives:
1. Build a web system to record equipment maintenance history.
2. Send reminders when a machine is due for servicing.
3. Show a simple dashboard of machine status.

Methodology:
The system will be developed using PHP and MySQL. Technicians log each service, and the system stores dates and notes. A reminder feature checks due dates and a dashboard lists machines that need attention. Basic testing will confirm the features work.

Scope:
The system is aimed at one small factory and covers logging and reminders. It will not include sensor data, cost analysis, or inventory management.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A functional maintenance logging web app.
2. A dashboard showing overdue machines.

Timeline:
About 14 weeks across analysis, development, and testing.

Title:
A Telemedicine Booking Platform for Community Clinics

Problem Statement:
Residents in some neighbourhoods find it hard to reach clinics quickly, especially during emergencies or busy hours. A simple telemedicine platform could let them consult a duty officer or nurse online and get basic guidance faster.

Objectives:
1. Build a web platform for booking online consultations.
2. Allow video calls between users and staff.
3. Store a basic record of each consultation.

Methodology:
The platform will use a JavaScript front end with a Node.js back end and a database for appointments. A third-party video API will handle calls. After building, a few test users will book and complete mock consultations to check usability.

Scope:
The platform covers booking, video consultation, and simple records for one community clinic. It excludes payment, prescriptions, and integration with hospital systems.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working booking and consultation platform.
2. Usability feedback from test users.

Timeline:
One semester, divided into design, build, and testing stages.

Title:
An E-Learning Platform with Adaptive Quizzes for Energy Efficiency Training

Problem Statement:
Facility staff often complete generic energy-saving courses that do not adjust to their existing knowledge, so confident learners are bored while weaker ones fall behind. An adaptive e-learning platform that adjusts quiz difficulty could make energy-efficiency training more effective.

Objectives:
1. Build an e-learning platform delivering energy-efficiency modules with quizzes.
2. Implement an adaptive engine that raises or lowers question difficulty based on recent answers.
3. Evaluate learning gains against a fixed-difficulty version.

Methodology:
The platform will be built with React and a Spring Boot backend storing content and results in MySQL. The adaptive engine uses a rule-based difficulty ladder driven by a rolling accuracy score. Evaluation compares pre/post quiz scores between an adaptive group and a control group of about 30 users, using a paired t-test.

Scope:
The system covers three energy-efficiency modules for office staff with text and quiz content. It excludes video production, certification, and SCADA integration.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working adaptive e-learning platform.
2. A comparison of learning gains between adaptive and fixed modes.

Timeline:
14 weeks: requirements (2), build (7), evaluation (3), reporting (2).

Title:
A QR-Based Payment and Bookkeeping App for Small Businesses

Problem Statement:
Small shop owners often accept cash and lose track of daily sales because they have no easy digital record. A lightweight QR payment app that also logs each transaction could help them accept cashless payments and review their earnings without expensive POS hardware.

Objectives:
1. Build a mobile app that generates payment QR codes for a shop.
2. Record each completed payment with a timestamp and amount.
3. Provide a daily and weekly sales summary view.

Methodology:
The app will be built in Flutter with a Firebase backend for authentication and transaction storage. Payments will be simulated through a sandbox payment gateway. Summaries are computed by aggregating stored transactions. Usability will be tested with five small business owners using task-based scenarios and a SUS questionnaire.

Scope:
The app targets single-owner micro-businesses and covers QR generation, transaction logging, and sales summaries. It excludes inventory, payroll, and real bank settlement.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A functional QR payment and bookkeeping app.
2. Usability scores from owner testing.

Timeline:
About one semester: analysis (2 weeks), development (8), testing (3), reporting (1).

Title:
Detecting Fraudulent Transactions in Agricultural Supply Cooperatives

Problem Statement:
Agricultural cooperatives handle many small payments to farmers, and manual checking makes it easy to miss duplicate or inflated claims. A machine-learning model could flag suspicious transactions for review and reduce financial losses for the cooperative.

Objectives:
1. Build a dataset of cooperative transactions with labelled normal and suspicious records.
2. Train a model to classify transactions as likely fraudulent or legitimate.
3. Evaluate detection performance and present flagged cases through a simple dashboard.

Methodology:
Using a public financial-fraud dataset adapted with synthetic cooperative features, the project trains logistic regression and random forest classifiers in Python with scikit-learn. Because fraud is rare, SMOTE handles class imbalance, and models are compared using precision, recall, and F1 with 5-fold cross-validation. The best model feeds a Flask dashboard listing flagged transactions.

Scope:
The project covers offline detection on historical transaction records and a review dashboard. It excludes real-time streaming and integration with live banking systems.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained fraud-detection model with reported precision/recall.
2. A dashboard showing flagged transactions.

Timeline:
14 weeks: data prep (3), modelling (5), dashboard (3), evaluation and write-up (3).

Title:
A Recommendation System for an Online Transport-Accessory Store

Problem Statement:
Online stores selling vehicle and transport accessories often show the same generic best-sellers to everyone, so customers struggle to find parts suited to their vehicle. A recommendation system tuned to past purchases could surface more relevant items and improve the shopping experience.

Objectives:
1. Build a product catalogue and simulated purchase history for a transport-accessory store.
2. Implement collaborative-filtering and content-based recommendation methods.
3. Compare the two approaches on recommendation quality.

Methodology:
The system uses Python with the Surprise library for item-based collaborative filtering and a TF-IDF content-based model over product descriptions. A public e-commerce ratings dataset is relabelled to the accessory domain. The two approaches are compared offline using precision@k and recall@k on a held-out test set, and the better model is exposed through a small Flask web store.

Scope:
The project covers offline recommendation generation and a demo storefront. It excludes payment processing, real inventory, and a mobile app.

Expected Outcomes:
1. Two working recommendation models with comparison metrics.
2. A demo storefront showing personalised suggestions.

Timeline:
One semester: data setup (3 weeks), modelling (6), web demo (3), evaluation (2).

Title:
A Chatbot to Answer Household Sustainability Questions

Problem Statement:
People who want to live more sustainably often have small everyday questions, such as how to recycle a specific item, but finding trustworthy answers takes time. A focused chatbot could give quick, consistent guidance drawn from official recycling and energy-saving resources.

Objectives:
1. Collect a knowledge base of sustainability and recycling guidance.
2. Build a chatbot that answers user questions from this knowledge base.
3. Evaluate answer accuracy and user satisfaction.

Methodology:
The chatbot uses a retrieval-based approach: documents are split into passages, embedded with Sentence-BERT, and stored in a FAISS index. User questions retrieve the closest passages, which a templated response presents. Accuracy is measured on a set of 50 test questions with known answers, and a short survey captures user satisfaction.

Scope:
The chatbot covers household recycling and basic energy-saving topics in English. It excludes legal advice, live web crawling, and multilingual support.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working retrieval-based sustainability chatbot.
2. Accuracy and satisfaction results from testing.

Timeline:
14 weeks: knowledge base (3), chatbot build (6), evaluation (3), reporting (2).

Title:
A Knowledge-Graph Search Tool for Warehouse Logistics Documents

Problem Statement:
Warehouse staff store procedures, supplier details, and shipment records across scattered documents, so finding how two things relate, such as which supplier ships to which zone, is slow. A knowledge-graph search tool could connect entities and let staff query relationships instead of just keywords.

Objectives:
1. Extract entities and relationships from logistics documents into a knowledge graph.
2. Build a search interface that answers relationship-style queries.
3. Compare retrieval quality against a plain keyword search baseline.

Methodology:
Entities such as suppliers, products, and zones are extracted with spaCy named-entity recognition and rules, then loaded into a Neo4j graph. A query interface translates user questions into Cypher for common patterns. The tool is evaluated on 40 relationship queries, comparing precision and answer completeness against an Elasticsearch keyword baseline.

Scope:
The project covers a fixed set of warehouse document types and predefined query patterns. It excludes free-form natural-language parsing and integration with a live warehouse system.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A populated knowledge graph with a working query interface.
2. A comparison against the keyword baseline.

Timeline:
One semester: extraction (4 weeks), graph and interface (5), evaluation (3), reporting (2).

Title:
Semantic Segmentation of Scanned Government Forms for Automated Field Extraction

Problem Statement:
E-government agencies still receive large volumes of scanned paper forms, and manual data entry from these documents is slow and error-prone. Reliable field extraction requires first segmenting each scan into regions such as printed labels, handwritten entries, checkboxes, and stamps, but layout variation across form types makes naive rule-based cropping fragile.

Objectives:
1. Assemble and annotate a dataset of scanned government forms with pixel-level region masks.
2. Train a U-Net segmentation model to label form regions and benchmark it against a thresholding baseline.
3. Quantify how segmentation quality affects downstream field-extraction accuracy.

Methodology:
Around 1,200 scanned forms are annotated into five region classes. A U-Net with a ResNet-34 encoder is trained in PyTorch using a combined Dice and cross-entropy loss, with augmentation for rotation, noise, and contrast to mimic scan variation. Performance is reported as mean IoU and per-class F1 under 5-fold cross-validation, compared against an Otsu-thresholding baseline. Segmented regions are then passed to an OCR step to measure end-to-end extraction accuracy.

Scope:
The work covers segmentation of three common form layouts and the extraction-accuracy analysis. It excludes building a full submission portal, multilingual handwriting recognition, and deployment to live agency systems.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained segmentation model with mIoU and per-class F1 against the baseline.
2. Evidence linking segmentation quality to downstream extraction accuracy.

Timeline:
14 weeks: data and annotation (4), modelling (5), evaluation (3), reporting (2).

Title:
Real-Time Detection of Classroom Engagement Cues from Lecture Video

Problem Statement:
In large lecture halls, instructors cannot easily gauge whether students are following along. Automatically detecting visible engagement cues, such as raised hands, phone use, and head-down posture, could give teachers anonymous, aggregate feedback, but classroom video is crowded, has varied lighting, and demands near-real-time inference.

Objectives:
1. Build an annotated dataset of classroom frames labelled with hand-raise, phone-use, and head-down behaviours.
2. Train and compare YOLOv8 detectors of two sizes for accuracy versus speed.
3. Evaluate whether the chosen model runs at an acceptable frame rate on a single GPU.

Methodology:
About 4,000 frames sampled from recorded lectures are annotated with bounding boxes for three behaviour classes. YOLOv8n and YOLOv8s are fine-tuned in PyTorch with transfer learning from COCO weights and standard augmentation. Detection quality is measured with mAP@0.5 and per-class average precision on a held-out test set, while inference speed is reported in FPS. Results are aggregated per minute to avoid identifying individuals.

Scope:
The project covers offline-trained detection of three behaviours evaluated on recorded video, plus a speed benchmark. It excludes face identification, emotion recognition, and live deployment in real classrooms.

Expected Outcomes:
1. Two trained detectors with mAP and FPS comparisons.
2. A recommendation on the accuracy-speed trade-off for classroom use.

Timeline:
One semester: data and annotation (4 weeks), training (5), evaluation (3), reporting (2).

Title:
Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis of Retail Product Reviews

Problem Statement:
Retailers receive thousands of product reviews, but an overall star rating hides which specific aspects, such as price, sizing, or delivery, customers are unhappy about. Aspect-based sentiment analysis can attach sentiment to each aspect, yet review text is noisy, informal, and often mixes positive and negative opinions in one sentence.

Objectives:
1. Prepare a labelled retail-review dataset annotated with aspect terms and their sentiment.
2. Fine-tune a transformer model for aspect-based sentiment classification and compare it to a lexicon baseline.
3. Summarise aspect-level sentiment per product for store managers.

Methodology:
The project uses a public retail/Amazon review dataset, with a subset re-annotated for four aspect categories and three sentiment polarities. A BERT-base model is fine-tuned in PyTorch for aspect-sentiment classification and compared against a VADER lexicon baseline. Evaluation uses macro F1 and per-aspect accuracy with a stratified train/validation/test split. Aspect sentiments are aggregated into per-product summaries.

Scope:
The work covers four aspect categories for English-language reviews in two product types, plus per-product summarisation. It excludes implicit-aspect extraction, sarcasm handling, and a production dashboard.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A fine-tuned aspect-based sentiment model with macro F1 against the baseline.
2. Per-product aspect-sentiment summaries.

Timeline:
14 weeks: annotation (3), modelling (6), evaluation (3), reporting (2).

Title:
Learned Cardinality Estimation for Faster Query Planning in a Smart-City Data Warehouse

Problem Statement:
Smart-city dashboards run analytical queries over large sensor tables, and slow queries often stem from the optimizer mis-estimating how many rows a predicate returns, leading it to pick poor join orders. Traditional histogram-based estimators struggle with correlated columns common in sensor data, so better cardinality estimates could meaningfully cut query latency.

Objectives:
1. Build a benchmark of analytical queries over a smart-city sensor schema with known result cardinalities.
2. Train a learned cardinality estimator and compare its accuracy to the database's built-in histogram estimator.
3. Measure the effect of improved estimates on end-to-end query latency.

Methodology:
Using a public sensor dataset loaded into PostgreSQL, a workload of parameterised analytical queries is generated with logged true cardinalities. A small multi-layer-perceptron estimator is trained in Python on featurised predicates, and its q-error is compared against PostgreSQL's default estimates. Selected estimates are then injected as planner hints to measure latency change, repeated across three runs to report medians.

Scope:
The project covers single-table and two-table-join cardinality estimation on one schema and the resulting latency analysis. It excludes modifying the optimizer source, distributed query execution, and write-heavy workloads.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A learned estimator with q-error compared to the histogram baseline.
2. Query-latency results showing the impact of better estimates.

Timeline:
One semester: benchmark setup (3 weeks), modelling (6), latency evaluation (3), reporting (2).

Title:
A Facial-Recognition Attendance System for Guided Tour Groups

Problem Statement:
Tour operators must repeatedly count members of large groups at each stop, which is slow and easy to get wrong when people wander off. An automatic facial-recognition attendance system could confirm who is present at each checkpoint, but outdoor lighting, varied angles, and the need to protect personal data make a reliable, privacy-conscious design challenging.

Objectives:
1. Build a check-in pipeline that enrols tour members and recognises them at each checkpoint.
2. Evaluate recognition accuracy under varied lighting and pose conditions.
3. Assess processing time per check-in and propose privacy safeguards.

Methodology:
Faces are detected with MTCNN and embedded with a pretrained FaceNet model; recognition is done by nearest-neighbour matching against enrolled embeddings. A test set of around 600 images covering different lighting and angles measures accuracy, precision, and recall, plus per-check-in latency. Embeddings are stored rather than raw images, and a confidence threshold flags uncertain matches for manual confirmation.

Scope:
The system covers enrolment and checkpoint recognition for groups of up to 30 people, evaluated on collected images. It excludes liveness/anti-spoofing detection, a mobile app, and integration with operator booking systems.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working recognition pipeline with accuracy under varied conditions.
2. Latency results and a set of privacy recommendations.

Timeline:
14 weeks: data collection (3), pipeline build (5), evaluation (4), reporting (2).

Title:
Robust OCR and Layout-Aware Extraction of Text from User-Generated Social-Media Images

Problem Statement:
A large share of social-media posts embed text inside images, such as memes, screenshots, and infographics, where decorative fonts, low contrast, emojis, and cluttered backgrounds defeat conventional document OCR. Reliable extraction of this in-image text would help moderation and accessibility, but general-purpose OCR trained on clean scans degrades sharply on this informal, stylised content, and the field lacks a domain-specific benchmark.

Objectives:
1. Construct and annotate a benchmark of 2,000 social-media images with transcribed text and reading-order boxes.
2. Compare an off-the-shelf engine (Tesseract) against a deep pipeline (CRAFT detection plus a fine-tuned TrOCR recognizer) on this benchmark.
3. Quantify the accuracy gain from domain fine-tuning and analyse remaining failure modes.

Methodology:
Images are sampled across four content types and double-annotated, with inter-annotator agreement reported. The deep pipeline uses CRAFT for text detection and TrOCR fine-tuned on a synthetic-plus-real training split in PyTorch, with augmentation for blur, compression, and colour shift. Models are evaluated with character error rate, word error rate, and end-to-end F1 against Tesseract, using a fixed train/validation/test split and bootstrapped confidence intervals. Errors are categorised by cause (font, contrast, emoji adjacency) to guide analysis. A key risk, scarce labelled data, is mitigated with synthetic text rendering.

Scope:
The project covers English in-image text across four social-media content types and a comparative evaluation. It explicitly excludes non-Latin scripts, video frames, real-time deployment, and downstream moderation decisions.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An annotated social-media OCR benchmark released for reuse.
2. CER/WER/F1 results showing the fine-tuned pipeline's gain over Tesseract, with a categorised failure analysis.

Timeline:
14 weeks: benchmark construction (4), pipeline implementation (3), fine-tuning (3), evaluation and error analysis (2), reporting (2).

Title:
Early Patient-Deterioration Alerts from Wearable Sensor Streams Using On-Device Anomaly Detection

Problem Statement:
Wearable vital-sign sensors generate continuous heart-rate, SpO2, and motion data, but raw thresholds raise too many false alarms and miss gradual deterioration, while sending all data to the cloud is costly and privacy-sensitive. An on-device model that flags early deterioration with few false alarms could enable timely intervention for monitored patients, yet sensor noise, drift, and class imbalance make this hard.

Objectives:
1. Define a labelled deterioration-detection task over multivariate wearable streams using a public clinical dataset.
2. Train and compare an LSTM autoencoder and a Transformer-based detector for early-warning detection.
3. Evaluate detection lead time, false-alarm rate, and feasibility of on-device inference within a memory budget.

Methodology:
Using the MIMIC-derived/WESAD-style vital-sign data resampled to fixed windows, deterioration episodes are labelled from documented events. An LSTM autoencoder (reconstruction-error scoring) and a compact Transformer classifier are trained in PyTorch with windowed cross-validation that respects patient boundaries to prevent leakage. Metrics include AUROC, AUPRC (given imbalance), median detection lead time before the event, and false alarms per patient-day, with a sliding-window baseline for comparison. The best model is quantised and profiled on a Raspberry Pi to confirm it fits a stated latency and memory budget.

Scope:
The project covers offline-trained detection on three vital signals and an embedded inference feasibility test. It excludes a clinical trial, medical-device certification, and real-time hospital integration.

Expected Outcomes:
1. Two trained detectors with AUROC/AUPRC, lead time, and false-alarm-rate comparisons against the baseline.
2. On-device profiling results confirming the memory/latency budget.

Timeline:
14 weeks: data and labelling (3), modelling (5), evaluation (3), on-device profiling (1), reporting (2).

Title:
Machine Learning for Factories

Problem Statement:
Factories make a lot of products and sometimes things go wrong. Companies want machine learning because it is popular now and helps a lot.

Objectives:
1. Use machine learning in the factory.
2. Make the factory better.
3. Get good results.

Methodology:
I will use Python and some algorithms to classify the data. I will do research online and try different things until it works.

Scope:
This can be used by all manufacturing companies everywhere to improve everything they do.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A machine learning system.
2. Better factory performance.

Title:
Deep Learning Camera System for Safety

Problem Statement:
Public places are not safe and there are many accidents and crimes. Deep learning and computer vision is very powerful so it can solve this problem.

Objectives:
1. Detect dangerous things with a camera.
2. Use deep learning.
3. Keep people safe.

Methodology:
I will train a neural network on images and use it to look at video. Deep learning is good at images so it will work well.

Scope:
The system will watch all public areas and stop crime and accidents from happening.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A safe city.
2. A working camera detector.

Title:
NLP for Energy

Problem Statement:
The energy sector has a lot of text and reports. NLP is a trending technology that can read text and understand it, which would be very useful for energy companies.

Objectives:
1. Apply NLP to energy text.
2. Understand the documents.
3. Help the energy industry.

Methodology:
I plan to use natural language processing and maybe some AI models. I will collect text and process it to get insights.

Scope:
It works for any energy company and any kind of document they have.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An NLP tool.
2. Useful insights for energy.

Title:
A Recommender System for Small Online Shops

Problem Statement:
Small businesses selling online struggle to show customers products they might like, unlike big platforms that have recommendation engines. This project builds a simple recommender so small shops can suggest relevant items and increase sales.

Objectives:
1. Build a product recommender for a small online store.
2. Use customer purchase history to make suggestions.
3. Test if the recommendations are useful.

Methodology:
The system will use collaborative filtering based on past purchases. I will build it in Python and connect it to a sample online store database. Recommendations will be shown on the product page.

Scope:
The project focuses on a single small online shop with a moderate catalogue. It will not handle real-time updates or very large datasets.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working recommender that suggests products.
2. An evaluation showing whether suggestions match customer interest.

Timeline:
The project will take about two semesters, starting with data collection and ending with testing.

Title:
Voice Commands for Farmers

Problem Statement:
Many farmers find it hard to use apps with typing, especially in the field with dirty hands. A speech recognition tool would let them record information by talking instead, making farm data entry easier.

Objectives:
1. Create a speech recognition feature for a farming app.
2. Let farmers log crop and field data by voice.
3. Check how accurate the voice recognition is.

Methodology:
I will use an existing speech recognition library to convert speech to text. The recognized text will be saved into a simple farm record form. Testing will involve recording sample farm phrases and checking the output.

Scope:
The tool covers basic farm data entry in English. It will not support multiple languages or offline use in the first version.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A voice input feature that records farm data.
2. A short accuracy report on recognized phrases.

Timeline:
Around two semesters, with the first focused on setup and the second on testing.

Title:
Detecting Network Attacks in Transport Systems

Problem Statement:
Transportation networks rely on connected computers, and attackers may try to break in. A network intrusion detection tool would help spot suspicious traffic so operators can react before damage is done.

Objectives:
1. Build an intrusion detection model for network traffic.
2. Train it to recognize common attack types.
3. Measure how well it detects attacks.

Methodology:
I will use a public network traffic dataset and train a classifier to label connections as normal or attack. The model will be built in Python using scikit-learn. Accuracy will be checked against the labelled data.

Scope:
The project looks at detecting a few common attack categories on sample traffic. It does not include blocking attacks or running on live transport networks.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained model that flags suspicious network traffic.
2. Results showing detection accuracy for the chosen attacks.

Timeline:
Two semesters: dataset preparation and modelling first, evaluation second.

Title:
Web Security Checker for Green Initiative Sites

Problem Statement:
Many sustainability and green-initiative organizations run websites without security checks, leaving them open to common attacks. A simple scanner could help these small organizations find basic vulnerabilities before attackers do.

Objectives:
1. Build a tool that scans a website for common security flaws.
2. Check for issues like SQL injection and cross-site scripting.
3. Produce a report of any problems found.

Methodology:
The tool will send test inputs to a target website and look for signs of vulnerabilities. It will be written in Python and check against the common OWASP issues. A test website will be set up to try it on.

Scope:
The scanner checks for a small set of well-known vulnerabilities on simple websites. It will not test complex authentication flows or fix the problems automatically.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A scanning tool that reports basic vulnerabilities.
2. A sample report from scanning a test site.

Timeline:
About two semesters, building the scanner first and testing it later.

Title:
Static and Dynamic Analysis of Malware in Logistics Software

Problem Statement:
Logistics companies depend on software to track shipments, and infected files can disrupt the whole supply chain. This project develops an analysis workflow that combines static and dynamic techniques to classify suspicious executables affecting logistics environments.

Objectives:
1. Collect a labelled set of benign and malicious Windows executables.
2. Extract static features (API calls, strings, PE headers) and dynamic behaviour from a sandbox.
3. Train and evaluate a classifier that distinguishes malware from clean files.

Methodology:
Static features will be extracted with pefile and disassembly tools, while dynamic behaviour will be captured by running samples in a Cuckoo sandbox. A random forest classifier will be trained on the combined features and evaluated using accuracy, precision, and recall on a held-out test set.

Scope:
The work targets Windows PE files relevant to logistics desktop software. It excludes mobile malware, kernel rootkits, and live deployment on company systems; analysis is done only in an isolated lab.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A combined static-dynamic feature pipeline for executables.
2. A classifier with reported accuracy and precision/recall on the test set.

Timeline:
Semester one for dataset and feature extraction; semester two for training, evaluation, and reporting.

Title:
A Responsive Citizen Services Portal for Local Government

Problem Statement:
Citizens often struggle to access local government services online because existing portals are hard to use on phones and scatter services across many pages. This project builds a responsive web portal that brings common services together in one accessible place.

Objectives:
1. Identify the most-used local government services through requirement gathering.
2. Build a responsive web portal where citizens can find and request these services.
3. Evaluate usability with a small group of test users.

Methodology:
The portal will be built with React and a Node.js backend using a relational database. Requirements will come from reviewing existing council websites and a short user survey. Usability will be measured with the System Usability Scale after task-based testing.

Scope:
The portal covers a defined set of common services such as complaints, bookings, and information lookup for one local council. It will not handle real payment processing or integrate with existing government back-end systems.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A responsive, mobile-friendly citizen services portal.
2. A usability evaluation report with SUS scores.

Timeline:
First semester for requirements and design, second for development and usability testing.

Title:
An Offline-Capable Progressive Web App for Revision

Problem Statement:
Students often want to revise on the go but lose access to learning material when their internet connection drops. A progressive web app (PWA) can cache content and quizzes so learners can study reliably even offline, without installing a native app.

Objectives:
1. Build a PWA that delivers revision notes and quizzes for a chosen subject.
2. Use service workers to cache content for offline access.
3. Evaluate offline reliability and student satisfaction.

Methodology:
The app will be developed with React and the Workbox service-worker library, storing content in IndexedDB for offline use. Quiz progress will sync when connectivity returns. Testing will measure offline load success and gather feedback through a short questionnaire.

Scope:
The PWA covers one subject area with notes and multiple-choice quizzes. It excludes video streaming, teacher dashboards, and large-scale multi-user accounts.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An installable PWA that works offline for revision.
2. A report on offline reliability and student feedback.

Timeline:
Semester one for design and core build; semester two for offline features and evaluation.

Title:
A Cross-Platform Mobile App for Small Retail Inventory

Problem Statement:
Small retailers often track stock on paper or spreadsheets, leading to errors and lost sales when items run out. A cross-platform mobile app would let shop owners manage inventory on both Android and iOS from one codebase without buying expensive systems.

Objectives:
1. Build a cross-platform mobile app for stock entry and tracking.
2. Add low-stock alerts and simple sales recording.
3. Evaluate the app with a small retailer for usefulness.

Methodology:
The app will be developed with Flutter so a single codebase runs on Android and iOS, with Firebase for data storage and authentication. Features will be drawn from interviewing one or two shop owners. Evaluation will use a task walkthrough and a satisfaction questionnaire.

Scope:
The app handles inventory and basic sales for a single small shop. It excludes barcode hardware integration, multi-branch syncing, and full accounting features.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working cross-platform inventory app with low-stock alerts.
2. A short evaluation report from a real shop owner.

Timeline:
First semester for requirements and core build, second for alerts, testing, and reporting.

Title:
A Native Android App for Reporting Smart City Issues

Problem Statement:
City residents notice problems like broken streetlights or potholes but lack an easy way to report them with location data. A native Android app would let citizens submit geo-tagged reports quickly, helping councils prioritize fixes in a smart-city setting.

Objectives:
1. Build a native Android app for submitting issue reports with photos and GPS.
2. Let users track the status of their submitted reports.
3. Evaluate the app's usability and report accuracy.

Methodology:
The app will be written in Kotlin using Android SDK location and camera APIs, sending reports to a Firebase backend. Reports will include category, photo, and GPS coordinates. Usability will be tested through task scenarios with a small group of student users.

Scope:
The app focuses on citizen-side reporting and status tracking on Android only. It excludes the council-side management dashboard and integration with real municipal systems.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A native Android reporting app with geo-tagged submissions.
2. A usability evaluation with collected feedback.

Timeline:
Semester one for design and core app; semester two for tracking, testing, and documentation.

Title:
An IoT Sensor Network for Monitoring Tourist Sites

Problem Statement:
Popular tourist sites can become overcrowded, harming visitor experience and the environment. An IoT sensor network could monitor visitor counts and environmental conditions so site managers can respond, but small attractions rarely have such monitoring.

Objectives:
1. Build an IoT sensor setup that counts visitors and measures temperature and humidity.
2. Send sensor data to a dashboard for site managers.
3. Test the accuracy and reliability of the readings.

Methodology:
ESP32 microcontrollers with PIR motion and DHT22 sensors will collect data and send it over Wi-Fi using MQTT to a server. A simple web dashboard will display live and historical readings. Accuracy will be checked by comparing counts against manual observation.

Scope:
The prototype covers one or two sensor nodes at a single test location. It excludes large-scale deployment, solar power, and predictive crowd forecasting.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working sensor network feeding a monitoring dashboard.
2. A reliability report comparing sensor counts to manual counts.

Timeline:
First semester for hardware and firmware; second for the dashboard and field testing.

Title:
A Smart Home Automation Hub That Posts Activity Summaries to Social Media

Problem Statement:
Existing smart home systems automate devices but rarely let users share curated activity with friends in a privacy-aware way. This project builds an automation hub that controls common devices and generates optional, user-filtered summaries to social media, addressing the gap between home automation and controlled social sharing.

Objectives:
1. Build a rule-based automation hub controlling at least three device types via MQTT.
2. Generate daily activity summaries and post them to a social platform through its API, with user-defined privacy filters.
3. Evaluate automation reliability and user trust in the sharing controls.

Methodology:
The hub will run on a Raspberry Pi using Home Assistant for device control and a Node.js service for summary generation. Privacy rules let users redact sensitive events before posting through the Twitter/X API. Evaluation measures rule execution success rate and gathers trust feedback via a questionnaire with ten participants.

Scope:
The system controls lights, plugs, and a temperature sensor, and posts to one social platform. It excludes voice assistants, camera streaming, and machine-learning behaviour prediction.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working automation hub with privacy-filtered social posting.
2. An evaluation of reliability and user trust.

Timeline:
Months 1-2 device integration, 3-4 summary and privacy module, 5-6 evaluation and write-up.

Title:
Edge-Based Real-Time Fall Detection for Elderly Care

Problem Statement:
Cloud-based health monitoring introduces latency and privacy risks when detecting falls among elderly patients. Running inference at the edge can reduce response time and keep sensitive video local, but lightweight models must stay accurate on constrained hardware. This project develops an edge fall-detection system balancing accuracy and latency.

Objectives:
1. Train a fall-detection model on accelerometer and pose data from public datasets (SisFall, UR Fall Detection).
2. Optimize and deploy the model on an edge device (Raspberry Pi 4) using TensorFlow Lite.
3. Evaluate detection accuracy, false-alarm rate, and on-device latency against a cloud baseline.

Methodology:
A lightweight CNN-LSTM will be trained on labelled fall and non-fall sequences, then quantized for edge inference. The system runs locally on a Raspberry Pi and raises alerts. Evaluation uses precision, recall, F1, and measured inference latency, comparing edge versus cloud round-trip times.

Scope:
The project covers single-person indoor fall detection using wearable and pose data. It excludes multi-person scenes, medical diagnosis, and clinical trials.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A quantized edge fall-detection model with reported F1 and latency.
2. A comparison showing edge latency and privacy gains over cloud.

Timeline:
Months 1-2 data and model, 3-4 edge optimization and deployment, 5-6 evaluation.

Title:
A Cloud-Native Microservices Architecture for Loan Processing

Problem Statement:
Monolithic banking applications make it hard to scale individual functions like credit checks during peak demand. This project designs and implements a cloud-native microservices architecture for a loan-processing workflow, demonstrating independent scaling and resilience compared with a monolithic baseline.

Objectives:
1. Decompose a loan-processing workflow into independent microservices (application, credit-check, decision, notification).
2. Containerize and orchestrate the services on Kubernetes with an API gateway.
3. Evaluate scalability and fault tolerance against a monolithic version under load.

Methodology:
Services will be built in Spring Boot, communicating via REST and a message queue (RabbitMQ), and deployed on a local Kubernetes cluster (Minikube) with Istio for routing. Load testing with k6 will measure throughput and latency, and chaos tests will kill pods to observe recovery. Results compare against an equivalent monolith.

Scope:
The prototype covers a simulated loan workflow with mock credit scoring. It excludes real banking integration, regulatory compliance, and production-grade security hardening.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A deployed microservices loan-processing prototype on Kubernetes.
2. A comparative report on scalability and fault recovery versus a monolith.

Timeline:
Months 1-2 service design and build, 3-4 orchestration, 5-6 load/chaos testing and analysis.

Title:
A CI/CD Pipeline with Automated Quality Gates for Manufacturing Software

Problem Statement:
Manufacturing software teams often deploy control and reporting tools manually, causing slow releases and inconsistent quality. This project builds a CI/CD pipeline with automated testing, security scanning, and deployment gates, and measures its effect on release reliability for a sample manufacturing application.

Objectives:
1. Build a CI/CD pipeline that automatically builds, tests, and deploys a sample app on each commit.
2. Add quality gates for unit tests, static analysis, and container vulnerability scanning.
3. Measure lead time and failure rate before and after pipeline adoption.

Methodology:
The pipeline will use GitHub Actions to build a containerized application, run JUnit tests and SonarQube analysis, scan images with Trivy, and deploy to a staging environment. DORA metrics (lead time, deployment frequency, change-failure rate) will be collected over a series of commits to quantify improvement against a manual baseline.

Scope:
The pipeline targets one sample manufacturing reporting application deployed to a staging cluster. It excludes production rollout, hardware-in-the-loop testing, and multi-team governance.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working CI/CD pipeline with automated quality gates.
2. A DORA-metrics comparison showing improvement over manual deployment.

Timeline:
Months 1-2 pipeline setup, 3-4 quality gates, 5-6 metric collection and evaluation.

Title:
A Big Data Pipeline for Crime Hotspot Analysis

Problem Statement:
Public safety agencies hold large volumes of incident data but lack accessible pipelines to process it into actionable hotspot insights. This project builds a scalable big-data pipeline that ingests, processes, and visualizes crime data to identify spatial-temporal hotspots for resource planning.

Objectives:
1. Build an ingestion and processing pipeline for a large public crime dataset.
2. Compute spatial-temporal hotspots using clustering and aggregation.
3. Visualize results on an interactive map and evaluate pipeline throughput.

Methodology:
Data from an open crime dataset (e.g., Chicago crimes) will be ingested into Apache Kafka and processed with Apache Spark for aggregation and DBSCAN-based hotspot clustering. Results will be stored in PostgreSQL/PostGIS and shown on a Leaflet map. Evaluation measures processing throughput, scalability with data volume, and clustering quality via silhouette score.

Scope:
The pipeline processes one historical open dataset in batch and micro-batch modes. It excludes real-time streaming from live police systems, predictive policing models, and any personal-data handling.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working big-data pipeline producing crime hotspot maps.
2. A throughput and clustering-quality evaluation.

Timeline:
Months 1-2 ingestion, 3-4 processing and clustering, 5-6 visualization and evaluation.

Title:
A Self-Service Business Intelligence Dashboard for Renewable Energy Plant Performance

Problem Statement:
Renewable energy operators monitoring multiple solar and wind sites struggle to consolidate generation, weather, and downtime data into a single decision-support view, and existing BI tools require costly licences and technical setup beyond small operators' reach. This project delivers an open, self-service BI dashboard that unifies these sources and benchmarks site performance against expected yield, addressing the gap in affordable, energy-specific analytics tooling.

Objectives:
1. Design a dimensional data model integrating generation, weather, and maintenance logs for at least three simulated sites.
2. Build an ETL process and interactive dashboard exposing KPIs (performance ratio, capacity factor, downtime) with drill-down and benchmarking.
3. Evaluate decision-support effectiveness via task-based usability testing (SUS) and query-performance benchmarks against a baseline flat-file approach.

Methodology:
A star-schema warehouse will be built in PostgreSQL, populated by an Apache Airflow ETL from public NREL generation and NASA POWER weather datasets. The dashboard will be implemented in Apache Superset with computed KPIs. Evaluation combines SUS scoring from eight operators completing defined analytical tasks, accuracy checks of computed KPIs against ground-truth, and query latency benchmarks versus a non-warehoused baseline.

Scope:
The system covers descriptive and diagnostic analytics for three simulated plant types using historical open data. It explicitly excludes real-time SCADA integration, predictive failure modelling, and financial trading analytics.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An open self-service BI dashboard with validated energy KPIs and benchmarking.
2. An evaluation reporting SUS scores, KPI accuracy, and query-performance gains over the baseline.

Timeline:
Months 1-2 data model and ETL, 3-4 dashboard and KPIs, 5 benchmarking, 6 usability evaluation and write-up.

Title:
Probabilistic Time-Series Forecasting of Daily Demand for Small Retail Businesses

Problem Statement:
Small retailers overstock or run out because they lack forecasting tools that handle short, noisy sales histories with holidays and promotions, while enterprise demand-planning software is too expensive and assumes long, clean data. This project develops and rigorously benchmarks a probabilistic forecasting approach tailored to short-history small-business data, quantifying the accuracy and inventory benefit of modern models over classical baselines in this specific low-data regime.

Objectives:
1. Assemble and clean daily sales data for several SKUs with calendar, holiday, and promotion features.
2. Implement and tune classical (SARIMA, ETS), machine-learning (LightGBM), and deep (DeepAR/N-BEATS) forecasters with prediction intervals.
3. Evaluate forecast accuracy and downstream inventory cost via rolling-origin cross-validation against a naive seasonal baseline.

Methodology:
Models will be built in Python using statsmodels, LightGBM, and GluonTS, with features for day-of-week, holidays, and promotions. Evaluation uses rolling-origin (time-series) cross-validation reporting MASE, sMAPE, and pinball loss for interval calibration, plus a simulated newsvendor inventory cost. Hyperparameters are tuned via Optuna on validation folds; statistical significance of differences is tested with a Diebold-Mariano test.

Scope:
The study covers daily-granularity demand for a defined set of fast-moving SKUs in one retail category using two years of history. It excludes intraday forecasting, new-product cold-start prediction, and live POS integration.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A benchmarked, reproducible forecasting pipeline producing calibrated probabilistic forecasts.
2. An evaluation showing accuracy and inventory-cost gains over the seasonal-naive baseline with significance testing.

Timeline:
Months 1-2 data and baselines, 3-4 ML and deep models, 5 cross-validation and tuning, 6 inventory simulation and reporting.

Blockchain for Social Media

VR Training for Finance
