Title:
A 3D Game to Teach Factory Safety

Problem Statement:
Factory workers sometimes do not follow safety rules and accidents happen. A game could make safety training more interesting than reading manuals, but most factories still use boring slides.

Objectives:
1. To design a 3D game about factory safety hazards
2. To build the game in Unity
3. To test if players enjoy it

Methodology:
The game will be made in Unity using C# and some free 3D models. Players walk around a factory and spot hazards. After building it, a few classmates will play it and fill in a short survey about how fun it was.

Scope:
The game covers basic manufacturing hazards like spills and machine guards. It is a single-player desktop game and will not include multiplayer or VR.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A playable 3D safety training game
2. Survey feedback from test players

Timeline:
The project will run over two semesters.

Title:
Serious Game for Public Safety Awareness

Problem Statement:
Many people don't know what to do during emergencies like fires or floods. Pamphlets are often ignored. A serious game might teach emergency response in a more engaging way, but few exist for the local public.

Objectives:
1. To develop a 2D serious game on emergency response
2. To include quiz-style decision points
3. To measure knowledge gain before and after playing

Methodology:
The game will be built with Unity for web. Levels present emergency scenarios where players choose actions and get feedback. A pre-test and post-test quiz will check if players learned anything, tested with about 15 volunteers.

Scope:
Focuses on fire and flood scenarios only. It is a 2D browser game for desktop, not mobile, and excludes earthquakes and medical emergencies.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A 2D public safety serious game
2. A short report comparing pre- and post-test scores

Timeline:
Roughly two semesters split into design, build and testing.

Title:
A Dashboard for Energy Use in Clinics

Problem Statement:
Small clinics use a lot of electricity for equipment and lighting but rarely track it. They get a monthly bill with no detail. Some way to see energy use per room could help them cut costs, but most clinic software ignores energy.

Objectives:
1. To build a web dashboard showing clinic energy use
2. To let staff enter meter readings
3. To show simple charts and monthly trends

Methodology:
A web app will be built with React and a small Node backend storing readings in MySQL. Staff type in readings and the dashboard draws line and bar charts. It will be demonstrated to one clinic for feedback.

Scope:
Manual data entry only; no IoT sensors. Covers electricity, not water or gas. Single clinic demo.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working energy dashboard web app
2. Feedback from clinic staff

Timeline:
Two semesters: requirements, development, then testing.

Title:
Telemedicine Booking Platform for Small Businesses

Problem Statement:
Small businesses such as independent physiotherapy studios struggle to offer remote consultations because existing telemedicine tools are expensive and built for big hospitals. A lightweight platform could let them book and run video calls cheaply, but cheap options are rare.

Objectives:
1. To build a web platform for booking online consultations
2. To integrate a video call feature
3. To add a basic patient record list

Methodology:
The platform uses React on the frontend and Spring Boot on the backend with a MySQL database. Video calls use a third-party API such as Jitsi. Functional testing checks that booking, calling and record-keeping work, with a walkthrough shown to two small clinic owners.

Scope:
Includes appointment booking, video calls and a simple record list. Excludes billing, insurance claims and prescription handling.

Expected Outcomes:

2. Informal usability feedback from two owners

Timeline:
Two semesters: planning, build, integration and testing.

Title:
An E-Learning System for Smallholder Farmers

Problem Statement:
Smallholder farmers often lack access to up-to-date guidance on crop management, and extension officers cannot reach everyone. Generic e-learning platforms ignore low-bandwidth rural settings and local crops, leaving a gap for an offline-friendly, crop-specific learning tool.

Objectives:
1. To develop a mobile-friendly e-learning system covering three local crops
2. To support offline access to lessons and quizzes
3. To evaluate usability with at least 20 farmers

Methodology:
The system will be built as a progressive web app using React with a Spring Boot backend and PostgreSQL. Lessons are cached locally via service workers for offline use. Content is drawn from public agricultural extension materials. Evaluation uses the System Usability Scale plus a short quiz to measure knowledge change with 20 farmers.

Scope:
Covers rice, maize and chili lessons. Includes offline lessons, quizzes and progress tracking. Excludes live video, payment and a recommendation engine.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working offline-capable e-learning PWA for three crops
2. A usability and knowledge-gain evaluation report

Timeline:
Semester 1: requirements, content and design. Semester 2: build, offline support, evaluation.

Title:
A Contactless Fare Payment App for Public Transport

Problem Statement:
Many local bus systems still rely on cash, causing slow boarding and lost revenue tracking. A mobile fare payment app with QR-based ticketing could speed boarding, but existing fintech wallets are not tailored to small transit operators with limited budgets.

Objectives:
1. To build a mobile app that lets riders top up and pay fares via QR codes
2. To provide operators with a basic trip and revenue report
3. To test payment success rate in a small pilot

Methodology:
A React Native app and Spring Boot backend will be built, with payments handled through a sandbox payment gateway such as Stripe test mode. QR codes encode fare and route data validated server-side. A pilot with 10 simulated riders measures payment success rate and average transaction time.

Scope:
Covers top-up, QR fare payment and operator reports. Excludes real bank settlement, refunds and multi-operator clearing.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working QR fare payment mobile app and operator dashboard
2. A pilot report on payment success rate and timing

Timeline:
Semester 1: design and gateway integration. Semester 2: app build, pilot, reporting.

Title:
Detecting Fraudulent Carbon Credit Claims with Machine Learning

Problem Statement:
Carbon credit markets are vulnerable to inflated or fake claims, undermining sustainability efforts. Manual auditing is slow and inconsistent. A machine learning classifier could flag suspicious credit claims for review, but most fraud research targets banking rather than sustainability data.

Objectives:
1. To build a classifier that flags suspicious carbon credit transactions
2. To compare logistic regression, random forest and gradient boosting
3. To evaluate using precision, recall and F1

Methodology:
A labelled dataset of synthetic and public carbon credit transactions will be assembled, with features such as claim size, frequency and project type. Three models (logistic regression, random forest, XGBoost) are trained in Python with scikit-learn, using 5-fold cross-validation. Class imbalance is handled with SMOTE. Metrics reported are precision, recall and F1.

Scope:
Focuses on offline batch classification. Excludes real-time scoring and blockchain integration. Uses a single curated dataset.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained fraud classifier with comparison of three algorithms
2. An evaluation report with precision, recall and F1

Timeline:
Semester 1: data and feature engineering. Semester 2: modelling and evaluation.

Title:
A Product Recommendation System for a Logistics Marketplace

Problem Statement:
On a B2B logistics marketplace, buyers struggle to find the right packaging and shipping products among thousands of listings. Generic e-commerce recommenders assume consumer behaviour and ignore bulk, recurring logistics purchases, so relevance is poor.

Objectives:
1. To build a recommendation system tuned for recurring logistics purchases
2. To compare collaborative filtering with a content-based approach
3. To evaluate ranking quality offline

Methodology:
Using a public e-commerce transaction dataset adapted to logistics categories, item-based collaborative filtering and a content-based TF-IDF model are implemented in Python. A hybrid that blends both is also tested. Offline evaluation uses precision@k and recall@k on a held-out split, comparing against a popularity baseline.

Scope:
Offline recommendation only, integrated into a demo web frontend. Excludes real-time personalization, pricing and inventory logic.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working hybrid recommender with a demo interface
2. An evaluation comparing models against a popularity baseline

Timeline:
Semester 1: data prep and baselines. Semester 2: hybrid model and evaluation.

Title:
A Conversational Agent for E-Government Service Queries

Problem Statement:
Citizens often struggle to find the right e-government service among scattered portals and forms. Call centres are overloaded. A chatbot that answers common service questions could reduce load, but generic chatbots give vague answers and miss local procedure details.

Objectives:
1. To build a chatbot that answers common e-government service questions
2. To ground answers in an official FAQ knowledge base
3. To evaluate answer accuracy and user satisfaction

Methodology:
A retrieval-based chatbot is built in Python using sentence embeddings and a FAISS index over a curated set of government FAQ documents. Intent matching retrieves the closest answer, with a fallback message when confidence is low. Evaluation uses a 50-question test set for top-1 accuracy plus a short satisfaction survey with 15 users.

Scope:
Covers three service categories such as licensing, taxes and registration. English only. Excludes live transaction processing and authentication.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working retrieval-based e-government chatbot
2. An accuracy and satisfaction evaluation report

Timeline:
Semester 1: knowledge base and retrieval. Semester 2: interface, evaluation, refinement.

Title:
Knowledge-Graph-Based Search for Course Materials

Problem Statement:
Students searching learning management systems get keyword matches that miss conceptual links between topics. Without showing how concepts relate, students cannot navigate prerequisite chains. A knowledge-graph search could surface related concepts, but most LMS search is plain keyword based.

Objectives:
1. To build a knowledge graph linking course concepts and materials
2. To provide graph-based concept search and related-topic suggestions
3. To compare retrieval relevance against keyword search

Methodology:
Concepts and relations are extracted from a sample course corpus using spaCy and stored in Neo4j. A search interface queries the graph to return materials plus related concepts. Relevance is evaluated on a set of 30 student queries, comparing precision@5 of graph search versus a baseline keyword search.

Scope:
One course's materials. Includes concept extraction, graph storage and search UI. Excludes automatic grading and personalized paths.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working knowledge graph and concept search interface
2. A relevance comparison against keyword search

Timeline:
Semester 1: extraction and graph build. Semester 2: search UI and evaluation.

Title:
Shelf Product Segmentation for Retail Stock Monitoring

Problem Statement:
Retail staff manually check shelves for out-of-stock and misplaced items, which is slow and error-prone. Existing object detectors give bounding boxes but cannot separate tightly packed adjacent products, so accurate shelf coverage estimation needs pixel-level segmentation that few retail studies provide.

Objectives:
1. To train an instance segmentation model for shelf products achieving mean IoU above 0.75 on a held-out set
2. To estimate per-shelf stock coverage from segmentation masks
3. To benchmark against a bounding-box detection baseline

Methodology:
The SKU-110K and a subset of the Grocery Shelves dataset are used, with manual mask annotation for a 500-image subset via Roboflow. Mask R-CNN with a ResNet-50 FPN backbone is fine-tuned in PyTorch using transfer learning, with data augmentation for lighting and angle. Evaluation reports mean IoU, mask AP and coverage error, compared against a YOLOv8 detection baseline using 5-fold validation.

Scope:
Packaged shelf goods only. Excludes fresh produce, video tracking and price recognition. Inference is offline on still images.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained segmentation model with mean IoU and coverage error reported
2. A documented comparison against the detection baseline

Timeline:
S1: dataset, annotation, baseline. S2: segmentation training, coverage estimation, evaluation.

Title:
Real-Time Pedestrian and Vehicle Detection for Smart City Intersections

Problem Statement:
Smart city traffic management needs accurate counts of pedestrians and vehicles at intersections, but generic detectors degrade under occlusion, low light and CCTV angles. Many city pilots report poor small-object recall, leaving a gap for a tuned, edge-deployable detector evaluated on local-style footage.

Objectives:
1. To fine-tune a detector reaching mAP@0.5 above 0.80 for pedestrians and vehicles
2. To sustain at least 20 FPS on an edge device
3. To analyse failure cases under occlusion and low light

Methodology:
Training uses a subset of the BDD100K and MIO-TCD datasets with class balancing. YOLOv8 is fine-tuned in PyTorch with augmentation for night and occlusion, then exported to ONNX and benchmarked on a Jetson Nano for FPS and latency. Evaluation reports mAP@0.5, per-class recall and an error analysis of occluded and low-light frames against a Faster R-CNN baseline.

Scope:
Pedestrians, cars, motorcycles and buses only. Excludes license plate recognition, tracking IDs across cameras and signal control logic.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A tuned detector with mAP and FPS reported on edge hardware
2. A failure-case analysis and baseline comparison

Timeline:
S1: data prep, baseline, training. S2: edge optimization, benchmarking, error analysis.

Title:
Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis of Tourist Reviews

Problem Statement:
Tourism operators get thousands of online reviews but overall star ratings hide which aspects (food, cleanliness, value) drive opinions. Generic sentiment classifiers give a single polarity per review, missing aspect-level nuance that operators need to prioritize improvements.

Objectives:
1. To build an aspect-based sentiment model identifying aspect terms and their polarity
2. To achieve macro-F1 above 0.75 on aspect polarity classification
3. To compare a fine-tuned transformer against a lexicon baseline

Methodology:
The SemEval-2014 restaurant/laptop ABSA datasets plus a scraped set of tourism reviews are used. BERT-base is fine-tuned in PyTorch for aspect-term extraction and aspect polarity, evaluated with precision, recall and macro-F1 under stratified train/validation/test splits. A VADER lexicon and a logistic-regression TF-IDF model serve as baselines, with error analysis on misclassified aspects.

Scope:
English reviews for hotels and restaurants. Four aspect categories. Excludes multilingual reviews, sarcasm handling and real-time streaming.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A fine-tuned ABSA model with macro-F1 reported per aspect
2. A comparison against lexicon and TF-IDF baselines with error analysis

Timeline:
S1: data, annotation alignment, baselines. S2: transformer fine-tuning and evaluation.

Title:
Learned Index Recommendation for Social Media Query Optimization

Problem Statement:
Social media backends run heavy read queries over large post and follower tables, and poorly chosen indexes cause slow timelines. Default cost-based optimizers miss workload patterns. There is a gap for a workload-aware tool that recommends indexes from real query logs and measures the speedup.

Objectives:
1. To build a tool that recommends indexes from a query workload
2. To measure query latency improvement against the default plan
3. To compare a heuristic recommender with a learning-based ranker

Methodology:
A synthetic social media schema is loaded into PostgreSQL and populated to 10 million rows. A workload of read queries is generated, and candidate indexes are scored using EXPLAIN ANALYZE costs. A heuristic frequency-based recommender is compared with a gradient-boosted ranker trained on query features. Evaluation measures average and p95 latency before and after, plus index storage overhead.

Scope:
Single-node PostgreSQL, read-heavy workload. Excludes write-cost modelling, partitioning and distributed sharding.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An index recommendation tool with measured latency improvements
2. A comparison of heuristic versus learned ranking

Timeline:
S1: schema, workload, heuristic baseline. S2: learned ranker, benchmarking, analysis.

Title:
Facial Recognition Attendance for Healthcare Staff Shifts

Problem Statement:
Hospitals track staff attendance with cards that can be shared, undermining shift records. Face-based attendance avoids buddy-punching, but ward lighting, masks and similar uniforms reduce accuracy, and few studies evaluate recognition under clinical masking and low light.

Objectives:
1. To build a face-recognition attendance system robust to mask wearing
2. To achieve recognition accuracy above 0.90 on a masked test set
3. To log check-in/out with anti-spoofing liveness checks

Methodology:
Faces are detected with MTCNN and embedded with FaceNet (or ArcFace), matched by cosine distance against an enrolled gallery in a Flask backend. A masked-face subset is created by augmenting enrolled images. A blink-based liveness check resists photo spoofing. Evaluation reports accuracy, false acceptance and false rejection rates on masked and unmasked sets, with a small 15-person enrollment trial.

Scope:
Up to 30 enrolled staff, indoor wards. Excludes payroll integration, multi-site sync and gait recognition.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working masked-robust attendance system with FAR/FRR reported
2. A trial report on recognition accuracy and spoofing resistance

Timeline:
S1: detection, embedding, enrollment. S2: liveness, masking tests, evaluation.

Title:
Robust OCR and Information Extraction for Financial Invoices

Problem Statement:
Finance teams manually key data from heterogeneous PDF and scanned invoices, which is slow and error-prone. Generic OCR returns raw text but does not extract structured fields (invoice number, totals, line items), and accuracy drops on noisy scans and varied layouts. The gap is an end-to-end pipeline that combines OCR with layout-aware field extraction and reports field-level accuracy on realistic noisy documents.

Objectives:
1. To build an OCR-plus-extraction pipeline returning structured fields with field-level F1 above 0.90 on clean invoices
2. To quantify accuracy degradation under controlled noise (blur, skew, low DPI)
3. To benchmark a layout-aware model (LayoutLMv3) against a Tesseract-plus-regex baseline

Methodology:
The FUNSD and SROIE datasets plus 300 self-collected anonymized invoices are used, split 70/15/15 with stratification by layout type. Tesseract provides OCR text; LayoutLMv3 is fine-tuned in PyTorch for token-level field tagging, compared against a Tesseract-plus-regex rule baseline. A noise generator applies graded blur, skew and DPI reduction to measure robustness curves. Metrics are field-level precision, recall and F1, plus character error rate, under 5-fold cross-validation. Risks (data scarcity, layout drift) are mitigated by augmentation and active sampling.

Scope:
English invoices and receipts only. Targets header fields and line-item totals. Excludes handwriting, multi-currency normalization and ERP integration. Inference is offline batch.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A reproducible OCR-plus-extraction pipeline with field-level F1 and CER reported
2. A robustness study showing accuracy versus noise level against the baseline

Timeline:
S1 (weeks 1-7): dataset assembly, annotation, baseline. S1 (8-14): LayoutLMv3 fine-tuning. S2 (1-7): noise study and ablation. S2 (8-14): evaluation, error analysis, write-up.

Title:
Anomaly Detection in Manufacturing Wireless Sensor Networks for Predictive Maintenance

Problem Statement:
Manufacturing lines instrument machines with wireless sensors (vibration, temperature, current), but raw streams are noisy and faults are rare, so simple thresholds either miss early degradation or flood operators with false alarms. The gap is a sensor-fusion anomaly detector that handles missing readings and class imbalance and is validated against labelled fault events with clear lead-time and false-alarm metrics.

Objectives:
1. To build a multivariate anomaly detector for sensor streams achieving F1 above 0.80 on labelled faults
2. To provide fault lead-time (early-warning horizon) and compare false-alarm rates against a threshold baseline
3. To evaluate robustness to missing and out-of-order sensor readings

Methodology:
The NASA CMAPSS and a public bearing-vibration dataset are used, resampled to fixed windows with feature extraction (RMS, FFT bands, rolling statistics). An LSTM autoencoder and an Isolation Forest are trained on healthy data in Python, scoring reconstruction/anomaly error against a control-chart threshold baseline. Class imbalance is addressed by training on normal data only; missing readings are simulated and imputed to test robustness. Metrics are precision, recall, F1, ROC-AUC and mean lead-time, with time-series cross-validation. Risks (label scarcity, concept drift) are noted with mitigation.

Scope:
Offline analysis of three sensor types on rotating machinery. Excludes live gateway deployment, RF protocol optimization and actuator control.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained anomaly detector with F1, ROC-AUC and lead-time reported
2. A robustness and false-alarm comparison against the threshold baseline

Timeline:
S1 (1-7): data, windowing, features. S1 (8-14): baseline and Isolation Forest. S2 (1-7): LSTM autoencoder and robustness tests. S2 (8-14): evaluation and reporting.

Machine Learning for Retail

Deep Learning Cameras for Smart City

NLP for Tourism

Title:
A Recommender System for a Social Media Platform

Problem Statement:
Social media users see a lot of posts and it is hard to find content they like. A recommender system could suggest posts based on what users interacted with before, but many small platforms do not have one.

Title:
Speech Recognition for Healthcare Notes

Problem Statement:
Doctors and nurses spend a lot of time typing notes. A speech recognition system could let them dictate notes instead, saving time. Existing tools are expensive and not always tuned for medical words.

Objectives:
1. Build a speech-to-text system for short clinical phrases.
2. Improve recognition of common medical terms.
3. Measure word error rate against a baseline.

Methodology:
I will use a pre-trained speech recognition model such as one based on wav2vec or a cloud API and adapt it with a small set of medical recordings. I will compute word error rate on a held-out test set. Python and a speech library will be used.

Scope:
The system covers English dictation of short clinical notes. It will not handle full conversations or multiple speakers at once. Patient privacy data will not be used; only synthetic or public recordings.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A prototype that transcribes spoken medical notes.
2. A comparison of word error rate before and after adaptation.

Timeline:
About 13 weeks across data prep, adaptation, and evaluation.

Title:
Network Intrusion Detection for a Finance Network

Problem Statement:
Financial systems are targets for network attacks. Intrusion detection systems help spot malicious traffic, but rule-based ones miss new attacks. A machine learning detector could flag suspicious flows, though training on realistic data is a challenge.

Objectives:
1. Build an ML classifier that labels network flows as normal or attack.
2. Use a public intrusion dataset for training.
3. Report accuracy and false positive rate.

Methodology:
I will use the NSL-KDD or CICIDS dataset and train classifiers like random forest and a simple neural network. Features will be the flow attributes already in the dataset. I will use scikit-learn and evaluate with accuracy, precision, and recall on a test split.

Scope:
The project is offline detection on a labelled dataset, not live deployment on a real bank network. It focuses on common attack categories in the dataset.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained intrusion detection model.
2. A report of detection metrics across attack types.

Timeline:
Roughly 12 weeks for data, modelling, and evaluation.

Title:
Web Application Security Scanner for Manufacturing Portals

Problem Statement:
Manufacturing companies run web portals for orders and inventory, but these often have security flaws. Many small firms cannot afford security audits. A lightweight scanner could check for common web vulnerabilities automatically.

Objectives:
1. Build a scanner that checks for common vulnerabilities like SQL injection and XSS.
2. Test it on a deliberately vulnerable web app.
3. Report which issues are found and missed.

Methodology:
I will write a Python tool that sends crafted requests to test for injection and cross-site scripting, drawing on the OWASP Top 10. I will test it against a known vulnerable app like DVWA and compare findings with an existing tool such as OWASP ZAP.

Scope:
The scanner targets a handful of common vulnerability types in web forms. It will not cover authentication bypass, business logic flaws, or network-level attacks.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working vulnerability scanner prototype.
2. A comparison of its detection rate with ZAP on a test app.

Timeline:
About 12 weeks across building and testing.

Title:
Static and Dynamic Malware Analysis Tool for Public Safety Agencies

Problem Statement:
Public safety agencies receive suspicious files but lack accessible tools to triage them quickly. Commercial sandboxes are costly. A combined static and dynamic analysis tool could give a fast risk indication and help analysts prioritise which samples to investigate further.

Objectives:
1. Extract static features (PE header fields, imported APIs, strings) from Windows executables.
2. Run samples in an isolated VM to capture behavioural indicators such as file and registry changes.
3. Classify samples as likely benign or malicious and present a readable report.

Methodology:
Static features will be parsed with the pefile library. Dynamic analysis will run samples in a snapshotted Windows VM via Cuckoo-style monitoring, logging API calls. A random forest classifier trained on a labelled set from VirusShare and benign system binaries will produce the verdict, evaluated with accuracy and F1 on a held-out split.

Scope:
The tool targets Windows PE files only. It excludes packed-binary unpacking, document macros, and live network malware. Analysis is single-sample, not bulk pipelines.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working triage tool with a combined static-dynamic report.
2. Classification metrics on a labelled malware dataset.

Timeline:
14 weeks: feature work (4), sandbox (4), classifier and report (4), evaluation (2).

Title:
A Responsive Web Platform for Household Energy Monitoring

Problem Statement:
Households want to understand their electricity use but utility bills give only a monthly total. A responsive web platform that shows daily and appliance-level consumption could help users spot waste and reduce costs, but most existing tools require proprietary hardware.

Objectives:
1. Build a responsive web dashboard that displays energy use over selectable time ranges.
2. Let users log appliances and estimate their share of consumption.
3. Provide simple tips based on usage patterns.

Methodology:
The frontend will use React with a charting library; the backend will be a Node.js REST API with a PostgreSQL store. Energy readings will come from a CSV upload or a simulated smart-meter feed. The layout will be tested across desktop and mobile breakpoints. Usability will be checked with a small group of test users.

Scope:
The platform handles single-household data from uploaded or simulated readings. It excludes real hardware integration, multi-home accounts, and billing.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A responsive web app with interactive consumption charts.
2. Usability feedback from a small user test.

Timeline:
13 weeks across design, build, and user testing.

Title:
A Progressive Web App for Small Business Inventory and Sales

Problem Statement:
Small shops often track stock on paper or spreadsheets, leading to errors and stockouts. A progressive web app that works offline and installs like a native app could let owners record sales and inventory on any device without app-store fees.

Objectives:
1. Build a PWA for recording sales and updating stock levels.
2. Support offline use with later synchronisation.
3. Generate a simple low-stock alert and sales summary.

Methodology:
The app will be built with React and a service worker for offline caching, using IndexedDB for local storage and background sync to a Firebase backend. Installability and offline behaviour will be verified with Lighthouse PWA audits. A few shop owners will trial the prototype and give feedback.

Scope:
The app covers single-store inventory and sales for a small catalogue. It excludes multi-branch sync, accounting, payroll, and payment processing.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An installable offline-capable inventory PWA.
2. A Lighthouse PWA score and user feedback summary.

Timeline:
13 weeks: design (2), core app (5), offline sync (3), testing (3).

Title:
A Cross-Platform Mobile App for Smallholder Crop Disease Guidance

Problem Statement:
Smallholder farmers often misidentify crop diseases and apply the wrong treatment. Expert advice is hard to reach in rural areas. A cross-platform mobile app that lets farmers photograph a leaf and get a likely-disease label with care tips could reduce crop loss.

Objectives:
1. Build a cross-platform app where farmers capture a leaf photo and get a disease prediction.
2. Run a lightweight image classifier on-device for a few common crops.
3. Show treatment guidance for each detected disease.

Methodology:
The app will be built with Flutter for Android and iOS. A MobileNet model trained on the PlantVillage dataset will be converted to TensorFlow Lite and run on-device. The classifier will be evaluated with top-1 accuracy on a held-out split. A small field trial with sample photos will check usability.

Scope:
The app covers three to four crops present in PlantVillage. It excludes pest identification, soil analysis, and real-time video. Predictions are advisory, not a replacement for an agronomist.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A cross-platform app with on-device leaf disease classification.
2. Accuracy results and field usability notes.

Timeline:
14 weeks across model, app build, and testing.

Title:
An Android Native App for Real-Time Public Bus Arrival Information

Problem Statement:
Commuters often wait at bus stops without knowing when the next bus arrives, leading to wasted time. Where a transit agency publishes location data, a native Android app could show live arrival estimates and stop information, but many small cities have no such app.

Objectives:
1. Build a native Android app showing nearby stops and predicted arrival times.
2. Consume a public transit feed (GTFS / GTFS-Realtime).
3. Provide route search and a favourites list.

Methodology:
The app will be built in Kotlin using Android Jetpack components, with Retrofit calling a GTFS-Realtime feed and Room for caching favourites. Arrival estimates come from the feed's vehicle positions and schedule. The UI will follow Material Design. Testing covers unit tests for the parsing layer and manual testing on two device sizes.

Scope:
The app targets one city's public transit feed and bus mode only. It excludes ticketing, payment, multi-modal routing, and offline maps.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working Android app with live arrival estimates.
2. Test results and basic performance notes.

Timeline:
13 weeks: setup (2), feed integration (4), UI (4), testing (3).

Title:
An IoT Sensor Network for Campus Water-Use Sustainability Monitoring

Problem Statement:
Campuses waste water through unnoticed leaks and inefficient usage, but facilities teams lack real-time visibility. A low-cost IoT sensor network could measure flow at several points and surface anomalies, supporting sustainability targets without expensive metering infrastructure.

Objectives:
1. Deploy flow sensors on a small set of points and stream readings over a network.
2. Store and visualise water-use data on a dashboard.
3. Detect simple anomalies such as unexpected overnight flow.

Methodology:
ESP32 microcontrollers with flow sensors will publish readings via MQTT to a Raspberry Pi broker, with data stored in InfluxDB and shown in Grafana. A threshold and moving-average rule will flag anomalies. The prototype will be validated on a small testbed with known leak scenarios simulated by opening a tap.

Scope:
The prototype covers three to four sensing points on a testbed, not a full campus rollout. It excludes pressure sensing, automated valve control, and billing integration.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working IoT testbed streaming and visualising water-use data.
2. Demonstrated detection of simulated leak events.

Timeline:
14 weeks across hardware, networking, dashboard, and testing.

Title:
A Smart-Home Automation Hub for Last-Mile Delivery Reception

Problem Statement:
Failed deliveries are costly in logistics because recipients are often absent when parcels arrive. Existing smart doorbells notify but cannot coordinate secure parcel reception. This project builds a smart-home automation hub that detects a delivery, grants one-time access to a secure drop box, and logs the event for the carrier, reducing missed deliveries for households.

Objectives:
1. Build a hub that integrates a camera, a smart lock, and a courier-facing one-time code.
2. Trigger an automation rule that unlocks a drop box only for a valid delivery code within a time window.
3. Evaluate reliability and access latency against a manual baseline over repeated trials.

Methodology:
The hub runs on a Raspberry Pi with Home Assistant orchestrating MQTT devices: an ESP32-CAM for motion and a ZigBee smart lock. Courier codes are issued via a web endpoint and verified server-side; an automation grants a single timed unlock. Evaluation measures successful-reception rate, false-grant rate, and unlock latency across 50 simulated delivery trials, compared to a no-automation baseline. Security review covers replay and code-reuse risks.

Scope:
The system handles single-household reception with one drop box and pre-issued courier codes. It excludes payment, multi-parcel queuing, and integration with real carrier APIs (simulated instead).

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working automation hub with secure one-time delivery access.
2. A reliability and latency report versus the manual baseline.

Timeline:
14 weeks: integration (4), automation logic (3), security hardening (3), evaluation (4).

Title:
Edge Computing for Low-Latency Document Verification in E-Government Kiosks

Problem Statement:
E-government kiosks that verify ID documents often send images to a central server, causing latency and privacy concerns in areas with poor connectivity. Running verification at the edge could cut response time and keep sensitive images local, but edge devices have limited compute, so model efficiency matters.

Objectives:
1. Deploy a document-verification pipeline (text region detection plus OCR field extraction) on an edge device.
2. Compare on-device inference latency and accuracy against a cloud baseline.
3. Quantify the accuracy-latency trade-off of model quantisation.

Methodology:
The pipeline uses a lightweight detector and Tesseract/EasyOCR running on a Jetson Nano. The detector will be quantised to INT8 with TensorRT and compared to an FP32 cloud deployment. Evaluation uses a public ID-document dataset (e.g. MIDV-500), measuring field-level accuracy, end-to-end latency, and throughput. A risk analysis covers degraded-image handling and offline operation.

Scope:
The project targets field extraction from a fixed set of document layouts under controlled lighting. It excludes liveness/anti-spoofing, biometric matching, and production security certification.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working edge verification prototype with measured latency and accuracy.
2. A quantisation trade-off analysis versus the cloud baseline.

Timeline:
15 weeks: pipeline (4), edge port and quantisation (4), evaluation (4), risk and write-up (3).

Title:
A Cloud-Native Microservices Architecture for an Online Learning Platform

Problem Statement:
Monolithic learning platforms struggle to scale individual features such as quiz grading during exam peaks, forcing the whole system to scale together and waste resources. Decomposing into microservices could let each service scale independently, but this introduces complexity in communication, data consistency, and observability that must be evaluated.

Objectives:
1. Design and implement core learning services (auth, course, enrolment, quiz-grading) as independent microservices.
2. Deploy on Kubernetes with autoscaling and a gateway.
3. Measure scalability and resilience under load versus a monolithic baseline.

Methodology:
Services are built in Spring Boot, communicating via REST and an event bus (Kafka) for enrolment events, each with its own PostgreSQL schema. They are containerised and deployed on a local Kubernetes (k3s) cluster with an API gateway, Horizontal Pod Autoscaler, and Prometheus/Grafana observability. Load tests with k6 measure latency and throughput as concurrent users rise; a chaos test kills a pod to check resilience, comparing against a monolithic build of the same features.

Scope:
The project implements four services and the grading scale path, not a full LMS. It excludes payment, video streaming, and multi-region deployment.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working microservices deployment with autoscaling and observability.
2. A scalability and resilience comparison report against a monolith.

Timeline:
15 weeks: services (5), Kubernetes and observability (4), load and chaos testing (4), analysis (2).

Title:
A CI/CD Automation Pipeline with Quality Gates for a Retail Web Service

Problem Statement:
Retail web teams that deploy manually face slow, error-prone releases and inconsistent quality checks. A well-designed CI/CD pipeline with automated testing, security scanning, and progressive delivery could cut release time and catch defects earlier, but teams need evidence of which gates give the most value for the added build time.

Objectives:
1. Build a CI/CD pipeline that runs tests, static analysis, and container scanning on every change.
2. Add automated deployment with a canary release stage and rollback.
3. Measure lead time, change-failure rate, and pipeline duration before and after the gates.

Methodology:
The pipeline uses GitHub Actions to build a containerised retail service, run unit and integration tests, SonarQube static analysis, and Trivy image scanning, then deploy to a Kubernetes staging cluster with an Argo Rollouts canary. DORA-style metrics (lead time, deployment frequency, change-failure rate, MTTR) are collected over a series of simulated changes, some intentionally faulty, to measure how many defects each gate catches and the cost in pipeline time.

Scope:
The project covers one service's pipeline on a staging cluster. It excludes production traffic, infrastructure provisioning automation, and multi-team governance.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working CI/CD pipeline with quality gates and canary deployment.
2. A before/after report on DORA metrics and defect-catch rate.

Timeline:
14 weeks: base pipeline (4), gates and canary (4), faulty-change experiments (3), analysis (3).

Title:
A Big-Data Analytics Pipeline for Smart-City Traffic Congestion Insights

Problem Statement:
Smart cities generate large volumes of traffic sensor and GPS data, but batch reporting is too slow to support timely decisions. A scalable analytics pipeline that ingests streaming data and produces near-real-time congestion metrics could help operators respond faster, though balancing throughput, latency, and cost is non-trivial.

Objectives:
1. Build a streaming pipeline that ingests vehicle-flow data and computes congestion metrics per road segment.
2. Store aggregates for both real-time dashboards and historical analysis.
3. Evaluate throughput and end-to-end latency as data volume scales.

Methodology:
Data from a public traffic dataset (replayed as a stream via Kafka) is processed with Apache Spark Structured Streaming to compute per-segment speed and congestion indices in tumbling windows. Results are written to a Parquet data lake for batch queries and to a serving store for a Grafana dashboard. The pipeline runs on Docker Compose locally; throughput and latency are measured as input rate increases, and partitioning strategies are compared.

Scope:
The pipeline covers congestion metrics from one city's replayed dataset. It excludes signal-control actuation, predictive modelling, and a managed-cloud deployment (run locally instead).

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working streaming analytics pipeline with a live congestion dashboard.
2. A throughput-latency scaling evaluation across input rates.

Timeline:
15 weeks: ingestion (3), streaming compute (4), storage and dashboard (4), scaling tests and analysis (4).

Title:
A Business-Intelligence Dashboard with Explainable Demand Drivers for Regional Tourism Boards

Problem Statement:
Regional tourism boards plan marketing and staffing using fragmented data (arrivals, bookings, weather, events) spread across spreadsheets, and existing BI dashboards show what changed but not why. The gap is an integrated dashboard that not only visualises tourism KPIs but attributes demand shifts to interpretable drivers, enabling evidence-based planning for boards without a data-science team.

Objectives:
1. Integrate arrivals, occupancy, weather, and event-calendar data into a governed star-schema warehouse with documented ETL.
2. Deliver a role-based BI dashboard exposing KPIs (occupancy, length-of-stay, seasonality) with drill-down by region and segment.
3. Add an explainable driver-attribution panel using SHAP on a gradient-boosted demand model, validated against a regression baseline.

Methodology:
ETL in dbt loads sources into a PostgreSQL star schema with data-quality tests. The dashboard is built in Apache Superset with row-level security per board role. A LightGBM model predicts weekly occupancy from weather, events, lag, and seasonality features; SHAP values surface per-period driver contributions. The model is evaluated with time-series cross-validation (rolling-origin), reporting MAE and MAPE against linear-regression and seasonal-naive baselines; attribution stability is checked across folds.

Scope:
Covers three pilot regions over three years of historical data, weekly granularity, occupancy-demand attribution only. Excludes real-time ingestion, individual-traveller PII, paid-ad ROI modelling, and automated budget allocation. Inclusions and exclusions are fixed at proposal sign-off.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A governed warehouse and role-based explainable BI dashboard validated with two tourism-board users.
2. A forecasting-and-attribution evaluation report (MAE/MAPE vs baselines, SHAP-driver findings).

Timeline:
16 weeks: ETL/warehouse (4), dashboard (4), demand model and SHAP (4), validation and reporting (4).

Title:
Forecasting Daily Engagement on a Social-Media Platform with Probabilistic Time-Series Models

Problem Statement:
Social-media operations teams need day-ahead engagement forecasts (active users, post volume) to schedule moderation and infrastructure, but engagement is volatile, holiday-sensitive, and exhibits multiple seasonalities. Point forecasts hide risk; teams need calibrated prediction intervals. The gap is a rigorous comparison of classical and modern probabilistic forecasters that quantifies both accuracy and interval calibration on real engagement series.

Objectives:
1. Build a reproducible pipeline that forecasts daily engagement with calibrated prediction intervals.
2. Compare SARIMAX, Prophet, and a Temporal Fusion Transformer against seasonal-naive and exponential-smoothing baselines.
3. Evaluate point accuracy and probabilistic calibration, and analyse failure cases around holidays and spikes.

Methodology:
Daily engagement series (public social-media activity datasets) are split with rolling-origin backtesting (expanding window, 14-day horizon). Models include SARIMAX with exogenous holiday/seasonality regressors, Prophet, and a Temporal Fusion Transformer, each tuned via time-aware validation to avoid leakage. Point accuracy uses MASE and sMAPE; probabilistic quality uses pinball loss and prediction-interval coverage (PICP) at the 80/95% levels. Statistical significance across models uses the Diebold-Mariano test. Residual diagnostics and a spike-driven error breakdown identify where each model fails.

Scope:
Covers univariate-plus-exogenous daily forecasting at a 14-day horizon for up to five engagement metrics, two years of history. Excludes intraday forecasting, causal-intervention modelling, and live production serving. Deliverables and exclusions are frozen at sign-off.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A reproducible forecasting library with backtesting and calibrated intervals.
2. An evaluation report ranking models by accuracy and calibration with significance tests and failure analysis.

Timeline:
16 weeks: data and backtest harness (3), baselines and classical models (4), TFT (4), evaluation and significance testing (3), write-up (2).

Title:
Blockchain for Logistics

Logistics has many problems and things get lost. Blockchain can fix this because it is secure and new technology that everyone is talking about now.

Objectives:

For all logistics companies everywhere.

AR App for Government

Problem Statement:
Government services are slow and people don't like going to offices. Augmented reality is cool and can make it better and more modern for citizens.

Objectives:
1. Build an AR app
2. For government

Methodology:
I will make an augmented reality app using a phone. People can point the camera and see government stuff. I will use Unity maybe.

Scope:
The whole government and all citizens.

1. An AR application
2. Better government

Title:
VR Training for Students

Problem Statement:
Students find learning boring and don't pay attention in class. Virtual reality is immersive and fun so it will help them learn better and remember more things.

Objectives:
1. Make a VR simulation
2. For training students
3. Improve learning

Methodology:
I will create a virtual reality simulation where students wear a headset and learn. I will use a game engine and 3D models from the internet.

All subjects and all students in the school.

1. A VR training app
2. Students learn better

Title:
A 2D Shopping Game for a Retail Store

Problem Statement:
Customers in retail stores are not engaged and loyalty programs are boring point counters. A simple 2D game tied to a shop could make shopping more fun and encourage repeat visits, but most small retailers do not have such tools.

Objectives:
1. Develop a 2D game where players collect items matching real store products
2. Add a points system linked to purchases
3. Test if users enjoy playing it

Methodology:
The game will be built in Unity with C# for a 2D side-scroller. Players move a character to catch falling products. Scores convert to discount coupons. I will design the sprites in a free tool and test with classmates.

Scope:
A single-player 2D game for one demo retail store, played on Android. Multiplayer and real payment integration are not included.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working 2D Android game
2. Survey feedback from at least 15 testers
