14 weeks: design, build, test.

Title:
A Serious Game to Teach Recycling in a Smart City

Problem Statement:
Smart cities want residents to recycle correctly, but flyers and posters are often ignored. People, especially younger ones, do not know which bin to use. A serious game could teach recycling rules in an engaging way, though few city-themed learning games exist locally.

Objectives:
1. Build a serious game that teaches correct waste sorting
2. Include city scenarios such as parks and streets
3. Measure knowledge improvement before and after playing

Methodology:
The game will be made in Unity as a 3D sorting game where the player drags trash into the right bin under a timer. Levels get harder. I will add a short quiz before and after to compare scores from around 20 players.

Scope:
A desktop educational game covering common household recyclables for one city theme. Real sensor data and a mobile version are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A playable serious game with three levels
2. A report on pre/post quiz score changes

Timeline:
One semester across four phases.

Title:
A Health Information App for Tourists

Problem Statement:
Tourists visiting a new country often do not know where the nearest clinic is or what local medicines are called. This causes stress during minor health issues abroad. There is no simple app combining basic health info with tourist locations for the destinations I looked at.

Objectives:
1. Build a mobile app listing nearby clinics and pharmacies for tourists
2. Provide basic first-aid and common medicine name translations
3. Let users save emergency contacts

Methodology:
The app will be built with Flutter and use the Google Maps API to show clinics. Health tips and medicine translations will be stored in a small local database. I will fill the data manually for one tourist city and test with a few users.

Scope:
An Android app for one tourist destination with English and one local language. Real-time appointment booking is excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working tourist health app
2. Usability feedback from testers

Timeline:
Roughly 13 weeks.

Title:
A Telemedicine Platform with Social Sharing Features

Problem Statement:
People delay seeing a doctor for minor issues and rely on unverified advice from social media groups. A telemedicine platform that lets patients consult doctors and share verified health posts could reduce misinformation, but most existing apps separate consultation from community discussion.

Objectives:
1. Build a web platform for booking video consultations with doctors
2. Add a moderated feed where doctors post verified health tips
3. Allow patients to follow doctors and react to posts

Methodology:
The platform will use React for the frontend and Node.js with MongoDB for the backend. Video calls will use a WebRTC library or a third-party SDK. A simple role system separates doctors and patients. I will seed the feed with sample posts and test core flows.

Scope:
A prototype web app with text/video consultation and a basic moderated feed. Payments, insurance, and prescription issuing are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working telemedicine prototype with consultation and feed
2. Feedback from a small pilot test

Timeline:
14 weeks in four stages.

Title:
An Adaptive E-Learning System for Nursing Students

Problem Statement:
Healthcare e-learning often delivers the same content to every learner regardless of their weak areas, so students waste time on topics they already know and skip ones they struggle with. Existing nursing course platforms rarely adapt question difficulty to individual performance, leaving knowledge gaps unaddressed before clinical placement.

Objectives:
1. Build an e-learning system that tracks each student's quiz performance per topic
2. Recommend the next module using a simple rule-based adaptive algorithm
3. Evaluate whether adaptive sequencing improves quiz scores compared to fixed order

Methodology:
The system will be built with Django and PostgreSQL. Each topic has a question bank tagged by difficulty. After each quiz, a mastery score per topic drives which module is shown next. I will run an A/B comparison with two small student groups (adaptive vs fixed) and compare average post-test scores.

Scope:
A web platform covering three nursing topics with multiple-choice quizzes. Video lectures and certification are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A functional adaptive e-learning web system
2. A comparison report of adaptive vs fixed learning paths

Timeline:
14 weeks: requirements, build, content, evaluation.

Title:
A QR-Based Micro-Payment System for Campus Vendors

Problem Statement:
Small campus vendors mostly take cash, which is slow during peak hours and hard to track. Existing fintech apps target large merchants and charge fees that small vendors find unattractive. A lightweight QR micro-payment system designed for low-value, high-frequency campus transactions is missing.

Objectives:
1. Build a mobile wallet supporting QR-based payments between students and vendors
2. Implement a transaction ledger with daily settlement summaries for vendors
3. Evaluate transaction speed and usability against cash payment

Methodology:
The app will use Flutter for clients and Spring Boot with MySQL for the backend, exposing REST APIs. Payments are simulated with a prepaid wallet balance (no real banking integration). QR codes encode vendor IDs; the server validates balance and records transactions. I will measure average transaction time and collect SUS usability scores from test users.

Scope:
A prototype with simulated balances for one campus food court. Real bank rails, KYC, and refunds are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working QR payment prototype with vendor dashboards
2. A report comparing speed and usability vs cash

Timeline:
Four phases over one semester.

Title:
Anomaly Detection for Defect Fraud in Manufacturing Claims

Problem Statement:
In manufacturing, suppliers sometimes file warranty or defect claims that are exaggerated or fraudulent, but reviewing every claim manually is slow. Rule-based checks miss novel patterns, and small factories lack data-science teams to flag suspicious claims for review.

Objectives:
1. Build a model that flags potentially fraudulent defect claims for human review
2. Compare an unsupervised approach (Isolation Forest) with a supervised one (logistic regression)
3. Provide a dashboard showing flagged claims with scores

Methodology:
Using a public manufacturing/claims-style dataset (or a synthetic one if needed), I will engineer features such as claim amount, frequency, and time since purchase. I will train Isolation Forest and logistic regression, evaluate with precision, recall, and ROC-AUC on a held-out split, and surface top-scored claims in a Flask dashboard.

Scope:
A prototype focused on tabular claim features and binary flagging. Image-based defect inspection and real-time streaming are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained detection model with evaluation metrics
2. A review dashboard listing flagged claims

Timeline:
14 weeks across data, modelling, dashboard, evaluation.

Title:
A Recommendation System for Public-Safety Equipment E-Commerce

Problem Statement:
An online store selling public-safety gear (helmets, vests, first-aid kits) for community groups offers many products, and buyers struggle to choose suitable bundles. Generic best-seller lists ignore the buyer's use case, leading to wrong purchases and returns.

Objectives:
1. Build a recommendation feature suggesting relevant safety products per user
2. Compare content-based filtering with item-based collaborative filtering
3. Evaluate recommendation quality offline using precision@k

Methodology:
The store will run on Laravel with MySQL. I will implement content-based filtering using product category/tag similarity (cosine), and item-based collaborative filtering from a synthetic purchase log. Offline evaluation will use a train/test split and precision@k and recall@k. The better method will be wired into the product page.

Scope:
A web store prototype with a seeded catalogue and synthetic interactions. Real payment and live user A/B testing are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working e-commerce site with recommendations
2. An offline comparison of the two methods

Timeline:
One semester, four milestones.

Title:
A Chatbot for Household Energy-Saving Advice

Problem Statement:
Households want to lower electricity bills but find energy reports confusing and rarely act on them. Utility FAQs are static and do not answer specific questions like "why is my bill high this month?" An interactive assistant could give tailored, plain-language advice.

Objectives:
1. Build a conversational agent answering common energy-saving questions
2. Personalize tips using the user's appliance list and monthly usage input
3. Evaluate answer helpfulness and intent-recognition accuracy

Methodology:
Intents will be handled with a retrieval approach: user questions are embedded with Sentence-BERT and matched to a curated FAQ knowledge base, with rule-based slots for appliance/usage inputs. The chatbot runs in a React widget over a Flask API. I will evaluate intent accuracy on a labelled test set and collect helpfulness ratings from testers.

Scope:
An English chatbot covering residential energy-saving topics with manual usage entry. Live smart-meter integration is excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working energy-advice chatbot
2. Intent-accuracy results and user helpfulness ratings

Timeline:
14 weeks in four phases.

Title:
A Knowledge-Graph Search Tool for Small-Business Suppliers

Problem Statement:
Small business owners searching for local suppliers rely on keyword search that misses related products and connections (e.g. a supplier offering both packaging and labels). Plain keyword lists do not show relationships, so owners spend time cross-checking multiple sites.

Objectives:
1. Build a knowledge graph linking suppliers, products, and categories
2. Provide graph-based search that returns related entities, not just keyword matches
3. Compare result relevance against plain keyword search

Methodology:
I will model suppliers/products/categories as nodes and relationships in Neo4j, populated from a scraped/seeded dataset of local business listings. Search uses Cypher traversals plus simple text matching. A small relevance study with sample queries will compare graph search and keyword search using relevance judgments and a precision metric.

Scope:
A web prototype for one business category in one region with a seeded graph. Automated continuous crawling is out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working knowledge-graph search prototype
2. A relevance comparison report

Timeline:
Four phases over one semester.

Title:
Semantic Segmentation of Crop and Weed Regions for Targeted Spraying

Problem Statement:
Uniform herbicide spraying wastes chemicals and harms soil because it cannot distinguish crops from weeds. Pixel-level separation of crop, weed, and soil from field images would enable targeted spraying, but lightweight models that run on edge hardware while staying accurate on real field conditions are still a challenge for smallholder farms.

Objectives:
1. Train a semantic segmentation model to label crop, weed, and soil pixels in field images
2. Compare U-Net and DeepLabV3+ (MobileNet backbone) on accuracy and inference cost
3. Quantify potential herbicide reduction from a targeted vs uniform spraying simulation

Methodology:
I will use the public CWFID and Sugar Beets datasets, applying augmentation (flips, colour jitter) to handle lighting variation. Both models train with the same split (70/15/15) using Dice + cross-entropy loss and early stopping. Evaluation uses mean IoU, per-class IoU, and inference time on CPU. A spraying simulation estimates chemical saved from predicted weed masks.

Scope:
RGB field images for two or three crop types under daytime conditions. Real-time drone deployment and hyperspectral imaging are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained segmentation model reporting per-class mean IoU
2. A model-comparison and herbicide-saving analysis

Timeline:
14 weeks: data prep (3), modelling (5), evaluation (4), write-up (2).

Title:
Real-Time Vehicle and Pedestrian Detection for Junction Safety Monitoring

Problem Statement:
Manual review of traffic-junction CCTV to spot near-misses is impractical at scale, and many junctions lack analytics. Detecting vehicles and pedestrians in real time enables automatic counting and conflict alerts, but balancing accuracy with the speed needed for live video on modest hardware remains difficult.

Objectives:
1. Train an object detector for vehicles and pedestrians at road junctions
2. Compare YOLOv8n and YOLOv8s on accuracy versus frames-per-second
3. Build a counting and proximity-alert module from detection outputs

Methodology:
I will fine-tune YOLOv8 (n and s) on a subset of the BDD100K dataset filtered to junction scenes, with augmentation for weather and lighting. Models are evaluated with mAP@0.5, mAP@0.5:0.95, and FPS on a GPU and a CPU fallback. Tracking via ByteTrack enables counting; a proximity rule flags close vehicle–pedestrian pairs as potential conflicts.

Scope:
Daytime and dusk footage at fixed junction angles for two object classes. Night-time, license-plate reading, and multi-camera fusion are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained detector with mAP and FPS results for both variants
2. A working counting and conflict-alert demo on test clips

Timeline:
Four phases across one semester with a risk buffer for annotation.

Title:
Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis of Consumer Reviews on Sustainable Products

Problem Statement:
Shoppers increasingly care about sustainability, but product reviews mix opinions on price, quality, and eco-friendliness, making it hard to gauge sentiment toward green attributes specifically. Document-level sentiment hides which aspect drives a complaint, so brands cannot tell whether eco-claims are trusted.

Objectives:
1. Build an aspect-based sentiment model targeting sustainability-related aspects
2. Compare a fine-tuned DistilBERT against a TF-IDF + SVM baseline
3. Analyse aspect-level sentiment trends across product categories

Methodology:
I will use the public SemEval ABSA datasets for pretraining/format and a scraped set of green-product reviews labelled for aspect sentiment (eco, price, quality). DistilBERT is fine-tuned for aspect-term sentiment classification; the baseline uses TF-IDF + linear SVM. Evaluation uses macro-F1 and per-aspect accuracy with a stratified split and 5-fold cross-validation on the labelled set.

Scope:
English reviews for three product categories and three predefined aspects. Multilingual reviews and sarcasm handling are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained ABSA model with macro-F1 against the baseline
2. An aspect-level sentiment trend report

Timeline:
14 weeks: data/labelling (4), modelling (5), analysis (3), write-up (2).

Title:
Learning-Based Cardinality Estimation for Logistics Query Optimization

Problem Statement:
Warehouse and shipment databases run analytical queries whose plans depend on the optimizer's cardinality estimates, which are often wrong for correlated columns (e.g. route and carrier), producing slow plans. Traditional histogram estimates ignore column correlation, hurting logistics dashboards that aggregate large shipment tables.

Objectives:
1. Build a learned cardinality estimator for multi-predicate queries on shipment data
2. Compare it against PostgreSQL's default estimates on estimation error and query latency
3. Measure where learned estimates change the chosen plan

Methodology:
On a logistics schema populated from a TPC-H-style/shipment dataset, I will generate a workload of multi-predicate queries with true cardinalities. A small neural estimator (MLP over featurized predicates) is trained to predict row counts, evaluated with q-error percentiles. Selected estimates are injected to compare resulting plan latency against the default optimizer over repeated runs.

Scope:
Read-only analytical queries on a fixed star schema with up to four predicates. Query rewriting, joins beyond the modelled set, and write workloads are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained estimator with q-error vs the PostgreSQL baseline
2. A latency comparison on a benchmark query set

Timeline:
Four phases over one semester with a tuning buffer.

Title:
A Face-Recognition Attendance System for Government Office Staff

Problem Statement:
Manual sign-in sheets and card swipes at government offices are easy to abuse through buddy-punching and are slow during shift changes. A face-recognition attendance system can reduce proxy attendance, but it must handle lighting variation and resist simple photo spoofing while protecting staff privacy.

Objectives:
1. Build an attendance system that identifies enrolled staff from a camera feed
2. Add a basic liveness check to reject printed-photo spoofing
3. Evaluate recognition accuracy and spoof-rejection rate

Methodology:
Faces are detected with MTCNN and embedded with FaceNet/ArcFace; identity is matched by cosine similarity to enrolled embeddings with a tuned threshold. A blink/eye-movement liveness check rejects static photos. I will evaluate verification accuracy, false-accept/false-reject rates on a small enrolled set plus LFW for tuning, and spoof rejection on printed-photo attempts. Logs write to a Spring Boot + MySQL backend.

Scope:
Indoor office lighting with up to ~30 enrolled staff and a single camera. Mask-wearing recognition and large-scale deployment are out of scope; embeddings are stored, not raw images.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working attendance system with a recognition dashboard
2. Accuracy, FAR/FRR, and spoof-rejection results

Timeline:
14 weeks across enrolment, modelling, liveness, and evaluation.

Title:
A Pipeline for Robust OCR and Field Extraction from Scanned Academic Transcripts

Problem Statement:
University admissions offices manually key data from scanned transcripts that vary in layout, font, and scan quality, which is slow and error-prone. General OCR transcribes text but does not reliably map it to structured fields (course code, grade, credit) across heterogeneous templates, and degraded scans further reduce accuracy. A pipeline combining quality-aware OCR with layout-driven field extraction, evaluated against a manual baseline, is the gap this project addresses.

Objectives:
1. Build an OCR-and-extraction pipeline that outputs structured (course, grade, credit) records from scanned transcripts with >=90% field-level F1 on the test set
2. Compare Tesseract against a deep recognizer (PaddleOCR/TrOCR) and quantify the gain from image preprocessing
3. Evaluate end-to-end extraction accuracy and time saved versus manual entry

Methodology:
Using a labelled corpus of ~400 transcript pages (public document datasets plus synthetically generated transcripts with ground-truth fields), images pass through deskew, denoise, and adaptive thresholding. Two OCR backends (Tesseract; PaddleOCR/TrOCR) are compared on CER/WER. Field extraction uses layout analysis (table/line detection) plus regex and a lightweight token classifier to assign values to fields. Evaluation uses field-level precision/recall/F1 with 5-fold cross-validation, an ablation on preprocessing, and a timing study versus manual entry. Risks (poor scans, template drift) are mitigated with augmentation and a confidence-flag review queue.

Scope:
English transcripts from a fixed set of three institutional templates, focused on the course/grade/credit table. Handwritten annotations, non-Latin scripts, and full document-management integration are explicitly excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A reproducible OCR-extraction pipeline reporting field-level F1 and CER/WER per backend
2. An ablation and time-saving analysis with a confidence-based human-review fallback

Timeline:
14 weeks: dataset+labelling (3), preprocessing+OCR (4), extraction (3), evaluation+ablation (2), write-up (2).

Title:
Edge Analytics for Footfall-Driven Shelf Restocking Using Wireless Sensors in Retail

Problem Statement:
Retailers restock shelves on fixed schedules rather than actual demand, causing stockouts on busy aisles and waste on slow ones. Wireless sensors (PIR motion, weight, and BLE counters) can reveal aisle footfall and shelf depletion, but raw streams are noisy and bandwidth-limited, and naive cloud upload is costly. The gap is a robust on-edge analytics pipeline that turns noisy multi-sensor streams into reliable restock alerts, evaluated against a fixed-schedule baseline.

Objectives:
1. Build an edge pipeline that fuses PIR, weight, and BLE-counter streams into per-aisle footfall and shelf-depletion estimates
2. Compare a threshold rule, an LSTM, and a lightweight gradient-boosted model for predicting restock-needed events, reporting precision/recall/F1 and latency
3. Quantify reduction in stockout minutes and data transmitted versus a fixed-schedule baseline

Methodology:
A sensor testbed (or the public Mall/retail footfall datasets plus a simulated weight-depletion model) provides labelled restock events. Signals are denoised (moving median, Kalman smoothing) and windowed into features. Three models are trained with a time-based split to avoid leakage: a tuned threshold, an LSTM, and LightGBM. Evaluation uses event-level precision/recall/F1, alert lead time, and on-device inference latency/memory on a Raspberry-Pi-class device. A discrete-event simulation compares stockout minutes and bytes transmitted against fixed-schedule restocking. Sensor dropout and drift are handled with imputation and periodic recalibration; this risk is tested by ablating sensors.

Scope:
One store layout with three sensor modalities across up to eight monitored aisles, indoor conditions. Camera-based vision counting, multi-store federation, and full ERP integration are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working edge pipeline with a restock-alert dashboard and per-model precision/recall/F1 and latency
2. A simulation report on stockout-minute and bandwidth reduction versus the baseline, with a sensor-dropout ablation

Timeline:
15 weeks: testbed+data (3), preprocessing (2), modelling (4), edge deployment (2), evaluation+simulation (2), write-up (2).

Title:
Crop Classification using Machine Learning

Problem Statement:
Farmers have many crops and it is hard to know which is which. Machine learning can help with this and make farming better for everyone.

Objectives:
1. To classify crops.
2. To use machine learning.
3. To help farmers.

Methodology:
I will use Python and some machine learning to classify the crops. I will do some research and testing.

Scope:
This project is for all farmers everywhere and all kinds of crops.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A system that classifies crops.
2. Happy farmers.

Title:
Deep Learning for Traffic

Problem Statement:
There are too many cars on the road and traffic is a big problem. Deep learning and computer vision are very powerful and can solve this.

Objectives:
1. To detect cars.
2. To use deep learning.
3. To reduce traffic.

Methodology:
I will use a neural network and computer vision to look at the cars. Then I will train it and see the results.

Scope:
The system will work for every city and all roads in the world.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A traffic detection system.
2. Less traffic jams.

Title:
NLP for the Environment

Problem Statement:
People talk a lot about sustainability online but nobody reads all of it. NLP is a smart technology that can understand text and help save the planet.

Objectives:
1. To analyze text.
2. To use NLP.
3. To help sustainability.

Methodology:
I will collect some text from the internet and use NLP techniques to understand it. Then I will show the results in a nice way.

Scope:
This covers all sustainability topics and any language people use.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A text analysis tool.
2. A greener world.

Title:
A Recommender System for Freight Delivery Routes

Problem Statement:
Logistics companies pick delivery routes manually and this wastes fuel and time. A recommender system could suggest better routes for drivers based on past deliveries, but small firms rarely have such tools.

Objectives:
1. To build a recommender system that suggests delivery routes.
2. To use past delivery data to make recommendations.
3. To evaluate if the recommendations save time.

Methodology:
The project will use collaborative filtering on a dataset of past deliveries. The system will be built in Python and tested by comparing suggested routes to actual routes taken. Some accuracy will be measured.

Scope:
The system focuses on road freight in one region and does not handle air or sea freight. It is a prototype for demonstration.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working route recommender prototype.
2. A report showing whether routes improved.

Timeline:
The project will take two semesters with development in the first and testing in the second.

Title:
Speech Recognition for Government Service Hotlines

Problem Statement:
Citizens calling government hotlines often wait long and repeat themselves to staff. A speech recognition system could transcribe and route calls automatically, but many e-government services still rely on manual operators.

Objectives:
1. To build a speech recognition module that transcribes citizen queries.
2. To classify queries into service categories.
3. To test the accuracy of transcription.

Methodology:
The project will use an existing speech-to-text library to convert audio to text, then apply keyword matching to route queries. It will be tested on a small set of recorded sample calls and word error rate will be checked.

Scope:
The prototype handles English queries for a few common services only and is not deployed to real call centres.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A speech recognition prototype that transcribes and routes queries.
2. An evaluation of transcription accuracy.

Timeline:
Two semesters: first for building, second for testing and writing up.

Title:
Network Intrusion Detection for Campus Networks

Problem Statement:
University networks face frequent attacks but small IT teams cannot watch all traffic. An intrusion detection system using machine learning could flag suspicious activity, yet many campuses still rely on basic firewalls only.

Objectives:
1. To build a machine learning model that detects network intrusions.
2. To train it on a public intrusion dataset.
3. To measure detection accuracy and false alarms.

Methodology:
The project will use the NSL-KDD dataset and train a decision tree and a random forest classifier in Python. Performance will be compared using accuracy and false positive rate. The better model will be chosen.

Scope:
The work is offline analysis on a public dataset and does not include real-time deployment on a live campus network.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained intrusion detection model.
2. A comparison of two classifiers with accuracy results.

Timeline:
The project runs over two semesters, with model building first and evaluation later.

Title:
Web Application Security Scanner for Online Stores

Problem Statement:
Small retail websites are often vulnerable to common attacks like SQL injection and cross-site scripting because owners lack security knowledge. A simple scanner could check for these flaws, but existing tools are too technical for small shop owners.

Objectives:
1. To build a scanner that checks retail web apps for common vulnerabilities.
2. To produce a readable report of findings.
3. To test it on sample vulnerable applications.

Methodology:
The scanner will send test inputs to web forms and check responses for SQL injection and XSS patterns. It will be built in Python and tested against intentionally vulnerable apps like DVWA. Detected issues will be listed.

Scope:
The tool checks for two vulnerability types only and is meant for small static online stores, not large platforms.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A vulnerability scanner prototype.
2. A sample security report.

Timeline:
Development in semester one, testing and documentation in semester two.

Title:
A Static Malware Analysis Tool for Smart City IoT Gateways

Problem Statement:
Smart city deployments connect many IoT gateways that can be infected by malware, but city operators often lack tools to inspect suspicious files before they spread. Manual analysis is slow and requires expertise that municipal teams rarely have.

Objectives:
1. To build a static analysis tool that extracts features from suspicious binaries.
2. To classify samples as benign or malicious using a machine learning model.
3. To evaluate accuracy against a labelled malware dataset.

Methodology:
The tool extracts static features such as imported API calls, byte n-grams, and header fields from PE files without executing them. A random forest classifier is trained on a labelled dataset combining benign Windows binaries and malware samples. Evaluation uses accuracy, precision, and recall with an 80/20 train-test split.

Scope:
The project covers static analysis of Windows PE files relevant to gateway management software. Dynamic sandbox analysis and live network deployment are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A static malware classification tool with a command-line interface.
2. An evaluation report with accuracy, precision, and recall.

Timeline:
Semester one: feature extraction and dataset preparation. Semester two: model training, evaluation, and reporting.

Title:
A Responsive Web Platform for Local Tourism Discovery

Problem Statement:
Tourists visiting smaller towns struggle to find local attractions, events, and small businesses because information is scattered across social pages and outdated brochures. A single responsive platform could centralise this, but most existing tourism sites focus only on major cities.

Objectives:
1. To design a responsive web platform listing local attractions and events.
2. To let businesses submit and manage their own listings.
3. To evaluate usability with a sample of users.

Methodology:
The platform is built with React on the front end and a Node.js and PostgreSQL back end. Listings support search and category filters. A small user study with around ten participants will collect System Usability Scale scores after completing typical tasks such as finding an attraction.

Scope:
The project targets one region's attractions and includes listing, search, and submission features. Online booking and payment processing are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A deployed responsive tourism platform prototype.
2. A usability evaluation summarising SUS scores and feedback.

Timeline:
Semester one: design and core development. Semester two: business submission feature, user testing, and write-up.

Title:
A Progressive Web App for Community Social Updates

Problem Statement:
Members of neighbourhood communities miss local updates because notices are spread across many social media groups with no reliable offline access. A progressive web app could deliver updates with push notifications and offline support, which most lightweight social tools lack.

Objectives:
1. To build a progressive web app for posting and viewing community updates.
2. To support offline reading and push notifications.
3. To evaluate performance and user satisfaction.

Methodology:
The app is built with React and a service worker for caching and offline access. Push notifications use the Web Push API. A Firebase back end stores posts. Lighthouse PWA audits measure installability and performance, and a small survey gathers user feedback.

Scope:
The app covers text and image posts, offline viewing, and notifications for a single community. Private messaging and video uploads are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An installable PWA with offline and notification support.
2. Lighthouse audit results and a user feedback summary.

Timeline:
Semester one: core PWA and offline support. Semester two: notifications, testing, and documentation.

Title:
A Cross-Platform Mobile App for Medication Reminders

Problem Statement:
Patients managing chronic conditions often forget to take medication on time, which affects treatment outcomes. A cross-platform reminder app could help, but many existing apps support only one platform or lack adherence tracking for caregivers.

Objectives:
1. To build a cross-platform app that schedules medication reminders.
2. To track adherence and let caregivers view it.
3. To evaluate usability and reminder reliability.

Methodology:
The app is built with Flutter to run on both Android and iOS from one codebase. Local notifications handle reminders and a Firebase back end stores schedules and adherence logs. Reminder reliability is tested across devices, and usability is assessed with a small user group using a questionnaire.

Scope:
The app covers scheduling, reminders, and adherence logging. Integration with hospital records and clinical advice features are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working cross-platform medication reminder app.
2. A usability and reliability evaluation report.

Timeline:
Semester one: app development and notifications. Semester two: caregiver view, testing, and reporting.

Title:
An Android Native App for Personal Budget Tracking

Problem Statement:
Young adults often struggle to track spending and stay within a budget because they record expenses inconsistently. A native Android app with quick entry and category insights could help, but many free apps overwhelm users with features or require subscriptions.

Objectives:
1. To build a native Android app for recording and categorising expenses.
2. To show spending summaries and budget alerts.
3. To evaluate usability with target users.

Methodology:
The app is built in Kotlin using Android Jetpack components and a local Room database for offline storage. Expenses are categorised and visualised with charts using MPAndroidChart. Budget alerts trigger when category spending nears a limit. A small usability test with students collects feedback and task completion times.

Scope:
The app handles manual expense entry, categories, summaries, and alerts on Android only. Bank account linking and cloud sync are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A functional native Android budgeting app.
2. A usability evaluation report.

Timeline:
Semester one: core entry and storage. Semester two: charts, alerts, testing, and write-up.

Title:
An IoT Sensor Network for Factory Environment Monitoring

Problem Statement:
Small manufacturing workshops rarely monitor temperature, humidity, and air quality, yet poor conditions affect product quality and worker comfort. An affordable IoT sensor network could provide continuous monitoring, which commercial industrial systems make too costly for small workshops.

Objectives:
1. To build an IoT sensor network that monitors workshop environmental conditions.
2. To collect and display readings on a dashboard.
3. To evaluate data accuracy and alert behaviour.

Methodology:
ESP32 microcontrollers with DHT22 and MQ-135 sensors send readings over MQTT to a Raspberry Pi broker. Data is stored in InfluxDB and shown on a Grafana dashboard with threshold alerts. Sensor readings are validated against a reference meter, and alert timing is tested.

Scope:
The project covers temperature, humidity, and air quality sensing with a dashboard and alerts for one workshop area. Machine vibration and predictive maintenance are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working IoT environmental monitoring prototype with dashboard.
2. An accuracy and alert evaluation report.

Timeline:
Semester one: hardware and data pipeline. Semester two: dashboard, alerts, validation, and reporting.

Title:
A Smart Home Automation System with Emergency Alerting for Public Safety

Problem Statement:
Elderly residents living alone are vulnerable to falls, fires, and gas leaks, but generic smart home kits focus on convenience rather than safety and rarely notify emergency contacts automatically. There is a gap for an affordable system that detects hazards and escalates alerts to neighbours or responders.

Objectives:
1. To build a smart home system that detects falls, smoke, and gas hazards.
2. To automatically alert designated contacts with location and event details.
3. To evaluate detection reliability and alert latency.

Methodology:
The system uses ESP32 nodes with PIR, smoke, and MQ-2 gas sensors, plus an accelerometer-based wearable for fall detection using a threshold-and-rule approach. Events publish over MQTT to a Raspberry Pi hub running Node-RED, which triggers SMS and app notifications. Detection reliability is measured through controlled trials with false positive and false negative counts, and alert latency is timed end to end.

Scope:
The project covers fall, smoke, and gas detection with automated alerting for a single household setup. Camera-based monitoring and direct integration with official emergency dispatch systems are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working hazard-detection and alerting prototype.
2. An evaluation of detection accuracy and alert latency.

Timeline:
Semester one: sensor nodes and hub. Semester two: alert logic, controlled trials, and reporting.

Title:
Edge Computing for Real-Time Solar Energy Forecasting

Problem Statement:
Small solar installations need short-term generation forecasts to manage battery use, but cloud-based forecasting adds latency and depends on stable connectivity that rural sites often lack. Running forecasts on edge devices could reduce dependence on the cloud, yet lightweight models suitable for constrained hardware are underexplored for this use.

Objectives:
1. To develop a lightweight forecasting model for short-term solar output.
2. To deploy and run inference on an edge device.
3. To compare edge accuracy and latency against a cloud baseline.

Methodology:
A compact LSTM and a gradient-boosting model are trained on historical irradiance and power data, then quantised with TensorFlow Lite for deployment on a Raspberry Pi. Forecast accuracy is measured with RMSE and MAE against held-out data, and end-to-end inference latency is compared with a cloud-hosted version of the same model. Resource use on the edge device is logged.

Scope:
The work targets one to four hour ahead forecasting for a single small installation using local sensor and weather data. Grid-scale forecasting and hardware accelerators are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A deployed edge forecasting prototype with logged latency and accuracy.
2. A comparison report of edge versus cloud performance.

Timeline:
Semester one: data preparation and model training. Semester two: edge deployment, benchmarking, and analysis.

Title:
A Cloud-Native Microservices Platform for Small Business Order Management

Problem Statement:
Small businesses outgrowing spreadsheets need order management software that can scale during busy periods, but monolithic off-the-shelf systems are hard to extend and costly to scale selectively. A microservices approach could let owners scale only the busy parts, yet such architectures are rarely demonstrated at small-business scale with clear trade-off analysis.

Objectives:
1. To design a microservices platform for orders, inventory, and notifications.
2. To deploy it on Kubernetes with independent scaling.
3. To evaluate scalability and resilience under load.

Methodology:
Services are built as containerised Spring Boot applications communicating via REST and a message queue, with separate databases per service. They are orchestrated on a Kubernetes cluster with horizontal pod autoscaling. Load testing with k6 measures throughput and latency as demand rises, and a fault-injection test verifies that one service failing does not take down the others.

Scope:
The project covers order, inventory, and notification services with autoscaling and a basic web client. Payment gateway integration and multi-region deployment are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A deployed microservices order-management prototype.
2. A scalability and resilience evaluation report.

Timeline:
Semester one: service design and containerisation. Semester two: Kubernetes deployment, load and fault testing.

Title:
A DevOps CI/CD Pipeline for Agricultural IoT Firmware Delivery

Problem Statement:
Agricultural IoT deployments run firmware on many field devices, but updates are often pushed manually, leading to inconsistent versions and slow security patching. A CI/CD pipeline tailored to firmware could automate building, testing, and staged rollout, yet most DevOps practice targets web services rather than constrained agricultural hardware.

Objectives:
1. To build a CI/CD pipeline that builds and tests IoT firmware automatically.
2. To support staged over-the-air rollout with rollback.
3. To evaluate deployment time and failure recovery.

Methodology:
The pipeline uses GitHub Actions to compile firmware, run unit tests on the build, and validate it on an emulator before publishing artifacts. A staged rollout service pushes updates over the air to a small fleet of ESP32 devices, monitors health checks, and rolls back on failure. Metrics include build-to-deploy time, rollout success rate, and recovery time after an induced bad update.

Scope:
The project covers automated build, test, staged rollout, and rollback for one firmware target on a small test fleet. Production-scale device fleets and hardware-in-the-loop farms are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working firmware CI/CD pipeline with staged rollout and rollback.
2. An evaluation of deployment time and recovery metrics.

Timeline:
Semester one: build and test automation. Semester two: rollout, rollback, and evaluation.

Title:
A Big Data Analytics Pipeline for Urban Public Transport Demand

Problem Statement:
City transit agencies collect large volumes of smart-card and GPS data but lack accessible pipelines to turn it into demand insights for route planning. Existing analyses are often ad hoc and do not scale as data grows, leaving smaller agencies without timely demand patterns.

Objectives:
1. To build a scalable pipeline that ingests and processes transit ridership data.
2. To derive demand patterns by route, time, and stop.
3. To evaluate pipeline scalability and the usefulness of the insights.

Methodology:
The pipeline ingests batch smart-card and GPS data into a data lake, processes it with Apache Spark for cleaning and aggregation, and stores results for querying. Demand patterns are computed by route and time window and visualised in a dashboard. Scalability is measured by processing time as the dataset size grows, and insight usefulness is checked against known peak periods.

Scope:
The project uses a publicly available or synthetic transit dataset for one city and produces batch demand analytics. Real-time streaming ingestion and predictive routing are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working batch analytics pipeline with a demand dashboard.
2. A scalability evaluation and validated demand insights.

Timeline:
Semester one: ingestion and processing. Semester two: aggregation, dashboard, and scalability testing.

Title:
A Business Intelligence Dashboard for Campus Sustainability Performance Benchmarking

Problem Statement:
University sustainability offices report energy, water, and waste figures in disconnected spreadsheets, making it hard to benchmark buildings, spot anomalies, or track progress against targets. Commercial BI suites are costly and assume clean integrated data, while existing campus dashboards rarely combine multiple resource streams with anomaly flagging and target tracking in one tool.

Objectives:
1. To design a star-schema data model integrating energy, water, and waste data from at least three source formats.
2. To build an interactive BI dashboard with building-level benchmarking, anomaly flags, and progress against targets.
3. To validate insight accuracy against ground-truth records and assess analyst usability with a SUS study.

Methodology:
An ETL process in Python ingests heterogeneous CSV and meter exports into a star schema in PostgreSQL, with data-quality checks logged. The dashboard is built in a BI tool exposing benchmarking, trend, and target views. Anomalies are flagged using a seasonal-decomposition residual threshold compared against a simple z-score baseline, evaluated by precision and recall on a labelled set of known anomalies. Eight sustainability staff complete tasks for a System Usability Scale score and think-aloud feedback.

Scope:
The dashboard covers three resource streams for one campus with benchmarking, anomaly flagging, and target tracking. Real-time meter streaming, automated control actions, and cross-institution data sharing are explicitly excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A validated BI dashboard with documented data model and anomaly detection compared to a baseline.

Title:
Probabilistic Time-Series Forecasting of Warehouse Outbound Volume for Logistics Staffing

Problem Statement:
Third-party logistics warehouses staff shifts using rough averages, leading to overstaffing on quiet days and missed service levels on peaks, because most forecasts give a single point estimate that ignores demand uncertainty. There is a need for probabilistic daily outbound-volume forecasts that quantify uncertainty so planners can set staffing against a service-level target, an angle underexplored in small-warehouse settings.

Objectives:
1. To build daily outbound-volume forecasting models that output prediction intervals, not just point forecasts.
2. To benchmark these against seasonal-naive and SARIMA baselines using rolling-origin cross-validation.
3. To translate forecasts into staffing recommendations and quantify cost versus service-level trade-offs.

Methodology:
Two years of daily outbound records with calendar and promotion features are modelled with SARIMA, Prophet, and a quantile-loss LightGBM producing P10/P50/P90 intervals. Models are evaluated with rolling-origin cross-validation reporting MASE for point accuracy and pinball loss and interval coverage for probabilistic quality, against seasonal-naive and SARIMA baselines. Forecast intervals feed a newsvendor-style staffing rule, and resulting cost and service level are compared with the current average-based policy on held-out weeks.

Scope:
The project forecasts daily outbound volume for one warehouse at the facility level over a one-to-fourteen-day horizon and converts forecasts into staffing numbers. SKU-level forecasting, inbound flows, and live integration with the warehouse system are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. Validated probabilistic forecasting models with documented MASE, pinball loss, and interval coverage versus baselines.
2. A staffing recommendation method with quantified cost and service-level improvement over the current policy.

Timeline:
Weeks 1-3 data cleaning and feature engineering; weeks 4-8 baseline and model development; weeks 9-12 rolling-origin evaluation; weeks 13-16 staffing rule and trade-off analysis; weeks 17-20 validation and write-up.

Title:
A Machine Learning System for Detecting Fraudulent Retail Returns

Problem Statement:
Retailers lose money to return fraud, where customers exploit return policies through wardrobing or receipt manipulation. Most small retailers rely on staff judgement, which is inconsistent and misses patterns across transactions.

Methodology:
Using a public retail transactions dataset (with synthetic fraud labels injected to balance classes), features such as return frequency, time-since-purchase, and value are engineered. A Random Forest and Logistic Regression are trained with 5-fold cross-validation and compared on precision, recall, and F1 against a simple threshold rule.

Scope:
Offline batch detection on historical transactions. Real-time deployment and integration with a live POS are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained fraud-detection model with reported precision/recall
2. A feature-importance analysis explaining the flags

Two semesters: data and modelling (weeks 1-16), evaluation and reporting (weeks 17-26).

Title:
A Recommendation Engine for a Smart-City Local Services Marketplace

Problem Statement:
Smart-city apps list many local services and shops, but residents face choice overload and rarely discover relevant nearby options. Generic best-seller lists ignore a user's location and past interactions.

Objectives:
1. Build a hybrid recommender combining collaborative filtering and location proximity
2. Compare it against a popularity baseline
3. Measure recommendation quality offline

Methodology:
A public e-commerce interaction dataset is augmented with synthetic location data. Item-based collaborative filtering (cosine similarity) is combined with a distance-decay weighting. The hybrid is evaluated offline with precision@k and recall@k via a leave-one-out split, against a most-popular baseline.

Scope:
Offline evaluation on a single dataset with simulated locations. A production mobile front end and real-time updates are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working hybrid recommendation prototype
2. An evaluation table comparing it with the baseline

Timeline:
Two semesters: literature and build (weeks 1-15), evaluation and write-up (weeks 16-26).

Title:
A Conversational Agent for Answering Tourist Questions About a City

Problem Statement:
Tourists often ask the same questions about attractions, transport, and opening hours, overwhelming information desks. Static FAQ pages are hard to search, and a chatbot could give quicker, natural-language answers.

Objectives:
1. Build a retrieval-based chatbot answering common tourism questions
2. Ground answers in a curated knowledge base of local attractions
3. Evaluate answer accuracy on a held-out question set

Methodology:
A knowledge base of attraction descriptions and FAQs is embedded with Sentence-BERT and stored in a FAISS index. User questions are matched by semantic similarity, and the top passage is returned. Accuracy is measured as top-1 retrieval correctness on 100 labelled questions, with a TF-IDF retriever as baseline.

Scope:
Retrieval-based answering for one city in English. Booking, payments, and multilingual support are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working tourism chatbot prototype
2. A retrieval-accuracy comparison against TF-IDF

Title:
A Knowledge-Graph Search Tool for Exploring Social-Media Topics

Problem Statement:
Researchers studying social-media discussions struggle to see how topics, accounts, and hashtags connect. Keyword search returns flat lists and hides the relationships between entities in a conversation.

Objectives:
1. Build a knowledge graph linking posts, hashtags, and users from a dataset
2. Provide a search interface that returns connected entities
3. Evaluate retrieval relevance against keyword search

Methodology:
A public Twitter-style dataset is parsed to extract entities and relations into a Neo4j graph. A web interface lets users query a term and view related hashtags and accounts as a subgraph. Relevance is judged by three annotators on a sample of queries, compared with a plain keyword baseline.

Scope:
One static dataset; entity extraction limited to users, hashtags, and post mentions. Real-time streaming and sentiment are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working knowledge-graph search prototype
2. A relevance comparison with keyword search

Two semesters: graph build (weeks 1-15), interface and evaluation (weeks 16-26).

Title:
Automated Segmentation of Skin Lesions in Dermoscopic Images Using U-Net

Problem Statement:
Accurate delineation of skin-lesion boundaries supports melanoma diagnosis, but manual segmentation is slow and varies between clinicians. While U-Net variants exist, many struggle on lesions with low contrast or hair artefacts, limiting reliability on routine images.

Objectives:
1. Train a U-Net to segment lesions on the ISIC 2018 dataset
2. Test whether attention gates improve boundary accuracy on low-contrast lesions
3. Benchmark against a baseline U-Net using Dice and IoU

Methodology:
Images from ISIC 2018 are pre-processed with hair-removal filtering and resized to 256x256. A baseline U-Net and an attention U-Net are trained with data augmentation (flips, rotation, colour jitter), Dice loss, and 5-fold cross-validation. Performance is reported as mean Dice and IoU with confidence intervals, plus qualitative review of the hardest cases.

Scope:
2D dermoscopic image segmentation only. 3D imaging, real-time clinical deployment, and final diagnosis classification are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained attention U-Net with Dice/IoU results versus the baseline
2. An error analysis on low-contrast and hair-occluded cases

Timeline:
Two semesters: data and baseline (weeks 1-12), attention model and evaluation (weeks 13-26).

Title:
Real-Time Detection of Filled Forms and Signature Fields in Financial Documents

Problem Statement:
Banks process many scanned financial forms, and locating signature, date, and amount fields manually is slow. Generic OCR finds text but not the layout regions that compliance checks depend on, so an object detector for these fields could speed verification.

Objectives:
1. Train a detector to locate signature, date, and amount fields on scanned forms
2. Compare a one-stage and two-stage detector on accuracy and speed
3. Assess robustness to scan noise and skew

Methodology:
A labelled set of 1,500 scanned form images (annotated in COCO format) is split 70/15/15. YOLOv8 (one-stage) and Faster R-CNN (two-stage) are trained with augmentation for rotation and Gaussian noise. Models are compared on mAP@0.5 and inference latency, with an ablation on augmentation to test robustness to skew.

Scope:
Detection of three field types on English-language forms. Reading field contents and downstream fraud decisions are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. Two trained detectors with mAP and latency comparison
2. A robustness analysis under noise and skew

Timeline:
Two semesters: annotation and YOLO (weeks 1-13), Faster R-CNN and evaluation (weeks 14-26).

Title:
Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis of Manufacturing Equipment Maintenance Reports

Problem Statement:
Maintenance technicians log free-text notes about machine faults, but managers cannot easily tell which components attract the most negative observations. Document-level sentiment hides the specific parts at fault, so an aspect-based approach is needed.

Objectives:
1. Build an aspect-based sentiment classifier for maintenance notes
2. Extract component-level sentiment (e.g. bearing, motor, valve)
3. Compare a fine-tuned transformer with a lexicon baseline

Methodology:
A corpus of maintenance notes is labelled for aspect terms and sentiment polarity. A BERT-base model is fine-tuned for joint aspect extraction and polarity classification, evaluated with macro-F1 on a held-out test set and 5-fold cross-validation. A VADER lexicon baseline provides comparison, and error cases are reviewed by component type.

Scope:
English maintenance notes for one equipment category. Multilingual notes and predictive failure modelling are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A fine-tuned aspect-based sentiment model with macro-F1 results
2. A component-level sentiment summary compared to the lexicon baseline

Timeline:
Two semesters: labelling and baseline (weeks 1-13), fine-tuning and analysis (weeks 14-26).

Title:
Learned Cost Estimation for Query Optimization in an Incident-Reporting Database

Problem Statement:
A public-safety incident database serves analytical queries whose plans the optimizer sometimes mis-costs, causing slow responses during emergencies. Traditional cardinality estimates are inaccurate on skewed incident data, hurting plan choice.

Objectives:
1. Build a learned cardinality estimator for incident-query predicates
2. Integrate its estimates into plan selection for a set of benchmark queries
3. Compare query latency against the default optimizer

Methodology:
A synthetic incident dataset is generated in PostgreSQL with realistic skew. A gradient-boosted model is trained on query-feature/true-cardinality pairs collected from logged executions. Estimated cardinalities feed plan hints, and end-to-end latency is measured over a 40-query benchmark with 10 repetitions, against the stock optimizer, reporting median and p95 latency.

Scope:
Single-node read-only analytical queries with up to three-table joins. Write workloads and distributed execution are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A learned estimator and an integrated plan-selection prototype
2. A latency comparison versus the default optimizer

Timeline:
Two semesters: data and estimator (weeks 1-13), integration and benchmarking (weeks 14-26).

Title:
A Facial-Recognition Attendance System for Energy-Plant Shift Workers

Problem Statement:
Energy plants need reliable attendance logging at shift gates, but badge cards are shared or lost and manual sign-in is slow. A facial-recognition system could automate this, yet lighting variation at outdoor gates challenges accuracy.

Objectives:
1. Build a face-recognition attendance pipeline for enrolled workers
2. Test accuracy under varied lighting at gate-like conditions
3. Compare two embedding models on accuracy and speed

Methodology:
Faces are detected with MTCNN and embedded with FaceNet and ArcFace, then matched by cosine similarity to an enrolment gallery. A test set of 30 volunteers captured under three lighting conditions is used; accuracy, false-accept and false-reject rates are reported, and the two embedding models are compared on accuracy and per-frame latency. A liveness check via blink detection mitigates photo spoofing.

Scope:
Recognition of pre-enrolled workers at one gate. Large-scale identification across plants and full anti-spoofing are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working attendance prototype with accuracy under varied lighting
2. A comparison of FaceNet and ArcFace embeddings

Timeline:
Two semesters: pipeline and enrolment (weeks 1-12), evaluation (weeks 13-26).

Title:
A Robust OCR Pipeline for Extracting Structured Data from Small-Business Receipts and Invoices

Problem Statement:
Small businesses spend hours manually keying receipt and invoice data into bookkeeping software. Off-the-shelf OCR transcribes text but does not reliably extract structured fields (vendor, date, line items, total) from the varied, often low-quality scans and phone photos that small businesses produce, and existing commercial APIs are costly and raise data-privacy concerns.

Objectives:
1. Build an end-to-end pipeline that detects, recognises, and extracts six structured fields from receipts/invoices, achieving field-level F1 above 0.85 on a held-out test set
2. Compare a layout-aware transformer (LayoutLMv3) against a CRNN+rule-based extractor under identical conditions
3. Quantify robustness to blur, skew, and low resolution through controlled degradation experiments

Methodology:
The public SROIE and CORD datasets (plus 200 self-collected local receipts) are annotated for six fields. Text regions are detected with DBNet and recognised with a CRNN; a rule/regex extractor and a fine-tuned LayoutLMv3 model are each evaluated for field extraction. Training uses an 80/10/10 split with 5-fold cross-validation; metrics are field-level precision/recall/F1 and full-document accuracy. A controlled study degrades images (Gaussian blur, rotation, downscaling) to measure F1 degradation. Risks (limited local data, class imbalance for rare fields) are mitigated with augmentation and active-learning sampling.

Scope:
English and Malay printed receipts/invoices with six target fields. Handwritten receipts, multi-page invoices, and live accounting-software integration are explicitly excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A reproducible OCR-to-structured-data pipeline with field-level F1 and full-document accuracy reported against both baselines
2. A robustness curve showing F1 versus image-degradation level, plus an open annotated local-receipt subset

Timeline:
Two semesters: data collection/annotation and baseline (weeks 1-10), LayoutLMv3 fine-tuning (weeks 11-18), robustness study and write-up (weeks 19-28).

Title:
Anomaly Detection and Irrigation Forecasting from Agricultural Wireless Sensor Network Data

Problem Statement:
Wireless sensor networks in farms stream soil-moisture, temperature, and humidity readings, but raw streams contain dropouts and faulty-sensor spikes, and farmers lack short-horizon guidance on when to irrigate. Naive threshold alerts misfire on noisy data, and most prior work studies anomaly detection and forecasting separately rather than as one usable pipeline.

Objectives:
1. Build a pipeline that flags sensor anomalies and forecasts soil moisture 6-12 hours ahead, with forecasting MAE at least 15% below a persistence baseline
2. Compare an LSTM forecaster against ARIMA and a persistence baseline under identical splits
3. Evaluate whether anomaly filtering before forecasting improves accuracy

Methodology:
A public agricultural WSN dataset is augmented with 60 days of self-logged readings from three low-cost soil sensors. Anomalies are detected with an Isolation Forest and validated against injected synthetic faults (precision/recall). Cleaned series feed an LSTM, ARIMA, and persistence model, evaluated with a rolling-origin (walk-forward) split on MAE and RMSE. An ablation compares forecasting with and without anomaly filtering. Hardware, connectivity, and data-loss risks are mitigated with redundant sensors and gap-imputation.

Scope:
Single-farm, three-sensor deployment forecasting soil moisture only. Multi-farm transfer learning, actuator control of irrigation valves, and energy-harvesting optimisation are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An anomaly-detection-plus-forecasting pipeline with MAE/RMSE reported against ARIMA and persistence baselines
2. An ablation quantifying the effect of anomaly filtering, plus the released self-logged sensor dataset

Timeline:
Two semesters: deployment and data logging (weeks 1-10), anomaly detection (weeks 11-16), forecasting and ablation (weeks 17-28).

Voice Commands for Energy Meter Reading

Title:
Intrusion Detection for Small Business Networks

Title:
Scanning Agriculture Web Portals for Common Vulnerabilities

Objectives:
1. Build a scanner that checks an agriculture portal for common web vulnerabilities.
2. Map findings to the OWASP Top 10 categories.
3. Generate a plain-language report for the operator.

Methodology:
I will write a Python scanner that probes for SQL injection, XSS, and missing security headers using crafted requests. I will test it against a deliberately vulnerable demo site such as DVWA. Findings are validated manually and summarised in a readable report.

Scope:
The scanner covers three vulnerability classes on a single test portal. It will not perform automated exploitation or business-logic testing.

Expected Outcomes:

2. A sample security report for a demo agriculture site.
