One semester divided into research, build, and testing.

Title:
Static and Dynamic Malware Analysis for Transport Fleet Systems

Problem Statement:
Transport companies run fleet management software on connected devices that are increasingly targeted by malware, yet smaller operators lack the expertise to triage suspicious binaries. Manual analysis is slow, and there is little tooling that combines lightweight static and behavioural signals into a single classification suited to a non-specialist operator.

Objectives:
1. Build a pipeline that extracts static features and runtime behaviour from sample executables.
2. Train a classifier to label samples as benign or malicious.
3. Evaluate the classifier against a held-out test set and report accuracy and false-negative rate.

Methodology:
Static features (imported APIs, byte n-grams, PE header fields) will be extracted with pefile, while dynamic features come from running samples in a Cuckoo sandbox to capture API call traces. A Random Forest and a gradient-boosted tree will be trained on a labelled subset of the EMBER dataset plus sandbox traces, then compared. Evaluation uses stratified cross-validation reporting accuracy, precision, recall.

Scope:
The work targets Windows PE samples relevant to fleet endpoints. Packed and kernel-level malware are excluded. The sandbox runs in an isolated VM only.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working static-plus-dynamic feature extraction pipeline.
2. A trained classifier with a comparative evaluation report.

Timeline:
14 weeks: setup and data (4), feature pipeline (4), modelling and evaluation (6).

Title:
A Responsive Web Platform for Tracking Campus Sustainability Pledges

Problem Statement:
University sustainability campaigns struggle to keep students engaged because pledges are made on paper and progress is never visible. There is no shared platform where students can log eco-actions, see aggregate impact, and stay motivated, so most pledges are forgotten within weeks.

Objectives:
1. Build a responsive web platform where students register and log sustainability actions.
2. Aggregate logged actions into a campus-wide impact dashboard.
3. Evaluate usability and engagement with a small group of student testers.

Methodology:
The platform will be built with React and a Node.js/Express backend backed by PostgreSQL. Users log actions from a predefined catalogue, each mapped to an estimated CO2 saving. A dashboard visualises totals using a charting library. Usability will be assessed with a System Usability Scale survey after a two-week pilot with around 15 students.

Scope:
The platform covers a fixed catalogue of individual eco-actions for one campus. It excludes payment, social-media integration, and verified measurement of actual emissions.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A deployed responsive web platform.
2. A usability report with SUS scores and engagement observations.

Timeline:
13 weeks across design, implementation, and a two-week pilot.

Title:
A Progressive Web App for Last-Mile Delivery Driver Coordination

Problem Statement:
Last-mile delivery drivers in small logistics firms often work with unreliable connectivity, so dispatch updates and proof-of-delivery captured on native apps are frequently lost or delayed. A progressive web app that works offline and syncs when reconnected could improve coordination without forcing app-store installs on every device.

Objectives:
1. Build a PWA that lets drivers view assigned stops and capture proof-of-delivery offline.
2. Implement background synchronisation so data uploads when connectivity returns.
3. Evaluate offline reliability and sync correctness under simulated network drops.

Methodology:
The PWA will use a service worker with the Workbox library for caching and IndexedDB for offline storage. Background Sync queues delivery confirmations. The backend is a REST API in Node.js. Testing simulates offline/online transitions using Chrome DevTools throttling, measuring data loss rate and sync latency across repeated trials.

Scope:
The app supports stop lists and photo proof-of-delivery for a single fictional courier. Route optimisation and live GPS tracking are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An installable offline-capable PWA prototype.
2. A test report on offline reliability and sync behaviour.

Timeline:
14 weeks: design (3), build (7), offline testing and reporting (4).

Title:
A Cross-Platform Mobile App for Local Council Service Requests

Problem Statement:
Residents reporting issues like potholes or broken streetlights to their local council often rely on phone calls or web forms that give no feedback on status. There is no convenient mobile channel that lets residents submit a geotagged report and track its progress, leading to duplicate complaints and frustration.

Objectives:
1. Build a cross-platform mobile app for residents to submit geotagged service requests with photos.
2. Provide status tracking and notifications for each request.
3. Evaluate the app's usability with a small group of residents.

Methodology:
The app will be built in Flutter so a single codebase targets Android and iOS, with a Firebase backend for authentication, storage, and push notifications. Requests are categorised and pinned on a map using a maps SDK. A two-week trial with around 12 users will gather feedback via a usability questionnaire and task-completion timing.

Scope:
The app covers report submission and status tracking for a defined set of issue categories in one council area. Backend dispatch to actual municipal systems is mocked, not integrated.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working cross-platform mobile prototype on Android and iOS.
2. A usability evaluation summarising feedback.

Timeline:
13 weeks across design, development, and a user trial.

Title:
An Android Native App for Spaced-Repetition Vocabulary Learning

Problem Statement:
Students learning a new language often forget vocabulary because they review words at the wrong intervals. Many existing apps are cloud-only and require constant connectivity, which is impractical in classrooms with poor Wi-Fi, and few are tuned to short course-specific word lists.

Objectives:
1. Build a native Android app that schedules vocabulary reviews using a spaced-repetition algorithm.
2. Store word lists and review history locally for full offline use.
3. Evaluate retention improvement through a short user study.

Methodology:
The app will be written in Kotlin using Android Jetpack components, with Room for local storage. Review scheduling implements the SM-2 spaced-repetition algorithm. A two-week study with around 15 students compares recall on words studied with the app against a paper flashcard control group, measured by a short post-test.

Scope:
The app handles text-based vocabulary for one course's word list, fully offline. Audio pronunciation and multi-device sync are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working offline Android vocabulary app.
2. A study report comparing retention against flashcards.

Timeline:
13 weeks: design (3), implementation (6), user study and write-up (4).

Title:
An IoT Sensor Network for In-Store Footfall and Shelf Monitoring

Problem Statement:
Small retail stores lack affordable ways to understand how customers move through aisles and which shelves draw attention, relying instead on intuition. A low-cost IoT sensor network could capture footfall and dwell time, but commercial retail analytics systems are expensive and closed.

Objectives:
1. Build an IoT sensor network that counts footfall and measures dwell time near shelves.
2. Aggregate sensor data into a backend for visualisation.
3. Evaluate counting accuracy against manual ground-truth counts.

Methodology:
Sensor nodes use ESP32 microcontrollers with PIR motion and ultrasonic distance sensors, publishing readings over MQTT to a Raspberry Pi broker. A Python service stores readings in a time-series database (InfluxDB) and a Grafana dashboard visualises footfall trends. Counting accuracy is validated by comparing sensor counts to manual tallies over several timed sessions.

Scope:
The deployment covers one mock store aisle with three sensor nodes. Individual customer identification and facial recognition are explicitly excluded for privacy.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working IoT footfall sensor network prototype.
2. An accuracy evaluation against manual counts.

Timeline:
14 weeks: hardware setup (4), data pipeline (4), evaluation (6).

Title:
An Energy-Aware Smart Home Automation Hub for Smart-City Demand Response

Problem Statement:
Smart-city demand-response programmes ask households to cut power during peak grid load, but most consumer smart-home hubs react only to manual rules and cannot respond automatically to dynamic grid signals. Households therefore miss savings and the grid loses a flexible load it could otherwise shed, partly because few open hubs integrate tariff signals with local device control.

Objectives:
1. Build a local smart-home hub that controls appliances based on simulated dynamic tariff and demand-response signals.
2. Implement a rule-plus-prediction policy that pre-cools or defers loads ahead of forecast peaks.
3. Evaluate cost and peak-load reduction against a fixed-schedule baseline.

Methodology:
The hub runs on a Raspberry Pi using Home Assistant with MQTT-connected smart plugs and a temperature sensor. A short-term load forecast (a simple LSTM trained on the UK-DALE dataset) feeds a scheduling policy that shifts deferrable loads. Demand-response events are replayed from a published tariff schedule. Evaluation compares total cost and peak demand of the policy against a naive always-on baseline over a simulated week, repeated across three scenarios.

Scope:
The system controls three deferrable appliance types in one simulated household. Real utility billing integration and multi-home coordination are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working automation hub with a forecasting-driven scheduling policy.
2. A quantified comparison of cost and peak reduction versus baseline.

Timeline:
15 weeks: hub setup (3), forecasting (4), policy and evaluation (8).

Title:
Edge-Based On-Device Landmark Recognition for Offline Tourism Guides

Problem Statement:
Tourists frequently explore areas with weak or costly mobile data, so cloud-based landmark recognition guides fail exactly when needed. Running recognition on the device avoids connectivity and privacy concerns, but naive on-device deep models are too large and slow for mid-range phones, and few tourism apps quantify the accuracy-versus-latency trade-off of edge deployment.

Objectives:
1. Build an on-device landmark recognition module that runs fully offline on a mid-range phone.
2. Apply model compression to meet a target inference latency.
3. Evaluate the accuracy-latency trade-off against an uncompressed baseline.

Methodology:
A MobileNetV3 classifier is fine-tuned on a curated set of 20 local landmarks (transfer learning from ImageNet weights) and converted to TensorFlow Lite with post-training quantisation. The compressed model is benchmarked on a real mid-range Android device for top-1 accuracy and per-image latency, compared against the full-precision model. Inputs include a held-out photo test set captured under varied lighting.

Scope:
Recognition covers a fixed catalogue of 20 landmarks in one city, image-only. Real-time AR overlays and audio narration are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An offline edge landmark-recognition app prototype.
2. A report on the accuracy-latency trade-off after quantisation.

Timeline:
15 weeks: dataset and training (5), compression and deployment (4), benchmarking (6).

Title:
A Cloud-Native Microservices Backend for a Social-Media Content Feed

Problem Statement:
Social-media platforms must serve personalised feeds under bursty load, but monolithic student projects rarely demonstrate how to decompose feed generation into independently scalable services. Without clear service boundaries and observability, performance bottlenecks under load are hard to locate, leaving a gap in understanding how microservices behave when feed traffic spikes.

Objectives:
1. Decompose a content-feed backend into independently deployable microservices.
2. Deploy the services on Kubernetes with horizontal autoscaling and observability.
3. Evaluate latency and throughput under load compared with a monolithic baseline.

Methodology:
Services (user, post, feed-assembly, notification) are built in Spring Boot, containerised with Docker, and orchestrated on a local Kubernetes cluster (Minikube). Inter-service calls use REST with a message queue (RabbitMQ) for fan-out. Prometheus and Grafana provide metrics. Load tests with k6 drive increasing request rates while measuring p95 latency and throughput, comparing the microservice deployment against a single-service monolith.

Scope:
The system implements feed read/write paths for a synthetic user set; it excludes real authentication hardening, media storage at scale, and content moderation.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A deployed microservices feed backend with autoscaling.
2. A comparative performance report versus the monolith.

Timeline:
15 weeks: design (3), service build (6), deployment and load testing (6).

Title:
A CI/CD Pipeline with Automated Testing and Deployment for a Clinic Booking System

Problem Statement:
Small healthcare software teams often deploy clinic booking updates manually, risking regressions in a domain where downtime affects patient appointments. Adopting CI/CD with automated testing can reduce defects and deployment time, yet many teams lack a concrete reference pipeline showing measured improvements over a manual process.

Objectives:
1. Build a CI/CD pipeline that automatically tests and deploys a clinic booking application.
2. Integrate automated unit, integration, and security scanning stages.
3. Measure deployment frequency, lead time, and defect escape rate against a manual baseline.

Methodology:
The pipeline is implemented in GitHub Actions, building a containerised booking app, running JUnit and integration tests, and a dependency vulnerability scan (Trivy) before deploying to a staging environment via Docker Compose. DORA-style metrics (deployment frequency, change lead time, change failure rate) are recorded across simulated change sets and compared with a manually deployed control over the same change set.

Scope:
The pipeline targets one booking application deployed to a single staging server. Production blue-green rollout and multi-region deployment are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working CI/CD pipeline with automated test and scan gates.
2. A comparison of DORA metrics against manual deployment.

Timeline:
14 weeks: app and tests (4), pipeline build (5), measurement and analysis (5).

Title:
A Batch and Streaming Big-Data Pipeline for Detecting Anomalous Financial Transactions

Problem Statement:
Financial institutions must process high-volume transaction streams to flag anomalies, but combining historical batch analysis with low-latency stream processing in one coherent pipeline is non-trivial. Student projects usually cover one mode in isolation, leaving a gap in demonstrating a unified architecture and its latency-versus-completeness trade-offs on realistic data volumes.

Objectives:
1. Build a pipeline that ingests transaction data in both batch and streaming modes.
2. Apply an anomaly-detection model to flag suspicious transactions in near real time.
3. Evaluate detection quality and end-to-end latency against a batch-only baseline.

Methodology:
Transaction data (the public IEEE-CIS Fraud dataset replayed as a stream) is ingested through Apache Kafka. Apache Spark Structured Streaming computes features and scores transactions with an Isolation Forest trained offline on the historical batch. Results land in PostgreSQL with a Grafana view. Evaluation reports precision/recall on labelled fraud and measures processing latency at increasing event rates, compared with a nightly batch-only configuration.

Scope:
The pipeline runs on a single multi-container host with a capped event rate. Real production-scale clusters and online model retraining are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working lambda-style batch-plus-streaming anomaly pipeline.
2. A report on detection quality and latency trade-offs.

Timeline:
15 weeks: ingestion (4), processing and model (6), evaluation (5).

Title:
A Business Intelligence Dashboard for Predictive OEE Monitoring on a Discrete Manufacturing Line

Problem Statement:
Discrete manufacturers track Overall Equipment Effectiveness (OEE) retrospectively, so quality and availability losses are diagnosed only after a shift ends. Plant supervisors lack a single interactive view that both explains historical OEE drivers and forecasts short-term downtime risk, leaving interventions reactive. Existing commercial BI suites are costly and rarely expose the modelling assumptions behind their forecasts, which limits trust on the shop floor.

Objectives:
1. Design a star-schema data model and ETL that consolidates machine, quality, and downtime logs into OEE measures.
2. Deliver an interactive BI dashboard that decomposes OEE into availability, performance, and quality with drill-down by line, shift, and fault code.
3. Add a calibrated short-horizon downtime-risk indicator and validate it against held-out shifts.

Methodology:
Synthetic-yet-realistic shop-floor logs (modelled on the SECOM and a Kaggle predictive-maintenance dataset) are loaded via a Python/dbt ETL into a PostgreSQL star schema. The dashboard is built in Apache Superset. A gradient-boosted classifier (XGBoost) predicts next-shift downtime risk; it is benchmarked against logistic-regression and a moving-average baseline using time-aware cross-validation, reporting ROC-AUC, Brier score, and calibration curves. Usefulness is checked with three supervisors via task-based walkthroughs.

Scope:
Covers one discrete line's three machines and a fixed fault taxonomy. Excludes real-time PLC integration, multi-plant rollout, and prescriptive scheduling; forecasting horizon is capped at one shift.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A reproducible ETL plus star-schema warehouse and an interactive OEE dashboard.
2. A validated downtime-risk indicator with a calibrated, baseline-compared evaluation report.

Timeline:
16 weeks: data model and ETL (4), dashboard (4), modelling and validation (5), usability and write-up (3).

Title:
Probabilistic Time-Series Forecasting of Emergency-Call Volume for Public-Safety Staffing

Problem Statement:
Emergency dispatch centres staff shifts against expected call volume, but point forecasts give no sense of uncertainty, so planners either over-staff or risk dangerous understaffing during surges. Public-safety demand is strongly seasonal and weather-sensitive, yet many forecasting studies report only mean error and omit calibrated prediction intervals that staffing decisions actually need.

Objectives:
1. Build hourly emergency-call-volume forecasts with calibrated prediction intervals.
2. Quantify the marginal value of weather and calendar covariates over a univariate baseline.
3. Evaluate probabilistic accuracy against classical and deep baselines using rolling-origin validation.

Methodology:
Using a public emergency-call dataset (Montgomery County 911 calls) aggregated hourly and joined with open weather and holiday calendars, I compare SARIMAX, Facebook Prophet, and a quantile-loss LSTM that emits prediction intervals. Models are tuned and evaluated with rolling-origin (time-series) cross-validation, reporting MASE and sMAPE for point accuracy plus pinball loss and empirical interval coverage for calibration. An ablation removes weather covariates to isolate their contribution. A persistence (seasonal-naive) model is the lower-bound baseline.

Scope:
Forecasts cover total hourly call volume for one county up to 24 hours ahead. Per-incident-type routing, geospatial hotspot prediction, and live API deployment are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A reproducible forecasting study comparing three models with calibrated intervals.
2. A covariate-ablation report quantifying the value of weather and calendar features.

Timeline:
16 weeks: data engineering (4), baseline models (4), deep model and tuning (5), evaluation and write-up (3).

Title:
Blockchain for Smart City

Problem Statement:
Smart cities have a lot of data and it is not secure. Blockchain is the future so we should use it for everything in the city.

Objectives:
1. Use blockchain
2. Make smart contracts
3. Help the city

Methodology:
I will study blockchain and write some smart contracts. Then I will test if they work.

Scope:
It can be used by any smart city in the world and all the government departments.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A blockchain system
2. Better security

Title:
AR Tourism App

Problem Statement:
Tourists get bored and don't know about places. Augmented reality is cool and can fix this problem easily.

Objectives:
1. Make an AR app
2. Show tourist places
3. Make tourism better

Methodology:
I will use Unity and some AR plugin to make an app that shows things on the phone camera.

Scope:
For all tourists everywhere who want to see information about anything.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A fun AR app
2. Happy tourists

Title:
VR Training for Social Media

Problem Statement:
People use social media wrong and get into trouble. We need VR to train them so they behave better online.

Objectives:
1. Build VR training
2. Teach social media
3. Stop bad behavior

Methodology:
I will make a VR simulation where people practice using social media in a headset.

Scope:
Everyone who uses social media including all ages and all countries.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A VR training app
2. People learn

Title:
A 2D Game to Teach Children About Hospitals

Problem Statement:
Many children are scared of going to the hospital because they do not understand what happens there. A simple game could make them less afraid before a visit.

Objectives:
1. Design a 2D game with hospital-themed levels
2. Add characters like doctors and nurses
3. Test if children enjoy the game

Methodology:
The game will be made in Unity using C# and 2D sprites. There will be a few mini-levels such as taking medicine and getting a check-up. After building it, I will let some children play and ask them questions.

Scope:
The game is for children aged 6 to 10 and covers basic hospital activities. It will be a single-player game on Windows.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A playable 2D hospital game
2. Feedback showing children feel less scared

Timeline:
About 14 weeks: design, build, test.

Title:
Serious Game for Learning Personal Finance

Problem Statement:
Young people often do not know how to budget or save money, and normal lessons are boring. A game might make learning about money more interesting and stick better.

Objectives:
1. Build a game where players manage a monthly budget
2. Include events like bills, savings, and unexpected costs
3. Measure if players learn finance basics

Methodology:
I will develop a 2D simulation game in Unity. Players get a virtual salary and must pay bills and save. I will add quizzes between levels and compare quiz scores before and after playing with a small group of students.

Scope:
The game covers budgeting, saving, and basic expenses for young adults. It will not cover investing or loans in detail.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working finance game
2. A short report on whether players improved their quiz scores

Timeline:
14 weeks split into planning, development, and testing.

Title:
A Dashboard for Tracking Machine Maintenance in a Factory

Problem Statement:
In manufacturing plants, machines break down and the records are often kept on paper. This makes it hard to know which machines need maintenance, so a digital system could help.

Objectives:
1. Build a web dashboard to record machine status
2. Let staff log breakdowns and repairs
3. Show simple charts of downtime

Methodology:
I will build a web application using React for the front end and a Node.js backend with a MySQL database. Staff can enter machine data through forms, and the dashboard will display tables and basic charts of repair history.

Scope:
The system records maintenance for one factory floor and shows reports. It does not include sensor data or automatic prediction.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working maintenance dashboard
2. Charts showing machine downtime over time

Timeline:
One semester: requirements, build, and user testing.

Title:
A Telemedicine Appointment Platform for Community Clinics

Problem Statement:
During emergencies, people in rural areas struggle to reach clinics for advice. A telemedicine platform where they can book and attend video consultations could reduce unnecessary travel and waiting.

Objectives:
1. Build a web platform for booking video consultations
2. Allow doctors to view patient details and notes
3. Add a simple video call feature

Methodology:
The platform will be a web app built with React and a Spring Boot backend storing data in MySQL. Video calls will use a third-party API such as Twilio. Patients book slots and doctors confirm them. I will test the workflow with a few volunteer users acting as patients and doctors.

Scope:
The platform handles booking, consultation notes, and video calls for one clinic. It does not include payment or prescription delivery.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working telemedicine web platform
2. Test feedback from volunteer users

Timeline:
14 weeks: design, development, testing.

Title:
An E-Learning System for Energy Efficiency Training

Problem Statement:
Building operators often lack training on how to reduce energy waste, and existing courses are generic. A targeted e-learning system with quizzes and progress tracking could help facility staff learn practical energy-saving habits.

Objectives:
1. Develop an e-learning platform with modular lessons on energy efficiency
2. Implement quizzes with automatic scoring and progress tracking
3. Evaluate usability and learning gain with a sample of facility staff

Methodology:
The system will be built with React, a Spring Boot REST API, and PostgreSQL. Lessons are organized into modules with embedded videos and quizzes. Progress is stored per user. I will run a pre-test/post-test with around 15 participants and collect System Usability Scale (SUS) scores to measure usability.

Scope:
The platform covers lesson delivery, quizzes, and progress dashboards for individual learners. It excludes live instructor sessions and certification issuance.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A functional e-learning platform with three energy modules
2. A usability report with SUS scores and pre/post quiz comparison

Timeline:
Weeks 1-3 requirements, 4-10 development, 11-14 testing and evaluation.

Title:
A QR-Based Payment App for Small Businesses

Problem Statement:
Small shops often rely on cash and lose customers who prefer cashless options, while existing payment providers charge high fees or need expensive hardware. A lightweight QR-based payment app could let small businesses accept digital payments cheaply.

Objectives:
1. Build a mobile app for merchants to generate payment QR codes and for customers to scan and pay
2. Integrate a sandbox payment gateway for transactions
3. Evaluate transaction success rate and merchant satisfaction

Methodology:
The app will be developed in Flutter with a Firebase backend for authentication and transaction records. Payments will use the Stripe test gateway. Merchants generate dynamic QR codes per sale; customers scan to confirm. I will test with mock merchant and customer accounts and record success and failure cases.

Scope:
The app covers QR generation, payment confirmation, and a transaction history list. It excludes real banking integration, refunds, and tax reporting.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working merchant-customer QR payment app on the sandbox gateway
2. A test report on transaction success rate and user feedback

Timeline:
14 weeks across analysis, development, and evaluation phases.

Title:
Fraud Detection for Agricultural Subsidy Claims

Problem Statement:
Government agricultural subsidy programmes lose money to duplicate or inflated claims, and manual review is slow. A machine learning model that flags suspicious claims for human review could reduce fraud while keeping a human in the loop.

Objectives:
1. Prepare a labelled dataset of subsidy claims with fraud indicators
2. Train and compare classifiers to flag suspicious claims
3. Evaluate the model using precision, recall, and F1

Methodology:
Using a public or synthetic subsidy-claims dataset, I will engineer features such as claim amount per hectare and claim frequency. I will train logistic regression and random forest models in scikit-learn and compare them against a rule-based baseline. Evaluation uses stratified 5-fold cross-validation reporting precision, recall, and F1, with attention to class imbalance via SMOTE.

Scope:
The project focuses on a binary fraud/no-fraud classifier and an explanation of flagged features. It excludes real-time deployment and integration with government systems.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained fraud-detection model with documented performance
2. A comparison report against the rule-based baseline

Timeline:
Weeks 1-4 data and features, 5-10 modelling, 11-14 evaluation and writing.

Title:
A Recommendation System for a Public Transport Ticketing Store

Problem Statement:
Online stores selling transport passes and travel add-ons show the same generic options to everyone, so commuters miss relevant deals. A recommendation feature could suggest passes and add-ons matched to a commuter's travel patterns.

Objectives:
1. Build an e-commerce prototype selling transport passes and add-ons
2. Implement a recommendation engine using collaborative and content-based filtering
3. Evaluate recommendation quality against a popularity baseline

Methodology:
The store will be a web app (React + Spring Boot + MySQL). I will use a public retail/interactions dataset adapted to transport items, applying item-based collaborative filtering and a content-based approach, then combine them in a simple hybrid. Offline evaluation uses precision@k and recall@k on a held-out test split compared to a most-popular baseline.

Scope:
The project covers browsing, cart, and personalized suggestions. It excludes real payment processing and live commuter data.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working store prototype with a recommendation panel
2. An evaluation report comparing hybrid recommendations to the baseline

Timeline:
14 weeks: requirements, build, model integration, evaluation.

Title:
A Chatbot for Household Sustainability Advice

Problem Statement:
People want to live more sustainably but find advice scattered and generic. A conversational agent that answers questions about recycling, energy, and water use in plain language could make practical guidance easier to access.

Objectives:
1. Build a chatbot that answers household sustainability questions
2. Ground answers in a curated knowledge base to reduce wrong advice
3. Evaluate answer relevance and user satisfaction

Methodology:
I will build a retrieval-augmented chatbot: a curated document set on sustainability is embedded with Sentence-BERT and stored in a FAISS index, and a language model generates answers from the retrieved passages. The web interface uses React with a Flask backend. Evaluation measures retrieval relevance (top-k accuracy on a question set) and collects user satisfaction ratings from around 12 testers.

Scope:
The chatbot covers recycling, home energy, and water saving for general households. It excludes purchasing advice and region-specific regulations.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working sustainability chatbot with a knowledge base
2. An evaluation report on relevance and user ratings

Timeline:
Weeks 1-3 knowledge base, 4-10 development, 11-14 evaluation.

Title:
A Knowledge-Graph Search Tool for Logistics Documents

Problem Statement:
Logistics companies store shipment, route, and customs information across many documents, making it hard to answer questions that span several records. A knowledge graph linking these entities could enable richer search than plain keyword lookup.

Objectives:
1. Extract entities and relations (shipments, routes, ports, carriers) from sample documents
2. Build a knowledge graph and a query interface
3. Compare graph-based search results to keyword search on sample queries

Methodology:
I will use spaCy for named-entity recognition and rule-based relation extraction over a sample document set, loading the results into a Neo4j graph database. A web interface lets users run Cypher-backed queries phrased in simple terms. I will define a set of test questions and compare answer completeness between the knowledge graph and a keyword baseline.

Scope:
The tool covers entity extraction, graph construction, and querying over a fixed sample corpus. It excludes live data feeds and automatic schema learning.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A populated logistics knowledge graph with a search interface
2. A comparison report against keyword search

Timeline:
14 weeks: extraction, graph build, interface, evaluation.

Title:
Semantic Segmentation of Scanned Government Forms for Automated Field Extraction

Problem Statement:
E-government services digitize millions of scanned forms, but extracting fields is error-prone when layouts vary and scans are noisy. Treating field localization as a pixel-level segmentation problem could outperform bounding-box methods on dense, overlapping form regions, reducing manual data entry.

Objectives:
1. Build a labelled dataset of scanned forms with pixel masks for key field regions (name, ID, date, signature)
2. Train and compare U-Net and DeepLabv3+ segmentation models for field-region extraction
3. Evaluate segmentation accuracy and downstream OCR field-extraction correctness

Methodology:
I will assemble around 1,500 form images from public datasets (e.g., FUNSD, RVL-CDIP subsets) plus synthetic augmentation, annotating region masks. U-Net and DeepLabv3+ (ResNet-50 backbone) will be trained in PyTorch with augmentation and a Dice+cross-entropy loss, against a connected-components baseline. Evaluation uses mean IoU and per-class Dice via 5-fold cross-validation; extracted regions feed Tesseract OCR and I report field-level accuracy.

Scope:
The project targets four field types on English-language single-page forms. It excludes handwriting recognition quality tuning and multi-page document linking.

Expected Outcomes:
1. Two trained segmentation models with mean IoU and Dice reported against the baseline
2. A field-extraction pipeline with measured downstream OCR accuracy

Timeline:
Weeks 1-3 dataset/annotation, 4-6 baseline, 7-11 model training, 12-14 evaluation and reporting.

Title:
Real-Time Detection of Classroom Engagement Cues Using Object Detection

Problem Statement:
In large lecture halls, instructors cannot gauge whether students are following along. Detecting engagement-related cues such as raised hands and phone usage from a classroom camera could give anonymized, aggregate feedback, but it must run fast enough for live use and respect privacy.

Objectives:
1. Build an annotated dataset of classroom frames labelled for hands-raised, phone-in-use, and head-down
2. Train and compare YOLOv8 and Faster R-CNN detectors for these cues
3. Evaluate accuracy and inference speed for real-time aggregate reporting

Methodology:
I will collect and annotate around 3,000 frames (with consent and face-blurring) plus relevant public images. YOLOv8 and Faster R-CNN will be trained in PyTorch with transfer learning from COCO weights and standard augmentation. Evaluation reports mAP@0.5 and mAP@0.5:0.95 on a held-out test set, plus frames-per-second on a mid-range GPU, comparing the two against each other for the speed/accuracy trade-off.

Scope:
The system outputs only aggregate counts of cues, never individual identities. It excludes emotion recognition and attendance tracking.

Expected Outcomes:
1. Two trained detectors with reported mAP and FPS
2. A privacy-preserving aggregate engagement dashboard prototype

Timeline:
Weeks 1-4 data and annotation, 5-10 training, 11-14 evaluation and dashboard.

Title:
Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis of Retail Product Reviews

Problem Statement:
Retailers receive thousands of product reviews, but an overall star rating hides which specific aspects (price, quality, delivery, sizing) customers complain about. Aspect-based sentiment analysis could surface aspect-level sentiment, but informal review language and sarcasm make this hard.

Objectives:
1. Build an aspect-labelled dataset of retail reviews across four aspect categories
2. Fine-tune and compare a fine-tuned BERT model against TF-IDF + SVM and a lexicon baseline
3. Evaluate aspect-sentiment classification with macro-F1 and per-aspect performance

Methodology:
I will use a public retail-review corpus (e.g., Amazon Reviews subset) and annotate aspect-sentiment pairs for a sampled set. A BERT-base model with an aspect-aware classification head will be fine-tuned in PyTorch/Hugging Face, compared against TF-IDF+SVM and a VADER lexicon baseline. Evaluation uses stratified train/validation/test splits reporting macro-F1, accuracy, and a per-aspect confusion analysis, with error analysis on misclassified sarcastic reviews.

Scope:
The project covers four predefined aspects in English reviews for one product category. It excludes implicit-aspect detection and multilingual reviews.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A fine-tuned aspect-based sentiment model with macro-F1 reported against two baselines
2. An aspect-sentiment summary view and error analysis

Timeline:
Weeks 1-3 data/annotation, 4-9 modelling, 10-14 evaluation and analysis.

Title:
Learning-Based Query Optimization for Smart-City Sensor Databases

Problem Statement:
Smart-city platforms run heavy analytical queries over large spatio-temporal sensor tables, and the database optimizer's cardinality estimates are often wrong, leading to slow plans. A learned cardinality estimator could improve plan selection for these workloads.

Objectives:
1. Build a workload of representative spatio-temporal queries over a sensor dataset
2. Train a learned cardinality-estimation model and integrate its estimates into plan selection
3. Evaluate query latency and estimation error against the native optimizer

Methodology:
Using an open smart-city sensor dataset loaded into PostgreSQL, I will generate a parametric query workload and capture true cardinalities. A lightweight neural cardinality estimator (MSCN-style) is trained in PyTorch on query features, and its estimates are used via hints to guide plan choice. Evaluation reports q-error for cardinality accuracy and end-to-end latency speedup over the default optimizer on a held-out query set, with cross-validation across query templates.

Scope:
The project focuses on select-join-aggregate read queries on one sensor schema. It excludes write-heavy workloads and modifying the database engine source.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained cardinality estimator with q-error reported against the native optimizer
2. A latency comparison across the query workload

Timeline:
Weeks 1-3 data/workload, 4-9 model, 10-14 integration and evaluation.

Title:
A Facial-Recognition Attendance System for Tour Group Check-Ins

Problem Statement:
Tour operators waste time at each stop manually counting and checking off group members. A facial-recognition attendance system could speed up check-ins, but it must handle outdoor lighting and avoid storing raw face images for privacy.

Objectives:
1. Build a facial-recognition pipeline for enrolling and matching tour-group members
2. Implement an attendance log that records check-in time and location
3. Evaluate recognition accuracy and speed under varied lighting

Methodology:
The pipeline uses MTCNN for face detection and a FaceNet embedding model; only embeddings (not raw images) are stored. Matching uses cosine similarity against enrolled embeddings with a tuned threshold. The app is built with Python/Flask and a SQLite log. I will evaluate on a small enrolled set under indoor and outdoor conditions, reporting accuracy, false-accept and false-reject rates, and per-check-in latency.

Scope:
The system handles enrolment, matching, and an attendance log for groups up to about 30 people. It excludes liveness/anti-spoofing detection and large-scale identification.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working face-recognition attendance prototype storing only embeddings
2. An accuracy and FAR/FRR report across lighting conditions

Timeline:
14 weeks: pipeline build, app, and evaluation.

Title:
Robust OCR for User-Generated Social-Media Images with Layout-Aware Post-Correction

Problem Statement:
Social-media platforms moderate text embedded in memes and screenshots, but standard OCR fails on stylized fonts, low resolution, and cluttered backgrounds, and produces character errors that break downstream policy filters. There is a gap in combining detection-robust recognition with a domain-adapted error-correction stage tuned for short, noisy social-media text rather than clean documents.

Objectives:
1. Curate and annotate a 4,000-image social-media OCR benchmark with ground-truth transcriptions and text-region boxes
2. Build a pipeline pairing a CRAFT detector and TrOCR recognizer with a fine-tuned seq2seq post-correction model
3. Quantify gains from post-correction over the raw recognizer and a Tesseract baseline using CER and word accuracy, with ablations

Methodology:
Detection uses CRAFT; recognition uses TrOCR-base fine-tuned on the curated set plus synthetic stylized text. A ByT5 post-corrector is trained on (OCR-output, ground-truth) pairs to fix character errors. Data is split 70/15/15 with 5-fold cross-validation on the train portion. Metrics are character error rate (CER), word accuracy, and normalized edit distance, reported against Tesseract and against the recognizer-without-correction. Ablations isolate the post-corrector and synthetic-data contributions; statistical significance is tested with bootstrap confidence intervals.

Scope:
The work targets English short-text in static social-media images. Explicitly excluded: handwriting, video frames, non-Latin scripts, and end-to-end moderation policy decisions, which are left as integration points.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A released benchmark and reproducible pipeline with CER/word-accuracy reported against two baselines
2. An ablation study isolating the post-correction and synthetic-data gains, with error analysis

Timeline:
Weeks 1-3 dataset curation, 4-6 baseline, 7-9 recognizer fine-tuning, 10-12 post-corrector and ablations, 13-14 analysis and writing.

Title:
Edge-Deployable Anomaly Detection in Wireless Body-Sensor Streams for Early Patient Deterioration

Problem Statement:
Wearable wireless sensors in hospital wards stream vitals continuously, but cloud-based analytics add latency and fail under network loss, while ward-level alarms suffer high false-alarm rates. There is a gap in lightweight, on-device multivariate anomaly detection that flags early deterioration from noisy, intermittently-dropped sensor streams without overwhelming staff with false alerts.

Objectives:
1. Construct a labelled multivariate vitals dataset (HR, SpO2, respiration, temperature) with deterioration episodes from a public ICU/ward source
2. Train and compare an LSTM-autoencoder, a Temporal Convolutional Network, and an Isolation Forest baseline for streaming anomaly detection
3. Quantize the best model for an edge device and evaluate detection quality, false-alarm rate, and latency

Methodology:
I will use MIMIC-derived waveform/vitals data, resampled and windowed, simulating packet loss to mirror wireless dropouts. Models are trained in PyTorch with reconstruction-error and forecasting-based anomaly scoring; thresholds are tuned on a validation split. Evaluation reports precision, recall, F1, AUPRC for episode detection, plus false-alarms-per-patient-hour and lead-time before clinical deterioration, using patient-disjoint cross-validation. The best model is INT8-quantized and benchmarked on a Raspberry Pi for inference latency and memory.

Scope:
The project covers four vital-sign channels and offline-then-on-device evaluation. Explicitly excluded: closed-loop intervention, FDA-style clinical validation, and live hospital deployment.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A compared set of anomaly detectors with F1/AUPRC and false-alarm-rate reported against the baseline
2. A quantized edge model with measured latency, memory footprint, and detection lead-time

Timeline:
Weeks 1-3 data preparation, 4-8 model training and comparison, 9-11 quantization and edge benchmarking, 12-14 evaluation and write-up.

Title:
Voice Assistant for Tourist Information

Title:
Detecting Suspicious Traffic on a Social Media Server

Problem Statement:
Social media platforms are targeted by automated attacks such as login floods and scraping bots. Small platforms lack the resources for commercial intrusion detection, so a lightweight detector trained on common attack patterns would help.

Objectives:
1. Use a public intrusion dataset to train a classifier.
2. Detect a few attack types relevant to web servers.
3. Measure detection accuracy.

Methodology:
I will use the NSL-KDD dataset and train a decision tree and a random forest with scikit-learn to classify traffic as normal or attack. Features will be the standard connection attributes in the dataset. I will report accuracy and a confusion matrix.

Scope:
The work is offline analysis on a public dataset, not a live deployment, and covers only the attack categories present in NSL-KDD.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained intrusion classifier.
2. A comparison of the two models.

14 weeks across data, training, and evaluation.

Title:
Scanning a Healthcare Web App for Common Vulnerabilities

Methodology:

Scope:

Title:
Static and Dynamic Analysis of Banking Trojan Samples

Problem Statement:
Financial institutions face banking trojans that steal credentials and inject fraudulent transactions. Analysts need to understand a sample's behaviour quickly, but manual reverse engineering is slow. A combined static-plus-dynamic workflow with a summary report could speed up triage of common families.

Objectives:
1. Collect labelled banking malware samples from a public repository and set up an isolated sandbox.
2. Extract static features (imports, strings, PE headers) and dynamic behaviours (API calls, network activity) for each sample.
3. Classify samples into families and summarise indicators of compromise.

Methodology:
Samples from theZoo and MalwareBazaar will be detonated in an isolated Cuckoo sandbox VM. Static features come from pefile and YARA rules; dynamic logs come from the sandbox API monitor. A random forest classifier in scikit-learn assigns family labels, evaluated with precision, recall, and F1 against ground-truth labels.

Scope:
Limited to Windows banking trojan families already labelled in the chosen feeds; no live network deployment and no obfuscation-resistant unpacking beyond the sandbox.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A reproducible analysis pipeline producing per-sample IOC reports.
2. A classification evaluation across the selected families.

Timeline:
14 weeks: sandbox setup, feature extraction, classification, reporting.

A Responsive Web Platform for Factory Maintenance Requests

Title:
A Cross-Platform Mobile App for Household Energy Tracking

Methodology:

Scope:
Manual logging only for a single household; excludes automatic metering, IoT plug integration, and utility-account linking.

Expected Outcomes:

2. A usability evaluation from trial users.

Timeline:
14 weeks across design, build, charts, and trial.

Title:
An Android Native App for Small-Business Inventory

Problem Statement:
Small retail businesses such as mini-marts often track stock in notebooks or spreadsheets, leading to stockouts and manual reordering. A simple Android app with barcode scanning could give owners real-time stock counts and low-stock alerts at low cost.

Title:
An IoT Sensor Network for Greenhouse Monitoring

Problem Statement:
Small-scale farmers running greenhouses often check temperature and soil moisture manually, which is time-consuming and misses overnight fluctuations that harm crops. A low-cost IoT sensor network that logs conditions and warns on threshold breaches could support better growing decisions.

Objectives:

Methodology:
ESP32 nodes with DHT22 and capacitive soil-moisture sensors will publish readings over MQTT to a Raspberry Pi broker, which forwards to a cloud database. A web dashboard charts the data, and a rules engine sends Telegram alerts on threshold breaches. Sensor accuracy will be checked against a reference meter.

Title:
Smart Home Automation That Adapts to Commuting Patterns

By linking home automation to live transportation data, the system could pre-condition the home and stagger EV charging around the actual expected arrival rather than a fixed clock.

Objectives:

2. Trigger automation rules (climate pre-conditioning, EV charge scheduling) keyed to predicted arrival.
3. Evaluate energy and comfort outcomes against a static-schedule baseline.

Methodology:
A Home Assistant instance will run on a Raspberry Pi controlling simulated devices via MQTT. Arrival estimates come from a transit/traffic API combined with a simple regression on logged commute times. A rules layer maps predicted arrival to device actions. Evaluation compares arrival-aware control against a fixed-schedule baseline over two weeks of recorded commute scenarios, measuring wasted heating minutes and charge timing accuracy.

Scope:
One simulated home with climate and EV-charging devices; excludes security devices, multi-occupant arbitration, and real grid pricing integration.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working arrival-aware automation prototype.
2. A quantified comparison versus the static baseline.

Timeline:
14 weeks: integration, rules, two-week evaluation, write-up.

Title:
Edge Computing for On-Device Waste-Bin Fill Detection

Problem Statement:
Cloud-based smart-waste systems stream camera images to servers, raising bandwidth cost and privacy concerns and failing where connectivity is poor. Running fill-level detection at the edge would cut data transfer and keep imagery local, supporting more sustainable, lower-bandwidth municipal waste collection.

Objectives:
1. Train a lightweight image classifier to estimate bin fill level (empty/half/full).
2. Deploy and quantise the model to run on an edge device, reporting only fill status.
3. Compare edge accuracy, latency, and bandwidth against a cloud-inference baseline.

Methodology:
A MobileNetV2 classifier will be trained on a labelled bin-image dataset (collected and augmented), then converted to TensorFlow Lite with INT8 quantisation and deployed on a Raspberry Pi 4 with a camera. The device publishes only a fill label over LoRaWAN. Evaluation measures on-device accuracy, inference latency, and bytes transmitted versus uploading full images to a cloud model.

Scope:
Three fill classes on static bin images; excludes object-level waste sorting, moving-vehicle capture, and multi-camera fusion.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A quantised on-device fill-detection model.
2. An accuracy/latency/bandwidth comparison versus cloud inference.

Timeline:
14 weeks: data, training, edge deployment, benchmarking.

Title:
A Cloud-Native Microservices Backend for Last-Mile Delivery Tracking

Problem Statement:
Monolithic delivery-tracking systems struggle to scale during demand spikes and couple unrelated functions, so a failure in one area can take down tracking entirely. A cloud-native microservices design with independent scaling and resilience could keep last-mile tracking responsive under load.

Objectives:
1. Decompose delivery tracking into independently deployable services (orders, drivers, tracking, notifications).
2. Containerise and orchestrate the services with health checks and autoscaling.
3. Evaluate latency and resilience under simulated load and induced failures.

Methodology:
Services will be built in Spring Boot, communicating via REST and a RabbitMQ event bus, each with its own PostgreSQL schema. They will be containerised with Docker and deployed to a local Kubernetes (minikube) cluster with horizontal pod autoscaling and liveness probes. Load testing with k6 measures p95 latency and throughput, and chaos tests kill pods to observe recovery. Results are compared with a single-service baseline.

Scope:
Backend services and their evaluation only; excludes a production mobile client, real payment processing, and multi-region deployment.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A deployable microservices tracking backend.
2. Latency and resilience results versus a monolithic baseline.

Timeline:
14 weeks: service build, orchestration, load/chaos testing, analysis.

Title:
A CI/CD Pipeline with Automated Security Gates for E-Government Services

Problem Statement:

Objectives:

2. Add automated quality and security gates that block releases failing defined thresholds.

A reference Spring Boot service will be wired into GitHub Actions running unit/integration tests, SonarQube for code quality, OWASP Dependency-Check and Trivy for vulnerability scanning, and a staging deploy to Docker. Gates fail the pipeline on critical findings or coverage below threshold. I will measure DORA-style metrics (lead time, deployment frequency, change-failure rate) across a series of seeded commits and compare with a manual release process.

Scope:
Pipeline and gating for one reference service; excludes infrastructure-as-code provisioning of cloud resources and production-grade secrets management.

Expected Outcomes:

2. A metrics comparison versus manual releases.

Timeline:

Title:

A batch-and-streaming analytics pipeline could turn raw event logs into early indicators of at-risk students for instructors.

Engagement features (clicks, active days, submission timing) train a logistic-regression at-risk classifier, evaluated with AUC and validated against held-out outcomes. Pipeline throughput is measured by records processed per second at increasing volumes.

Scope:
Offline/near-real-time analytics on one LMS schema; excludes live integration with a production LMS and personalised intervention delivery.

Expected Outcomes:

2. Throughput benchmarks and an at-risk model evaluation.

14 weeks: ingestion, processing, modelling, benchmarking.

Title:
A Business-Intelligence Dashboard with Explainable Sales-Driver Attribution for Omnichannel Retail

Problem Statement:
Mid-size retailers run separate online and in-store systems, so managers see fragmented sales reports and cannot tell which factors (promotions, weather, footfall, stockouts) actually drove a change in revenue. Conventional BI dashboards visualise what happened but not why, leaving buyers to guess at causes. This project delivers an integrated dashboard that pairs descriptive KPIs with explainable attribution of weekly sales movements.

Objectives:
1. Build an ETL layer consolidating online and in-store transactions into a star-schema warehouse.
2. Deliver a dashboard of core retail KPIs (revenue, basket size, conversion, sell-through) sliced by store, channel, and category.
3. Add a driver-attribution panel that quantifies each factor's contribution to weekly revenue change with confidence indicators.

Methodology:
ETL in dbt loads the public Olist plus synthesised in-store data into a PostgreSQL star schema; the dashboard is built in a React front-end over a cached query API. Attribution uses a gradient-boosting model (XGBoost) with SHAP values to attribute weekly revenue change to drivers, benchmarked against a linear-regression baseline and validated with time-based cross-validation (rolling origin). Accuracy is reported as MAPE on held-out weeks; attribution stability is checked across folds. A heuristic usability test with three retail-analyst proxies validates the interface.

Scope:
Covers descriptive KPIs and explainable attribution for one retailer's two-channel data; explicitly excludes prescriptive optimisation, real-time streaming ingestion, and demand forecasting beyond the attribution horizon.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An integrated, documented BI dashboard with KPI and attribution views.
2. An evaluation of attribution accuracy and stability versus the baseline, plus usability findings.

Timeline:
14 weeks — Wk1-3 warehouse/ETL, Wk4-7 KPI dashboard, Wk8-11 attribution model and validation, Wk12-14 usability test and write-up.

Title:
Probabilistic Short-Term Forecasting of Urban Water Demand for Smart-City Operations

Problem Statement:
Smart-city water utilities need hour-ahead demand forecasts to schedule pumping and reduce energy cost, but most deployed models output a single point value and ignore uncertainty, so operators cannot size safety margins for peak events. There is little open comparison of classical and deep sequence models with calibrated prediction intervals on municipal water data, which this project addresses.

Objectives:
1. Build a reproducible pipeline producing 24-hour-ahead district water-demand forecasts with prediction intervals.
2. Compare SARIMA, gradient-boosted trees, and an LSTM/Temporal Fusion Transformer under identical features and splits.
3. Evaluate both point accuracy and interval calibration, and quantify the operational pumping-cost implication.

Methodology:
Hourly demand from a public municipal water dataset is joined with weather and calendar features. Models are SARIMA (statsmodels), LightGBM with quantile loss, and a Temporal Fusion Transformer (PyTorch Forecasting), all trained with rolling-origin time-series cross-validation to prevent leakage. Point accuracy uses MAE and sMAPE against a seasonal-naive baseline; probabilistic quality uses pinball loss and PICP/MPIW for interval calibration. A simple pumping-cost simulation translates forecast error into estimated kWh, and ablations test feature and horizon sensitivity.

Scope:
Hour-ahead to day-ahead forecasting for district-level demand on one city's historical data; excludes leak detection, pipe-network hydraulic simulation, and live SCADA integration.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An open, reproducible forecasting pipeline with calibrated intervals.
2. A benchmarked comparison across models with point and probabilistic metrics and an operational cost analysis.

Timeline:
14 weeks — Wk1-3 data/features, Wk4-7 baseline and tree models, Wk8-11 deep model and calibration, Wk12-14 cost simulation and reporting.

Title:

Objectives:
1. Develop a serious game that visualizes sorting and searching algorithms
2. Include interactive levels where students arrange elements to match an algorithm's behaviour
3. Evaluate engagement and perceived learning with a student group

Methodology:
The game will be developed in Unity with C#. Each level animates an algorithm (bubble sort, binary search) and asks the player to predict the next step. A pre/post quiz and a short engagement survey will be used with around 20 students.

Scope:
The game covers four basic algorithms and targets first-year students. Advanced algorithms and automated difficulty adjustment are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A serious game covering four algorithms
2. Quiz and survey results comparing before and after play

Timeline:
Two semesters: design and asset creation, then development, then user testing.

Title:
A Healthcare Records App for a Retail Pharmacy

Problem Statement:
Small retail pharmacies often keep customer medication records on paper or in spreadsheets, making it hard to track repeat prescriptions and flag drug interactions. A simple informatics app could store this data and give basic alerts.

Objectives:
1. Build an app to store customer medication records for a pharmacy
2. Add a basic alert when two recorded drugs may interact
3. Test the app with sample pharmacy data

Methodology:
The app will be a web application built with PHP and MySQL. A small lookup table of common drug interactions will be used to generate alerts. The system will be tested with made-up customer records to check that alerts appear correctly.

Scope:
The app covers a single pharmacy branch and a limited list of common drugs. Insurance, billing, and multi-branch sync are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working pharmacy records web app with interaction alerts
2. Test results showing alerts trigger for known drug pairs

Timeline:
Two semesters, starting with database design then development and testing.

Title:
A Telemedicine Booking Platform for a Smart City Clinic Network

Problem Statement:
In a city with many small clinics, residents struggle to find which clinic has an available doctor for a video consultation, leading to long waits. A shared telemedicine platform could let residents book and join video appointments across participating clinics.

Objectives:
1. Build a web platform where residents book telemedicine appointments
2. Integrate a video call feature for consultations
3. Provide clinics with a simple dashboard to manage their available slots

Methodology:
The platform will be built with React and a Node.js backend with MySQL. Video calls will use a third-party WebRTC library such as Jitsi. Clinics set their availability, residents book a slot, and both join a video room. The system will be tested with a few simulated clinics and users.

Scope:
The project covers appointment booking and video consultation for general practitioners. Prescriptions, payments, and emergency services are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A telemedicine platform with booking and video consultation
2. A clinic dashboard for managing availability

Timeline:
Two semesters: requirements and design, then build, then testing with sample users.

Title:
An Adaptive E-Learning System for Tourism Industry Workers

Problem Statement:
Tourism workers such as tour guides and hotel staff need ongoing training on destinations, languages, and service standards, but generic online courses do not adapt to each worker's existing knowledge, wasting their limited time. An adaptive e-learning system that adjusts content difficulty to the learner could make training more efficient.

Objectives:
1. Develop a web-based e-learning system with tourism training modules
2. Implement an adaptive engine that recommends the next lesson based on quiz performance
3. Evaluate learning gains and user satisfaction against a non-adaptive version

Methodology:
The system will be built with React and Django, backed by PostgreSQL. The adaptive engine uses a rule-based mastery model: each topic has a mastery score updated from quiz results, and the next lesson is chosen from topics below a mastery threshold. Evaluation will use an A/B test with two groups of around 15 learners each, comparing post-test scores and a usability survey (SUS).

Scope:
The system covers three tourism training modules and one language. Content authoring tools and offline mobile access are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working adaptive e-learning web system for tourism training
2. A comparison report showing learning-gain and satisfaction differences between adaptive and non-adaptive versions

Timeline:
Semester 1: requirements, content, and core LMS. Semester 2: adaptive engine, A/B evaluation, and reporting.

Title:
A Peer-to-Peer Micro-Payment Feature for a Social Media Platform

Problem Statement:
Content creators on social media platforms struggle to receive small tips from followers because existing payment options have high fees and friction for amounts under a few dollars. A lightweight in-app micro-payment feature could let followers tip creators quickly while keeping fees low.

Objectives:
1. Design and build a micro-payment module that integrates with a mock social media app
2. Implement a wallet and tipping flow using a sandbox payment gateway
3. Evaluate transaction speed, fee handling, and user trust through a usability study

Methodology:
A prototype social feed will be built with React Native and a Spring Boot backend. The micro-payment module uses the Stripe sandbox API with a local wallet ledger to batch small tips and reduce per-transaction fees. Testing covers functional correctness of the ledger and a usability study with about 12 participants rating trust and ease of use.

Scope:
The project covers tipping between users within one mock app using sandbox (non-real) money. Real banking integration, fraud detection, and regulatory compliance are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working micro-payment and tipping prototype inside a sample social app
2. A report on transaction performance and usability findings

Timeline:
Semester 1: app shell and wallet ledger. Semester 2: gateway integration, batching, and usability evaluation.

Title:
Machine Learning Detection of Fraudulent Healthcare Insurance Claims

Problem Statement:
Healthcare insurers lose money to fraudulent claims such as duplicate billing or services never rendered, and manual auditing reviews only a small fraction of claims. A machine learning classifier could flag suspicious claims for auditors to prioritize, but class imbalance makes naive models miss real fraud.

Objectives:
1. Build a classifier that flags potentially fraudulent healthcare claims
2. Address class imbalance and compare resampling strategies
3. Evaluate detection performance using metrics suited to imbalanced data

Methodology:
Using a public healthcare claims dataset (e.g., a Medicare-style claims dataset), features such as billing amount, provider frequency, and procedure codes will be engineered. Logistic regression, random forest, and XGBoost will be trained, with SMOTE and class weighting compared against an unbalanced baseline. Evaluation uses precision, recall, F1, and PR-AUC with stratified 5-fold cross-validation.

Scope:
The project focuses on offline batch classification on one dataset. Real-time scoring, deployment, and provider-network graph analysis are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained fraud-detection model with a comparison of resampling strategies
2. An evaluation report ranking models on PR-AUC and recall at fixed precision

Timeline:
Semester 1: data prep, feature engineering, baseline models. Semester 2: imbalance handling, tuning, and evaluation.

Title:
A Hybrid Recommendation System for an Online Financial Products Store

Problem Statement:
An e-commerce platform selling financial products such as insurance plans and savings accounts struggles to recommend relevant products, because purchases are infrequent and each customer buys few items, weakening collaborative filtering. A hybrid recommender combining content and behaviour could improve relevance.

Objectives:
1. Build a hybrid recommender combining content-based and collaborative filtering
2. Handle the cold-start problem for new users with limited history
3. Evaluate recommendation quality against single-method baselines

Methodology:
A dataset of product attributes and simulated user interactions will be used (or a public financial-product interaction dataset where available). Content-based filtering uses TF-IDF over product attributes; collaborative filtering uses matrix factorization (SVD). The hybrid weights both, falling back to content-based for cold-start users. Evaluation uses Precision@K, Recall@K, and NDCG with a train/test split, compared against content-only and CF-only baselines.

Scope:
The system is an offline recommender producing ranked lists. Live A/B testing, real-time updates, and regulatory suitability checks are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A hybrid recommendation prototype with cold-start handling
2. An evaluation comparing the hybrid against content-only and CF-only baselines

Timeline:
Semester 1: data, content-based model, CF model. Semester 2: hybrid combination, cold-start, evaluation.

Title:
A Maintenance-Support Chatbot for Factory Floor Operators

Problem Statement:
When machines fault on a manufacturing line, operators waste time searching paper manuals for troubleshooting steps, increasing downtime. A conversational agent that answers maintenance questions from the machine manuals could speed up first-line fixes.

Objectives:
1. Build a chatbot that answers troubleshooting questions from machine manuals
2. Use retrieval over the manual content to ground answers and reduce wrong replies
3. Evaluate answer accuracy and operator-rated usefulness

Methodology:
Manual PDFs for two machine types will be parsed and chunked, embedded with a sentence-transformer model, and stored in a FAISS index. A retrieval-augmented pipeline retrieves relevant chunks and passes them to a language model to compose answers. Evaluation uses a set of about 40 question/answer pairs scored for correctness, plus a small usefulness survey with operators or proxy users.

Scope:
The chatbot covers troubleshooting for two specified machine types in English. Live machine sensor integration and multi-language support are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working retrieval-augmented maintenance chatbot for two machine types
2. An accuracy and usefulness evaluation report

Timeline:
Semester 1: manual parsing, embedding, retrieval. Semester 2: answer generation, evaluation, and refinement.

Title:
A Knowledge-Graph-Based Search Tool for Public Safety Incident Reports

Problem Statement:
Public safety agencies store incident reports as free text, so analysts cannot easily find related incidents linked by location, people, or vehicles. A knowledge graph built from these reports could let analysts search by entities and relationships rather than keywords alone.

Objectives:
1. Extract entities and relationships from incident report text to build a knowledge graph
2. Provide a search interface that queries the graph by entity and relationship
3. Evaluate retrieval quality against a keyword-search baseline

Methodology:
Using a public set of crime or incident reports, named-entity recognition (spaCy) will extract people, locations, vehicles, and dates, with rule-based patterns for relationships. Triples will be stored in Neo4j. A search UI lets users query connected entities. Evaluation compares the graph search against keyword search on a set of analyst-style queries using precision and recall of relevant incidents.

Scope:
The tool covers one report dataset in English and a fixed set of entity types. Real-time ingestion and predictive policing are explicitly out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A knowledge graph and search tool over incident reports
2. A comparison report of graph search versus keyword search

Timeline:
Semester 1: entity/relation extraction and graph building. Semester 2: search UI and evaluation.

Title:
Semantic Segmentation of Solar Panels in Aerial Imagery for Energy Asset Mapping

Problem Statement:
Energy utilities need accurate maps of rooftop solar installations to plan grid capacity, but manual annotation of aerial imagery is slow and expensive. Existing segmentation models often fail on small or partially shaded panels and across varying roof types, leaving coverage estimates inaccurate.

Objectives:
1. Train a semantic segmentation model to delineate rooftop solar panels from aerial imagery
2. Improve performance on small and shaded panels through targeted augmentation and loss weighting
3. Evaluate against a U-Net baseline using IoU and boundary-aware metrics

Methodology:
The public solar-panel aerial dataset (e.g., the Distributed Solar PV dataset) will be tiled and split patient-wise to avoid spatial leakage. A U-Net baseline and a DeepLabv3+ model with a ResNet-50 encoder will be trained, comparing cross-entropy against a Dice+focal loss to handle class imbalance and small objects. Augmentations include rotation, brightness/shadow simulation, and scale jitter. Evaluation uses mean IoU, per-class IoU, and boundary F1, with 5-fold spatial cross-validation and significance testing.

Scope:
The work covers rooftop PV segmentation in RGB aerial tiles for one region. Panel power-output estimation and real-time inference on drones are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A segmentation model exceeding the U-Net baseline mean IoU on shaded/small panels
2. An ablation report quantifying the contribution of loss weighting and shadow augmentation

Timeline:
S1 weeks 1-7 data/tiling and baseline; weeks 8-14 DeepLabv3+ and loss study. S2: augmentation ablation, evaluation, write-up.

Title:
Real-Time Shelf Stock Object Detection for Small Retail Businesses

Problem Statement:
Small retail shops cannot afford enterprise inventory systems, so out-of-stock shelves go unnoticed and sales are lost. A lightweight object detector running on a cheap camera could flag empty or low-stock shelf regions, but small-business settings have cluttered shelves and limited labelled data.

Objectives:
1. Build an object detector that identifies products and empty shelf gaps from shelf images
2. Optimize the model to run in near real time on low-cost hardware
3. Evaluate accuracy and inference speed against a baseline detector

Methodology:
A shelf-image dataset (e.g., SKU-110K plus a small self-labelled set of empty-gap examples) will be used. YOLOv8-nano will be trained for product and gap detection, with transfer learning to handle the small custom set. Model size and speed will be compared between the nano and small variants, and post-training quantization will be applied for edge deployment on a Raspberry Pi or similar. Evaluation uses mAP@0.5, mAP@0.5:0.95, and frames-per-second, against a Faster R-CNN baseline.

Scope:
The project targets packaged-goods shelves under reasonable lighting and one camera angle. Multi-camera fusion and automatic re-ordering are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained shelf-detection model meeting a target FPS on low-cost hardware
2. An accuracy/speed comparison against the Faster R-CNN baseline with quantization results

Timeline:
S1: dataset assembly, labelling, baseline. S2: YOLO training, quantization, edge benchmarking, evaluation.

Title:
Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis of Farmer Feedback on Agricultural Inputs

Problem Statement:
Agricultural suppliers receive feedback from farmers about seeds, fertilizers, and equipment, but a single overall sentiment hides which aspect (price, yield, durability) drives dissatisfaction. Aspect-based sentiment analysis could pinpoint problem areas, yet agricultural text mixes local terms and code-switching that general models handle poorly.

Objectives:
1. Build an aspect-based sentiment model for farmer feedback across defined aspects
2. Adapt a transformer model to agricultural-domain vocabulary
3. Evaluate aspect extraction and sentiment classification against a lexicon baseline

Methodology:
Feedback text will be collected/compiled and annotated for aspects (price, yield, durability, service) and polarity, with inter-annotator agreement reported (Cohen's kappa). A BERT-based model will be fine-tuned for joint aspect-term extraction and aspect sentiment, with domain-adaptive pretraining on unlabelled agricultural text. A VADER/lexicon approach serves as the baseline. Evaluation uses F1 for aspect extraction and macro-F1 for sentiment, with a held-out test set and 5-fold cross-validation.

Scope:
The project handles English (with some code-switched terms) and four predefined aspects. Real-time streaming and multilingual coverage beyond the collected data are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An aspect-based sentiment model outperforming the lexicon baseline on macro-F1
2. An annotated dataset and an error analysis of code-switching failures

Timeline:
S1: data collection, annotation, baseline. S2: fine-tuning, domain adaptation, evaluation, error analysis.

Title:
Learned Cardinality Estimation for Query Optimization in a Transportation Database

Problem Statement:
Transportation systems run analytical queries over large trip and route tables, and slow queries often stem from the optimizer's poor cardinality estimates on correlated columns (e.g., route and time-of-day). Traditional histogram estimators ignore column correlations, leading to bad join orders and high latency.

Objectives:
1. Build a learned cardinality estimator for multi-column predicates on transportation data
2. Compare its estimates and resulting query plans against the database's default estimator
3. Evaluate end-to-end query latency improvements on a benchmark workload

Methodology:
Using a transportation dataset (e.g., NYC taxi trips) loaded into PostgreSQL, a workload of join and filter queries will be generated. A learned estimator (a small neural network / lightweight model trained on query feature vectors and true cardinalities) will predict selectivities, fed back via hints. Evaluation compares estimation q-error and actual execution time against PostgreSQL's default and a sampling-based estimator, across a held-out query set, reporting median and 95th-percentile q-error and latency.

Scope:
The work targets single-table and two-table-join cardinality estimation on one dataset and one DBMS. Full optimizer replacement and distributed query processing are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A learned estimator with lower q-error than the default on correlated predicates
2. A latency comparison showing improved plans on a subset of the benchmark workload

Timeline:
S1: data load, workload generation, baseline measurement. S2: estimator training, integration, latency evaluation.

Title:
Privacy-Aware Facial Recognition Attendance for a Campus Sustainability Program

Problem Statement:
A campus sustainability program runs frequent volunteer sessions where paper sign-in sheets waste paper and time and are easy to falsify. A facial-recognition attendance system could automate sign-in without printouts, but it must handle varying outdoor lighting and protect participant biometric data.

Objectives:
1. Build a facial-recognition attendance system that logs participant check-ins
2. Improve robustness to lighting and pose variation common in outdoor sessions
3. Evaluate recognition accuracy and measure spoof resistance and privacy safeguards

Methodology:
Face detection uses MTCNN and recognition uses FaceNet/ArcFace embeddings compared by cosine similarity against an enrolled gallery; only embeddings (not raw images) are stored, encrypted at rest. A small enrolled set plus augmented samples (brightness, blur, pose) will be used. Evaluation reports identification accuracy, false-accept and false-reject rates at chosen thresholds, and a basic presentation-attack test using printed photos. A non-ML QR fallback handles failures.

Scope:
The system covers up to about 50 enrolled participants in semi-outdoor conditions. Large-scale crowds, liveness hardware (depth/IR), and cross-campus deployment are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working attendance prototype with encrypted embedding storage and a QR fallback
2. An accuracy, FAR/FRR, and basic spoof-resistance evaluation report

Timeline:
S1: detection/recognition pipeline and enrollment. S2: robustness augmentation, privacy/spoof testing, evaluation.

Title:
Robust OCR and Information Extraction for Multi-Format Logistics Shipping Documents

Problem Statement:
Freight forwarders manually key data from heterogeneous shipping documents (bills of lading, commercial invoices, packing lists) that vary in layout, language, scan quality, and contain rotated or stamped regions. Generic OCR achieves high character accuracy on clean text but degrades on these documents, and existing key-information-extraction benchmarks (SROIE, CORD) cover receipts, not multi-page logistics forms, leaving a domain gap in layout-aware extraction under noise.

Objectives:
