1. Build an end-to-end pipeline that OCRs shipping documents and extracts a defined set of fields (shipper, consignee, container number, HS code, totals) with confidence scores
2. Improve extraction robustness to skew, low-resolution scans, and stamps via preprocessing and layout-aware modelling, quantifying each component's contribution
3. Evaluate field-level extraction against a regex-plus-Tesseract baseline and a layout-only baseline, with an error taxonomy and a human-correction-effort metric

Methodology:
A corpus combining public sets (SROIE, RVL-CDIP invoices) with a self-annotated set of logistics documents will be labelled at the field level with double annotation and adjudication (Cohen's kappa reported). The pipeline: deskew and denoise (Hough/CRAFT), OCR with Tesseract and PaddleOCR (compared), then field extraction with a fine-tuned LayoutLMv3 token classifier; outputs carry calibrated confidences (temperature scaling). Baselines are Tesseract+regex and a text-only RoBERTa tagger. Evaluation uses field-level precision/recall/F1, character/word error rate, and end-to-end exact-match per document, with 5-fold cross-validation, paired bootstrap significance tests, and an ablation isolating deskew, OCR engine, and layout features. Risks (label scarcity, class imbalance for rare fields) are mitigated with augmentation and active learning on low-confidence samples.

Scope:
Covers English-language single- and multi-page scanned PDFs/images for three document types and seven target fields. Handwritten free-text fields, non-Latin scripts, and production system integration are explicitly excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A reproducible OCR-plus-extraction pipeline with calibrated confidences and a released annotated logistics-document subset
2. An evaluation and ablation report showing field-F1 gains over both baselines, with an error taxonomy and an estimate of reduced manual-correction effort

Timeline:
S1 w1-4 dataset assembly/annotation; w5-9 preprocessing+OCR comparison and baselines; w10-14 LayoutLMv3 fine-tuning. S2 w1-5 confidence calibration+active learning; w6-10 ablation and significance testing; w11-14 error analysis and write-up.

Title:
Anomaly Detection in Wireless Sensor Network Data for E-Government Facility Monitoring

Problem Statement:
Government buildings increasingly deploy wireless sensor networks (temperature, occupancy, power, air quality) for smart facility management, but the streams are noisy, contain missing values from node dropout, and exhibit drift, so naive threshold alarms produce excessive false positives. Existing public anomaly benchmarks are largely univariate or synthetic, under-representing the correlated, intermittently-missing multivariate streams of real WSN deployments, which limits operator trust and timely fault response.

Objectives:
1. Build a multivariate anomaly detector for WSN telemetry that is robust to missing values and sensor drift, emitting ranked alerts with severity
2. Compare reconstruction-based and forecasting-based deep models against classical baselines under realistic missingness, isolating the effect of each design choice
3. Evaluate detection quality and operational practicality (alert volume, lead time) and analyse failure cases

Methodology:
Public multivariate datasets (SWaT/WADI for infrastructure plus Intel Lab WSN sensor data) will be used, with injected node-dropout and drift to mimic facility conditions; train/validation/test split chronologically to prevent leakage. Models: an LSTM-autoencoder and a Transformer-based forecaster (Anomaly Transformer) with masking to tolerate gaps, benchmarked against Isolation Forest, a seasonal-ARIMA residual detector, and a moving-z-score baseline. Preprocessing handles missingness via masked inputs and imputation comparison. Evaluation uses point-adjusted precision/recall/F1, PR-AUC, and a delay-aware detection score, with 5-fold time-series CV, threshold selection on validation only, and statistical comparison via paired tests. Risks (label scarcity, distribution shift) are handled with semi-supervised training and a drift-monitoring check.

Scope:
Covers offline batch and streaming-replay detection on the listed multivariate datasets with four to six sensor channels. Live deployment to actual government hardware, root-cause diagnosis, and automated actuation are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A robust multivariate WSN anomaly detector with documented tolerance to missing data and drift
2. A benchmark report ranking deep and classical methods on detection quality and alert practicality, with an ablation and failure-case analysis

Timeline:
S1 w1-4 data prep, dropout/drift injection, baselines; w5-9 LSTM-AE; w10-14 Anomaly Transformer. S2 w1-5 missingness/drift robustness study; w6-10 delay-aware evaluation and significance tests; w11-14 failure analysis and write-up.

Title:
Machine Learning for E-Government

Problem Statement:
Government online services are slow and people are not happy. We want to use machine learning to fix this and classify things automatically.

Objectives:
1. Make a machine learning system
2. Classify government data
3. Help citizens

Methodology:
I will use Python and some ML algorithms to classify the data. I will collect some data and train a model. Then I will check if it works.

Scope:
This project is for all government departments and can be used by any citizen in the country.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working classifier
2. Happier citizens

Title:
Deep Learning Computer Vision in Education

Problem Statement:
Schools have a lot of images and videos but nobody knows what to do with them. Deep learning is very powerful so it can help education become smarter.

Objectives:
1. Use deep learning
2. Do computer vision on education images
3. Improve learning

Methodology:
I will build a deep learning model using neural networks. The model will look at pictures and understand them. I will use a GPU to train it faster.

Scope:
The system will work for every school and every subject and all kinds of images.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A smart vision system
2. Better education

Title:
NLP for Retail Shops

Problem Statement:
Retail shops get many customer messages and reviews. Reading them takes too long. Natural language processing can read text very fast so it will solve this problem.

Objectives:
1. Apply NLP to retail text
2. Understand customers
3. Increase sales

Methodology:
I plan to use natural language processing techniques to analyse the text. I will use a library and do some processing on the words. After that I will see the results and write a report.

Scope:
It is for all retail businesses everywhere and works on any language.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An NLP tool for retail
2. More profit for shops

Title:
A Recommender System for Smart City Services

Problem Statement:
Residents in a smart city have access to many public services such as transport, libraries and recreation centres, but they often do not know which ones are relevant to them. A recommender system could suggest useful services, but most city portals only show a static list.

Objectives:
1. Collect data about city services and resident usage
2. Build a recommender system that suggests services
3. Test whether residents find the suggestions useful

Methodology:
I will use collaborative filtering to recommend services based on what similar residents used. The system will be built as a web application with a Python backend. I will gather some usage data and evaluate the recommendations with a small group of users.

Scope:
The project focuses on one city's public services and a limited set of categories. Real-time location data is not included.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working recommender web application
2. Feedback from test users on recommendation quality

Timeline:
The project will run over two semesters with development in the first and testing in the second.

Title:
Speech Recognition for a Tourism Assistant

Problem Statement:
Tourists visiting a new region often need information but find typing on a phone slow, especially when their hands are busy. A voice-based assistant could help, yet many existing tourism apps only support text input and ignore spoken queries.

Objectives:
1. Build a speech recognition module for tourist questions
2. Connect it to a simple tourism information database
3. Measure how accurately spoken queries are understood

Methodology:
I will use an existing speech-to-text engine to convert voice into text, then match the text to answers about attractions and transport. The app will be developed for Android. Accuracy will be checked by recording sample questions and comparing the recognised text.

Scope:
The assistant covers one tourist city and supports English speech only. Offline use and multiple languages are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A voice-driven tourism information app
2. An accuracy report on recognised queries

Timeline:
Development takes place across two semesters, with testing near the end.

Title:
Network Intrusion Detection for Social Media Platforms

Problem Statement:
Social media platforms are frequent targets of network attacks such as port scans and denial-of-service attempts. Administrators need to spot suspicious traffic early, but reviewing raw logs manually is impractical given the volume of connections.

Objectives:
1. Prepare a labelled network traffic dataset
2. Train a classifier to detect intrusion attempts
3. Evaluate detection accuracy and false alarms

Methodology:
I will use a public intrusion dataset such as NSL-KDD and train a decision tree and a random forest to classify traffic as normal or attack. The models will be compared using accuracy and false positive rate. Preprocessing will handle feature scaling.

Scope:
The project works offline on an existing dataset and focuses on a few common attack types. Live deployment on a real platform is excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained intrusion detection model
2. A comparison of the two classifiers

Timeline:
Two semesters: data and training first, evaluation second.

Title:
Web Application Security Testing for a Healthcare Portal

Problem Statement:
Healthcare portals store sensitive patient records, so security flaws can have serious consequences. Small clinics often deploy web portals without thorough security testing, leaving common vulnerabilities such as injection and weak authentication unchecked.

Objectives:
1. Identify common web vulnerabilities in a sample healthcare portal
2. Apply automated and manual testing to find them
3. Recommend fixes for the issues found

Methodology:
I will build a small sample healthcare portal and test it using tools such as OWASP ZAP for automated scanning, plus manual checks against the OWASP Top 10. Found issues will be documented and basic fixes applied and re-tested.

Scope:
The project tests one self-built portal and focuses on the OWASP Top 10. Network and physical security are not covered.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A vulnerability report on the sample portal
2. A patched version with fixes verified

Timeline:
Building and testing in semester one, fixing and reporting in semester two.

Title:
Static and Dynamic Malware Analysis for Financial Sector Threats

Problem Statement:
Financial institutions are heavily targeted by banking trojans and ransomware that evade signature-based antivirus. Analysts need to understand the behaviour of suspicious samples, but combining static indicators with runtime behaviour into a single readable report is time consuming and inconsistent across teams.

Objectives:
1. Collect a set of labelled malicious and benign Windows samples
2. Extract static features and observe dynamic behaviour in a sandbox
3. Build a classifier that flags likely banking malware and produce an analysis report

Methodology:
Static analysis will extract PE header fields, imported API calls and strings, while dynamic analysis will run samples in a Cuckoo sandbox to capture API call traces and file/registry activity. Features from both will train a random forest classifier, evaluated with precision, recall and a confusion matrix on a held-out test set.

Scope:
The project targets Windows executables and a curated sample set from public repositories. It excludes packed-sample unpacking research and mobile malware.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained classifier with reported precision and recall
2. A combined static-dynamic analysis report template

Timeline:
Semester one: dataset and sandbox setup. Semester two: feature extraction, training and evaluation.

Title:
A Responsive Web Platform for Manufacturing Production Tracking

Problem Statement:
Small manufacturing firms often track production orders on spreadsheets and whiteboards, which makes it hard for supervisors and floor workers to see live status. A responsive web platform accessible from desktops on the floor and phones on the move could centralise this, but off-the-shelf ERP systems are too costly and complex for small plants.

Objectives:
1. Gather requirements from a small manufacturing workflow
2. Build a responsive web platform to record and track production orders
3. Evaluate usability with floor staff

Methodology:
The platform will use a React frontend and a Spring Boot REST API with a MySQL database. The layout will be made responsive with a CSS framework so it works on phones and desktops. Role-based access will separate supervisors from operators. Usability will be assessed with a SUS questionnaire after a trial.

Scope:
The system covers production order tracking and status updates for one product line. Inventory procurement and payroll are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A deployed responsive web platform
2. A usability evaluation report

Timeline:
Requirements and design first semester; build and evaluation second semester.

Title:
A Progressive Web App for Public Safety Incident Reporting

Problem Statement:
Residents who witness hazards such as flooding, road damage or fires often have no quick way to report them to local authorities, and native apps require installation that many users avoid. A progressive web app could allow fast reporting from any device, including offline capture when connectivity is poor during emergencies.

Objectives:
1. Design an incident reporting workflow for residents and authority staff
2. Build a progressive web app with offline submission and location tagging
3. Evaluate report turnaround and user satisfaction in a small trial

Methodology:
The PWA will be built with React and a service worker for offline caching, storing pending reports in IndexedDB and syncing when online. Geolocation will tag incidents and an authority dashboard will triage them. A small trial will measure submission success and gather feedback via a short survey.

Scope:
The project covers resident reporting and a basic triage dashboard for one municipality. Dispatch integration with emergency services is excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An installable PWA with offline reporting
2. A trial report on usability and turnaround

Timeline:
Design and core build in semester one; offline sync, dashboard and trial in semester two.

Title:
A Cross-Platform Mobile App for Household Energy Monitoring

Problem Statement:
Households rarely understand which appliances drive their electricity bills because utility statements arrive monthly and show only a total. A mobile app that visualises consumption could encourage saving, but building separate iOS and Android apps doubles the effort for a single developer.

Objectives:
1. Let users log appliance usage and import meter readings
2. Build a cross-platform app that visualises consumption trends
3. Evaluate whether the app changes user awareness of usage

Methodology:
The app will be built with Flutter so a single codebase targets Android and iOS. Users enter readings or appliance hours, and the app charts daily and weekly usage with simple tips. Data is stored locally with optional cloud backup via Firebase. A two-week trial with a short pre/post survey will assess awareness change.

Scope:
The app relies on manual readings and basic appliance estimates for individual households. Direct smart-meter hardware integration is out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A cross-platform energy monitoring app
2. Survey results on awareness change

Timeline:
Semester one: design and core app. Semester two: charts, backup and the user trial.

Title:
An Android Native App for Small Business Appointment Booking

Problem Statement:
Small service businesses such as salons and repair shops still manage bookings by phone and paper diaries, leading to double bookings and missed appointments. An affordable Android app for managing appointments could reduce these errors, but existing booking platforms charge monthly fees that small owners are reluctant to pay.

Objectives:
1. Capture the booking needs of a small service business
2. Build a native Android app for scheduling and reminders
3. Evaluate booking errors and owner satisfaction

Methodology:
The app will be developed natively in Kotlin using Android Jetpack components and a Room database for offline storage, with optional sync to a Firebase backend. It will support creating, editing and cancelling appointments and sending local notification reminders. A trial with one business will compare booking errors before and after, plus an owner interview.

Scope:
The app targets single-location businesses on Android phones. Online customer self-booking and payment processing are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working Android booking app with reminders
2. A short evaluation of booking accuracy and satisfaction

Timeline:
Requirements and UI in semester one; scheduling, reminders and trial in semester two.

Title:
An IoT Sensor Network for Greenhouse Crop Monitoring

Problem Statement:
Smallholder greenhouse farmers struggle to maintain ideal growing conditions because they check temperature and soil moisture manually and infrequently. Poor timing of watering and ventilation reduces yield, and commercial monitoring kits are priced for large commercial farms rather than small operations.

Objectives:
1. Build a low-cost sensor node measuring temperature, humidity and soil moisture
2. Transmit readings to a dashboard and alert on threshold breaches
3. Evaluate measurement reliability over a trial period

Methodology:
Sensor nodes based on an ESP32 with DHT22 and capacitive soil-moisture sensors will publish readings over Wi-Fi using MQTT to a Raspberry Pi broker. A web dashboard will chart trends and send alerts when readings cross set thresholds. Reliability will be checked by comparing sensor readings against a reference meter over two weeks.

Scope:
The prototype covers one greenhouse with a few nodes and three measured variables. Automated actuation of irrigation or vents is excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working sensor network with a live dashboard
2. A reliability report comparing sensor and reference readings

Timeline:
Hardware and firmware in semester one; dashboard, alerts and field trial in semester two.

Title:
Context-Aware Smart Home Automation Linked to Commute Conditions

Problem Statement:
Smart home routines today fire on fixed schedules and ignore the occupant's actual commute, so heating, charging and lighting waste energy when arrival is delayed by traffic. There is little work connecting live transportation conditions to home automation decisions for a single household, leaving a gap between mobility data and home energy control.

Objectives:
1. Integrate live transit and traffic estimates into a home automation controller by week 6
2. Implement a rule-and-prediction engine that adjusts heating, EV charging and lighting based on predicted arrival time
3. Evaluate energy use and comfort against a fixed-schedule baseline over a four-week trial

Methodology:
A Home Assistant instance will control simulated and real smart plugs and a thermostat. A Python service will pull travel-time estimates from a routing API and predict arrival with a regression model, triggering automations a tuned lead time before arrival. Evaluation compares energy consumption (kWh) and a comfort metric against the default schedule, using paired comparison across matched days.

Scope:
The project covers one occupant's commute and three device categories. It excludes multi-occupant scheduling and security automation.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working commute-aware automation controller
2. A measured energy-versus-comfort comparison against the baseline

Timeline:
Weeks 1-6 integration, 7-10 prediction engine, 11-14 trial and analysis.

Title:
Edge Computing for On-Device Litter Detection in Sustainability Monitoring

Problem Statement:
City sustainability programmes want to map littering hotspots, but streaming camera footage to the cloud for analysis is bandwidth-heavy and raises privacy concerns. Running detection on the edge avoids both, yet deploying accurate object detection on low-power devices forces a trade-off between accuracy and latency that is rarely quantified for this task.

Objectives:
1. Curate and label a litter image dataset for model training by week 5
2. Train and compress a detector to run on an edge device within a latency budget
3. Quantify the accuracy-versus-latency trade-off across model variants

Methodology:
A YOLOv8-nano model will be trained on the TACO litter dataset plus self-collected images. The model will be quantised with INT8 and deployed to a Raspberry Pi with a Coral TPU and to a Jetson Nano. Mean average precision (mAP) will be measured on a held-out test set, and inference latency and power draw will be logged per device and per quantisation level, with a no-compression baseline.

Scope:
The project covers static-mounted single-camera detection of common litter classes. Multi-camera tracking and on-device retraining are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A deployable edge litter detector with reported mAP
2. An accuracy/latency/power trade-off analysis across devices

Timeline:
Weeks 1-5 data, 6-9 training and compression, 10-14 deployment and benchmarking.

Title:
A Cloud-Native Microservices Backend for Last-Mile Logistics Tracking

Problem Statement:
Last-mile delivery firms run monolithic tracking systems that struggle to scale during peak periods and couple parcel, driver and notification logic together, making independent deployment risky. A cloud-native microservices design promises elastic scaling, but small logistics teams lack a clear reference for how the services should be decomposed and how they behave under load.

Objectives:
1. Decompose tracking into parcel, routing, driver and notification services by week 6
2. Deploy the services on Kubernetes with an API gateway and asynchronous messaging
3. Measure scalability and resilience under simulated peak load

Methodology:
Each service will be a Spring Boot application communicating via REST and Kafka events, containerised with Docker and orchestrated on a local Kubernetes cluster with horizontal pod autoscaling. A PostgreSQL-per-service pattern will enforce data ownership. Load will be generated with k6 to measure p95 latency and throughput, and chaos tests will kill pods to observe recovery against a monolithic baseline.

Scope:
The project delivers four core services and a load/resilience evaluation. Real courier hardware, billing and a production UI are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A deployable microservices tracking backend on Kubernetes
2. A scalability and resilience report versus a monolith

Timeline:
Weeks 1-6 decomposition, 7-10 orchestration, 11-14 load and chaos testing.

Title:
A DevOps CI/CD Pipeline with Automated Quality Gates for E-Government Services

Problem Statement:
E-government teams often deploy citizen services manually, which is slow and error-prone and makes security regressions easy to miss before release. Adopting CI/CD with automated quality gates could shorten lead time, but there is limited guidance on which gates matter most for public-sector web services and how they affect deployment speed and defect escape.

Objectives:
1. Build a CI/CD pipeline for a sample citizen-service application by week 5
2. Add automated quality gates for tests, code quality and security scanning
3. Measure the effect of the gates on lead time and defect escape

Methodology:
The pipeline will use GitHub Actions to build, run unit and integration tests, run SonarQube static analysis and run an OWASP dependency and ZAP security scan, blocking merges that fail thresholds. Deployment will target a staging Kubernetes namespace. DORA-style metrics (lead time, deployment frequency, change failure rate) will be measured with and without the gates using a seeded set of changes.

Scope:
The project automates one sample service and four gate types. Multi-team governance and production rollout to real citizens are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working CI/CD pipeline with enforced quality gates
2. A before/after analysis of delivery and defect metrics

Timeline:
Weeks 1-5 pipeline, 6-9 gates, 10-14 metric collection and analysis.

Title:
A Big Data Analytics Pipeline for Early Detection of Student Disengagement

Problem Statement:
Universities collect large volumes of learning-management-system logs, yet most early-warning systems run on small samples and cannot process clickstream data at scale or in near real time. As a result, signs of disengagement are noticed too late for timely intervention, and there is little work on a streaming pipeline that turns raw LMS events into actionable risk signals.

Objectives:
1. Ingest and clean LMS clickstream events into a scalable store by week 5
2. Build a batch-and-streaming pipeline that computes engagement features
3. Train and evaluate a model that flags at-risk students with calibrated thresholds

Methodology:
Events from the OULAD dataset, replayed through Kafka, will be processed by Spark Structured Streaming to compute per-student engagement features into a Parquet/Delta store. A gradient-boosted model will predict disengagement, evaluated with AUC, precision-recall and calibration on a temporal hold-out, against a logistic-regression baseline. The pipeline's throughput and latency will also be reported.

Scope:
The project uses an existing public LMS dataset and produces weekly risk flags. Live integration with a real LMS and intervention delivery are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working batch/streaming analytics pipeline
2. An evaluated disengagement model with throughput figures

Timeline:
Weeks 1-5 ingestion, 6-9 feature pipeline, 10-14 modelling and evaluation.

Title:
A Self-Service Business Intelligence Dashboard with Explainable Markdown Recommendations for Fashion Retail

Problem Statement:
Mid-sized fashion retailers hold excess seasonal stock because category managers rely on static weekly spreadsheets that show what sold but not why, and existing BI dashboards visualise sales without suggesting concrete, defensible markdown actions. The unmet need is a dashboard that not only surfaces sell-through and margin metrics but also recommends markdown timing per SKU with a transparent justification managers can trust and override.

Objectives:
1. Design a star-schema warehouse and load 18 months of point-of-sale and inventory data by week 4
2. Implement an interactive dashboard exposing sell-through, weeks-of-cover and margin at SKU, category and store levels by week 9
3. Add an explainable markdown-timing recommender and evaluate its decisions against historical outcomes and a manager baseline by week 13

Methodology:
Data will be modelled as a Kimball star schema in PostgreSQL and transformed with dbt, with the dashboard built in a React frontend backed by a metrics API. The recommender will estimate per-SKU sell-through trajectories with a gradient-boosted survival-style model and trigger markdown suggestions using inventory-cover thresholds, with SHAP values rendered as plain-language reasons. Evaluation will back-test against held-out historical seasons, comparing realised gross margin and end-of-season residual stock against the retailer's actual markdowns, with a manager-rule baseline and sensitivity analysis on thresholds.

Scope:
The project covers womenswear apparel for one retailer across up to five stores and excludes price elasticity from competitor data, e-commerce returns modelling and automated repricing execution; recommendations are advisory only.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A deployed self-service BI dashboard with drill-down and role-based views
2. A back-tested evaluation showing margin and residual-stock impact of the explainable recommender versus baselines

Timeline:
Weeks 1-4 warehouse and ETL, 5-9 dashboard, 10-13 recommender and back-testing, 14 documentation; key risk is data-quality gaps in historical POS, mitigated by an early profiling and cleaning pass.

Title:
Probabilistic Short-Term Forecasting of Smart-City Parking Occupancy with Calibrated Uncertainty

Problem Statement:
Smart-city parking guidance fails drivers when it shows only a single predicted occupancy number, because point forecasts hide the risk that a lot is actually full on arrival. Most published parking models report only mean error and ignore calibrated uncertainty, so guidance systems cannot express confidence and over-direct drivers to lots that fill within minutes. There is a need for a short-horizon forecaster that produces calibrated probability intervals usable by a routing layer.

Objectives:
1. Assemble and clean a multi-lot occupancy time series with weather and event covariates by week 4
2. Build and compare point and probabilistic forecasters at 15-, 30- and 60-minute horizons by week 10
3. Evaluate calibration and sharpness against baselines and quantify guidance impact in simulation by week 13

Methodology:
Using the Birmingham parking dataset augmented with calendar, weather and event covariates, I will engineer lag and rolling features and train seasonal-naive and SARIMAX baselines, a LightGBM quantile-regression model and a Temporal Fusion Transformer for probabilistic forecasts. Models are evaluated with rolling-origin cross-validation using MAE and RMSE for point accuracy, plus pinball loss, prediction-interval coverage probability and a reliability diagram for calibration. A routing simulation then measures reduced over-recommendation of soon-full lots versus a point-forecast strategy.

Scope:
The project covers short-horizon occupancy forecasting for one city's monitored lots using historical and covariate data; live sensor integration, payment systems and the production routing UI are explicitly excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A calibrated probabilistic parking forecaster with documented coverage and sharpness
2. A reproducible benchmark comparing models and a simulated guidance-quality improvement

Timeline:
Weeks 1-4 data, 5-10 modelling and tuning, 11-13 evaluation and simulation, 14 write-up; main risk is sensor gaps, mitigated with imputation and gap-aware cross-validation folds.

Title:
Machine Learning for Energy

Problem Statement:
Energy is very important for everyone and there is a lot of data about power. Machine learning can help classify this data and make energy companies better.

Objectives:
1. To classify energy data.
2. To use machine learning.
3. To help energy.

Methodology:
I will get some energy data and run machine learning classification in Python to see the results. Then I will check the accuracy.

Scope:
This will work for all power plants and energy companies in the world for any kind of energy.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A machine learning classifier.
2. Better energy management.

Title:
Deep Learning Vision for Small Business

Problem Statement:
Small businesses have many photos and images. Deep learning and computer vision are powerful trending technologies that can look at pictures and help shops do better.

Objectives:
1. To use deep learning.
2. To analyze business images.
3. To help small business owners.

Methodology:
I will use a neural network with computer vision to look at the images. I will train it and test it using Python libraries.

Scope:
The system covers every small business and any photo they have, anywhere.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A computer vision model.
2. Happy small business owners.

Title:
NLP for Farming

Problem Statement:
Agriculture has a lot of text like reports and notes. NLP is a modern technology that reads text and understands it so farmers can grow more crops.

Objectives:
1. To use natural language processing.
2. To read farming text.
3. To help agriculture.

Methodology:
I will collect agriculture text and apply NLP techniques in Python to process the words. After that I will look at whether it works well.

Scope:
This project helps all farms and farmers everywhere with any text about crops or animals.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An NLP system for farming.
2. More crops for farmers.

Title:
A Recommender System for Public Bus Routes

Problem Statement:
Many commuters in the city struggle to pick the best bus route, especially new residents who do not know the network. A recommender system could suggest suitable routes based on a user's past trips, but most current apps only show schedules without personalised suggestions.

Objectives:
1. To collect bus trip and route data for a city.
2. To build a recommender system that suggests bus routes.
3. To evaluate the recommendations with users.

Methodology:
The project will use collaborative filtering to recommend routes based on similar commuters. A dataset of trips will be gathered or simulated, and Python with the Surprise library will be used to build the model. The output will be shown in a simple web interface.

Scope:
The system focuses on bus routes in one city only and does not cover trains or taxis. It will handle a limited set of routes for testing.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working bus route recommender prototype.
2. An evaluation showing whether users find the routes helpful.

Timeline:
The project runs over two semesters, with data collection first, then model building, then testing.

Title:
Voice Command Recognition for an Eco-Friendly Home Assistant

Problem Statement:
People want to control devices by voice to save effort, and a voice assistant could help households reduce wasted electricity by switching off idle appliances. However, building accurate speech recognition for simple home commands is still a challenge for non-experts.

Objectives:
1. To record a small set of spoken commands for controlling appliances.
2. To train a speech recognition model for these commands.
3. To connect the recognised commands to a simulated smart plug.

Methodology:
The project will use an open speech dataset plus self-recorded samples. A model will be trained using Python and a library such as TensorFlow or a pretrained model like Wav2Vec, then tested on held-out audio. Recognised words will trigger actions in a small simulation.

Scope:
Only about ten English commands are covered. Continuous conversation and other languages are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A speech recognition prototype for home commands.
2. A report on recognition accuracy.

Timeline:
Roughly two semesters: data preparation, training, then integration and testing.

Title:
Network Intrusion Detection for a Logistics Company Network

Problem Statement:
Logistics firms increasingly rely on connected systems for tracking shipments, which makes them targets for network attacks. Smaller firms often cannot afford commercial intrusion detection, so a lightweight machine-learning detector could help flag suspicious traffic.

Objectives:
1. To study a public intrusion detection dataset.
2. To train a classifier that detects malicious network traffic.
3. To measure detection accuracy.

Methodology:
The NSL-KDD dataset will be used to train and test classifiers such as Random Forest and Decision Tree in Python with scikit-learn. Features will be selected to reduce dimensionality, and accuracy and false-positive rate will be reported on a test split.

Scope:
The project works offline on an existing dataset and does not deploy on live company traffic. Only common attack categories in the dataset are considered.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained intrusion detection model.
2. A comparison of accuracy across the chosen algorithms.

Timeline:
Two semesters covering dataset study, model training, and evaluation.

Title:
A Vulnerability Scanner for E-Government Web Portals

Problem Statement:
E-government portals handle citizen data, so security flaws can be serious. Common issues like SQL injection and cross-site scripting still appear in many portals, and a simple scanning tool could help developers catch these before deployment.

Objectives:
1. To identify common web vulnerabilities relevant to e-government portals.
2. To build a tool that scans a test web application for these issues.
3. To validate the tool on a deliberately vulnerable application.

Methodology:
The tool will be written in Python and will send crafted requests to detect SQL injection and XSS, inspired by how OWASP ZAP works. It will be tested against the intentionally vulnerable DVWA application, and detected issues will be compared with known ones.

Scope:
Only SQL injection and XSS are covered, on test applications under my control. No scanning of real government sites is done.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working scanner prototype for two vulnerability types.
2. A test report on detection coverage against DVWA.

Timeline:
Two semesters: research, tool building, then testing on DVWA.

Title:
Static and Dynamic Analysis of Android Malware in Educational Apps

Problem Statement:
Students increasingly install learning apps from unofficial stores, some of which carry malware that steals credentials or data. There is little guidance aimed at school IT staff on how to quickly triage a suspicious education-related APK. This project builds a small analysis pipeline to classify Android samples as benign or malicious and explain the indicators found.

Objectives:
1. To assemble a labelled set of benign and malicious Android samples relevant to education apps.
2. To extract static features (permissions, API calls) and basic dynamic behaviour in a sandbox.
3. To train and evaluate a classifier and produce a readable indicator report.

Methodology:
Static features will be extracted with Androguard, and dynamic traces collected by running samples in an emulator. A Random Forest classifier will be trained on combined features and evaluated with accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 using a held-out test set. Results will be compared against a permissions-only baseline.

Scope:
The work covers Android only and a few hundred samples; iOS, packed/obfuscated malware, and full reverse engineering are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working static-plus-dynamic classification pipeline.
2. An evaluation report comparing the model with the baseline.

Timeline:
Semester 1: dataset and feature extraction. Semester 2: modelling, evaluation, and reporting.

Title:
A Responsive Web Platform for Local Retail Inventory and Orders

Problem Statement:
Small retail shops often track stock on paper or spreadsheets, leading to stock-outs and lost sales. Affordable, easy-to-use web tools tailored to single-store retailers are scarce. This project develops a responsive web platform where a shop owner can manage inventory, record sales, and view low-stock alerts on any device.

Objectives:
1. To gather requirements from two or three local shop owners.
2. To build a responsive web application for inventory and order management.
3. To evaluate usability and the accuracy of stock tracking.

Methodology:
The platform will be built with React on the front end and a Node.js/Express REST API backed by PostgreSQL. Development follows an iterative approach with feedback from shop owners. Usability will be assessed with the System Usability Scale, and stock accuracy will be checked against manual counts.

Scope:
The system targets a single store with one user account type and excludes multi-branch support, payment gateways, and supplier integrations.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A deployed responsive web platform for retail inventory and orders.
2. A usability and accuracy evaluation report.

Timeline:
Semester 1: requirements and core build. Semester 2: alerts, testing, and evaluation.

Title:
A Progressive Web App for Citizen Reporting of Smart City Issues

Problem Statement:
Residents often have no easy way to report potholes, broken lights, or illegal dumping, and existing portals work poorly on low-end phones with patchy connectivity. A progressive web app that works offline and installs without an app store could lower the barrier to reporting and help city teams prioritise repairs.

Objectives:
1. To design a citizen reporting flow with photo and geolocation capture.
2. To build a progressive web app with offline submission and background sync.
3. To evaluate offline reliability and usability with test users.

Methodology:
The PWA will use a service worker for caching and IndexedDB to queue reports made offline, syncing when connectivity returns. The front end uses a framework such as Vue, with a lightweight backend storing reports. Offline behaviour will be tested under simulated network loss, and ten users will complete tasks rated with the System Usability Scale.

Scope:
The project covers reporting and status viewing for one issue category set in one district; routing reports to real city departments is out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An installable PWA supporting offline citizen reports.
2. A test report on offline reliability and usability.

Timeline:
Semester 1: design and core PWA. Semester 2: offline sync, testing, evaluation.

Title:
A Cross-Platform Mobile App for Personalised Local Tourism Itineraries

Problem Statement:
Tourists visiting a city often rely on scattered blogs and generic listings, making it hard to plan a day that fits their interests and time. A mobile app that builds a simple itinerary from chosen interests and available hours could improve the visitor experience for a single destination city.

Objectives:
1. To collect a curated dataset of attractions with categories, hours, and locations.
2. To build a cross-platform mobile app that generates a day itinerary from user preferences.
3. To evaluate itinerary quality and app usability with test users.

Methodology:
The app will be built with Flutter for Android and iOS, calling a Firebase backend for attraction data. A rule-based itinerary builder will order attractions by category match, opening hours, and travel time from map data. Usability will be measured with the System Usability Scale, and itinerary relevance rated by ten test users.

Scope:
One destination city and a fixed attraction dataset are covered; live bookings, payments, and real-time crowd data are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A cross-platform tourism app producing day itineraries.
2. An evaluation of itinerary relevance and usability.

Timeline:
Semester 1: data and app skeleton. Semester 2: itinerary logic, testing, evaluation.

Title:
A Native Android App for Detecting Misinformation Cues on Social Media Posts

Problem Statement:
Users scrolling social media struggle to judge whether a post is reliable. While full fact-checking is hard, surface cues such as sensational wording, missing sources, and known-suspicious links can flag posts worth a second look. This project builds a native Android app that highlights such cues for text users paste in.

Objectives:
1. To define a set of detectable misinformation cues from existing literature.
2. To build a native Android app that scores pasted post text against these cues.
3. To evaluate the app's flagging against a small labelled set of posts.

Methodology:
The app will be developed in Kotlin using Android Studio. A lightweight on-device rule and keyword model will score text for sensational language, absence of cited sources, and blacklisted domains. The flagging will be compared against a labelled sample of 100 posts using precision and recall, and five users will rate usability.

Scope:
English text-only posts pasted by the user are handled; images, video, and automatic scraping of live feeds are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A native Android app that highlights misinformation cues.
2. A small evaluation of flagging accuracy and usability.

Timeline:
Semester 1: cue research and app build. Semester 2: scoring logic, evaluation, reporting.

Title:
An IoT Sensor Network for Monitoring Vaccine Refrigerator Conditions in Clinics

Problem Statement:
Vaccines lose potency if storage temperature drifts outside a safe range, yet small clinics often check fridges manually and miss overnight excursions. A low-cost IoT sensor network that logs temperature and humidity and alerts staff to breaches could reduce spoiled stock and improve patient safety.

Objectives:
1. To build temperature and humidity sensor nodes for clinic refrigerators.
2. To collect readings centrally and raise alerts when thresholds are breached.
3. To evaluate measurement accuracy and alert reliability over a trial period.

Methodology:
Each node uses an ESP32 with a DHT22/DS18B20 sensor publishing readings over MQTT to a Raspberry Pi broker and a small dashboard. Alerts trigger when readings exceed configured thresholds. Sensor accuracy will be checked against a calibrated thermometer, and alert reliability assessed by inducing controlled excursions over a two-week test.

Scope:
The prototype covers up to three sensor nodes in a single clinic setting; integration with national cold-chain systems is excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working IoT monitoring prototype with alerting.
2. An evaluation of accuracy and alert reliability.

Timeline:
Semester 1: hardware and data pipeline. Semester 2: alerting, trial, evaluation.

Title:
A Privacy-Preserving Smart Home Automation Hub with On-Device Energy-Cost Optimisation

Problem Statement:
Most smart home hubs send usage data to vendor clouds and optimise comfort rather than cost, which concerns privacy-conscious households facing time-of-use electricity tariffs. There is a gap for a local-first hub that schedules appliances to cut electricity bills under variable tariffs without exporting data off-device. This project builds and evaluates such a hub against a cloud-dependent baseline.

Objectives:
1. To design a local automation hub that ingests appliance and tariff data without cloud dependence.
2. To implement a rule-plus-optimisation scheduler that shifts flexible loads to cheaper tariff windows.
3. To evaluate cost savings, privacy properties, and scheduling latency against a cloud-rule baseline.

Methodology:
The hub runs on a Raspberry Pi with Home Assistant and MQTT, controlling simulated and two physical smart plugs. A linear-programming scheduler (PuLP) minimises cost given a published time-of-use tariff and appliance flexibility windows. Evaluation uses a one-week simulated load profile, reporting percentage bill reduction versus an always-on baseline, scheduling latency, and a data-flow analysis confirming no off-device transmission.

Scope:
The work covers deferrable loads (washer, dryer, water heater) under a single residential tariff; HVAC modelling, battery storage, and multi-home coordination are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A local-first smart home hub with a cost-aware scheduler.
2. An evaluation quantifying bill savings and confirming data stays on-device.

Timeline:
Semester 1: hub setup, device integration, baseline. Semester 2: scheduler, evaluation, write-up.

Title:
Edge-Based Real-Time Defect Detection for a Manufacturing Conveyor Line

Problem Statement:
Manufacturers want to catch surface defects on parts before they move downstream, but sending high-frame-rate video to the cloud adds latency and bandwidth cost. Running detection on the edge is appealing yet constrained by limited compute. This project evaluates whether a quantised vision model on an edge device can detect defects in near real time with acceptable accuracy.

Objectives:
1. To build a labelled image set of defective and good parts using a public surface-defect dataset plus captured samples.
2. To train and quantise a compact detector that runs on an edge device.
3. To evaluate accuracy and end-to-end latency on the edge versus a cloud-inference baseline.

Methodology:
A MobileNetV2-based classifier (and a YOLOv8-nano detector for localisation) will be trained in PyTorch on the NEU surface-defect dataset augmented with captured images, then quantised to INT8 and deployed via TensorFlow Lite on a Raspberry Pi with a camera over a small conveyor rig. Metrics include precision, recall, F1, frames per second, and per-frame latency, compared against full-precision cloud inference.

Scope:
One part type and three defect classes on a bench-scale conveyor are covered; full PLC integration and multi-camera setups are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An edge-deployed defect detector running in near real time.
2. An accuracy-versus-latency comparison against a cloud baseline.

Timeline:
Semester 1: dataset, model training. Semester 2: quantisation, edge deployment, evaluation.

Title:
A Cloud-Native Microservices Backend for Public-Safety Incident Reporting and Dispatch

Problem Statement:
Public-safety incident systems must stay available during surges when many reports arrive at once, yet monolithic backends scale poorly and fail as a unit. A microservices architecture promises independent scaling and fault isolation, but the trade-offs in complexity and latency are worth measuring for a student-scale system. This project builds and load-tests such a backend.

Objectives:
1. To decompose incident reporting, dispatch assignment, and notification into independent services.
2. To deploy the services on Kubernetes with an API gateway and asynchronous messaging.
3. To evaluate scalability, fault isolation, and latency under load against a monolithic baseline.

Methodology:
Services are built in Spring Boot, communicating via REST and a Kafka event stream, containerised with Docker, and deployed to a local Kubernetes (k3s) cluster with an NGINX ingress and Prometheus/Grafana monitoring. Load tests with k6 ramp concurrent reports; metrics include p95 latency, throughput, and recovery time after killing a pod, all compared with an equivalent monolith.

Scope:
Three core services and a simulated dispatcher are implemented; real CAD integration, mapping, and mobile clients are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A deployed microservices backend with monitoring.
2. A measured comparison of scalability and resilience versus a monolith.

Timeline:
Semester 1: service design, build, monolith baseline. Semester 2: Kubernetes deploy, load tests, analysis.

Title:
A CI/CD Pipeline with Automated Testing and Deployment for a Smart-Metering Web Service

Problem Statement:
Teams maintaining energy-sector web services need fast, reliable releases, but manual build-and-deploy steps cause errors and slow turnaround. A well-structured CI/CD pipeline can automate testing and deployment, yet there is value in measuring how much it actually reduces lead time and failure rate for a representative service. This project builds and quantifies such a pipeline.

Objectives:
1. To containerise a sample smart-metering web service and define its automated test suite.
2. To build a CI/CD pipeline that runs tests, security scans, and staged deployments automatically.
3. To evaluate the pipeline using DORA metrics against a manual-deployment baseline.

Methodology:
The pipeline uses GitHub Actions to run unit and integration tests, container image build, Trivy vulnerability scanning, and deployment to a staging and production environment with a blue-green strategy on Docker. Evaluation tracks the four DORA metrics (deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change-failure rate, mean time to restore) over a set of seeded changes versus a manual process.

Scope:
One sample service and a single cloud/VM target are covered; multi-region deployment and full infrastructure-as-code provisioning are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working automated CI/CD pipeline with testing and scanning.
2. A DORA-metric comparison showing improvement over manual deployment.

Timeline:
Semester 1: service, tests, basic pipeline. Semester 2: scanning, blue-green deploy, metric evaluation.

Title:
A Big-Data Analytics Pipeline for Foot-Traffic Insights Aimed at Small Retail Businesses

Problem Statement:
Small retailers rarely have the tooling to turn raw point-of-sale and footfall logs into actionable insight, while enterprise analytics stacks are too costly and complex. This project builds an affordable batch-plus-streaming analytics pipeline that ingests transaction and door-counter data and surfaces peak-hour and basket insights, evaluated for correctness and throughput on realistic data volumes.

Objectives:
1. To design an ingestion and processing pipeline for transaction and footfall data.
2. To compute peak-hour, basket-affinity, and conversion metrics in both batch and streaming modes.
3. To evaluate correctness against ground truth and measure throughput and latency at scale.

Methodology:
Data is ingested via Kafka, processed with Apache Spark (batch) and Spark Structured Streaming (near-real-time), and stored in a partitioned Parquet data lake with results served from PostgreSQL. A synthetic generator produces months of transactions at controllable rates. Correctness is checked against hand-computed aggregates on a sample; performance is measured as records-per-second throughput and end-to-end latency across increasing volumes.

Scope:
A single-store data model and pre-defined metric set are covered; predictive forecasting and a full BI front end are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working batch-and-streaming analytics pipeline.
2. A report on correctness and on throughput/latency scaling.

Timeline:
Semester 1: ingestion, batch metrics, validation. Semester 2: streaming, scaling tests, write-up.

Title:
An Interactive Business-Intelligence Dashboard for Smallholder Crop Yield and Input Efficiency

Problem Statement:
Smallholder farmers and cooperative agronomists collect yield, weather, and input (seed, fertiliser, water) records but lack accessible tools to compare plots, detect underperformance, and decide where inputs are wasted. Existing agri-BI tools assume enterprise data warehouses and reliable connectivity that cooperatives do not have. The specific gap this project addresses is a lightweight, offline-capable BI dashboard that turns heterogeneous plot-level records into per-plot input-efficiency and yield-gap insights with clear drill-down.

Objectives:
1. To consolidate cleaned plot-level yield, weather, and input data from at least three cooperatives into a documented star-schema model by week 6.
2. To deliver an interactive dashboard exposing yield-gap, input-efficiency, and seasonal-trend views with plot-level drill-down by week 14.
3. To evaluate decision usefulness with eight agronomists via task-based testing and SUS, targeting a mean SUS at or above 75 by week 18.

Methodology:
Data from cooperative spreadsheets and a public weather API is profiled, cleaned with Python/pandas, and loaded into a PostgreSQL star schema. Yield gap is computed against an attainable-yield benchmark; input efficiency as yield per unit input, normalised per crop. The dashboard is built in a React front end with a metrics API, validated against hand-computed figures on a holdout sample. Usefulness is assessed through eight task-based sessions measuring task success, time-on-task, and the System Usability Scale, compared against participants' current spreadsheet workflow as baseline.

Scope:
Included: two crop types, three cooperatives, descriptive and diagnostic analytics, and offline caching of the latest sync. Explicitly excluded: predictive yield forecasting, satellite imagery, real-time IoT feeds, and write-back to farm-management systems.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A validated, offline-capable BI dashboard delivering per-plot yield-gap and input-efficiency insights with drill-down.
2. An evaluation report quantifying decision usefulness (task success, time-on-task, SUS) against the spreadsheet baseline.

Timeline:
Weeks 1-6 data modelling and ETL; weeks 7-14 dashboard build and metric validation; weeks 15-18 user evaluation and analysis; weeks 19-24 refinement, threat-to-validity review, and reporting.

Title:
Short-Horizon Passenger-Demand Forecasting for Urban Bus Stops Using Temporal Models with Calibrated Uncertainty

Problem Statement:
Transit operators need accurate 15-to-60-minute-ahead passenger-demand forecasts per stop to adjust headways and reduce both overcrowding and empty runs, yet many deployed systems use simple historical averages that ignore weather, events, and recent trends, and almost none report calibrated uncertainty that operators can act on. The specific gap this project targets is short-horizon, per-stop demand forecasting that combines temporal models with prediction intervals and is benchmarked against strong classical baselines on a public transit dataset.

Objectives:
1. To assemble and clean a stop-level boarding time series with weather and calendar features from a public transit feed by week 5.
2. To train and tune SARIMAX, LightGBM, and an LSTM forecaster, selecting hyperparameters via rolling-origin cross-validation by week 13.
3. To evaluate point accuracy (MAE, RMSE, MASE) and interval calibration (PICP, MPIW) against a seasonal-naive baseline, demonstrating a statistically significant MASE improvement by week 17.

Methodology:
GTFS and automatic-passenger-count data are aggregated to 15-minute per-stop bins and enriched with weather-API and calendar features. Three model families - SARIMAX, gradient-boosted trees (LightGBM), and an LSTM - are trained with rolling-origin (time-series) cross-validation to avoid leakage. Prediction intervals come from conformal prediction for the ML models and model-based intervals for SARIMAX. Models are compared with MAE, RMSE, scale-free MASE, and interval metrics (PICP, MPIW); significance is tested with a Diebold-Mariano test against a seasonal-naive baseline. Risks (sparse low-traffic stops, missing counts) are mitigated by stop clustering and imputation, documented in a threats-to-validity section.

Scope:
Included: 30 high-traffic stops on two routes, horizons of 15/30/60 minutes, and reproducible code with fixed seeds. Excluded: network-wide routing optimisation, real-time online retraining, fare and origin-destination modelling, and deployment into operator systems.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A reproducible forecasting pipeline producing calibrated short-horizon per-stop demand predictions across three horizons.
2. A benchmarking report quantifying accuracy and calibration gains over classical baselines with significance testing and a threats-to-validity discussion.

Timeline:
Weeks 1-5 data engineering; weeks 6-13 modelling and cross-validated tuning; weeks 14-17 evaluation, calibration, and significance testing; weeks 18-24 ablations, reproducibility packaging, and reporting.

Title:
Blockchain for Finance

Problem Statement:
Banks and finance companies have a lot of problems with money and trust. Blockchain is a new technology that can fix this and make everything secure.

Objectives:
1. To study blockchain.
2. To make smart contracts.
3. To help finance.

Methodology:
I will use blockchain and smart contracts to build the system. Research will be done online and some coding.

This can be used by all banks and finance companies everywhere to handle their money safely.

Title:
AR App for Factory

Problem Statement:
Factories are complicated and workers do not always know what to do. Augmented reality is cool and can show things on the phone to help them.

Objectives:
1. To make an AR app.
2. To use it in a factory.
3. To help workers.

Methodology:
I will build an augmented reality app using a phone. The app will show information on top of machines.

Scope:
The app is for manufacturing factories and the workers there.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An AR app.
2. Workers are happier.

Title:
VR Training for Safety

Problem Statement:
Public safety is very important and training people is hard and expensive. VR can make training better and safer for everyone.

Objectives:
1. To create a VR simulation.
2. To train people.
3. To improve safety.

Methodology:
I will use VR technology and a headset to make a training simulation. Some research will be done.

Scope:
It is for fire fighters, police and all public safety workers.

Expected Outcomes:
