2. People are trained better.

Title:
2D Energy Saving Game

Problem Statement:
Many people waste electricity at home because they do not understand how their daily habits add up. A simple game could teach energy-saving habits in a fun way, but most existing apps are boring and just show numbers.

Objectives:
1. To design a 2D game about saving energy at home.
2. To include levels where players turn off appliances to score points.
3. To test if players learn anything about energy.

Methodology:
The game will be built in Unity using C#. It will have a few 2D levels with a house and appliances. Players click appliances to turn them off and earn points. Sprites will be drawn or taken from free asset packs.

Scope:
The game covers a single home environment with about five appliances. It runs on Windows desktop only. Multiplayer is not included.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A playable 2D energy game with several levels.
2. A short survey result showing whether players found it useful.

Timeline:
Semester 1 design and assets, Semester 2 build and testing.

Title:
Serious Game for Small Business Training

Problem Statement:
Small business owners often lack time and money for formal management training. Reading manuals is dull and many owners give up. A serious game that simulates running a small shop could make learning basic management more engaging, though current options are mostly generic quizzes.

Objectives:
1. To build a simulation game where the player runs a small shop.
2. To teach budgeting, stock control and customer service through gameplay.
3. To gather feedback from a small group of users on whether they learned anything.

Methodology:
The game will be made in Unity with simple 2D graphics. The player manages cash, inventory and customers across in-game days. Decisions affect a score. Content on budgeting will be based on common small-business advice from online sources.

Scope:
The game models one retail shop with limited products. It is single player on desktop. Real financial integration is excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working shop-management serious game.
2. Survey feedback from around ten testers.

Timeline:
First semester planning and prototype, second semester full build and user testing.

Title:
Health Records App for Farmers

Problem Statement:
Farmers in rural areas often have poor access to clinics and keep no record of their health. When they do visit a doctor they cannot recall past symptoms or medicines. A simple app to store basic health information could help, but most health apps assume good internet and are too complex for this group.

Objectives:
1. To build a mobile app that stores basic health records for farmers.
2. To let users record symptoms, medicines and clinic visits.
3. To make the interface simple with large buttons and local language labels.

Methodology:
The app will be developed in Android Studio using Java and SQLite for offline storage. Screens will let users add records and view a history list. Some farmers will be asked to try it and give feedback.

Scope:
The app stores personal records on one device offline. It does not connect to hospital systems or provide diagnosis.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working offline health-record app.
2. Feedback from a few farmer users.

Timeline:
Design in semester one, development and testing in semester two.

Title:
Telemedicine Platform for Transport Drivers

Problem Statement:
Long-haul drivers spend days on the road and rarely see a doctor, so minor health issues become serious. A telemedicine platform that lets drivers consult a doctor by video during rest stops could help, but existing apps are not designed around irregular driver schedules and weak mobile signal.

Objectives:
1. To build a web platform where drivers can book and join video consultations.
2. To let doctors view a short driver health profile before the call.
3. To test the booking flow with a few users.

Methodology:
The platform will use React for the front end and Node.js with MongoDB for the back end. Video calls will use a third-party API such as a free WebRTC service. The booking system stores appointments and a basic profile.

Scope:
The system covers booking, a driver profile and video consultation. Payment, prescriptions and full medical records are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working telemedicine web platform with video calls.
2. Usability feedback from test users.

Timeline:
Semester one requirements and design, semester two implementation and testing.

Title:
E-Learning Platform for Sustainability Education

Problem Statement:
Sustainability topics are often taught through static slides that fail to keep students engaged or track their progress. Schools want an online platform that delivers structured lessons on climate and waste while measuring learning outcomes, but most free tools lack progress analytics tailored to sustainability content.

Objectives:
1. To develop a web e-learning platform with course modules on sustainability themes.
2. To add quizzes and a progress dashboard that tracks completion and scores.
3. To evaluate learner engagement through usage logs and a post-use survey.

Methodology:
The platform will be built with React, a Spring Boot REST API and MySQL. It will support lesson content, multiple-choice quizzes, and a dashboard summarising progress per student. Usage events such as lesson views and quiz attempts will be logged. A pilot with around twenty students will provide survey and log data.

Scope:
The system targets secondary-school sustainability modules with three sample courses. Live video and payment are excluded. Role support is limited to learner and instructor.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A functioning e-learning platform with quizzes and a progress dashboard.
2. An evaluation report comparing engagement metrics against the pilot survey.

Timeline:
Weeks 1-5 requirements and design, 6-11 development, 12-14 pilot and evaluation.

Title:
Mobile Payment System for Logistics Drivers

Problem Statement:
Logistics companies still settle many cash-on-delivery payments manually, causing reconciliation errors and delays. A mobile payment system that lets drivers record and confirm payments at delivery would speed up reconciliation, yet generic payment apps do not link a transaction to a specific delivery order.

Objectives:
1. To build a mobile app that records cash and digital payments against delivery orders.
2. To provide an admin dashboard that reconciles payments with orders daily.
3. To evaluate accuracy and time saved compared with the manual process.

Methodology:
The app will be developed in Flutter with a Firebase back end for authentication and data storage. A sandbox payment gateway will simulate digital transactions. Each payment is tied to an order ID, and the dashboard flags mismatches. Evaluation compares reconciliation time on sample data against a manual baseline.

Scope:
The system handles payment capture, order linking and reconciliation reporting. Real banking integration and tax handling are out of scope. It supports driver and admin roles only.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working payment-and-reconciliation app with an admin dashboard.
2. A comparison report on reconciliation accuracy and time saved.

Timeline:
Weeks 1-4 design, 5-10 build, 11-14 testing and evaluation.

Title:
Fraud Detection for E-Government Subsidy Claims

Problem Statement:
Government subsidy programmes lose funds to duplicate and falsified claims that manual auditors cannot review at scale. An automated fraud-detection layer that flags suspicious claims for human review would help, but off-the-shelf rules miss patterns that span multiple applications.

Objectives:
1. To build a system that scores subsidy claims for fraud risk.
2. To combine rule checks with a machine-learning classifier on claim features.
3. To evaluate detection performance against a labelled sample.

Methodology:
A synthetic dataset of claims will be generated with injected fraud patterns. Features such as claim frequency, amount anomalies and duplicate identities will be engineered. A logistic regression and a random forest will be trained with scikit-learn, evaluated by precision, recall and F1 using a held-out test split. Flagged claims appear in a reviewer dashboard.

Scope:
The project covers one subsidy type with a synthetic dataset. Real citizen data, payment disbursement and appeals workflow are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A fraud-scoring service with a reviewer dashboard.
2. An evaluation comparing the rule-only baseline against the combined model.

Timeline:
Weeks 1-3 data and features, 4-9 modelling, 10-14 dashboard and evaluation.

Title:
Course Recommendation for an Education Marketplace

Problem Statement:
Online course marketplaces overwhelm learners with thousands of options, and simple popularity lists ignore each learner's background. A recommendation feature that suggests relevant courses based on past enrolments could improve completion, but small platforms rarely have the data scale that collaborative filtering assumes.

Objectives:
1. To build a course recommender for an education marketplace.
2. To compare content-based and collaborative-filtering approaches.
3. To evaluate recommendation quality on a public course-interaction dataset.

Methodology:
A public dataset of course enrolments will be used. A content-based recommender will use TF-IDF over course descriptions, and an item-based collaborative-filtering recommender will use cosine similarity on the rating matrix. Both will be evaluated with precision@k and recall@k on a held-out split. The better model is exposed through a small web demo.

Scope:
The work focuses on the recommendation algorithm and a demo UI. Payment, course hosting and real user accounts are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working recommender demo with two comparable approaches.
2. An evaluation report ranking the approaches by precision@k.

Timeline:
Weeks 1-3 data prep, 4-9 modelling, 10-14 demo and evaluation.

Title:
Customer Support Chatbot for Retail

Problem Statement:
Retail stores receive many repetitive customer questions about orders, returns and stock that tie up staff time. A chatbot that answers common queries would reduce load, but rule-based bots break on phrasing they were not scripted for, frustrating customers.

Objectives:
1. To build a chatbot that answers common retail customer queries.
2. To use intent classification so the bot handles varied phrasing.
3. To evaluate intent accuracy and fallback rate on test queries.

Methodology:
A set of retail intents such as order status, returns and store hours will be defined with example utterances. An intent classifier will be trained using a sentence-embedding model with a simple classifier head. Responses are template-based per intent, with a fallback for low confidence. The bot is served through a web chat widget, and intent accuracy is measured on a held-out query set.

Scope:
The chatbot covers a fixed set of around eight intents in English. Live agent handoff and payment actions are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working retail chatbot with intent classification.
2. An accuracy and fallback-rate report on the test set.

Timeline:
Weeks 1-4 intent design and data, 5-10 model and integration, 11-14 evaluation.

Title:
Knowledge Graph Search for Smart City Services

Problem Statement:
Smart-city portals scatter information about transport, permits and facilities across many pages, so keyword search returns disconnected results. A knowledge-graph-backed search could answer questions that span entities, such as which facilities a permit applies to, but most city portals still rely on flat full-text search.

Objectives:
1. To build a knowledge graph of selected smart-city services and their relationships.
2. To provide a search interface that answers entity-linked queries over the graph.
3. To compare answer relevance against a keyword-search baseline.

Methodology:
Entities such as services, locations and permits will be modelled in Neo4j with defined relationships, populated from a curated sample of open city data. A search layer maps user queries to graph traversals returning connected results. A keyword baseline over the same content is built for comparison, and relevance is judged on a set of test questions with manual relevance scoring.

Scope:
The graph covers three service categories for one city sample. Real-time data feeds and citizen accounts are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working knowledge-graph search demo.
2. A relevance comparison against the keyword baseline.

Timeline:
Weeks 1-4 graph modelling, 5-10 search layer, 11-14 evaluation.

Title:
Semantic Segmentation of Tourist Landmarks in Street Imagery

Problem Statement:
Tourism apps that overlay information on photos need to know which pixels belong to a landmark versus background, but generic segmentation models trained on urban-driving data perform poorly on cluttered tourist scenes with crowds and signage. A landmark-focused segmentation model would enable cleaner overlays.

Objectives:
1. To train a semantic segmentation model that separates landmarks, sky, people and background in tourist photos.
2. To compare a U-Net baseline against a DeepLabV3+ model with a ResNet-50 backbone.
3. To evaluate segmentation quality using mean IoU and per-class IoU on a held-out set.

Methodology:
A dataset will be assembled from a public landmark image set with masks generated by fine-tuning on a subset and manual correction. Models will be implemented in PyTorch, trained with data augmentation (flips, colour jitter) and a Dice-plus-cross-entropy loss. Evaluation uses mean IoU, per-class IoU and qualitative overlays, with the U-Net as the baseline and DeepLabV3+ as the candidate.

Scope:
The project targets five landmark categories in daytime outdoor photos. Video, night scenes and real-time mobile inference are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained segmentation model with reproducible training scripts.
2. A report comparing mean IoU of the two architectures with error analysis.

Timeline:
Weeks 1-3 dataset and masks, 4-8 baseline, 9-12 DeepLabV3+, 13-14 evaluation.

Title:
Detecting Harmful Imagery in Social Media Posts

Problem Statement:
Social platforms must flag posts containing weapons or graphic content, but human moderation does not scale and simple keyword filters miss image-only posts. An object-detection model tuned for a small set of harmful object classes could pre-filter posts for review, reducing moderator exposure.

Objectives:
1. To train an object detector for a small set of harmful object classes in user images.
2. To compare YOLOv8 against Faster R-CNN on detection accuracy and speed.
3. To evaluate performance using mAP at IoU 0.5 and inference latency.

Methodology:
Public detection datasets containing the target classes will be filtered and merged, with annotations standardised to COCO format. YOLOv8 and Faster R-CNN will be trained in PyTorch with transfer learning from pretrained weights, using augmentation and a fixed train/validation/test split. Evaluation reports mAP@0.5, mAP@0.5:0.95, per-class AP and frames per second.

Scope:
The detector targets three harmful object classes in still images. Text moderation, video and deployment to a live platform are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. Two trained detectors with a reproducible evaluation pipeline.
2. A report comparing accuracy and latency trade-offs between the models.

Timeline:
Weeks 1-3 data and annotation, 4-8 YOLOv8, 9-12 Faster R-CNN, 13-14 comparison.

Title:
Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis of Patient Feedback

Problem Statement:
Hospitals collect free-text patient feedback but reduce it to a single star rating, losing detail about which aspect, such as waiting time or staff attitude, drove the sentiment. Aspect-based sentiment analysis could surface actionable signals, yet general sentiment models give only an overall polarity.

Objectives:
1. To build an aspect-based sentiment model that assigns polarity to predefined care aspects in patient reviews.
2. To compare a fine-tuned DistilBERT model against a TF-IDF plus SVM baseline.
3. To evaluate aspect-level accuracy and macro-F1 on a labelled test set.

Methodology:
A public patient-review corpus will be annotated for four aspects (waiting time, staff, facilities, treatment) with polarity labels, using a held-out split. The baseline uses TF-IDF features with a linear SVM per aspect. The candidate fine-tunes DistilBERT with an aspect-marked input format in PyTorch. Evaluation reports per-aspect accuracy and macro-F1, with confusion analysis on misclassified aspects.

Scope:
The model covers four aspects in English reviews. Real-time integration with hospital systems and multilingual input are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained aspect-based sentiment model with an inference script.
2. A report comparing macro-F1 of the baseline and DistilBERT with error analysis.

Timeline:
Weeks 1-4 annotation, 5-8 baseline, 9-12 DistilBERT, 13-14 evaluation.

Title:
Learned Index Tuning for Financial Time-Series Queries

Problem Statement:
Financial analytics workloads run heavy range and aggregation queries over large time-series tables, where poor index choices cause slow scans. Database engines pick indexes with cost models that ignore workload skew, so a workload-aware index recommender could cut query latency on these patterns.

Objectives:
1. To build a tool that recommends indexes for a financial time-series query workload.
2. To compare the tool's recommendations against the default optimizer choices.
3. To evaluate latency improvement and index storage overhead on a benchmark.

Methodology:
A synthetic financial dataset and a representative query workload will be generated in PostgreSQL. Candidate indexes are enumerated from query predicates, and a greedy selection ranks them by estimated benefit using EXPLAIN ANALYZE costs under a storage budget. The recommended configuration is compared against the default by measuring median and p95 query latency over repeated runs, plus added index size.

Scope:
The work targets single-node PostgreSQL with B-tree and partial indexes on one schema. Distributed databases and write-heavy workloads are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An index-recommendation tool with the selection algorithm.
2. A benchmark report on latency gains versus storage overhead.

Timeline:
Weeks 1-3 workload setup, 4-9 recommender, 10-14 benchmarking.

Title:
Facial Recognition Attendance for a Manufacturing Plant

Problem Statement:
Manufacturing plants track shift attendance with cards that are shared or forgotten, causing buddy-punching and inaccurate payroll. A facial-recognition attendance system at plant entrances could remove cards, but plant lighting and workers wearing masks or helmets challenge off-the-shelf recognition.

Objectives:
1. To build a facial-recognition attendance system that logs entry and exit.
2. To evaluate recognition accuracy under varied lighting and partial occlusion.
3. To compare two embedding models on accuracy and false-acceptance rate.

Methodology:
Face detection uses MTCNN, and recognition uses FaceNet and ArcFace embeddings compared by cosine distance against an enrolled gallery. A test set will include images under bright, dim and partially occluded conditions. Evaluation reports recognition accuracy, false-acceptance and false-rejection rates, with a threshold tuned on a validation split. Attendance events are written to a database with a simple dashboard.

Scope:
The system handles enrolment, recognition and an attendance log for a fixed roster. Payroll integration and liveness anti-spoofing are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working attendance system with a recognition pipeline and dashboard.
2. An accuracy report across lighting and occlusion conditions.

Timeline:
Weeks 1-3 data and enrolment, 4-9 recognition pipeline, 10-14 evaluation.

Title:
Robust OCR for Handwritten Incident Report Forms in Public Safety

Problem Statement:
Public-safety agencies still capture field incident reports on standardised paper forms, then re-key them manually, introducing delays and transcription errors. Off-the-shelf OCR handles clean printed text but degrades on mixed printed-and-handwritten fields, stamps and creases typical of these forms, and gives no per-field confidence to route uncertain entries for human checking.

Objectives:
1. To build an OCR pipeline that extracts structured fields from scanned incident forms, separating printed labels from handwritten values.
2. To compare a Tesseract baseline against a TrOCR-based handwritten recognizer, with layout detection via a fine-tuned LayoutLMv3 region model.
3. To evaluate field-level accuracy, character error rate and the precision of confidence-based routing for human review.

Methodology:
A dataset of synthetic and scanned forms (target 1,500 forms) will be annotated with field bounding boxes and ground-truth values, split 70/15/15. Layout detection localises fields; printed fields go to Tesseract and handwritten fields to a fine-tuned TrOCR model in PyTorch. Per-field softmax confidence drives a routing threshold tuned on validation. Evaluation reports character error rate, field-exact-match accuracy and the human-review precision/recall trade-off, with a Tesseract-only baseline and an error analysis by field type and image degradation.

Scope:
The pipeline covers one bilingual form template with twelve fields. Free-form narrative paragraphs, real-time mobile capture and downstream case-management integration are explicitly excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A reproducible OCR pipeline with layout detection, dual recognizers and confidence routing.
2. An evaluation report quantifying CER and accuracy gains over the baseline plus a routing analysis showing review effort saved.

Timeline:
Weeks 1-3 data collection and annotation, 4-6 layout model, 7-10 recognizers, 11-12 routing, 13-14 evaluation and risk review.

Title:
Anomaly Detection and Forecasting for Wireless Sensor Energy Telemetry

Problem Statement:
Energy grids increasingly rely on dense wireless sensor networks reporting voltage, current and temperature, but readings arrive irregularly with dropout and drift, so simple threshold alarms produce false positives and miss slow degradation. Operators need a method that both forecasts short-term load and flags genuine anomalies under noisy, gap-prone telemetry, with awareness of the sensor-failure failure mode versus real grid events.

Objectives:
1. To build a pipeline that imputes gaps, forecasts short-horizon sensor load and flags anomalies in wireless energy telemetry.
2. To compare an LSTM autoencoder and a Temporal Convolutional Network against an ARIMA and seasonal-naive baseline.
3. To evaluate forecasting error and anomaly-detection performance, distinguishing sensor faults from grid events.

Methodology:
A public energy-telemetry dataset will be resampled to fixed intervals with gap masks; missing values are imputed by interpolation with a missingness indicator. Models are trained in PyTorch with a sliding-window split that preserves time order to avoid leakage. Forecasting is scored by MAE and RMSE against ARIMA and seasonal-naive baselines; anomaly detection uses reconstruction error with a threshold tuned on validation, scored by precision, recall and F1 against injected and labelled anomalies, separated into sensor-fault and grid-event types.

Scope:
The work covers one substation's sensor stream at one-minute resolution over a fixed period. Real-time streaming deployment and control actions are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A reproducible forecasting-and-anomaly pipeline with imputation and tuned thresholds.
2. An evaluation report comparing models on MAE/RMSE and F1, with a fault-versus-event breakdown and a leakage-and-risk discussion.

Timeline:
Weeks 1-3 data prep and imputation, 4-7 forecasting models, 8-10 anomaly models, 11-12 thresholding, 13-14 evaluation.

Title:
Tourism Prediction Using Machine Learning

Problem Statement:
Tourism is a big industry and there is a lot of data. Companies want to predict things about tourists so they can make better decisions and earn more money.

Objectives:
1. To predict tourism using machine learning.
2. To help tourism companies.
3. To make a good system.

Methodology:
I will use Python and machine learning to classify the data. I will collect some data and train a model and then test it to see if it works.

Scope:
This project is for all tourism companies in the whole world and anyone can use it.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A machine learning system.
2. Happy tourism companies.

Title:
Image Detection for Social Media with Deep Learning

Problem Statement:
Social media has many images. We need deep learning to understand them because there are too many to look at by hand.

Objectives:
1. To detect images on social media.
2. To use deep learning.

Methodology:
I will use a neural network and computer vision to look at the images. Deep learning is very powerful so it should work well for this.

Scope:
The project covers all images on all social media apps like Instagram, Facebook, TikTok and others.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An image detection app.
2. Better social media.

Title:
NLP System for Healthcare

Problem Statement:
Hospitals have a lot of text and documents. Doctors are busy and cannot read everything. NLP can help read the text and find useful things.

Objectives:
1. To build an NLP system for healthcare.
2. To process medical text.
3. To help doctors save time.

Methodology:
I will apply natural language processing techniques to medical text and do some analysis. I plan to use Python libraries to handle the words and sentences.

Scope:
The system will work for any hospital and any medical document in any language.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working NLP tool.
2. Doctors save time.

Title:
A Recommender System for Personal Finance Products

Problem Statement:
Many bank customers do not know which savings or loan products suit them, and bank websites list everything without guidance. A recommender system could suggest relevant products based on a customer profile, but most online banking portals still rely on static menus.

Objectives:
1. To build a recommender system that suggests finance products to users.
2. To use collaborative filtering on customer data.
3. To evaluate the recommendations.

Methodology:
The project will use a collaborative filtering approach. Customer transaction data will be collected and a model will recommend products based on similar users. Python and a recommendation library will be used. The output will be tested to see if recommendations are reasonable.

Scope:
The system focuses on retail banking products such as savings accounts, credit cards and personal loans. It will use a sample dataset rather than live bank data.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working product recommender prototype.
2. A short evaluation of recommendation quality.

Timeline:
The project will be done over two semesters.

Title:
Speech Recognition for Factory Floor Commands

Problem Statement:
Factory workers often have their hands full and cannot operate touchscreens to log machine status. A voice command system could let them control simple actions hands-free, but factory environments are noisy and standard assistants struggle there.

Objectives:
1. To build a speech recognition system for short factory commands.
2. To handle a small set of command words.
3. To test accuracy in a noisy setting.

Methodology:
The project will record a set of spoken commands and train a speech recognition model using an existing toolkit. Background noise samples will be added to test robustness. Recognition accuracy will be measured on a held-out set of recordings.

Scope:
The system recognises around ten fixed commands such as start, stop and report. It does not handle full conversations or multiple languages.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A prototype voice command recogniser.
2. Accuracy figures under quiet and noisy conditions.

Timeline:
Roughly six months across two semesters.

Title:
Network Intrusion Detection for Public Safety Networks

Problem Statement:
Public safety agencies run networks that connect cameras, sensors and dispatch systems, and an intrusion could disrupt emergency response. Many small agencies cannot afford commercial intrusion detection, so a lightweight machine-learning detector would help flag suspicious traffic.

Objectives:
1. To build an intrusion detection model using network flow data.
2. To classify traffic as normal or attack.
3. To measure detection accuracy.

Methodology:
The project will use a public intrusion dataset such as NSL-KDD. Features will be extracted from flow records and a classifier such as a random forest will be trained. Performance will be reported using accuracy and a confusion matrix.

Scope:
The work focuses on offline detection from captured flow data for a single small network. Real-time deployment and packet payload inspection are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained intrusion detection model.
2. A report comparing two classifiers.

Timeline:
Two semesters, with model training in the second.

Title:
A Web Application Vulnerability Scanner for Energy Sector Portals

Problem Statement:
Energy utilities increasingly expose customer portals and operator dashboards on the web, and these are attractive targets. Small utilities rarely run regular security tests, so a simple scanner that checks for common web flaws would be useful.

Objectives:
1. To build a scanner that checks for common web vulnerabilities.
2. To test it against a deliberately vulnerable web app.
3. To produce a readable findings report.

Methodology:
The tool will send crafted requests to detect issues from the OWASP Top 10 such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting. It will be tested against an intentionally vulnerable application like DVWA. Detected issues will be logged with severity.

Scope:
The scanner targets a handful of common vulnerability classes on standard HTTP applications. It does not cover authenticated multi-step workflows or industrial control protocols.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A command-line vulnerability scanner.
2. A sample scan report on a test application.

Timeline:
About six months over two semesters.

Title:
Static and Dynamic Malware Analysis Toolkit for Small Businesses

Problem Statement:
Small businesses are frequent ransomware targets but rarely have security staff to inspect suspicious files. Commercial sandboxes are expensive, so an affordable analysis toolkit that combines basic static and dynamic checks would help a small business triage a file before opening it.

Objectives:
1. To build a toolkit that performs static feature extraction and dynamic behaviour logging on Windows executables.
2. To classify samples as likely benign or malicious using extracted features.
3. To evaluate the classifier against a labelled malware dataset.

Methodology:
Static analysis will extract PE header fields, imported APIs and string indicators. Dynamic analysis will run samples in an isolated virtual machine and log file, registry and network activity. A gradient-boosted classifier will be trained on features from a labelled corpus such as EMBER, and evaluated using precision, recall and F1 with a held-out test set.

Scope:
The toolkit targets Windows PE files only. It excludes packed-binary unpacking, document macros and mobile malware. The sandbox uses a single snapshot VM.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working analysis toolkit with a report per sample.
2. Classification metrics compared against a simple baseline.

Timeline:
Semester one: static module and dataset. Semester two: dynamic module, classifier and evaluation.

Title:
A Responsive Web Platform for Smallholder Crop Advisory

Problem Statement:
Smallholder farmers often lack timely advice on planting and pest control, and existing agriculture portals are desktop-only and hard to use on the cheap phones farmers actually carry. A responsive web platform that works on small screens and slow connections could deliver advisory content more reliably.

Objectives:
1. To build a responsive web platform delivering crop advisory and a pest reporting form.
2. To support extension officers in posting localised advisories.
3. To evaluate usability with a small group of users.

Methodology:
The platform will be built with React and a Spring Boot backend over MySQL, using a mobile-first responsive layout. Content will be entered by extension officers and shown to farmers by crop and region. A System Usability Scale survey will be run with around ten participants and the score reported.

Scope:
The platform covers three crops and one region, with content in one local language. It does not include offline sync, payments or marketplace features.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A deployed responsive web platform.
2. A usability evaluation with SUS results.

Timeline:
Semester one: design and core CRUD. Semester two: advisory module and usability testing.

Title:
A Progressive Web App for Public Bus Arrival Information

Problem Statement:
Commuters in mid-sized cities often wait without knowing when the next bus arrives, and native transit apps are too heavy for older phones. A progressive web app could deliver installable, offline-capable arrival information without a large download.

Objectives:
1. To build a PWA that shows nearby stops and estimated bus arrivals.
2. To cache route and schedule data for offline viewing.
3. To measure load performance and offline behaviour.

Methodology:
The app will be built with a service worker for caching and a manifest for installability. Schedule data will come from a published GTFS feed, and arrival estimates will be computed from scheduled times. Performance will be measured with Lighthouse, focusing on first load and repeat offline load.

Scope:
The PWA covers one city's bus network using static GTFS data. Real-time GPS feeds, fare payment and multi-modal routing are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An installable PWA with offline stop lookup.
2. Lighthouse performance and PWA scores before and after caching.

Timeline:
Semester one: UI and GTFS import. Semester two: offline caching and performance evaluation.

Title:
A Cross-Platform Mobile App for Household Recycling Tracking

Problem Statement:
Households that want to reduce waste have little feedback on how much they recycle, and most sustainability apps are region-locked or single-platform. A cross-platform app that lets users log recyclables and see their impact could encourage better habits.

Objectives:
1. To build a cross-platform app for logging recyclable items and weights.
2. To show weekly recycling summaries and simple impact estimates.
3. To evaluate user engagement over a short trial.

Methodology:
The app will be built with Flutter targeting Android and iOS, backed by Firebase for authentication and data storage. Users log items by category, and the app aggregates weekly totals with a CO2-saved estimate from published conversion factors. A two-week trial with a small user group will record daily active use.

Scope:
The app supports five recyclable categories and manual entry only. Barcode scanning, municipal pickup integration and gamified rewards are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working cross-platform app on Android and iOS.
2. Engagement figures from the trial period.

Timeline:
Semester one: data model and logging UI. Semester two: summaries, impact estimates and trial.

Title:
An Android Native App for Last-Mile Delivery Proof of Delivery

Problem Statement:
Small courier firms often confirm deliveries with paper or phone calls, leading to disputes and lost records. An Android app that captures signatures, photos and GPS at the drop-off point would give drivers and dispatchers a reliable digital record.

Objectives:
1. To build a native Android app that captures proof of delivery with photo, signature and location.
2. To sync completed deliveries to a backend when connectivity returns.
3. To evaluate the app with a small set of test deliveries.

Methodology:
The app will be built natively in Kotlin using CameraX for photos, a canvas view for signatures and the fused location provider for GPS. Records will be stored locally with Room and synced to a REST backend, queuing when offline. Testing will run a set of simulated delivery runs and check that all records sync correctly.

Scope:
The app targets Android phones for single-driver routes. Route optimisation, multi-stop planning and customer-facing tracking are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working Android proof-of-delivery app with offline queueing.
2. A test report on sync reliability.

Timeline:
Semester one: capture features and local storage. Semester two: offline sync and testing.

Title:
An IoT Sensor Network for Public Facility Air Quality Monitoring

Problem Statement:
City-run facilities such as libraries and clinics rarely monitor indoor air quality, yet poor ventilation affects visitor comfort and health. A low-cost IoT sensor network that reports readings to an e-government dashboard would let facility managers act on real data.

Objectives:
1. To build IoT nodes that measure CO2, temperature and humidity.
2. To collect readings on a server and show them on a dashboard.
3. To validate sensor readings against a reference meter.

Methodology:
Each node uses an ESP32 with a CO2 and temperature-humidity sensor, publishing readings over MQTT to a broker. A backend stores time-stamped data and a web dashboard plots trends per facility. Readings will be compared against a calibrated reference meter to estimate measurement error.

Scope:
The prototype deploys three nodes in one building and reports three parameters. Particulate sensing, outdoor deployment and automated ventilation control are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working sensor network feeding a live dashboard.
2. A validation report comparing nodes to a reference meter.

Timeline:
Semester one: node assembly and data pipeline. Semester two: dashboard and validation.

Title:
A Smart Home Automation Hub for Focused Study Environments

Problem Statement:
Students studying at home are easily distracted, and existing smart-home tools automate comfort but not concentration. There is little work tying home automation to study sessions, so a hub that adjusts lighting, notifications and reminders around a student's planned study blocks could measurably support focus.

Objectives:
1. To build a local automation hub that triggers lighting and do-not-disturb scenes from a student's study schedule.
2. To integrate a Pomodoro timer that drives device actions and logs session adherence.
3. To evaluate the effect on self-reported focus and completed study blocks across a two-week trial.

Methodology:
The hub runs on a Raspberry Pi with Home Assistant, controlling Zigbee bulbs and a smart plug, and exposes a study-session API. A companion app starts sessions, and rule automations switch scenes and suppress notifications. The evaluation uses a within-subject design: one baseline week and one intervention week with eight participants, comparing completed study blocks and a focus questionnaire, analysed with a paired test.

Scope:
The system covers one room with lighting, a plug and notification control. It excludes HVAC, security devices, cloud control and voice assistants.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working schedule-driven automation hub with a study app.
2. A within-subject evaluation reporting focus and adherence changes.

Timeline:
Semester one: hub, device integration and app. Semester two: trial, analysis and write-up.

Title:
Edge-Based Real-Time Shelf Stock Detection for Retail

Problem Statement:
Out-of-stock shelves cost retailers sales, and cloud-based shelf cameras raise bandwidth and privacy concerns. Running detection at the edge avoids streaming video offsite, but small stores need a model light enough for a low-power device, a gap this project targets.

Objectives:
1. To deploy an object detector on an edge device that flags empty shelf regions from a camera feed.
2. To compare a quantised lightweight model against a server-side baseline on accuracy and latency.
3. To evaluate end-to-end alert latency under realistic store conditions.

Methodology:
A YOLO-based detector will be trained on the SKU-110K shelf dataset plus a small set of locally captured empty-shelf images, then quantised with INT8 and deployed to a Jetson Nano with TensorRT. A server-side full-precision model serves as the baseline. Evaluation reports mAP, frames per second and on-device latency, plus a privacy note since frames never leave the device.

Scope:
The system detects empty versus stocked shelf regions for one product category on fixed cameras. Restock prediction, planogram compliance and multi-store coordination are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An edge-deployed stock detector with an alerting threshold.
2. An accuracy-versus-latency comparison of edge and server models.

Timeline:
Semester one: dataset, training and baseline. Semester two: quantisation, edge deployment and evaluation.

Title:
A Cloud-Native Microservices Backend for Smart-City Incident Reporting

Problem Statement:
Smart-city incident reporting platforms often run as monoliths that struggle under bursty load during events and are hard to update without downtime. A cloud-native microservices design with independent scaling could handle these spikes, but trade-offs between service granularity and operational complexity are rarely measured in a student-scale prototype.

Objectives:
1. To decompose an incident-reporting backend into containerised microservices with a defined API gateway.
2. To deploy the services on Kubernetes with autoscaling and observability.
3. To evaluate scalability and resilience under load and induced failures.

Methodology:
The backend will be split into reporting, notification, user and analytics services in Spring Boot, communicating via REST and a message queue. Services run as Docker containers on a Kubernetes cluster with horizontal pod autoscaling, and observability uses Prometheus and Grafana. Load tests with k6 will measure throughput and latency, and chaos tests will kill pods to observe recovery.

Scope:
The prototype implements four services with synthetic load. Multi-region deployment, service mesh and production data are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A deployed microservices backend with autoscaling and dashboards.
2. A load-and-resilience report against a monolith baseline.

Timeline:
Semester one: service decomposition and containerisation. Semester two: Kubernetes deployment and load testing.

Title:
A CI/CD Pipeline with Automated Quality Gates for a Tourism Booking Platform

Problem Statement:
Small tourism software teams often deploy manually, causing slow releases and regressions during peak season. Adopting CI/CD with automated testing and quality gates can reduce defects, yet teams lack a measured reference showing the effect on deployment frequency and failure rate for a realistic booking application.

Objectives:
1. To build a CI/CD pipeline that automates build, test, security scan and deployment for a sample booking app.
2. To add quality gates that block releases on failing tests or coverage thresholds.
3. To measure DORA metrics before and after introducing the pipeline.

Methodology:
The pipeline will be implemented in GitHub Actions with stages for unit and integration tests, a coverage gate, a dependency vulnerability scan and containerised deployment to a staging environment. A blue-green strategy enables rollback. The evaluation tracks four DORA metrics: deployment frequency, lead time, change failure rate and recovery time, comparing a manual baseline against the automated pipeline over a series of changes.

Scope:
The pipeline targets one booking application deployed to a single staging environment. Production rollout, multi-cloud and infrastructure provisioning are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working CI/CD pipeline with enforced quality gates.
2. A before-and-after DORA metrics comparison.

Timeline:
Semester one: sample app and basic pipeline. Semester two: quality gates, blue-green deploy and metrics.

Title:
A Big Data Pipeline for Streaming Social Media Sentiment

Problem Statement:
Tracking public sentiment on social media during fast-moving events needs a pipeline that ingests high-volume streams and produces near-real-time aggregates, but most student projects process static dumps offline. Building a streaming pipeline reveals practical trade-offs in throughput and latency that batch approaches hide.

Objectives:
1. To build an ingestion-to-dashboard pipeline that streams posts and computes rolling sentiment.
2. To compute trending topics and sentiment over sliding time windows.
3. To evaluate pipeline throughput, end-to-end latency and the effect of partition count.

Methodology:
Posts will be ingested through Kafka, processed by Spark Structured Streaming for cleaning, language filtering and a transformer-based sentiment classifier, with windowed aggregates written to a store feeding a dashboard. A replayable archived dataset will drive reproducible load. Evaluation measures sustained throughput in messages per second, end-to-end latency at increasing rates, and how Kafka partition count affects both.

Scope:
The pipeline handles English text and binary positive-negative sentiment on a replayed dataset. Live platform APIs, multilingual handling and sarcasm detection are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working streaming sentiment pipeline with a live dashboard.
2. A throughput-and-latency evaluation across configurations.

Timeline:
Semester one: ingestion and processing. Semester two: windowed analytics, dashboard and load evaluation.

Title:
A Business Intelligence Dashboard for Hospital Bed-Occupancy and Patient Flow

Problem Statement:
Mid-sized hospitals struggle to anticipate ward congestion because occupancy, admissions and discharge data sit in separate systems with no unified view. Without consolidated indicators, bed managers react to overcrowding rather than pre-empt it. This project addresses the gap by delivering a governed BI dashboard that integrates these sources and surfaces leading indicators of congestion, validated with clinical-operations users.

Objectives:
1. To design a star-schema data warehouse integrating admissions, discharges and bed-status feeds with daily ETL.
2. To build an interactive dashboard exposing occupancy rate, average length of stay and a 24-hour congestion risk flag.
3. To evaluate analytical accuracy and decision usefulness against current manual reports with bed managers.

Methodology:
A dimensional warehouse will be modelled in PostgreSQL and loaded by an Airflow ETL from anonymised exports of a public MIMIC-derived admissions dataset and a synthetic bed feed. The dashboard will be built in a BI tool with role-based access. The congestion risk flag uses a logistic-regression baseline compared against a gradient-boosted model, evaluated by AUROC with five-fold cross-validation and a temporal hold-out to avoid leakage. Decision usefulness is assessed via a task-based study with six bed managers using a standardised usability and trust questionnaire.

Scope:
The dashboard covers inpatient wards for one hospital's data, with daily refresh. Real-time HL7 integration, outpatient flow and identifiable patient data are explicitly excluded; only de-identified data is used.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A governed BI dashboard with documented metric definitions and role-based access.
2. A validation report covering predictive AUROC, cross-validation results and a user trust evaluation.

Timeline:
Weeks 1-4 requirements and warehouse design; 5-9 ETL and dashboard; 10-13 risk model and cross-validation; 14-18 user study; 19-24 analysis, risk review and write-up.

Title:
Probabilistic Time-Series Forecasting of Intraday Electricity Trading Prices

Problem Statement:
Intraday power-market traders need not just a point forecast but a calibrated sense of uncertainty, yet many student forecasting projects report only single-value predictions and ignore the non-stationarity and volatility clustering of price series. This project targets that gap by producing probabilistic intraday price forecasts with calibrated prediction intervals and rigorously benchmarking them against established baselines.

Objectives:
1. To build a probabilistic forecasting model that outputs prediction intervals for 30-minute-ahead electricity prices.
2. To benchmark it against seasonal-naive, ARIMA and gradient-boosting baselines under identical conditions.
3. To evaluate point accuracy and interval calibration using a walk-forward protocol.

Methodology:
Using a public intraday price dataset with calendar and load features, the project compares a quantile-regression LightGBM and a Temporal Fusion Transformer producing quantile forecasts, against seasonal-naive, ARIMA and a plain gradient-boosting baseline. All models use the same feature set and a strict walk-forward (rolling-origin) split to prevent leakage. Point error is reported as MAE and RMSE, and interval quality as pinball loss and empirical coverage of the 90% interval, with significance tested via the Diebold-Mariano test. Hyperparameters are tuned only on inner validation folds.

Scope:
The work forecasts one market's day-ahead-to-intraday price at 30-minute resolution for a defined two-year window. Live trading execution, order-book microstructure and cross-market spillover are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A reproducible forecasting pipeline with logged configurations and seeds.
2. A benchmark report covering point error, calibration and statistical significance versus baselines.

Timeline:
Weeks 1-4 data and feature pipeline; 5-8 baselines; 9-13 probabilistic models; 14-17 walk-forward evaluation; 18-21 significance testing and ablations; 22-24 write-up.

Blockchain for Schools

Schools have a lot of records and sometimes they get lost or changed. Blockchain is a new technology that is very secure so it can help education.

AR Shopping App

Shopping is sometimes boring and people cannot see the products well. Augmented reality is cool and can make shopping better and more fun for everyone.

Title:
VR City Training

Cities are getting bigger and workers need training. VR is good for training because it feels real and people learn faster maybe.

Title:
A 3D Tourism Exploration Game for Local Heritage Sites

Problem Statement:
Many young people do not know much about local heritage sites and tourism brochures are not very engaging. A game could make learning about these places more interesting and encourage people to visit them.

Objectives:
1. Design a 3D game with explorable heritage locations
2. Add quizzes and collectibles about each site

The game will be built in Unity using free 3D assets and some custom models. It will have a few levels each based on a real heritage site with information popups. A small group of players will be asked to give feedback after playing.

Title:
A Serious Game to Teach Safe Social Media Habits to Teenagers

Problem Statement:
Teenagers spend a lot of time on social media but often do not understand privacy risks, scams, or cyberbullying. Traditional lessons are boring, so a serious game might teach these topics in a more memorable way.

Objectives:
1. Create a 2D game with scenarios about social media risks
2. Include decision points where players choose safe or unsafe actions
3. Evaluate learning using a before and after quiz

Methodology:
The game will be built with Unity and C#. Each level presents a story scenario such as a suspicious friend request or a phishing message, and the player chooses how to respond with feedback given. A small class of students will play it and complete quizzes to measure learning.

Scope:
The game covers three topics: privacy, scams, and cyberbullying. It is a single player browser game and does not cover all online safety topics or include teacher dashboards.

1. A working educational game on social media safety
2. Quiz results indicating any improvement in knowledge
