Roughly 6 months across design, development, and a small evaluation.

Title:
A Web System for Managing Clinic Patient Records

Problem Statement:
Small clinics often still keep patient records on paper, which makes it slow to find information and easy to lose files. A simple digital system could help staff manage appointments and patient history more easily.

Objectives:
1. Build a web application to store patient records and appointments
2. Allow staff to search and update records
3. Add basic reports such as daily appointment lists

Methodology:
The system will be developed using PHP and MySQL with a Bootstrap front end. It will have login roles for receptionist and doctor. After building, clinic staff will be asked to try it and give usability feedback.

Scope:
The system handles patient records, appointments, and simple reports for one small clinic. It does not include billing, insurance claims, or integration with hospital systems.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A functional clinic record management web system
2. Usability feedback from clinic staff

Timeline:
Around 6 months: requirements, development, and testing.

Title:
A Telemedicine Appointment Platform with Online Payment

Problem Statement:
People sometimes find it hard to see a doctor in person, and paying for consultations can be inconvenient. A telemedicine platform that lets patients book video calls and pay online could make healthcare more accessible.

Objectives:
1. Build a platform for booking online doctor consultations
2. Add video calls and an online payment option
3. Test the booking and payment flow

Methodology:
The platform will be built using React and Node.js with a third party video API and a payment gateway sandbox. Patients can register, book a slot, join a call, and pay. A few test users will check the main flows.

Scope:
The platform covers registration, booking, video consultation, and sandbox payments. It does not include real money transactions, prescriptions, or medical record storage.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working telemedicine booking platform with sandbox payment
2. Test results for the main user flows

Timeline:
About 6 months for analysis, development, and testing.

Title:
An E-Learning Platform for Manufacturing Machine Operator Training

Problem Statement:
Manufacturing companies need to train new machine operators quickly, but in-person training is time consuming and inconsistent. There is no convenient self-paced system that combines short lessons with assessments tailored to specific machines, leading to slower onboarding.

Objectives:
1. Develop a web-based e-learning platform delivering modular lessons for three machine types
2. Implement quizzes with automatic scoring and a progress tracker per operator
3. Evaluate the platform with a small group of trainees and supervisors using a usability questionnaire

Methodology:
The system will be built with Django and PostgreSQL, with lesson content as text, images, and embedded videos. Each module ends with a multiple-choice quiz, and an admin dashboard shows completion and scores. Evaluation uses a System Usability Scale survey with about 15 participants plus task-completion observation.

Scope:
The platform covers course delivery, quizzes, and progress tracking for three machines. It excludes VR simulation, live instructor sessions, and integration with company HR systems.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working e-learning platform with three training modules and assessments
2. Usability results and completion data from the trainee evaluation

Timeline:
8 months: requirements (1), design (1), development (4), evaluation and writing (2).

Title:
A Mobile Payment App for Reporting and Funding Public Safety Issues

Problem Statement:
Residents often notice public safety problems such as broken streetlights or damaged signs but have no easy way to report them or contribute to community fixes. Existing reporting channels are slow and rarely let citizens crowd-fund small repairs, so issues remain unresolved.

Objectives:
1. Build a mobile app where users report public safety issues with photo and location
2. Add a small payment feature so users can contribute to a community repair fund
3. Test the reporting and payment flow with sample users

Methodology:
The app will be developed in Flutter with a Firebase backend and a payment gateway sandbox for contributions. Reports are geotagged and shown on a map, and an admin view lists pending issues. Testing involves around 10 users submitting reports and trial contributions, with feedback collected by survey.

Scope:
The project covers reporting, mapping, and sandbox payments for one city district. It excludes real fund disbursement, government system integration, and identity verification.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A functional reporting and contribution mobile app
2. User feedback and test results on the main flows

Timeline:
8 months across analysis, development, and evaluation.

Title:
Machine Learning Detection of Anomalous Energy Consumption for Billing Fraud

Problem Statement:
Energy providers lose revenue from meter tampering and irregular consumption that go unnoticed in manual checks. Reviewing every account is impractical, and simple threshold rules miss subtle fraud patterns, so suspicious accounts need to be flagged automatically for inspection.

Objectives:
1. Build a model that flags anomalous electricity consumption patterns from smart meter data
2. Compare a rule-based baseline against Isolation Forest and an autoencoder
3. Evaluate detection using precision, recall, and F1 on labelled cases

Methodology:
Using a public smart-meter dataset, features such as daily load profile, variance, and night/day ratio will be engineered. An Isolation Forest and a small autoencoder will be trained in Python with scikit-learn and Keras, and compared to a threshold baseline. Evaluation uses precision, recall, and F1 with a held-out test set and a confusion matrix.

Scope:
The project focuses on residential meter anomaly detection on one dataset. It excludes real-time deployment, hardware tampering sensors, and live integration with billing systems.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained anomaly detection model with reported metrics
2. A comparison showing which method best flags suspicious accounts

Timeline:
8 months: data and features (2), modelling (3), evaluation (2), writing (1).

Title:
A Product Recommendation System for a Small Business Online Store

Problem Statement:
Small online businesses cannot afford the recommendation engines large platforms use, so customers see generic listings and miss relevant products. This lowers average order value and repeat purchases for small retailers that already operate on thin margins.

Objectives:
1. Build a recommendation module for a small e-commerce store using collaborative and content-based filtering
2. Combine both into a hybrid recommender and integrate it into a sample storefront
3. Evaluate recommendation quality offline using precision@k and recall@k

Methodology:
A public retail transactions dataset will be used to build item-item collaborative filtering and a content-based model on product attributes, then combined into a weighted hybrid. The module is implemented in Python and exposed via a Flask API to a demo store. Offline evaluation uses precision@k, recall@k, and a train/test split, with a small user survey on perceived relevance.

Scope:
The system handles "you may also like" recommendations for one product catalogue. It excludes real-time personalization at scale, payment processing, and inventory management.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working hybrid recommendation module integrated into a demo store
2. Offline metrics and survey feedback comparing the approaches

Timeline:
8 months: data and models (3), integration (2), evaluation (2), writing (1).

Title:
A Conversational Agent to Answer Farmers' Crop and Pest Questions

Problem Statement:
Smallholder farmers often lack quick access to agricultural advice on pests, fertilizer, and planting times. Extension officers are stretched thin, so farmers rely on guesswork. A chatbot answering common questions in simple language could give timely guidance.

Objectives:
1. Build a chatbot that answers common crop and pest questions for selected local crops
2. Use intent classification and a curated knowledge base of agricultural advice
3. Evaluate answer accuracy and user satisfaction with sample farmers

Methodology:
The chatbot uses intent classification (a fine-tuned transformer or Rasa) over a curated set of crop and pest FAQs compiled from agricultural extension guides. Responses are retrieved from a structured knowledge base. It is deployed as a web/WhatsApp-style chat interface. Evaluation measures intent accuracy on a labelled test set and satisfaction from about 12 users.

Scope:
The chatbot covers three staple crops and common pests, in English. It excludes image-based disease diagnosis, real-time weather integration, and full open-domain conversation.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working agricultural chatbot for three crops
2. Accuracy metrics and user satisfaction results

Timeline:
8 months across knowledge base building, development, and evaluation.

Title:
A Knowledge Graph Search System for Public Transport Information

Problem Statement:
Public transport information is scattered across routes, stops, schedules, and fares, making it hard to answer connected questions like "which routes near this stop reach the hospital." Keyword search returns flat results without understanding these relationships, frustrating commuters.

Objectives:
1. Build a knowledge graph linking routes, stops, schedules, and points of interest
2. Implement semantic search and relationship queries over the graph
3. Evaluate retrieval quality against a keyword search baseline

Methodology:
Transport open data (GTFS) and a small set of points of interest will be modelled as a knowledge graph in Neo4j, with entities and relationships defined in a simple ontology. A query interface translates user questions into Cypher queries. Evaluation compares answer relevance and query success rate against an Elasticsearch keyword baseline on a set of test questions.

Scope:
The system covers one city's bus network and selected points of interest. It excludes real-time vehicle tracking, multimodal trip planning, and natural-language generation of full itineraries.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working knowledge graph search prototype for transport queries
2. A comparison showing graph search versus keyword baseline performance

Timeline:
8 months: data modelling (2), development (3), evaluation (2), writing (1).

Title:
Semantic Segmentation of Rooftop Solar Panels from Aerial Imagery for Sustainability Planning

Problem Statement:
City sustainability teams need to estimate rooftop solar adoption and remaining potential, but manual inspection of aerial imagery is slow and inconsistent. Automatically segmenting existing solar panels would let planners quantify installed capacity and target incentives, yet panels are small, varied, and easily confused with skylights and dark roofs.

Objectives:
1. Train a semantic segmentation model to delineate rooftop solar panels in aerial images
2. Compare U-Net and DeepLabV3+ against a thresholding baseline
3. Evaluate using IoU, F1, and per-area capacity error on a held-out region

Methodology:
Using a public aerial solar-panel dataset, images will be tiled and augmented (rotation, flips, brightness). U-Net and DeepLabV3+ with a ResNet encoder will be trained in PyTorch with a Dice plus cross-entropy loss and early stopping. Models are compared to an HSV-threshold baseline, evaluated with mean IoU and F1 via geographic train/test split to avoid leakage, with error analysis on confusing roof types.

Scope:
The project covers binary panel-vs-background segmentation on one city's imagery at a fixed resolution. It excludes panel-type classification, 3D roof modelling, and real-time inference on live drone feeds.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained segmentation model with reported IoU/F1 and estimated rooftop capacity
2. A comparison of architectures and an error analysis report

Timeline:
9 months: data prep (2), modelling (3), evaluation and error analysis (2), writing (2).

Title:
Real-Time Pallet and Forklift Object Detection for Warehouse Logistics Safety

Problem Statement:
Warehouse near-misses between forklifts and pedestrians or misplaced pallets cause delays and injuries. Manual CCTV monitoring is unreliable, and generic detectors are not tuned to overhead warehouse views, so an accurate, fast detector for pallets, forklifts, and people is needed to support safety alerts.

Objectives:
1. Train an object detector for pallets, forklifts, and people from warehouse camera footage
2. Compare YOLOv8 against Faster R-CNN on accuracy and inference speed
3. Evaluate using mAP@0.5, mAP@0.5:0.95, and frames per second

Methodology:
A combination of a public logistics dataset and self-annotated frames (labelled in Roboflow) will be split by camera location to prevent leakage. YOLOv8 and Faster R-CNN will be trained in PyTorch with augmentation (mosaic, scaling, occlusion) and transfer learning from COCO weights. Models are evaluated with mAP and FPS on GPU, with a confusion analysis of class mix-ups under occlusion.

Scope:
The project targets three classes from fixed overhead cameras in one warehouse layout. It excludes multi-camera tracking, depth estimation, and embedded-device deployment.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained detector with reported mAP and FPS for the three classes
2. A speed-versus-accuracy comparison guiding which model suits safety alerts

Timeline:
9 months: annotation and data (2), training (3), evaluation (2), writing (2).

Title:
Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis of Citizen Feedback on E-Government Services

Problem Statement:
E-government portals collect large volumes of citizen feedback, but agencies struggle to know which specific aspects (ease of use, response time, staff helpfulness) drive dissatisfaction. Overall star ratings hide this, so aspect-level sentiment is needed to prioritize service improvements.

Objectives:
1. Build an aspect-based sentiment model identifying aspects and their polarity in citizen feedback
2. Compare a fine-tuned BERT model against TF-IDF with logistic regression and a lexicon baseline
3. Evaluate using macro-F1 for aspect detection and sentiment classification

Methodology:
A labelled dataset of service reviews (public review corpora adapted, plus manual annotation of a government-feedback sample) will be used. A fine-tuned BERT model performs joint aspect-category and polarity classification, compared with TF-IDF plus logistic regression and a VADER lexicon baseline. Evaluation uses macro-F1 and per-aspect breakdown with stratified k-fold cross-validation and inter-annotator agreement reporting.

Scope:
The project covers four predefined service aspects in English text feedback. It excludes multilingual feedback, sarcasm-specific handling, and live portal integration.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained aspect-based sentiment model with macro-F1 results per aspect
2. A baseline comparison and analysis of which aspects most affect satisfaction

Timeline:
9 months: data and annotation (2), modelling (3), evaluation (2), writing (2).

Title:
A Learned Index Advisor for Query Optimization in a Student Records Database

Problem Statement:
University records systems run many ad-hoc reporting queries, and poorly chosen indexes cause slow responses and wasted storage. DBAs tune indexes manually, which is error-prone. An advisor that recommends indexes from observed query workloads could improve query latency without manual tuning.

Objectives:
1. Build an index-recommendation tool that analyzes a SQL query workload and suggests candidate indexes
2. Compare its recommendations against no-index and full-index baselines using PostgreSQL's cost estimates
3. Evaluate using measured query latency and total index storage on a benchmark workload

Methodology:
A synthetic student-records schema will be populated with realistic data, and a workload generator will produce mixed read queries. Candidate indexes are derived from parsed predicates and join columns, then ranked using EXPLAIN ANALYZE cost feedback in a greedy what-if loop. Evaluation runs the workload under recommended versus baseline configurations, measuring median and p95 latency and storage, repeated across three workload mixes.

Scope:
The advisor targets single-column and two-column B-tree indexes on one PostgreSQL schema. It excludes materialized views, partitioning, and multi-database deployment.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working index advisor with measured latency improvements over baselines
2. An analysis of the latency-versus-storage trade-off across workloads

Timeline:
9 months: schema and workload (2), advisor logic (3), benchmarking (2), writing (2).

Title:
A Facial Recognition Attendance System for Retail Staff with Anti-Spoofing

Problem Statement:
Retail chains use buddy-punching-prone card and PIN attendance, causing payroll inaccuracies. Face-based attendance is convenient but vulnerable to photo spoofing. A system combining accurate recognition with basic liveness detection is needed for reliable, low-fraud staff check-in.

Objectives:
1. Build a face-recognition attendance system that enrolls and identifies retail staff
2. Add a liveness/anti-spoofing check to reject photo and screen attacks
3. Evaluate recognition accuracy and spoof-rejection rate under varied lighting

Methodology:
Faces are detected with MTCNN and embedded with a pretrained FaceNet/ArcFace model, matched by cosine similarity against an enrolled gallery. A liveness module uses a blink/texture-based check trained on a small real-versus-spoof set. The system runs as a desktop app logging timestamps. Evaluation measures identification accuracy, false acceptance/rejection rates, and spoof-rejection rate across lighting and angle conditions with around 15 enrolled participants.

Scope:
The system covers enrollment, identification, and basic liveness for up to a few dozen staff at one entry point. It excludes mask-occluded recognition, large-scale crowds, and payroll system integration.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working face-attendance prototype with anti-spoofing
2. Accuracy and spoof-rejection results across test conditions

Timeline:
9 months: setup and enrollment (2), recognition and liveness (3), evaluation (2), writing (2).

Title:
A Robust OCR Pipeline for Extracting Structured Fields from Smart-City Permit Documents

Problem Statement:
Smart-city departments receive scanned permit and inspection forms in varied layouts and image quality, and manual data entry is slow and error-prone. Generic OCR returns raw text without field structure, and accuracy drops on skewed, low-contrast scans, so a pipeline that both reads text reliably and extracts key fields (permit number, address, date, status) is needed to populate municipal databases.

Objectives:
1. Build an OCR pipeline that preprocesses scans and extracts six structured fields from two permit form types
2. Compare Tesseract against a deep model (PaddleOCR/TrOCR) and a layout-aware extractor (LayoutLMv3) for field extraction
3. Evaluate using character error rate, field-level precision/recall/F1, and end-to-end accuracy, with ablation of the preprocessing steps

Methodology:
A dataset of 800 anonymized permit scans (plus synthetic augmentations: skew, blur, noise) will be annotated with field bounding boxes and ground-truth values. Preprocessing applies deskewing, adaptive binarization, and denoising. Text recognition compares Tesseract, PaddleOCR, and TrOCR; field extraction compares a regex/rule layer against fine-tuned LayoutLMv3. Models are evaluated with CER and field F1 under document-stratified 5-fold cross-validation, with an ablation isolating preprocessing impact and error analysis by degradation type. Risks (small labelled set) are mitigated with synthetic data and transfer learning.

Scope:
The pipeline targets two English permit form types and six fields, processed in batch. It excludes handwritten free-text fields, real-time mobile capture, and direct write-back to live municipal systems.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An OCR-plus-extraction pipeline with reported CER and field-level F1 per model
2. An ablation and error analysis identifying the best-performing, most robust configuration

Timeline:
10 months: data collection and annotation (2), preprocessing and OCR (2), extraction modelling (3), evaluation/ablation (2), writing (1).

Title:
Predicting Tourist Foot-Traffic Hotspots from Wireless Sensor Network Data Using Spatio-Temporal Models

Problem Statement:
Tourism boards want to anticipate crowding at attractions to manage congestion and staffing, but they lack short-horizon forecasts of visitor density. Wi-Fi probe and BLE sensors at sites produce noisy, irregular counts, and simple averages ignore spatial spillover between nearby zones, so a spatio-temporal model that forecasts per-zone foot traffic is needed for proactive crowd management.

Objectives:
1. Build a forecasting model predicting next-hour visitor counts per zone from wireless sensor data across a tourist precinct
2. Compare a seasonal ARIMA and LSTM baseline against a spatio-temporal graph neural network (ST-GCN)
3. Evaluate using MAE, RMSE, and MAPE per horizon, plus a peak-detection F1 for hotspot alerts

Methodology:
Anonymized Wi-Fi/BLE counts from multiple sensors will be cleaned (de-duplication, MAC-randomization handling), aggregated to 15-minute bins, and arranged on a zone-adjacency graph. After feature engineering (time-of-day, day-of-week, weather, lag features), an ST-GCN is trained in PyTorch and compared with ARIMA and a vanilla LSTM. Evaluation uses a chronological train/validation/test split with walk-forward validation, reporting MAE/RMSE/MAPE by horizon and hotspot-alert F1, with sensitivity analysis on sensor dropout to test robustness.

Scope:
The project forecasts foot traffic for one precinct's defined zones at 15-minute resolution up to a 2-hour horizon. It excludes individual-level tracking, indoor positioning, and live integration with signage systems.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained spatio-temporal forecaster with reported error metrics versus baselines
2. A robustness analysis and hotspot-alert evaluation supporting crowd-management decisions

Timeline:
10 months: data pipeline (2), baselines (2), ST-GCN modelling (3), evaluation and robustness (2), writing (1).

Title:
Machine Learning for Sustainability

Problem Statement:
The world has a lot of sustainability problems and we need machine learning to solve them. Companies want to be green but they don't know how.

Objectives:
1. Use machine learning.
2. Help sustainability.
3. Make a classification.

Methodology:
I will collect some data and use Python to classify things. Machine learning will be used to get good results.

Scope:
This can be used by everyone who cares about the environment and all companies in the world.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A model that classifies stuff.
2. Better sustainability.

Title:
Deep Learning Vision for Logistics

Problem Statement:
Logistics is very big and there are many trucks and boxes. Deep learning and computer vision are powerful so they should help logistics somehow.

Objectives:
1. Do deep learning.
2. Use computer vision.
3. Improve logistics.

Methodology:
I plan to use a neural network and some images. The computer will look at the images and learn. This is computer vision.

Scope:
The project covers all logistics companies and warehouses everywhere.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A vision system.
2. Faster logistics.

Title:
NLP for E-Government

Problem Statement:
Governments have many documents and citizens are confused. NLP is a trending technology that can read text, so it would be good for e-government services.

Objectives:
1. Apply NLP.
2. Help citizens.
3. Read documents.

Methodology:
I will use natural language processing and AI to understand text. Some libraries will be used and I will train a model.

Scope:
All government departments and all citizens can use this innovative system.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An NLP tool.
2. Happier citizens.

Title:
A Course Recommender System for Online Learning Students

Problem Statement:
Students on e-learning platforms struggle to pick which course to take next because there are too many choices. A recommender system could suggest relevant courses based on what they have already studied.

Objectives:
1. Build a recommender system for online courses.
2. Suggest courses based on student history.
3. Test if students like the recommendations.

Methodology:
I will use collaborative filtering to recommend courses. The system will look at what similar students took and suggest the same. I will build it in Python with a simple web interface and use a public course dataset.

Scope:
The system focuses on recommending online courses to university students. It will not handle payments or video streaming.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working recommender web app.
2. A set of recommendations for each student.

Timeline:
The project will take about two semesters from planning to testing.

Title:
Voice-Based Product Search for Retail Customers

Problem Statement:
Customers in online retail stores sometimes find it hard to type product names, especially on mobile phones. A speech recognition feature could let them search by voice instead of typing.

Objectives:
1. Add voice search to a retail website.
2. Convert spoken words into search queries.
3. Check how accurate the voice search is.

Methodology:
I will use a speech recognition library such as the Web Speech API or Google Speech-to-Text to turn voice into text, then feed the text into a normal product search. The prototype will be a small online shop built with React.

Scope:
The project covers English voice search for a demo retail catalogue. It will not support multiple languages or payment processing.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A retail demo with working voice search.
2. An accuracy report on recognized queries.

Timeline:
Around two semesters, split into build and testing phases.

Title:
A Network Intrusion Detection Prototype for Smart City Networks

Problem Statement:
Smart city systems connect many devices over networks, which makes them targets for attacks. Detecting suspicious network traffic early can help protect city infrastructure.

Objectives:
1. Build an intrusion detection system using machine learning.
2. Classify network traffic as normal or attack.
3. Measure detection accuracy.

Methodology:
I will use a public intrusion dataset like NSL-KDD and train a classifier such as a decision tree or random forest to detect attacks. The model will be evaluated on accuracy. Python with scikit-learn will be used.

Scope:
The project uses an existing offline dataset and focuses on detecting common attack types. It will not be deployed on a live smart city network.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained intrusion detection model.
2. A report comparing accuracy of two classifiers.

Timeline:
Two semesters covering data preparation, modeling, and evaluation.

Title:
A Vulnerability Scanner for Tourism Booking Websites

Problem Statement:
Many small tourism and hotel booking websites are built quickly and may contain common security flaws like SQL injection or cross-site scripting. Owners often cannot afford professional security audits.

Objectives:
1. Build a tool that scans tourism websites for common vulnerabilities.
2. Detect SQL injection and XSS issues.
3. Produce a simple report for the website owner.

Methodology:
I will develop a Python scanner that sends test inputs to web forms and checks responses for signs of SQL injection and XSS. I will test it against a deliberately vulnerable practice site such as DVWA.

Scope:
The tool focuses on two vulnerability types for small booking sites. It will not fix the vulnerabilities, only report them, and will not scan APIs.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working scanner with a report output.
2. Test results from a practice vulnerable website.

Timeline:
About two semesters from design to testing.

Title:
Static and Dynamic Analysis of Malicious Links Shared on Social Media

Problem Statement:
Social media platforms are frequently used to spread links that lead to malware or phishing pages. Users click these links without knowing the risk. A lightweight analysis tool that combines static URL features with sandbox behaviour could flag dangerous links before users open them.

Objectives:
1. Collect a labelled dataset of benign and malicious URLs shared on social media.
2. Extract static features such as domain age, URL length, and use of redirects.
3. Train a classifier and validate it against a behavioural sandbox check.

Methodology:
I will combine the PhishTank and a benign Alexa-based list to build a dataset, extract lexical and host-based features, and train a random forest classifier with scikit-learn evaluated by precision, recall, and F1. A subset of flagged URLs will be checked in an isolated sandbox to confirm behaviour.

Scope:
The project targets HTTP/HTTPS links only and uses pre-collected datasets. It will not perform full binary malware reverse engineering or live social media crawling.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained URL classifier with reported precision and recall.
2. A comparison between static-only and static-plus-sandbox results.

Timeline:
Semester one for data and feature work, semester two for modeling and evaluation.

Title:
A Responsive Appointment and Records Platform for Small Clinics

Problem Statement:
Small private clinics often rely on paper records and phone calls for appointments, which causes double bookings and lost patient histories. A responsive web platform would let staff manage appointments and basic records from any device.

Objectives:
1. Design a responsive web platform for clinic appointment booking.
2. Allow staff to store and retrieve basic patient records securely.
3. Evaluate usability with clinic staff.

Methodology:
I will build the platform with React on the front end and a Node.js/Express REST API backed by PostgreSQL. Authentication will use JWT with role-based access for staff and doctors. Usability will be evaluated with a System Usability Scale survey given to a small group of testers.

Scope:
The platform covers appointment scheduling and basic patient records for a single clinic. It excludes billing, insurance claims, and integration with national health systems.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A deployed responsive web application.
2. A usability evaluation report with SUS scores.

Timeline:
Two semesters: requirements and design first, then build and evaluation.

Title:
A Progressive Web App for Personal Budget Tracking

Problem Statement:
Many young adults lose track of daily spending because finance apps are heavy, require accounts, or need a constant connection. A progressive web app (PWA) that works offline and installs like a native app could make budget tracking easier and more private.

Objectives:
1. Build a PWA for tracking income and expenses that works offline.
2. Provide category-based spending summaries and charts.
3. Evaluate offline reliability and user satisfaction.

Methodology:
I will develop the PWA using React with a service worker for offline caching and IndexedDB for local storage so data stays on the device. Charts will be rendered with Chart.js. Offline behaviour will be tested by toggling network conditions, and satisfaction measured with a short questionnaire.

Scope:
The app handles manual expense entry and local summaries for a single user. It excludes bank account syncing, multi-currency conversion, and cloud backup.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An installable offline-capable budgeting PWA.
2. A short evaluation of offline reliability and user feedback.

Timeline:
About two semesters, divided into development and testing.

Title:
A Cross-Platform Mobile App for Shop-Floor Defect Reporting

Problem Statement:
On manufacturing shop floors, workers often report machine faults or product defects verbally or on paper, so reports get lost and managers lack a clear record. A cross-platform mobile app would let workers log defects with photos in real time.

Objectives:
1. Build a cross-platform mobile app for logging defects with photos.
2. Let supervisors view and filter reported defects on a dashboard.
3. Evaluate the app with a small group of workers.

Methodology:
I will develop the app with Flutter so it runs on both Android and iOS from one codebase, using Firebase for authentication, storage of photos, and a real-time database. Supervisors will see a filtered list view. The app will be evaluated through a task-based usability test.

Scope:
The app covers defect logging and viewing for one factory line. It excludes integration with existing ERP systems and predictive maintenance.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working Android and iOS defect-reporting app.
2. A usability test summary.

Timeline:
Two semesters split between development and field testing.

Title:
An Android Native App for Community Incident Reporting in Public Safety

Problem Statement:
Residents who witness hazards such as broken streetlights, flooding, or accidents often have no quick way to report them to local authorities. An Android app with location tagging could speed up reporting and routing to the right department.

Objectives:
1. Build a native Android app for reporting public safety incidents with location.
2. Categorise incidents and attach photos and GPS coordinates.
3. Evaluate report accuracy and user experience.

Methodology:
I will develop the app natively in Kotlin using Android Jetpack components, the Fused Location Provider for GPS, and a Firebase backend to store reports. Reports will be categorised and viewable on a map. Evaluation will use a small pilot with simulated incident reports and a usability questionnaire.

Scope:
The app focuses on citizen-side reporting for one municipality. It excludes the authority dispatch system and emergency calling.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A functioning Android incident-reporting app with map view.
2. A pilot evaluation report.

Timeline:
Two semesters, design then implementation and evaluation.

Title:
An IoT Sensor Network for Household Energy Monitoring

Problem Statement:
Households often cannot see which appliances consume the most electricity, so they cannot reduce waste effectively. A low-cost IoT sensor network could measure per-circuit consumption and present it on a dashboard.

Objectives:
1. Build an IoT node that measures electrical current and sends readings wirelessly.
2. Aggregate readings from multiple nodes into a central dashboard.
3. Evaluate measurement accuracy against a reference meter.

Methodology:
I will use ESP32 microcontrollers with non-invasive SCT-013 current sensors, publishing readings over MQTT to a Raspberry Pi broker. Data will be stored in InfluxDB and visualised with Grafana. Accuracy will be validated by comparing readings against a calibrated plug-in power meter.

Scope:
The system monitors up to three circuits in one home for demonstration. It excludes automated appliance control and utility-grade billing certification.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working multi-node energy monitoring dashboard.
2. An accuracy comparison against a reference meter.

Timeline:
Two semesters covering hardware assembly, software, and validation.

Title:
An Occupancy-Aware Smart Home Automation Controller for Small Businesses

Problem Statement:
Small businesses such as cafes and salons waste energy because lighting and air-conditioning run on fixed schedules regardless of whether anyone is present. Off-the-shelf smart home kits are consumer-focused and lack occupancy-driven logic suited to irregular small-business hours.

Objectives:
1. Design a rule-and-occupancy-based automation controller for small commercial spaces.
2. Integrate PIR and door sensors to drive lighting and HVAC switching.
3. Evaluate energy savings against a fixed-schedule baseline over two weeks.

Methodology:
The controller will run on a Raspberry Pi using Home Assistant, with ESP32-based PIR/door sensors over Zigbee and smart relays for switching. Occupancy is inferred from sensor fusion with a debounce timer. I will run an A/B comparison: one week on a fixed schedule, one week with occupancy-aware control, logging kWh via smart plugs and comparing means with a paired test.

Scope:
The system targets a single small commercial unit with up to six controllable zones. It excludes cloud dependence, voice assistants, and security-camera analytics.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A deployed occupancy-aware controller with documented rules.
2. A quantified energy-saving comparison versus the baseline schedule.

Timeline:
Weeks 1-4 requirements and hardware, 5-10 integration, 11-14 two-week trial and analysis.

Title:
Edge-Based Crop Disease Detection on Low-Power Devices for Smallholder Farms

Problem Statement:
Smallholder farmers often lack reliable internet, so cloud-based crop disease detection apps fail in the field. Running detection directly on an affordable edge device would give offline, real-time diagnosis where it is needed.

Objectives:
1. Train a lightweight CNN to classify common leaf diseases on three crops.
2. Quantise and deploy the model on an edge device for offline inference.
3. Benchmark accuracy, latency, and power against a cloud baseline.

Methodology:
I will fine-tune MobileNetV2 on the PlantVillage dataset for selected crops, apply post-training INT8 quantisation with TensorFlow Lite, and deploy on a Raspberry Pi 4 with a camera. Evaluation reports top-1 accuracy with a confusion matrix, on-device inference latency, and measured power draw, compared against the same model served from a cloud API.

Scope:
The project covers three crops and a fixed disease set under controlled lighting. It excludes pest detection, yield prediction, and a full mobile UI beyond a demo viewer.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A quantised on-device disease classifier with reported accuracy and latency.
2. An edge-versus-cloud trade-off analysis.

Timeline:
Weeks 1-5 data and training, 6-9 quantisation and deployment, 10-14 benchmarking and write-up.

Title:
A Cloud-Native Microservices Backend for Real-Time Bus Tracking

Problem Statement:
City bus passengers lack reliable real-time arrival information, and monolithic transit backends struggle to scale during peak load. A cloud-native microservices design could ingest vehicle GPS streams and serve arrival predictions elastically.

Objectives:
1. Decompose a bus-tracking backend into independently deployable microservices.
2. Stream and process live vehicle positions to compute arrival estimates.
3. Evaluate scalability and latency under simulated peak load.

Methodology:
The system will use Spring Boot services (ingestion, tracking, prediction, gateway) containerised with Docker and orchestrated on Kubernetes, with Kafka for GPS event streaming and Redis for hot-position caching. Arrival estimates use a simple speed-and-distance model. Load tests with k6 will measure p95 latency and throughput while horizontal pod autoscaling is enabled, using a simulated GTFS feed.

Scope:
The project covers backend services and a minimal map demo using simulated GPS traces for a few routes. It excludes a production mobile app and real fleet hardware integration.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A deployed microservices backend with autoscaling.
2. A load-test report on latency and throughput under peak load.

Timeline:
Weeks 1-4 design, 5-9 service build, 10-12 load testing, 13-14 analysis.

Title:
A CI/CD Pipeline with Carbon-Aware Build Scheduling for Green Software Delivery

Problem Statement:
Continuous integration pipelines run builds on demand without regard to the carbon intensity of the electricity grid at that moment. Deferring non-urgent builds to lower-carbon periods could cut emissions without harming developer workflow, but few teams have tooling to do so.

Objectives:
1. Build an automated CI/CD pipeline for a sample microservice application.
2. Add a carbon-aware scheduler that defers non-urgent jobs to low-intensity windows.
3. Measure emissions and developer wait-time trade-offs against a default pipeline.

Methodology:
I will set up GitHub Actions with build, test, container-image, and deploy stages to a staging cluster. A scheduler will query a grid carbon-intensity API and delay jobs tagged non-urgent until intensity falls below a threshold. I will estimate per-build emissions from runtime and intensity, comparing a carbon-aware run against a baseline over two weeks and reporting emissions saved versus added delay.

Scope:
The pipeline targets one sample application and one region's carbon data. It excludes multi-cloud cost optimisation and production-critical deployments.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working carbon-aware CI/CD pipeline.
2. A report quantifying emission savings versus scheduling delay.

Timeline:
Weeks 1-4 pipeline setup, 5-9 scheduler, 10-14 two-week measurement and analysis.

Title:
A Batch-and-Stream Big Data Pipeline for Last-Mile Delivery Analytics

Problem Statement:
Last-mile delivery operators generate large volumes of GPS pings, order events, and traffic data, but often analyse them only in slow daily batches, so dispatchers cannot react to delays as they happen. A unified pipeline supporting both historical batch and near-real-time stream analytics is needed.

Objectives:
1. Build a big data pipeline ingesting delivery events into both batch and streaming layers.
2. Compute late-delivery risk indicators in near real time.
3. Evaluate throughput and end-to-end latency on a simulated event volume.

Methodology:
Following a lambda-style architecture, events will flow through Kafka into Spark Structured Streaming for real-time aggregates and into a data lake (Parquet on MinIO) for batch processing with Spark SQL. Results land in PostgreSQL feeding a dashboard. I will generate a synthetic dataset of millions of delivery events and measure ingestion throughput and processing latency, with a small late-delivery heuristic validated against held-out labels.

Scope:
The project uses simulated data for one metropolitan region and a fixed schema. It excludes route optimisation and integration with live courier APIs.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working batch-plus-stream analytics pipeline with a dashboard.
2. A performance report on throughput and latency.

Timeline:
Weeks 1-4 architecture and data generation, 5-10 pipeline build, 11-14 benchmarking and write-up.

Title:
A Business Intelligence Dashboard for Municipal Service-Request Resolution with Anomaly Flagging

Problem Statement:
Municipal e-government portals collect thousands of citizen service requests (potholes, waste, lighting) but officials lack a consolidated view of resolution performance across departments, so backlogs and outlier delays go unnoticed. Existing open-data portals publish raw counts without department-level SLA tracking or statistically grounded anomaly flagging, leaving decision-makers without actionable insight.

Objectives:
1. Design a BI dashboard that tracks service-request resolution KPIs (volume, median time-to-close, SLA compliance) by department and ward.
2. Implement an anomaly-flagging layer that highlights wards or weeks whose delays deviate significantly from historical norms.
3. Evaluate decision usefulness through a task-based study with proxy officials, against a baseline raw-table view.

Methodology:
Using the public SF311 service-request dataset, I will model a star schema (fact table plus date/department/ward dimensions) in PostgreSQL, build incremental ETL with dbt, and surface KPIs in a Metabase dashboard. Anomalies are flagged with seasonal-trend (STL) decomposition plus a robust z-score on residuals, tuned by precision against manually labelled known backlog periods. A within-subjects study (n approx 12) compares task accuracy and completion time on the dashboard versus a raw-table baseline, analysed with a paired t-test.

Scope:
The work covers descriptive KPIs and statistical anomaly flagging for one city's open dataset over three years. It explicitly excludes predictive forecasting of future demand, citizen-facing features, and personally identifiable data, which is absent from the source.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A deployed BI dashboard with documented KPI definitions and a validated anomaly-flagging module (reported precision/recall on labelled backlogs).
2. An empirical usability study showing measured improvement in decision-task accuracy and time over the baseline.

Timeline:
Weeks 1-3 data modelling and ETL, 4-7 dashboard and KPIs, 8-10 anomaly module and tuning, 11-13 user study, 14 analysis and reporting.

Title:
Short-Term Forecasting of University E-Learning Server Load for Capacity Planning

Problem Statement:
University e-learning platforms suffer slowdowns during predictable but under-planned spikes (assignment deadlines, exam weeks), yet IT teams provision capacity from intuition rather than data. Accurate short-term load forecasts that account for academic-calendar effects would let teams pre-scale resources, but generic forecasters ignore these domain-specific exogenous signals.

Objectives:
1. Build a forecasting pipeline predicting hourly e-learning request load 24 hours ahead using historical load plus academic-calendar features.
2. Compare classical, machine-learning, and deep-learning forecasters under a unified rolling-origin evaluation.
3. Quantify the marginal value of calendar exogenous features and translate accuracy into a capacity-planning rule.

Methodology:
From two years of hourly server logs, I will engineer calendar features (deadline proximity, exam period, weekday, holiday). Models compared: seasonal-naive and SARIMA baselines, gradient-boosted trees (LightGBM) with lagged and exogenous features, and an LSTM. Evaluation uses rolling-origin (time-series) cross-validation reporting MAE, RMSE, and MASE, with significance via Diebold-Mariano tests, and an ablation removing calendar features. The best model feeds a threshold rule estimating servers needed per hour.

Scope:
The study forecasts aggregate request load for one institution's LMS at hourly granularity, 24 hours ahead. It excludes per-course forecasting, autoscaling actuation, and cost modelling of specific cloud SKUs.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A reproducible forecasting pipeline with a benchmarked model table (MAE/RMSE/MASE) and an ablation isolating calendar-feature contribution.
2. A capacity-planning recommendation mapping forecasts to provisioning decisions, with documented limitations and risk notes.

Timeline:
Weeks 1-3 data cleaning and feature engineering, 4-6 baselines, 7-9 ML/DL models, 10-11 evaluation and ablation, 12-13 capacity rule, 14 write-up.

Title:
Blockchain for Small Business

Problem Statement:
Small businesses lose money and trust is a big problem. Blockchain is a new technology that is very secure and cannot be hacked, so it can help them a lot.

Objectives:
1. To use blockchain.
2. To make small business better.
3. To use smart contracts.

Methodology:
I will study blockchain and make some smart contracts. Then I will see if it works for shops.

Scope:
This will be for all small businesses in the world to do their payments and contracts safely.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A blockchain system.
2. Small businesses that are happy and safe.

Title:
AR App for Farming

Problem Statement:
Farmers have many problems with their crops and they need help. Augmented reality is cool and shows things on the phone so it can help farmers grow food.

Objectives:
1. To make an AR app.
2. To help farmers.
3. To show crops on phone.

Methodology:
I will use Unity and make an app with AR. Then farmers can point the phone at plants.

Scope:
For all farmers everywhere who grow any kind of crop.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An AR app for farms.
2. More food and happy farmers.

Title:
VR Training for Transport

Problem Statement:
Drivers and transport workers need training but it is dangerous and costs money. VR is the future and feels very real so it can train them better.

Objectives:
1. To build VR training.
2. To train transport people.
3. To make it safe.

Methodology:
I will use a VR headset and make a simulation. Then people can practice driving inside it.

Scope:
This will train all transport workers and drivers in the whole industry.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A VR training simulation.
2. Safer and smarter workers.

Title:
A 2D Game to Teach Sustainability Habits

Problem Statement:
Many young people do not think about recycling or saving energy in daily life. Reading posters is boring, so a fun 2D game might get them more interested in sustainable habits, but most existing apps are just quizzes.

Objectives:
1. To design a 2D game about recycling and energy saving.
2. To add levels and a scoring system.
3. To test if players enjoy it.

Methodology:
I will build the game in Unity using C#. The player sorts trash and turns off lights to earn points across several levels. I will use free sprite assets and design the levels myself. After it is done I will ask some classmates to play it and give feedback.

Scope:
The game will be a single-player 2D platformer with about five levels focused on recycling and energy. It will run on Windows PC only.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A playable 2D sustainability game with five levels.
2. Feedback from a small group of testers.

Timeline:
About four months to design, build and test.

Title:
Serious Game for Learning Warehouse Logistics

Problem Statement:
Logistics students learn about warehouse picking and routing from slides, which is hard to picture. A serious game could let them practice ordering and picking goods in a simulated warehouse, though it will be a simplified version of real systems.

Objectives:
1. To build a game that simulates picking orders in a warehouse.
2. To include a simple routing puzzle between shelves.
3. To measure if players improve their picking time.

Methodology:
The game will be made with Unity and C#. Players receive orders, walk a character to shelves, and pack items before a timer runs out. I will record completion times to see if players get faster. Level data will be stored in simple files. Testing will be done with a few logistics diploma students.

Scope:
A single-player 2D top-down game with three warehouse layouts. Real inventory systems and multiplayer are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working warehouse logistics game.
2. A short report on whether play improves picking speed.

Timeline:
Roughly five months across design, build, and testing.

Title:
A Healthcare Records Portal for a Local Government Clinic

Problem Statement:
Many small government clinics still keep patient visit records on paper, which is slow to search and easy to misplace. A simple web portal could let clinic staff store and look up patient visits, but it will not integrate with national health systems.

Objectives:
1. To build a web system that stores patient and visit records.
2. To let staff search records by name or ID.
3. To add basic login roles for nurses and admins.

Methodology:
I will use PHP and MySQL with a Bootstrap front end. Staff create patient profiles and add visit notes, which are saved in the database. Login will separate nurse and admin roles. I will test the search and record forms with sample data and ask one clinic staff member for feedback.

Scope:
A web app for a single clinic covering patient profiles, visit notes, and search. Billing, insurance, and inter-clinic sharing are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working clinic records portal with role-based login.
2. Staff feedback on usability.

Timeline:
Around five months including requirements, build, and testing.

Title:
A Telemedicine Platform for Online Tutoring Support

Problem Statement:
Students in rural areas sometimes cannot reach tutors easily, and existing video tools are not built for scheduling lessons. A telemedicine-style platform adapted for tutoring could let students book and join video sessions with tutors, though it will rely on an existing video API rather than custom streaming.

Objectives:
1. To build a platform where students book tutoring sessions.
2. To add video calls using a third-party API.
3. To let tutors manage their availability.

Methodology:
The system will be built with React and Node.js with a MongoDB database. Students browse tutors, pick a time slot, and join a video call powered by an embedded API such as Jitsi. Tutors set available hours. I will test booking and joining flows with a few volunteer users and fix issues found.

Scope:
A web platform for one-to-one tutoring with booking and embedded video. Payments and group classes are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working booking-plus-video tutoring platform.
2. Test feedback from a small group of students and tutors.

Timeline:
Approximately five months over four phases.

Title:
An Adaptive E-Learning System for Retail Staff Onboarding

Problem Statement:
Retail chains onboard new staff with the same fixed training modules regardless of prior experience, which wastes time for experienced hires and overwhelms beginners. There is room for a system that adjusts module order based on quiz performance, though full intelligent tutoring is beyond this project.

Objectives:
1. To build an e-learning system with product, till, and customer-service modules for retail staff.
2. To add a rule-based adaptation that reorders or skips modules based on pre-quiz scores.
3. To evaluate learning gain using pre- and post-tests with a small user group.

Methodology:
The platform will use Django with PostgreSQL and a Bootstrap front end. Each module has content, a quiz, and a difficulty tag. A rule engine routes learners: high pre-quiz scores skip ahead, low scores get remedial modules first. I will compare adaptive versus fixed paths with about fifteen testers, measuring post-test scores and time spent, and gather a short usability survey.

Scope:
A web app covering three retail training modules with rule-based adaptation. Mobile apps and machine-learning personalisation are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working adaptive e-learning system for retail onboarding.
2. A comparison report of adaptive versus fixed paths on learning gain and time.

Timeline:
Six months: requirements (1), build (3), evaluation (1.5), write-up (0.5).

Title:
A QR-Based Fintech Payment App for Smart City Parking

Problem Statement:
In many cities, paying for street parking still relies on coin meters or separate apps per operator, which frustrates drivers. A unified QR-based payment app could let drivers pay any participating bay from one wallet, though it will run in a sandbox rather than handle real bank settlement.

Objectives:
1. To build a mobile app that pays for parking by scanning a bay QR code.
2. To implement a wallet with top-up and transaction history using a sandbox payment gateway.
3. To evaluate transaction success rate and task time against a meter baseline.

Methodology:
The app will be built in Flutter with a Spring Boot backend and MySQL. Scanning a QR identifies the bay; the user confirms duration and pays from a wallet topped up via the Stripe test gateway. Sessions and receipts are stored server-side. I will run a usability test with around twelve users timing how long payment takes versus a simulated coin meter, and log transaction success and failure cases.

Scope:
A prototype Android app plus backend with sandbox payments and a simulated city bay map. Real banking integration and enforcement systems are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working QR parking payment app with wallet and history.
2. An evaluation comparing payment time and success rate to a meter baseline.

Timeline:
Six months across design, backend, app, and evaluation phases.

Title:
Fraud Detection for Online Tourism Bookings

Problem Statement:
Tourism booking sites face fraudulent reservations made with stolen cards, causing chargebacks. Manual review does not scale and simple rules miss new patterns. A machine-learning classifier on transaction features could flag risky bookings for review, but it will be trained on a public dataset rather than live operator data.

Objectives:
1. To engineer features from booking transactions such as amount, time-to-travel, and country mismatch.
2. To train and compare logistic regression, random forest, and XGBoost classifiers for fraud.
3. To evaluate using precision, recall, F1, and ROC-AUC with attention to class imbalance.

Methodology:
I will use a public credit-card or booking fraud dataset on Kaggle and frame travel-style features. After cleaning, I will handle imbalance with SMOTE and class weighting, then train logistic regression, random forest, and XGBoost with 5-fold cross-validation and a grid search on key hyperparameters. Models are compared on precision, recall, F1, and ROC-AUC, with a confusion matrix on a held-out test set. A small Flask demo will score sample bookings.

Scope:
An offline model plus a demo UI, trained on a public dataset. Real-time deployment and integration with a live booking engine are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained fraud classifier with a documented comparison of three models.
2. A Flask demo that flags sample bookings as low or high risk.

Timeline:
Six months: data and features (1.5), modelling (2.5), evaluation (1), demo and write-up (1).

Title:
A Hybrid Recommendation Engine for a Social Media Marketplace

Problem Statement:
Social-commerce feeds often show items unrelated to what a user actually wants, lowering engagement. Pure popularity ranking ignores personal taste, while pure collaborative filtering struggles with new users. A hybrid recommender could blend both, though it will be evaluated offline on a public dataset.

Objectives:
1. To build collaborative-filtering and content-based recommenders for marketplace items.
2. To combine them into a weighted hybrid that handles cold-start users.
3. To evaluate ranking quality using Precision@K, Recall@K, and NDCG against baselines.

Methodology:
Using a public e-commerce interaction dataset, I will implement item-based collaborative filtering with matrix factorisation (SVD via the Surprise library) and a content-based model on item categories and text via TF-IDF. A weighted hybrid falls back to content features for cold-start users. I will evaluate with an 80/20 temporal split, reporting Precision@10, Recall@10, and NDCG against popularity and single-method baselines. A small web demo shows recommendations for a chosen user.

Scope:
An offline recommender with a demo UI on a public dataset. Live A/B testing and real social-graph signals are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A hybrid recommender beating popularity and single-method baselines on ranking metrics.
2. A demo showing top-N items for sample users.

Timeline:
Six months across data prep, modelling, evaluation, and demo.

Title:
A Retrieval-Augmented Chatbot for Hospital FAQ Support

Problem Statement:
Hospital reception staff repeatedly answer the same questions about visiting hours, departments, and document requirements, while generic chatbots invent wrong answers. A retrieval-augmented chatbot grounded in the hospital's own FAQ could give accurate replies, but it will not give medical or diagnostic advice.

Objectives:
1. To build a chatbot that answers hospital FAQ questions from a curated document set.
2. To ground answers using retrieval over embedded FAQ passages to reduce hallucination.
3. To evaluate answer accuracy and intent coverage against a manually labelled test set.

Methodology:
FAQ documents will be chunked and embedded with a sentence-transformer model and stored in a FAISS index. At query time the system retrieves top passages and passes them with the question to an LLM to compose a grounded answer; out-of-scope questions return a safe fallback. I will build a test set of about eighty questions with expected answers and measure retrieval hit rate and answer correctness by manual rating, plus handling of medical questions that must be refused.

Scope:
A web chatbot answering administrative hospital FAQs in English. Clinical advice, appointment booking, and multilingual support are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working retrieval-grounded FAQ chatbot with a safe refusal path.
2. An evaluation of retrieval hit rate and answer accuracy on the labelled set.

Timeline:
Six months: corpus and retrieval (2), chatbot (2), evaluation (1), write-up (1).

Title:
A Knowledge-Graph Search Tool for Financial Filings

Problem Statement:
Analysts searching company filings rely on keyword search, which misses relationships such as which firm acquired another or who sits on which board. A knowledge graph built from filings could answer relationship queries directly, though it will cover a limited set of companies and entity types.

Objectives:
1. To extract companies, people, and relationships from a sample of financial filings.
2. To build a knowledge graph and expose relationship queries through a search interface.
3. To evaluate extraction accuracy and query usefulness against keyword search.

Methodology:
I will collect a sample of public filings, run named-entity recognition with spaCy and rule patterns to extract companies, people, and relations like acquired, owns, and board-member. Triples are loaded into Neo4j. A web UI lets users run relationship queries (for example, companies acquired by X) translated to Cypher. I will measure extraction precision and recall on a hand-labelled subset and compare answers to keyword search on a set of test questions.

Scope:
A graph over about fifty filings with three entity types and a handful of relations. Real-time ingestion and full legal-language parsing are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A populated financial knowledge graph with a relationship search UI.
2. An evaluation of extraction accuracy and a comparison with keyword search.

Timeline:
Six months across extraction, graph build, UI, and evaluation.

Title:
Semantic Segmentation of Surface Defects on Manufactured Metal Parts

Problem Statement:
Visual inspection of metal parts for scratches, cracks, and stains is manual and inconsistent, and bounding-box detection cannot capture defect shape or area for quality grading. Pixel-level segmentation would quantify defect extent, but generalising across lighting and part types remains hard, and this project targets a constrained set of defect classes.

Objectives:
1. To prepare a segmentation dataset from a public surface-defect benchmark with pixel masks.
2. To train and compare U-Net and DeepLabv3+ segmentation models on three defect classes.
3. To evaluate per-class IoU and Dice against a classical thresholding baseline and analyse failure cases.

Methodology:
I will use a public metal surface-defect dataset (such as NEU or Severstal-style masks), splitting it 70/15/15 with augmentation for rotation, brightness, and flips. U-Net and DeepLabv3+ with a ResNet encoder are trained in PyTorch using a combined cross-entropy and Dice loss, with early stopping on validation Dice. Evaluation reports mean IoU and Dice per class on the held-out test set, compared with an Otsu-threshold baseline, plus qualitative analysis of false positives under uneven lighting.

Scope:
Offline segmentation of three defect classes on one part family from a public dataset. Real-time line deployment and 3D inspection are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. Two trained segmentation models with per-class IoU and Dice reported.
2. A failure-case analysis and a recommendation between U-Net and DeepLabv3+.

Timeline:
Seven months: data and masks (1.5), training (2.5), evaluation (1.5), analysis and write-up (1.5).

Title:
Real-Time Detection of Unattended Bags for Public-Safety Monitoring

Problem Statement:
CCTV operators in stations cannot watch every screen, and unattended bags are a recognised safety concern. An object detector that flags stationary bags separated from people could assist operators, but crowded scenes, occlusion, and false alarms from luggage in transit make reliable detection difficult, so this project focuses on a constrained indoor setting.

Objectives:
1. To assemble an annotated dataset of bags and people from public CCTV-style footage.
2. To fine-tune and compare YOLOv8 and Faster R-CNN for bag and person detection.
3. To add a simple abandonment rule and evaluate detection mAP and alert precision against ground truth.

Methodology:
Frames from public surveillance datasets will be annotated for person and bag classes. I will fine-tune YOLOv8 and Faster R-CNN in PyTorch with augmentation, comparing mAP@0.5 and inference speed on a held-out test set. A lightweight tracker links bags across frames; a bag stationary beyond a threshold and far from any person raises an alert. Alert precision and recall are measured against manually labelled abandonment events, and false alarms in crowding are analysed.

Scope:
Offline detection on recorded indoor footage with a rule-based abandonment trigger. Live camera integration, re-identification, and outdoor crowds are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. Two trained detectors compared on mAP and speed, with a chosen model.
2. An abandonment-alert evaluation reporting precision, recall, and false-alarm analysis.

Timeline:
Seven months across annotation, training, rule and tracking, and evaluation.

Title:
Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis of Customer Feedback on Energy Providers

Problem Statement:
Energy retailers receive thousands of reviews mixing praise and complaints about billing, outages, and customer service in a single text, so a single overall sentiment hides which aspect is failing. Aspect-based sentiment analysis can separate these, but informal language and sarcasm reduce accuracy, and this project limits itself to a defined set of aspects.

Objectives:
1. To build an annotated dataset of energy-provider reviews labelled by aspect and sentiment.
2. To fine-tune a transformer (BERT) for aspect-based sentiment and compare it to a TF-IDF plus SVM baseline.
3. To evaluate per-aspect macro-F1 and produce an aspect-level sentiment summary dashboard.

Methodology:
I will collect public energy-provider reviews and label about 1,500 of them for four aspects (billing, reliability, service, pricing) with positive, negative, or neutral sentiment, double-checking a subset for inter-annotator agreement. A BERT model is fine-tuned in PyTorch with stratified splits and compared to a TF-IDF plus linear SVM baseline. Evaluation reports per-aspect and macro-averaged F1 on a held-out set, with error analysis on sarcastic and mixed reviews. A small dashboard aggregates aspect sentiment over time.

Scope:
Offline aspect-based sentiment on English reviews for four fixed aspects. Real-time streaming and multilingual reviews are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A labelled dataset and a fine-tuned BERT model beating the SVM baseline on macro-F1.
2. An aspect-level sentiment dashboard and an error analysis.

Timeline:
Seven months: data and labelling (2), modelling (2), evaluation (1.5), dashboard and write-up (1.5).

Title:
Learning-Based Index Recommendation for Small-Business Database Workloads

Problem Statement:
Small businesses run off-the-shelf apps on databases that slow down as data grows, and owners lack DBAs to tune indexes. Default indexing and trial-and-error are common, yet poor index choices waste query time. A tool that recommends indexes from observed query logs could help, though it targets single-node MySQL and a bounded query set rather than arbitrary workloads.

Objectives:
1. To capture and characterise query workloads from a sample small-business schema.
2. To implement and compare a cost-based heuristic and a learning-based index recommender.
3. To evaluate end-to-end query latency before and after recommended indexes on a benchmark.

Methodology:
Using a TPC-C-style or sample retail schema on MySQL, I will generate a mixed read-write workload and parse query logs for candidate columns. A cost-based heuristic ranks indexes via the optimizer's estimates; a learning-based approach trains a regression model to predict latency improvement per candidate index from query and table features. I will apply each method's top recommendations and measure total workload latency and storage overhead against the un-indexed and default-indexed baselines, repeating runs to control variance.

Scope:
Single-node MySQL, B-tree index recommendation on one schema and workload mix. Distributed databases, materialised views, and write-amplification tuning are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. Two index recommenders compared on workload latency and storage cost.
2. A report quantifying speedup over default indexing on the benchmark.

Timeline:
Seven months across workload setup, heuristic, learning model, and evaluation.

Title:
Facial Recognition Attendance System for Farm Workers

Problem Statement:
Farms employ many seasonal workers and track attendance on paper, which is slow and easy to fake through buddy-punching. A facial recognition system could log attendance automatically when workers arrive, though outdoor lighting and dust may affect accuracy.

Objectives:
1. To build a facial recognition attendance system for farm workers.
2. To store attendance records with timestamps in a database.
3. To test recognition accuracy under different lighting.

Methodology:
I will use Python with OpenCV and a pre-trained face-recognition library (dlib/face_recognition) to detect and match enrolled faces from a webcam. Recognised workers are logged with a timestamp into a MySQL database, viewable in a simple web dashboard. I will enrol about twenty volunteers and test recognition accuracy indoors and in bright outdoor light, recording how often it matches the right person.

Scope:
A prototype that enrols and recognises around twenty workers from a single camera and logs attendance. Anti-spoofing, multi-camera setups, and very large worker pools are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working face-recognition attendance prototype with a dashboard.
2. An accuracy report across lighting conditions.

Timeline:
Six months across enrolment, recognition, logging, and testing.

Title:
A Robust OCR Pipeline for Extracting Structured Fields from Vehicle Consignment Notes in Transportation

Problem Statement:
Freight operators receive consignment notes and delivery orders as scanned images and phone photos, then re-key fields such as consignment number, vehicle plate, origin, destination, and weight by hand, which is slow and error-prone. General OCR engines transcribe raw text but do not reliably map it to these fields under skew, low contrast, stamps, and varied layouts. The gap is a layout-tolerant pipeline that not only reads text but extracts a validated structured record, evaluated against a labelled ground truth rather than judged informally.

Objectives:
1. To assemble and annotate a dataset of at least 600 transportation consignment-note images with field-level ground truth (consignment number, plate, origin, destination, date, weight).
2. To build a pipeline combining preprocessing (deskew, denoise, adaptive thresholding), text detection and recognition, and a layout-plus-regex field-extraction stage, comparing Tesseract against a deep recognizer (TrOCR/PaddleOCR).
3. To evaluate end-to-end performance using character error rate, field-level precision/recall/F1, and exact-match accuracy per field, with ablations on each preprocessing step.

Methodology:
Images will be collected from public freight-document sources and synthetically augmented (rotation, blur, JPEG noise, stamp overlays) to reach the target size, with field-level annotation and a held-out 70/15/15 split. The pipeline preprocesses with OpenCV (Hough-based deskew, CLAHE, adaptive thresholding), detects regions, and recognises text with two backends compared on equal footing: Tesseract LSTM and a transformer recognizer (TrOCR or PaddleOCR). A hybrid field extractor combines positional layout cues with regular-expression and dictionary validation (for example, plate and date formats) to populate the structured record. I will run 5-fold cross-validation on the training portion for the extraction rules, report CER, per-field F1, and exact-match on the test set, and conduct ablations removing each preprocessing stage. Risks (poor scans, unseen layouts) are mitigated with a confidence threshold that routes low-confidence fields to manual review.

Scope:
The project covers English-language transportation consignment notes for six fixed fields, delivered as an offline batch tool with a review UI. Real-time mobile capture, handwriting recognition, and integration with a live transport-management system are explicitly excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A labelled benchmark of 600+ consignment-note images and a reproducible OCR-to-structured-record pipeline.
2. A quantitative comparison of OCR backends with CER, per-field F1, exact-match accuracy, and a preprocessing ablation study.

Timeline:
Eight months: data collection and annotation (2), preprocessing and OCR integration (2), field extraction (1.5), evaluation and ablations (1.5), write-up (1).

Title:
Anomaly Detection and Predictive Analytics for a Wireless Sensor Network Monitoring Building Sustainability Metrics

Problem Statement:
Wireless sensor networks deployed for sustainability monitoring (energy, temperature, humidity, CO2) produce noisy, sometimes missing time-series data, and faults such as drifting sensors or sudden spikes are often noticed only after waste has occurred. Simple fixed-threshold alarms either miss gradual drift or flood operators with false alarms. The gap is a data-driven pipeline that imputes missing readings and detects anomalies on multivariate sensor streams, evaluated against labelled fault events rather than by eyeballing charts.

Objectives:
1. To build a preprocessing pipeline for a public building-sensor dataset that handles missing values and resampling, with injected synthetic faults for ground truth.
2. To implement and compare anomaly detectors — an LSTM autoencoder, an Isolation Forest, and a seasonal statistical baseline — on multivariate sensor streams.
3. To evaluate detection using precision, recall, F1, and detection delay, and to quantify short-horizon forecasting error for energy use.

Methodology:
I will use a public building/energy sensor dataset (for example, a BMS or ASHRAE-style set), resample to fixed intervals, and impute gaps with forward-fill and interpolation, comparing both. Realistic faults (drift, stuck-at, spikes) are injected to create labelled anomalies. An LSTM autoencoder flags points whose reconstruction error exceeds a validation-tuned threshold; Isolation Forest and a seasonal-decomposition statistical method serve as baselines. For forecasting, an LSTM predicts next-hour energy and is compared to ARIMA on RMSE and MAE. Models are tuned with time-series cross-validation to avoid leakage, and detectors are scored on precision, recall, F1, and mean detection delay against the injected labels. A dashboard visualises live anomalies and forecasts.

Scope:
Offline analysis of one public multivariate building-sensor dataset with three anomaly detectors and one forecasting task, packaged with a visualisation dashboard. Live network deployment, radio-layer/MAC optimisation, and edge-device implementation are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A reproducible preprocessing-plus-detection pipeline with three compared anomaly detectors reported on precision, recall, F1, and detection delay.
2. A short-horizon energy forecaster compared against ARIMA and a dashboard for anomalies and forecasts.

Timeline:
Eight months: data and fault injection (1.5), detectors (2.5), forecasting (1.5), evaluation (1.5), dashboard and write-up (1).

Title:
Machine Learning for Factories

Problem Statement:
Factories make a lot of products and sometimes things go wrong. We need machine learning to fix this and help the manufacturing industry be better.

Objectives:
1. Use machine learning in the factory
2. Make predictions
3. Improve the production

Methodology:
I will collect some data from the factory and use Python to do machine learning classification. Then I will train a model and see the results.

Scope:
This project is for all factories and manufacturing companies everywhere. It will work on any kind of product line.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A machine learning system
2. Better factories

Title:
Deep Learning Camera System for Safety
