Public places are not safe and there are many dangers. Cameras can use deep learning to watch people and keep everyone safe from bad things happening.

Objectives:
1. Build a camera system
2. Detect dangerous things
3. Keep the public safe

Methodology:
The system will use deep learning computer vision. I will use a camera and some AI to look at the video and find problems. Neural networks will be used.

Scope:
The project covers all public safety situations including crime, accidents, and emergencies in any city.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working safety camera
2. Safer streets for people

Title:
NLP System for the Energy Sector

Problem Statement:
Energy companies have lots of text documents and reports. Natural language processing can read these and find useful information so the energy sector works better.

Objectives:
1. Apply NLP to energy documents
2. Find important information
3. Help energy companies

Methodology:
I plan to use natural language processing techniques in Python. The system will read text and understand it. I will use some libraries and do research on the topic.

Scope:
This applies to the whole energy industry including oil, gas, solar, and electricity providers around the world.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An NLP tool for energy
2. Faster document reading

Title:
Product Recommendation System for Small Online Shops

Problem Statement:
Small online businesses struggle to suggest relevant products to customers because they lack the resources that large retailers have. As a result, customers often leave without buying, and shop owners miss sales opportunities they could otherwise capture.

Objectives:
1. Build a recommendation feature for a small e-commerce shop
2. Use customer purchase history to suggest products
3. Test whether the suggestions are relevant

Methodology:
The system will use collaborative filtering based on past purchases. I will gather sample transaction data from a small shop and apply a similarity-based algorithm to recommend items. The recommendations will be shown on a simple web page and checked by a few users.

Scope:
The project focuses on one small retail shop and product recommendations only. It does not cover payment, inventory, or shipping features.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working recommendation module integrated into a shop page
2. Feedback from users about whether suggestions were helpful

Timeline:
The project will run across two semesters, with data collection first and development later.

Title:
Voice Command Tool for Farm Workers

Problem Statement:
Farm workers often have their hands busy and dirty, making it hard to type data into devices while working in the field. A speech recognition tool could let them record information by voice, but most existing apps are not designed for noisy outdoor farm settings.

Objectives:
1. Build a speech recognition app for recording farm data
2. Let workers add crop and livestock notes by voice
3. Check accuracy in outdoor conditions

Methodology:
I will use an existing speech-to-text library to convert voice into text and store the results in a small database. Sample recordings will be made on a farm to test how well the system handles background noise. Accuracy will be measured by comparing recognized text to what was actually said.

Scope:
The app covers English voice input for basic farm record-keeping. It does not support other languages or full farm management features.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A mobile speech tool that records farm notes
2. A short report on recognition accuracy in field conditions

Timeline:
Two semesters: build in the first, test and refine in the second.

Title:
Intrusion Detection for Transport Network Systems

Problem Statement:
Transportation systems increasingly rely on connected networks for ticketing and traffic control, which exposes them to cyber attacks. Operators need a way to spot suspicious network traffic, but commercial intrusion detection tools are often too expensive or generic for transport-specific traffic patterns.

Objectives:
1. Build a network intrusion detection prototype for transport network traffic
2. Train it to flag common attack types
3. Measure detection accuracy and false alarms

Methodology:
The prototype will use a machine learning classifier trained on a public intrusion dataset such as NSL-KDD. Network features will be extracted and the model will label traffic as normal or malicious. Detection rate and false positive rate will be reported.

Scope:
The work focuses on detecting a few known attack categories on simulated transport-like traffic. Live deployment and prevention actions are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained detection model with accuracy results
2. A comparison of false positive rates across attack types

Timeline:
Spread over two semesters from dataset preparation to evaluation.

Title:
Web Application Vulnerability Scanner for Green Tech Sites

Problem Statement:
Many small sustainability and green-technology organisations run websites with limited security review, leaving them open to common web attacks. They usually cannot afford professional penetration testing, so basic vulnerabilities such as injection or weak forms go unnoticed.

Objectives:
1. Build a scanner that checks a website for common web vulnerabilities
2. Cover issues like SQL injection and cross-site scripting
3. Produce a readable report for non-experts

Methodology:
The tool will send crafted requests to a target site and analyse responses for signs of common vulnerabilities, following the OWASP Top 10 as a checklist. I will test it against a deliberately vulnerable practice application to confirm detections. Findings will be summarised in a simple report.

Scope:
The scanner focuses on a handful of common web vulnerabilities for small static and form-based sites. It does not exploit issues or test complex authenticated flows.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A scanning tool that reports common vulnerabilities
2. A test report against a sample vulnerable site

Timeline:
Two semesters: research and build first, then testing.

Title:
Static and Dynamic Analysis Tool for Logistics Malware Samples

Problem Statement:
Logistics companies depend on warehouse and fleet software, which makes them targets for malware that disrupts shipments. Smaller logistics firms rarely have malware analysts on staff, so they cannot tell quickly whether a suspicious file is dangerous. A lightweight analysis tool that summarises a sample's behaviour would help their IT staff make faster decisions.

Objectives:
1. Build a tool that performs basic static and dynamic analysis on suspicious files
2. Extract indicators such as suspicious API calls and network activity
3. Classify samples as likely benign or malicious and present a summary

Methodology:
Static analysis will extract strings, imports, and hashes, while dynamic analysis will run samples in a sandboxed virtual machine to observe behaviour. Features from both stages will feed a simple classifier trained on a labelled malware dataset. The classifier will be evaluated using accuracy and confusion-matrix metrics on a held-out test set.

Scope:
The project targets Windows executable samples and a defined set of behavioural indicators. It excludes advanced evasion techniques and packed-binary unpacking.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An analysis tool that outputs an indicator summary and verdict
2. Evaluation results showing classification accuracy on test samples

Timeline:
Semester one for sandbox setup and feature extraction; semester two for classification and evaluation.

Title:
Responsive Citizen Services Portal for Local e-Government

Problem Statement:
Residents in many small municipalities still apply for permits and certificates in person because the local council website is outdated and not mobile-friendly. This causes long queues and wasted trips. A responsive web portal would let residents submit and track requests online from any device.

Objectives:
1. Build a responsive web portal for submitting and tracking council service requests
2. Provide role-based views for residents and staff
3. Evaluate usability across desktop and mobile screens

Methodology:
The portal will be built with a React front end and a REST API backed by a relational database. Responsive layouts will be implemented with a CSS framework and tested across common screen sizes. Usability will be assessed through a small task-based test with sample users and a standard usability questionnaire.

Scope:
The portal covers two or three common services such as permit applications and certificate requests, with resident and staff roles. Online payment and digital signatures are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working responsive portal with request submission and tracking
2. A usability evaluation report with findings and improvements

Timeline:
First semester for design and core build; second semester for remaining features and usability testing.

Title:
Progressive Web App for Offline-First Learning in Rural Schools

Problem Statement:
Students in rural schools often have unreliable internet, so browser-based learning tools fail when connectivity drops. A progressive web app that caches lessons and works offline could keep learning going during outages and sync progress once a connection returns.

Objectives:
1. Build a progressive web app delivering lessons and quizzes
2. Support offline access and background synchronisation of progress
3. Evaluate performance and usability on low-end devices

Methodology:
The app will use service workers to cache lesson content and an IndexedDB store for offline progress, syncing to a backend when online. It will be developed with a standard PWA framework and tested under simulated offline and slow-network conditions using browser dev tools. Load time and offline reliability will be measured, and students will rate usability.

Scope:
The app covers one subject's lessons and quizzes with offline support. Live video and real-time collaboration are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An installable PWA that works offline and syncs progress
2. A report on offline reliability and usability on low-end devices

Timeline:
Semester one for core app and offline caching; semester two for sync, testing, and refinement.

Title:
Cross-Platform Mobile Loyalty App for Independent Retailers

Problem Statement:
Independent retail shops want loyalty programmes to keep customers returning, but separate iOS and Android development is too costly for them. A cross-platform mobile app would let small shops offer digital loyalty cards and promotions without maintaining two codebases.

Objectives:
1. Build a cross-platform mobile app for digital loyalty cards
2. Let shop owners create promotions and track customer points
3. Evaluate the app on both Android and iOS

Methodology:
The app will be built with Flutter so a single codebase runs on Android and iOS, backed by a cloud database for points and promotions. Core flows such as earning and redeeming points will be implemented and tested on both platforms. A small group of users will trial the app and give feedback on ease of use.

Scope:
The app covers loyalty points, promotions, and a shop dashboard for one pilot retailer. Payment processing and supplier integration are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A cross-platform loyalty app working on Android and iOS
2. User feedback summarised with suggested improvements

Timeline:
First semester for app build; second semester for testing and the pilot trial.

Title:
Android App for Reporting Smart-City Maintenance Issues

Problem Statement:
City residents notice problems like broken streetlights and potholes but lack an easy way to report them with precise location data. Phone calls and emails are slow and hard for councils to track. A native Android app with GPS tagging could let residents report issues and let staff monitor them on a map.

Objectives:
1. Build a native Android app for reporting city maintenance issues
2. Capture photo and GPS location for each report
3. Provide a staff dashboard to view and update report status

Methodology:
The app will be developed natively in Kotlin using Android location and camera APIs, sending reports to a backend with a map-based dashboard. Reports will be stored with status fields so staff can mark them in progress or resolved. Functionality will be verified on several Android versions, and a small user test will check reporting ease.

Scope:
The project covers issue reporting, photo and location capture, and a basic staff dashboard. Automatic routing to specific departments is out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working Android reporting app with a staff dashboard
2. Test results on reporting accuracy and usability

Timeline:
Semester one for the app and backend; semester two for the dashboard and testing.

Title:
IoT Sensor Network for Monitoring Tourist Site Crowds

Problem Statement:
Popular tourist sites often become overcrowded, hurting visitor experience and safety. Site managers usually lack real-time data on how many people are in each area. A low-cost IoT sensor network could estimate crowd levels and display them so visitors and staff can avoid congestion.

Objectives:
1. Deploy IoT sensors to estimate crowd density at site zones
2. Send readings to a central dashboard in near real time
3. Evaluate accuracy of crowd-level estimates

Methodology:
Sensor nodes based on microcontrollers will count nearby devices or use motion sensing to estimate occupancy, transmitting data over Wi-Fi or MQTT to a server. A dashboard will display per-zone crowd levels with colour indicators. Estimates will be validated against manual head counts during test sessions.

Scope:
The prototype covers a few zones at one site using a small number of sensor nodes. Precise individual tracking and outdoor large-scale coverage are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working sensor network feeding a live crowd dashboard
2. An accuracy comparison between sensor estimates and manual counts

Timeline:
First semester for hardware and data pipeline; second semester for the dashboard and validation.

Title:
Smart Home Automation with Social-Media-Triggered Routines

Problem Statement:
Existing smart home systems automate routines from time schedules or motion, but they ignore a user's social-media context, such as posting that they are travelling or hosting an event. Manually adjusting devices for these situations is tedious. There is little work connecting social-media signals to home automation in a privacy-conscious way, leaving an opportunity to make routines context-aware.

Objectives:
1. Build a smart home controller that adjusts routines based on opt-in social-media signals
2. Map a defined set of post categories to safe device actions
3. Evaluate responsiveness and user trust through a small study

Methodology:
The system will pull posts via official platform APIs with explicit user consent, classify them into a small set of intents using a fine-tuned text classifier, and trigger MQTT commands to simulated and real devices. A rules layer will gate which intents may control which devices. Evaluation will measure classification accuracy, end-to-end latency, and user-reported trust from a short questionnaire, compared against a schedule-only baseline.

Scope:
The project supports a fixed set of intent categories and a small number of device types in a controlled home lab. Continuous location tracking and third-party data sharing are explicitly excluded for privacy.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working context-aware automation prototype with a privacy gating layer
2. Evaluation results on intent accuracy, latency, and user trust versus the baseline

Timeline:
Semester one: device integration and intent classifier. Semester two: rules layer, user study, and evaluation.

Title:
Edge-Based Real-Time Fall Detection for Elderly Home Care

Problem Statement:
Cloud-based fall detection for elderly care suffers from latency and raises privacy concerns because video leaves the home. Sending continuous footage to the cloud is costly and risky, yet timely alerts are critical for at-risk residents. Running detection on an edge device could cut latency and keep raw video local, but model accuracy must hold on constrained hardware.

Objectives:
1. Deploy a fall-detection model on an edge device that processes video locally
2. Keep end-to-end alert latency under a defined threshold while preserving accuracy
3. Compare edge inference against a cloud baseline on latency, accuracy, and privacy exposure

Methodology:
A lightweight pose-estimation model will feed a fall classifier, quantised and deployed on a Raspberry Pi or Jetson Nano. It will be trained and validated on public fall-detection datasets using precision, recall, and F1 with cross-validation. The edge build will be benchmarked against a cloud-inference baseline on latency and accuracy, and data leaving the device will be quantified to assess privacy.

Scope:
The system targets single-occupant indoor scenes and a defined set of fall types on one edge device. Multi-person tracking and outdoor scenarios are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An edge fall-detection prototype meeting the latency target
2. A benchmark report comparing edge and cloud on latency, accuracy, and privacy

Timeline:
Semester one: dataset work and model training. Semester two: edge deployment, optimisation, and benchmarking.

Title:
Cloud-Native Microservices Platform for Real-Time Fraud Screening

Problem Statement:
Monolithic transaction systems in small fintech firms struggle to scale fraud checks during traffic spikes, causing slow approvals or missed fraud. Scaling the whole monolith for one hot path wastes resources. A cloud-native microservices design could scale the fraud-screening path independently, but the team needs evidence that decomposition improves latency and resilience without overcomplicating operations.

Objectives:
1. Design a microservices architecture isolating the fraud-screening path from core transaction handling
2. Achieve independent autoscaling and graceful degradation under load
3. Compare the microservices design against a monolithic baseline on latency and resilience

Methodology:
Services will be containerised with Docker and orchestrated on Kubernetes, communicating via REST and an event queue, with a rule-plus-ML fraud check service. Load tests with k6 will measure p95 latency and throughput, and fault injection will test resilience under simulated service failures. Results will be benchmarked against an equivalent monolithic implementation, with circuit breakers and health checks for graceful degradation.

Scope:
The project covers the fraud-screening path and supporting services on a single cluster with synthetic transaction data. Real banking integration and production-grade compliance are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working microservices platform with independent scaling of the fraud path
2. A benchmark report comparing latency and resilience against the monolith

Timeline:
Semester one: service decomposition and deployment pipeline. Semester two: load and fault testing plus benchmarking.

Title:
CI/CD Automation Pipeline for Manufacturing Control Software

Problem Statement:
Manufacturing firms updating their machine-control software often deploy manually, which is slow and error-prone and risks shop-floor downtime. Without automated testing and staged rollout, a bad release can halt a line. A CI/CD pipeline tailored to this setting could shorten release cycles and reduce failed deployments, but it must respect the safety constraints of control software.

Objectives:
1. Build a CI/CD pipeline that automates build, test, and staged deployment of control software
2. Add automated tests and a gated promotion step before production rollout
3. Measure deployment frequency, lead time, and change-failure rate against the manual process

Methodology:
The pipeline will use GitHub Actions for build and test, containerised artifacts, and a staging-to-production promotion gate requiring passing tests and manual approval. A sample control application will exercise unit, integration, and smoke tests, with automatic rollback on failed health checks. DORA metrics will be collected before and after automation to quantify improvement.

Scope:
The project covers the pipeline and a representative sample application in a staging environment. Integration with live production machinery is out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working CI/CD pipeline with automated testing and rollback
2. A before-and-after comparison of DORA delivery metrics

Timeline:
Semester one: pipeline setup and test automation. Semester two: staged deployment, rollback, and metric evaluation.

Title:
Big Data Analytics Pipeline for Emergency Call Hotspot Detection

Problem Statement:
Emergency-response agencies collect large volumes of call records but often analyse them in batches days later, missing emerging incident hotspots. Manual spreadsheet analysis cannot keep up with the volume or velocity of data. A streaming big-data pipeline could surface hotspots in near real time to guide resource placement, but it must handle high throughput reliably.

Objectives:
1. Build a streaming analytics pipeline that ingests emergency-call records and detects geographic hotspots
2. Surface near-real-time hotspot dashboards for dispatchers
3. Evaluate pipeline throughput, latency, and hotspot-detection accuracy

Methodology:
Records will be ingested through Apache Kafka, processed with Spark Structured Streaming for windowed spatial aggregation, and stored for a dashboard layer. A clustering method such as DBSCAN will flag hotspots, evaluated against labelled historical incidents using precision and recall. Throughput and end-to-end latency will be measured under replayed high-volume loads using a public or synthetic emergency-call dataset.

Scope:
The pipeline covers ingestion, hotspot detection, and a dashboard over one synthetic or anonymised dataset. Predictive forecasting of future incidents is out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working streaming pipeline with a near-real-time hotspot dashboard
2. An evaluation of throughput, latency, and detection accuracy

Timeline:
Semester one: ingestion and streaming aggregation. Semester two: hotspot detection, dashboard, and load evaluation.

Title:
A Self-Service Business Intelligence Dashboard for Building Energy Efficiency Benchmarking

Problem Statement:
Facility managers across a building portfolio receive energy data as disconnected utility reports, making it hard to benchmark buildings, spot anomalies, or justify retrofits. Existing commercial BI tools are costly and rarely encode energy-specific normalisation such as weather and floor-area adjustment, so comparisons are misleading. The gap is an affordable, energy-aware self-service dashboard that normalises consumption and ranks efficiency opportunities.

Objectives:
1. Build a self-service BI dashboard that ingests meter data and produces weather- and area-normalised energy benchmarks across buildings
2. Detect consumption anomalies and rank retrofit opportunities by estimated savings
3. Evaluate decision usefulness and benchmark accuracy against a documented baseline with facility managers

Methodology:
A dimensional star-schema warehouse will store meter, weather, and building metadata, populated by a scheduled ETL job. Energy Use Intensity will be degree-day and floor-area normalised, and anomalies flagged using a seasonal-decomposition residual threshold validated against labelled events with precision and recall. The dashboard will be built in a BI tool, compared against a raw-report baseline. Eight to ten facility managers will complete benchmark tasks measured by accuracy, time-on-task, and a SUS questionnaire.

Scope:
The project covers electricity benchmarking for ten to fifteen non-residential buildings with hourly or monthly meter data. Real-time control, sub-metering by appliance, and carbon accounting are explicitly excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A deployed BI dashboard with normalised benchmarks, anomaly flags, and ranked retrofit opportunities
2. An evaluation report quantifying benchmark accuracy and decision usefulness versus the raw-report baseline

Timeline:
Weeks 1-3 requirements and data audit; 4-7 warehouse and ETL; 8-11 normalisation and anomaly modelling; 12-15 dashboard build; 16-20 user evaluation, analysis, and write-up.

Title:
Probabilistic Demand Forecasting for Inventory Decisions in Small Independent Retailers

Problem Statement:
Small independent retailers typically forecast demand with simple moving averages, which ignore seasonality, promotions, and uncertainty, leading to stockouts and overstock that tie up scarce cash. Off-the-shelf forecasting suites assume clean, high-volume histories that small shops lack, and they output single-point forecasts that hide risk. The gap is a robust, uncertainty-aware forecasting method suited to short, noisy, intermittent sales data and tied directly to reorder decisions.

Objectives:
1. Build a probabilistic SKU-level demand forecaster handling seasonality, promotions, and intermittent demand
2. Convert forecast distributions into reorder recommendations under a service-level target
3. Evaluate forecast and inventory performance against naive and classical baselines

Methodology:
Using two to three years of daily sales from a partner shop plus promotion and calendar features, I will compare seasonal-naive, ETS, and a gradient-boosted model with quantile loss, plus Croston's method for intermittent SKUs, under rolling-origin cross-validation. Accuracy will use MASE and pinball loss; reorder points derived from forecast quantiles will be back-tested for fill rate and holding cost against current practice. Risks such as data sparsity and promotion leakage will be mitigated by SKU grouping and strict temporal splits.

Scope:
The work covers offline forecasting and reorder recommendations for one retailer's top SKUs. Live POS integration, supplier automation, and price optimisation are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A reproducible forecasting pipeline producing probabilistic forecasts and reorder points
2. An evaluation showing accuracy and inventory-cost gains over baselines with documented limitations

Timeline:
Weeks 1-3 data collection and cleaning; 4-7 baselines and cross-validation; 8-11 probabilistic and intermittent models; 12-15 inventory back-testing; 16-20 analysis and report.

Blockchain for Social Media

AR App for Hospitals

Hospitals are confusing and patients get lost. Augmented reality is cool and can show things on the phone screen to help people.

VR Training for Finance

Problem Statement:
Finance workers need training but it is boring. Virtual reality can make training fun and immersive so people learn better in the finance world.

Objectives:
1. To make a VR simulation.
2. To train finance people.
3. To use VR headsets.

I will use VR and Unity probably. The user will wear a headset and do finance tasks in the virtual world.

For all banks and finance companies.

Title:
A 2D Game to Teach Factory Safety

Problem Statement:
New factory workers often skip safety briefings or forget them quickly. A game could make safety rules more memorable, but most manufacturing training is still paper-based and dull.

Objectives:
1. To design a 2D game where players spot hazards on a factory floor.
2. To include three levels covering machinery, chemicals, and fire safety.
3. To test whether players remember the rules afterwards.

Methodology:
I will build the game in Unity using C# and 2D sprites. Levels will be designed around common factory hazards found from online safety guides. A short quiz before and after play will check what players learned.

The game focuses on basic manufacturing safety for entry-level workers. It will not cover advanced machinery or real-time IoT sensors.

2. Survey results showing whether the game improves recall.

Roughly 12 weeks, split between design, development, and testing.

Title:
Serious Game for Public Safety Awareness

Problem Statement:
Many citizens do not know what to do during emergencies like floods or fires. Traditional pamphlets are easy to ignore. A serious game might engage people better, but few such tools exist for community public safety.

Objectives:
1. To develop a game teaching emergency response steps.
2. To cover three scenarios: flood, fire, and earthquake.
3. To evaluate user engagement and knowledge gain.

Methodology:
The game will be built in Unity with branching choices. Players make decisions in each scenario and get feedback. Content will be based on government safety guidelines. A questionnaire will measure learning.

Scope:
The project targets general adult users and three emergency scenarios. It will not include multiplayer or VR.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working serious game with three scenarios.
2. A short evaluation report on knowledge gain.

About 14 weeks across design, build, and evaluation.

Title:
A Dashboard for Monitoring Hospital Energy Use

Problem Statement:
Hospitals use a lot of electricity, and staff rarely see where it goes. Without clear data, waste is hard to reduce. Existing building systems exist but are often expensive and not tailored to ward-level monitoring.

Objectives:
1. To build a web dashboard showing energy use per hospital ward.
2. To highlight wards with unusually high consumption.
3. To let staff view trends over time.

Methodology:
I will create a web app using React and a Node backend. Energy data will be simulated from sample datasets since real meters are unavailable. Charts will show usage per ward, and simple thresholds will flag high usage.

Scope:
The dashboard covers electricity only and uses sample data. It will not control devices or integrate with real meters.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working energy dashboard with ward-level charts.
2. Threshold alerts for high consumption.

Timeline:
Around 13 weeks for build and testing.

Title:
A Simple Telemedicine Platform for Small Clinics

Problem Statement:
Small clinics often cannot afford telemedicine systems, so patients must visit in person even for minor follow-ups. Cheaper, lightweight tools could let small businesses offer remote consultations, but most platforms target large hospitals.

Objectives:
1. To build a web platform for booking and holding video consultations.
2. To let clinics manage appointments and patient notes.
3. To keep the system affordable for a single small clinic.

Methodology:
The platform will use React for the front end and Node.js with MySQL for the back end. Video calls will use the WebRTC library or a free API. Basic appointment and note features will be added. Testing will use a few sample clinic accounts.

Scope:
The system supports one clinic with appointment booking, video calls, and notes. It excludes billing, insurance, and prescriptions.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working telemedicine web app with video consultations.
2. An appointment and notes management module.

Timeline:
About 14 weeks for development and testing.

Title:
An Offline-Capable E-Learning System for Rural Farmers

Problem Statement:
Agricultural extension services struggle to reach rural farmers who have weak internet. Existing e-learning platforms assume stable connectivity, leaving many farmers without access to crop and pest management knowledge in their own language.

Objectives:
1. To build a mobile e-learning app delivering short agricultural lessons that work offline.
2. To support content sync when connectivity is available.
3. To evaluate usability with a small group of test users.

Methodology:
The app will be developed in Flutter with local SQLite storage so lessons remain available offline. A Firebase backend will handle sync and content updates. Lessons will be drawn from public agricultural guides and structured into modules with quizzes. Usability will be assessed using the System Usability Scale with around ten participants.

Scope:
The project covers lesson delivery, offline access, and quizzes for two crop types. It excludes live expert chat, payment, and large-scale deployment.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working offline-first e-learning app for farmers.
2. A usability evaluation report with SUS scores.

Timeline:
Phase 1 requirements (2 weeks), Phase 2 development (8 weeks), Phase 3 testing and evaluation (4 weeks).

Title:
A QR-Based Mobile Payment App for Public Transport

Problem Statement:
Cash and physical cards slow down boarding on buses and create queues. While e-wallets exist, many are not optimized for the quick, low-value, offline-tolerant payments that public transport needs in areas with patchy coverage.

Objectives:
1. To build a mobile app that pays transport fares via QR codes.
2. To support a prepaid wallet with transaction history.
3. To handle brief offline periods by queuing transactions.

Methodology:
The app will be built in React Native with a Spring Boot backend and MySQL. Fares are paid by scanning a route QR code, deducting from a prepaid balance. Offline transactions are stored locally and synced once online. Security will use JWT authentication and HTTPS. Testing covers wallet top-up, fare deduction, and sync correctness.

Scope:
The prototype covers single-operator fares, wallet top-up, and offline queuing. It excludes real bank integration, refunds, and multi-operator settlement.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working fare-payment app with QR scanning and a prepaid wallet.
2. Test results verifying offline sync accuracy.

Timeline:
Requirements (2 weeks), development (9 weeks), testing (3 weeks).

Title:
Fraud Detection for Carbon Credit Transactions

Problem Statement:
Carbon credit markets are growing but vulnerable to double-counting and fraudulent claims, which undermine sustainability goals. Manual auditing is slow, and few accessible tools flag suspicious transactions automatically for smaller registries.

Objectives:
1. To build a machine learning model that flags suspicious carbon credit transactions.
2. To compare it against a rule-based baseline.
3. To present results through a simple review dashboard.

Methodology:
Using a public or synthetic transaction dataset, features such as transaction frequency, amount, and counterparty patterns will be engineered. A Random Forest classifier will be trained and compared to a logistic regression and a rule-based baseline. Models will be evaluated with precision, recall, and F1 using stratified train-test splits. Flagged transactions will appear on a Flask dashboard.

Scope:
The project covers model training, baseline comparison, and a review dashboard on one dataset. It excludes real-time streaming and blockchain ledger integration.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained fraud-detection model with precision/recall reported.
2. A dashboard showing flagged transactions.

Timeline:
Data and features (3 weeks), modeling (6 weeks), dashboard and evaluation (4 weeks).

Title:
A Product Recommendation Engine for a Logistics Supply Store

Problem Statement:
Online stores selling logistics supplies carry thousands of similar SKUs, making it hard for buyers to find the right item. Generic recommendation widgets rarely account for the bulk, compatibility, and reorder patterns typical of logistics purchasing.

Objectives:
1. To build a recommendation engine suggesting relevant logistics products.
2. To combine collaborative filtering with content-based features.
3. To evaluate recommendation quality offline.

Methodology:
A dataset of purchase histories (public e-commerce data adapted, or synthetic) will be used. Item-based collaborative filtering will be implemented with cosine similarity, combined with content features like category and pack size. The hybrid will be compared against a popularity baseline using precision@k and recall@k on a held-out test set. The engine will be served through a small web demo.

Scope:
The project covers offline recommendation for one product catalog with a web demo. It excludes real-time personalization, A/B testing, and live inventory.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A hybrid recommender with precision@k reported against a baseline.
2. A web demo showing recommendations for sample users.

Timeline:
Data prep (3 weeks), modeling (6 weeks), demo and evaluation (4 weeks).

Title:
A Conversational Agent for Government Service Enquiries

Problem Statement:
Citizens often struggle to find the right e-government procedure among scattered web pages, leading to call-center load and abandoned applications. A focused chatbot could answer common procedural questions, but generic bots give vague, unsourced replies.

Objectives:
1. To build a chatbot answering questions about selected government services.
2. To ground answers in an official document knowledge base.
3. To evaluate answer accuracy against a question set.

Methodology:
A retrieval-augmented chatbot will be built. Official service documents will be chunked and embedded into a FAISS index; user questions retrieve relevant passages that feed a language model to generate grounded answers. A test set of around 50 real-style questions with known answers will measure top-k retrieval accuracy and answer correctness. The interface will be a simple web chat.

Scope:
The chatbot covers three government service categories and English-language queries. It excludes transactions, login, and live policy updates.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working retrieval-augmented chatbot grounded in official documents.
2. An accuracy report on the test question set.

Timeline:
Knowledge base (3 weeks), chatbot build (6 weeks), evaluation (4 weeks).

Title:
Knowledge-Graph Search for University Course Materials

Problem Statement:
University students searching course materials get keyword matches that miss conceptual links between topics, prerequisites, and related lectures. A knowledge graph could expose these relationships, but most learning platforms still rely on flat keyword search.

Objectives:
1. To build a knowledge graph linking course concepts, topics, and resources.
2. To enable semantic search and concept exploration over it.
3. To evaluate search relevance against keyword search.

Methodology:
Course syllabi and lecture notes will be processed to extract concepts and relationships using simple NLP and manual curation, stored in Neo4j. A search interface will let students query concepts and traverse related topics. Relevance will be evaluated by comparing the graph search against a keyword baseline on a set of sample queries judged for relevance.

Scope:
The graph covers two courses and their materials with a search interface. It excludes automatic full-syllabus ingestion and personalization.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A populated knowledge graph with a working search interface.
2. A relevance comparison against keyword search.

Timeline:
Graph construction (4 weeks), search interface (5 weeks), evaluation (4 weeks).

Title:
Shelf Product Segmentation for Retail Stock Monitoring

Problem Statement:
Retailers want to monitor shelf stock from camera images, but counting and locating products requires pixel-level segmentation of densely packed, visually similar items. Generic object detectors give bounding boxes that overlap heavily on crowded shelves, so a segmentation approach is needed to separate adjacent products and detect gaps.

Objectives:
1. To train an instance segmentation model that delineates individual products on retail shelves.
2. To detect empty shelf regions as out-of-stock indicators.
3. To benchmark the model against a bounding-box detector baseline.

Methodology:
The SKU-110K and a subset of the Grocery Shelves dataset will be used, with annotations adapted to masks where needed. A Mask R-CNN with a ResNet-50 FPN backbone will be fine-tuned, augmented with flips, scaling, and color jitter. Evaluation uses mask mAP at IoU 0.5:0.95, plus precision and recall for gap detection, against a Faster R-CNN baseline. A held-out test split and 5-fold validation on the training portion guard against overfitting.

Scope:
The project covers segmentation and gap detection on static shelf images for packaged goods. It excludes video tracking, price recognition, and edge deployment.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained segmentation model with mask mAP reported against the baseline.
2. A gap-detection evaluation with precision and recall.

Timeline:
Data and annotation (3 weeks), training (5 weeks), evaluation and write-up (4 weeks).

Title:
Real-Time Vehicle and Pedestrian Detection for Smart-City Intersections

Problem Statement:
Smart-city traffic management needs reliable counts of vehicles and pedestrians at intersections, but lighting changes, occlusion, and small distant objects degrade accuracy. Many deployments use heavy models unsuited to the limited compute available at roadside cabinets.

Objectives:
1. To train an object detector for vehicles and pedestrians tuned for intersection footage.
2. To optimize the model for near-real-time inference on modest hardware.
3. To benchmark accuracy and speed against a standard baseline.

Methodology:
A subset of the BDD100K and UA-DETRAC datasets will be used for training and evaluation. YOLOv8 will be fine-tuned, with augmentation for lighting and occlusion, then compared against a Faster R-CNN baseline. Accuracy is measured by mAP@0.5 and mAP@0.5:0.95; efficiency by FPS and model size on a CPU and a low-end GPU. A class-balanced split and validation set control overfitting; failure cases on small/occluded objects are analyzed.

Scope:
The work covers detection of two classes in daytime and night intersection images. It excludes multi-camera tracking, signal control logic, and on-vehicle deployment.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A fine-tuned detector with mAP and FPS reported against the baseline.
2. An error analysis of occlusion and small-object cases.

Timeline:
Data prep (3 weeks), training and tuning (6 weeks), benchmarking and analysis (4 weeks).

Title:
Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis of Tourist Reviews

Problem Statement:
Tourism operators receive thousands of reviews, but an overall star rating hides which aspects—cleanliness, location, service, value—drive satisfaction. Document-level sentiment models miss this, so operators lack actionable, aspect-level insight for improving specific services.

Objectives:
1. To build an aspect-based sentiment model that classifies sentiment per aspect in tourist reviews.
2. To compare a transformer model against classical baselines.
3. To summarize aspect sentiment trends for operators.

Methodology:
The SemEval-2014 restaurant/laptop ABSA datasets and a scraped sample of hotel reviews will be used, with aspect terms and polarities labeled. A fine-tuned BERT-base model for aspect-term sentiment classification will be compared against TF-IDF with SVM and an LSTM baseline. Evaluation uses accuracy and macro-F1 with stratified train/validation/test splits and early stopping. An aggregation step produces per-aspect sentiment summaries.

Scope:
The project covers English reviews and four predefined aspects with a summary view. It excludes multilingual reviews, sarcasm handling, and live scraping pipelines.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An ABSA model with macro-F1 reported against two baselines.
2. Aspect-level sentiment summaries for a sample of operators.

Timeline:
Data and labeling (3 weeks), modeling (6 weeks), aggregation and evaluation (4 weeks).

Title:
Learned Index Selection for Social-Media Query Optimization

Problem Statement:
Social-media backends run heavy mixes of timeline and search queries whose optimal indexes shift as workloads change. Manual index tuning is slow and error-prone, and default optimizers often miss good multi-column indexes, leading to slow queries under load.

Objectives:
1. To build a tool that recommends indexes for a social-media query workload.
2. To estimate the speedup of recommended indexes against the default configuration.
3. To evaluate recommendations on a realistic benchmark.

Methodology:
A PostgreSQL instance loaded with a social-media-style schema and synthetic data will run a workload derived from common timeline, follow, and search queries. The tool parses queries, generates candidate single- and multi-column indexes, and uses the optimizer's cost estimates plus actual EXPLAIN ANALYZE timings to rank them, with a greedy selection under a storage budget. Results compare query latency before and after, against a baseline of no tuning and of naive single-column indexes.

Scope:
The project covers index recommendation for one schema and read-heavy workload on PostgreSQL. It excludes materialized views, sharding, and write-amplification tuning.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An index-recommendation tool with measured latency improvements.
2. A comparison against default and naive-index baselines.

Timeline:
Setup and workload (3 weeks), tool development (6 weeks), benchmarking (4 weeks).

Title:
Face-Recognition Attendance for Hospital Staff Shifts

Problem Statement:
Hospitals track staff attendance across rotating shifts, but card-based systems allow buddy-punching and queues at shift change. A face-recognition system could speed check-in and reduce fraud, yet must handle masks, varied lighting, and privacy concerns in a clinical setting.

Objectives:
1. To build a face-recognition attendance system robust to masks and lighting changes.
2. To log check-in and check-out against staff shift schedules.
3. To evaluate recognition accuracy and processing time.

Methodology:
Face detection will use RetinaFace, and recognition will use FaceNet/ArcFace embeddings matched by cosine similarity against an enrolled gallery. A small enrolled set plus public masked-face data (e.g., MFR2/RMFD subsets) will test masked and unmasked accuracy. Evaluation reports recognition accuracy, false-accept and false-reject rates, and per-check-in latency. The system logs attendance to a database and flags failed matches for manual review. Embeddings are stored, not raw images, for privacy.

Scope:
The prototype covers enrollment, check-in/out, and a small staff gallery in one environment. It excludes liveness/anti-spoofing, multi-site sync, and payroll integration.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working attendance system with accuracy and FAR/FRR reported.
2. Attendance logs linked to shift schedules.

Timeline:
Setup and enrollment (3 weeks), recognition build (6 weeks), evaluation (4 weeks).

Title:
An OCR and Information-Extraction Pipeline for Financial Invoices

Problem Statement:
Finance back-offices manually key data from heterogeneous supplier invoices—PDFs, scans, and photos—which is slow and error-prone. Off-the-shelf OCR returns raw text without structure, and template-based extractors break on unseen layouts, so a layout-aware extraction approach is needed to pull key fields reliably across vendors.

Objectives:
1. To build a pipeline that detects and recognizes text on invoices and extracts structured fields (vendor, invoice number, date, line items, total).
2. To handle unseen invoice layouts without per-template rules.
3. To benchmark field-level extraction accuracy against a regex-on-OCR baseline.

Methodology:
Images are pre-processed (deskew, denoise, binarize) and passed through a detector-recognizer; Tesseract and PaddleOCR are compared for the recognition stage. Structured extraction uses a fine-tuned LayoutLMv3 model that fuses text and layout, trained and evaluated on the public SROIE and FUNSD datasets plus a small annotated in-house set. Metrics are character error rate for OCR and field-level precision, recall, and F1 for extraction, reported with 5-fold cross-validation on the in-house set and a fixed test split for SROIE. The LayoutLMv3 pipeline is compared against a regex-and-keyword baseline applied to OCR text, and a confidence threshold routes low-confidence fields to manual review. Risks (skewed scans, low-resolution photos) are addressed with augmentation and an ablation on pre-processing steps.

Scope:
The pipeline targets English single-page invoices and five key fields plus line items. It explicitly excludes multi-page contracts, handwriting, multilingual documents, and ERP integration.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An extraction pipeline reporting CER and field-level F1 against the baseline, with the LayoutLMv3 model improving F1 on unseen layouts.
2. An ablation quantifying the contribution of pre-processing and layout features, plus a review-routing mechanism for low-confidence fields.

Timeline:
Phase 1 data and annotation (3 weeks), Phase 2 OCR comparison (2 weeks), Phase 3 extraction model and tuning (5 weeks), Phase 4 evaluation, ablation, and write-up (4 weeks).

Title:
Anomaly Detection and Predictive Maintenance from Wireless Sensor Streams on a Production Line

Problem Statement:
Manufacturing lines instrument machines with wireless vibration and temperature sensors, but the resulting high-rate, noisy, sometimes-dropped streams are hard to turn into early failure warnings. Threshold alarms fire too late or too often, and labeled failure data is scarce, so an approach combining unsupervised anomaly detection with remaining-useful-life estimation is needed under realistic sensor noise and dropout.

Objectives:
1. To build a streaming pipeline that ingests multi-sensor data and detects anomalies indicating incipient machine faults.
2. To estimate remaining useful life (RUL) and trigger maintenance alerts ahead of failure.
3. To benchmark detection and RUL accuracy against statistical and threshold baselines under simulated packet loss.

Methodology:
The NASA C-MAPSS turbofan degradation dataset and the CWRU bearing vibration dataset provide labeled run-to-failure data; sliding-window features (RMS, kurtosis, spectral energy) are extracted. An LSTM autoencoder flags anomalies by reconstruction error, and a separate LSTM regressor predicts RUL, compared against an Isolation Forest plus a moving-average threshold baseline. Evaluation uses precision, recall, and F1 with detection lead-time for anomalies, and RMSE plus a scoring function for RUL, on subject-wise train/validation/test splits to avoid leakage. Robustness is tested by injecting synthetic packet loss and noise, with an ablation on window size; an MQTT-fed simulator demonstrates near-real-time operation. Class imbalance is handled with weighting, and risks (sensor dropout, domain shift between machines) are explicitly evaluated.

Scope:
The project covers anomaly detection and RUL estimation on two public datasets with a streaming simulator and dashboard. It excludes physical sensor deployment, control-loop actuation, and multi-factory federated training.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A streaming anomaly-detection and RUL pipeline with F1, lead-time, and RMSE reported against baselines.
2. A robustness study under simulated packet loss and a window-size ablation, surfaced through a live monitoring dashboard.

Timeline:
Phase 1 data and feature pipeline (3 weeks), Phase 2 anomaly model (4 weeks), Phase 3 RUL model and baselines (4 weeks), Phase 4 robustness, dashboard, and evaluation (3 weeks).

Title:
Machine Learning for Retail

Problem Statement:
Shops have a lot of data and they don't know what to do with it. Machine learning can help them sell more things to customers.

Objectives:
1. Make a machine learning model
2. Help the shop
3. Get good results

Methodology:
I will use Python and some machine learning to classify the customers. I will download a dataset and train it. Then I will see if it works.

Scope:
This can be used by any retail shop, supermarket, or online store anywhere.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working model
2. Happy customers

Title:
Deep Learning Camera System for Smart City

Problem Statement:
Cities have many cameras but nobody can watch all of them. Deep learning and computer vision is very powerful and can solve this problem for the smart city.

Objectives:
1. Use deep learning
2. Detect things in the city
3. Build a smart system

Methodology:
I will use a neural network and computer vision to look at the city camera images. The AI will learn by itself and detect important stuff automatically.

Scope:
The whole city including roads, parks, buildings and traffic.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A smart city system
2. Better safety for everyone

Title:
NLP Chatbot for Tourism

Problem Statement:
Tourists ask many questions when they travel and there is nobody to answer them all the time. Natural language processing can understand what people say and reply to them.

Objectives:
1. Build a chatbot
2. Use NLP
3. Help tourists

Methodology:
The system will use natural language processing to read the tourist questions and give answers. I will make it talk like a human using AI.

Scope:
For all tourists visiting any country who need help with hotels, food and attractions.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A chatbot that answers questions
2. Tourists will be happy

Title:
A Recommender System for Suggesting Posts on a Social Media Platform

Problem Statement:
Social media users are shown too many posts and often miss content they actually care about. A recommendation engine could rank posts so users see relevant content first, which keeps them engaged.

Objectives:
1. Collect user interaction data such as likes and shares
2. Build a recommender system to suggest posts
3. Test whether the recommendations are accurate

Methodology:
I plan to use collaborative filtering to recommend posts based on what similar users liked. The system will be built in Python with a small web interface. A public social media dataset will be used for training, and accuracy will be checked.

Scope:
The project focuses on recommending text posts for one social media platform. It will not cover video or live streaming recommendations.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A recommender system that suggests relevant posts
2. An evaluation showing the recommendations are reasonably accurate

Timeline:
The project will take about two semesters from data collection to testing.

Title:
Speech Recognition System for Recording Patient Symptoms

Problem Statement:
Doctors spend a lot of time typing notes during consultations, which takes attention away from the patient. A speech recognition tool that transcribes spoken symptoms could save time in a healthcare setting.

Objectives:
1. Capture doctor or patient speech as audio
2. Convert the speech to text automatically
3. Display the transcribed notes on a simple screen

Methodology:
The system will use an existing speech-to-text library to convert recorded audio into text. It will be tested with a few sample medical phrases to see how accurate it is. A basic web page will show the results.

Scope:
The project handles English speech only and focuses on short symptom descriptions. It will not handle full medical diagnosis or multiple languages.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working speech-to-text tool for symptom notes
2. A short accuracy report on the sample phrases

Timeline:
Roughly two semesters, with the first for setup and the second for testing.

Title:
Network Intrusion Detection for Online Banking Traffic

Problem Statement:
Financial institutions face constant network attacks, and manually monitoring traffic logs is slow. A system that flags suspicious network activity could help security teams react faster to intrusions on banking infrastructure.

Objectives:
1. Use a public network traffic dataset with labelled attacks
2. Train a classifier to detect intrusion attempts
3. Measure how well it distinguishes normal from malicious traffic

Methodology:
I will use the NSL-KDD dataset and train a decision tree or random forest classifier in Python with scikit-learn. The model will be evaluated using accuracy and a confusion matrix. Features will be selected from the traffic records.

Scope:
The work focuses on offline detection using a known dataset, not real-time deployment on a live bank network. Encrypted payload inspection is out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained intrusion detection classifier
2. An accuracy and confusion-matrix report on the test set

Timeline:
About two semesters: dataset preparation first, then model training and evaluation.

Title:
A Web Application Vulnerability Scanner for Manufacturing Dashboards

Problem Statement:
Manufacturing companies increasingly use web dashboards to monitor production lines, but these are often built quickly and may contain security flaws. A scanner that checks for common vulnerabilities would help small manufacturers find issues early.

Objectives:
1. Identify common web vulnerabilities such as SQL injection and XSS
2. Build a scanning tool that tests a target web application
3. Generate a report listing the issues found

Methodology:
The tool will be written in Python and will send crafted requests to a test web application to check for SQL injection and cross-site scripting. I will use a deliberately vulnerable practice site to test it and produce a findings report.

Scope:
Only SQL injection and XSS checks are included. Authentication bypass and network-level attacks are not covered. Testing is done on a sandbox site, not a live system.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A scanner that detects basic SQL injection and XSS
2. A sample vulnerability report

Timeline:
Two semesters, split between building the scanner and testing it.

Title:
Static and Dynamic Malware Analysis Tool for Public Safety Agencies

Problem Statement:
Public safety and law enforcement teams sometimes receive suspicious files but lack the resources for deep malware analysis. A combined static and dynamic analysis tool could give a quick risk assessment of a submitted file without needing a specialist on hand.

Objectives:
1. Extract static features such as file headers, strings, and imported API calls
2. Run samples in a sandbox to capture dynamic behaviour like file and registry changes
3. Classify samples as benign or malicious and produce a readable report

Methodology:
Static analysis will use the pefile and YARA libraries to extract indicators. Dynamic analysis will run samples inside a Cuckoo sandbox virtual machine to log behaviour. A random forest classifier will be trained on features from a public malware dataset and evaluated with accuracy and F1-score. All testing is isolated in a VM.

Scope:
The tool targets Windows PE executables only. It will not handle obfuscated packers beyond UPX, mobile malware, or live network propagation analysis.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working analysis tool producing static and dynamic reports
2. A classifier with measured accuracy and F1 on a held-out test set

Timeline:
Semester one: feature extraction and sandbox setup. Semester two: classifier training, evaluation, and reporting.

Title:
A Responsive Web Platform for Household Energy Consumption Tracking

Problem Statement:
Households often have no clear view of how much electricity each appliance uses, making it hard to reduce bills. A responsive web platform that lets users log and visualise their energy usage could encourage more efficient habits.

Objectives:
1. Let users record appliance usage and meter readings
2. Visualise consumption trends with charts on any device
3. Provide simple tips based on the highest-consuming appliances

Methodology:
The platform will be built with React on the front end and a Node.js and Express backend with a MySQL database. Charts will be rendered with Chart.js, and the layout will use responsive CSS so it works on phones and desktops. Usability will be tested with a small group of users using a short questionnaire.

Scope:
The system handles manual entry and uploaded CSV meter exports. Direct integration with smart meters or utility company APIs is out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A responsive web platform with usage dashboards
2. Usability feedback from a small test group

Timeline:
First semester for design and core features; second semester for visualisation, tips, and user testing.

Title:
A Progressive Web App for Small Business Inventory Management

Problem Statement:
Small retailers often track stock on paper or spreadsheets, leading to errors and stockouts. A progressive web app that works offline and on any device could give them a low-cost way to manage inventory without installing native software.

Objectives:
1. Allow shop owners to add, edit, and search inventory items
2. Support offline use with later synchronisation
3. Alert users when stock falls below a set threshold

Methodology:
The app will be built as a PWA using React and a service worker for offline caching, with IndexedDB for local storage and a Firebase backend for sync. Low-stock alerts will be triggered client-side. Functionality will be tested across mobile and desktop browsers, and three shop owners will trial it.

Scope:
The app covers single-store inventory only. Multi-warehouse transfers, supplier ordering, and accounting integration are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An installable PWA that works offline and syncs when online
2. Trial feedback from a few small business owners

Timeline:
Semester one: core CRUD and offline support. Semester two: sync, alerts, and user trials.

Title:
A Cross-Platform Mobile App for Crop Disease Reporting in Agriculture

Problem Statement:
Smallholder farmers often struggle to identify crop diseases early and lack an easy way to seek advice. A cross-platform mobile app that lets farmers photograph affected plants and log symptoms could help track outbreaks and connect them to guidance.

Objectives:
1. Let farmers capture photos and describe crop symptoms
2. Store reports with location data for mapping
3. Show common disease information and basic advice

Methodology:
The app will be built with Flutter so a single codebase runs on Android and iOS. Reports and images will be stored in a Firebase backend, and locations shown on a map using a maps SDK. A small library of disease descriptions will be included. Five farmers or agriculture students will test the app and give feedback.

Scope:
The app focuses on reporting and information lookup, not automatic image-based diagnosis. Only three common local crops are covered.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working Android and iOS app for crop reporting
2. Tester feedback on usability and usefulness

Timeline:
First semester: app structure and reporting. Second semester: mapping, info library, and testing.

Title:
An Android Native App for Public Bus Arrival Times in Transportation

Problem Statement:
Commuters who rely on public buses often wait without knowing when the next bus will arrive. An Android app that shows estimated arrival times and route information could reduce uncertainty and waiting frustration for daily transport users.

Objectives:
1. Display bus routes and stops for a selected city area
2. Estimate arrival times from schedule and location data
3. Let users save favourite routes for quick access

Methodology:
The app will be built natively in Kotlin using Android Studio, with Room for local storage of saved routes and Retrofit to fetch schedule data from a transit API or an open GTFS feed. Arrival estimates will be computed from the timetable and current time. The app will be tested on two physical devices and an emulator.

Scope:
The app covers one city's bus network using available open data. Real-time GPS tracking of individual buses is out of scope where the feed is unavailable.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A native Android app showing routes and arrival estimates
2. A test report across devices and screen sizes

Timeline:
Semester one: UI and route display. Semester two: arrival estimation, favourites, and testing.

Title:
An IoT Sensor Network for Monitoring Water Usage in Sustainability

Problem Statement:
Reducing water waste requires knowing where and when water is consumed, but most buildings lack fine-grained monitoring. A low-cost IoT sensor network could measure water flow at several points and report usage to help identify waste and leaks.

Objectives:
1. Build sensor nodes that measure water flow
2. Send readings wirelessly to a central server
3. Visualise usage and flag unusual consumption

Methodology:
Each node uses an ESP32 microcontroller with a flow sensor, sending readings over Wi-Fi using MQTT to a Raspberry Pi broker. Data is stored in InfluxDB and visualised with a Grafana dashboard. A simple threshold rule flags abnormal flow that may indicate a leak. The setup will be tested on a small rig over two weeks.

Scope:
The prototype uses up to three sensor nodes in a controlled test setup. Whole-building deployment and integration with utility billing are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working sensor network reporting water flow data
2. A dashboard with leak alerts validated on the test rig

Timeline:
Semester one: hardware and communication. Semester two: storage, dashboard, alerts, and testing.

Title:
A Smart Home Automation Hub for Last-Mile Logistics Parcel Handling

Problem Statement:
As home delivery volumes grow, parcels are frequently left unattended, leading to theft and missed deliveries. Existing smart-home setups rarely coordinate door access, secure storage, and courier notification. This project builds an automation hub that links a smart lockbox, sensors, and courier alerts to streamline last-mile parcel handling at the home.

Objectives:
1. Integrate a smart lockbox, motion sensor, and camera into one hub
2. Automate one-time access codes for verified couriers and notify residents on delivery
3. Evaluate delivery success rate and event latency against a manual baseline

Methodology:
The hub runs on Home Assistant on a Raspberry Pi, integrating ESP32-controlled lock hardware over MQTT. A rules engine issues time-limited access codes validated against expected delivery windows from a mock courier API, triggering camera capture and push notifications. The system is evaluated over 30 simulated deliveries, measuring successful secure deposits and end-to-end notification latency against a manual no-automation baseline.

Scope:
The prototype handles a single home lockbox and one courier integration via a mock API. Multi-home fleet coordination, real carrier integration, and outdoor robotics are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working automation hub with code-based courier access and alerts
2. A comparison report on delivery success and latency versus the manual baseline

Timeline:
Phase 1 (weeks 1-5): hardware and Home Assistant setup. Phase 2 (weeks 6-11): access logic and notifications. Phase 3 (weeks 12-16): evaluation and reporting.

Title:
Edge Computing for On-Site Document Verification in E-Government Services

Problem Statement:
E-government counters often verify scanned identity documents by sending images to central servers, which raises latency and privacy concerns over citizen data leaving the premises. Running verification at the edge keeps sensitive images local while still flagging tampered or low-quality scans. This project evaluates an edge-based document verification pipeline for a service counter.

Objectives:
1. Deploy a document classification and quality-check model on an edge device
2. Detect blurred, cropped, or mismatched document scans locally
3. Compare edge inference latency and accuracy against a cloud baseline

Methodology:
A MobileNetV2 model is trained to classify document types and flag quality issues, then quantised with TensorFlow Lite and deployed on an NVIDIA Jetson Nano. A public document image dataset plus augmented samples provides training and test data. Evaluation reports accuracy, precision, and recall for the quality flags, and measures inference latency on the edge device against the same model served from a cloud VM.

Scope:
The prototype covers three document types and three quality-defect classes on one edge device. Full OCR text extraction and live integration with a government database are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A quantised edge model performing local document quality checks
2. A latency and accuracy comparison against the cloud baseline

Timeline:
Phase 1 (weeks 1-5): data prep and model training. Phase 2 (weeks 6-10): quantisation and edge deployment. Phase 3 (weeks 11-16): evaluation and write-up.

Title:
A Cloud-Native Microservices Architecture for an Online Learning Platform

Problem Statement:
Monolithic e-learning systems struggle to scale during exam periods when enrolment, content delivery, and quiz grading spike unevenly. Decomposing the platform into independently scalable microservices could improve resilience and resource use. This project designs and evaluates a cloud-native microservices backend for an online learning platform under varying load.

Objectives:
1. Split core e-learning functions into separate services with their own data stores
2. Deploy the services to Kubernetes with autoscaling and a gateway
3. Measure scalability and fault tolerance under simulated load against a monolith baseline

Methodology:
Four Spring Boot services (auth, courses, quizzes, notifications) communicate via REST and a RabbitMQ event bus, each with a PostgreSQL schema. They are containerised with Docker and deployed on a local Kubernetes cluster with a horizontal pod autoscaler and an NGINX ingress. Load tests with k6 simulate enrolment and quiz spikes, measuring throughput, p95 latency, and recovery time when a pod is killed, compared to an equivalent monolith.

Scope:
The project implements four services and load-tests them locally on Minikube. A full production UI, payment processing, and multi-region deployment are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working microservices backend deployed on Kubernetes with autoscaling
2. A benchmark report on scalability and recovery versus the monolith

Timeline:
Phase 1 (weeks 1-5): service decomposition and APIs. Phase 2 (weeks 6-11): containerisation and Kubernetes. Phase 3 (weeks 12-16): load testing and analysis.

Title:
A DevOps CI/CD Automation Pipeline for a Retail E-Commerce Application

Problem Statement:
Retail e-commerce teams often deploy manually, causing slow releases and inconsistent environments that lead to production errors during promotions. An automated CI/CD pipeline with quality gates could shorten release times and reduce failed deployments. This project builds and measures such a pipeline for a sample retail web application.

Objectives:
1. Automate build, test, and container image creation on every commit
2. Add quality gates for unit tests, linting, and security scanning
3. Enable automated staging deployment with rollback and measure release metrics

Methodology:
The pipeline is built with GitHub Actions for build and test, SonarQube for code quality, and Trivy for image vulnerability scanning. Passing builds produce Docker images pushed to a registry and deployed to a staging Kubernetes namespace via Argo CD using a blue-green strategy with automatic rollback on failed health checks. Effectiveness is measured using DORA metrics, deployment frequency, lead time, and change failure rate, before and after automation.

Scope:
The pipeline targets one sample retail application deployed to a staging environment. Production rollout, multi-cloud deployment, and infrastructure provisioning automation are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working CI/CD pipeline with quality gates and automated rollback
2. A DORA-metrics comparison showing the impact of automation

Phase 1 (weeks 1-4): CI build and tests. Phase 2 (weeks 5-10): quality gates and CD. Phase 3 (weeks 11-16): rollback, metrics, and reporting.

Title:
A Big Data Analytics Pipeline for Smart City Traffic Flow Analysis

Problem Statement:
Smart cities generate large volumes of traffic sensor and GPS data, but batch-only processing makes it hard to spot congestion as it forms. A streaming big-data pipeline could ingest and analyse traffic events in near real time to surface congestion hotspots. This project builds and evaluates such a pipeline on open traffic data.

Objectives:
1. Ingest streaming traffic events and store historical records
2. Compute rolling congestion metrics per road segment in near real time
3. Visualise hotspots and evaluate pipeline throughput and latency

Methodology:
Traffic events from an open dataset are replayed into Apache Kafka, processed by Apache Spark Structured Streaming to compute per-segment average speed and congestion in sliding windows, and written to a data lake (Parquet on MinIO) plus a serving store. A dashboard built with Grafana shows live hotspots. The pipeline is evaluated on ingestion throughput, end-to-end latency, and correctness of windowed metrics against a batch recomputation.

Scope:
The project uses one replayed open dataset on a single-node cluster. Live city sensor integration, predictive traffic modelling, and multi-node tuning are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working streaming pipeline producing near-real-time congestion metrics
2. A performance report on throughput, latency, and metric correctness

Timeline:
Phase 1 (weeks 1-5): ingestion and storage. Phase 2 (weeks 6-11): stream processing and dashboard. Phase 3 (weeks 12-16): benchmarking and analysis.

Title:
A Business Intelligence Dashboard for Destination Demand Analysis in Tourism

Problem Statement:
Regional tourism boards collect bookings, occupancy, and visitor-survey data in disconnected systems, so analysts cannot quickly compare destinations or detect demand shifts before a season. Existing off-the-shelf dashboards rarely combine these heterogeneous sources with a clear data model, leaving a gap for a tailored, well-governed BI solution. This project delivers a dimensional-model-backed dashboard that unifies these sources for destination demand analysis.

Objectives:
1. Design a star-schema warehouse integrating bookings, occupancy, and survey data with documented ETL
2. Build interactive dashboards reporting demand KPIs (RevPAR, occupancy, seasonality, origin mix) by destination
3. Evaluate decision usefulness and query performance against a spreadsheet baseline with five tourism analysts

Methodology:
Three source datasets (a public hotel-bookings dataset, synthetic occupancy records, and survey extracts) are cleaned and loaded into a PostgreSQL star schema via Python ETL scripts, with data-quality checks and a documented grain per fact table. Power BI connects to the warehouse to deliver drill-down dashboards and a seasonality forecast view. Evaluation uses a task-based usability study (five analysts completing eight analytical tasks), measuring task success, time-on-task, and a System Usability Scale score, plus query latency versus the spreadsheet baseline.

Scope:
The solution covers domestic-destination demand reporting for one region with three integrated sources and a fixed KPI set. Real-time streaming ingestion, predictive pricing optimisation, and live PMS connectors are explicitly excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A documented star-schema warehouse with reproducible ETL and data-quality checks
2. An interactive BI dashboard plus an evaluation report on usability and query performance versus the baseline

Timeline:
Phase 1 (weeks 1-4): requirements and dimensional modelling. Phase 2 (weeks 5-9): ETL and warehouse build. Phase 3 (weeks 10-13): dashboard development. Phase 4 (weeks 14-16): usability study, benchmarking, and reporting.

Title:
Time-Series Forecasting of Daily Engagement Volume on a Social Media Platform

Problem Statement:
Community managers on social media platforms need short-term forecasts of daily engagement (posts, comments, reactions) to schedule moderation staff and content, yet engagement series exhibit strong weekly seasonality, holiday effects, and bursty spikes that simple moving averages miss. The gap is a rigorously evaluated forecasting approach that handles these patterns and quantifies uncertainty. This project compares classical and deep-learning forecasters for next-7-day engagement prediction.

Objectives:
1. Build a clean daily engagement series with calendar and holiday features from a public platform dataset
2. Develop and tune SARIMA, Prophet, and an LSTM forecaster for a 7-day horizon
3. Evaluate accuracy and uncertainty against a seasonal-naive baseline using rolling-origin cross-validation

Methodology:
A public social-media activity dataset is aggregated to a daily engagement series and enriched with day-of-week and holiday indicators. Three models are compared: SARIMA (order selected via AIC), Facebook Prophet with added regressors, and an LSTM (hyperparameters tuned by validation grid). Models are assessed with rolling-origin (time-series) cross-validation using MAE, RMSE, and MAPE, plus prediction-interval coverage at 80% and 95%, all benchmarked against a seasonal-naive baseline. Statistical significance of differences is checked with a Diebold-Mariano test, and residual diagnostics confirm assumptions.

Scope:
The work forecasts one platform-level daily engagement series at a 7-day horizon. Per-user prediction, content-level virality modelling, and real-time online retraining are out of scope. The risk of dataset distribution shift is mitigated by holding out the most recent months as a final test set.

Expected Outcomes:
1. Three tuned forecasting models with reproducible code and a documented feature pipeline
2. A comparative evaluation report with cross-validated error metrics, interval coverage, and significance testing against the baseline

Timeline:
Phase 1 (weeks 1-4): data engineering and feature design. Phase 2 (weeks 5-9): classical models. Phase 3 (weeks 10-13): LSTM and tuning. Phase 4 (weeks 14-16): cross-validation, significance testing, and reporting.

Title:

Title:
Fraud Detection for Manufacturing Procurement Invoices

Methodology:

Performance is measured with stratified 5-fold cross-validation and compared to a simple rule-based filter. The best model is wrapped in a small Flask dashboard.

Scope:
The project covers tabular invoice anomaly detection. It excludes image-based invoice scanning and real ERP integration.

Expected Outcomes:

2. A dashboard that lists flagged invoices.

Title:

A content-based recommender uses product category and tag similarity, while item-based collaborative filtering uses a purchase co-occurrence matrix. Both are evaluated with precision@k and coverage on a held-out test split, then exposed through a web demo.

Scope:
The work focuses on the recommendation algorithm and a demo storefront. Payment, logistics, and live user accounts are excluded.

Title:

Title:
A Knowledge-Graph Search Tool for Small Business Records

Problem Statement:
Small business owners keep customers, suppliers, and invoices in separate spreadsheets, making it hard to answer questions that span documents, such as which supplier links to an overdue customer. Keyword search alone cannot follow these relationships.

Objectives:

2. Provide a search interface that answers relationship queries.
3. Evaluate retrieval quality against keyword search on sample questions.

Methodology:
Spreadsheet data is parsed and loaded into Neo4j as nodes and edges. A query layer translates simple natural-language questions into Cypher templates. A set of 30 test questions compares the graph tool's answers with a plain keyword search baseline using precision and recall.

Scope:
The project covers a single small business's three record types and a fixed set of query templates. Free-form natural-language understanding is out of scope.
