Title:
Semantic Segmentation of Crop and Weed Regions in Field Images

Problem Statement:
Precision agriculture needs to distinguish crops from weeds so herbicide is applied only where needed, but manual annotation in the field is slow. Pixel-level segmentation can automate this, yet lighting variation and overlapping foliage challenge simple thresholding methods used by many growers.

Objectives:
1. Train a segmentation model that labels each pixel as crop, weed, or soil.
2. Compare a U-Net baseline against DeepLabV3+ on the same data.
3. Evaluate using mean IoU and per-class IoU on a held-out test set.

Methodology:
The project uses the public CWFID and Sugar Beets crop/weed datasets. Images are augmented with flips, rotation, and colour jitter. U-Net and DeepLabV3+ (ResNet-50 backbone) are trained in PyTorch with the Dice+cross-entropy loss, early stopping, and a fixed 70/15/15 split. Mean IoU, per-class IoU, and inference time are reported, with qualitative overlays for error analysis.

Scope:
The work targets RGB field images of one to two crop types. Real-time on-tractor deployment and multispectral imagery are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. Two trained segmentation models with a quantitative comparison.
2. An error-analysis report with visual overlays.

Timeline:
Phase 1 data and baseline (6 wks), Phase 2 models (6 wks), Phase 3 evaluation and write-up (6 wks).

Title:
Real-Time Detection of Road Hazards for Driver Assistance

Problem Statement:
Potholes and road debris cause vehicle damage and accidents, and city reporting relies on slow manual complaints. A dashcam-based detector could flag hazards automatically, but it must run fast enough on modest hardware while keeping false alarms low on cluttered roads.

Objectives:
1. Train an object detector to locate potholes and debris in dashcam frames.
2. Compare YOLOv8n and YOLOv8s for the accuracy/speed trade-off.
3. Evaluate using mAP@0.5, mAP@0.5:0.95, and frames per second on a CPU.

Methodology:
A pothole/road-damage dataset (RDD2022 subset plus a public pothole set) is annotated in YOLO format and split 80/10/10. Both models are trained in Ultralytics PyTorch with augmentation (mosaic, HSV shift). Evaluation reports mAP, precision, recall, and FPS on a laptop CPU. A confusion analysis examines misses on shadowed road sections.

Scope:
The project covers daytime road hazard detection from forward dashcam views. Night-vision, lane detection, and embedded deployment are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained hazard detector with an accuracy/speed comparison.
2. A short demo running on recorded video clips.

Timeline:
Three phases over 18 weeks: dataset (5), training (7), evaluation/demo (6).

Title:
Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis of Consumer Reviews on Sustainable Products

Methodology:
A labelled subset of the Amazon and SemEval ABSA review data is filtered for sustainability-related products. DistilBERT is fine-tuned for aspect-term sentiment classification and compared with a TF-IDF + linear SVM baseline. Evaluation uses macro-F1 and per-aspect accuracy with 5-fold cross-validation; error cases are inspected for sarcasm and mixed sentiment.

Scope:

Expected Outcomes:

2. A breakdown of sentiment per sustainability aspect.

Timeline:

Title:
Learned Cost Estimation for Query Optimization in a Logistics Database

Problem Statement:
Logistics systems run complex joins over shipment, route, and order tables, and the database optimizer sometimes chooses poor plans because its cardinality estimates are inaccurate. Better cost estimates could cut query latency, but building them must not require changing the underlying engine.

Objectives:
1. Build a learned cardinality/cost estimator for a set of logistics query templates.
2. Compare its plan choices against PostgreSQL's default optimizer.
3. Evaluate using estimation error (q-error) and end-to-end query latency.

Methodology:
A synthetic logistics schema is populated with TPC-H-style data scaled to shipments. Query features (join count, predicate selectivity, table sizes) are extracted, and a gradient-boosted regressor predicts cardinality. Predicted estimates feed plan-hint selection. Evaluation measures median and 95th-percentile q-error and wall-clock latency over 200 test queries versus the native optimizer.

Scope:
The project covers read-only analytical queries on a fixed schema. Write workloads, index tuning, and distributed databases are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained cost estimator integrated via query hints.
2. A latency and q-error comparison report.

Timeline:
18 weeks: schema and data (5), modelling (7), evaluation (6).

Title:
A Facial-Recognition Attendance System for E-Government Offices

Problem Statement:
Government offices still use sign-in sheets or fingerprint scanners that spread contact and allow buddy-punching. A contactless face-based attendance system could speed check-in, but it must handle varied lighting and resist simple photo spoofing to be trustworthy.

Objectives:
1. Build a face-recognition attendance system that logs staff entry and exit.
2. Add a basic liveness check to reject printed-photo spoofing.
3. Evaluate recognition accuracy and spoof-rejection rate.

Methodology:
Face detection uses MTCNN and embeddings come from a pre-trained FaceNet model; identities are matched by cosine distance against an enrolled gallery. A blink/texture-based liveness check rejects static photos. The system is tested on the LFW set for verification accuracy plus a self-collected enrolment of 30 volunteers, reporting accuracy, false-accept and false-reject rates, and spoof-rejection on photo attacks.

Scope:
The project covers indoor staff attendance with cooperative subjects. Mask-occluded recognition and large-scale crowds are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working attendance system with a web dashboard of logs.
2. An evaluation of accuracy, FAR/FRR, and spoof rejection.

Timeline:
Three phases across 18 weeks: enrolment pipeline, liveness, evaluation.

Title:
A Robust OCR Pipeline for Handwritten Student Assessment Forms

Problem Statement:
Schools digitise stacks of handwritten assessment forms by hand, which is slow and error-prone, and off-the-shelf OCR struggles with mixed printed/handwritten fields, faint ink, and skewed scans. A targeted pipeline with explicit pre-processing and field-level validation is needed to make extraction reliable enough for record-keeping.

Objectives:
1. Build an end-to-end OCR pipeline that extracts named fields (student ID, scores, remarks) from scanned forms.
2. Compare a Tesseract LSTM baseline against a fine-tuned TrOCR model on handwritten fields.
3. Evaluate with character error rate (CER), word error rate (WER), and field-level exact-match accuracy.

Methodology:
A dataset is assembled from the public IAM handwriting corpus plus 300 self-scanned forms annotated per field. Pre-processing applies deskew, adaptive binarisation, and layout-based field cropping. Tesseract (LSTM) is the baseline; TrOCR-base is fine-tuned on the handwritten crops. Evaluation uses CER/WER and field exact-match with 5-fold cross-validation, a confidence-threshold rejection option, and ablations removing each pre-processing step. A regex/checksum validator flags low-confidence numeric fields for human review.

Scope:
The pipeline targets single-language English forms with a known layout. Free-form multi-page documents and table reconstruction are explicitly excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A reproducible OCR pipeline with the baseline-vs-TrOCR comparison and ablation results.
2. A field-validation module routing low-confidence extractions to manual review, with an error-analysis report.

Timeline:
Phase 1 dataset and pre-processing (5 wks), Phase 2 baseline and fine-tuning (7 wks), Phase 3 evaluation, ablations, and write-up (6 wks); risk buffer for annotation included.

Title:
Anomaly Detection in Retail Wireless Sensor Streams for Cold-Chain Monitoring

Problem Statement:
Retailers run wireless temperature and humidity sensors across refrigerated displays, but staff notice spoilage-risk excursions late, and naive threshold alarms flood operators with false positives from door openings and defrost cycles. A method that separates genuine cold-chain faults from benign transients is needed to cut waste without alert fatigue.

Objectives:
1. Build an anomaly-detection model for multivariate WSN streams (temperature, humidity, door state).
2. Compare an LSTM autoencoder against an Isolation Forest and a fixed-threshold baseline.
3. Evaluate detection with precision, recall, F1, and mean time-to-detect on labelled excursion events.

Methodology:
Data combines the public Intel Lab WSN dataset with a self-collected fridge log labelled for excursion events. Streams are windowed (sliding 15-min) with lag and rate-of-change features. An LSTM autoencoder flags windows by reconstruction error; Isolation Forest and a static threshold serve as baselines. Evaluation uses event-level precision/recall/F1, PR-AUC, and mean time-to-detect with time-series cross-validation; sensitivity to window size and contamination rate is analysed, and packet-loss robustness is tested by dropping readings.

Scope:
The project covers offline analysis of three sensor types in one store layout. Live gateway deployment and predictive maintenance of compressors are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained anomaly-detection model with a baseline comparison and ROC/PR curves.
2. An alert-quality report quantifying false-positive reduction and time-to-detect, plus robustness findings.

Timeline:
Phase 1 data and labelling (5 wks), Phase 2 modelling and baselines (7 wks), Phase 3 evaluation and robustness study (6 wks), with a buffer for sensor data collection.
