I will build the system using PHP and MySQL with a simple Bootstrap interface. Pharmacy staff can add customers, record prescriptions, and see refill reminders. One small pharmacy will trial it and give feedback through interviews.

Scope:
Aimed at single-branch retail pharmacies. It handles records and reminders only, not insurance claims or stock ordering, and is not a certified medical device.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working prescription record web app
2. Feedback from a pilot pharmacy

Timeline:
Requirements month 1, build months 2-5, pilot month 6.

Title:
A Simple Telemedicine Booking Platform for a Smart City Clinic

Problem Statement:
Residents in growing smart-city neighbourhoods often wait a long time to see a doctor for minor issues and have no easy way to book a video consultation. A lightweight telemedicine platform could let them book and join calls online.

Objectives:
1. Build a web platform where patients book video consultations
2. Integrate a video call feature for doctor-patient sessions
3. Allow doctors to write simple notes after each call

Methodology:
The platform will be built with React on the front end and Node.js with MySQL on the back end. Video calls use a third-party API such as Jitsi. Patients register, choose a slot, and join a call. I will demo it to a few volunteers acting as patients and doctors.

Scope:
Covers booking, video calls, and basic consultation notes for one clinic. It does not handle payment, e-prescriptions, or integration with hospital systems.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working booking and video consultation web app
2. A short usability evaluation with volunteers

Timeline:
Months 1-2 design, 3-5 development, 6 testing.

Title:
An Adaptive E-Learning System for Local Tourism Guides

Problem Statement:
Trainee tourism guides need to learn about local heritage sites, but generic e-learning courses do not adapt to what each learner already knows, so confident learners get bored and weaker ones fall behind. There is room for a system that adjusts the difficulty of content based on quiz performance.

Objectives:
1. Build an e-learning platform with modules on local heritage and guiding skills
2. Implement an adaptive engine that selects the next module based on quiz scores
3. Evaluate learning gains against a fixed-order version of the same content

Methodology:
The system will be built with Django and PostgreSQL. The adaptive logic uses a rule-based mastery threshold: learners scoring below 70% repeat related content, while higher scorers skip ahead. I will run a small study with two groups, one using the adaptive version and one using a fixed sequence, and compare pre/post-test scores.

Scope:
Covers around five tourism training modules for one region. The adaptation is rule-based, not machine-learning, and the content set is fixed.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working adaptive e-learning platform
2. A comparison of learning gains between adaptive and fixed groups

Timeline:
Months 1-2 content and design, 3-4 build, 5 adaptive engine, 6 study and write-up.

Title:
In-App Peer Payments for a Campus Social Media Platform

Problem Statement:
Students on a campus social network frequently split costs for food and events but currently leave the app to use separate banking apps, which is clumsy. Embedding a simple peer-to-peer payment feature could keep these small transactions inside the social platform.

Objectives:
1. Add a wallet and peer-to-peer transfer feature to a social media web app
2. Record a transaction history with split-bill support
3. Evaluate transaction reliability and user satisfaction

Methodology:
The feature will be built on a React and Node.js stack with a MySQL ledger table. Payments use a sandbox payment gateway (Stripe test mode) rather than real money. I will implement split-bill logic, then test with a group of students completing scripted payment tasks and collect a usability and trust questionnaire.

Scope:
A prototype within one social media app, using sandbox payments only. Real bank settlement, fraud handling, and regulatory compliance are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working in-app peer payment prototype with split bills
2. Reliability and satisfaction results from user testing

Timeline:
Months 1-2 design, 3-5 build, 6 testing.

Title:
Detecting Anomalous Healthcare Insurance Claims with Machine Learning

Problem Statement:
Healthcare insurers process large volumes of claims, and a small fraction are fraudulent or erroneous, but manual review cannot scale. A supervised model that flags suspicious claims for human review could reduce losses while keeping a human in the loop.

Objectives:
1. Build a labelled dataset of claims with engineered features
2. Train and compare classifiers to flag suspicious claims
3. Evaluate the models using metrics suited to imbalanced data

Methodology:
Using a public healthcare claims dataset, I will engineer features such as claim amount, provider frequency, and procedure codes. I will train logistic regression, random forest, and XGBoost models, handling class imbalance with SMOTE. Evaluation uses precision, recall, F1, and ROC-AUC with stratified cross-validation, and I will inspect feature importance to explain flags.

Scope:
A research prototype on a single public dataset. It outputs a risk score for review and does not auto-reject claims or connect to a live insurer system.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained anomaly-flagging model with reported metrics
2. A comparison of the three classifiers and key predictive features

Timeline:
Month 1 data prep, 2-3 features, 4 modelling, 5 evaluation, 6 write-up.

Title:
A Hybrid Product Recommendation Engine for an Online Finance Marketplace

Problem Statement:
Users browsing an online marketplace for financial products such as loans and insurance plans face too many options and often leave without choosing. A recommendation engine tailored to their stated needs could surface relevant products and improve engagement.

Objectives:
1. Build a recommendation engine combining content-based and collaborative filtering
2. Generate ranked product suggestions from user profiles and behaviour
3. Evaluate recommendation quality offline and with a small user test

Methodology:
I will use a public or synthetic dataset of user-product interactions. Content-based filtering matches product attributes to user preferences, while collaborative filtering uses matrix factorisation on interaction history; a weighted hybrid combines both. Offline evaluation uses precision@k and recall@k on held-out data, followed by a small survey on perceived relevance.

Scope:
A prototype web demo for one category of financial products, using sample data. It does not give regulated financial advice or connect to live product providers.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working hybrid recommendation engine with a demo interface
2. Offline and survey-based evaluation of recommendation quality

Timeline:
Months 1-2 data and design, 3-4 build, 5 evaluation, 6 write-up.

Title:
A Conversational Assistant for Factory Floor Maintenance Queries

Problem Statement:
Maintenance technicians on a manufacturing floor lose time searching long PDF manuals for equipment procedures. A chatbot that answers questions from these manuals in plain language could speed up troubleshooting and reduce downtime.

Objectives:
1. Build a chatbot that answers maintenance questions from equipment manuals
2. Ground answers in the manual content using retrieval
3. Evaluate answer accuracy against a set of technician questions

Methodology:
I will use a retrieval-augmented approach: manuals are chunked and embedded into a FAISS vector store, and a question retrieves the most relevant passages, which are passed to a language model to compose an answer. I will create a test set of about 40 real maintenance questions with expected answers and measure accuracy and retrieval relevance, comparing against keyword search.

Scope:
Covers manuals for a small set of machines in one factory. It answers procedural questions only and is not connected to live machine sensors or control systems.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working retrieval-augmented maintenance chatbot
2. Accuracy results against a technician question set with a keyword baseline

Timeline:
Months 1-2 setup and ingestion, 3-4 retrieval and generation, 5 evaluation, 6 write-up.

Title:
Knowledge-Graph Search over Public Safety Incident Reports

Problem Statement:
Public safety analysts struggle to connect related incidents because reports are stored as free text, so links between locations, people, and event types are hidden. A knowledge graph built from these reports could let analysts search by relationships rather than keywords.

Objectives:
1. Extract entities and relations from incident reports into a knowledge graph
2. Build a query interface that answers relationship-based questions
3. Evaluate search quality against keyword search on sample queries

Methodology:
I will use spaCy for named-entity recognition to pull out locations, dates, and event types, then build a graph in Neo4j linking them. A query interface translates analyst questions into Cypher queries. Using a public crime/incident dataset, I will define a set of relationship queries and compare results from the graph against a keyword search baseline using precision and recall.

Scope:
A prototype on one public incident dataset. Entity extraction targets a fixed set of types; it is an analyst tool, not a live operational system.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A populated knowledge graph with a relationship search interface
2. A precision/recall comparison against keyword search

Timeline:
Month 1 data, 2-3 extraction and graph, 4 query interface, 5 evaluation, 6 write-up.

Title:
Semantic Segmentation of Solar Panels in Aerial Imagery for Energy Auditing

Problem Statement:
Energy auditors estimating rooftop solar capacity must manually trace panels in aerial photos, which is slow and inconsistent. Automatic pixel-level segmentation of solar arrays would let auditors quantify installed capacity across a region quickly, but cluttered rooftops and varying panel colours make this non-trivial.

Objectives:
1. Assemble and annotate an aerial dataset of rooftop solar panels
2. Train and compare segmentation models for pixel-level panel detection
3. Evaluate segmentation accuracy and estimate panel area from masks

Methodology:
I will use a public aerial solar dataset and augment it with manually annotated tiles. I will train a U-Net and a DeepLabV3+ model, both with pretrained encoders, comparing them against a thresholding baseline. Data augmentation includes rotation and brightness shifts. Evaluation uses IoU, Dice coefficient, and pixel accuracy with a held-out test set, plus an estimate of panel area error against ground truth.

Scope:
Segments solar panels only, from RGB aerial tiles at a fixed resolution. Capacity estimation in kilowatts and detection of other rooftop objects are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained segmentation model with IoU and Dice results
2. A comparison of U-Net and DeepLabV3+ and area-estimation error

Timeline:
Month 1 data and annotation, 2 baseline, 3-4 model training, 5 evaluation, 6 write-up.

Title:
Real-Time Shelf Stock Detection for Small Retail Businesses

Problem Statement:
Small shop owners cannot afford enterprise inventory systems and often discover empty shelves only when customers complain. An object detector running on a cheap camera feed could flag out-of-stock shelf sections in near real time, but small businesses need it to run on modest hardware.

Objectives:
1. Build an annotated dataset of shelf images with stocked and empty regions
2. Train an object detection model to locate products and gaps on shelves
3. Evaluate detection accuracy and inference speed on low-cost hardware

Methodology:
I will collect and label shelf images using bounding boxes for product packs and empty gaps. I will train YOLOv8 in nano and small variants and compare against an SSD-MobileNet baseline. Evaluation uses mAP at IoU 0.5, precision, recall, and frames-per-second measured on a CPU and a Raspberry Pi to test feasibility on cheap hardware. I will analyse failure cases such as reflections.

Scope:
Detects product presence and empty gaps on shelves for one product category. It does not identify specific brands or count exact units.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained shelf-gap detector with mAP and speed results
2. A feasibility comparison across hardware targets

Timeline:
Month 1 data collection, 2 annotation, 3-4 training, 5 evaluation on hardware, 6 write-up.

Title:
Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis of Farmer Feedback on Agricultural Apps

Problem Statement:
Developers of agricultural advisory apps receive thousands of reviews but cannot tell which features farmers like or dislike, since overall star ratings hide the detail. Aspect-based sentiment analysis could break feedback down by feature, such as weather accuracy or usability, but agricultural reviews mix local terms and code-switching.

Objectives:
1. Build a labelled dataset of agricultural app reviews tagged by aspect and sentiment
2. Train models to extract aspects and classify their sentiment
3. Compare a fine-tuned transformer against a classical baseline

Methodology:
I will scrape and manually label reviews into aspect categories (advice quality, weather, usability, price) with positive/negative/neutral sentiment. I will fine-tune DistilBERT for joint aspect-sentiment classification and compare it against a TF-IDF plus SVM baseline. Evaluation uses macro-F1 per aspect and overall accuracy with stratified k-fold cross-validation, plus an error analysis of code-switched reviews.

Scope:
Covers English and mixed English-Malay reviews for a small set of aspects. It classifies sentiment but does not generate developer recommendations.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A labelled aspect-sentiment dataset and trained model
2. Macro-F1 comparison between the transformer and baseline

Timeline:
Month 1 scraping, 2 labelling, 3 baseline, 4 transformer, 5 evaluation, 6 write-up.

Title:
Learned Index Tuning for Queries on a Public Transport Trip Database

Problem Statement:
Public transport analytics platforms run heavy queries over large trip records, and poorly chosen indexes slow them down, yet manual index tuning needs an expert. An automated advisor that recommends indexes from observed query workloads could improve query latency for transport datasets.

Objectives:
1. Build a benchmark of representative transport analytics queries
2. Implement an index-recommendation method driven by the query workload
3. Measure latency improvement against the default and a naive index set

Methodology:
Using a public transit trip dataset loaded into PostgreSQL, I will define a workload of around 20 representative queries. I will use the database's hypothetical-index and EXPLAIN cost estimates to drive a greedy index-selection algorithm that picks indexes maximising estimated cost reduction under a storage budget. Evaluation measures actual query latency and total index size against no tuning and an all-columns naive baseline.

Scope:
Tunes single-column and simple composite B-tree indexes on one PostgreSQL schema. Query rewriting, partitioning, and other database engines are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A workload-driven index advisor prototype
2. Latency and storage results versus default and naive baselines

Timeline:
Month 1 data and workload, 2-3 algorithm, 4 integration, 5 evaluation, 6 write-up.

Title:
A Facial-Recognition Attendance System for Campus Sustainability Events

Problem Statement:
Sustainability volunteer events on campus track attendance with paper sign-in sheets, which waste paper and are easy to falsify. A facial-recognition attendance system would cut paper use and give reliable records, but lighting variation and privacy concerns must be handled carefully.

Objectives:
1. Build an enrolment and recognition pipeline for event attendance
2. Record attendance automatically and export reports
3. Evaluate recognition accuracy under different lighting conditions

Methodology:
The system uses MTCNN for face detection and FaceNet embeddings, matching faces against an enrolled gallery with a cosine-similarity threshold. A Flask app logs check-ins to a database and exports CSV reports. I will evaluate on a self-collected set of volunteers under indoor and outdoor lighting, reporting accuracy, false acceptance and false rejection rates, and will store only embeddings with consent rather than raw images.

Scope:
Handles enrolment, check-in, and reporting for events of up to about fifty participants. Liveness/anti-spoofing detection and integration with the campus student system are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working facial-recognition attendance app with report export
2. Accuracy and error-rate results across lighting conditions

Timeline:
Month 1 pipeline, 2-3 app and database, 4 data collection, 5 evaluation, 6 write-up.

Title:
An OCR Pipeline for Automated Extraction of Structured Fields from Logistics Shipping Documents

Problem Statement:
Freight forwarders manually key fields such as consignee, tracking number, weight, and HS code from scanned bills of lading and delivery orders, which is slow and error-prone, especially when documents are skewed, low-resolution, or use varied layouts. A general OCR alone returns raw text without knowing which token is the tracking number, so the bottleneck is structured field extraction, not just character recognition. This project targets reliable key-value extraction from heterogeneous logistics documents.

Objectives:
1. Assemble and annotate a dataset of 800+ scanned logistics documents with labelled key-value fields across at least three layout types
2. Build a pipeline combining OCR with a layout-aware extraction model and benchmark it against a regex-and-rules baseline
3. Evaluate field-level extraction accuracy and quantify robustness to skew and resolution degradation

Methodology:
Pages are preprocessed with deskewing and adaptive thresholding, then passed through Tesseract and a comparison with the PaddleOCR engine for text and bounding boxes. For field extraction I will fine-tune LayoutLMv3, which fuses text, layout, and image features, against a rule-based regex baseline. Training uses an 80/10/10 split with five-fold cross-validation on the train portion. Evaluation reports per-field precision, recall, and F1, exact-match accuracy, and normalised edit distance, with a controlled robustness study injecting synthetic skew and downsampling. Annotation quality is checked with inter-annotator agreement on a subset.

Scope:
Covers three logistics document types (bill of lading, delivery order, commercial invoice) in English, extracting a fixed schema of about ten fields. Handwriting recognition, non-Latin scripts, and downstream ERP integration are explicitly excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An annotated benchmark dataset and an OCR-plus-extraction pipeline with reproducible code
2. A documented per-field F1 comparison showing the layout-aware model versus the rules baseline and its robustness profile

Timeline:
Month 1 dataset collection and annotation, month 2 preprocessing and baseline, months 3-4 LayoutLMv3 fine-tuning, month 5 robustness evaluation, month 6 analysis and write-up.

Title:
Anomaly Detection and Predictive Analytics for a Smart-Building Wireless Sensor Network Supporting e-Government Facilities

Problem Statement:
Government office buildings increasingly deploy wireless sensor networks measuring temperature, occupancy, power, and air quality, but the raw streams are noisy, contain dropouts, and are rarely analysed beyond simple dashboards. Facility managers cannot easily tell a genuine fault, such as an HVAC failure, from a transient sensor glitch, leading to wasted energy and late maintenance. This project develops an analytics pipeline that cleans sensor streams and detects anomalies indicative of equipment faults in e-government building data.

Objectives:
1. Build an ingestion and cleaning pipeline that handles missing values and clock drift across heterogeneous sensor streams
2. Develop and compare unsupervised anomaly-detection models on multivariate time-series sensor data
3. Evaluate detection performance against labelled fault windows and measure forecasting accuracy for short-term demand

Methodology:
Using a public smart-building sensor dataset supplemented with injected synthetic faults for ground truth, I will resample and impute streams and engineer time and lag features. I will compare an Isolation Forest, an LSTM autoencoder reconstruction-error detector, and a seasonal-decomposition baseline for anomaly detection, and an SARIMA versus a lightweight LSTM for short-term load forecasting. Anomaly detection is evaluated with precision, recall, F1, and point-adjusted F1 against labelled fault windows; forecasting with MAE and RMSE. Time-series cross-validation with rolling windows prevents leakage, and I will run an ablation on feature groups.

Scope:
Covers four sensor types in one building dataset for offline analysis. Real-time streaming deployment, actuator control, and multi-building federation are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A reproducible cleaning-plus-anomaly-detection pipeline with a model comparison and ablation
2. Reported detection and forecasting metrics against labelled faults and baselines

Timeline:
Month 1 data and cleaning, month 2 feature engineering and baselines, months 3-4 anomaly and forecasting models, month 5 evaluation and ablation, month 6 write-up.

Title:
Crop Disease Detection Using Machine Learning

Problem Statement:
Farmers lose crops every year because of diseases. They do not always know what is wrong with their plants. Machine learning can help solve this big problem for farmers everywhere.

Objectives:
1. To detect crop diseases.
2. To help farmers.
3. To use machine learning.

Methodology:
I will collect some pictures of plants and use Python to train a model. Then it will classify the disease. I will use machine learning algorithms to make it accurate.

Scope:
This system can be used by all farmers in the world to check their crops and save money.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working system.
2. Happy farmers.

Title:
Smart Traffic with Deep Learning

Problem Statement:
There is too much traffic on the roads and people are stuck. Cameras see the cars but nobody uses them properly. Deep learning is very powerful and can fix traffic.

Objectives:
1. To make traffic better.
2. To use deep learning and computer vision.
3. To help drivers.

Methodology:
I will use a neural network to look at the cameras and find the cars. Deep learning will do the rest. I will train it on a computer until it works.

Scope:
The project is about traffic and cars on roads in the city.

Expected Outcomes:
1. Less traffic.
2. A smart camera system.

Title:
NLP for a Greener Planet

Problem Statement:
Climate change is a serious issue and people talk about it online a lot. We need to understand what they are saying so we can be more sustainable and save the environment.

Objectives:
1. To use NLP.
2. To analyse text about the environment.
3. To make the planet greener.

Methodology:
I will take text from the internet and use natural language processing to read it. The program will tell us the opinions. I will use Python libraries for the NLP part.

Scope:
This covers all text about sustainability and the environment online.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A text analysis tool.
2. Better awareness of climate change.

Title:
A Product Recommender System for an Online Logistics Marketplace

Problem Statement:
Logistics marketplaces list many carriers and freight services, and shippers struggle to find a suitable provider quickly. A recommender could suggest carriers based on past bookings, but the current platform only offers keyword search, which ignores user history and preferences.

Objectives:
1. To build a recommender that suggests carriers to shippers.
2. To use past booking data to personalise suggestions.
3. To evaluate whether the recommendations are useful.

Methodology:
The system will use collaborative filtering on historical booking records. I plan to use Python with the Surprise library to build a matrix-factorisation model. A web interface will display the top recommended carriers. Accuracy will be checked by comparing predictions to held-out bookings.

Scope:
The project focuses on freight carrier recommendations for one marketplace dataset. It will not handle pricing negotiation or real-time tracking.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working recommender prototype with a simple web front end.
2. An accuracy comparison against a popularity baseline.

Timeline:
The project will run over two semesters, with data work first and the model and interface later.

Title:
Voice Input for an E-Government Service Portal

Problem Statement:
Many citizens find online government forms hard to fill in, especially older users and those who type slowly. Adding speech recognition could let them dictate answers, but most e-government portals only accept typed input, which excludes some groups.

Objectives:
1. To add speech-to-text input to a sample government form.
2. To test how accurately it captures spoken answers.
3. To gather user feedback on ease of use.

Methodology:
I will integrate an existing speech recognition engine (such as the Web Speech API or Vosk) into a prototype web form. Spoken responses will be transcribed into the relevant fields. I will measure word error rate on a set of recorded test phrases and run a small usability test.

Scope:
The prototype covers one form type and English input only. It excludes authentication, payments, and multilingual support.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A web form prototype that accepts voice input.
2. A short report on transcription accuracy and user feedback.

Timeline:
Roughly two semesters: prototype build first, then testing and evaluation.

Title:
Detecting Network Intrusions on a Campus Education Network

Problem Statement:
University networks carry sensitive student and research data and face frequent scanning and intrusion attempts. Administrators often rely on manual log review, which is slow. A machine learning classifier on network traffic could flag suspicious flows earlier, but it is unclear how well standard models work on campus traffic.

Objectives:
1. To build a classifier that distinguishes normal from malicious network flows.
2. To train and test it on a public intrusion dataset.
3. To report detection accuracy and false alarms.

Methodology:
I will use the NSL-KDD dataset and train a Random Forest classifier with scikit-learn after basic feature scaling. The model will be evaluated using accuracy, precision, and recall on a held-out test split. Results will be compared with a simple decision-tree baseline.

Scope:
The work is limited to offline analysis of one public dataset modelling a campus-like network. Live deployment and encrypted-traffic analysis are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained intrusion-detection model with reported metrics.
2. A comparison against the baseline classifier.

Timeline:
Two semesters: dataset preparation and modelling in the first, evaluation and write-up in the second.

Title:
A Vulnerability Scanner for Small Retail Web Stores

Problem Statement:
Small online retailers often deploy web stores without security testing and remain exposed to common flaws like SQL injection and cross-site scripting. Commercial scanners can be costly, so a lightweight scanner aimed at small shops could help owners find obvious issues before launch.

Objectives:
1. To build a scanner that checks a retail web store for common vulnerabilities.
2. To detect SQL injection and XSS on test pages.
3. To present findings in a readable report.

Methodology:
The tool will be written in Python and will crawl a target site, then send crafted payloads to input fields to probe for SQL injection and reflected XSS. Detected issues will be logged with the affected URL. I will test it against a deliberately vulnerable app such as DVWA.

Scope:
The scanner targets two vulnerability types on small web stores. It excludes authenticated scanning, business-logic flaws, and automated fixing.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A command-line scanner that reports detected SQLi and XSS points.
2. A test report against a known vulnerable application.

Timeline:
About two semesters: crawler and payload engine first, testing and reporting later.

Title:
Static Malware Analysis for Smart-City IoT Gateways

Problem Statement:
Smart-city deployments connect many IoT gateways that are attractive targets for malware aiming at lighting, transport, and surveillance systems. Operators rarely have tools to triage suspicious binaries collected from these gateways. A static analysis pipeline that extracts features and classifies samples could speed up triage without running the malware live.

Objectives:
1. To extract static features (opcode n-grams, imported APIs, byte histograms) from a labelled malware/benign sample set.
2. To train a classifier that flags likely malicious binaries.
3. To evaluate detection performance and report which features matter most.

Methodology:
Samples will be drawn from a public dataset such as EMBER. Using Python and the LIEF and scikit-learn libraries, I will parse binaries, build feature vectors, and train a gradient-boosted tree classifier. Evaluation uses stratified train/test splits with accuracy, precision, recall, and ROC-AUC, and feature importance will be inspected.

Scope:
The project covers static analysis of Windows-style executables representative of gateway payloads. Dynamic sandbox analysis, packed-binary unpacking, and live deployment on real gateways are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A static-analysis classifier with reported metrics.
2. An analysis of the most informative features for detection.

Timeline:
Semester one: dataset, feature extraction, baseline model. Semester two: tuning, evaluation, and documentation.

Title:
A Responsive Web Platform for Local Tourism Discovery

Problem Statement:
Independent travellers visiting smaller towns struggle to find attractions, local eateries, and events in one place, as information is scattered across social pages and outdated brochures. A responsive web platform that aggregates curated local listings and lets users plan a short itinerary would make trip planning easier on any device.

Objectives:
1. To design a responsive platform listing attractions, food, and events for a chosen region.
2. To let users search, filter, and save places to a simple itinerary.
3. To evaluate usability with a small group of testers.

Methodology:
The platform will be built with React and a Node/Express REST API backed by PostgreSQL. Listing data will be seeded from publicly available tourism sources. Responsive layouts will be implemented with CSS grid and tested across phone, tablet, and desktop breakpoints. Usability will be assessed with a System Usability Scale questionnaire after task-based testing.

Scope:
The platform covers one region's listings and itinerary planning. Online booking, payments, and native mobile apps are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A deployed responsive web platform with search and itinerary features.
2. A usability evaluation summarising SUS scores and feedback.

Timeline:
Two semesters: design and core features first, then itinerary feature, testing, and refinement.

Title:
A Progressive Web App for Community Social Updates

Problem Statement:
Neighbourhood and hobby communities often share updates through fragmented chat groups, where posts get lost and offline access is poor. A progressive web app (PWA) could give these communities a single feed that loads quickly, works offline, and sends push notifications, without forcing members to install a native app.

Objectives:
1. To build a PWA feed where members post, comment, and react to community updates.
2. To support offline reading and push notifications.
3. To measure load performance and offline behaviour.

Methodology:
The app will use React with a service worker for caching and the Web Push API for notifications. A Firebase backend will store posts and handle authentication. Offline reading will be implemented with cached responses and an app-shell model. Performance will be measured with Lighthouse, focusing on PWA score, time-to-interactive, and offline page availability.

Scope:
The project delivers one community feed with text and image posts. Live video, direct messaging, and moderation tooling are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An installable PWA with offline support and push notifications.
2. A Lighthouse-based performance and PWA-compliance report.

Timeline:
Semester one: feed and auth. Semester two: offline, notifications, and evaluation.

Title:
A Cross-Platform Mobile App for Medication Reminders

Problem Statement:
Patients managing several daily medications frequently miss doses, which reduces treatment effectiveness. Existing reminder apps are often single-platform or cluttered. A clean cross-platform app that schedules reminders, logs adherence, and shows simple progress could help patients and let them share a summary with their doctor.

Objectives:
1. To build a cross-platform app that schedules medication reminders.
2. To log taken/missed doses and display an adherence summary.
3. To evaluate usability and reminder reliability with test users.

Methodology:
The app will be built with Flutter so a single codebase runs on Android and iOS. Local notifications will trigger reminders, and dose logs will be stored in a local SQLite database with optional cloud sync via Firebase. Reminder reliability will be tested across several schedules, and usability will be checked with a small task-based test and SUS questionnaire.

Scope:
The app handles personal medication scheduling and adherence logging. Prescription verification, pharmacy integration, and clinical decision support are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working cross-platform app with reminders and adherence logging.
2. A short evaluation of usability and reminder reliability.

Timeline:
Two semesters: core scheduling and logging first, then sync, summaries, and testing.

Title:
A Native Android App for Personal Expense Tracking

Problem Statement:
Many young adults struggle to track everyday spending because manual logging is tedious and generic apps bury simple budgeting behind paywalls. A focused native Android app that makes quick entry easy and shows clear monthly category breakdowns could help users build better spending habits.

Objectives:
1. To build a native Android app for fast expense entry and categorisation.
2. To show monthly summaries and per-category budget limits with alerts.
3. To evaluate usability and entry speed with test users.

Methodology:
The app will be written in Kotlin using Android Jetpack components, with Room for local storage and MVVM architecture. Charts will be drawn with MPAndroidChart, and budget-limit alerts will use scheduled notifications. Entry speed will be timed during user tasks, and usability assessed with a SUS questionnaire after a short test session.

Scope:
The app covers manual expense entry, categorisation, and budgeting on Android only. Bank-account syncing, multi-currency, and shared budgets are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working native Android app with budgeting and category charts.
2. A usability and entry-speed evaluation report.

Timeline:
Semester one: data model and entry/summary screens. Semester two: budgets, alerts, and testing.

Title:
An IoT Sensor Network for Factory Machine Condition Monitoring

Problem Statement:
Small manufacturers often run machines until they fail because they lack affordable condition monitoring. Unplanned downtime is costly. A low-cost IoT sensor network that streams vibration and temperature data to a dashboard could give early warning of abnormal behaviour without an expensive industrial system.

Objectives:
1. To build a sensor node that measures vibration and temperature on a machine.
2. To stream readings to a server and dashboard over Wi-Fi.
3. To flag readings that exceed learned normal thresholds and evaluate the alerts.

Methodology:
Nodes will use an ESP32 with an accelerometer (MPU-6050) and a temperature sensor, publishing readings via MQTT to a Raspberry Pi broker. Data will be stored in InfluxDB and visualised in Grafana. Simple statistical thresholds (mean plus standard deviations from a baseline window) will trigger alerts. The setup will be validated on a small motor with induced imbalance.

Scope:
The project covers two sensor node prototypes, data collection, dashboarding, and threshold alerts. Predictive remaining-life modelling and plant-wide deployment are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working IoT monitoring prototype with a live dashboard.
2. A short evaluation of alert accuracy on induced fault conditions.

Timeline:
Semester one: hardware and data pipeline. Semester two: alerting, testing, and write-up.

Title:
A Smart-Home Automation Hub with Public-Safety Hazard Detection

Problem Statement:
Consumer smart-home hubs focus on convenience and rarely coordinate safety responses across devices. When a hazard such as smoke, a gas leak, or a water leak occurs, sensors often act in isolation, and residents or neighbours may not be alerted in time. There is room for a local-first hub that fuses multiple safety sensors and escalates alerts reliably, even when cloud connectivity is down.

Objectives:
1. To design a local hub that ingests smoke, gas, water, and motion sensor events over a common protocol.
2. To implement rule-based automation that escalates hazards (local alarm, app push, and SMS to a chosen contact).
3. To evaluate detection latency, escalation reliability, and behaviour during simulated network outages.

Methodology:
The hub will run on a Raspberry Pi using Home Assistant with Zigbee sensors via a Zigbee2MQTT bridge. Automation rules will be authored in YAML and tested against scripted hazard scenarios. SMS escalation will use a Twilio fallback, and the system will be designed to run automations locally without internet. Evaluation will measure end-to-end alert latency and the success rate of escalations across normal and offline conditions, compared against a single-sensor baseline.

Scope:
The project covers a single-home setup with four sensor types and a defined escalation chain. Whole-building systems, regulatory certification, and integration with municipal emergency services are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working local-first safety hub with multi-sensor hazard escalation.
2. An evaluation of latency and reliability under normal and offline conditions.

Timeline:
Semester one: hub setup, sensor integration, and automation rules. Semester two: offline resilience, escalation, evaluation, and documentation.

Title:
Edge-Computing Anomaly Detection for Household Energy Meters

Problem Statement:
Cloud-only energy analytics introduce latency, recurring costs, and privacy concerns because raw consumption data leaves the home. For households wanting early warning of unusual energy use (a faulty appliance or a forgotten high-draw device), processing data at the edge is attractive but constrained by limited compute. The challenge is running useful anomaly detection on a low-power device while keeping data local.

Objectives:
1. To deploy a lightweight anomaly-detection model on an edge device reading a smart energy meter.
2. To detect abnormal consumption patterns locally and notify the user without sending raw data to the cloud.
3. To evaluate detection quality and on-device latency and resource use against a cloud baseline.

Methodology:
An ESP32/Raspberry Pi class device will read power data via a CT-clamp sensor. A compact model (autoencoder or isolation forest) will be trained offline on collected household traces, then converted with TensorFlow Lite for on-device inference. Detection quality will be measured with precision/recall on labelled anomaly events injected into the data. Latency, memory, and CPU use will be profiled and compared to an equivalent cloud-hosted model.

Scope:
The work targets single-household, single-meter monitoring with edge inference. Multi-home federated training, billing integration, and grid-level analytics are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An edge device performing local energy-anomaly detection with user alerts.
2. A comparative evaluation of accuracy, latency, and resource use versus a cloud baseline.

Timeline:
Semester one: data capture, model training, edge deployment. Semester two: anomaly injection tests, profiling, and evaluation.

Title:
A Cloud-Native Microservices Platform for Small-Business Order Management

Problem Statement:
Small businesses outgrowing spreadsheets often adopt monolithic order tools that are hard to scale and update. A cloud-native microservices design could let them scale individual functions (catalogue, orders, payments) independently and deploy changes safely, but it is unclear how much operational overhead this adds for a small team. This project builds and evaluates such a platform at small-business scale.

Objectives:
1. To design an order-management system as independently deployable microservices (catalogue, orders, inventory, notifications).
2. To containerise and orchestrate the services with health checks, service discovery, and an API gateway.
3. To evaluate scalability, fault isolation, and deployment effort versus an equivalent monolith.

Methodology:
Services will be built with Spring Boot, communicating via REST and an event bus (RabbitMQ), and packaged as Docker containers orchestrated on Kubernetes (k3s). An API gateway will handle routing and auth, and Prometheus/Grafana will collect metrics. Load tests with k6 will measure latency and throughput under increasing traffic, and a fault-injection test will verify that one failing service does not take down others. A small monolith version will serve as a comparison baseline.

Scope:
The platform covers four core services for a single small-business tenant. Multi-tenancy, real payment-gateway certification, and production-grade autoscaling tuning are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working containerised microservices platform with monitoring.
2. A comparative report on scalability, fault isolation, and deployment effort.

Timeline:
Semester one: service design, containerisation, orchestration. Semester two: monitoring, load and fault testing, evaluation.

Title:
A CI/CD Pipeline for Reproducible Agricultural Data-Science Models

Problem Statement:
Agricultural data teams often retrain yield and disease models by hand, leading to inconsistent results and slow, error-prone deployment. DevOps practices common in software are rarely applied to these data-science workflows. This project builds a CI/CD pipeline that automatically tests, builds, and deploys an agriculture model so updates are reproducible and traceable.

Objectives:
1. To automate testing, packaging, and deployment of a crop-yield model via a CI/CD pipeline.
2. To version data, code, and models so any deployment can be reproduced.
3. To evaluate deployment time, failure recovery, and reproducibility against a manual workflow.

Methodology:
The pipeline will use GitHub Actions to run unit and data-validation tests, build a Docker image of the model service, and deploy to a staging environment on each push. Data and model versioning will use DVC, and model performance gates (a minimum validation score) will block bad deployments. Infrastructure will be described with Docker Compose. Metrics collected will include pipeline duration, rollback time after an injected failing build, and whether a tagged release reproduces identical predictions.

Scope:
The project covers one model service with automated test, build, deploy, and rollback. Multi-cloud deployment, GPU training clusters, and full feature-store tooling are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working CI/CD pipeline that deploys a versioned agriculture model.
2. A comparison of deployment time, recovery, and reproducibility versus manual operation.

Timeline:
Semester one: test automation and build/deploy stages. Semester two: versioning, gates, rollback, and evaluation.

Title:
A Big-Data Pipeline for Public-Transport Demand Analytics

Problem Statement:
Transit agencies collect large volumes of ticketing and vehicle-location data but often analyse only small samples in spreadsheets, missing demand patterns that could improve scheduling. Building a scalable pipeline to ingest, process, and aggregate this data is non-trivial. This project develops a batch-and-streaming pipeline that turns raw transit feeds into demand insights for a chosen city's bus network.

Objectives:
1. To ingest historical and near-real-time transit data into a scalable processing pipeline.
2. To compute demand metrics (boardings per route, peak-hour load, dwell patterns) and store them for querying.
3. To evaluate pipeline throughput, latency, and the usefulness of the resulting demand metrics.

Methodology:
Batch processing of historical GTFS and ticketing data will use Apache Spark, while a streaming path using Kafka and Spark Structured Streaming will handle live vehicle-position feeds. Processed metrics will land in a columnar store (Parquet on object storage) and be served to a query/dashboard layer. The pipeline will run in Docker containers. Evaluation will measure records-per-second throughput, end-to-end streaming latency, and will validate computed demand against a manually aggregated sample.

Scope:
The pipeline targets one city's bus network with a defined set of demand metrics. Fare-policy modelling, multi-modal integration, and predictive demand forecasting are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working batch-and-streaming pipeline producing queryable demand metrics.
2. An evaluation of throughput, latency, and metric accuracy against a manual baseline.

Timeline:
Semester one: ingestion and batch processing. Semester two: streaming path, serving layer, and evaluation.

Title:
A Decision-Support Business-Intelligence Dashboard for Campus Sustainability with Driver Attribution

Problem Statement:
Universities publish annual sustainability figures but rarely give facilities staff an operational tool to see why electricity, water, and waste metrics move week to week, so interventions are reactive. Existing BI dashboards visualise totals without attributing change to drivers (weather, occupancy, building schedules), leaving staff unable to prioritise actions. This project builds a decision-support dashboard that not only reports campus sustainability KPIs but attributes period-over-period changes to specific drivers and flags anomalous buildings.

Objectives:
1. To model and load two years of campus electricity, water, and waste data into a star-schema warehouse with conformed time, building, and weather dimensions.
2. To compute KPIs (intensity per m2, per-occupant use) and decompose period-over-period change into weather-, occupancy-, and baseline-driver contributions using a regression-based attribution.
3. To deliver an interactive dashboard with anomaly flags and to evaluate attribution accuracy and decision usefulness with facilities staff.

Methodology:
Data from meters, the timetable system, and a public weather API will be cleaned and loaded via a dbt/Python ETL into a PostgreSQL star schema. Driver attribution will use degree-day-adjusted regression per building, with the change decomposition validated against held-out months (target MAPE below 10 percent) and compared to a naive year-on-year baseline. Anomaly flags use seasonal-residual thresholds. The dashboard will be built in a BI tool (Apache Superset) and evaluated through task-based sessions with facilities staff using a SUS questionnaire and decision-time measurement, plus a backtest of whether flagged anomalies matched logged faults.

Scope:
The project covers electricity, water, and waste for ten instrumented buildings on one campus over a two-year window. Carbon scope-3 accounting, real-time control of building systems, and financial budgeting modules are explicitly excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A populated warehouse and interactive BI dashboard with KPI, attribution, and anomaly views.
2. A validated attribution method (reported MAPE versus baseline) and a usability/decision-usefulness evaluation with staff.

Timeline:
Weeks 1-4 data modelling and ETL; weeks 5-9 KPI and attribution modelling with validation; weeks 10-13 dashboard and anomaly flags; weeks 14-18 staff evaluation and write-up.

Title:
Probabilistic Time-Series Forecasting of Warehouse Outbound Demand for Logistics Staffing

Problem Statement:
Third-party logistics warehouses staff pickers based on rough manual demand guesses, causing both overstaffing costs and missed cutoffs during surges. Point-forecast models give a single number that ignores uncertainty, so planners cannot size buffer staff for risk. This project develops a probabilistic forecasting approach that predicts daily and hourly outbound order volume with calibrated prediction intervals to support risk-aware staffing decisions.

Objectives:
1. To build daily and intraday forecasting models of outbound order volume that output calibrated prediction intervals, not just point estimates.
2. To incorporate calendar, promotion, and lag features and benchmark several model families under a unified backtesting protocol.
3. To evaluate forecast accuracy, interval calibration, and the staffing-cost impact versus the current manual method.

Methodology:
Eighteen months of order data will be cleaned and split with rolling-origin (time-series) cross-validation to prevent leakage. Baselines (seasonal-naive, ETS, SARIMA) will be compared against gradient-boosted quantile regression (LightGBM) and a global model (Prophet/N-BEATS), all evaluated on MAE, MASE, pinball loss, and prediction-interval coverage. Feature importance and ablations will isolate the value of promotion and calendar features. A simple staffing simulator will translate forecasts and intervals into picker counts and compute expected cost (overstaffing plus penalty for missed cutoffs) against the historical manual plan. Risks such as data gaps and regime changes are addressed with documented imputation and a holdout on the most recent quarter.

Scope:
The study covers outbound demand forecasting for one warehouse with one product mix over the available 18-month window. Inbound forecasting, route optimisation, and live integration with the warehouse management system are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A benchmarked probabilistic forecasting model with calibrated intervals and reproducible backtests.
2. A staffing-cost evaluation quantifying savings versus the current manual approach.

Timeline:
Weeks 1-3 data preparation and CV harness; weeks 4-9 baseline and probabilistic model development; weeks 10-13 calibration and staffing simulation; weeks 14-18 evaluation, ablations, and write-up.

Title:
Blockchain for Public Safety

Problem Statement:
Public safety is very important and the police need better technology. Blockchain is a new trend that can help with safety problems in the city.

Objectives:
1. Make a blockchain system
2. Help public safety
3. Use smart contracts

Methodology:
I will use blockchain and smart contracts to do public safety. Some coding will be done and I will research online about it.

Scope:
For all police and the public everywhere.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A safer city
2. A working blockchain

Title:
AR App for Energy

Problem Statement:
Energy is wasted a lot and people do not know how much they use. An AR app would be cool and help people see energy.

Objectives:
1. Build an AR app
2. Show energy data
3. Save energy

Methodology:
Augmented reality will be used to make an app for energy. I will look at some tutorials and build it on the phone.

Scope:
Everyone who uses energy in their house and offices too.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An AR app
2. Less energy wasted

Title:
VR Training for Small Business

Problem Statement:
Small businesses have many problems with training their workers. VR is the future and can train people in a virtual world which is better than normal training.

Objectives:
1. Create a VR training
2. Train workers
3. Help small business

Methodology:
I will make a VR simulation using a headset so workers can train. Research will be done and then I build the simulation.

Scope:
Any small business that wants to train staff.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A VR training simulation
2. Better trained workers

Title:
A 2D Farming Game for Agriculture Awareness

Problem Statement:
Many young people do not understand how farming works or the challenges farmers face. A simple 2D game could teach the basics of crop planting and harvesting in a fun way, but few free games focus on real agricultural concepts.

Objectives:
1. Develop a 2D farming simulation game using Unity.
2. Teach players about crop cycles and weather effects.
3. Test whether players learn farming basics after playing.

Methodology:
The game will be built in Unity with C#. Players plant crops, manage water, and deal with seasons. Sprites will be drawn or taken from free asset packs. A short quiz before and after play will check what players learned.

Scope:
The game covers three crops and basic weather. It is a single-player desktop game and does not include multiplayer or real farm data.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A playable 2D farming game.
2. Some evidence that players learn farming basics.

Timeline:
Around 4 months total, split between design, building, and testing.

Title:
Serious Game for Road Safety Education in Transportation

Problem Statement:
Road accidents are common among new drivers who lack practical hazard awareness. Traditional classroom lessons are boring and students forget the rules. A serious game could make learning road safety more engaging, but most existing apps are just quizzes.

Objectives:
1. Design a serious game teaching road safety rules and hazard spotting.
2. Include scenarios like crossings, traffic lights, and bad weather driving.
3. Measure player knowledge improvement after playing.

Methodology:
The game will be developed in Unity with simple 2.5D scenes. Players drive through scenarios and make decisions; correct choices earn points. A pre-test and post-test questionnaire will measure learning gains across about 20 student testers.

Scope:
The game focuses on basic road rules for new drivers in an urban setting. It excludes highway driving, vehicle physics realism, and licensing exam content.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working serious game with at least five scenarios.
2. Test results comparing knowledge before and after play.

Timeline:
Five months covering design, development, and a small user study.

Title:
A Web System for Tracking Hospital Resource Sustainability

Problem Statement:
Hospitals consume large amounts of energy, water, and disposable supplies, but small clinics rarely track this. Without data, clinics cannot find waste or report on sustainability. A simple informatics dashboard could help clinic managers monitor usage.

Objectives:
1. Build a web dashboard for recording clinic resource usage.
2. Show trends in energy, water, and supply consumption over time.
3. Flag months where usage is unusually high.

Methodology:
The system will be a web application built with React and a Node.js backend storing data in MySQL. Clinic staff enter monthly readings, and the dashboard shows charts. A simple threshold rule flags high-usage months. The tool will be demonstrated with sample data from one clinic.

Scope:
The system handles manual data entry for one small clinic and basic charts. It excludes automated meter integration and predictive forecasting.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working resource-tracking dashboard.
2. Example reports showing usage trends.

Timeline:
About five months including requirements, development, and demonstration.

Title:
Telemedicine Platform for Remote Logistics Workers

Problem Statement:
Logistics workers like long-haul drivers often cannot reach clinics during working hours, so minor health issues go untreated. A telemedicine platform could let them consult a doctor online, but general platforms do not consider their irregular schedules.

Objectives:
1. Develop a web-based telemedicine platform for booking and video consultations.
2. Let workers upload symptoms and view doctor notes.
3. Allow scheduling that fits shift-based work hours.

Methodology:
The platform will use React for the frontend and a Spring Boot backend with MySQL. Video calls will use a third-party API such as Jitsi. Appointments, notes, and prescriptions are stored in the database. The system will be tested with a few mock users acting as drivers and doctors.

Scope:
The project covers appointment booking, video consultation, and basic records for one company's drivers. It excludes payment processing, insurance, and medical device integration.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A functional telemedicine web platform.
2. A demonstration of a full consultation flow.

Timeline:
Roughly five months across analysis, build, and testing phases.

Title:
An E-Learning System for Citizen Training on E-Government Services

Problem Statement:
Many citizens struggle to use online government services such as tax filing and permit applications, leading to errors and call-centre load. There is no dedicated training platform that walks citizens through these services interactively. This project builds an e-learning system with guided lessons and practice simulations for common e-government tasks.

Objectives:
1. Develop an e-learning platform with modular courses on three e-government services.
2. Provide interactive simulations that mimic real service portals without affecting live data.
3. Track learner progress and quiz scores to measure completion and accuracy.

Methodology:
The platform uses React, Spring Boot, and MySQL. Courses are structured as lessons, simulations, and quizzes. Simulations are sandboxed HTML mockups of portals. Progress and scores are stored per user. The system will be evaluated through a usability test with around 15 participants using a System Usability Scale survey, plus pre/post quiz scores to measure learning gain.

Scope:
The system covers three e-government services with guided tutorials and quizzes for desktop browsers. It excludes integration with real government APIs, mobile apps, and multilingual content beyond English.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working e-learning platform with three courses and simulations.
2. Usability and learning-gain results from the user test.

Timeline:
Six months: month 1 requirements, months 2-4 development, month 5 testing, month 6 evaluation and write-up.

Title:
A Micro-Payment System for School Fee and Activity Collection

Problem Statement:
Schools collect many small payments for fees, trips, and meals, often in cash, which is hard to track and prone to loss. Existing payment apps charge high fees per transaction, making micro-payments costly. This project develops a fintech payment system tailored to schools that batches small payments to reduce cost.

Objectives:
1. Build a web and mobile-friendly payment system for parents to pay school charges.
2. Implement a wallet model that batches micro-payments before settlement.
3. Provide administrators a dashboard for reconciliation and reporting.

Methodology:
The system uses React and Spring Boot with MySQL, integrating a sandbox payment gateway such as Stripe test mode. Parents top up a wallet and pay charges; the system batches transactions and reconciles them in the admin dashboard. Evaluation compares simulated transaction-fee totals between per-charge and batched models, and gathers feedback from five mock administrators.

Scope:
The project covers wallet top-up, charge payment, batching, and reconciliation in a sandbox environment for one school. It excludes real money settlement, refunds processing, and integration with national banking systems.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working sandbox payment system with batching.
2. A cost comparison showing fee savings from batching.

Timeline:
Six months across requirements, development, integration, and evaluation.

Title:
Fraud Detection for Retail Return Abuse

Problem Statement:
Retailers lose revenue to return fraud, where customers exploit lenient return policies through wardrobing or receipt manipulation. Manual review does not scale, and simple rules miss patterns. This project builds a machine-learning model to flag suspicious return transactions for human review.

Objectives:
1. Build a labelled dataset of retail return transactions with fraud indicators.
2. Train and compare classifiers to detect likely fraudulent returns.
3. Provide a dashboard that ranks flagged returns by risk score.

Methodology:
Using a public retail transactions dataset augmented with synthetic fraud labels, features such as return frequency, time since purchase, and refund amount will be engineered. Logistic regression, random forest, and gradient boosting will be trained and compared using precision, recall, and F1, with an 80/20 train-test split and 5-fold cross-validation. The best model feeds a Flask dashboard listing high-risk returns.

Scope:
The project covers offline model training and a review dashboard for one synthetic retail dataset. It excludes real-time POS integration, image-based receipt analysis, and deployment at scale.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained fraud-detection model with reported metrics.
2. A dashboard ranking returns by fraud risk.

Timeline:
Six months: data prep, modelling, dashboard, and evaluation.

Title:
A Recommendation Engine for a Smart-City Local Marketplace

Problem Statement:
Smart-city initiatives promote local commerce, but residents browsing a city marketplace face too many listings and weak discovery. Generic e-commerce recommenders ignore proximity and local availability. This project builds a recommendation engine that blends user preference with location to surface nearby relevant products.

Objectives:
1. Develop a recommendation engine combining collaborative filtering with location proximity.
2. Integrate it into a simple marketplace web app for browsing local listings.
3. Evaluate recommendation quality against a popularity baseline.

Methodology:
The system uses item-based collaborative filtering computed from a synthetic ratings dataset, then re-ranks candidates by distance to the user. The marketplace is a React and Spring Boot app with MySQL. Evaluation uses offline metrics precision@10 and recall@10 on held-out interactions, comparing the hybrid recommender to a popularity baseline, plus a small user survey on perceived relevance.

Scope:
The project covers recommendation logic and a basic marketplace UI using synthetic data for one city. It excludes real seller onboarding, payments, and live geolocation tracking.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working hybrid recommendation engine in a marketplace app.
2. Evaluation results comparing the recommender to the baseline.

Timeline:
Six months across data, engine development, integration, and evaluation.

Title:
A Conversational Agent for Tourist Trip Planning

Problem Statement:
Tourists planning a trip search across many sites for attractions, hours, and routes, which is time-consuming and fragmented. Static FAQ pages cannot answer specific itinerary questions. This project develops a chatbot that answers tourism questions and suggests day plans for a chosen city.

Objectives:
1. Build a chatbot that answers attraction, opening-hour, and transport questions.
2. Generate a simple day itinerary based on user interests and time.
3. Evaluate answer accuracy and user satisfaction.

Methodology:
The chatbot uses intent classification over a curated knowledge base of attractions stored as structured data, with a retrieval step to fetch relevant entries and a templated response generator. It is built in Python with Flask and a React chat UI. Evaluation measures intent-classification accuracy on a labelled test set and collects satisfaction ratings from about 12 testers planning a sample trip.

Scope:
The chatbot covers one city's attractions and basic itinerary suggestions in English. It excludes real-time booking, live transit data, and multi-city trips.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working tourism chatbot with itinerary suggestions.
2. Accuracy and satisfaction results from the evaluation.

Timeline:
Six months: knowledge base build, chatbot development, UI, and evaluation.

Title:
A Knowledge-Graph Search Tool for Social-Media Topic Exploration

Problem Statement:
Researchers studying social-media discussions struggle to see how topics, hashtags, and users connect, because keyword search returns flat result lists. A knowledge graph could reveal relationships and let users explore connected entities. This project builds a search tool over a knowledge graph extracted from social-media posts.

Objectives:
1. Build a knowledge graph linking posts, hashtags, users, and topics from a dataset.
2. Provide graph-based search and visualisation of connected entities.
3. Evaluate retrieval relevance against keyword search.

Methodology:
A public social-media dataset will be processed to extract entities and relations using rule-based and NER methods, stored in Neo4j. A React frontend queries the graph and visualises neighbourhoods. Evaluation compares relevance of graph-expanded results versus keyword search on a set of test queries using precision@k judged by manual relevance labels.

Scope:
The tool covers one social-media dataset with entity extraction, graph search, and visualisation. It excludes real-time streaming ingestion, sentiment analysis, and account-level privacy handling beyond anonymised data.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working knowledge-graph search and visualisation tool.
2. A relevance comparison against keyword search.

Timeline:
Six months across extraction, graph build, UI, and evaluation.

Title:
Automated Segmentation of Skin Lesions in Dermoscopy Images

Problem Statement:
Accurate delineation of skin-lesion boundaries supports early melanoma diagnosis, but manual segmentation is slow and varies between clinicians. Existing tools often underperform on lesions with low contrast or hair occlusion. This project develops and evaluates a deep-learning segmentation model that is robust to these artefacts, supporting downstream clinical analysis.

Objectives:
1. Train a U-Net-based model to segment skin lesions from dermoscopy images.
2. Improve robustness to hair and low-contrast cases via targeted augmentation.
3. Benchmark against a baseline U-Net using standard segmentation metrics.

Methodology:
The ISIC 2018 segmentation dataset will be used with an 80/10/10 train/validation/test split. A U-Net with a pretrained encoder is trained with Dice plus binary cross-entropy loss, using augmentations including simulated hair, rotation, and contrast jitter. Performance is measured by Dice coefficient, IoU, and Hausdorff distance, compared against a vanilla U-Net baseline. Five-fold cross-validation estimates variance; ablations isolate the augmentation contribution.

Scope:
The project covers binary lesion-versus-skin segmentation on dermoscopy images only. It excludes multi-class diagnosis, clinical deployment, and non-dermoscopy modalities such as histopathology.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained segmentation model with reported Dice, IoU, and Hausdorff scores.
2. An ablation showing the augmentation effect on hair and low-contrast cases.

Timeline:
Month 1 data and baseline, months 2-4 model and augmentation, month 5 evaluation, month 6 write-up.

Title:
Object Detection for Cheque and Form Field Extraction in Finance

Problem Statement:
Banks process large volumes of scanned cheques and forms where key fields such as amount boxes, signatures, and date fields must be located before reading. Manual templating is brittle across layouts. This project develops an object-detection model that locates structured fields on financial documents to support automated processing.

Objectives:
1. Train an object-detection model to localise key fields on scanned financial forms.
2. Handle layout variation across multiple form templates.
3. Compare detection accuracy against a template-matching baseline.

Methodology:
A dataset of scanned forms will be annotated with bounding boxes for field classes. A YOLOv8 model is fine-tuned on an 80/20 split with augmentation for rotation, blur, and brightness to mimic scan noise. Performance is reported as mAP@0.5 and mAP@0.5:0.95 per class, compared to a template-matching baseline. Error analysis examines failures on skewed and low-quality scans.

Scope:
The project covers field localisation on a fixed set of form types and outputs bounding boxes. It excludes optical character recognition of field contents, fraud detection, and live banking integration.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained detector with per-class mAP results.
2. A comparison against template matching plus error analysis.

Timeline:
Six months: annotation, training, baseline comparison, and evaluation.

Title:
Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis of Manufacturing Equipment Reviews

Problem Statement:
Manufacturers buying industrial equipment rely on reviews and forum posts, but overall ratings hide whether issues concern reliability, support, or cost. Document-level sentiment is too coarse for purchasing decisions. This project develops an aspect-based sentiment-analysis system that scores sentiment per equipment aspect.

Objectives:
1. Build an aspect-based sentiment model identifying aspects and their polarity in equipment reviews.
2. Cover aspects such as reliability, maintenance, support, and price.
3. Evaluate against a document-level sentiment baseline.

Methodology:
A dataset of equipment reviews will be annotated for aspect terms and polarity. A fine-tuned BERT model performs aspect-term extraction and aspect-sentiment classification. Training uses an 80/10/10 split with class-weighted loss for imbalance. Metrics are F1 for aspect extraction and macro-F1 for polarity, compared to a document-level baseline and a lexicon method. Error analysis covers mixed-sentiment and negation cases.

Scope:
The project covers English text reviews and four predefined aspects. It excludes multilingual reviews, sarcasm detection, and integration into procurement software.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained aspect-based sentiment model with F1 results per aspect.
2. A comparison against document-level and lexicon baselines.

Timeline:
Six months across annotation, modelling, evaluation, and reporting.

Title:
Learned Cost Estimation for Query Optimization in Public-Safety Databases

Problem Statement:
Public-safety dispatch systems run analytical queries over large incident databases, where poor query plans cause slow responses during emergencies. Traditional optimizers rely on inaccurate cardinality estimates for complex joins. This project explores a learned cardinality estimator to improve plan selection for these workloads.

Objectives:
1. Build a learned cardinality estimator for multi-join queries over an incident schema.
2. Integrate estimates into plan selection and measure query latency impact.
3. Compare against the database's default optimizer estimates.

Methodology:
Using a synthetic incident-records database generated to mimic public-safety data, a workload of join queries is created with true cardinalities collected via execution. A gradient-boosted model predicts cardinality from query features. Predicted estimates are injected to guide plan choice. Evaluation measures q-error of estimates and end-to-end latency on a held-out query set, compared to PostgreSQL's native estimator, across cold and warm caches.

Scope:
The project covers select-project-join queries on one synthetic schema and read-only workloads. It excludes updates, distributed databases, and full optimizer replacement.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A learned estimator with reported q-error improvements.
2. Latency comparison against the native optimizer.

Timeline:
Six months: workload generation, model training, integration, and evaluation.

Title:
Facial-Recognition Attendance for Energy-Sector Field Sites

Problem Statement:
Energy companies operate remote field sites where worker attendance is logged manually, causing errors and slow safety roll-calls during incidents. Card systems fail when badges are lost or shared. This project develops a facial-recognition attendance system suited to outdoor, variable-lighting conditions at field sites.

Objectives:
1. Build a facial-recognition attendance system that records check-in and check-out.
2. Maintain accuracy under varied lighting and partial occlusion such as helmets.
3. Evaluate recognition accuracy and speed against a controlled baseline.

Methodology:
Face detection uses MTCNN and recognition uses FaceNet embeddings with a cosine-similarity threshold against an enrolled gallery. A small dataset is collected under indoor and simulated outdoor lighting with helmet occlusion. Evaluation reports true-accept and false-accept rates, rank-1 accuracy, and per-frame latency, comparing performance across lighting conditions. Liveness via a simple blink check mitigates photo spoofing.

Scope:
The project covers enrolment, recognition, and attendance logging for a small enrolled group as a prototype. It excludes large-scale identity databases, payroll integration, and full anti-spoofing hardware.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working attendance prototype with logged check-ins.
2. Accuracy and latency results across lighting conditions.

Timeline:
Six months across data collection, system build, and evaluation.

Title:
A Robust OCR Pipeline for Small-Business Invoice and Receipt Processing

Problem Statement:
Small businesses spend significant time manually keying data from supplier invoices and receipts, which are noisy, varied in layout, and often photographed on phones. General OCR engines read text but do not reliably extract structured fields (vendor, date, line items, total) across heterogeneous, low-quality documents. This project develops and rigorously evaluates an OCR-plus-extraction pipeline targeting exactly this small-business setting, with explicit attention to degraded images and layout variation.

Objectives:
1. Build a pipeline that detects, recognises, and extracts six key fields from invoices and receipts with field-level F1 above 0.85 on a held-out test set.
2. Quantify robustness to photo degradations (blur, skew, low light) via controlled perturbation experiments.
3. Benchmark the layout-aware extractor against a baseline of Tesseract plus regex rules.

Methodology:
The public SROIE and CORD receipt datasets supply annotated fields, split 70/15/15. Text detection uses a pretrained CRAFT/EasyOCR stage; structured extraction uses a fine-tuned LayoutLMv3 model consuming text, position, and image features. Training uses class-weighted cross-entropy with early stopping; hyperparameters are selected on validation. Evaluation reports field-level precision, recall, and F1, plus end-to-end document accuracy, against the Tesseract+regex baseline, with 5-fold cross-validation for variance. A perturbation suite (Gaussian blur, rotation, brightness) measures degradation curves, and an ablation removes layout features to isolate their contribution. Risks (small annotated data, GPU limits) are mitigated with augmentation and gradient accumulation.

Scope:
The pipeline targets English invoices and receipts and the six listed fields, exported as JSON. Excluded: handwritten documents, non-Latin scripts, multi-page contracts, accounting-software integration, and live deployment hardening.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained extraction pipeline meeting the field-level F1 target, with full metric reporting.
2. Robustness degradation curves and an ablation quantifying the layout-feature contribution versus the baseline.

Timeline:
Month 1 data and baseline; months 2-3 model and training; month 4 perturbation and ablation studies; month 5 evaluation and error analysis; month 6 documentation and write-up.

Title:
Anomaly Detection in Agricultural Wireless Sensor Networks for Early Crop-Stress Warning

Problem Statement:
Farms deploy wireless sensor networks measuring soil moisture, temperature, and humidity, but raw streams contain faulty-node readings and miss early crop-stress onset, so farmers react too late. Simple threshold alarms produce false alerts and ignore spatial-temporal correlations between nodes. This project develops and evaluates a spatio-temporal anomaly-detection method that separates sensor faults from genuine crop-stress events, giving earlier, more reliable warnings.

Objectives:
1. Build a model that flags crop-stress anomalies from multivariate sensor streams with recall above 0.85 at a controlled false-alarm rate.
2. Distinguish sensor-fault anomalies from environmental-stress anomalies.
3. Benchmark against threshold and univariate baselines using labelled events.

Methodology:
The public Intel/agricultural sensor datasets plus a synthetic stress-injection generator provide labelled normal, fault, and stress windows, split temporally to avoid leakage. An LSTM autoencoder models normal spatio-temporal patterns; reconstruction error drives anomaly scoring, with a secondary classifier separating fault from stress using cross-node consistency features. Training uses early stopping on a validation period; thresholds are set on validation to fix the false-alarm rate. Evaluation reports precision, recall, F1, and detection latency (lead time before visible stress), compared to fixed-threshold and ARIMA baselines, with sensitivity analysis over window length and an ablation on the cross-node features. Risks include limited real stress labels, mitigated by synthetic injection and domain-informed validation.

Scope:
The project covers offline analysis of three sensor modalities and the two anomaly types, outputting alerts with lead-time estimates. Excluded: on-device deployment, actuator/irrigation control, satellite imagery fusion, and live field trials.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained spatio-temporal detector meeting the recall target with reported metrics and detection latency.
2. A fault-versus-stress separation result and ablation versus the baselines.

Timeline:
Month 1 data and labelling; months 2-3 modelling; month 4 fault/stress separation; month 5 evaluation and sensitivity analysis; month 6 write-up.

Title:
A Recommender System for Community Safety Tips

Problem Statement:
Residents in a neighbourhood receive generic safety advice that does not match their local risks. A personalised recommender could surface safety tips that are more relevant to each user based on their area and past interactions, but most local safety apps just show the same list to everyone.

2. To use collaborative filtering on user interaction data.
3. To evaluate whether recommendations are relevant.

Methodology:
The project will collect ratings of safety tips from users and apply collaborative filtering. I plan to use Python with the Surprise library to build the model and a simple web front end to show recommendations. Accuracy will be checked by looking at how users rate the suggestions.

Scope:
The system focuses on one type of community safety content and a small group of test users. It will not handle emergency dispatch.
