Title:
Voice Commands for Energy Meter Reading

Problem Statement:
Field workers who read energy meters often have their hands busy and typing readings into a phone is slow. A speech recognition feature could let them speak readings aloud, but existing apps rely on manual entry and few support hands-free input in noisy environments.

Objectives:
1. To add speech recognition for entering meter readings by voice.
2. To convert spoken numbers into structured data.
3. To test recognition accuracy in field-like conditions.

Methodology:

Scope:
The prototype covers reading numeric values only, in English, for a single utility company format. It excludes full conversational control.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A voice-input prototype for meter readings.
2. An accuracy report comparing voice and manual entry.

Two semesters covering build and field testing.

Title:
Intrusion Detection for a Small Business Network

Problem Statement:
Small businesses rarely afford enterprise security monitoring, so suspicious network traffic often goes unnoticed until damage is done. A lightweight intrusion detection setup could flag common attacks, yet most affordable tools require expertise these owners do not have.

Objectives:
1. To build a network intrusion detection prototype for a small office.
2. To train a classifier that distinguishes normal from malicious traffic.
3. To present alerts in a simple dashboard.

Methodology:
I will use the NSL-KDD dataset to train a Random Forest classifier in Python with scikit-learn, then test it on held-out traffic. Flagged events will be shown in a basic web dashboard. Accuracy and false positive rate will be reported.

Scope:
The work targets detecting a few common attack categories on captured traffic. It does not include automatic blocking or live deployment on a production network.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained intrusion detection classifier.
2. A dashboard prototype showing alerts.

Timeline:
Phased over two semesters: data, model, dashboard, evaluation.

Title:
Security Testing for an Agriculture Marketplace Website

Problem Statement:
Online marketplaces that connect farmers and buyers handle payments and personal data but small projects rarely test for web vulnerabilities. This leaves them exposed to attacks like SQL injection and cross-site scripting, and there is little awareness of secure coding among such platforms.

Objectives:
1. To assess common web vulnerabilities in an agriculture marketplace app.
2. To apply fixes following OWASP guidelines.
3. To show before-and-after security improvements.

Methodology:
I will build a sample marketplace in PHP and test it using OWASP ZAP and manual checks against the OWASP Top 10. After identifying issues I will patch them and re-scan to confirm the fixes. Results will be documented in a comparison table.

Scope:
The project covers a demo marketplace and a subset of the OWASP Top 10. It excludes penetration testing of live third-party services.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A vulnerability assessment report.
2. A hardened version of the demo app.

Timeline:
Two semesters from build to re-testing.

Title:
Static and Dynamic Analysis of Android Malware Targeting Ride-Hailing Apps

Problem Statement:
Transportation apps such as ride-hailing clients store location and payment data, making them attractive targets for repackaged malicious clones. Users struggle to tell a tampered app from a legitimate one, and there is limited public analysis of how such malware behaves on the Android platform.

Objectives:
1. To collect and analyse a sample set of malicious Android transport-app variants using static analysis.
2. To observe runtime behaviour through dynamic analysis in a sandbox.
3. To summarise indicators that distinguish malicious clones from legitimate apps.

Methodology:
Samples will be drawn from public repositories such as AndroZoo and decompiled with JADX and Apktool for static inspection of permissions and API calls. Dynamic behaviour will be captured in an Android emulator with Frida and network logging. Findings will be organised into a small indicator catalogue, validated against a few known-clean apps.

Scope:
The study focuses on Android transport-related samples and behavioural indicators, not automated detection at scale or iOS. A modest sample set is used due to time limits.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An analysis report on malicious transport-app behaviour.
2. A catalogue of distinguishing indicators.

Timeline:
Semester 1 setup and static analysis; Semester 2 dynamic analysis and write-up.

Title:
A Responsive Web Platform for Tracking Household Sustainability Habits

Problem Statement:
Households that want to reduce waste and energy use lack a simple place to record habits and see progress over time. Existing apps are often paywalled or device-specific, so a responsive web platform that works across phones and laptops could lower the barrier to sustainable behaviour change.

Objectives:

2. To provide progress visualisations and weekly goals.
3. To evaluate usability with a small group of users.

Methodology:

The system supports manual habit logging and basic visual feedback for individual users. It excludes automatic IoT meter integration and social networking features.

Title:
A Progressive Web App for Last-Mile Delivery Drivers

Problem Statement:

A progressive web app could give drivers route lists and proof-of-delivery capture that keep working offline and sync when signal returns, but many small logistics firms still rely on paper or fragile web forms.

Objectives:
1. To build a progressive web app that shows assigned deliveries and routes.
2. To support offline data capture with background sync.
3. To evaluate offline reliability and load performance.

Methodology:
The PWA will use service workers and IndexedDB for offline caching, built with React and Workbox. Proof-of-delivery photos and statuses are queued offline and synced to a Node.js backend when online. Reliability will be tested under simulated network loss, and load time measured with Lighthouse.

Scope:
The app covers delivery listing, offline capture, and sync for a single small fleet. It excludes live GPS dispatch optimisation and payment handling.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An installable PWA with offline support.
2. A performance and offline-reliability report.

Timeline:
Semester 1 build core and offline layer; Semester 2 sync, testing, evaluation.

Title:
A Cross-Platform Mobile App for Booking Local Government Services

Problem Statement:
Citizens often queue physically or navigate confusing portals to book appointments for e-government services such as licence renewals. 2. To let users track application status and receive reminders.
3. To test the app on both Android and iOS for usability.

Methodology:
The app will be developed in Flutter with a Firebase backend for authentication, bookings, and notifications. Appointment slots are managed through Firestore, and push reminders use Firebase Cloud Messaging. Usability testing will be run with a small set of users on both platforms.

Scope:
The prototype covers appointment booking and status tracking for a few service types. It excludes real integration with official government databases and payment of fees.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A cross-platform booking app prototype.
2. A usability test report across Android and iOS.

Timeline:
Two semesters: requirements and build, then cross-platform testing.

Title:
A Native Android App for Peer Tutoring at a University

Problem Statement:
Students seeking peer tutoring rely on noisy chat groups where requests get lost and tutor quality is unclear. A native Android app could match students with peer tutors by subject and availability and keep a record of sessions, but no dedicated tool exists for this campus.

Objectives:

2. To support session scheduling and ratings.
3. To evaluate matching usefulness with student feedback.

Methodology:
The app will be developed in Kotlin using Android Jetpack components and a Firebase backend for accounts, listings, and scheduling. A simple filter matches requests to available tutors by subject and time. Feedback will be gathered through an in-app rating flow and a short post-trial survey.

The app targets one faculty's subjects and basic scheduling and rating. It excludes payment processing and video calling.

Title:
An IoT Sensor Network for Monitoring Retail Store Conditions

Problem Statement:
Retail stores need to keep shelves stocked and conditions comfortable, but staff check temperature, humidity, and footfall manually and inconsistently. A low-cost IoT sensor network could collect this data continuously and alert managers to issues, yet small retailers seldom have such monitoring.

Objectives:
1. To deploy an IoT sensor network measuring temperature, humidity, and footfall in a store layout.
2. To stream readings to a central dashboard.
3. To trigger alerts when thresholds are crossed.

Methodology:
ESP32 nodes with DHT22 and PIR sensors will publish readings over MQTT to a Raspberry Pi broker, which stores data in InfluxDB and visualises it in Grafana. Threshold rules generate alerts. The setup will be tested in a mock store environment over several days to check data reliability.

Scope:
The prototype covers a few sensor nodes and three measured variables in a controlled setup. It excludes inventory-level RFID tracking and multi-store rollout.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working IoT monitoring prototype with a dashboard.
2. A report on data reliability and alerting.

Semester 1 hardware and data pipeline; Semester 2 dashboard, alerts, testing.

Title:
A Smart Home Automation Hub Contributing to Smart-City Energy Goals

Problem Statement:
Smart-city energy programmes depend on households shifting consumption away from peak hours, but most home automation systems optimise only for comfort and ignore grid-level demand signals. There is a gap for an open hub that automates appliances in response to both user preferences and time-of-use pricing, helping aggregate demand response at the neighbourhood scale.

Objectives:
1. To build a home automation hub that controls appliances using rules combining user comfort and time-of-use tariffs.
2. To shift schedulable loads to off-peak windows automatically.
3. To quantify the reduction in peak-hour energy use against an always-on baseline.

Methodology:
The hub will run on a Raspberry Pi using Home Assistant with Zigbee smart plugs for a few schedulable appliances. A rule engine reads a published time-of-use schedule and user constraints to defer loads. Evaluation compares peak-window consumption and cost over a two-week trial against an unmanaged baseline, using logged power data, and notes comfort-violation events.

Scope:
The prototype covers a small set of schedulable appliances in one dwelling and rule-based control. It excludes machine-learned occupancy prediction and direct utility integration.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working automation hub with tariff-aware scheduling.
2. A measured comparison of peak-use and cost reduction versus baseline.

Timeline:
S1: hardware, integration, rule engine. S2: trial, baseline comparison, analysis.

Title:
Edge Computing for Offline Landmark Recognition in a Tourism App

Problem Statement:
Tourists frequently explore areas with poor or costly connectivity, where cloud-based landmark recognition fails or drains data. Running inference at the edge on the device could give instant offline recognition, but naive on-device models are large and slow. The challenge is fitting an accurate landmark recogniser within a phone's compute and latency budget.

Objectives:
1. To deploy a quantised landmark-recognition model on-device for offline use.
2. To compare on-device latency and accuracy against a cloud baseline.
3. To measure the trade-off between model size, accuracy, and battery impact.

Methodology:
A MobileNetV3 classifier will be trained on a curated set of local landmark images, then quantised and converted to TensorFlow Lite for on-device inference in an Android app. Latency, top-1 accuracy, and energy use will be measured on real devices and compared with a server-hosted full-precision model. Test images cover varied lighting and angles.

Scope:
The project covers a defined set of landmarks in one city and image classification only. It excludes AR overlays and continuous video recognition.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An offline landmark-recognition app running at the edge.
2. A trade-off study of latency, accuracy, size, and battery against cloud.

Timeline:
S1: dataset, model training, quantisation. S2: app integration, on-device benchmarking, analysis.

Title:
A Cloud-Native Microservices Backend for a Social Media Feed

Problem Statement:
Monolithic social platforms struggle to scale independent functions like posting, timeline assembly, and notifications under uneven load. A cloud-native microservices design promises independent scaling and resilience, but students rarely measure whether decomposition actually improves scalability versus the added operational complexity.

Objectives:
1. To design a microservices backend for a simplified social feed with separate post, timeline, and notification services.
2. To deploy it on Kubernetes with autoscaling and a message queue.
3. To compare throughput and latency under load against a monolithic version.

Methodology:
Services will be built in Spring Boot, containerised with Docker, and orchestrated on a local Kubernetes cluster (minikube/kind), communicating via REST and a RabbitMQ event bus, with PostgreSQL per service. A monolithic baseline implements the same features. Load tests with k6 will measure throughput, p95 latency, and behaviour under horizontal pod autoscaling.

Scope:
The system implements a core feed workflow with three services and load comparison. It excludes media storage at scale, real user traffic, and multi-region deployment.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A deployable microservices feed backend with autoscaling.
2. A benchmarked comparison against a monolith under load.

Timeline:
S1: service design, containerisation, monolith baseline. S2: Kubernetes deployment, load testing, analysis.

Title:
A CI/CD Pipeline with Automated Quality Gates for a Healthcare Web Service

Problem Statement:
Healthcare software demands traceable, tested releases, yet small teams often deploy manually with inconsistent checks, risking defects in sensitive systems. A DevOps pipeline with automated quality and security gates could enforce standards on every change, but the value of each gate is rarely measured against deployment speed.

Objectives:
1. To build a CI/CD pipeline that automates build, test, security scan, and deployment for a sample healthcare service.
2. To enforce quality gates for coverage, static analysis, and dependency vulnerabilities.
3. To measure lead time and defect-escape rate before and after the gates.

Methodology:
The pipeline will use GitHub Actions to run unit tests, JaCoCo coverage thresholds, SonarQube static analysis, and OWASP Dependency-Check, deploying to a staging container on pass. Two-week before/after periods on a sample service will be compared using DORA-style metrics: lead time, deployment frequency, and change-failure rate, with seeded defects to test gate effectiveness.

Scope:
The work covers one service's pipeline and a defined gate set. It excludes production clinical deployment and full regulatory certification.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working CI/CD pipeline with enforced quality gates.
2. A measured before/after comparison of delivery and quality metrics.

Timeline:
S1: pipeline build and gate integration. S2: metric collection, defect seeding, analysis.

Title:
A Big Data Pipeline for Detecting Anomalous Financial Transactions

Problem Statement:
Financial fraud detection must process high-volume transaction streams with low latency, but simple batch scripts cannot keep up and miss timely alerts. A scalable streaming analytics pipeline could ingest, enrich, and score transactions in near real time, though the engineering trade-offs of such a pipeline are seldom evaluated at student scale.

Objectives:
1. To build a streaming big-data pipeline that ingests and scores transactions for anomalies.
2. To compute rolling features and apply an anomaly model in near real time.
3. To evaluate detection quality and processing latency under varying throughput.

Methodology:
Transactions from a public dataset (e.g. IEEE-CIS or PaySim) will be replayed through Apache Kafka into Apache Spark Structured Streaming, which computes windowed aggregates and applies an Isolation Forest scorer, writing flagged events to a store with a dashboard. Precision/recall against labelled fraud and end-to-end latency will be measured as input rate scales.

Scope:
The pipeline covers ingestion, feature computation, scoring, and visualisation on replayed data. It excludes live bank integration and deep-learning model research.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working streaming anomaly-detection pipeline.
2. An evaluation of detection metrics and latency under load.

Timeline:
S1: ingestion and streaming features. S2: scoring, dashboard, throughput/latency evaluation.

Title:
A Business Intelligence Dashboard for Predictive Downtime Insight on a Manufacturing Line

Problem Statement:
Mid-sized manufacturers collect machine and production data but consume it through static end-of-shift reports that surface problems too late to act on. Operators lack a near-real-time view that links current conditions to likely downtime, so unplanned stoppages persist. The specific gap this project addresses is the absence of an integrated BI layer that combines descriptive line metrics with a short-horizon downtime risk indicator on the same operator-facing dashboard.

Objectives:
1. To build an ETL layer consolidating machine telemetry and production logs into a dimensional star schema, refreshed at five-minute intervals.
2. To deliver OEE, throughput, and defect KPIs in an interactive dashboard with drill-down by line, shift, and machine.
3. To embed a downtime-risk indicator from a trained classifier and evaluate it against a logistic-regression baseline using AUC and precision at fixed recall, with time-based cross-validation.

Methodology:
Telemetry and logs from the AI4I 2020 predictive-maintenance dataset, augmented with simulated shift metadata, will be staged via an Apache Airflow ETL into a PostgreSQL star schema. KPIs and a downtime-risk gauge will be exposed in a Metabase dashboard. A gradient-boosting classifier (XGBoost) predicting failure within a short horizon will be compared against a logistic-regression baseline using rolling time-series cross-validation, reporting AUC and precision at 80% recall, with feature importance for interpretability.

Scope:
The project covers one simulated production line, a fixed KPI set, and a binary short-horizon risk indicator. Explicit exclusions: no remaining-useful-life regression, no PLC hardware integration, and no multi-plant rollout; the dashboard is read-only for operators.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A refreshable BI dashboard presenting OEE/throughput/defect KPIs with drill-down and an embedded downtime-risk indicator.
2. A documented evaluation showing the classifier's AUC and precision-at-recall versus the baseline, plus an ETL and schema report.

Timeline:
S1 (wk1-6) ETL and schema; (wk7-14) KPI dashboard. S2 (wk1-7) model and baseline; (wk8-12) integration and evaluation; (wk13-14) usability check and write-up.

Title:
Short-Horizon Time-Series Forecasting of Emergency Call Volume for Public-Safety Staffing

Problem Statement:
Emergency dispatch centres staff shifts largely on historical averages, leaving them under- or over-resourced when call demand spikes, which lengthens response times. While time-series forecasting is well studied, few student projects rigorously compare classical and modern forecasters on hourly public-safety demand with proper temporal validation and calibrated prediction intervals. This project targets that gap with a reproducible, interval-aware forecast of hourly emergency-call volume to inform staffing.

Objectives:
1. To produce hourly call-volume forecasts up to 24 hours ahead with calibrated 80% prediction intervals.
2. To benchmark SARIMA and Prophet against a Temporal Fusion Transformer and a seasonal-naive baseline using rolling-origin evaluation.
3. To quantify accuracy with MASE, RMSE, and interval coverage, and translate forecasts into a staffing-band recommendation.

Methodology:
A public hourly emergency-call dataset (e.g. Montgomery County 911) will be cleaned and enriched with calendar and weather covariates. Models — seasonal-naive baseline, SARIMA, Prophet, and a TFT (via PyTorch Forecasting) — will be trained and compared under rolling-origin cross-validation that strictly respects time order. Metrics are MASE and RMSE for point accuracy and empirical coverage for the 80% intervals; statistical significance of differences is checked with a Diebold-Mariano test.

Scope:
The work forecasts aggregate hourly call counts for one region with a 24-hour horizon and maps them to coarse staffing bands. Explicit exclusions: no per-incident-type forecasting, no geospatial routing, and no live dispatch-system integration.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A reproducible forecasting pipeline with the four models and rolling-origin evaluation.
2. A benchmark report ranking models by MASE/RMSE and interval coverage, with a staffing-band mapping and limitations.

Timeline:
S1 (wk1-5) data and baseline+SARIMA; (wk6-14) Prophet and TFT. S2 (wk1-6) rolling-origin evaluation and intervals; (wk7-11) staffing mapping; (wk12-14) validation and report.

Title:
Serious Game for Teaching Personal Budgeting
