Objectives:
1. Build a game where players manage a monthly salary and expenses.
2. Include events like emergencies and bills that affect the budget.
3. Check if players understand budgeting better after playing.

Methodology:
The game will be made in Unity. Players start with a virtual salary and must allocate it to rent, food, and savings while random events occur. A short quiz before and after play will compare scores. I will recruit around fifteen classmates to play and answer the quiz.

Scope:
The game focuses on monthly personal budgeting for individuals, not businesses or investing. It is a single-player web build.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working budgeting serious game.
2. Quiz results suggesting some learning improvement.

Timeline:
Three months for design, development, and a small test.

Title:
A Dashboard for Tracking Manufacturing Machine Maintenance

Problem Statement:
Small factories often log machine maintenance on paper or spreadsheets, so it is hard to see which machines break down most or when servicing is due. This leads to unexpected stoppages.

Objectives:
1. Build a web system to record machine maintenance events.
2. Show a dashboard of breakdown frequency per machine.
3. Send reminders when scheduled servicing is due.

Methodology:
I will build a web application using PHP and MySQL. Staff enter maintenance records through a form, and the system stores machine ID, date, and issue. A dashboard page will use Chart.js to display breakdown counts. A simple date check will flag overdue servicing. Testing will involve sample data and a walkthrough with one factory supervisor.

Scope:
The system covers maintenance logging and basic reporting for one small factory. It does not predict failures or connect to machine sensors.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working maintenance-tracking web app.
2. A dashboard showing breakdown statistics.

Timeline:
Roughly 14 weeks including testing.

Title:
Telemedicine Appointment Platform for Community Clinics

Problem Statement:
In some areas people travel far to clinics for minor consultations, wasting time. A basic telemedicine platform could let patients book and hold video consultations from home, easing clinic crowding.

Objectives:
1. Build a web platform where patients book appointments with doctors.
2. Add a video-call feature for remote consultations.
3. Let doctors write simple notes after each session.

Methodology:
The platform will be developed with React on the frontend and Node.js with MongoDB on the backend. Video calls will use a third-party WebRTC library. Patients register, pick a slot, and join a call link at the booked time. I will test the booking and call flow with a few volunteers acting as patients and doctors.

Scope:
The project covers booking, video consultation, and note-taking for general consultations. It excludes prescriptions, payments, and emergency cases.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A functional telemedicine booking and video platform.
2. Positive usability feedback from test volunteers.

Timeline:
About 15 weeks across two semesters.

Title:
An Adaptive E-Learning System for Energy-Efficiency Training

Problem Statement:
Workers in facilities management need training on energy-saving practices, but standard e-learning delivers the same content to everyone regardless of prior knowledge, leaving experts bored and beginners overwhelmed.

Objectives:
1. Develop an e-learning platform delivering modules on energy efficiency.
2. Implement an adaptive quiz that adjusts difficulty based on learner answers.
3. Evaluate learner satisfaction and quiz-score improvement against a fixed-content version.

Methodology:
The system will be built with Django and PostgreSQL. Content covers lighting, HVAC, and equipment scheduling. An adaptive engine using a rule-based item-difficulty model will select the next question from an easy/medium/hard pool based on a running accuracy score. I will run a small A/B comparison with around thirty participants split between adaptive and fixed versions, measuring pre/post quiz gains and a usability survey.

Scope:
The platform covers three energy-efficiency topics for workplace learners. It uses rule-based adaptation, not machine learning, and excludes mobile apps and certification.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working adaptive e-learning web system.
2. Evidence on whether adaptation improves quiz gains versus fixed content.

Timeline:
Weeks 1-4 requirements and content, 5-11 development, 12-14 A/B testing and analysis.

Title:
A QR-Based Payment App for Small Business Owners

Problem Statement:
Small vendors often lack affordable point-of-sale tools and rely on cash, making sales tracking and reconciliation hard. A lightweight QR payment app could record transactions and provide simple sales summaries.

Objectives:
1. Build a mobile app letting customers pay vendors by scanning a QR code.
2. Record each transaction with amount, time, and item category.
3. Generate daily and weekly sales summaries for the vendor.

Methodology:
The app will be built in Flutter with a Firebase backend. Payment will integrate a sandbox payment-gateway API (no real money in scope). Each completed transaction is stored in Firestore and aggregated for summary charts. Testing will use the gateway's sandbox and a walkthrough with three small vendors, collecting feedback on usability and report usefulness.

Scope:
The project covers QR-based payment capture and sales reporting for single-owner businesses, using a sandbox gateway. It excludes inventory, payroll, and multi-branch support.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working QR payment and sales-summary mobile app.
2. Vendor feedback on whether the summaries aid tracking.

Timeline:
14 weeks: design, build, sandbox integration, and vendor testing.

Title:
Machine-Learning Fraud Detection for Agricultural Subsidy Claims

Problem Statement:
Agricultural subsidy programs receive many claims, and a minority are fraudulent (duplicate plots, inflated acreage). Manual review is slow, and there is no automated flagging to prioritize which claims auditors should inspect first.

Objectives:
1. Build a classifier that flags potentially fraudulent subsidy claims.
2. Engineer features from claim records such as acreage, location overlap, and claim frequency.
3. Evaluate the model using precision, recall, and F1 against a logistic-regression baseline.

Methodology:
Using a public or synthetic subsidy-claim dataset, I will preprocess and engineer features, then train a Random Forest classifier and compare it to a logistic-regression baseline. The data will be split with stratified cross-validation, and class imbalance handled with SMOTE. Evaluation reports precision, recall, F1, and a confusion matrix, since false negatives matter most for fraud.

Scope:
The project covers a supervised binary classifier on tabular claim data, comparing two models. It excludes real-time scoring, image-based plot verification, and deployment.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained fraud-detection model with evaluation results.
2. A comparison showing whether Random Forest beats the baseline.

Timeline:
Weeks 1-3 data and features, 4-9 modeling, 10-13 evaluation, 14 write-up.

Title:
A Recommendation System for a Public-Transport Ticketing Store

Problem Statement:
Online stores selling transport passes and add-ons (route maps, travel insurance) show the same products to everyone, so relevant add-ons are missed. A recommendation feature could suggest items based on a commuter's past purchases.

Objectives:
1. Build an e-commerce module recommending transport-related products.
2. Implement item-based collaborative filtering from purchase history.
3. Evaluate recommendation quality using precision@k on held-out purchases.

Methodology:
I will use a public retail-style transaction dataset adapted to transport products, or generate synthetic purchase logs. Item-based collaborative filtering with cosine similarity will produce top-N suggestions. I will hold out the last purchase per user and measure precision@5 and recall@5, comparing against a popularity-based baseline. The recommender will be exposed through a small Flask web demo.

Scope:
The project covers offline collaborative filtering plus a demo interface for a single store's transport products. It excludes deep-learning models, real-time updates, and A/B testing with live users.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working recommendation module with a web demo.
2. Precision@k results versus a popularity baseline.

Timeline:
About 14 weeks: data prep, modeling, evaluation, and demo build.

Title:
A Chatbot for Answering Household Sustainability Questions

Problem Statement:
People want to live more sustainably but find advice scattered across websites. A conversational agent that answers questions on recycling, energy, and water use could give quick, consistent guidance in one place.

Objectives:
1. Build a chatbot answering common household sustainability questions.
2. Use intent classification to map questions to curated answers.
3. Evaluate intent-recognition accuracy and answer relevance.

Methodology:
The chatbot will use the Rasa framework with a curated FAQ knowledge base covering recycling, energy, and water. Intents and training phrases will be defined, and a fallback message handles unknown queries. I will evaluate intent classification accuracy on a held-out set of test phrases and ask ten users to rate answer helpfulness on a 1-5 scale.

Scope:
The chatbot handles a fixed set of sustainability FAQ intents in English through a web widget. It excludes open-domain chat, multilingual support, and live data such as local recycling schedules.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working sustainability FAQ chatbot.
2. Intent-accuracy and user-rating results.

Timeline:
Weeks 1-3 knowledge base, 4-9 bot development, 10-13 evaluation, 14 reporting.

Title:
A Knowledge-Graph Search Tool for Logistics Shipment Records

Problem Statement:
Logistics staff search shipment data with keyword queries that miss connections between shipments, carriers, and routes. A knowledge graph could let users find related entities (e.g. all delayed shipments via a given hub) that flat keyword search cannot easily surface.

Objectives:
1. Build a knowledge graph linking shipments, carriers, routes, and hubs.
2. Provide a search interface that answers relationship queries over the graph.
3. Compare retrieval relevance against a keyword-search baseline.

Methodology:
Shipment records (synthetic or public) will be modeled as a graph in Neo4j, with nodes for shipments, hubs, and carriers and edges for routes and delays. A web interface will translate selected query templates into Cypher. I will define a set of test queries with known relevant answers and measure precision and recall versus a SQL keyword-search baseline on the same data.

Scope:
The project covers graph construction, template-based querying, and an evaluation against keyword search for one logistics dataset. It excludes natural-language query parsing and real-time data ingestion.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working knowledge-graph search tool.
2. Relevance comparison against keyword search.

Timeline:
Weeks 1-4 graph modeling, 5-10 interface, 11-13 evaluation, 14 write-up.

Title:
Semantic Segmentation of Scanned Government Forms for Automated Field Extraction

Problem Statement:
E-government agencies digitize large volumes of scanned paper forms, but extracting field values requires knowing each field's region. Layouts vary across form types, and fixed-coordinate templates break when scans are skewed or a form is redesigned, forcing manual correction.

Objectives:
1. Train a segmentation model that labels form regions (header, field label, field value, signature) on scanned forms.
2. Achieve mean IoU above 0.75 on a held-out test set across at least three form layouts.
3. Compare a U-Net model against a template-matching baseline on extraction accuracy.

Methodology:
I will assemble a dataset of scanned forms (public document-layout corpora such as FUNSD plus synthetic augmentations for skew and noise) with pixel-level region annotations. A U-Net with an encoder backbone will be trained using data augmentation and Dice plus cross-entropy loss, validated with an 80/10/10 split. Evaluation reports mean IoU and per-class IoU, and downstream field-extraction accuracy is compared to a coordinate-template baseline.

Scope:
The project covers four region classes on printed (not handwritten-heavy) forms across three layouts. It excludes OCR of the extracted text and live integration with agency systems.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained segmentation model with reported mean IoU.
2. Evidence that segmentation-based extraction beats template matching on skewed scans.

Timeline:
Weeks 1-3 dataset and annotation, 4-9 model training, 10-13 evaluation, 14 reporting.

Title:
Real-Time Object Detection for Monitoring Classroom Engagement Cues

Problem Statement:
In large lecture halls, instructors cannot easily gauge whether students are attentive. Manual observation is impractical, and existing analytics tools rarely use vision. Detecting visible engagement cues (hand-raising, phone use, head-down) could give anonymized aggregate feedback to teachers.

Objectives:
1. Train an object detector to recognize three engagement-cue classes in classroom video frames.
2. Reach at least 0.70 mAP@0.5 on a held-out test set while running near real time.
3. Produce per-session aggregate counts rather than identifying individuals.

Methodology:
I will collect and annotate classroom-style images (consented recordings plus public datasets) for the three cue classes, labeling bounding boxes in YOLO format. A YOLOv8 model will be fine-tuned with augmentation, validated on an 80/10/10 split. Evaluation reports mae mAP@0.5, per-class AP, and inference FPS on a mid-range GPU, compared against a YOLOv5 baseline. Outputs are aggregated counts to preserve anonymity.

Scope:
The project covers three engagement-cue classes from a fixed camera angle and reports aggregate counts. It excludes face recognition, identity tracking, and emotion inference.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained near-real-time engagement-cue detector.
2. mAP and FPS results versus a baseline, with aggregate session reports.

Timeline:
Weeks 1-4 data collection and annotation, 5-10 training, 11-13 evaluation, 14 write-up.

Title:
Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis of Retail Product Reviews

Problem Statement:
Retail managers read thousands of product reviews but cannot easily tell which aspects (price, quality, delivery, support) drive satisfaction. Overall star ratings hide which specific aspect a complaint targets, so improvement efforts are misdirected.

Objectives:
1. Build an aspect-based sentiment model classifying sentiment per aspect in retail reviews.
2. Achieve macro-F1 above 0.75 on a labeled test set across four aspect categories.
3. Compare a fine-tuned transformer against a TF-IDF plus SVM baseline.

Methodology:
Using a public retail-review dataset (e.g. Amazon reviews) with aspect annotations, or augmenting with manual aspect labels, I will preprocess text and define four aspect categories. A fine-tuned DistilBERT model will predict sentiment per aspect, evaluated with stratified train/validation/test splits and reporting per-aspect precision, recall, and macro-F1. A TF-IDF plus linear SVM serves as the baseline, and errors are analyzed by aspect.

Scope:
The project covers four predefined aspects with sentiment classification on English reviews for one product category. It excludes aspect-term extraction from scratch, multilingual reviews, and a deployed dashboard.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained aspect-based sentiment model with per-aspect metrics.
2. A comparison showing whether the transformer beats the baseline.

Timeline:
Weeks 1-3 data and labeling, 4-9 modeling, 10-13 evaluation, 14 reporting.

Title:
A Learned Cost-Estimation Module for Query Optimization on Smart-City Sensor Data

Problem Statement:
Smart-city platforms store huge volumes of sensor readings, and analytical queries over them can be slow. Traditional optimizers rely on static cost models with cardinality estimates that are often wrong on skewed sensor data, leading to poor join orders and long runtimes.

Objectives:
1. Build a learned cardinality-estimation model for queries over a smart-city sensor dataset.
2. Reduce estimation error (q-error) compared to the database's default estimator.
3. Measure whether better estimates improve chosen plan runtime on a benchmark query set.

Methodology:
Using a sensor dataset loaded into PostgreSQL, I will generate a workload of parameterized analytical queries and collect true cardinalities. A gradient-boosted regression model (and a small neural baseline) will predict cardinalities from query features. Models are evaluated by median and 95th-percentile q-error on held-out queries, and I will compare end-to-end runtimes when plan hints reflect the learned estimates versus the default.

Scope:
The project covers single- and two-table predicate cardinality estimation on one sensor schema, with offline training. It excludes multi-join deep models, write workloads, and modifying the optimizer internals beyond hints.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A learned cardinality estimator with q-error results.
2. Runtime comparison showing whether improved estimates help.

Timeline:
Weeks 1-3 workload setup, 4-9 modeling, 10-13 evaluation, 14 write-up.

Title:
A Facial-Recognition Attendance System for Guided Tour Groups

Problem Statement:
Tour operators take manual headcounts to confirm all members are present before departing each stop, which is slow and error-prone with large groups. An automated face-based check-in could speed boarding and flag missing members.

Objectives:
1. Build a system that enrolls tour-group members and marks attendance from a camera feed.
2. Achieve at least 95% verification accuracy under varied lighting on a test set.
3. Compare a FaceNet-embedding approach against an LBPH baseline.

Methodology:
Members are enrolled with a few reference photos; face embeddings are computed with a pretrained FaceNet model and stored. At each stop, detected faces (via MTCNN) are matched to enrolled embeddings by cosine distance with a threshold. I will evaluate verification accuracy, false-accept and false-reject rates on a test set with lighting and angle variation, comparing against an LBPH recognizer. A liveness check (blink) mitigates photo spoofing.

Scope:
The project covers enrollment, recognition-based attendance, and a missing-member alert for groups up to about thirty, evaluated offline. It excludes large-scale crowds, full anti-spoofing hardware, and cloud deployment.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working face-attendance prototype with accuracy and error-rate results.
2. A comparison of FaceNet versus the LBPH baseline.

Timeline:
Weeks 1-3 enrollment pipeline, 4-9 recognition, 10-13 evaluation, 14 reporting.

Title:
Robust OCR Post-Correction for User-Generated Social-Media Image Text

Problem Statement:
Social-media images (memes, screenshots, posters) embed text that standard OCR transcribes poorly because of stylized fonts, low resolution, and cluttered backgrounds. Raw OCR output therefore contains errors that hurt downstream moderation and search. There is a gap in lightweight post-correction tuned to noisy social-media text rather than clean scanned documents.

Objectives:
1. Build a pipeline that OCRs social-media images and applies a learned post-correction step to reduce transcription errors.
2. Reduce Character Error Rate (CER) by at least 20% relative to raw Tesseract output on a held-out test set.
3. Benchmark the post-corrector against a dictionary-based spell-checker baseline and conduct an ablation on the correction component.

Methodology:
The dataset combines public scene-text corpora (COCO-Text, ICDAR) with a manually transcribed sample of social-media images, split 80/10/10. The pipeline runs CRAFT for text detection and Tesseract for recognition, then a fine-tuned ByT5 sequence-to-sequence model for post-correction trained on (OCR-output, ground-truth) pairs. Evaluation uses CER and Word Error Rate with bootstrap confidence intervals, compared against raw OCR and a SymSpell baseline, plus an ablation removing the post-corrector. Risks (limited labeled social-media data) are mitigated with synthetic noise injection.

Scope:
The project covers English text post-correction for static social-media images, including detection, recognition, and correction. It explicitly excludes non-Latin scripts, handwriting, video frames, and real-time deployment.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An OCR-plus-post-correction pipeline with reproducible CER/WER results and confidence intervals.
2. A documented comparison and ablation showing the post-corrector's contribution over baselines.

Timeline:
Weeks 1-3 dataset assembly and annotation, 4-6 detection/recognition pipeline, 7-10 post-corrector training, 11-13 evaluation and ablation, 14 thesis write-up.

Title:
Early Detection of Patient Deterioration from Wearable Sensor Streams Using Multivariate Time-Series Models

Problem Statement:
In post-discharge and ward monitoring, wearable sensors stream heart rate, SpO2, respiration, and motion, but clinicians cannot watch every stream continuously. Single-threshold alarms produce high false-alarm rates and fire late, missing the gradual multivariate drift that precedes deterioration. There is a need for an early-warning model that fuses sensor channels while keeping false alarms low enough for clinical trust.

Objectives:
1. Develop a multivariate time-series model that predicts patient deterioration several hours before a clinical event from wearable sensor windows.
2. Achieve AUROC above 0.85 and improve early-warning lead time over a single-threshold and an early-warning-score baseline.
3. Evaluate the false-alarm rate per patient-day and analyze calibration for clinical usability.

Methodology:
Using a public vital-signs dataset (e.g. MIMIC-derived waveforms or the WESAD/PhysioNet sensor sets), I will window the multivariate streams and label deterioration events. A Temporal Convolutional Network and an LSTM are trained with patient-level grouped cross-validation to prevent leakage, against a NEWS-style threshold baseline. Evaluation reports AUROC, AUPRC, lead time, and alarms-per-patient-day, with calibration curves and bootstrap confidence intervals. Class imbalance is handled with focal loss, and a sensitivity analysis varies the alert threshold.

Scope:
The project covers offline modeling and evaluation on retrospective sensor data for adult patients, fusing four channels. It excludes prospective deployment, real-time edge inference, and regulatory clearance, which are noted as future work.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained deterioration-prediction model with AUROC, lead-time, and false-alarm metrics versus baselines.
2. A calibration and threshold-sensitivity analysis informing a clinically usable operating point.

Timeline:
Weeks 1-3 data preparation and labeling, 4-6 baseline implementation, 7-10 model training, 11-13 evaluation and calibration, 14 write-up.

Title:
Machine Learning for Government

Problem Statement:
Government services are slow and people complain a lot. We need machine learning to fix this and make things better for citizens.

Objectives:
1. Use machine learning
2. Make government better
3. Help citizens

Methodology:
I will use Python and some algorithms to classify the data. I will train a model and check if it works.

Scope:
This will work for all government departments and all citizens everywhere.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A good system
2. Happy citizens

Title:
Deep Learning Vision in Schools

Problem Statement:
Schools have many images and videos but nobody looks at them properly. Deep learning computer vision can solve this problem and improve education.

Objectives:
1. Apply deep learning
2. Detect things in images
3. Improve learning

Methodology:
I plan to use a neural network with computer vision to recognise images. I will collect some pictures and run the model on them.

Scope:
For students and teachers in education to use anytime.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An image system that works
2. Better education results

Title:
NLP for Shops

Problem Statement:
Shops get a lot of customer text and reviews. Natural language processing is a powerful technology that can read this text and help shops understand customers.

Objectives:
1. Do natural language processing
2. Read customer reviews
3. Help shops sell more

Methodology:
I will use NLP libraries and process the text. The system will analyse the words and give results. Some testing will be done.

Scope:
All retail shops and all kinds of products.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A text analysis tool
2. More sales for shops

Title:
A Recommender System for Smart City Services

Problem Statement:
Smart city residents have access to many public services such as transport, libraries, and events, but there is no single place that suggests relevant services to them. This project builds a recommender system to suggest city services to residents.

Objectives:
1. Collect data about city services and usage
2. Build a recommendation model
3. Test the recommendations with users

Methodology:
The system will use collaborative filtering to recommend services based on what similar residents used. Python and a basic web interface will be built. Some sample data will be gathered and the model will be evaluated by checking if users like the suggestions.

Scope:
The project focuses on a small set of city services in one city and does not include real-time updates.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working recommender prototype
2. A report on recommendation accuracy

Timeline:
The project will take two semesters to finish.

Title:
Speech Recognition for Tourist Assistance

Problem Statement:
Tourists often struggle to ask for directions or information when they do not speak the local language well. A speech recognition app could let tourists speak and get useful answers, but few simple tools target tourism.

Objectives:
1. Build a speech recognition module for short tourist phrases
2. Connect it to a simple information lookup
3. Test the accuracy with a few users

Methodology:
The app will use an existing speech-to-text library to convert spoken phrases into text, then match keywords to a small database of tourist information. A mobile or web interface will be developed and tested with sample recordings.

Scope:
The project covers English and a limited set of tourist questions in one city, and does not handle full conversation.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A prototype speech tourist assistant
2. Accuracy results on the test phrases

Timeline:
Two semesters, split into design and implementation.

Title:
Network Intrusion Detection for Social Media Platforms

Problem Statement:
Social media platforms face many network attacks that can leak user data. Intrusion detection systems can spot suspicious traffic, but many are complex. This project builds a simpler machine-learning detector for common attacks.

Objectives:
1. Use a public intrusion dataset
2. Train a classifier to detect attacks
3. Measure detection accuracy

Methodology:
The project will use the NSL-KDD dataset and train a decision tree or random forest classifier to label traffic as normal or attack. Features will be selected from the dataset and accuracy and false positive rate will be measured. Python with scikit-learn will be used.

Scope:
The work is limited to offline analysis of the chosen dataset and does not include live deployment on a real platform.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained intrusion detection model
2. A comparison of accuracy between two classifiers

Timeline:
Two semesters with data preparation first, then modelling.

Title:
Web Application Security Scanner for Healthcare Portals

Problem Statement:
Healthcare web portals store sensitive patient data and are common targets for attacks like SQL injection and cross-site scripting. Small clinics rarely test their portals. This project builds a basic scanner to flag common vulnerabilities.

Objectives:
1. Identify common web vulnerabilities to check
2. Build a scanner that tests for them
3. Evaluate the scanner on a sample portal

Methodology:
The scanner will send crafted inputs to web forms and check responses for signs of SQL injection and XSS, similar to simple penetration testing. It will be tested against a deliberately vulnerable demo healthcare app such as a custom-built test site.

Scope:
Only two or three vulnerability types are covered and the tool is tested on a demo site, not a live hospital system.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working vulnerability scanner prototype
2. A report listing detected issues on the demo site

Timeline:
Two semesters from research to testing.

Title:
Static and Dynamic Malware Analysis for Financial Applications

Problem Statement:
Financial institutions are frequently targeted by malware that steals credentials and transaction data. Analysts must triage many suspicious files, yet purely static analysis misses packed samples and pure dynamic analysis is slow. A combined lightweight approach could speed up triage for banking-related malware.

Objectives:
1. Build a pipeline that extracts static features (PE headers, imported APIs, strings) from Windows samples
2. Run samples in a sandbox to capture API call traces and network behaviour
3. Train a classifier to flag financial malware and compare it against a static-only baseline

Methodology:
Samples will be drawn from a labelled corpus such as a subset of the EMBER dataset plus collected banking trojan samples in an isolated VM. Static features will be extracted with pefile, and dynamic traces captured using Cuckoo Sandbox. A random forest classifier will be trained, with accuracy, precision, and recall reported and compared to a static-only model.

Scope:
The project targets Windows PE financial malware only; mobile and macro-based malware are excluded, and analysis runs offline in a controlled lab.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A combined static-dynamic analysis tool with a labelled report per sample
2. Evaluation showing detection improvement over the static baseline

Timeline:
Semester one: dataset, static features, sandbox setup. Semester two: dynamic features, classifier, evaluation.

Title:
A Responsive Web Platform for Manufacturing Production Tracking

Problem Statement:
Small manufacturers often track production on paper or spreadsheets, making it hard for supervisors to see job status across machines and shifts. A responsive web platform accessible from desktop and shop-floor tablets could centralise this tracking.

Objectives:
1. Design a database for jobs, machines, and production logs
2. Build a responsive web application for entering and viewing production status
3. Provide dashboards summarising throughput and delays per machine

Methodology:
The platform will use a React frontend with a Node.js and PostgreSQL backend, following a responsive layout that adapts to tablet and desktop. Requirements will be gathered from a small manufacturer, and usability will be evaluated with a System Usability Scale survey from a few operators and a supervisor.

Scope:
The system covers job tracking and basic dashboards for a single small factory; it excludes machine sensor integration and payroll. Data is entered manually.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A deployed responsive web platform with role-based access
2. Usability results and a summary of measured tracking time savings

Timeline:
Semester one: requirements and core CRUD. Semester two: dashboards, testing, evaluation.

Title:
A Progressive Web App for Community Public Safety Reporting

Problem Statement:
Residents who witness hazards such as broken streetlights, flooding, or accidents often have no quick way to report them to local authorities, especially when connectivity is poor. A progressive web app that works offline and syncs later could improve public safety reporting.

Objectives:
1. Build a PWA for submitting geotagged safety reports with photos
2. Support offline capture and background synchronisation
3. Provide an authority dashboard to view and update report status

Methodology:
The app will be built with React and a service worker for offline caching, using IndexedDB to queue reports and the Background Sync API to upload when online. Reports will be stored in a Firebase backend with location captured via the Geolocation API. Testing will cover offline scenarios and a usability check with a small group of residents.

Scope:
The project covers report submission, offline sync, and a basic status dashboard for one neighbourhood; it excludes automated dispatch and integration with official emergency systems.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An installable PWA that captures and syncs reports offline
2. A dashboard plus test results on offline reliability

Timeline:
Semester one: PWA shell and offline storage. Semester two: sync, dashboard, evaluation.

Title:
A Cross-Platform Mobile App for Household Energy Monitoring

Problem Statement:
Households often have little visibility into which appliances drive their electricity bills, so they cannot change habits to save energy. A cross-platform mobile app that lets users log appliance usage and view consumption estimates could help them reduce waste.

Objectives:
1. Build a cross-platform app for logging appliances and usage hours
2. Estimate and visualise energy consumption and cost
3. Give simple saving tips based on usage patterns

Methodology:
The app will be developed in Flutter so it runs on both Android and iOS, with a SQLite local store and an optional cloud sync. Consumption is estimated from appliance wattage and logged usage hours, shown in charts. The app will be tested with a small group of users who log usage for two weeks, and feedback collected via a survey.

Scope:
The app relies on manual logging and wattage estimates; it does not connect to smart meters or real-time sensors. One country's tariff is used.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working cross-platform energy monitoring app
2. User feedback and observed changes in awareness

Timeline:
Semester one: app core and logging. Semester two: visualisation, tips, user trial.

Title:
An Android Native App for Small Business Inventory Management

Problem Statement:
Owners of small retail and grocery businesses often track stock manually, leading to stockouts and overstocking. A native Android app could let them manage inventory, scan barcodes, and get low-stock alerts on the phones they already own.

Objectives:
1. Build a native Android app for adding products and recording stock movements
2. Add barcode scanning and low-stock alert notifications
3. Provide simple sales and stock reports

Methodology:
The app will be built natively in Kotlin using Android Jetpack components and a Room (SQLite) local database, with barcode scanning via the ML Kit barcode API and local notifications for low-stock thresholds. It will be tested with two small business owners over two weeks, with usability assessed by a short survey.

Scope:
The app targets single-store inventory on Android phones only; multi-branch sync, supplier ordering, and accounting integration are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A functioning Android inventory app with barcode scanning and alerts
2. Usability feedback and notes on time saved versus manual tracking

Timeline:
Semester one: data model and core CRUD. Semester two: scanning, alerts, reports, testing.

Title:
An IoT Sensor Network for Smart Crop Field Monitoring

Problem Statement:
Smallholder farmers often water and fertilise based on guesswork because they lack data on soil and weather conditions, which wastes water and reduces yield. A low-cost IoT sensor network could provide soil moisture and temperature readings to guide irrigation.

Objectives:
1. Build sensor nodes that measure soil moisture, temperature, and humidity
2. Transmit readings to a central gateway and store them
3. Provide a dashboard with trends and simple irrigation alerts

Methodology:
Sensor nodes will use ESP32 microcontrollers with capacitive soil moisture and DHT22 sensors, sending data over Wi-Fi/MQTT to a Raspberry Pi gateway running an MQTT broker and InfluxDB. A Grafana or custom dashboard will display trends, and a threshold rule will trigger irrigation alerts. The system will be tested in a small plot over several weeks.

Scope:
The prototype uses three to five nodes on one small field; automated valve control and machine-learning yield prediction are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working multi-node sensor network feeding a live dashboard
2. Field test results on data reliability and alert usefulness

Timeline:
Semester one: node and gateway build. Semester two: dashboard, alerts, field deployment.

Title:
Smart Home Automation Linked to Commuter Transportation Schedules

Problem Statement:
Smart home routines today run on fixed schedules and ignore the user's actual commute, so heating, charging, and departure reminders are often mistimed when transit is delayed. Coupling home automation to live public-transport data could reduce wasted energy and missed connections, yet few open systems integrate the two.

Objectives:
1. Integrate live transit arrival data with a home automation hub to trigger context-aware routines
2. Implement rules that adjust departure reminders, EV charging, and thermostat setback based on predicted leave time
3. Evaluate timing accuracy and energy impact against a fixed-schedule baseline

Methodology:
A Home Assistant hub will subscribe to a transit agency's GTFS-Realtime feed; a rule engine computes recommended leave time from journey duration plus delays and triggers routines via MQTT-connected smart plugs and a thermostat. Predicted-versus-actual leave-time error and standby energy will be logged over a multi-week trial in one household, compared to a static-schedule control period.

Scope:
The project targets one home, one commute route, and three device types; multi-occupant scheduling and citywide rollout are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working transit-aware automation system with documented rules
2. Measured improvement in reminder timing and energy use versus the baseline

Timeline:
S1: hub, GTFS-RT ingestion, rules. S2: device integration, trial, evaluation.

Title:
Edge Computing for On-Device Energy Disaggregation in Sustainable Buildings

Problem Statement:
Cloud-based energy monitoring raises latency, bandwidth, and privacy concerns because raw household power data leaves the premises. Running non-intrusive load monitoring (NILM) at the edge keeps data local, but model size and inference cost on constrained devices remain challenging for sustainability applications.

Objectives:
1. Train a compact NILM model to disaggregate appliance use from aggregate power
2. Optimise and deploy it for low-latency inference on an edge device
3. Compare on-device accuracy, latency, and energy use against a cloud baseline

Methodology:
A 1D-CNN/LSTM model will be trained on the UK-DALE dataset, then quantised and pruned with TensorFlow Lite and deployed on a Raspberry Pi 4. Disaggregation F1, inference latency, and device power draw will be measured and compared to the same model served from the cloud, with mains data captured via a CT-clamp sensor.

Scope:
Five common appliances and one edge device are in scope; transfer to unseen homes and large appliance vocabularies are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A deployed edge NILM prototype with a reproducible benchmark
2. A quantified accuracy-versus-latency-versus-energy trade-off report

Timeline:
S1: data, model, training. S2: quantisation, edge deployment, benchmarking.

Title:
A Cloud-Native Microservices Platform for Last-Mile Logistics Tracking

Problem Statement:
Monolithic delivery-tracking systems are hard to scale during demand spikes and tightly couple order, routing, and notification logic. A cloud-native microservices design with independent scaling could improve resilience and deployment speed for last-mile logistics, but student projects rarely measure these benefits concretely.

Objectives:
1. Decompose delivery tracking into independently deployable services (orders, tracking, routing, notifications)
2. Containerise and orchestrate them with Kubernetes, with an API gateway and async messaging
3. Evaluate scalability and fault tolerance under simulated load against a monolithic baseline

Methodology:
Services will be built in Spring Boot, communicate via REST and a Kafka event bus, and deploy to a local Kubernetes (k3s) cluster with an Ingress gateway and Prometheus/Grafana monitoring. Load tests with k6 will measure throughput, p95 latency, and recovery time when a service is killed, compared to an equivalent monolith.

Scope:
The platform covers four services and a simulated courier feed; real payment processing and production-scale deployment are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A running microservices platform with CI-built container images
2. Benchmarks showing scaling and fault-recovery differences versus the monolith

Timeline:
S1: service decomposition and containers. S2: orchestration, load tests, evaluation.

Title:
A CI/CD Pipeline with Automated Quality Gates for E-Government Services

Problem Statement:
Public-sector software releases are often manual and infrequent, increasing downtime risk and slowing security patches. A DevOps CI/CD pipeline with automated testing and security gates could shorten lead time and reduce failed deployments, but the impact is rarely measured in an e-government context with its compliance constraints.

Objectives:
1. Build a CI/CD pipeline that builds, tests, scans, and deploys a sample e-government web service
2. Add automated quality gates: unit/integration tests, SAST, dependency scanning, and a staging smoke test
3. Measure DORA metrics (lead time, deployment frequency, change-failure rate) before and after automation

Methodology:
A GitHub Actions pipeline will containerise a sample citizen-request service, run JUnit and integration tests, scan with SonarQube and Trivy, and deploy to a staging environment via blue-green release with automatic rollback on failed smoke tests. DORA metrics will be collected across a manual baseline period and the automated period and compared.

Scope:
One representative service and a staging environment are in scope; production rollout and full accessibility certification are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A reusable pipeline definition with passing quality gates
2. A before/after DORA comparison demonstrating delivery improvements

Timeline:
S1: pipeline, tests, scanning. S2: deployment automation, metrics, evaluation.

Title:
A Big Data Analytics Pipeline for Student Engagement in Online Learning

Problem Statement:
Universities collect large volumes of learning-management-system logs but rarely turn them into timely signals of student disengagement. A scalable analytics pipeline could process clickstream data to surface at-risk students, yet building one that handles volume while remaining reproducible is non-trivial for an institution.

Objectives:
1. Ingest and process large LMS clickstream logs in a batch-and-streaming pipeline
2. Engineer engagement features and compute weekly at-risk indicators
3. Validate indicators against course outcomes and benchmark pipeline throughput

Methodology:
Clickstream events from the public OULAD dataset (augmented with synthetic streaming) will be ingested via Kafka, processed in Apache Spark (batch) and Spark Structured Streaming, and stored in Parquet on a data lake. Engagement features feed a logistic-regression risk score; the pipeline's throughput and latency are benchmarked, and risk indicators validated against pass/fail labels with AUC.

Scope:
The pipeline targets engagement analytics on one dataset; live integration with a production LMS and intervention delivery are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A reproducible big-data pipeline producing weekly at-risk reports
2. Validation metrics and throughput benchmarks

Timeline:
S1: ingestion and batch processing. S2: streaming, risk model, benchmarking.

Title:
A Business Intelligence Dashboard with Explainable Demand Drivers for Omnichannel Retail

Problem Statement:
Mid-sized omnichannel retailers run BI dashboards that report what sold but not why, forcing category managers to guess the drivers behind weekly swings. Existing dashboards lack integrated, explainable attribution linking sales movements to promotions, weather, and stock-outs, leaving decisions slow and subjective. This project delivers a BI dashboard that pairs standard KPIs with model-based, explainable demand-driver attribution.

Objectives:
1. Build a star-schema warehouse and dashboard covering sales, margin, and inventory KPIs across online and store channels
2. Fit a gradient-boosting demand model and surface per-week SHAP-based driver attributions in the dashboard
3. Evaluate forecast accuracy (MAPE/WAPE) and validate driver usefulness with category managers via a structured task study

Methodology:
Data from the public M5 (Walmart) dataset plus simulated promotion and weather features will be modelled into a star schema in PostgreSQL/dbt and visualised in a React + Apache ECharts dashboard. An XGBoost demand model is trained with time-based cross-validation against naive and seasonal-naive baselines; SHAP values produce weekly driver attributions shown beside each KPI. A within-subjects study with five managers compares decision speed and confidence against a KPI-only dashboard.

Scope:
Three product categories, two channels, and weekly granularity are in scope; real-time streaming, price optimisation, and supplier integration are explicitly excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A deployed explainable BI dashboard with documented ETL and data model
2. Accuracy results beating both baselines plus study evidence of improved decision speed

Timeline:
S1 (wk1-6 ETL/warehouse, wk7-13 dashboard+model). S2 (wk1-6 SHAP attribution, wk7-13 user study, evaluation, write-up).

Title:
Probabilistic Multi-Horizon Forecasting of Urban Air Quality for Smart-City Alerting

Problem Statement:
Smart-city air-quality alerts rely on single-point forecasts that hide uncertainty, causing either missed exceedance warnings or alert fatigue from false alarms. Few municipal-scale studies provide calibrated probabilistic forecasts across multiple horizons that also account for spatial correlation between monitoring stations. This project builds and rigorously evaluates a probabilistic multi-horizon PM2.5 forecaster for city-wide alerting.

Objectives:
1. Build a multi-station dataset aligning PM2.5 with meteorological and temporal features
2. Develop probabilistic 1-to-24-hour forecasts and calibrated exceedance alerts
3. Benchmark accuracy, calibration, and alert quality against statistical and naive baselines

Methodology:
Using the public Beijing Multi-Site Air-Quality dataset, features (lags, weather, calendar) are built per station. A Temporal Fusion Transformer producing quantile forecasts is compared against SARIMA, gradient-boosted quantile regression, and a seasonal-naive baseline using blocked time-series cross-validation. Evaluation reports MAE/RMSE, pinball loss, PICP/coverage for calibration, and exceedance-alert precision/recall/lead-time; ablations test the value of meteorological and spatial features.

Scope:
Twelve stations in one city and PM2.5 only are in scope; source apportionment, other pollutants, and live sensor deployment are explicitly excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A reproducible probabilistic forecasting pipeline with calibration diagnostics
2. Evidence the model improves calibrated alert lead-time over all baselines

Timeline:
S1 (wk1-5 data+features, wk6-13 baselines+TFT). S2 (wk1-6 calibration+ablations, wk7-13 alert evaluation, write-up).

Title:
Blockchain for Transport

Problem Statement:
Transportation has many problems and blockchain can help fix them. Smart contracts are a good technology that everyone is talking about now.

Objectives:
1. Use blockchain in transport
2. Make smart contracts
3. Help people

Methodology:
I will study blockchain and write some smart contracts. I will use the computer and do testing to see if it works.

Scope:
This is for all transport companies everywhere and buses and trains and cars too.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A blockchain system
2. Happy users

Title:
AR App for Sustainability

Problem Statement:
The environment is in danger and we need to be more sustainable. Augmented reality is cool and can teach people about this.

Objectives:
1. Build an AR app
2. Make it about sustainability
3. Get users to download it

Methodology:
I will make an AR application using a phone. People will point the camera and see things about nature and recycling.

Scope:
For everyone who cares about the planet and wants to save it.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An AR app
2. People learn to be green

Title:
VR Training for Logistics

Problem Statement:
Logistics workers need training but it is hard and expensive. Virtual reality is a modern solution that can make training fun and easy for the warehouse.

Objectives:
1. Create a VR simulation
2. Train logistics staff
3. Save money for companies

Methodology:
I will use a VR headset and build a simulation where workers can practice. Then I will let some people try it and ask if they liked it.

Scope:
This covers all logistics and warehouse and shipping training around the world.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working VR training simulation
2. Better trained workers

Title:
A 3D Game to Teach Citizens About E-Government Services

Problem Statement:
Many citizens find online government portals confusing and avoid using them, instead queuing at physical counters. A playful, interactive way to introduce these services could lower the barrier for first-time users, especially older adults unfamiliar with digital forms.

Objectives:
1. Design a 3D game where the player completes virtual e-government tasks such as renewing a licence.
2. Build the game using a common game engine.
3. Test whether players feel more confident about real e-government portals afterwards.

Methodology:
The game will be developed in Unity with simple 3D environments representing a virtual town hall. Players walk to counters and complete mini-tasks that mirror real online services. A small group of users will play it and answer a short questionnaire about their confidence.

Scope:
The project focuses on three common services and a single-player desktop game. Mobile and multiplayer are not included.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A playable 3D educational game covering three e-government services.
2. Survey feedback on user confidence before and after playing.

Timeline:
Roughly 12 weeks split between design, building, and testing.

Title:
A Serious Game for Learning Basic Programming Concepts

Problem Statement:
First-year students often struggle to grasp abstract programming ideas like loops and variables from lectures alone. A game-based approach might keep them engaged while practising these concepts repeatedly, though motivation tends to drop with traditional exercises.

Objectives:
1. Develop a 2D puzzle game where solving levels requires applying loops, conditionals, and variables.
2. Include increasing difficulty so concepts build on each other.
3. Measure whether students who play score better on a short concept quiz.

Methodology:
The game will be built in Unity with a 2D tile-based interface. Each level presents a puzzle that the player solves by arranging code-like blocks. A class of students will be split into a group that plays and a group that does not, and both take the same quiz.

Scope:
Limited to three introductory concepts and a browser-playable build. It will not cover functions, recursion, or real code syntax.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A 2D educational game covering three programming concepts.
2. A comparison of quiz scores between players and non-players.

Timeline:
About 13 weeks across design, development, and a classroom test.

Title:
A Health Tracking System for Retail Pharmacy Customers

Problem Statement:
Retail pharmacies handle many walk-in customers who ask about medication and basic health metrics, but staff rarely keep a record customers can revisit. A simple system letting customers log purchases and reminders might improve adherence, although current paper slips are easily lost.

Objectives:
1. Build a web system where pharmacy customers register and log their medication.
2. Add reminders for when to take or refill medicine.
3. Let pharmacy staff view a basic summary for each customer.

Methodology:
The system will be a web application built with a standard framework and a MySQL database. Customers create accounts, enter their medicines, and receive reminder notifications. Staff have a separate login to look up customer records. Some pharmacy users will try it and give feedback.

Scope:
Focused on one pharmacy branch and over-the-counter plus common prescription logging. It will not handle insurance or e-prescriptions.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working web system for medication logging and reminders.
2. Informal feedback from pharmacy staff and customers.

Timeline:
Around 12 weeks total.

Title:
A Telemedicine Platform for a Smart City Clinic Network

Problem Statement:
Residents in a smart city often travel across town for minor consultations that could be handled remotely, adding congestion and wait times. A video-based telemedicine platform connecting residents to nearby clinics could reduce unnecessary trips, though video quality and scheduling remain practical concerns.

Objectives:
1. Build a platform where residents book and join video consultations with clinic doctors.
2. Provide doctors a queue to manage appointments.
3. Store basic consultation notes for follow-up.

Methodology:
A web platform will be developed with a frontend for patients and doctors and a backend handling appointments. Video calls will use an existing third-party API. The database stores users, appointments, and notes. A few test users will simulate booking and consulting.

Scope:
Covers appointment booking, video consultation, and note-taking for one clinic network. Prescriptions, payment, and integration with hospital records are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A functioning telemedicine web platform with booking and video calls.
2. Test-user feedback on the consultation flow.

Timeline:
Approximately 14 weeks across requirements, build, and testing.

Title:
An Adaptive E-Learning System for Tourism Industry Training

Problem Statement:
Tourism staff such as guides and hotel front-desk workers need ongoing training on destinations and service standards, but generic courses ignore each learner's existing knowledge, wasting time on material they already know. An adaptive system that adjusts content to performance could make training more efficient.

Objectives:
1. Develop an e-learning platform delivering tourism modules with quizzes.
2. Implement an adaptive engine that routes learners to easier or harder content based on quiz results.
3. Evaluate whether adaptive sequencing improves quiz scores compared with a fixed sequence.

Methodology:
The platform will be built as a web application with a content bank tagged by difficulty. A rule-based adaptive engine uses recent quiz accuracy to select the next module. Evaluation uses an A/B setup: one group receives adaptive sequencing, another a fixed order, comparing pre- and post-test gains with a t-test.

Scope:
Covers three tourism topics for one training centre, web-based, English only. It excludes mobile apps, certification, and machine-learning-based recommendation.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An adaptive e-learning web platform for tourism training.
2. A measured comparison of learning gains between adaptive and fixed groups.

Timeline:
14 weeks: 3 design, 6 development, 3 content, 2 evaluation.

Title:
A Peer-to-Peer Payment Feature Integrated into a Social Media Prototype

Problem Statement:
Users increasingly want to send money within the same apps where they chat, but standalone payment apps require switching contexts and re-entering recipient details. Embedding a lightweight peer-to-peer payment flow into a social feed could reduce friction, while raising clear concerns about transaction security and verification.

Objectives:
1. Build a social media prototype with messaging and a profile feed.
2. Add a peer-to-peer payment flow using a sandbox payment gateway.
3. Evaluate transaction success rate and user-perceived ease through a usability test.

Methodology:
The prototype will be a web app with a backend handling users, posts, and a simulated wallet. Payments use a sandbox gateway API with OTP confirmation. A usability test with around ten participants measures task completion time and SUS scores, and transaction logs are checked for failures.

Scope:
Limited to in-app transfers between registered users using sandbox funds. Real money, currency conversion, and fraud detection are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working social-media prototype with an integrated payment flow.
2. Usability and transaction-success metrics from the test sessions.

Timeline:
13 weeks across design, build, integration, and evaluation.

Title:
Machine-Learning Fraud Detection for Healthcare Insurance Claims

Problem Statement:
Healthcare insurers process large volumes of claims, a small fraction of which are fraudulent through inflated or duplicate billing. Manual auditing catches only a sample, so an automated classifier flagging suspicious claims could focus human reviewers where they matter most, provided false positives stay manageable.

Objectives:
1. Build a classifier that labels insurance claims as likely-fraudulent or legitimate.
2. Compare logistic regression, random forest, and gradient boosting on the task.
3. Evaluate using precision, recall, and AUC with attention to class imbalance.

Methodology:
A public health-insurance claims dataset will be cleaned and feature-engineered (provider, amount, frequency, diagnosis codes). Class imbalance is addressed with SMOTE on the training fold only. Three models are trained with 5-fold cross-validation and tuned via grid search. Metrics reported are precision, recall, F1, and AUC, with the strongest model inspected for feature importance.

Scope:
Offline analysis on one historical dataset; covers binary fraud classification only. Real-time scoring, deep learning, and deployment are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained fraud-detection model with documented performance.
2. A comparison of three algorithms under class imbalance.

Timeline:
14 weeks: 2 data, 7 modelling, 3 evaluation, 2 reporting.

Title:
A Hybrid Recommendation System for a Personal-Finance Product Marketplace

Problem Statement:
Comparison sites for financial products such as loans and credit cards list many options, but users struggle to pick ones suited to their profile, often abandoning the search. A recommender that combines product attributes with similar-user behaviour could surface more relevant options, though cold-start users with no history are a known difficulty.

Objectives:
1. Build a hybrid recommender combining content-based filtering and collaborative filtering for financial products.
2. Handle cold-start users via a content-based fallback.
3. Evaluate ranking quality with precision@k and compare against a popularity baseline.

Methodology:
Using a synthesized interaction dataset over a catalogue of financial products, a content-based model encodes product attributes and a collaborative model uses matrix factorization. A weighted hybrid blends both scores. Evaluation uses a held-out test split with precision@k and recall@k against a most-popular baseline, and cold-start cases are tested separately.

Scope:
Web prototype recommending within one product category set, offline evaluation. Live A/B testing and real customer PII are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A hybrid recommendation prototype with a fallback for new users.
2. Ranking metrics comparing the hybrid against a popularity baseline.

Timeline:
13 weeks across data prep, modelling, integration, and evaluation.

Title:
A Retrieval-Based Chatbot for Manufacturing Shop-Floor Support

Problem Statement:
Machine operators on a manufacturing floor frequently need quick answers about maintenance steps and error codes, but flipping through PDF manuals slows them down and supervisors get repeated questions. A chatbot answering from the manuals could speed up troubleshooting, while hallucinated answers would be unacceptable on safety-relevant tasks.

Objectives:
1. Build a chatbot that answers operator questions from a corpus of machine manuals.
2. Use retrieval to ground answers in the source documents and cite the section.
3. Evaluate answer relevance against a set of test questions.

Methodology:
Manuals are chunked and embedded into a vector store. User questions are embedded and matched to the nearest chunks, which a template assembles into a grounded answer with a citation. A test set of operator questions with expected sources measures retrieval accuracy (top-k hit rate) and answer relevance rated by two reviewers.

Scope:
Covers one machine family's manuals, English, text-only chat. Voice input, live machine data, and open-ended generation are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A retrieval-based chatbot grounded in machine manuals with citations.
2. Retrieval-accuracy and relevance results on the test question set.

Timeline:
13 weeks: 3 corpus prep, 6 build, 2 test set, 2 evaluation.

Title:
A Knowledge-Graph-Powered Search Tool for Public-Safety Incident Records

Problem Statement:
Public-safety agencies hold incident records linking people, locations, and event types, but keyword search misses connected information spread across reports. Representing records as a knowledge graph could let analysts ask relationship questions, such as incidents near a location involving a vehicle type, that flat search cannot answer well.

Objectives:
1. Build a knowledge graph from structured incident records linking entities and events.
2. Provide a search interface translating user queries into graph traversals.
3. Evaluate retrieval quality against keyword search on a set of relationship queries.

Methodology:
Records are parsed into entities (person, location, vehicle, incident) and relationships loaded into a Neo4j graph. A query layer maps a small set of natural-language patterns to Cypher traversals. Evaluation compares precision and recall of the graph search versus a keyword baseline on twenty relationship queries with manually labelled relevant results.

Scope:
Uses an anonymized or synthetic incident dataset, focuses on relationship queries over four entity types. Free-text NLP parsing and real classified data are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A knowledge graph and search interface over incident records.
2. Precision/recall comparison against keyword search on relationship queries.

Timeline:
14 weeks across data modelling, graph build, interface, and evaluation.

Title:
Semantic Segmentation of Solar-Panel Defects from Aerial Thermal Imagery

Problem Statement:
Utility-scale solar farms inspect panels with drone thermal cameras, but locating defective cells in thousands of images by eye is slow and inconsistent. Pixel-level segmentation of hotspots and cracks would let operators quantify affected area per panel, yet thermal images are low-contrast and defects are small relative to the frame.

Objectives:
1. Train a semantic segmentation model to delineate hotspot and crack regions in thermal panel images.
2. Compare U-Net and DeepLabv3+ backbones on segmentation accuracy.
3. Evaluate with mean IoU and per-class Dice, reporting performance on small defects specifically.

Methodology:
A public infrared solar-panel dataset will be annotated or used with existing masks, split per-site to avoid leakage. Images are normalized and augmented (rotation, flip, brightness). U-Net and DeepLabv3+ with a ResNet-50 encoder are trained with a combined cross-entropy and Dice loss, using early stopping on a validation set. Models are compared by mean IoU, per-class Dice, and a size-stratified analysis of small versus large defects.

Scope:
Two defect classes plus background on single-panel crops; offline inference only. Drone flight control, RGB fusion, and real-time edge deployment are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained segmentation model with documented mean IoU and Dice per class.
2. A U-Net versus DeepLabv3+ comparison including small-defect performance.

Timeline:
14 weeks: 3 data/annotation, 6 training, 3 evaluation, 2 reporting.

Title:
On-Shelf Product Detection for Small-Business Inventory Auditing

Problem Statement:
Small retailers cannot afford automated shelf-scanning systems and rely on manual stock counts that are error-prone and infrequent. A phone-photo object detector that counts product facings on a shelf could give owners a quick audit, but dense, overlapping products and varied lighting make detection on a single low-cost camera hard.

Objectives:
1. Train an object detector to locate and count product facings in shelf photos.
2. Compare YOLOv8 against Faster R-CNN on detection accuracy and inference speed.
3. Evaluate with mAP@0.5 and counting error against manual ground-truth counts.

Methodology:
A shelf-image dataset (public SKU dataset plus a small self-captured set) is annotated with bounding boxes and split by shelf to prevent leakage. Images are augmented with scaling, mosaic, and brightness shifts. YOLOv8 and Faster R-CNN are trained with transfer learning, tuned on a validation split. Evaluation reports mAP@0.5, mAP@0.5:0.95, mean absolute counting error per shelf, and per-image inference time on CPU.

Scope:
Detects packaged products as a single generic class for counting, on still photos. Per-brand classification, video, and price-tag OCR are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained shelf-detection model with documented mAP and counting error.
2. A YOLOv8 versus Faster R-CNN accuracy/speed comparison.

Timeline:
13 weeks: 3 data, 5 training, 3 evaluation, 2 reporting.

Title:
Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis of Farmer Feedback on Agricultural Inputs

Problem Statement:
Farmers discuss seeds, fertilizers, and equipment in forums and reviews, but suppliers and extension services cannot easily tell which aspects draw complaints. Document-level sentiment hides this; aspect-based sentiment analysis could attribute opinions to specific aspects like yield or price, though agricultural slang and code-switching complicate the language.

Objectives:
1. Build an aspect-based sentiment model that extracts aspects and classifies sentiment per aspect from farmer reviews.
2. Fine-tune a transformer (DistilBERT) and compare it against a TF-IDF plus SVM baseline.
3. Evaluate with macro-F1 per aspect category and overall accuracy.

Methodology:
A corpus of agricultural product reviews is collected and annotated with aspect terms and sentiment labels using a defined guideline, with inter-annotator agreement checked on a subset. Text is cleaned and tokenized. A DistilBERT model is fine-tuned for aspect-sentiment classification and compared against TF-IDF features with a linear SVM, using a stratified train/validation/test split. Metrics are macro-F1, per-aspect F1, and accuracy.

Scope:
Three aspect categories (price, quality, availability) in English-Malay mixed reviews. Real-time monitoring and aspect-opinion phrase extraction are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An aspect-based sentiment model with per-aspect F1 reported.
2. A transformer-versus-baseline comparison with error analysis.

Timeline:
14 weeks: 4 data/annotation, 5 modelling, 3 evaluation, 2 reporting.

Title:
Learned Cardinality Estimation for Query Optimization in a Transportation Database

Problem Statement:
Query optimizers choose plans using cardinality estimates, but on a transportation schema with correlated columns (route, time, vehicle type) traditional histogram estimates are often wrong, leading to slow plans on analytic queries. A learned estimator trained on the workload could give tighter estimates, though it must stay cheap enough to query at plan time.

Objectives:
1. Build a learned cardinality estimator for multi-predicate queries on a transportation dataset.
2. Compare its estimation error against the database's built-in histogram estimator.
3. Measure the effect of improved estimates on chosen plan latency for a query set.

Methodology:
A transportation trips dataset is loaded into PostgreSQL. A supervised model (a small neural network over featurized predicates) is trained on sampled queries labelled with true cardinalities. Estimation accuracy is measured by q-error against the built-in estimator. For a held-out query set, plans guided by the learned estimates are timed and compared with default-plan latency, averaged over repeated runs.

Scope:
Read-only analytic queries with up to three conjunctive predicates on one schema. Joins across many tables, updates, and optimizer integration internals are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A learned cardinality estimator with q-error compared to the baseline.
2. Plan-latency results showing where better estimates help or hurt.

Timeline:
14 weeks: 3 setup/data, 6 modelling, 3 evaluation, 2 reporting.

Title:
A Facial-Recognition Attendance System for Campus Sustainability Reporting

Problem Statement:
Card-based attendance in lecture halls wastes printed slips and gives no reliable occupancy data, which sustainability teams need to optimize lighting and air-conditioning. A face-recognition attendance system could automate logging and feed occupancy analytics, but accuracy under crowding, masks, and lighting plus privacy handling are real concerns.

Objectives:
1. Build a face-recognition system that logs attendance from a classroom camera.
2. Compare recognition accuracy of a FaceNet embedding pipeline against a dlib baseline.
3. Evaluate accuracy, false-acceptance rate, and end-to-end logging latency.

Methodology:
Enrolled student faces are encoded into embeddings; MTCNN handles detection and FaceNet produces embeddings matched by cosine similarity against the gallery. A dlib ResNet baseline is compared. Testing uses a recorded classroom session with labelled ground truth, reporting top-1 accuracy, false-acceptance and false-rejection rates, and processing time per frame. Embeddings are stored hashed, not raw images, for privacy.

Scope:
One classroom, a gallery of up to fifty enrolled students, frontal-to-moderate angles. Mask-occluded and outdoor recognition and multi-camera tracking are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working attendance system with accuracy and error-rate results.
2. A FaceNet-versus-dlib comparison and a privacy-handling note.

Timeline:

Title:
A Robust OCR Pipeline for Automated Extraction of Logistics Shipping Documents

Problem Statement:
Freight forwarders manually key data from scanned bills of lading and commercial invoices that arrive in inconsistent layouts, skews, and print quality, causing delays and transcription errors. General OCR engines read characters but do not reliably map them to structured fields (consignee, container number, HS code), and existing commercial extractors are costly and closed. A pipeline pairing OCR with layout-aware field extraction, evaluated on real document variability, addresses a concrete gap for small forwarders.

Objectives:
1. Build an end-to-end pipeline that detects, recognizes, and extracts six target fields from scanned logistics documents.
2. Compare a Tesseract-plus-rules approach against a LayoutLMv3 field-extraction model on the same labelled set.
3. Evaluate field-level precision/recall/F1 and end-to-end accuracy, and analyze failures by degradation type (skew, noise, low DPI).

Methodology:
A dataset of bills of lading and invoices is collected and annotated with field bounding boxes and values, split document-wise into train/validation/test to prevent template leakage. Preprocessing applies deskewing, denoising, and adaptive thresholding. Two pipelines are built: Tesseract OCR with regex-and-position rules, and a fine-tuned LayoutLMv3 that jointly uses text and layout. Both are evaluated with field-level precision, recall, and F1 plus exact-match end-to-end accuracy. A stratified error analysis groups failures by image-degradation type, and a small ablation removes preprocessing to quantify its contribution. Risks (limited annotated volume, sensitive data) are mitigated by augmentation and using anonymized samples.

Scope:
Two document types, six fields, English documents, batch processing. Handwriting, multilingual documents, table line-item extraction, and live system integration are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A reproducible OCR-plus-extraction pipeline with per-field and end-to-end metrics.
2. A rules-versus-LayoutLMv3 comparison and a degradation-stratified error analysis.

Timeline:
14 weeks: 3 data/annotation, 2 preprocessing, 5 modelling, 2 evaluation/ablation, 2 reporting.

Title:
Anomaly Detection in Wireless-Sensor Streams for E-Government Building Monitoring

Problem Statement:
Government buildings increasingly deploy wireless sensor networks for temperature, humidity, power, and occupancy, but raw streams are noisy and faults (drift, dropout, spikes) get noticed only after equipment damage or wasted energy. Threshold alarms miss contextual anomalies, and labelled fault data is scarce because faults are rare. An unsupervised, time-aware anomaly detector evaluated against labelled fault episodes targets this monitoring gap.

Objectives:
1. Build an unsupervised anomaly detector for multivariate wireless-sensor time series in a building-monitoring context.
2. Compare an LSTM-autoencoder reconstruction approach against Isolation Forest and a seasonal-decomposition baseline.
3. Evaluate with point-adjusted precision, recall, F1, and detection delay on labelled anomaly episodes.

Methodology:
A public building-sensor dataset (and an injected-fault variant for controlled labels) is resampled to a fixed interval, gap-filled, and normalized per sensor, split chronologically to avoid leakage. An LSTM-autoencoder is trained on nominal windows; reconstruction error over a sliding window flags anomalies with a threshold set on a validation quantile. Baselines are Isolation Forest on windowed features and STL residual thresholding. Evaluation uses point-adjusted precision/recall/F1, PR-AUC, and mean detection delay, with sensitivity analysis over window length and threshold. Limited real labels are addressed by synthetic fault injection (drift, dropout, spike) with known timestamps.

Scope:
Four sensor modalities from one building, offline streaming-style evaluation. Real-time deployment on gateways, root-cause diagnosis, and network-layer faults are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained anomaly-detection model with point-adjusted metrics and detection delay.
2. A three-way method comparison and a window/threshold sensitivity analysis.

Timeline:
14 weeks: 3 data/injection, 5 modelling, 2 baselines, 2 evaluation, 2 reporting.

Title:

Excluded: predictive yield modelling, market-price forecasting, and accounting-grade tax reporting. Title:
Probabilistic Short-Term Forecasting of Urban Bus Arrival Times

Problem Statement:
Commuters distrust transit apps because point estimates of bus arrival ignore uncertainty, so a predicted "3 minutes" that varies by ten erodes confidence. Most published transit predictors output single values and are benchmarked only against naive schedules, leaving a gap for calibrated probabilistic forecasts that quantify and communicate arrival uncertainty at the stop level.

Objectives:
1. Produce 5-30 minute-ahead probabilistic arrival forecasts whose 90% prediction intervals achieve empirical coverage within +/-3 percentage points of nominal.
2. Beat naive-schedule and seasonal-mean baselines on MAE and pinball loss by a statistically significant margin.
3. Quantify the marginal value of weather and traffic features via ablation.

Methodology:
Using six months of GTFS-Realtime feeds plus weather and incident data, I will engineer lag, headway, and calendar features, then compare a LightGBM quantile-regression model and a Temporal Fusion Transformer against ARIMA and seasonal-naive baselines. Evaluation uses blocked rolling-origin cross-validation with MAE, RMSE, pinball loss, and PICP/MPIW for interval calibration; significance is tested with Diebold-Mariano. An ablation isolates weather and traffic contributions.

Scope:
Included: arrival forecasting for three high-frequency routes with calibrated intervals and feature ablation. Excluded: full-network routing, fleet reassignment, and a production mobile UI. Risk: feed gaps are handled by documented imputation and gap-aware evaluation.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A calibrated probabilistic forecaster with reproducible benchmarks against baselines.
2. An analysis quantifying interval calibration and feature value.

Timeline:
Weeks 1-3 data pipeline; 4-7 feature engineering; 8-13 modelling and baselines; 14-18 calibration and ablation; 19-24 significance testing and thesis write-up.
