2. A usability summary from test users.

Timeline:
Around 13 weeks of development and testing.

Title:
An E-Learning Platform with Sustainability Modules and Progress Tracking

Problem Statement:
University students are increasingly interested in sustainability topics, but course material is scattered across slides, PDFs, and videos with no unified way to track progress or test understanding. Existing learning management systems are generic and do not tailor content sequencing to the sustainability theme.

Objectives:
1. To develop a web-based e-learning platform delivering structured sustainability modules with quizzes.
2. To implement progress tracking and adaptive module recommendations based on quiz performance.
3. To evaluate usability and learning outcomes through a controlled student trial.

Methodology:
The platform will be built with React, Spring Boot, and PostgreSQL. A rule-based recommendation component will suggest the next module from quiz scores. Evaluation uses a pre/post knowledge test plus the System Usability Scale with about 25 students, comparing adaptive against fixed sequencing.

Scope:
The platform covers three sustainability modules and supports individual learners. Instructor authoring tools and mobile apps are excluded. English content only.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A functional e-learning platform with progress tracking and adaptive recommendations.
2. Trial results reporting SUS scores and pre/post knowledge gains.

Timeline:
14 weeks: requirements (2), development (7), trial (3), analysis and writing (2).

Title:
A Digital Wallet for Small Logistics Operators with Settlement Tracking

Problem Statement:
Small logistics operators handle many cash-on-delivery payments and struggle to reconcile collections against deliveries, leading to disputes and slow settlement to drivers. General payment apps do not link a payment to a specific delivery job, leaving a reconciliation gap.

Objectives:
1. To build a fintech wallet that ties each payment to a delivery job and driver.
2. To provide automatic daily settlement summaries per driver.
3. To evaluate reconciliation accuracy against a manual baseline.

Methodology:
The system uses a React Native app and a Spring Boot backend with MySQL. Payments are simulated through a sandbox payment gateway API. Settlement logic groups transactions by job and driver. Accuracy is tested on a generated dataset of 500 transactions with injected mismatches, comparing the system's flags to ground truth.

Scope:
The project covers cash-on-delivery reconciliation and settlement reporting only. Real banking integration, refunds, and multi-currency support are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working wallet app with job-linked payments and settlement reports.
2. Accuracy metrics for mismatch detection on the test dataset.

Timeline:
14 weeks across analysis, build, testing, and evaluation.

Title:
Fraud Detection for E-Government Subsidy Applications

Problem Statement:
E-government portals that process subsidy applications receive duplicate and falsified submissions that are hard to catch by manual review. Officers lack a tool that flags suspicious applications for closer inspection, and simple rule checks miss patterns spanning multiple records.

Objectives:
1. To build a system that scores subsidy applications for fraud risk.
2. To combine rule-based checks with a machine-learning classifier.
3. To evaluate detection performance against a labelled dataset.

Methodology:
A synthetic dataset of subsidy applications with labelled fraud cases will be generated. Features include duplicate identity fields, income inconsistencies, and submission timing. A Random Forest classifier will be trained and compared with a logistic-regression baseline using precision, recall, and F1 under 5-fold cross-validation. A dashboard will display flagged cases.

Scope:
The project focuses on detection and ranking only, not investigation workflow or automatic rejection. A single subsidy scheme is modelled.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A fraud-scoring service with an officer dashboard.
2. A performance report comparing the model and baseline.

Timeline:
14 weeks: data and features (3), modelling (4), dashboard (3), evaluation and writeup (4).

Title:
A Course Recommendation Engine for an Education Marketplace

Problem Statement:
On online learning marketplaces, students browse thousands of courses and often cannot find ones suited to their goals and prior activity. Plain popularity rankings push the same few courses to everyone and ignore individual learning history.

Objectives:
1. To build a recommendation engine that suggests courses from a learner's enrolment and rating history.
2. To compare collaborative filtering with a content-based approach.
3. To evaluate recommendation quality offline against held-out interactions.

Methodology:
Using a public course-interaction dataset, item-based collaborative filtering (matrix factorization via SVD) and a TF-IDF content-based recommender will be implemented in Python. Evaluation uses Precision@10, Recall@10, and NDCG with a temporal train/test split, plus a popularity baseline. A small web front end demonstrates recommendations.

Scope:
The engine covers course recommendation for registered learners only. Real-time updates, pricing, and a cold-start solution for brand-new users are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. Two working recommenders with a demo interface.
2. A comparison report on ranking metrics versus the baseline.

Timeline:
14 weeks: data prep (2), implementation (5), evaluation (4), writeup (3).

Title:
A Retail Customer Service Chatbot with Intent Classification

Problem Statement:
Online retailers receive repetitive customer questions about orders, returns, and stock that overwhelm small support teams during peak periods. Keyword-based auto-replies misread phrasing and frustrate customers, so a chatbot that understands intent is needed.

Objectives:
1. To build a chatbot that classifies customer messages into common retail intents.
2. To return appropriate answers and hand off uncertain cases to a human.
3. To evaluate intent-classification accuracy and response relevance.

Methodology:
Intents are defined from a public retail support dataset and augmented with paraphrases. A fine-tuned DistilBERT classifier handles intent detection, with a confidence threshold triggering human handoff. The bot is served through a web widget. Evaluation reports accuracy and macro-F1 on a held-out test set against a TF-IDF plus logistic-regression baseline.

Scope:
The chatbot covers order status, returns, and stock queries only. Live order-system integration and multilingual support are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working retail chatbot with handoff logic.
2. Classification metrics compared to the baseline.

Timeline:
14 weeks of data work, modelling, integration, and evaluation.

Title:
A Knowledge-Graph Search Tool for Smart-City Open Data

Problem Statement:
Smart-city open-data portals publish datasets on transport, utilities, and amenities, but residents and analysts struggle to connect related facts across separate tables. Keyword search returns isolated datasets and cannot answer questions that span multiple entities like "bus stops near flooded roads".

Objectives:
1. To build a knowledge graph linking smart-city entities such as roads, stops, and facilities.
2. To provide a search interface that answers relationship queries over the graph.
3. To evaluate answer correctness against a set of benchmark questions.

Methodology:
Selected open datasets are mapped to an RDF schema and loaded into a Neo4j graph. A query layer translates a constrained natural-language form into Cypher. A benchmark of 30 relationship questions with known answers measures precision and recall. A baseline keyword search over the raw tables is used for comparison.

Scope:
The graph covers three linked domains for one city's open data. Live streaming updates and full open-domain natural language are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A populated knowledge graph with a search interface.
2. Accuracy results versus keyword-search baseline.

Timeline:
14 weeks: modelling (3), ingestion (3), query layer (4), evaluation (4).

Title:
Semantic Segmentation of Tourist Landmarks for an Auto-Tagging Travel App

Problem Statement:
Travel apps that auto-tag user photos rely on whole-image classification, which fails when a landmark occupies only part of a cluttered scene with crowds and signage. Pixel-level segmentation of the landmark region would improve tagging and enable background blurring, but tourism-specific segmentation datasets are scarce.

Objectives:
1. To assemble and annotate a landmark segmentation dataset from public tourism images.
2. To train a semantic segmentation model that isolates landmark regions from background.
3. To benchmark the model against established baselines using standard segmentation metrics.

Methodology:
About 1,500 images of ten landmarks will be annotated with polygon masks. A U-Net and a DeepLabV3+ (ResNet-50 backbone, ImageNet-pretrained) will be trained with augmentation. Evaluation uses mean IoU, Dice, and pixel accuracy on a held-out 20% test split with 5-fold cross-validation, comparing against an FCN baseline. Class imbalance is handled with weighted loss.

Scope:
The work covers single-landmark-per-image segmentation for ten landmarks. Video, real-time mobile inference, and instance segmentation are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An annotated dataset and two trained segmentation models.
2. A benchmark report on mIoU and Dice against the baseline.

Timeline:
15 weeks: annotation (4), training (5), evaluation (3), writeup (3).

Title:
Detecting Harmful Visual Content in Social-Media Images via Object Detection

Problem Statement:
Social platforms must flag images containing specific harmful objects such as weapons before they spread, yet manual moderation does not scale and generic classifiers cannot localize the offending object for reviewer context. An object detector that both flags and bounds the object would speed moderation, but class imbalance and small objects make this hard.

Objectives:
1. To curate a labelled dataset of harmful-object images with bounding boxes.
2. To train an object-detection model that localizes the target objects.
3. To evaluate detection accuracy and inference speed against baselines.

Methodology:
A dataset is built from public sources and annotated in YOLO format for three object classes. YOLOv8 and Faster R-CNN are trained with augmentation and class-balanced sampling. Evaluation uses mAP@0.5, mAP@0.5:0.95, precision, recall, and frames-per-second on a held-out test set, with an SSD baseline. Failure cases on small and occluded objects are analysed.

Scope:
Detection covers three harmful object classes in still images. Text moderation, video, and deployment to a live platform are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An annotated dataset and two trained detectors.
2. A comparative report on mAP and speed versus the baseline.

Timeline:
15 weeks across annotation, training, evaluation, and analysis.

Title:
Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis of Patient Feedback for Hospital Services

Problem Statement:
Hospitals collect large volumes of free-text patient feedback, but overall star ratings hide which aspects—staff attitude, waiting time, cleanliness—drive dissatisfaction. Document-level sentiment tools give a single polarity and cannot attribute sentiment to specific service aspects that managers can act on.

Objectives:
1. To build an aspect-based sentiment model that links sentiment to predefined hospital service aspects.
2. To compare a transformer approach with a classical machine-learning baseline.
3. To evaluate aspect-level performance on annotated patient feedback.

Methodology:
Around 4,000 patient reviews will be labelled for four aspects and their sentiment polarity. A fine-tuned BERT model performs joint aspect detection and polarity classification, compared with an SVM over TF-IDF features. Evaluation reports per-aspect F1 and macro-F1 with 5-fold cross-validation and McNemar's test for significance. Preprocessing handles medical abbreviations.

Scope:
The model covers four service aspects in English reviews only. Real-time dashboards and multilingual feedback are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An annotated dataset and a trained aspect-based sentiment model.
2. A statistically tested comparison against the baseline.

Timeline:
15 weeks: annotation (4), modelling (5), evaluation (3), writeup (3).

Title:
Learned Cardinality Estimation for Query Optimization in Financial Databases

Problem Statement:
Query optimizers in relational databases pick execution plans using cardinality estimates, but on skewed, correlated financial data the histogram-based estimators built into engines like PostgreSQL produce large errors, leading to slow plans. A learned estimator could reduce error, though training cost and generalization to unseen queries are open concerns.

Objectives:
1. To build a learned cardinality estimator for multi-predicate queries on financial tables.
2. To integrate the estimates into plan selection and measure runtime impact.
3. To benchmark estimation error and query latency against the native optimizer.

Methodology:
A workload of analytical queries is generated over a synthetic financial schema (TPC-H-style with skew). A multi-set convolutional network is trained on query-cardinality pairs. Q-error quantifies estimation accuracy; end-to-end latency is measured after feeding estimates back via plan hints. Baselines are PostgreSQL's default estimator and a sampling estimator, evaluated on held-out query templates.

Scope:
The work targets single-table and two-way join selectivity for SELECT queries. Updates, transactions, and full optimizer replacement are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained cardinality estimator with an integration harness.
2. Q-error and latency results versus both baselines.

Timeline:
15 weeks: workload (3), model (5), integration (3), evaluation (4).

Title:
A Facial-Recognition Attendance System for a Manufacturing Plant Floor

Problem Statement:
Manufacturing plants track worker attendance with badge taps, which allow buddy-punching and slow shift changeovers at the gate. Facial recognition could automate check-in, but plant conditions—poor lighting, helmets, masks, and motion—degrade accuracy, and existing demos assume clean frontal faces.

Objectives:
1. To build a facial-recognition attendance pipeline robust to partial occlusion and varied lighting.
2. To evaluate recognition accuracy under simulated plant conditions.
3. To measure anti-spoofing effectiveness against printed-photo attacks.

Methodology:
Face detection uses MTCNN, and embeddings come from a pretrained FaceNet model, matched by cosine similarity against an enrolled gallery. A simulated dataset adds occlusion (masks/helmets) and brightness variation to a public face set. Evaluation reports verification accuracy, false-accept and false-reject rates, and ROC-AUC, with a basic blink-based liveness check tested against photo spoofs. A Haar-cascade pipeline is the baseline.

Scope:
The system handles enrolment and one-to-many identification for up to 100 workers. Payroll integration and 3D-mask spoofing defence are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working attendance pipeline with liveness check.
2. Accuracy, FAR/FRR, and spoofing-resistance results versus the baseline.

Timeline:
15 weeks of dataset prep, pipeline build, and evaluation.

Title:
Robust OCR Pipeline for Degraded Public-Safety Incident Reports with Layout-Aware Post-Correction

Problem Statement:
Public-safety agencies hold decades of handwritten and typed incident reports on degraded, multi-column forms. Off-the-shelf OCR mis-reads these due to noise, stamps, and mixed print/handwriting, and downstream search fails on the resulting garbled text. There is no openly evaluated pipeline that pairs robust recognition with layout-aware, domain-lexicon post-correction for this report type, leaving a gap this project targets.

Objectives:
1. To assemble and ground-truth a benchmark of 600 degraded incident-report pages spanning typed, handwritten, and mixed forms.
2. To build an end-to-end pipeline combining document layout analysis, recognition, and a domain-lexicon post-correction model.
3. To rigorously evaluate accuracy and downstream search retrieval against established baselines with statistical significance and error analysis.

Methodology:
Layout regions are detected with LayoutParser; text is recognized with a fine-tuned TrOCR (transformer) model and compared against Tesseract 5 and PaddleOCR baselines. A character-level seq2seq post-corrector trained on a public-safety lexicon refines output. Evaluation uses Character and Word Error Rate plus retrieval Precision@10 on a search task, with 5-fold cross-validation, bootstrap confidence intervals, and a paired t-test. Annotation uses double-coding with inter-annotator agreement (Cohen's kappa). Risks (annotation cost, privacy) are mitigated by redaction and a phased annotation plan.

Scope:
The pipeline covers English incident reports with up to two-column layouts; included are typed, handwritten, and mixed pages. Excluded: non-English text, table-structure extraction, and live capture from scanners. Data is de-identified before use.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A de-identified annotated benchmark and a reproducible OCR-plus-post-correction pipeline.
2. A CER/WER and retrieval evaluation showing significant gains over Tesseract and PaddleOCR, with documented failure modes.

Timeline:
16 weeks: annotation and IAA (4), pipeline integration (4), post-correction training (3), evaluation and significance testing (3), writeup (2).

Title:
Anomaly Detection in Wireless Sensor Networks for Predictive Maintenance of Energy Substations

Problem Statement:
Energy substations rely on wireless sensor networks reporting temperature, vibration, and current, but readings drift, drop, and spike under interference, making faults hard to distinguish from sensor noise. Threshold alarms produce many false positives and miss slow degradations. No openly benchmarked, resource-aware anomaly detector exists that separates true equipment faults from sensor faults on multivariate substation streams under realistic packet loss.

Objectives:
1. To curate a labelled multivariate sensor dataset with injected equipment and sensor faults plus realistic packet loss.
2. To develop a lightweight anomaly-detection model distinguishing equipment faults from sensor faults within node compute limits.
3. To evaluate detection quality, latency, and on-node cost against statistical and deep baselines with ablations.

Methodology:
A semi-supervised LSTM-autoencoder with a reconstruction-error threshold is trained on normal windows, augmented by a fault classifier separating equipment from sensor anomalies. Baselines are an ARIMA residual detector, Isolation Forest, and a Transformer detector. Evaluation reports precision, recall, F1, PR-AUC, and detection latency under 5-fold time-series cross-validation, with bootstrap confidence intervals and an ablation on input channels and window size. Model size and inference time are measured against an embedded memory budget. Risks (label scarcity, drift) are mitigated with synthetic injection and a drift-monitoring check.

Scope:
The work covers three sensor modalities on one substation topology with offline analysis and an on-node feasibility estimate. Excluded: live deployment, network-routing optimization, and multi-substation transfer learning.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A labelled benchmark dataset and a resource-aware anomaly detector with fault-type separation.
2. An evaluation report with significance testing, ablations, and an on-node cost analysis showing gains over all baselines.

Timeline:
16 weeks: dataset and fault injection (3), model development (5), baselines and ablations (4), evaluation and writeup (4).

Title:
Tourism Prediction System with Machine Learning

Problem Statement:
Tourism is very big and there is a lot of data. People want to know about tourists so my project will help with that using AI and machine learning which is very popular now.

Objectives:
1. To use machine learning
2. To classify tourists
3. To make a good system

Methodology:
I will use Python and some machine learning algorithms to classify the tourism data. I will do research online and find datasets and then train the model to get results.

Scope:
This can be used by hotels, airlines, travel agencies and the government for all of tourism everywhere.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working system

Title:
Deep Learning Image Detection for Social Media

Problem Statement:
Social media has many images and videos and it is hard to understand all of them. Deep learning and computer vision is a trending technology that can solve this problem in a smart way.

Objectives:
1. To detect images
2. To use deep learning
3. To help social media

Methodology:
I plan to use deep learning and neural networks to look at the social media images. I will get pictures from the internet and train the computer to see them.

Scope:
The project covers all social media platforms like Facebook, Instagram, TikTok and others.

Expected Outcomes:
1. The system can detect images
2. High performance

Title:
NLP Healthcare Text Project

Problem Statement:
Hospitals have many documents and text that nobody can read fast. Natural language processing is a powerful AI field so I want to apply it to healthcare to make things better and faster for everyone.

Objectives:
1. To do natural language processing
2. To read healthcare text
3. To assist doctors and patients

Methodology:
I will use NLP techniques and some libraries in Python to process the medical text. After that I will analyze and show the output to the user.

Scope:
It will work for all hospitals, clinics and medical records across the whole country.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A text processing tool
2. Useful results for healthcare

Timeline:
Around one semester or two.

Title:
A Recommender System for Personal Finance Products

Problem Statement:
Many young customers struggle to pick suitable financial products such as savings accounts or credit cards because banks list dozens of options with confusing terms. A recommendation tool could suggest products that match a user's spending habits, but most current banking apps only show static lists.

Objectives:
1. To collect a dataset of financial products and sample user profiles.
2. To build a recommender that suggests products based on user spending.
3. To evaluate whether users find the recommendations helpful.

Methodology:
The system will use collaborative filtering and content-based filtering to match users with products. I will build it as a web app in Python using Flask, and store data in a MySQL database. A small survey will be used to test user satisfaction.

Scope:
The project focuses on personal finance products for individual users. It will not handle real banking transactions or live account data, and uses synthetic profiles instead.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A web-based recommender prototype.
2. A short evaluation report on recommendation quality.

Timeline:
The project will run over two semesters, with development in the first and testing in the second.

Title:
Voice Command Recognition for Factory Machine Control

Problem Statement:
On factory floors workers often have their hands busy and cannot easily operate control panels. A speech recognition interface could let operators give simple voice commands to machines, but noisy environments make this difficult and few small factories have such systems.

Objectives:
1. To record a small set of spoken machine commands.
2. To train a speech recognition model for these commands.
3. To test recognition accuracy in a noisy setting.

Methodology:
I will collect audio samples of around ten commands and use a pre-trained speech model with fine-tuning. The recogniser will be connected to a simple simulator that shows which command was understood. Accuracy will be measured by counting correct recognitions.

Scope:
The project handles a fixed vocabulary of about ten English commands for one demonstration machine. It does not cover continuous speech, multiple languages, or real machinery integration.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working voice command demo for the fixed vocabulary.
2. An accuracy comparison between quiet and noisy recordings.

Timeline:
Data collection and model training in semester one, evaluation in semester two.

Title:
Machine Learning Based Network Intrusion Detection for Public Safety Networks

Problem Statement:
Public safety agencies run networks that carry sensitive emergency data, making them targets for attacks. Traditional rule-based firewalls miss new attack patterns. A machine learning intrusion detector could flag unusual traffic, but choosing the right features and avoiding false alarms is challenging.

Objectives:
1. To use a public intrusion dataset to study attack traffic.
2. To train a classifier that separates normal and malicious traffic.
3. To measure detection accuracy and false positive rate.

Methodology:
I will use the NSL-KDD dataset and train models such as decision trees and random forests with scikit-learn. Features will be selected from the dataset columns. Performance will be reported using accuracy, precision, and recall.

Scope:
The work is an offline study on an existing dataset, simulating a public safety context. It does not include live network capture, real-time blocking, or deployment on agency hardware.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained intrusion detection model with reported metrics.
2. A comparison of two or three algorithms.

Timeline:
Literature review and data preparation first, then training and evaluation in the second semester.

Title:
Web Application Vulnerability Scanner for Energy Sector Portals

Problem Statement:
Energy companies increasingly run web portals for customers to view bills and usage, and these portals can have security holes like SQL injection or cross-site scripting. Small energy providers often lack security testing tools, leaving their sites exposed.

Objectives:
1. To study common web vulnerabilities affecting customer portals.
2. To build a scanner that checks a target site for a few vulnerability types.
3. To test the scanner on a deliberately vulnerable practice site.

Methodology:
The scanner will be written in Python and send crafted requests to detect SQL injection and XSS, similar to basic features of existing tools. I will test it against a sandbox app such as DVWA and record which issues are found.

Scope:
The tool checks a small set of vulnerability categories on a single web app at a time, framed around an energy portal example. It will not perform exploitation, authenticated scanning, or scanning of real production systems.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A command-line vulnerability scanner prototype.
2. A test report listing detected and missed vulnerabilities.

Timeline:
Two semesters, with build then testing.

Title:
A Static and Dynamic Malware Analysis Toolkit for Small Business IT Staff

Problem Statement:
Small businesses rarely employ security specialists, so when a suspicious file appears staff cannot easily judge whether it is malware. Commercial sandboxes are costly and complex. A lightweight toolkit that combines basic static and dynamic analysis with plain-language reports would help non-expert IT staff triage files.

Objectives:
1. To collect a labelled set of benign and malicious Windows samples from public sources.
2. To implement static feature extraction (PE headers, imported APIs, strings) and dynamic behaviour logging in a sandbox VM.
3. To classify samples and produce a readable risk report, evaluating accuracy against the labels.

Methodology:
Static features will be extracted with pefile and a strings parser; dynamic behaviour will be captured by running samples in an isolated Windows VM with API monitoring. A random forest classifier trained on these features will output a risk score. Evaluation uses an 80/20 split with accuracy, precision, and recall, compared against a strings-only baseline.

Scope:
The toolkit targets Windows PE executables and uses public datasets such as samples from VirusShare for malware and clean system binaries for benign cases. It excludes mobile malware, packed-binary unpacking, and real-time endpoint protection.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working analysis toolkit with a plain-language report generator.
2. An evaluation comparing combined static-plus-dynamic features against a baseline.

Timeline:
Semester one: dataset and static analysis. Semester two: dynamic analysis, classifier, evaluation.

Title:
A Responsive Web Platform for Connecting Smallholder Farmers to Buyers

Problem Statement:
Smallholder farmers often sell produce through middlemen who take large margins, partly because farmers lack a direct channel to reach buyers. Existing marketplaces are not tailored to local crops or low-end devices. A responsive web platform could let farmers list produce and buyers browse nearby listings.

Objectives:
1. To gather requirements from a small group of farmers and buyers through interviews.
2. To build a responsive web platform for posting and searching produce listings.
3. To evaluate usability with representative users.

Methodology:
The platform will be built with React on the front end and a Node.js and PostgreSQL back end, using responsive CSS so it works on phones and desktops. Core features include listing creation, search by crop and location, and a contact channel. Usability will be assessed with a System Usability Scale survey after task-based testing.

Scope:
The platform covers listing, searching, and contacting for a single region's common crops. It excludes online payments, delivery logistics, and a native mobile app.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A deployed responsive web platform with the core listing and search features.
2. A usability evaluation summarising SUS scores and feedback.

Timeline:
Requirements and design in semester one; build and usability testing in semester two.

Title:
A Progressive Web App for Real-Time Public Bus Tracking

Problem Statement:
Bus passengers in many cities cannot tell when the next bus will arrive, leading to long waits and uncertainty. Dedicated native apps require installation and updates, which discourages occasional riders. A progressive web app that works offline and installs from the browser could give arrival estimates without an app store download.

Objectives:
1. To design a PWA that displays bus routes and live positions on a map.
2. To compute and show estimated arrival times from position updates.
3. To evaluate the app's offline behaviour and arrival-estimate error.

Methodology:
The PWA will use React with a service worker for offline caching and a manifest for installability. Bus positions will come from a public GTFS-Realtime feed (or a simulated feed if none is available), displayed with Leaflet maps. Arrival estimates will be computed from position and route data, and estimate error will be measured against logged actual arrivals over several runs.

Scope:
The app covers a small number of bus routes in one city and focuses on tracking and arrival estimation. It excludes ticketing, payment, and trip planning across multiple transport modes.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An installable PWA with offline route viewing and live tracking.
2. A report on arrival-estimate accuracy and offline performance.

Timeline:
Semester one for data integration and UI; semester two for arrival logic and evaluation.

Title:
A Cross-Platform Mobile App for Household Carbon Footprint Tracking

Problem Statement:
Many people want to reduce their environmental impact but have no clear sense of how daily choices like transport and electricity use add up. Existing carbon calculators are one-off web forms that do not track change over time, so users get little ongoing feedback.

Objectives:
1. To design a cross-platform mobile app that logs household activities and estimates their carbon footprint.
2. To show trends and personalised reduction tips over time.
3. To evaluate estimate plausibility and user engagement.

Methodology:
The app will be built with Flutter so a single codebase runs on Android and iOS, with local storage via SQLite and charts for trends. Carbon estimates use published emission factors for electricity, transport, and diet. A two-week trial with a small user group will gather engagement data and feedback through a questionnaire.

Scope:
The app covers electricity, personal transport, and diet categories for individual households. It excludes corporate carbon accounting, automatic smart-meter integration, and carbon offset purchasing.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working cross-platform app with logging, trends, and tips.
2. An evaluation of user engagement and estimate plausibility.

Timeline:
Design and build in semester one; user trial and analysis in semester two.

Title:
An Android Native App for Last-Mile Delivery Driver Coordination

Problem Statement:
Last-mile delivery drivers for small courier firms often manage their stops with paper lists or generic chat apps, which makes route order and proof of delivery hard to track. This causes missed parcels and disputes. A purpose-built Android app could organise stops and capture delivery confirmation.

Objectives:
1. To build a native Android app that lists assigned delivery stops in route order.
2. To capture proof of delivery via photo and signature, syncing to a back end.
3. To evaluate task completion time and driver feedback.

Methodology:
The app will be developed natively in Kotlin using Android Jetpack components, with Room for offline storage and Retrofit to sync with a Spring Boot back end. Stops will be ordered using a simple nearest-neighbour heuristic from device location. A usability test with a few drivers will compare completion time against their current paper method.

Scope:
The app targets Android phones for a single courier company's drivers and covers stop management and proof of delivery. It excludes dispatcher route optimisation at scale, customer-facing tracking, and iOS support.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working Android app with offline stop lists and proof-of-delivery capture.
2. An evaluation comparing the app to the existing paper workflow.

Timeline:
Semester one: app build and back end. Semester two: sync, testing, evaluation.

Title:
An IoT Sensor Network for Monitoring Public Facility Conditions in E-Government

Problem Statement:
Local government offices and public facilities often discover problems like overheating server rooms or flooded basements only after damage occurs, because monitoring relies on occasional manual checks. A low-cost IoT sensor network feeding a dashboard could give staff early warnings and support more responsive public service management.

Objectives:
1. To deploy temperature, humidity, and water-leak sensors on microcontrollers in a test area.
2. To collect readings to a central server and display them on a web dashboard with alerts.
3. To evaluate sensor reliability and alert timeliness.

Methodology:
Sensors will be wired to ESP32 boards publishing readings over MQTT to a Mosquitto broker and stored in InfluxDB. A web dashboard built with Grafana will visualise data and trigger threshold alerts by email. Reliability will be assessed by measuring missed-reading rate over a multi-day run, and alert latency will be timed against induced events.

Scope:
The prototype covers three sensor types in one small test environment standing in for a public facility. It excludes city-wide deployment, mains-power safety certification, and integration with existing government IT systems.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working IoT monitoring prototype with a live dashboard and alerts.
2. An evaluation of reliability and alert timeliness.

Timeline:
Hardware and data pipeline in semester one; dashboard, alerts, and evaluation in semester two.

Title:
A Smart Home Automation System to Support Focused Study Environments for Students

Problem Statement:
Students studying at home struggle to maintain a distraction-free environment, with lighting, noise, and device use working against concentration. General smart-home platforms automate comfort but are not tuned to study sessions, and there is little work linking automated environmental control to measured study focus.

Objectives:
1. To design a rule-and-schedule automation system that adjusts lighting and notifies on noise during declared study sessions.
2. To integrate a Pomodoro-style session manager that controls connected devices automatically.
3. To evaluate whether the automation improves self-reported focus and reduces phone interruptions compared with a manual baseline.

Methodology:
The system uses Home Assistant on a Raspberry Pi as the hub, controlling smart bulbs and a noise sensor via MQTT and Zigbee. A custom session-manager component sets lighting scenes per Pomodoro phase and logs ambient noise and phone-unlock counts. A within-subjects study with around ten participants compares automated versus manual sessions, using a focus questionnaire and interruption counts analysed with a paired t-test.

Scope:
The system controls lighting and noise alerting in a single room for individual study, integrating commodity Zigbee devices. It excludes HVAC control, multi-room orchestration, and voice assistants.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working study-focused automation system with a session manager.
2. An evaluation reporting focus and interruption differences between conditions.

Timeline:
Weeks 1-4 requirements and hardware setup; 5-10 automation and session manager; 11-16 user study and analysis.

Title:
Edge-Based Real-Time Shelf Stock Detection for Retail Stores

Problem Statement:
Out-of-stock shelves cost retailers sales, yet manual shelf audits are infrequent and cloud-based vision systems raise latency, bandwidth, and privacy concerns. Running stock detection at the edge could give near real-time alerts without streaming video off-site, but edge devices have limited compute, so model efficiency is the key challenge.

Objectives:
1. To train an object detection model that identifies empty shelf regions from shelf images.
2. To optimise and deploy the model on an edge device with quantisation, meeting a latency target.
3. To evaluate the accuracy-latency trade-off against a non-quantised baseline.

Methodology:
A YOLOv8-nano model will be trained on the public SKU-110K and an annotated empty-shelf set, then quantised with TensorRT and deployed on an NVIDIA Jetson Nano. Detection of empty regions triggers a restock alert. Evaluation reports mAP and per-frame latency on the edge device, comparing FP32, FP16, and INT8 variants, with attention to the accuracy lost through quantisation.

Scope:
The system detects empty-shelf regions from a fixed camera view in a controlled mock-shelf setup. It excludes product-level SKU identification, multi-camera coverage, and integration with store inventory systems.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A deployed edge stock-detection prototype with restock alerting.
2. An evaluation of the accuracy-latency trade-off across precision levels.

Timeline:
Weeks 1-5 data and training; 6-10 edge optimisation and deployment; 11-16 evaluation and reporting.

Title:
A Cloud-Native Microservices Architecture for a Smart City Parking Service

Problem Statement:
Smart city parking systems must handle bursty demand and combine several functions such as availability, reservations, and payments. Monolithic designs scale poorly and are hard to update independently. A cloud-native microservices architecture promises independent scaling and deployment, but adds complexity in service communication, data consistency, and observability that must be evaluated rather than assumed.

Objectives:
1. To design and implement a microservices-based parking backend with separate availability, reservation, and notification services.
2. To deploy it on Kubernetes with an API gateway, service discovery, and centralised logging.
3. To evaluate scalability and resilience under load compared with a monolithic version.

Methodology:
Services will be built in Spring Boot, containerised with Docker, and orchestrated on a local Kubernetes cluster (k3s) with an Ingress gateway and Prometheus/Grafana monitoring. Asynchronous events use RabbitMQ. A functionally equivalent monolith serves as the baseline. Load tests with k6 measure throughput, latency, and behaviour under a simulated pod failure to assess resilience.

Scope:
The project covers three core services and their orchestration in a simulated smart-city parking scenario with synthetic data. It excludes real payment gateways, mobile front ends, and multi-cloud deployment.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A deployed microservices parking backend on Kubernetes.
2. A comparative evaluation of scalability and resilience versus a monolith.

Timeline:
Weeks 1-4 design and core services; 5-10 orchestration and observability; 11-16 load testing and comparison.

Title:
A DevOps CI/CD Pipeline with Automated Quality Gates for Tourism Web Services

Problem Statement:
Small tourism software teams often deploy manually, leading to slow releases and avoidable defects reaching production. Adopting CI/CD can help, but teams lack guidance on which automated quality gates meaningfully reduce defects without slowing delivery. This project builds and measures such a pipeline for a sample tourism booking service.

Objectives:
1. To implement a CI/CD pipeline that builds, tests, scans, and deploys a tourism booking service automatically.
2. To add quality gates for unit-test coverage, static analysis, and container vulnerability scanning.
3. To evaluate the effect of the pipeline on lead time and defect escape rate against a manual baseline.

Methodology:
The pipeline will use GitHub Actions to run tests, enforce a coverage threshold, run SonarQube static analysis and Trivy image scanning, and deploy to a staging environment via Docker Compose. DORA-style metrics (lead time for changes, deployment frequency, change failure rate) will be collected over a series of seeded change requests and compared with a manual release process on the same service.

Scope:
The work targets one sample tourism booking service and its pipeline, with quality gates limited to testing, static analysis, and image scanning. It excludes production traffic, blue-green or canary release strategies, and infrastructure provisioning automation.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working CI/CD pipeline with enforced quality gates.
2. A measured comparison of delivery and defect metrics versus manual releases.

Timeline:
Weeks 1-4 base pipeline; 5-10 quality gates; 11-16 metric collection and analysis.

Title:
A Big Data Analytics Pipeline for Detecting Trending Topics in Social Media Streams

Problem Statement:
Social media generates high-velocity text streams where emerging topics matter for moderation and public communication, but processing this volume in near real time is hard for simple scripts. A scalable streaming analytics pipeline is needed, and design choices around windowing and aggregation strongly affect both timeliness and accuracy of trend detection.

Objectives:
1. To build a streaming pipeline that ingests social media posts and computes trending terms over time windows.
2. To apply a burst-detection method to flag genuinely rising topics rather than constantly popular ones.
3. To evaluate detection timeliness and precision against a labelled set of known events.

Methodology:
Posts (from a public Twitter/Reddit dataset replayed as a stream) will be ingested through Apache Kafka and processed with Apache Spark Structured Streaming using sliding windows. Term frequencies feed a z-score burst-detection algorithm to surface trends. Results are stored in Elasticsearch and shown on a Kibana dashboard. Evaluation compares detected trends against manually labelled events using detection latency and precision/recall.

Scope:
The pipeline processes English text posts replayed from a fixed dataset to simulate a live stream. It excludes multimedia content, multilingual handling, and production-scale cluster deployment beyond a small local setup.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working Kafka-plus-Spark trend-detection pipeline with a dashboard.
2. An evaluation of trend-detection timeliness and accuracy.

Timeline:
Weeks 1-4 ingestion setup; 5-10 streaming analytics and burst detection; 11-16 evaluation and dashboard.

Title:
A Business Intelligence Dashboard for Reducing Outpatient Clinic Appointment No-Shows

Problem Statement:
Outpatient clinics lose capacity and revenue to appointment no-shows, yet many clinics lack the analytics to see which appointments are at risk or which interventions help. A business intelligence dashboard that combines descriptive analytics with a predictive no-show indicator could let clinic managers target reminders, but such tools must be both accurate and interpretable to be trusted and acted upon by non-technical staff.

Objectives:
1. To design a dimensional data model and ETL process over an appointment dataset capturing patient, scheduling, and outcome attributes.
2. To build an interactive BI dashboard surfacing no-show rates by clinic, time, and patient segment, with a calibrated per-appointment no-show risk score.
3. To evaluate predictive performance with AUROC and calibration, and to assess decision usefulness with clinic staff via a structured walkthrough.

Methodology:
Using the public Kaggle "Medical Appointment No Shows" dataset, an ETL pipeline in Python will clean and load data into a star schema in PostgreSQL. A gradient-boosted model (XGBoost) will predict no-show probability, benchmarked against logistic regression and a prior-rate baseline using stratified 5-fold cross-validation, AUROC, and Brier-score calibration; SHAP values provide interpretable risk drivers. The dashboard, built in Power BI, embeds the risk score and segment views. A think-aloud session with clinic staff assesses interpretability and intended actions.

Scope:
The project covers descriptive analytics and a no-show risk indicator over historical appointment data for outpatient scheduling. It explicitly excludes live electronic-health-record integration, automated sending of reminders, and any clinical diagnostic prediction; all data is de-identified public data.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A deployed BI dashboard with calibrated no-show risk scoring and segment analytics.
2. An evaluation report covering model AUROC, calibration, baseline comparison, and staff-perceived decision usefulness.

Timeline:
Weeks 1-3 data modelling and ETL; 4-7 model development and validation; 8-12 dashboard build; 13-16 staff walkthrough, evaluation, and write-up.

Title:
Probabilistic Day-Ahead Forecasting of Intraday Cryptocurrency Volatility with Transformer and Classical Baselines

Problem Statement:
Risk management for crypto assets depends on anticipating volatility, not just price, yet much student work forecasts only point prices and ignores forecast uncertainty. Realised volatility is highly non-stationary and exhibits clustering, so it is unclear whether modern sequence models meaningfully outperform well-tuned classical econometric methods for day-ahead volatility, especially when forecasts are required as calibrated intervals rather than single numbers.

Objectives:
1. To construct a clean dataset of daily realised volatility for several major crypto assets from minute-level price data.
2. To build and tune classical (GARCH, HAR-RV) and deep (LSTM, Temporal Fusion Transformer) models that produce probabilistic day-ahead volatility forecasts.
3. To evaluate point and probabilistic accuracy with a rolling-origin backtest, and to test whether deep models significantly beat the classical baselines.

Methodology:
Minute-level OHLCV data from a public exchange API will be aggregated into daily realised volatility (Parkinson and realised-variance estimators). HAR-RV and GARCH(1,1) serve as baselines; an LSTM and a Temporal Fusion Transformer (implemented in PyTorch with quantile loss) provide probabilistic forecasts. A walk-forward rolling-origin backtest avoids look-ahead bias. Evaluation uses RMSE and MAE for point forecasts and pinball loss plus interval coverage for probabilistic forecasts; differences are tested with the Diebold-Mariano test. Hyperparameters are tuned on a validation window only.

Scope:
The study forecasts day-ahead daily realised volatility for three to five major cryptocurrencies using historical price data only. It excludes intraday and multi-step horizons, order-book and sentiment features, live trading deployment, and any portfolio or execution strategy.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A reproducible forecasting codebase with classical and deep models and a documented dataset.
2. A backtested comparison reporting point and probabilistic accuracy with statistical significance versus the classical baselines.

Timeline:
Weeks 1-3 data pipeline and feature construction; 4-7 baseline models; 8-11 deep models and tuning; 12-14 rolling backtest and significance testing; 15-16 analysis and write-up.

Title:
Blockchain for Schools

Problem Statement:
Schools have many records and sometimes they get lost or changed. Blockchain is a new technology that is very secure so it can help.

Objectives:
1. Use blockchain in education
2. Make it secure
3. Help schools

Methodology:
I will study blockchain and smart contracts and then build something using it. I will use Solidity maybe and do testing.

Scope:
This can be used by all schools and universities everywhere to store all their data safely on the blockchain.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A blockchain system for schools
2. More security

Title:
AR Shopping App

Problem Statement:
Shopping is boring sometimes and people want new things. Augmented reality is cool and can make shopping fun and better for customers.

Objectives:
1. Make an AR app for shops
2. Let people see products
3. Make shopping fun

Methodology:
I will use Unity and AR to make the app. I will add some products and let users point their phone at things.

Scope:
The app will work for any shop and any product and any customer who has a phone.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An AR app
2. Happy customers

Title:
VR City Training

Problem Statement:
Smart cities are the future and workers need training. VR is good for training because it feels real. So I want to make a VR thing.

Objectives:
1. Build a VR simulation
2. Train city workers
3. Use new technology

Methodology:
I will use a VR headset and some software to make a virtual city. People can walk around and learn things in it.

Scope:
It will cover everything about smart cities and can be used by all city workers and councils.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A VR training program
2. Better trained workers

Title:
A 2D Adventure Game to Promote Local Tourism

Problem Statement:
Many young people do not know about local tourist attractions in their state. A simple game could introduce these places in an entertaining way while players explore levels based on real landmarks.

Objectives:
1. Design a 2D side-scrolling game featuring three local landmarks
2. Add quiz checkpoints about each location
3. Test whether players remember the landmarks after playing

Methodology:
The game will be built in Unity using C#. Sprites and backgrounds will be drawn to resemble real places. Each level ends with a short quiz. A small group of students will play it and answer a survey.

Scope:
The game focuses on one state with three landmarks and runs on Windows desktop only. Multiplayer and mobile are not included.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A playable 2D tourism game
2. Survey results on landmark recall

Timeline:
Design month 1, development months 2-4, testing month 5.

Title:
Serious Game for Teaching Safe Social Media Habits

Problem Statement:
Teenagers often share too much personal information online and fall for scams. A serious game could let them practise safe choices in a low-risk setting instead of just reading guidelines.

Objectives:
1. Build a scenario-based game where players manage a fake social media profile
2. Include events such as phishing messages and oversharing prompts
3. Measure score improvement between a first and second playthrough

Methodology:
The game will be developed in Unity with branching scenarios. Each choice affects a privacy score. Around fifteen secondary students will play twice, and pre/post scores will be compared with a short questionnaire.

Scope:
Covers four common online-safety scenarios for English-speaking teenagers on desktop. It does not cover real account integration or parental controls.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working serious game with four scenarios
2. A comparison of pre/post privacy scores

Timeline:
Months 1-2 design, 3-4 build, 5 testing, 6 reporting.

Title:
A Patient Appointment and Records Web System for a Small Clinic

Problem Statement:
Small clinics still rely on paper files, which makes finding patient history slow and appointments easy to double-book. A simple web system could centralise records and bookings for a single clinic.

Objectives:
1. Build a web app for patient registration and appointment booking
2. Allow staff to view and update basic patient records
3. Generate a daily appointment list for the front desk

Methodology:
The system will be built with PHP and MySQL using a standard three-tier design. Staff log in with roles. The clinic's current paper forms will guide the database fields. Two staff members will trial it and give feedback.

Scope:
One clinic, front-desk and doctor roles only. Billing, insurance, and lab integration are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working clinic web system
2. Feedback from trial staff

Timeline:
Requirements month 1, build months 2-4, testing month 5.

Title:
A Telemedicine Booking Platform with Simple Payment

Problem Statement:
Patients in rural areas struggle to reach clinics for minor consultations. A telemedicine platform that books video calls and takes a small payment could reduce unnecessary travel for basic advice.

Objectives:
1. Build a web platform to book and join video consultations
2. Add a basic online payment step before confirmation
3. Let doctors record a short consultation note

Methodology:
The platform uses React on the front end and Node.js with MongoDB on the back end. Video uses an embedded WebRTC library, and payment uses a sandbox gateway. A few volunteers will test booking and joining a call.

Scope:
Single specialty, web only, sandbox payments. Prescriptions, insurance, and real money are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working telemedicine booking platform
2. A test report on the booking and call flow

Timeline:
Months 1-2 design, 3-5 build, 6 test.

Title:
An Adaptive E-Learning Module for Machine-Operator Safety Training

Problem Statement:
New factory operators are usually trained with the same fixed slideshow regardless of prior knowledge, which wastes time for experienced workers and overwhelms beginners. A small e-learning module that adapts content based on quiz performance could make onboarding more efficient.

Objectives:
1. Build an e-learning module covering five machine-safety topics with embedded quizzes
2. Implement a rule-based adaptation that skips or repeats topics based on quiz scores
3. Compare completion time and post-test scores against a fixed-sequence version

Methodology:
The module will be built with Django and a PostgreSQL backend storing quiz results. A rule engine routes learners to the next topic using threshold scores. Twenty trainees will be split into adaptive and fixed groups, and post-test scores plus completion time will be compared with a t-test.

Scope:
Five safety topics for one machine type, desktop browser, English only. Video production and VR are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working adaptive e-learning module
2. A comparison of learning outcomes between adaptive and fixed groups

Timeline:
Months 1-2 content and design, 3-4 development, 5 user study, 6 analysis.

Title:
A QR-Based Mobile Payment App for Community Public-Safety Volunteers

Problem Statement:
Neighbourhood patrol groups collect cash contributions and reimburse volunteers manually, which is hard to track and audit. A lightweight mobile payment and ledger app could record contributions and payouts transparently for a single community group.

Objectives:
1. Build a mobile app for QR-based contributions and volunteer reimbursements
2. Maintain an auditable transaction ledger viewable by the group treasurer
3. Evaluate transaction accuracy and treasurer satisfaction in a small trial

Methodology:
The app will be built with Flutter and Firebase, using a sandbox payment gateway and QR codes for transfers. Each transaction is written to a ledger with timestamp and category. A four-week trial with one patrol group will check whether the ledger matches manual records, plus a usability survey.

Scope:
One community group, sandbox payments, contributions and reimbursements only. Bank integration and tax reporting are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working payment and ledger app
2. A trial report comparing app and manual records

Timeline:
Month 1 design, 2-4 build, 5 trial, 6 reporting.

Title:
Detecting Anomalous Billing in Household Electricity Data

Problem Statement:
Utility billing errors and meter tampering produce unusual consumption patterns that are easy to miss in monthly bills. A model that flags anomalous household electricity readings could help analysts prioritise which accounts to inspect.

Objectives:
1. Engineer features from hourly household smart-meter consumption data
2. Train and compare anomaly-detection models for flagging unusual usage
3. Evaluate detection performance using precision, recall, and a labelled subset

Methodology:
Using a public smart-meter dataset, I will build features such as daily averages and weekday/weekend ratios. Isolation Forest and a simple autoencoder will be compared against a statistical z-score baseline. A manually labelled subset of anomalies will provide ground truth, and models will be scored with precision, recall, and F1.

Scope:
Residential meters from one public dataset, offline batch detection. Real-time streaming and theft localisation are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained anomaly-detection pipeline with comparison results
2. A report on which method best flags billing anomalies

Timeline:
Month 1 data prep, 2-3 modelling, 4 evaluation, 5-6 writing.

Title:
A Product Recommendation Feature for a Small Online Craft Store

Problem Statement:
Small online stores rarely have personalised recommendations, so customers miss related items and owners lose cross-sell opportunities. A lightweight recommender suited to a small catalogue could suggest relevant products without a large data-science team.

Objectives:
1. Build a recommendation module using purchase and view history from a sample store
2. Compare item-based collaborative filtering with a content-based approach
3. Evaluate suggestions using precision@5 on held-out purchases

Methodology:
A sample dataset of orders and product attributes will be used. I will implement item-based collaborative filtering with cosine similarity and a content-based model using product tags, then combine them as a simple hybrid. Offline evaluation uses precision@5 and coverage on a held-out split.

Scope:
One small catalogue under 500 products, offline web prototype. Real-time personalisation and A/B testing on live traffic are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working recommendation module with a comparison table
2. A short integration demo on the sample storefront

Timeline:
Month 1 data, 2-3 models, 4 evaluation, 5 demo, 6 report.

Title:
A Bilingual Chatbot for Smallholder Crop and Pest Queries

Problem Statement:
Smallholder farmers often cannot reach an extension officer quickly when a pest or disease appears. A chatbot that answers common crop and pest questions in simple language could give first-line guidance while officers handle complex cases.

Objectives:
1. Build a chatbot answering questions on three common crops and their pests
2. Support both English and a local language for queries
3. Evaluate answer accuracy against an officer-reviewed question set

Methodology:
Intents and answers will be curated from agricultural extension guides. The bot uses an intent-classification model with a fallback to retrieval over a small FAQ knowledge base. A set of 60 test questions reviewed by an extension officer will measure top-1 answer accuracy and fallback rate.

Scope:
Three crops, text only, two languages. Image-based disease diagnosis and live officer chat are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working bilingual crop-and-pest chatbot
2. An accuracy report against the reviewed question set

Timeline:
Month 1 knowledge base, 2-3 build, 4 testing, 5-6 reporting.

Title:
A Knowledge-Graph Search Tool for Public Bus Route Information

Problem Statement:
Bus information is scattered across route lists, stop names, and schedules, so answering questions like which routes connect two districts requires manual cross-referencing. A knowledge graph linking stops, routes, and areas could power richer search than keyword lookup.

Objectives:
1. Build a knowledge graph of stops, routes, and districts from open transit data
2. Support relationship queries such as routes connecting two stops
3. Compare answer completeness against keyword search on a question set

Methodology:
Open GTFS data for one city will be modelled as a graph in Neo4j, with nodes for stops, routes, and districts and typed edges. A query interface translates a small set of question templates into Cypher. Twenty questions will compare the graph's answer completeness and correctness against a keyword baseline over the same data.

Scope:
One city's bus network, predefined question templates. Real-time arrivals and multi-modal routing are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A populated transit knowledge graph with a query interface
2. A comparison of graph vs keyword search results

Timeline:
Month 1 data modelling, 2-3 graph build, 4 query interface, 5 evaluation, 6 report.

Title:
Semantic Segmentation of Rooftop Solar-Panel Area from Aerial Imagery

Problem Statement:
Estimating rooftop solar adoption usually relies on manual surveys, which are slow and quickly outdated. Automatically segmenting installed panels from aerial imagery would let planners track adoption and estimate generated capacity over time. The challenge is reliable segmentation under varied roof colours, shadows, and panel orientations.

Objectives:
1. Train a U-Net and a DeepLabV3+ model to segment solar panels from aerial tiles
2. Compare both against a thresholding baseline using IoU and F1 at the pixel level
3. Estimate per-rooftop panel area and quantify error against manually traced masks

Methodology:
I will use a public aerial solar dataset, splitting tiles 70/15/15 with stratification by region. Both networks use a ResNet-50 encoder with augmentation for rotation and brightness. Training uses Dice plus cross-entropy loss, early stopping, and 5-fold cross-validation on the training split. Evaluation reports mean IoU, F1, and area-estimation error, with a per-class error analysis.

Scope:
Fixed-resolution RGB aerial tiles for residential rooftops. Tilt/azimuth estimation and energy-yield modelling are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained segmentation model with IoU/F1 reported against baselines
2. A rooftop panel-area estimation report with error analysis

Timeline:
M1 data and baseline, M2-3 model training, M4 cross-validation, M5 area estimation, M6 writing.

Title:
Detecting Damaged and Mislabelled Parcels on a Conveyor Using Object Detection

Problem Statement:
Warehouses manually spot dented boxes and missing labels on conveyors, which is tiring and inconsistent across shifts. An object detector that flags damaged or unlabelled parcels in real time could route them for manual review. The difficulty is small defects, motion blur, and class imbalance for rare damage cases.

Objectives:
1. Train YOLOv8 to detect parcels and classify label-present, label-missing, and visibly-damaged
2. Compare against a Faster R-CNN baseline using mAP@0.5 and per-class recall
3. Measure inference latency to confirm near-real-time feasibility on a single GPU

Methodology:
A dataset of conveyor frames will be annotated with bounding boxes for three classes, augmented with motion blur and brightness jitter, and split 70/15/15. YOLOv8 and Faster R-CNN are trained with the same augmentations; class imbalance is handled with weighted sampling. Evaluation reports mAP@0.5, per-class precision/recall, confusion analysis, and frames-per-second.

Scope:
Single conveyor view, three defect classes, offline-recorded video. Multi-camera tracking and robotic sorting are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained detector with mAP and latency reported against the baseline
2. An error analysis of missed damage and false label-missing cases

Timeline:
M1 annotation, M2-3 training, M4 baseline and tuning, M5 latency tests, M6 reporting.

Title:
Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis of Citizen Feedback on E-Government Services

Problem Statement:
E-government portals collect large volumes of free-text feedback, but agencies struggle to know which specific service aspects, such as login, payment, or response time, frustrate citizens. Overall sentiment alone hides these details. Aspect-based sentiment analysis could route concerns to the right team.

Objectives:
1. Build an aspect-based sentiment pipeline tagging feedback by service aspect and polarity
2. Fine-tune a transformer model and compare it with a TF-IDF plus SVM baseline
3. Evaluate using macro-F1 per aspect on a manually annotated test set

Methodology:
A corpus of public service reviews will be annotated for five aspects and three polarities by two annotators, with Cohen's kappa reported. I will fine-tune a pretrained transformer for joint aspect and polarity classification and compare against a TF-IDF plus linear SVM baseline using a stratified 80/20 split and 5-fold cross-validation. Metrics are macro-F1 and per-aspect confusion.

Scope:
English feedback, five predefined aspects, offline analysis. Multilingual input and live dashboard deployment are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An annotated dataset and a trained aspect-based sentiment model
2. A per-aspect performance comparison against the baseline

Timeline:
M1 annotation, M2 baseline, M3-4 fine-tuning, M5 evaluation, M6 writing.

Title:
A Learned Index-Recommendation Advisor for Student-Records Query Workloads

Problem Statement:
University student-records databases run repeating reporting queries that often scan tables because indexes are chosen by intuition. Manually tuning indexes is error-prone and rarely revisited. An advisor that recommends indexes from an observed query workload could cut query time without a DBA's constant attention.

Objectives:
1. Capture a representative student-records query workload and parse predicates and joins
2. Generate candidate indexes and rank them by an estimated cost-benefit model
3. Measure actual query-time improvement against the unindexed and full-index baselines

Methodology:
Using PostgreSQL with a synthetic but realistic student-records schema, I will log a workload of reporting queries and extract filtered and joined columns. Candidate single- and multi-column indexes are generated, then ranked using the planner's cost estimates against storage cost. The top recommendations are applied and measured with EXPLAIN ANALYZE over a fixed query set, compared to no-index and index-everything baselines.

Scope:
One relational schema, read-heavy reporting queries, single node. Write-heavy workloads and distributed sharding are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An index-recommendation tool with a ranked candidate list
2. A benchmark of query-time improvement against both baselines

Timeline:
M1 workload capture, M2 candidate generation, M3-4 ranking model, M5 benchmarking, M6 reporting.

Title:
A Liveness-Aware Facial-Recognition Attendance System for a Retail Store

Problem Statement:
Retail outlets track staff attendance with badge swipes that allow buddy-punching, where one worker clocks in for another. Facial recognition can reduce this, but naive systems can be fooled by a photo. A liveness check is needed so attendance is both convenient and harder to spoof.

Objectives:
1. Build a face-recognition attendance pipeline with enrolment and daily check-in
2. Add a blink-based liveness check to reject printed-photo spoofing attempts
3. Evaluate recognition accuracy and spoof-rejection rate on a small enrolled cohort

Methodology:
Faces are detected with MTCNN and embedded with a pretrained FaceNet model; identity is matched by cosine distance against enrolled embeddings with a tuned threshold. A blink-detection step using eye-aspect-ratio over consecutive frames provides liveness. Evaluation covers fifteen enrolled staff, reporting recognition accuracy, false-accept and false-reject rates, and spoof-rejection against printed photos and screen replays.

Scope:
One store, up to twenty enrolled staff, indoor lighting, blink-based liveness only. Mask occlusion and large-scale recognition are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working attendance system with enrolment and liveness check
2. An accuracy and spoof-rejection evaluation report

Timeline:
M1 enrolment pipeline, M2-3 recognition, M4 liveness, M5 evaluation, M6 reporting.

Title:
End-to-End Extraction of Structured Fields from Multilingual Smart-City Permit Documents

Problem Statement:
City permit offices receive scanned application forms in mixed English and Malay layouts and re-key fields such as applicant name, address, permit type, and dates by hand, which is slow and error-prone. Generic OCR returns raw text without structure, and off-the-shelf form parsers fail on the varied, low-quality scans typical of counter submissions. A document-processing pipeline that both recognises text and extracts named fields would cut manual data entry while remaining auditable.

Objectives:
1. Build a pipeline that detects, recognises, and extracts eight key fields from scanned permit forms
2. Compare a layout-aware model (LayoutLMv3) against a Tesseract-OCR-plus-regex baseline on field-level F1
3. Quantify robustness to scan degradation (skew, blur, low DPI) and report a human-review fallback rate at a target precision

Methodology:
I will assemble and annotate 800 scanned permit forms (bilingual) with field-level bounding boxes and values, splitting 70/15/15 stratified by form template. Preprocessing applies deskew and adaptive thresholding. The baseline uses Tesseract with regular-expression field rules; the proposed system fine-tunes LayoutLMv3 for token classification over OCR tokens. Models are tuned via 5-fold cross-validation on the training split. Evaluation reports field-level precision, recall, and F1, edit distance on values, and a degradation study with synthetic skew/blur. A confidence threshold sets the human-review fallback rate, and inter-annotator agreement (kappa) is reported. Risks (label noise, template drift) are mitigated by double annotation and a held-out unseen-template set.

Scope:
Eight predefined fields on three permit templates, English and Malay, single-page forms. Handwriting recognition, signature verification, and live counter deployment are explicitly out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An annotated bilingual permit dataset and a reproducible extraction pipeline
2. A field-level F1 comparison with degradation analysis and a precision-controlled review-fallback report

Timeline:
M1 data collection and annotation guidelines, M2 annotation and baseline, M3-4 LayoutLMv3 fine-tuning and cross-validation, M5 degradation and threshold analysis, M6 unseen-template evaluation and writing.

Title:
Short-Horizon Visitor-Density Forecasting from Wireless Sensor Streams at Tourist Sites

Problem Statement:
Popular heritage sites experience crowding spikes that strain staff and degrade visitor experience, yet managers react only after queues form. Wireless sensors (Wi-Fi probe counters and PIR motion units) already produce footfall streams, but raw counts are noisy and offer no lead time. A forecasting model that predicts visitor density fifteen to sixty minutes ahead per zone would let managers redirect flow before congestion. The technical challenge is noisy, intermittently missing sensor data and spatial correlation between adjacent zones.

Objectives:
1. Clean and align multi-sensor footfall streams into a per-zone density time series with imputation
2. Train and compare an LSTM, a Temporal Convolutional Network, and a SARIMA baseline for 15/30/60-minute-ahead forecasts
3. Evaluate accuracy with MAE, RMSE, and MAPE per horizon and a peak-detection lead-time metric

Methodology:
Using a public Wi-Fi/footfall sensor dataset (or a 6-week site deployment if access is granted), I will resample to 5-minute bins, impute short gaps with interpolation and flag long gaps, and engineer calendar and weather features. Data is split by time (no leakage) with a rolling-origin validation scheme. The LSTM and TCN use the same lookback window and are tuned over learning rate and hidden size; SARIMA serves as the statistical baseline. Metrics are MAE, RMSE, MAPE per horizon plus a lead-time measure for crowding peaks above a threshold. Risks (sensor outages, concept drift across seasons) are addressed with gap flagging and a held-out later period.

Scope:
One site with four to six zones, indoor footfall sensors, horizons up to 60 minutes. Individual tracking, identity inference, and outdoor weather sensing are out of scope on privacy and feasibility grounds.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A reproducible pipeline from raw sensor streams to per-zone density forecasts
2. A per-horizon accuracy comparison with lead-time analysis for crowd-management decisions

Timeline:
M1 data ingestion and cleaning, M2 feature engineering and baseline, M3-4 LSTM/TCN training and rolling validation, M5 lead-time and drift analysis, M6 evaluation and writing.

Title:
Speech Recognition for Reporting Environmental Issues

Title:
Network Intrusion Detection for Logistics Networks

Problem Statement:
Logistics companies run networked warehouse and tracking systems that are increasingly targeted by cyberattacks. Many small operators have no intrusion detection in place. This project explores a machine-learning-based detector for suspicious network traffic.

Objectives:
1. Train a classifier on labelled network traffic.
2. Detect common attack types.
3. Measure detection accuracy.

Methodology:
I will use a public dataset such as NSL-KDD and train a model (for example a decision tree or random forest) to separate normal from malicious traffic. Features will be taken from the dataset directly. Accuracy and false positive rate will be reported.

Scope:
The work is limited to offline analysis of an existing dataset and a few attack categories. Live deployment on a real logistics network is out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained intrusion detection model.
2. Accuracy and false-positive results.

Two semesters: literature, dataset preparation, training, and evaluation.

Title:
Detecting Web Vulnerabilities in E-Government Portals

Problem Statement:
E-government portals hold sensitive citizen data and are common targets for web attacks such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting. Smaller agencies rarely run regular security checks. This project builds a scanner that flags common web vulnerabilities.

1. Review common web vulnerability types.
2. Build a scanner for a test web app.
3. Report which vulnerabilities are found.

Methodology:
I will set up a deliberately vulnerable test application and write a scanner in Python that sends crafted inputs to detect SQL injection and XSS. Results will be compared against the known vulnerabilities planted in the test app.

About two semesters from research to testing.

Title:
Static and Dynamic Malware Analysis for a Campus Education Network

Problem Statement:
University networks host thousands of student devices, and malware spreading through shared drives and downloads disrupts learning. IT teams often lack time to analyse each suspicious file. This project develops a small malware analysis pipeline that combines static and dynamic checks to triage Windows samples on a campus network.

Objectives:
1. Build a static analyser extracting features such as imported APIs and strings from PE files.
2. Add a sandboxed dynamic stage that logs runtime behaviour.
3. Classify samples as benign or malicious and evaluate accuracy.

Methodology:
Static features will be extracted with the pefile library and combined with behavioural logs from a Cuckoo-style sandbox. A random forest classifier will be trained on a labelled set drawn from a public malware corpus and benign system binaries. Evaluation uses precision, recall, and F1 on a held-out split.

Scope:
The work targets Windows PE malware only and uses a few hundred samples. Polymorphic evasion, mobile malware, and real-time campus deployment are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working static plus dynamic analysis pipeline.
2. A classification report with precision and recall.

Timeline:
Semester one for setup and static stage; semester two for dynamic stage, classification, and evaluation.

Title:
A Responsive Web Platform for Independent Retail Stores

Problem Statement:

Title:

Scope:
The project covers report submission, offline sync, and a map dashboard for one city district. Automated routing of reports to departments and push notifications are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:

Title:
A Cross-Platform Mobile Travel Companion for Local Tourism

Scope:
The app covers one tourist region with a fixed dataset of attractions. Real-time booking and in-app payments are out of scope.

Semester one for core app and data; semester two for itineraries, offline mode, and testing.

Title:
A Native Android App for Interest-Based Local Social Groups

Problem Statement:
People moving to a new city find it hard to meet others who share their hobbies, and large social platforms feel impersonal for this. A focused native Android app could connect nearby users around shared interests and local meetups. This project builds that app.

Title:
An IoT Sensor Network for Ward Environment Monitoring in Healthcare

Problem Statement:
Hospital wards need stable temperature, humidity, and air quality for patient comfort and infection control, yet many smaller facilities still check conditions manually and irregularly. An IoT sensor network could monitor wards continuously and alert staff to deviations. This project builds a prototype monitoring network.

Objectives:

2. Stream readings to a central dashboard in near real time.
3. Trigger alerts when readings cross configured thresholds.

Methodology:
Each node uses an ESP32 with DHT22 and an air-quality sensor, publishing readings over Wi-Fi via MQTT to a Raspberry Pi broker. Data is stored in InfluxDB and shown on a Grafana dashboard. Threshold alerts are sent by email. The prototype is validated in a lab setting against a reference meter.

Scope:
The prototype uses three nodes in a simulated ward environment. Integration with hospital information systems and medical-grade certification are out of scope.
