Title:
A Smart-Home Automation Hub with On-Device Budget-Aware Energy Control

Problem Statement:
Smart-home energy devices typically optimise comfort without regard to a household's financial constraints, and cloud-dependent hubs raise privacy and outage concerns. There is a gap for a local hub that schedules appliances against a household budget and time-of-use tariffs while keeping data on the premises. This project addresses that finance-aware, privacy-preserving gap.

Objectives:
1. Build a local hub integrating smart plugs, thermostats, and a tariff feed.
2. Implement a scheduler that shifts deferrable loads to minimise cost under a monthly budget.
3. Evaluate cost savings and comfort impact against a baseline always-on schedule.

Methodology:
The hub runs on a Raspberry Pi using Home Assistant for device integration over Zigbee and MQTT. A constraint-based scheduler (formulated as a linear program solved with PuLP) shifts deferrable loads using time-of-use tariff data and forecasted usage. Evaluation replays two weeks of recorded household consumption, comparing total cost, budget adherence, and comfort violations against an unscheduled baseline.

Scope:
The system controls deferrable loads (water heater, dishwasher, EV charger) for a single household. Generation-side control such as solar and battery dispatch is excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working budget-aware automation hub.
2. A comparative evaluation showing cost savings versus the baseline.

Timeline:
Months 1-2 integration; 3-4 scheduler; 5-6 evaluation and write-up.

Title:
Edge-Based Real-Time Defect Detection for Manufacturing Lines

Problem Statement:
Visual quality inspection on manufacturing lines is often manual or relies on sending images to the cloud, adding latency and bandwidth cost that make in-line decisions impractical. Running inference at the edge could enable real-time defect flagging, but model size and latency on constrained hardware are the obstacles. This project builds and evaluates an edge-deployed defect detector.

Objectives:
1. Train a defect classifier on a surface-defect image dataset.
2. Optimise and deploy the model on edge hardware within a latency budget.
3. Measure accuracy, latency, and throughput against a server baseline.

Methodology:
A MobileNetV2 classifier is trained on the NEU surface-defect dataset, then quantised with TensorFlow Lite and deployed to a Raspberry Pi 4 and a Coral Edge TPU. Inference latency, frames per second, and accuracy after quantisation are compared against the full model on a server. A simple conveyor mock-up feeds test images.

Scope:
The work targets one metal-surface defect dataset and image classification only. Multi-camera fusion and integration with line PLCs are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A quantised model running in real time on edge hardware.
2. An accuracy-versus-latency comparison across devices.

Timeline:
Months 1-2 training; 3-4 optimisation and deployment; 5-6 benchmarking and reporting.

Title:
A Cloud-Native Microservices Platform for Public-Safety Incident Coordination

Problem Statement:
Public-safety agencies often run monolithic incident systems that scale poorly during emergencies and are hard to update without downtime. A cloud-native microservices design could scale individual functions and remain available under load, but careful service decomposition and resilience patterns are needed. This project designs and benchmarks such a platform.

Objectives:
1. Decompose incident intake, dispatch, and status tracking into independent microservices.
2. Deploy on Kubernetes with autoscaling and resilience patterns.
3. Evaluate availability and latency under simulated load spikes.

Methodology:
Services are built in Spring Boot, containerised, and orchestrated on a local Kubernetes cluster (kind or minikube), communicating via REST and a message queue (RabbitMQ). Resilience uses circuit breakers (Resilience4j) and horizontal pod autoscaling. Load is generated with k6 to simulate surge traffic, measuring p95 latency, error rate, and recovery time after an induced service failure.

Scope:
The prototype covers three core services and runs on a local cluster. Production cloud hosting, real CAD radio integration, and authentication hardening are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working microservices incident platform on Kubernetes.
2. A resilience and performance report under load.

Timeline:
Months 1-2 service design; 3-4 orchestration and resilience; 5-6 load testing and analysis.

Title:
A CI/CD Pipeline with Automated Quality Gates for Energy-Sector Software

Problem Statement:
Software for energy operations must be reliable, yet many teams still deploy manually, risking regressions in safety-relevant code. A well-designed CI/CD pipeline with automated quality gates could catch defects before release, but choosing effective gates and measuring their impact is non-trivial. This project builds and assesses such a pipeline.

Objectives:
1. Build a CI/CD pipeline that automates build, test, and deployment.
2. Add quality gates for tests, coverage, static analysis, and security scanning.
3. Measure the effect of the gates on defect escape and lead time.

Methodology:
The pipeline uses GitHub Actions to build a sample energy-monitoring service, running unit and integration tests, enforcing coverage and SonarQube quality gates, and scanning dependencies with OWASP Dependency-Check before deploying via Docker to a staging environment. A set of seeded defects is used to measure how many are caught by the gates, alongside DORA-style metrics for lead time and deployment frequency.

Scope:
The work covers one sample service and a single staging target. Multi-environment promotion and blue-green production rollout are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working CI/CD pipeline with enforced quality gates.
2. A report on defects caught and pipeline metrics.

Timeline:
Months 1-2 base pipeline; 3-4 quality gates; 5-6 measurement and reporting.

Title:
A Big-Data Analytics Pipeline for Small-Business Sales Insights

Problem Statement:
Small businesses accumulate sales, inventory, and web-traffic data across disconnected tools but lack the means to combine and analyse it at scale. An affordable batch-and-stream analytics pipeline could surface trends and anomalies, yet building one within small-business resource limits is challenging. This project designs and evaluates such a pipeline.

Objectives:
1. Ingest sales and clickstream data through batch and streaming paths.
2. Process and aggregate the data into queryable insight tables.
3. Evaluate pipeline throughput and the usefulness of generated insights.

Methodology:
Data is ingested with Apache Kafka for streaming and scheduled batch loads, processed with Apache Spark (Structured Streaming and batch jobs), and stored in a partitioned Parquet data lake queried via Spark SQL. Anomaly flags on daily sales use a simple z-score method. Throughput and latency are benchmarked on a generated dataset of one year of synthetic transactions, and insight quality is reviewed against known seeded patterns.

Scope:
The pipeline targets one synthetic small-business dataset and runs on a single multi-core machine in pseudo-distributed mode. Real-time dashboards and ML forecasting are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working batch-and-stream analytics pipeline.
2. A throughput benchmark and validation of detected patterns.

Timeline:
Months 1-2 ingestion; 3-4 processing and storage; 5-6 benchmarking and evaluation.

Title:
A Business-Intelligence Dashboard for Smallholder-Farmer Cooperative Decision Support

Problem Statement:
Agricultural cooperatives aggregate produce from many smallholders but make pricing, storage, and procurement decisions from spreadsheets, with no consolidated view of yields, prices, and spoilage. Existing farm dashboards target large agribusiness and ignore cooperative-level aggregation. The gap is a low-cost BI layer that turns cooperatives' own transactional records into decision-ready indicators with defensible data quality.

Objectives:
1. Model a cooperative star schema over members, crops, deliveries, sales, and spoilage by week 4.
2. Build an ETL layer and an interactive dashboard exposing eight KPIs (yield per hectare, price realisation, spoilage rate, member contribution) by week 12.
3. Evaluate decision usefulness via a task-based study with cooperative managers (n=8), targeting a SUS score above 70.

Methodology:
Transactional data is modelled as a Kimball star schema in PostgreSQL; ETL is built in dbt with tested data-quality assertions (not-null, referential, range). The dashboard uses Apache Superset with drill-down and parameterised date ranges. Evaluation pairs a task-completion study (time and error rate on six realistic decisions) with the System Usability Scale, benchmarked against the cooperatives' current spreadsheet workflow.

Scope:
Two cooperatives and three crop types over one year of historical records are included. Predictive forecasting, mobile field-data capture, and live IoT feeds are explicitly excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A deployed, data-quality-tested BI dashboard with eight validated KPIs.
2. An evaluation report comparing task time, errors, and SUS against the spreadsheet baseline.

Timeline:
Weeks 1-4 modelling and ETL; 5-8 dashboard and KPIs; 9-12 data-quality tests; 13-16 user study and write-up.

Title:
Probabilistic Short-Term Forecasting of Urban Bus Passenger Demand

Problem Statement:
Transit operators schedule buses from static historical averages, leaving services crowded at peaks and empty off-peak. Most published demand models give a single point forecast, which is poorly suited to capacity decisions that hinge on the upper tail of demand. The gap is a calibrated probabilistic short-term forecaster of stop-level boarding demand that quantifies uncertainty for headway planning.

Objectives:
1. Assemble and clean a stop-level boarding dataset with weather and calendar covariates by week 4.
2. Build and compare probabilistic models (seasonal-naive baseline, SARIMAX, LightGBM quantile regression, and a Temporal Fusion Transformer) for 30-to-120-minute-ahead demand by week 12.
3. Evaluate calibration and sharpness with pinball loss and prediction-interval coverage against the seasonal-naive baseline.

Methodology:
Boarding counts are aggregated to 30-minute stop intervals and joined with weather and holiday covariates. Models are trained with rolling-origin (expanding-window) cross-validation to respect temporal order, with hyperparameters tuned on a validation fold. Evaluation uses mean pinball loss across quantiles, P50 MAE/MAPE, and 80%/90% interval coverage; statistical significance of the best model over the baseline is tested with a Diebold-Mariano test. Identified risks (sparse low-traffic stops, holiday distribution shift) are handled by stop clustering and a held-out holiday test set.

Scope:
One city's bus network for stops above a minimum daily ridership over two years of data is covered. Real-time GPS feeds, fare-pricing optimisation, and rail demand are explicitly excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A reproducible probabilistic forecasting pipeline with four compared models.
2. A calibration-and-accuracy report with significance testing versus the baseline.

Timeline:
Weeks 1-4 data and baseline; 5-8 statistical models; 9-12 deep model and tuning; 13-16 evaluation and write-up.

Title:

Title:
Static and Dynamic Analysis of Malicious Links Shared on Social Media

Problem Statement:
Social media platforms are frequently used to spread malware through shortened or disguised links, and ordinary users cannot tell a safe link from a harmful one. While URL blacklists exist, they miss newly created malicious links, so a combined analysis approach that inspects link behaviour could give earlier warnings.

Objectives:
1. Build a tool that extracts and analyses links from social media posts.
2. Apply both static features and dynamic sandbox behaviour to classify links as safe or malicious.
3. Evaluate detection accuracy against a labelled URL dataset.

Methodology:
The tool will collect URLs from sample posts, extract static features such as domain age and URL structure, and run unfamiliar links in an isolated sandbox to observe redirects and downloads. A classifier trained on a public malicious-URL dataset (e.g. PhishTank/URLhaus) will combine these features. Performance will be measured with precision, recall and F1.

Scope:
The project analyses URLs only, not attachments, and works on collected sample posts rather than live platform integration. Mobile malware is excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A link-analysis prototype combining static and dynamic features.
2. An evaluation report with precision, recall and F1.

Timeline:
Semester 1 for data collection and static analysis; semester 2 for sandboxing, classification and evaluation.

Title:
A Responsive Web Platform for Community Clinic Appointment Booking

Problem Statement:
Small community clinics often manage appointments by phone or paper, leading to double bookings and long waits. A responsive web platform that lets patients book online and staff manage slots could reduce these problems, but existing systems are usually too expensive or complex for a single clinic.

Objectives:
1. Develop a responsive web platform for booking and managing clinic appointments.
2. Provide separate patient and staff views with role-based access.
3. Evaluate usability with a small group of test users.

Methodology:
The platform will be built with a React front end and a Node/Express back end backed by a relational database. Patients can browse free slots and book; staff can confirm, reschedule or cancel. The interface will be tested on phone and desktop widths, and usability will be assessed with the System Usability Scale on around eight participants.

Scope:
The system covers booking, rescheduling and a basic admin view for one clinic. It excludes payment, electronic medical records and SMS reminders.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working responsive booking platform.
2. A usability evaluation summary.

Timeline:
Semester 1: requirements and core booking; semester 2: staff features, responsive polish and usability testing.

Title:
A Progressive Web App for Personal Budget Tracking

Problem Statement:
Many people want to track daily spending but find native finance apps heavy and dependent on a constant connection. A progressive web app could offer offline entry and quick access from any device, yet most free budgeting tools do not work well offline or do not install like an app.

Objectives:
1. Build a progressive web app for recording income and expenses.
2. Support offline entry that syncs when the connection returns.
3. Test installability and offline behaviour across browsers.

Methodology:
The PWA will be built with a service worker for caching and IndexedDB for local storage so entries persist offline. A small charting library will summarise spending by category. I will verify installability and offline support using Lighthouse and manual tests on Chrome and Firefox, including airplane-mode entry and later sync.

Scope:
The app handles manual income and expense entry with category summaries. It will not connect to bank accounts or handle multiple currencies.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An installable budget-tracking PWA that works offline.
2. A test report on offline sync and Lighthouse PWA scores.

Timeline:
Semester 1: core entry and storage; semester 2: offline sync, charts and cross-browser testing.

Title:
A Cross-Platform Mobile App for Factory Machine Maintenance Logging

Problem Statement:
On small factory floors, machine maintenance is often recorded on paper, making it hard to track which machines were serviced and when. A mobile app that technicians can use on either Android or iOS would centralise these records, but building two separate native apps is beyond a small team's budget.

Objectives:
1. Build a cross-platform mobile app for logging machine maintenance.
2. Let technicians scan a machine QR code and record service details.
3. Provide a summary view of overdue maintenance.

Methodology:
The app will be developed with Flutter so a single codebase runs on Android and iOS. Each machine carries a QR code that technicians scan to open its log; entries are stored in Firebase. A dashboard highlights machines past their service interval. The app will be tested on two physical devices for core flows.

Scope:
The project covers logging, QR scanning and an overdue list for one factory's machines. It excludes spare-part inventory and integration with existing ERP systems.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A cross-platform maintenance-logging app.
2. An overdue-maintenance dashboard.

Timeline:
Semester 1: data model and logging; semester 2: QR scanning, dashboard and device testing.

Title:
A Native Android App for Community Hazard Reporting

Problem Statement:
Residents who notice public safety hazards such as broken streetlights, open drains or fallen trees often have no easy way to report them, so issues go unfixed for weeks. A native Android app that captures the hazard with a photo and GPS location could speed up reporting to local authorities.

Objectives:
1. Develop a native Android app for reporting neighbourhood hazards.
2. Attach a photo and automatic GPS location to each report.
3. Show submitted reports on a map for follow-up.

Methodology:
The app will be built in Kotlin using Android's camera and location APIs. A report contains a category, photo, GPS coordinates and description, stored in a cloud database. Submitted reports appear as pins on a Google Map. Core flows will be tested on two Android versions to check camera and location permissions.

Scope:
The app covers citizen submission and a map view of reports. It excludes an authority-side admin console and real dispatch to government systems.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A native Android hazard-reporting app.
2. A map view of submitted reports.

Timeline:
Semester 1: capture and storage; semester 2: map view, permissions handling and testing.

Title:
An IoT Sensor Network for Household Energy Monitoring

Problem Statement:
Households rarely know which appliances drive their electricity bill because the meter only shows a total. A low-cost IoT sensor network that measures power use at a few points could reveal where energy goes, but commercial whole-home monitors are expensive and closed.

Objectives:
1. Build an IoT setup that measures power usage at several plug points.
2. Send readings to a central dashboard over WiFi.
3. Display consumption trends so users can spot heavy appliances.

Methodology:
Each sensor node uses an ESP32 with a current sensor to estimate power at a socket and publishes readings over MQTT to a small server. The server stores readings and a web dashboard charts usage per node over time. The prototype will be validated by comparing its readings against a reference plug-in power meter on a few appliances.

Scope:
The prototype covers three to four monitored sockets in one home. It excludes automatic appliance control and billing integration.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working multi-node energy-monitoring prototype.
2. A dashboard showing per-socket consumption trends.

Timeline:
Semester 1: hardware nodes and data pipeline; semester 2: dashboard, accuracy check and reporting.

Title:
A Rule-Based Smart Home Automation Hub for Small Retail Shops

Problem Statement:
Small retail shops waste energy because lighting, signage and air-conditioning are switched manually and often left on after closing. Consumer smart-home apps target homes and lack shop-oriented logic like opening-hours schedules and per-zone control, so owners get little benefit. A configurable automation hub aimed at small shops could cut waste with simple, owner-defined rules.

Objectives:
1. Build a local automation hub that controls lights, signage and AC through smart plugs and relays.
2. Provide a rule engine where owners set schedules and condition-based triggers (e.g. close-time off, motion-based aisle lighting).
3. Evaluate energy savings and rule reliability against a manual baseline over a two-week simulated shop schedule.

Methodology:
A Raspberry Pi hub runs a rule engine that subscribes to sensor events (motion, light level, door) over MQTT and actuates Zigbee/WiFi smart plugs. Owners configure rules through a web UI. Evaluation compares logged energy use under automated rules versus a manual baseline using a plug-in meter, and measures rule firing accuracy and latency.

Scope:
The project covers lighting, signage and AC for a single small shop with up to eight controlled devices. It excludes CCTV, access control and cloud multi-store management.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working automation hub with a rule-configuration UI.
2. An energy-saving and reliability report versus manual operation.

Timeline:
Phase 1 (weeks 1-5): hardware and MQTT integration. Phase 2 (weeks 6-10): rule engine and UI. Phase 3 (weeks 11-14): evaluation and reporting.

Title:
Edge-Based Plant Disease Detection for Smallholder Farms

Problem Statement:
Smallholder farmers often lack reliable internet, so cloud-based crop disease apps are unusable in the field. Running inference on-device would help, but full deep networks are too heavy for low-cost hardware. There is a gap for an edge-deployable, quantised model that detects common leaf diseases offline on affordable boards.

Objectives:
1. Train a lightweight CNN to classify common leaf diseases from the PlantVillage dataset.
2. Quantise and deploy the model on a Raspberry Pi 4 for offline inference.
3. Measure accuracy, inference latency and memory use against a server-class baseline.

Methodology:
A MobileNetV2 classifier will be trained on PlantVillage with data augmentation and an 80/10/10 split, using transfer learning. The model will be converted to TensorFlow Lite with INT8 quantisation and deployed on a Pi 4 with a camera. Evaluation reports top-1 accuracy, per-class F1, on-device latency and RAM use, compared to the unquantised model on a laptop GPU as baseline.

Scope:
The project targets a handful of leaf diseases for two or three crops under controlled lighting. Field robustness to varied backgrounds and pest damage is out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A quantised on-device disease classifier running offline on a Pi.
2. A comparison report of accuracy versus latency and memory trade-offs.

Timeline:
Phase 1 (weeks 1-4): dataset and training. Phase 2 (weeks 5-9): quantisation and deployment. Phase 3 (weeks 10-14): edge evaluation and write-up.

Title:
A Cloud-Native Microservices Backend for Ride-Booking

Problem Statement:
Monolithic ride-booking backends become hard to scale when trip demand spikes, because the whole application must scale together. Splitting concerns into independently deployable microservices can improve scalability and fault isolation, but students rarely demonstrate this with measured evidence on a realistic transport workload.

Objectives:
1. Design a microservices backend for ride booking with separate user, trip, pricing and notification services.
2. Deploy the services on Kubernetes with an API gateway and per-service databases.
3. Evaluate scalability and fault isolation against a monolithic version under load.

Methodology:
Each service is a containerised Spring Boot app communicating via REST and a message queue for trip events. Services run on a local Kubernetes cluster (kind/minikube) behind an API gateway, with horizontal pod autoscaling. A monolithic baseline implements the same features. Load tests with k6 measure throughput and latency at increasing request rates, and a fault-injection test kills one service to compare degradation.

Scope:
The project covers four core services and a booking flow, evaluated under synthetic load. Real payment gateways, driver mobile apps and production deployment are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A deployable microservices ride-booking backend on Kubernetes.
2. A scalability and fault-isolation comparison against the monolith.

Timeline:
Phase 1 (weeks 1-5): service design and implementation. Phase 2 (weeks 6-10): Kubernetes deployment and gateway. Phase 3 (weeks 11-14): load testing, fault injection and analysis.

Title:
A CI/CD Pipeline with Automated Carbon-Aware Build Scheduling

Problem Statement:
Software teams run continuous integration pipelines constantly, but builds are scheduled without regard to the carbon intensity of the electricity grid at that moment. Shifting non-urgent builds to greener periods could lower emissions, yet mainstream CI tools offer no carbon-aware scheduling, so the idea is rarely measured in practice.

Objectives:
1. Build a CI/CD pipeline that automates test, build and deploy for a sample web app.
2. Add a scheduler that delays non-urgent jobs to lower-carbon-intensity windows using grid carbon data.
3. Measure build throughput and estimated carbon savings versus immediate scheduling.

Methodology:
The pipeline uses GitHub Actions to lint, test and containerise a sample app, deploying to a staging environment. A scheduling layer queries a public grid carbon-intensity API and defers jobs tagged non-urgent to greener windows within a deadline. Experiments compare estimated emissions and average job delay against a baseline that runs everything immediately, over a one-week trace.

Scope:
The work covers one application's pipeline and a single grid region's carbon data. Urgent and release builds always run immediately and are out of the deferral scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working CI/CD pipeline with carbon-aware scheduling.
2. A report on carbon savings versus added delay.

Timeline:
Phase 1 (weeks 1-4): base pipeline. Phase 2 (weeks 5-9): carbon-aware scheduler. Phase 3 (weeks 10-14): experiments and evaluation.

Title:
A Big Data Analytics Pipeline for Delivery Route Performance

Problem Statement:
Logistics firms generate large volumes of GPS and delivery-event data, but small operators cannot analyse it because their tools choke on the volume and the data arrives continuously. A scalable batch-and-stream pipeline that turns raw delivery events into route performance metrics would let them spot slow routes, yet building such a pipeline end-to-end is rarely demonstrated at student scale.

Objectives:
1. Build an ingestion-to-dashboard pipeline for delivery GPS and event data.
2. Compute route performance metrics (on-time rate, average delay per route) in both batch and streaming modes.
3. Evaluate pipeline throughput and metric correctness on a public logistics-style dataset.

Methodology:
Delivery events are ingested through Kafka, processed with Spark (batch for history, Structured Streaming for live), and stored in a columnar store for querying. Computed metrics feed a dashboard. A public taxi/delivery trajectory dataset is replayed to simulate load. Evaluation measures events-per-second throughput, end-to-end latency, and checks streaming metrics against batch ground truth for correctness.

Scope:
The pipeline computes a fixed set of route metrics on a single dataset replayed locally. Predictive routing and live integration with a courier's systems are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working batch-and-stream analytics pipeline with a metrics dashboard.
2. A throughput and correctness evaluation report.

Timeline:
Phase 1 (weeks 1-5): ingestion and batch metrics. Phase 2 (weeks 6-10): streaming and dashboard. Phase 3 (weeks 11-14): load testing and evaluation.

Title:
A Self-Service Business Intelligence Dashboard for Municipal Service Requests

Problem Statement:
City councils receive thousands of citizen service requests (potholes, waste, lighting) but resolution data sits in disconnected systems, so managers cannot see which categories or districts lag. Existing commercial BI suites are costly and require data-engineering staff that small councils lack. There is a gap for an open, governance-aware self-service dashboard that turns raw 311-style request logs into actionable performance indicators while respecting role-based data access.

Objectives:
1. Design a dimensional data model and ETL that ingests 311-style request logs into a star schema.
2. Build a self-service BI dashboard exposing SLA compliance, backlog ageing and per-district KPIs with role-based filtering.
3. Evaluate decision usefulness via task-based testing and query performance against a denormalised baseline.

Methodology:
Using the public Chicago 311 dataset, an ETL process (Python/dbt) cleans and loads records into a star schema in PostgreSQL. A dashboard (Apache Superset) presents KPIs with drill-down and row-level security per role. Query performance is benchmarked on star schema versus a flat table at three data volumes. Decision usefulness is assessed by eight participants completing five analytical tasks, measuring task success, time-on-task and SUS, with comparison to reading raw exports as baseline.

Scope:
The project covers descriptive analytics on one city's historical request data with three user roles. Predictive forecasting, live API ingestion and write-back to source systems are explicitly excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A governed self-service BI dashboard backed by a documented star schema and ETL.
2. An evaluation report covering query performance and task-based decision usefulness.

Timeline:
Phase 1 (weeks 1-4): data modelling and ETL. Phase 2 (weeks 5-9): dashboard, KPIs and role-based access. Phase 3 (weeks 10-12): performance benchmarking. Phase 4 (weeks 13-14): user task study and reporting.

Title:
Forecasting Daily Student Engagement on an LMS with Comparative Time-Series Models

Problem Statement:
Learning management systems log daily engagement (logins, submissions, resource views), and early dips often precede course dropout. However, most LMS analytics report only past activity without forecasting, and the few that predict use a single model without testing whether classical methods suffice before adopting heavier deep models. A rigorous comparison on real engagement data is missing, leaving institutions unsure which forecasting approach is worth deploying.

Objectives:
1. Build daily engagement time series per course from the public OULAD learning-analytics dataset.
2. Compare SARIMA, Prophet and an LSTM for forecasting next-week engagement under a unified evaluation.
3. Quantify accuracy gains versus computational cost to guide model selection.

Methodology:
Daily aggregated engagement series are constructed and split with a rolling-origin (time-series cross-validation) scheme to avoid leakage. SARIMA and Prophet serve as classical baselines; an LSTM with tuned look-back is the deep model. All models forecast a 7-day horizon and are scored with MAE, RMSE and MASE against a seasonal-naive baseline; differences are checked with a Diebold-Mariano test. Training time and inference cost are recorded. Hyperparameters are tuned only on training folds.

Scope:
The study forecasts aggregate engagement for a fixed set of courses one week ahead. Per-student dropout prediction and causal intervention are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A reproducible forecasting pipeline comparing three model families with statistical significance testing.
2. An evidence-based recommendation on the accuracy-versus-cost trade-off for LMS engagement forecasting.

Timeline:
Phase 1 (weeks 1-3): data preparation and series construction. Phase 2 (weeks 4-8): baseline models and CV harness. Phase 3 (weeks 9-12): LSTM and tuning. Phase 4 (weeks 13-14): significance testing, cost analysis and reporting.

Title:
Blockchain App for Small Business

Problem Statement:
Small businesses have many problems with payments and trust. Blockchain is a new technology that can help them a lot because it is secure and modern.

Objectives:
1. Make a blockchain system
2. Use smart contracts
3. Help small businesses

Methodology:
I will use blockchain and smart contracts to build the app. I will do research online and watch tutorials to learn how it works.

Scope:
This project is for all small businesses everywhere. It will be very useful and save money.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working blockchain app
2. Happy small businesses

Title:
AR App for Farming

Problem Statement:
Farmers do not have good technology. Augmented reality is cool and can show things on the phone screen so farmers can see better.

Objectives:
1. Build an AR app
2. Help farmers
3. Make farming easy

Methodology:
I will use augmented reality and a phone to make the app. Unity has AR features that I can try.

Scope:
The app is for farmers and agriculture. It will be good for crops.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An AR farming app
2. Better farming

Title:
VR Training for Transport

Problem Statement:
Training drivers is hard and dangerous in real life. Virtual reality can let people practice without danger which is safer and better.

Objectives:
1. Create a VR simulation
2. Train transport workers
3. Be safe

Methodology:
I will make a VR simulation using a headset and game software. I will learn from YouTube how to do VR.

Scope:
This is for transportation companies and drivers. Everyone can use it.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A VR training program
2. Safer drivers

Title:
A 3D Game to Teach Sustainability Habits

Problem Statement:
Many young people do not understand everyday sustainability choices like recycling and saving energy. Lectures and posters are boring, so a game might keep players engaged while teaching these habits.

Objectives:
1. Design a 3D game with levels about recycling, water saving and energy use
2. Build the game so players earn points for correct eco-choices
3. Test if players enjoy the game

Methodology:
The game will be built in Unity with C# scripting. Levels will present scenarios where the player sorts waste or turns off appliances. A scoring system rewards correct actions. After building, a few classmates will play it and give feedback through a short survey.

Scope:
The game focuses on three sustainability topics and runs on Windows desktop. Mobile and multiplayer are not included.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A playable 3D sustainability game with three levels
2. Survey feedback on whether players found it fun and educational

Timeline:
About 12 weeks: design, build, then test.

Title:
Serious Game for Learning Warehouse Logistics Basics

Problem Statement:
New warehouse staff often struggle to learn picking, packing and stock placement quickly, and on-the-job mistakes are costly. A serious game could let trainees practice these tasks in a safe simulated warehouse before working on the real floor.

Objectives:
1. Build a 2D simulation where the player fulfils orders by picking items from shelves
2. Add a time and accuracy score to mimic real performance pressure
3. Evaluate whether players improve their picking speed across attempts

Methodology:
The game will be developed in Unity. The warehouse layout, order list and inventory will be modelled in simple 2D. Each round generates random orders and tracks the player's time and error rate. A small group of testers will play multiple rounds so improvement can be observed.

Scope:
The game covers order picking and basic stock placement only. Real inventory systems integration and 3D graphics are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working 2D logistics training game
2. Data showing whether repeated play improves picking accuracy and speed

Timeline:
Roughly one semester across design, development and testing phases.

Title:
A Web Portal for Citizen Health Record Requests in E-Government

Problem Statement:
Citizens who need copies of their public clinic health records often must visit offices in person and fill paper forms. This is slow and inconvenient. A simple e-government web portal could let them request records online and track the status.

Objectives:
1. Build a web portal where citizens log in and submit record requests
2. Let clinic staff view, approve and upload the requested records
3. Add status tracking so citizens see if their request is pending or ready

Methodology:
The system will be built with a standard web stack such as React for the front end and a Node or PHP backend with a MySQL database. User roles separate citizens from staff. Requests and their statuses are stored in the database. Basic testing will check that the request workflow works end to end.

Scope:
The portal handles record requests and status updates only. It does not include payment, full electronic medical records, or integration with national systems.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A functioning record-request web portal with two user roles
2. A working request-status workflow

Timeline:
One semester: requirements, build, and testing.

Title:
A Telemedicine Platform for Online Student Counselling Sessions

Problem Statement:
University students often need counselling but find it hard to book and attend in-person sessions because of stigma and timetable clashes. A telemedicine-style platform tailored to campus counselling could let students book and join video sessions privately.

Objectives:
1. Build a booking system where students reserve counselling slots online
2. Integrate video calls so the session happens inside the platform
3. Provide counsellors a simple dashboard of upcoming appointments

Methodology:
The platform will use a web framework with a database to store users and appointments. Video calling will be added through an existing API such as a WebRTC service. Students and counsellors have separate logins. The booking and joining flow will be tested with sample accounts to confirm it works.

Scope:
The platform covers booking and video counselling for one university's counselling unit. Prescriptions, payments and medical diagnosis features are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working booking-and-video telemedicine platform
2. A counsellor dashboard listing appointments

Timeline:
About 14 weeks across planning, development and testing.

Title:
An Adaptive E-Learning System for Retail Staff Product Knowledge

Problem Statement:
Retail employees must learn details about a constantly changing product catalogue, but generic training modules waste time on items staff already know. There is a need for an e-learning system that adapts the next lesson to each learner's demonstrated weak areas rather than showing fixed content to everyone.

Objectives:
1. Build an e-learning platform delivering product-knowledge quizzes to retail staff
2. Implement a rule-based adaptive engine that selects the next topic based on past quiz performance
3. Compare learner improvement under the adaptive path versus a fixed linear path

Methodology:
The system uses a web stack (React, Spring Boot, MySQL). Each quiz result updates a per-topic mastery score; an adaptive rule then routes weak topics back sooner using a spaced-repetition style schedule. To evaluate, two groups of testers use the adaptive and fixed versions, and pre/post test score gains are compared.

Scope:
The project covers one retail category's product catalogue and text-based quizzes. Video content, gamified rewards and mobile apps are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working adaptive e-learning web system with mastery tracking
2. A comparison report of score gains between adaptive and fixed groups

Timeline:
Weeks 1-3 requirements, 4-10 development, 11-13 evaluation, 14 reporting.

Title:
A Mobile Micropayment System for Smart City Parking

Problem Statement:
Drivers in city parking zones often lack coins and existing apps require large minimum top-ups, leaving small unused balances. A fintech micropayment system that charges exact per-minute parking fees could reduce waste and speed up payment at smart-city parking bays.

Objectives:
1. Build a mobile app that starts and stops a parking session and charges per minute
2. Integrate a payment gateway in sandbox mode to handle the transactions
3. Measure transaction completion time and compare it with manual coin payment

Methodology:
The app is built in Flutter with a backend storing sessions and a sandbox payment gateway such as Stripe test mode. A QR code at each bay identifies the location. Per-minute charges are computed when the user stops the session. Evaluation times how long a payment takes across several test users versus a simulated coin process.

Scope:
The project covers per-minute parking payments using a sandbox gateway. Real banking settlement, refunds and enforcement integration are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working per-minute parking payment mobile app
2. Timing data comparing app payment against manual payment

Timeline:
14 weeks: design, build payment flow, integrate gateway, test, report.

Title:
Machine-Learning Fraud Detection for Online Tour Bookings

Problem Statement:
Online tourism booking sites face fraudulent bookings made with stolen cards, causing chargebacks and lost inventory. Manual review is slow and inconsistent, so an automated model that flags likely fraudulent bookings before confirmation would help operators act faster.

Objectives:
1. Engineer features from booking data such as booking-to-travel gap, amount and device mismatch
2. Train and compare logistic regression and random forest classifiers to flag suspicious bookings
3. Evaluate the models using precision, recall and AUC on a held-out test set

Methodology:
A public or synthetic transaction dataset adapted to tourism bookings will be used. Features are extracted with pandas, and scikit-learn trains the classifiers. Because fraud is rare, class imbalance is handled with SMOTE. Models are compared with stratified train/test splits and ROC-AUC, with attention to recall since missed fraud is costly.

Scope:
The project covers offline model training and evaluation on a single dataset. Real-time deployment and integration into a live booking site are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. Trained fraud-detection models with a documented feature set
2. An evaluation comparing classifiers on precision, recall and AUC

Timeline:
Weeks 1-2 data, 3-8 modelling, 9-12 evaluation, 13-14 writing.

Title:
A Hybrid Recommendation Engine for a Social-Commerce Marketplace

Problem Statement:
On social-media-driven marketplaces, users browse many items shared by friends but struggle to find products that match their taste, and pure popularity feeds ignore individual preference. A recommendation engine combining what similar users bought with item content could surface more relevant products.

Objectives:
1. Build a recommender combining collaborative filtering with content-based item features
2. Incorporate a simple social signal so items liked by a user's connections are weighted higher
3. Evaluate recommendation quality with precision@k and compare against a popularity baseline

Methodology:
Using a public e-commerce ratings dataset augmented with simulated social links, item-based collaborative filtering produces base scores that are blended with TF-IDF content similarity and a social-boost term. The system is built in Python. Evaluation uses an offline train/test split reporting precision@k and recall@k against a most-popular baseline.

Scope:
The project covers offline recommendation generation and evaluation. A production-scale live feed, real-time updates and a full social network backend are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working hybrid recommender with a social-boost component
2. Evaluation results showing improvement over the popularity baseline

Timeline:
14 weeks split across data, modelling, evaluation and reporting.

Title:
A Triage Chatbot for Hospital Outpatient Appointment Guidance

Problem Statement:
Hospital call centres are overwhelmed with routine questions about which department a patient should book and what to prepare. Patients wait on hold for simple guidance. A conversational agent that asks about symptoms and directs patients to the right department could reduce call load.

Objectives:
1. Build a chatbot that classifies a user's described symptoms into a likely department
2. Provide preparation instructions and a booking link for the suggested department
3. Evaluate intent-classification accuracy on a labelled set of sample queries

Methodology:
Intents and symptom categories are defined with a domain reference. A retrieval-and-intent approach is used: user text is classified with a fine-tuned lightweight transformer or an intent classifier, mapping to a department. Responses come from a curated answer bank, not free generation, to avoid unsafe medical advice. Accuracy and confusion between departments are measured on held-out test queries.

Scope:
The chatbot guides outpatient department selection and preparation only. It gives no diagnosis, dosage or emergency advice, and covers one hospital's departments.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working triage chatbot with a curated response bank
2. An accuracy report on department-routing classification

Timeline:
Weeks 1-3 intent design, 4-9 build, 10-12 evaluation, 13-14 report.

Title:
A Knowledge-Graph Search Assistant for Company Financial Filings

Problem Statement:
Analysts searching company financial filings rely on keyword search that misses relationships, such as which subsidiaries a company owns or which executives sit on multiple boards. A knowledge-graph-based search could let users ask relationship questions that plain full-text search cannot answer well.

Objectives:
1. Extract entities and relations (companies, executives, subsidiaries) from a set of filings into a graph
2. Build a query interface that answers relationship questions over the graph
3. Compare answer relevance against a keyword-search baseline on a set of test questions

Methodology:
A corpus of public filings is processed with spaCy named-entity recognition plus pattern rules to extract relations, which are loaded into Neo4j. A query layer translates a fixed set of question templates into Cypher. Evaluation uses a small benchmark of relationship questions, scoring precision of returned entities against the keyword baseline.

Scope:
The project covers a limited entity/relation schema over a fixed filing set. Open-ended natural-language querying and live data ingestion are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A populated financial knowledge graph with a template query interface
2. A relevance comparison against keyword search

Timeline:
14 weeks: extraction, graph build, query layer, evaluation, writing.

Title:
Semantic Segmentation of Surface Defects on Manufactured Metal Parts

Problem Statement:
Visual inspection of metal parts for scratches, dents and corrosion is manual and inconsistent on production lines. Existing defect classifiers only label whether a part is defective, but quality engineers need the exact defect region to assess severity and root cause. Pixel-level segmentation of defects remains underused on small in-house factory datasets.

Objectives:
1. Build a labelled defect-segmentation dataset from the public NEU and Severstal steel-defect images
2. Train and compare U-Net and DeepLabV3+ models to segment defect regions at pixel level
3. Evaluate segmentation with mean IoU and Dice, and analyse failure cases by defect type

Methodology:
Images are annotated with masks for defect classes and split 70/15/15 with stratification by defect type. U-Net and DeepLabV3+ (ResNet-50 backbone) are trained in PyTorch with data augmentation (flips, brightness, elastic) to offset limited data, using a combined Dice-plus-cross-entropy loss. Models are compared on mean IoU and Dice on the held-out test set, with a classification-only baseline for context, and a qualitative review of false positives near surface texture.

Scope:
The project segments three defect classes on flat steel surfaces from the named datasets. Real-time camera integration, 3D parts and non-metal materials are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. Trained U-Net and DeepLabV3+ models with reproducible mean IoU and Dice scores
2. A failure-case analysis identifying where each model under-performs

Timeline:
Weeks 1-2 data and annotation, 3-8 training, 9-12 evaluation, 13-14 reporting.

Title:
Real-Time Detection of Unattended Bags in Public Spaces for Safety Monitoring

Problem Statement:
Security staff monitoring crowded public spaces cannot continuously watch every screen, and unattended bags are a known safety concern. Generic object detectors find bags but do not reason about whether a bag has been left without a nearby person, which is the actual alert condition operators care about.

Objectives:
1. Fine-tune a YOLOv8 detector to locate persons and bags in public-area CCTV-style footage
2. Add a tracking-and-rule layer that flags a bag as unattended when no person stays near it beyond a time threshold
3. Evaluate detection mAP and the unattended-bag alert precision/recall on annotated clips

Methodology:
A subset of the public ABODA and PETS abandoned-object datasets is used. YOLOv8 is fine-tuned in PyTorch for person and bag classes, and a ByteTrack tracker associates detections across frames. A rule computes bag-to-nearest-person distance and dwell time to raise an alert. Detection is measured with mAP@0.5; the alert logic is scored on precision and recall against labelled abandonment events, with attention to false alarms from crowd occlusion.

Scope:
The system processes pre-recorded clips at moderate resolution and detects bag abandonment only. Face recognition, multi-camera handoff and live deployment are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A fine-tuned detector plus tracking-rule pipeline that flags unattended bags
2. An evaluation reporting detection mAP and alert precision/recall

Timeline:
Weeks 1-2 data prep, 3-7 detector training, 8-10 rule layer, 11-13 evaluation, 14 report.

Title:
Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis of Customer Feedback on Home Energy Providers

Problem Statement:
Energy providers receive large volumes of free-text feedback covering billing, outages, customer service and pricing, but overall sentiment scores hide which specific aspect is driving dissatisfaction. Document-level sentiment is too coarse for operations teams who need to know whether complaints concern billing or reliability.

Objectives:
1. Build an aspect-labelled dataset of energy-provider reviews across four aspects
2. Fine-tune a DistilBERT model for aspect-based sentiment and compare it with a TF-IDF plus SVM baseline
3. Evaluate per-aspect macro-F1 and analyse where aspect confusion occurs

Methodology:
Reviews are collected from public app-store and complaint sources, then annotated per aspect with positive/negative/neutral labels using a defined guideline and a second-annotator agreement check. A DistilBERT model is fine-tuned in Hugging Face Transformers for aspect-sentiment pairs, and a TF-IDF plus linear SVM serves as the baseline. Evaluation uses stratified 5-fold cross-validation reporting macro-F1 per aspect and a confusion analysis between aspects.

Scope:
The study covers English reviews and four predefined aspects only. Real-time streaming, sarcasm detection and multilingual input are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An annotated aspect-sentiment dataset and a fine-tuned DistilBERT model
2. A comparison showing per-aspect macro-F1 against the baseline

Timeline:
Weeks 1-3 data and annotation, 4-9 modelling, 10-12 evaluation, 13-14 writing.

Title:
A Learning-Based Index Advisor for Query Optimization in Small-Business Databases

Problem Statement:
Small businesses run reporting queries on databases with no dedicated DBA, and missing or redundant indexes cause slow queries and wasted storage. Default database optimizers choose plans but do not recommend which indexes to create for a given workload, leaving non-experts guessing.

Objectives:
1. Capture a representative query workload and benchmark baseline execution times on PostgreSQL
2. Build an index-advisor that ranks candidate indexes by estimated cost benefit using the optimizer's what-if cost estimates
3. Measure end-to-end workload speedup and storage overhead from the recommended indexes

Methodology:
A workload is generated from a TPC-H-derived schema scaled to small-business size. Candidate single- and multi-column indexes are enumerated from query predicates; each is evaluated using PostgreSQL hypothetical-index (HypoPG) cost estimates so no index is physically built during search. A greedy selection respects a storage budget. The recommended set is then created and the full workload re-timed, reporting total runtime improvement, per-query change and added storage versus the no-extra-index baseline.

Scope:
The advisor targets single-node PostgreSQL and B-tree indexes for a fixed read-mostly workload. Distributed databases, write-heavy tuning and partitioning are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working index-advisor tool with a storage-budget constraint
2. Benchmark results quantifying workload speedup against storage cost

Timeline:
Weeks 1-2 workload, 3-8 advisor, 9-12 benchmarking, 13-14 reporting.

Title:
A Facial-Recognition Attendance System for Farm Worker Shift Logging

Problem Statement:
Farms employing seasonal workers still log attendance on paper or shared cards, which allows buddy-punching and slows payroll. A face-recognition attendance terminal could log shift start and end automatically, but outdoor lighting and dust make naive recognition unreliable, so robustness must be addressed explicitly.

Objectives:
1. Build an enrolment and recognition pipeline using face embeddings for a fixed worker roster
2. Add a liveness check and a confidence threshold to reject spoofing and uncertain matches
3. Evaluate recognition accuracy and false-acceptance rate under varied lighting conditions

Methodology:
Faces are detected with MTCNN and embedded with a pre-trained FaceNet model; identity is assigned by nearest-neighbour cosine distance against enrolled embeddings above a tuned threshold. A simple blink-based liveness step deters photo spoofing. A small enrolled roster is tested with images captured in bright, shaded and low-light conditions to report top-1 accuracy, false-acceptance and false-rejection rates, and the threshold is chosen from a validation split.

Scope:
The system handles a fixed enrolled roster on a single terminal and logs shift in/out times. Large-scale identification, payroll integration and mask-occluded faces are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working face-attendance prototype with liveness and thresholding
2. An accuracy and false-acceptance report across lighting conditions

Timeline:
Weeks 1-2 setup, 3-7 pipeline, 8-10 liveness, 11-13 evaluation, 14 report.

Title:
End-to-End OCR Pipeline for Freight Consignment Notes with Layout-Aware Post-Correction

Problem Statement:
Logistics back offices manually key data from scanned freight consignment notes, where fields such as consignee, weight and reference number sit in inconsistent layouts and are degraded by stamps, creases and faxing. General OCR transcribes characters but ignores document structure, so field extraction accuracy stays low and errors propagate into shipment records. The gap is a pipeline that combines robust text recognition with layout-aware field extraction and a domain post-correction step, evaluated on the realistic noisy scans these offices actually handle.

Objectives:
1. Assemble and annotate a 600-note corpus with field-level bounding boxes for eight target fields, with double-annotation on 15% to report agreement
2. Build a pipeline pairing a CRNN/Tesseract text recognizer with a LayoutLMv3 field extractor and a dictionary-and-regex post-correction module
3. Evaluate field-level exact-match accuracy and character error rate against a Tesseract-plus-regex baseline, with an ablation isolating the post-correction contribution

Methodology:
Scanned notes are preprocessed (deskew, adaptive binarization) and split 70/15/15 stratified by template. Text lines are recognized, then LayoutLMv3 is fine-tuned in PyTorch to tag tokens with field labels using OCR-provided positions; a post-correction module applies a consignee/port dictionary, checksum rules for reference numbers, and unit normalization for weights. Evaluation reports per-field exact-match, overall CER and end-to-end field accuracy, compared against a Tesseract-plus-regex baseline; an ablation removes post-correction to quantify its effect. Risks (template overfitting, annotation cost) are mitigated by augmentation (synthetic stamps, blur) and template-stratified splits.

Scope:
The project targets eight predefined fields on English single-page consignment notes from three known templates. Handwriting recognition, multi-page bundles and live scanner integration are explicitly excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An annotated 600-note dataset and a reproducible OCR-plus-extraction pipeline with the trained LayoutLMv3 model
2. A benchmarked evaluation with ablation showing field accuracy and CER gains over the baseline

Timeline:
Weeks 1-3 data collection and annotation, 4-6 preprocessing and recognizer, 7-10 layout extractor and post-correction, 11-13 evaluation and ablation, 14 reporting.

Title:
Anomaly Detection in Wireless Sensor Networks for Building Energy-and-Water Sustainability

Problem Statement:
Green-certified buildings deploy wireless sensor networks for energy, water and occupancy, but raw streams are noisy and contain gaps and drift from low-cost nodes. Facility teams want early warning of waste events such as overnight HVAC running or a hidden water leak, yet fixed thresholds either miss gradual drift or flood operators with false alarms. The gap is an evaluated anomaly-detection approach robust to missing data that distinguishes genuine waste events from benign sensor noise on real building telemetry.

Objectives:
1. Build a cleaned multivariate dataset from public building-telemetry sources with labelled or expert-confirmed anomaly windows
2. Implement and compare three detectors (seasonal-decomposition residual thresholding, Isolation Forest, and an LSTM autoencoder) on energy and water streams
3. Evaluate event-level precision, recall and detection delay, and assess robustness when 10-20% of readings are dropped

Methodology:
Sensor streams are resampled to a fixed interval; gaps are imputed and features include rolling statistics and time-of-day context. The three detectors are trained in Python (statsmodels, scikit-learn, PyTorch) on normal-operation periods; the LSTM autoencoder flags windows by reconstruction error above a validation-tuned percentile. Evaluation uses event-level matching (a true event counted if any alarm falls in its window) to report precision, recall, F1 and mean detection delay, compared against a static-threshold baseline. A controlled experiment drops readings at increasing rates to measure robustness, and time-ordered splits prevent leakage.

Scope:
The study covers energy and water streams from the chosen building dataset and point/contextual anomalies. Live deployment, actuation control and multi-building transfer are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A cleaned, labelled telemetry dataset and three reproducible detector implementations
2. A comparative evaluation reporting event-level metrics, detection delay and robustness to missing data

Timeline:
Weeks 1-3 data preparation, 4-9 detector implementation, 10-12 evaluation and robustness tests, 13-14 reporting.

Title:
Machine Learning for Factory

Factories have a lot of machines and sometimes things go wrong. We need machine learning to fix this and make the factory better.

I will use Python and some algorithms to classify the data. Then I will check if it works.

This can be used by all factories everywhere to improve everything in manufacturing.

Title:
Deep Learning Camera for Safety

Problem Statement:
People are not safe in public and there are many problems. Cameras can watch but they are not smart. Deep learning will make them smart.

Objectives:

2. Detect danger.

The system will work in any city, airport, mall, or street to stop all crimes.

Title:
NLP for Energy

Problem Statement:
Energy companies have many documents and text. It is hard to read them all. NLP can help understand the text and save energy.

Objectives:
1. Read the text with NLP.
2. Understand energy data.
3. Save power.

Methodology:
I will do natural language processing on the text using some libraries and get the meaning. After that I will show the results.

For all energy companies in the world to manage their text and reduce cost.
