2. Energy saving.

Title:
A Product Recommender for Small Online Shops

Problem Statement:
Small online businesses often lose customers because their websites show the same products to everyone. Bigger companies have recommendation engines, but small shops cannot afford them, so they miss chances to suggest items a buyer might like.

Objectives:
1. Build a recommendation feature for a small shop website.
2. Suggest products based on what users viewed or bought.
3. Test if recommendations increase clicks.

Methodology:
I will collect purchase history data and use collaborative filtering to find similar users. The recommender will be built in Python and connected to a simple web store. I will measure accuracy by checking if suggested items match what users actually buy.

Scope:
The project covers one demo shop with a sample catalog. It will not handle payment or real-time stock.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A recommender that suggests products to shoppers.
2. A short report on whether suggestions improve engagement.

Timeline:
About four months from data collection to testing.

Title:
Voice Commands for Farmers in the Field

Problem Statement:
Farmers often have their hands full and cannot type on a phone while working. A speech recognition tool could let them record crop notes or check information by talking, but most apps are built for office use and do not handle farm vocabulary well.

Objectives:
1. Build a speech recognition app that records spoken farm notes.
2. Recognise common crop and task words.
3. Test accuracy with a few users.

Methodology:
I will use an existing speech-to-text library and record sample voice clips of farming terms. The app will convert speech to text and save notes. I will compare recognised words against the spoken words to measure error rate.

Scope:
The tool will support English voice input for a small set of farm tasks. It will not work offline or support multiple languages.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working voice note app for farm use.
2. An accuracy measurement on the test clips.

Timeline:
Roughly one semester of development and testing.

Title:
Detecting Network Attacks in a Transport System

Problem Statement:
Public transport systems now rely on connected networks for ticketing and scheduling, which makes them targets for cyberattacks. Operators need a way to spot unusual traffic that might signal an intrusion before it disrupts service.

Objectives:
1. Build a system that flags suspicious network traffic.
2. Train it to tell normal traffic from attacks.
3. Measure how often it is correct.

Methodology:
I will use a public intrusion dataset and train a classifier such as a decision tree or random forest to separate attack traffic from normal traffic. The model will be evaluated using accuracy and a confusion matrix on held-out data.

Scope:
The project focuses on offline detection using an existing dataset. It will not be deployed on a live transport network or handle encrypted payloads.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained intrusion detection model with reported accuracy.
2. A comparison of two algorithms on the dataset.

Timeline:
Two semesters, split between training and evaluation.

Title:
Finding Vulnerabilities in Sustainability Reporting Websites

Problem Statement:
Many organisations now run web portals to publish sustainability and carbon data, but smaller teams build these sites quickly and leave security holes. Common flaws like injection or weak authentication can expose sensitive figures.

Objectives:
1. Scan a sample web application for common security flaws.
2. Identify the most frequent vulnerability types.
3. Suggest fixes for each finding.

Methodology:
I will build a small sustainability-reporting web app and test it with open-source scanning tools and manual checks against the OWASP Top 10. Findings will be recorded and rated by severity.

Scope:
The work covers one test web application and a fixed list of common vulnerabilities. It will not cover network-level or physical security.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A vulnerability report for the test application.
2. A checklist of recommended fixes.

Timeline:
One academic year including build and testing phases.

Title:
Static and Dynamic Analysis of Malware Targeting Logistics Software

Problem Statement:
Logistics firms depend on warehouse and fleet-management software, and a single malware infection can stall deliveries across a supply chain. Analysts need clearer ways to characterise samples that target these systems, but most coursework treats malware analysis only at a surface level.

Objectives:
1. Collect a labelled set of malware and benign samples relevant to enterprise software.
2. Extract static features (imported APIs, strings) and observe dynamic behaviour in a sandbox.
3. Compare a feature-based classifier against signature matching for detection accuracy.

Methodology:
Samples will be drawn from a public malware repository. Static features are extracted with PE-parsing tools, and dynamic behaviour is captured in an isolated Cuckoo sandbox. A random forest classifier is trained on the combined features and evaluated with precision, recall, and F1 against a signature baseline.

Scope:
The study covers Windows PE malware analysed offline in a sandbox. It excludes live network propagation, mobile malware, and real logistics infrastructure.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A labelled feature dataset and a trained detection classifier.
2. A comparison showing where behavioural features outperform signatures.

Timeline:
Semester one: sample collection and feature extraction. Semester two: training, evaluation, and write-up.

Title:
A Responsive Citizen Services Portal for Local e-Government

Problem Statement:
Residents often struggle to access local council services online because existing portals are not mobile-friendly and force users through long forms. This leads to repeat office visits and slow request handling for staff.

Objectives:
1. Design a responsive web portal where residents submit and track service requests.
2. Provide a staff dashboard to manage and update request status.
3. Evaluate usability with a small group of test users.

Methodology:
The portal will be built with React and a Node/Express backend over a relational database. Requirements come from reviewing two existing council sites. After build, I will run a usability test using task-completion time and a System Usability Scale questionnaire.

Scope:
The system covers request submission, status tracking, and a basic staff view for one service category. It excludes payments, identity verification, and integration with real council systems.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working responsive portal with citizen and staff roles.
2. A usability evaluation report with SUS scores.

Timeline:
Semester one: requirements and design. Semester two: development and usability testing.

Title:
A Progressive Web App for Offline Study in Low-Connectivity Schools

Problem Statement:
Students in areas with unreliable internet often lose access to learning materials when connectivity drops. Native apps are costly to maintain across devices, while plain websites fail offline, leaving a gap for lightweight cross-device learning tools.

Objectives:
1. Build a progressive web app that caches lessons for offline use.
2. Sync student progress when connectivity returns.
3. Test offline reliability and load performance.

Methodology:
The PWA will use service workers and IndexedDB for offline caching, built on React with a workbox setup. Progress sync uses a queue that flushes to a backend when online. Testing covers offline page loads, cache-hit rates, and Lighthouse PWA scores.

Scope:
The app delivers text and image lessons plus quizzes for one subject. It excludes video streaming, real-time collaboration, and account billing.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An installable PWA that works offline and syncs progress.
2. Performance and offline-reliability test results.

Timeline:
Four months build, then one month of testing and refinement.

Title:
A Cross-Platform Mobile App for Small Retail Inventory

Problem Statement:
Small retailers often track stock on paper or spreadsheets, leading to stockouts and overordering. Affordable mobile tools exist but are usually single-platform, so shops with mixed Android and iOS devices cannot share one system.

Objectives:
1. Build a cross-platform app to record stock levels and sales.
2. Alert staff when items fall below a reorder threshold.
3. Test the app with a small shop's sample data.

Methodology:
The app will be built in Flutter so a single codebase runs on Android and iOS, backed by a Firebase datastore. Low-stock alerts trigger from threshold rules. Evaluation uses a usability session with shop staff and a check that alerts fire correctly on seeded data.

Scope:
The app covers inventory entry, sales deduction, and low-stock alerts for one store. It excludes supplier ordering, barcode hardware integration, and accounting.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A cross-platform inventory app with alerting.
2. A usability and correctness test report.

Timeline:
Semester one: design and core build. Semester two: alerts, testing, documentation.

Title:
A Native Android App for Reporting Smart City Issues

Problem Statement:
City residents notice problems like broken streetlights or potholes but lack an easy way to report them with location. Calls and emails get lost, so issues stay unresolved and councils have no clear picture of recurring problem areas.

Objectives:
1. Build a native Android app for residents to report issues with photo and GPS.
2. Show reported issues on a map for council review.
3. Evaluate the app with a small user group.

Methodology:
The app is built natively in Kotlin using the device camera and fused location provider, sending reports to a backend with a map view. Requirements are gathered from a short survey. Evaluation uses task-based testing and a usability questionnaire.

Scope:
The app supports citizen reporting and a map display for a fixed set of issue types. It excludes work-order assignment, in-app messaging, and live council system integration.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working Android reporting app with map visualisation.
2. A usability evaluation summary.

Timeline:
Semester one: build core reporting. Semester two: map view, testing, write-up.

Title:
An IoT Sensor Network for Crowd Monitoring at Tourist Sites

Problem Statement:
Popular tourist attractions struggle to manage crowding, which harms visitor experience and safety. Manual headcounts are slow and inaccurate, and most venues lack a low-cost way to see how busy different areas are in near real time.

Objectives:
1. Deploy low-cost sensors to estimate visitor counts in zones of a site.
2. Send readings to a dashboard showing current crowd levels.
3. Evaluate counting accuracy against manual reference counts.

Methodology:
Sensor nodes built on ESP32 with PIR and Wi-Fi-probe counting publish readings over MQTT to a backend that aggregates per-zone counts. A web dashboard displays levels. Accuracy is checked by comparing sensor estimates to manual counts during test sessions.

Scope:
The prototype covers a few zones in one test area with relative crowd levels. It excludes individual identification, outdoor weatherproofing for long-term use, and precise headcounts.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working sensor-to-dashboard crowd-monitoring prototype.
2. An accuracy report comparing sensor and manual counts.

Timeline:
Semester one: hardware and firmware. Semester two: dashboard, testing, evaluation.

Title:
A Smart Home Hub that Shares Safe Activity Updates to Social Media

Problem Statement:
Smart home owners increasingly want to share moments such as a garden camera capturing wildlife, but existing automations either over-share private data or require manual posting. There is little work on privacy-aware automation that decides what is safe to publish to social platforms.

Objectives:
1. Build a home automation hub that triggers actions from sensor and camera events.
2. Apply a rule-based privacy filter before any content is shared to social media.
3. Evaluate the hub's responsiveness and the filter's correctness against test scenarios.

Methodology:
The hub runs on a Raspberry Pi using Home Assistant and MQTT to ingest sensor events. A privacy filter applies user-defined rules (face presence, location tags, time windows) before posting through a social API. Evaluation measures end-to-end latency and the filter's precision and recall on a labelled set of share/no-share events.

Scope:
The project covers a small device set (motion, door, one camera) and posting to a single social platform. It excludes facial recognition of identities, video editing, and commercial-grade reliability.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working privacy-aware automation hub with a configurable share filter.
2. An evaluation reporting latency and filter precision/recall.

Timeline:
Phase 1 (6 wk): hub and sensor integration. Phase 2 (6 wk): privacy filter. Phase 3 (4 wk): evaluation and write-up.

Title:
Edge-Based Fall Detection for Elderly Home Care

Problem Statement:
Continuous fall monitoring for elderly people raises privacy concerns and bandwidth costs when video is streamed to the cloud, and cloud round-trips add latency that delays alerts. Running detection on the edge could keep data local and cut response time, but accuracy on constrained hardware is uncertain.

Objectives:
1. Implement a fall-detection model that runs on an edge device.
2. Quantise and optimise the model to meet on-device latency limits.
3. Compare edge accuracy and latency against a cloud baseline.

Methodology:
A lightweight CNN/LSTM on accelerometer and pose data is trained on a public fall dataset, then converted to TensorFlow Lite and deployed on a Raspberry Pi/Coral edge device. Evaluation reports accuracy, precision, recall, on-device inference latency, and power use, benchmarked against a server-side model.

Scope:
The system targets fall events from wearable/pose input in a single-room setting. It excludes multi-person tracking, medical certification, and long-term clinical trials.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A deployable edge fall-detector meeting a stated latency budget.
2. An edge-vs-cloud comparison of accuracy, latency, and privacy trade-offs.

Timeline:
Phase 1 (5 wk): model training. Phase 2 (5 wk): edge optimisation/deployment. Phase 3 (4 wk): benchmarking and analysis.

Title:
A Cloud-Native Microservices Backend for Personal Finance

Problem Statement:
Personal finance apps often start as monoliths that become hard to scale and deploy as features like budgeting, transactions, and alerts grow. Students rarely see how to decompose such a system into independently deployable services with resilient communication.

Objectives:
1. Decompose a personal-finance backend into bounded microservices.
2. Add resilient inter-service communication with observability.
3. Measure scalability and fault tolerance under load.

Methodology:
Services (accounts, transactions, budgeting, notifications) are built with Spring Boot, containerised, and orchestrated on Kubernetes with an API gateway. Asynchronous events flow through Kafka, with circuit breakers for resilience and Prometheus/Grafana for metrics. Load testing with k6 measures throughput and latency, and fault injection tests recovery.

Scope:
The project delivers four services with a gateway and observability stack on a local cluster. It excludes real banking integration, production security hardening, and mobile front-end work.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A deployable microservices backend with gateway and monitoring.
2. A report on scalability, latency, and fault-recovery behaviour.

Timeline:
Phase 1 (5 wk): service design and build. Phase 2 (5 wk): messaging and resilience. Phase 3 (4 wk): load/fault testing and analysis.

Title:
A CI/CD Pipeline for Manufacturing Control Software

Problem Statement:
Teams maintaining factory control and monitoring software often deploy manually, causing slow releases and inconsistent test coverage that risk plant downtime. A reproducible CI/CD pipeline with automated quality gates could reduce these risks, but few studies tailor such pipelines to embedded/industrial constraints.

Objectives:
1. Build an automated CI/CD pipeline for a sample control application.
2. Add automated testing, security scanning, and staged deployment gates.
3. Measure the pipeline's effect on lead time and failure rate.

Methodology:
The pipeline uses GitHub Actions with build, unit/integration test, SAST scanning, container build, and deployment stages to a staging environment via Docker. Infrastructure is defined with Terraform, and DORA metrics (lead time, deployment frequency, change-failure rate) are collected before and after automation for comparison.

Scope:
The work covers one sample control application and a simulated deployment target. It excludes real PLC hardware deployment and safety certification.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A reproducible CI/CD pipeline with automated quality gates.
2. A before/after comparison using DORA metrics.

Timeline:
Phase 1 (4 wk): base pipeline. Phase 2 (6 wk): testing/security/IaC. Phase 3 (4 wk): metrics collection and analysis.

Title:
A Big Data Pipeline for Emergency Incident Analytics

Problem Statement:
Public-safety agencies collect large volumes of incident and sensor data but often lack a scalable pipeline to ingest, process, and analyse it for hotspots and response trends. Batch-only tools miss timely patterns, while ad-hoc scripts do not scale.

Objectives:
1. Build a pipeline that ingests and processes incident data at scale.
2. Produce aggregated analytics on incident hotspots and response times.
3. Evaluate throughput and query latency against data volume.

Methodology:
Streaming incident records flow through Kafka into Spark Structured Streaming for cleaning and aggregation, with results stored in a columnar warehouse and surfaced via a query layer. The pipeline is benchmarked on a public incident dataset (e.g. city 911/crime data) for ingestion throughput, processing latency, and query response across growing data sizes.

Scope:
The project covers ingestion, processing, and aggregate analytics on a historical dataset replayed as a stream. It excludes real-time dispatch integration and predictive modelling of future incidents.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working scalable analytics pipeline with aggregate dashboards.
2. A performance evaluation across throughput and latency.

Timeline:
Phase 1 (5 wk): ingestion/storage. Phase 2 (5 wk): processing and analytics. Phase 3 (4 wk): benchmarking and reporting.

Title:
A Self-Service Business Intelligence Dashboard for Building Energy Management

Problem Statement:
Facility managers in commercial buildings receive energy data from disparate meter and BMS exports but lack a unified, drill-down view, so they cannot quickly link consumption spikes to specific zones, equipment, or tariff periods. Existing vendor dashboards are costly and closed, and prior student projects stop at static charts without supporting interactive root-cause analysis against a baseline.

Objectives:
1. Design a dimensional data model that consolidates half-hourly meter, weather, and tariff data for three building zones.
2. Build an interactive BI dashboard with drill-down KPIs (kWh, cost, CO2, intensity per m2) benchmarked against a degree-day-adjusted baseline.
3. Validate decision usefulness with five facility staff using task-based scenarios and a SUS questionnaire.

Methodology:
ETL in Python (pandas) loads cleaned meter, weather (degree-day), and tariff data into a star schema in PostgreSQL. A dashboard in a tool such as Metabase/Superset exposes filtered drill-downs and anomaly highlighting via z-score thresholds on degree-day-normalised consumption. Evaluation combines task-completion time and error rate against a spreadsheet baseline, plus SUS scoring, with results reported as means and confidence intervals.

Scope:
Included: three zones, twelve months of historical half-hourly data, electricity only, drill-down and anomaly flagging. Excluded: real-time streaming, automated control actions, gas/water meters, and predictive forecasting (left to related work).

Expected Outcomes:
1. A validated dimensional model and interactive energy BI dashboard.
2. An evaluation showing faster, more accurate analysis tasks versus the spreadsheet baseline with reported SUS scores.

Timeline:
Wk 1-3 requirements and data audit; Wk 4-7 ETL and star schema; Wk 8-12 dashboard build; Wk 13-15 user evaluation; Wk 16 write-up.

Title:
Short-Term Demand Forecasting for a Small Bakery to Reduce Waste

Problem Statement:
Small bakeries overproduce or run short because owners forecast daily demand by intuition, driving food waste and lost sales. Generic forecasting tools ignore local drivers like weekday patterns, weather, and holidays, and few student projects rigorously compare classical and modern methods on real small-business data with proper backtesting.

Objectives:
1. Assemble and clean two years of daily product-level sales for one bakery with weather and holiday covariates.
2. Build and compare forecasting models (seasonal naive baseline, SARIMA, Prophet, and LightGBM with lag features) for 7-day-ahead demand.
3. Quantify waste-reduction potential by simulating production decisions from forecasts versus current practice.

Methodology:
Data is aggregated to daily per-product series with calendar, weather, and promotion features. Models are evaluated with rolling-origin (walk-forward) cross-validation using MAE, RMSE, and MASE against a seasonal-naive baseline; statistical significance of differences is checked with a Diebold-Mariano test. A simple newsvendor simulation translates forecast error into expected waste and stockout costs.

Scope:
Included: top 10 products, daily horizon up to 7 days, one store, backtested offline. Excluded: real-time POS integration, multi-store transfer, intraday forecasting, and pricing optimisation.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A benchmarked forecasting study identifying the best model per product class with error metrics.

Title:
An Offline-Capable E-Learning System for Rural Agriculture Training

Problem Statement:

Title:
Fraud Detection for Carbon-Credit Transaction Records

Because fraud is rare, I will apply SMOTE for class imbalance and report precision, recall, and F1 rather than accuracy. A rule-based threshold detector serves as the baseline.

Scope:
The work covers offline detection on historical records. It excludes real-time streaming and blockchain registry integration.

Title:
A Recommendation System for a Logistics Spare-Parts Marketplace

Methodology:

The system is built in Python with a Flask API. I will evaluate using precision@k and recall@k on a train/test split and compare against a popularity baseline.

Scope:
The recommender works on one catalogue category. It excludes pricing optimisation and inventory forecasting.

Expected Outcomes:

2. Precision@k and recall@k results versus the baseline

One semester: data prep (3), modelling (6), evaluation (5).

Title:
A Conversational Agent for Government Service Enquiries

Problem Statement:
Citizens struggle to find the right form or office for services like licence renewal, often calling busy hotlines. Government websites bury this information in long pages, so a chatbot that answers procedural questions could reduce call volume.

Objectives:

3. Measure answer accuracy against a set of test questions

Methodology:
I will use a retrieval-augmented approach: official documents are chunked and embedded into a FAISS vector store, and a language model answers using retrieved passages. The interface is a web widget built with React talking to a Flask backend. I will build a 50-question test set with known answers and measure how many are answered correctly.

Scope:
The chatbot covers three service categories and answers in English. It excludes account login, payments, and form submission.

Title:
A Knowledge-Graph Search Tool for Course Materials

Problem Statement:
Students searching lecture notes by keyword miss results when terminology differs across courses, and they cannot see how concepts connect. A knowledge graph linking concepts could support exploratory search that plain keyword search cannot.

Evaluation uses a set of student queries with relevant documents judged manually, reporting precision and recall against an Elasticsearch keyword baseline.

Title:
Shelf Image Segmentation for Retail Out-of-Stock Detection

Problem Statement:
Retail audits of shelf availability are mostly manual, so out-of-stock gaps go unnoticed for hours, losing sales. Existing object detectors give bounding boxes but struggle to delineate empty shelf regions precisely, which segmentation can address by producing pixel-level masks of gaps and products.

Objectives:
1. Build a semantic segmentation pipeline that masks products and empty shelf gaps from shelf photos
2. Train and evaluate the model on the SKU-110K-derived and annotated shelf images
3. Benchmark mask quality against a baseline and report per-class IoU

Methodology:
I will fine-tune a U-Net and a DeepLabV3+ (ResNet-50 backbone) on shelf images I annotate with product/gap/background masks, augmenting with flips and brightness jitter to handle lighting. Training uses a Dice-plus-cross-entropy loss with 5-fold cross-validation. Evaluation reports mean IoU and per-class IoU, with a thresholded-edge baseline for comparison.

Scope:
The work covers single-camera frontal shelf images in one store category. It excludes multi-camera stitching, real-time video, and price-tag reading.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained segmentation model with reproducible mean and per-class IoU
2. A comparison report between U-Net, DeepLabV3+, and the baseline

Timeline:
14 weeks: annotation (3), training (5), evaluation (3), write-up (3).

Title:
Real-Time Pedestrian and Vehicle Detection for Smart-City Junctions

Problem Statement:
Traffic signals on fixed timers waste green time on empty approaches and delay pedestrians. Adaptive control needs reliable counts of road users at junctions, but edge devices have limited compute, so detection must balance accuracy with speed on modest hardware.

Objectives:
1. Detect and count pedestrians, cars, and motorcycles from junction camera frames
2. Achieve real-time throughput on a single GPU edge-class device
3. Evaluate detection accuracy and speed against a heavier baseline

Methodology:
I will fine-tune YOLOv8-nano and YOLOv8-small on junction frames drawn from the UA-DETRAC and a self-labelled local subset, using mosaic augmentation. I will report mAP@0.5 and mAP@0.5:0.95 plus frames-per-second on a Jetson-class device, comparing the nano and small variants and a Faster R-CNN baseline to quantify the accuracy-speed trade-off.

Scope:
The work covers daytime detection at fixed junction cameras. It excludes night/IR footage, tracking across frames, and signal-control integration.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained detector with mAP and FPS measured on edge hardware
2. An accuracy-versus-speed comparison across the three models

Timeline:
14 weeks: data and labelling (3), training (5), edge benchmarking (3), report (3).

Title:
Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis of Tourist Reviews

Problem Statement:
Destination managers read overall star ratings but cannot tell whether complaints concern cleanliness, price, or staff. Document-level sentiment hides this, so aspect-based sentiment analysis is needed to attribute opinion to specific facets of a tourist attraction.

Objectives:
1. Extract review aspects (such as cleanliness, value, staff) and their sentiment polarity
2. Fine-tune a transformer for aspect-based sentiment on tourism reviews
3. Compare against a lexicon-based and a classic ML baseline

Methodology:
I will fine-tune BERT-base for aspect-based sentiment using the SemEval-2014/2016 review datasets adapted to tourism categories, plus scraped attraction reviews labelled for aspects. Preprocessing includes tokenisation and aspect-term tagging. Evaluation uses macro F1 per aspect with stratified cross-validation, benchmarked against a VADER lexicon baseline and an SVM with TF-IDF.

Scope:
The system handles English reviews and a fixed set of five aspects. It excludes multilingual reviews, sarcasm handling, and a live dashboard.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A fine-tuned aspect-based sentiment model with per-aspect F1
2. A benchmark table against the lexicon and SVM baselines

Timeline:

Title:
Learned Index Hints for Query Optimization on a Social-Media Workload

Problem Statement:
Social-media feeds issue skewed, repetitive queries, yet the database planner picks plans from static statistics and can mis-estimate cardinality for these patterns. Better optimization could cut latency, but rewriting the planner is impractical, so a lightweight hint layer is worth exploring.

Objectives:
1. Profile a representative social-media query workload and find slow, mis-estimated queries
2. Train a model to predict good join orders / index hints for recurring query templates
3. Measure latency improvement against the default planner

Methodology:
Using PostgreSQL and a synthetic social-graph workload generated to mimic feed and follower queries, I will log plans and runtimes. A gradient-boosted model maps query template features to a recommended index/join hint, applied via pg_hint_plan. Evaluation compares median and p95 latency with and without hints on a held-out query set, and notes any regressions.

Scope:
The work targets read-heavy SELECT queries on a fixed schema. It excludes writes, distributed sharding, and changing the planner source.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A hint-recommendation model integrated via pg_hint_plan
2. Latency results (median, p95) versus the default planner

Timeline:
14 weeks: workload setup (3), profiling (3), model and hints (5), evaluation (3).

Title:
Facial-Recognition Attendance for Hospital Staff with Spoof Checks

Problem Statement:
Hospitals need accurate shift attendance, but card systems suffer buddy-punching and fingerprint readers raise hygiene concerns in clinical areas. Face-based attendance is contactless, yet naive systems can be fooled by photos, so liveness checking must be part of the design.

Objectives:
1. Build a face-recognition attendance system that logs staff clock-in/out
2. Add a basic anti-spoofing check to reject printed photos
3. Evaluate recognition accuracy and spoof-rejection on a held-out test set

Methodology:
Face embeddings come from a pre-trained FaceNet/ArcFace model with cosine-similarity matching against an enrolled gallery. A blink/texture-based liveness check screens out static photos. The backend is Flask with an SQLite log. Evaluation reports recognition accuracy, false-acceptance and false-rejection rates, and spoof-attack rejection on photo attacks, across varied lighting.

Scope:
The system covers a small enrolled set of staff at one entry point under indoor lighting. It excludes mask-occluded faces, video-replay attacks, and payroll integration.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working face-attendance system with logging
2. Accuracy, FAR/FRR, and spoof-rejection results

Timeline:
14 weeks: enrolment and pipeline (4), liveness (3), evaluation (4), report (3).

Title:
An OCR Pipeline for Automated Extraction of Financial Invoice Fields

Problem Statement:
Finance teams manually key fields from scanned supplier invoices, which is slow and error-prone, and generic OCR returns raw text without structure. The gap is reliable field-level extraction (invoice number, date, totals, line items) from heterogeneous, noisy scans, where layout variety and degraded quality defeat template-based parsers used in many small finance departments.

Objectives:
1. Build a pipeline that detects, recognises, and structures key fields from scanned invoices into validated JSON
2. Achieve field-level F1 above 0.90 on a held-out invoice set while flagging low-confidence fields for human review
3. Quantify gains over a Tesseract-plus-regex baseline and a layout-aware model, including an error and ablation analysis

Methodology:
Scans are deskewed and denoised with OpenCV, then text is detected and recognised; I will compare Tesseract OCR against a TrOCR recogniser. Field extraction fine-tunes LayoutLMv3 (text+layout) on the public SROIE and FUNSD datasets plus a self-annotated invoice set, with stratified 5-fold cross-validation. Metrics are per-field precision/recall/F1 and end-to-end exact-match, with a Tesseract+regex baseline. A confidence threshold routes uncertain fields to manual review; I include an ablation removing layout features and an error analysis by scan quality.

Scope:
The pipeline targets English single-page invoices in PDF/image form for the listed fields. It explicitly excludes handwriting, multi-currency normalisation, multi-page tables, and ERP posting, which are noted as future work.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A reproducible OCR-to-JSON pipeline with per-field F1 and a confidence-routing report
2. A benchmark and ablation showing improvement over the baseline, with documented failure modes and a risk note on dataset bias

Timeline:
14 weeks: data/annotation (3), preprocessing+OCR (3), LayoutLM fine-tuning (4), evaluation+ablation (2), write-up (2).

Title:
Anomaly Detection in Wireless Sensor Streams for Predictive Maintenance

Problem Statement:
Manufacturing lines instrument machines with wireless vibration and temperature sensors, but operators react only after breakdowns. The gap is early, interpretable anomaly detection on noisy, intermittently-dropping sensor streams, where labelled faults are scarce and naive thresholds drift with load, making both supervised methods and fixed limits unreliable on the factory floor.

Objectives:
1. Build an unsupervised anomaly detector for multivariate wireless sensor streams that tolerates gaps and sensor drift
2. Detect emerging faults earlier than a fixed-threshold baseline, measured as lead time before recorded failures
3. Provide interpretable alerts attributing each anomaly to contributing sensors, evaluated with precision/recall and PR-AUC

Methodology:
On the public NASA bearing and a synthetic streaming dataset with injected drift and dropouts, I will window the multivariate signals and compare an LSTM autoencoder against an Isolation Forest and a Matrix Profile detector, scoring anomalies by reconstruction error. Missing-packet handling uses forward-fill plus a missingness flag. Evaluation reports precision, recall, PR-AUC, and detection lead time with time-series cross-validation that avoids look-ahead leakage; SHAP-style attribution highlights the sensors driving each alert. Risks (concept drift, false-alarm fatigue) are mitigated with an adaptive threshold and discussed.

Scope:
The work is offline analysis on recorded/simulated streams from one machine class with three sensor types. It excludes on-device deployment, control-loop actuation, and RF/networking optimisation, which are noted as future work.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A reproducible anomaly-detection pipeline with PR-AUC, lead-time results, and per-sensor attribution
2. A comparative study across the three detectors with an ablation on the missingness handling and a documented risk analysis

Timeline:
14 weeks: data+simulation (3), modelling (4), evaluation+attribution (4), write-up (3).

Title:

14 weeks across literature, dataset prep, modelling and write-up.

Title:
A Web Application Vulnerability Scanner for Manufacturing Company Portals

Manufacturing firms run internal web portals that may contain common security flaws. Manual checking is slow. A simple automated scanner that looks for a few known vulnerability types could help their IT staff.

Title:
Static and Dynamic Analysis of Android Malware for a Public Safety Threat Catalogue

Problem Statement:
Public safety agencies increasingly track malicious Android apps that target citizens, but manually triaging samples is slow. A combined static and dynamic analysis pipeline that summarises a sample's behaviour and assigns a family label would speed early triage and feed a shared threat catalogue.

Objectives:
1. Extract static features (permissions, API calls) from APK samples using Androguard
2. Capture dynamic behaviour by running samples in an emulator sandbox
3. Classify samples into malware families and output a structured threat report

Methodology:
Samples from the Drebin and CICMalDroid datasets will be used. Static features are extracted with Androguard; dynamic logs are collected from the Android emulator with network and API monitoring. A Random Forest classifier is trained on the combined feature set, evaluated by accuracy and per-family F1 with an 80/20 split.

Scope:
The project targets Android only and a fixed set of families present in the datasets. Live malware collection, iOS, and obfuscation-resistant unpacking are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An analysis pipeline producing per-sample behaviour reports
2. A family classifier with measured accuracy and F1

Timeline:
14 weeks: 3 setup, 4 static, 4 dynamic, 3 evaluation.

2. Visualise consumption by day, week and appliance category
3. Generate basic saving suggestions from usage patterns

Methodology:

Scope:
The platform consumes pre-exported meter CSV files; live meter integration and billing are out of scope. It supports a single household account model.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working responsive dashboard with three chart views
2. A usability score and feedback summary

13 weeks across design, frontend, backend and user testing.

Title:
A Progressive Web App for Small Business Inventory and Offline Sales

Small shop owners often use paper or spreadsheets for stock and lose track when offline. A progressive web app that works without a constant connection and syncs later could give them reliable inventory and sales records on cheap devices.

1. Build a PWA for adding stock and recording sales that works offline
2. Sync local changes to a server when connectivity returns
3. Provide a low-stock alert view

Methodology:
The app uses React with a service worker and IndexedDB for offline storage, packaged as an installable PWA. A Firebase backend handles sync and conflict resolution by last-write-wins. Offline behaviour is tested by toggling network conditions in Chrome DevTools, and sync correctness is verified with scripted edits.

Scope:
Single-store, single-currency use is covered. Multi-branch stock transfer, accounting, and barcode hardware are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An installable offline-capable inventory PWA
2. A verified sync log showing offline edits reconciled

Timeline:
13 weeks: 2 design, 6 build, 3 offline/sync testing, 2 write-up.

Title:
A Cross-Platform Mobile App for Crop Disease Reporting by Smallholder Farmers

Problem Statement:
Smallholder farmers often spot crop disease late and lack an easy way to record and share what they see with extension officers. A cross-platform mobile app for photographing and logging suspected disease cases could improve early reporting in rural areas.

Objectives:
1. Build a cross-platform app for capturing crop photos with location and notes
2. Let officers view submitted reports on a shared list
3. Allow basic offline capture with later upload

Methodology:
The app will be built in Flutter for Android and iOS from one codebase. Reports with image, GPS and timestamp are sent to a Firebase backend. Offline captures are queued locally and uploaded on reconnect. Testing covers two physical Android devices and an iOS simulator, plus a small field trial with 5 users.

Scope:
The app handles reporting and viewing only; automated disease diagnosis from images is out of scope. It targets one region's crop list.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working cross-platform reporting app
2. A field-trial feedback summary from 5 users

Timeline:
14 weeks across design, build, offline support and field testing.

Title:
An Android Native App for Real-Time Public Bus Arrival Estimates

Problem Statement:
Commuters often wait at stops without knowing when the next bus will arrive, leading to wasted time. An Android app that combines a published bus schedule with live position feeds to estimate arrival could make daily commuting more predictable.

Objectives:
1. Build a native Android app showing nearby stops and routes on a map
2. Compute and display estimated arrival times from live position data
3. Let users save favourite stops for quick access

Methodology:
The app is built natively in Kotlin using the Google Maps SDK and Room for local storage. It consumes a GTFS schedule plus a GTFS-Realtime vehicle position feed; arrival estimates use remaining stops and average segment speed. Estimate error is measured against logged actual arrivals for one route over a week.

Scope:
One city's bus network with an available GTFS feed is covered. Multi-modal routing and ticketing are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working native Android bus-arrival app
2. A measured arrival-estimate error report for one route

Timeline:
13 weeks: 2 design, 6 development, 3 data validation, 2 evaluation.

Title:
An IoT Sensor Network for Monitoring Water Use in a Campus Sustainability Project

Problem Statement:
Campuses waste water through leaks and unmonitored usage, but data on where water is consumed is rarely available. A low-cost IoT sensor network that logs flow at several points could give facilities staff the data they need to target reductions.

Objectives:
1. Deploy flow sensors on multiple taps reporting to a central gateway
2. Store and visualise usage trends per location over time
3. Trigger an alert when usage exceeds a set threshold

Methodology:
ESP32 nodes with water-flow sensors publish readings over MQTT to a Raspberry Pi gateway running Mosquitto and InfluxDB. Grafana visualises per-node trends. Threshold alerts are sent by email. The setup is validated by comparing logged volume against manual bucket measurements for calibration.

Scope:
A small testbed of three to four sensor nodes is built; campus-wide rollout and automated valve control are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working multi-node water-monitoring testbed with a dashboard
2. A calibration accuracy result against manual measurement

Timeline:
14 weeks across hardware setup, networking, dashboard and calibration.

Title:
A Smart Home Automation Hub for Optimising Last-Mile Parcel Pickup Readiness

Problem Statement:
In last-mile logistics, failed deliveries to homes are costly, often because no one is ready to receive a parcel. A smart home hub that links delivery ETA notifications to home presence and locker state could raise first-attempt success, yet existing smart-home setups rarely coordinate with delivery windows.

Objectives:
1. Build a hub that ingests delivery ETA events and home occupancy/locker signals
2. Implement a rule engine that prepares the home (unlocks a smart locker, notifies the occupant) within the predicted window
3. Evaluate first-attempt readiness against a baseline of notification-only handling

Methodology:
The hub runs on a Raspberry Pi using Home Assistant with MQTT-connected sensors (door, motion) and a smart-lock simulator. Delivery ETAs are fed from a courier webhook stub. A rule engine in Python triggers locker readiness when ETA confidence and occupancy align. Evaluation uses 30 simulated delivery scenarios comparing readiness rate and false-unlock rate against a notification-only baseline, with sensitivity analysis on ETA error.

Scope:
A single-home testbed with simulated courier and locker is built. Real courier API integration and multi-home fleet scheduling are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working automation hub with a documented rule engine
2. A comparative readiness and false-unlock evaluation across scenarios

Timeline:
14 weeks: 2 setup, 5 hub/rules, 3 simulation harness, 3 evaluation, 1 write-up.

Title:
Edge Computing for Low-Latency Document Verification at E-Government Service Counters

Problem Statement:
E-government counters that verify scanned ID documents often send images to a central server, adding latency and exposing citizen data over the network. Running verification at the edge could cut response time and keep raw images local, but the trade-off between on-device model size and accuracy is not well characterised for this setting.

Objectives:
1. Deploy a document-classification and field-extraction model on an edge device
2. Compare edge inference latency and accuracy against a centralised baseline
3. Quantify the accuracy cost of model quantisation on the edge

Methodology:
A MobileNetV2 classifier plus a Tesseract OCR field extractor run on a Jetson Nano. The same pipeline runs on a server as baseline. Models are quantised to INT8 with TensorRT. A labelled set of 600 synthetic ID-style documents is used; metrics are end-to-end latency, classification accuracy and field-level character accuracy. Network-off behaviour confirms edge data locality.

Scope:
Three synthetic document types are covered using generated data, not real citizen IDs. Counter hardware integration and identity-database lookups are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working edge verification pipeline with quantised models
2. A latency/accuracy comparison table against the centralised baseline

Timeline:
14 weeks: 3 data, 4 model, 3 edge deployment, 3 evaluation, 1 write-up.

Title:
A Cloud-Native Microservices Backend for a Course Enrolment Platform

Problem Statement:
University enrolment systems built as monoliths struggle during peak registration when load spikes on a few features. Decomposing enrolment into independently scalable microservices may improve resilience under load, but students rarely measure the actual benefit versus the added operational complexity.

Objectives:
1. Design a microservices backend (catalogue, enrolment, payment-stub, notification) with clear APIs
2. Deploy on Kubernetes with autoscaling and a message broker for async enrolment
3. Compare latency and error rate under load against an equivalent monolith

Methodology:
Services are written in Spring Boot, containerised, and deployed to a local Kubernetes (k3s) cluster with horizontal pod autoscaling. Enrolment events flow through RabbitMQ. A monolith version is built as the baseline. Load is generated with k6 at increasing virtual users; p95 latency, throughput and error rate are recorded for both architectures.

Scope:
Four core services with stubbed payment are implemented; real payment gateways, multi-cluster deployment and full auth federation are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A deployed microservices backend with autoscaling
2. A load-test comparison of microservices versus monolith

Timeline:
14 weeks: 3 design, 5 services, 2 k8s/deploy, 3 load testing, 1 write-up.

Title:
A CI/CD Pipeline With Automated Quality Gates for a Retail Web Application

Problem Statement:
Small retail dev teams often deploy manually, causing slow, error-prone releases and inconsistent quality. A CI/CD pipeline with automated build, test and security gates could shorten lead time, but the effect of each gate on lead time and defect escape is rarely measured in a controlled way.

Objectives:
1. Build a CI/CD pipeline that automates build, test, scan and deploy for a sample retail app
2. Add quality gates (unit-test coverage threshold, SAST, container scan) that block bad builds
3. Measure deployment lead time and gate effectiveness across simulated commits

Methodology:
GitHub Actions orchestrates stages: Maven build and JUnit tests, coverage gate via JaCoCo, SAST with SonarQube, container scan with Trivy, then deploy to a staging Docker host. A set of 25 seeded commits (some with injected defects/vulnerabilities) is pushed to measure lead time and how many bad commits each gate catches. Results compare gated versus ungated flow.

Scope:
One sample Spring Boot retail app and a single staging environment are used. Production rollout strategies (canary, blue-green) are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working gated CI/CD pipeline
2. A report on lead time and defect-catch rate per gate

Timeline:
13 weeks: 2 app prep, 5 pipeline, 3 experiment, 2 analysis, 1 write-up.

Title:
A Big Data Analytics Pipeline for Smart-City Traffic Congestion Patterns

Problem Statement:
Smart cities collect large volumes of traffic-sensor and GPS data, but turning streaming and historical feeds into congestion insight at scale is hard for ad-hoc scripts. A structured big data pipeline could ingest, process and aggregate this data, yet students rarely test how batch and streaming layers compare on the same congestion task.

Objectives:
1. Build an ingestion and processing pipeline for traffic-sensor data
2. Compute congestion metrics in both a batch and a streaming layer
3. Compare freshness and resource use between the two layers

Methodology:
Data from an open city-traffic dataset is replayed into Kafka. Spark Structured Streaming computes rolling congestion indices, while a Spark batch job recomputes daily aggregates into Parquet on HDFS/MinIO. Results feed a small dashboard. Evaluation compares end-to-end latency, throughput and CPU/memory between batch and streaming on identical windows, with a documented data schema.

Scope:
One open dataset replayed in a single-node cluster is used; real-time city feeds, geospatial routing and ML prediction are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working batch-plus-streaming analytics pipeline with a dashboard
2. A comparison of latency and resource use between the two layers

Timeline:
14 weeks: 3 ingestion, 4 batch, 3 streaming, 3 evaluation, 1 write-up.

Title:
An Interactive Business Intelligence Dashboard for Destination Demand Analysis in Domestic Tourism

Problem Statement:
Regional tourism boards hold fragmented data on arrivals, bookings and seasonality but lack an integrated, drill-down BI view, so planning relies on static yearly reports. Commercial BI tools exist, yet few open student projects document an end-to-end dimensional model plus governed, role-filtered dashboards for destination demand, leaving a reproducible gap this project addresses.

Objectives:
1. Design a star-schema warehouse integrating arrivals, accommodation and event datasets with documented ETL
2. Deliver an interactive dashboard with drill-down by region, season and visitor segment
3. Evaluate decision-task accuracy and time against the existing static-report workflow

Methodology:
Public tourism datasets are cleaned and loaded via a Python/dbt ETL into a PostgreSQL star schema (fact: visits; dimensions: date, region, segment, accommodation). Apache Superset provides drill-down dashboards with row-level filters per board role. Evaluation is a within-subjects study with 12 participants performing 6 planning tasks on dashboard versus static reports, measuring task time, accuracy and SUS, analysed with paired t-tests. Data-quality checks and a documented refresh schedule address reliability.

Scope:
Three integrated public datasets for one country's domestic tourism are covered. Real-time feeds, predictive forecasting and write-back planning are explicitly excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A documented dimensional warehouse with reproducible ETL
2. An interactive role-filtered dashboard plus a statistically analysed usability and decision-efficiency study

Timeline:
15 weeks: 2 requirements, 3 ETL/modelling, 4 dashboard, 3 user study, 2 analysis, 1 write-up.

Title:
Forecasting Daily User Engagement on a Social Media Platform: A Comparative Time-Series Study

Problem Statement:
Social media teams plan content and capacity around expected daily engagement, but simple moving averages miss weekly seasonality and event spikes. While many models exist, students rarely compare classical, machine-learning and deep-learning forecasters under one rigorous protocol with proper backtesting on the same engagement series, which this project provides as a reproducible benchmark.

Objectives:
1. Build a clean daily engagement series with calendar and event features
2. Compare SARIMA, Prophet, XGBoost and an LSTM under identical backtesting
3. Quantify accuracy and prediction-interval calibration, with an ablation on event features

Methodology:
A public social media activity dataset is aggregated to daily active-engagement counts. Features include day-of-week, holiday flags and lagged values. Models (SARIMA, Prophet, gradient-boosted XGBoost on lags, and an LSTM) are evaluated with rolling-origin cross-validation. Metrics are MAE, RMSE, MAPE and 80% interval coverage; a naive seasonal model is the baseline. Statistical significance of differences uses the Diebold-Mariano test, and an ablation removes event features to isolate their effect.

Scope:
One platform's aggregate daily engagement over at least two years is used. Per-user prediction, multivariate cross-platform modelling and live deployment are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A reproducible forecasting benchmark across four model families with intervals
2. A significance-tested accuracy comparison and an event-feature ablation report

Timeline:
15 weeks: 2 data, 3 features, 5 modelling, 3 evaluation, 2 write-up.

Title:
Blockchain for Logistics

Problem Statement:
Logistics companies have a lot of problems with tracking and trust. Blockchain can fix this because it is secure and modern.

Objectives:
1. To use blockchain.
2. To make logistics better.
3. To do smart contracts.

Methodology:
I will study blockchain and use smart contracts to track things. Some coding will be done.

Scope:
This will work for all logistics companies everywhere and save money.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A blockchain system.
2. Happy companies.

Title:
AR App for Government

Problem Statement:
People do not like going to government offices. Augmented reality is cool and can make things easier for everyone.

Objectives:
1. Make an AR app.
2. Help citizens.
3. Use new technology.

Methodology:
I will download an AR tool and build an app with it. Then I will test if it works on my phone.

Scope:
For all government services and all citizens in the country.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An AR application.
2. Better government.

Title:
VR Training Simulation

Problem Statement:
Students get bored in class and do not learn well. Virtual reality is the future and can make learning fun and interesting.

Objectives:
1. Build a VR simulation.
2. Train students.
3. Make learning fun.

Methodology:
I will use a VR headset and some software to make a 3D world where students can learn. Research will also be done online.

Scope:
This is for education and all schools can use it for any subject.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A VR training app.
2. Students learn more.

Title:
A 2D Mobile Game for Retail Shopping

Problem Statement:
Many retail stores want to keep customers engaged but shopping apps are boring. A small game that rewards shoppers with points could make the experience more enjoyable and encourage repeat visits.

Objectives:
1. To design a 2D game where players collect items linked to store products.
2. To add a points and reward system tied to purchases.
3. To test the game with a small group of users.

Methodology:
I will build the game in Unity using C#. The game will have a few levels and a simple scoring system. A basic backend will store the points. I will ask around ten people to play it and give feedback through a short survey.

Scope:
The project covers a single-player 2D game for Android only. It will not include real payment integration or multiplayer.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working 2D Android game with a reward feature.
2. Survey feedback on whether users found it engaging.

Timeline:
About 14 weeks, split into design, development, and testing.

Title:
A Serious Game to Teach Smart City Concepts

Problem Statement:
Residents in growing cities often do not understand how smart city systems like traffic sensors or energy grids work. A game-based approach could help people learn these ideas in a more interactive way than reading documents.

Objectives:
1. To develop a serious game that explains three smart city concepts.
2. To include short quizzes inside the game to check understanding.
3. To measure whether players learn from playing.

Methodology:
The game will be made in Unity. Players manage a small virtual city and make decisions about traffic and energy. After each level there is a quiz. I will run a pre-test and post-test with around fifteen students to see if scores improve.

Scope:
The game focuses on three concepts only and is for desktop. It will not model a full city or use real sensor data.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A playable educational game covering three smart city topics.
2. Pre/post test results showing any learning gain.

Timeline:
14 weeks across design, build, and evaluation phases.

Title:
A Health Information App for Tourists

Problem Statement:
Tourists visiting a new country often struggle to find nearby clinics or understand local health advice. A simple app that lists health facilities and basic guidance could reduce stress when travellers feel unwell abroad.

Objectives:
1. To build a mobile app that shows nearby clinics and pharmacies.
2. To provide simple first-aid and health tips for travellers.
3. To let users save important emergency contacts.

Methodology:
The app will be built with Flutter and use a maps API to show facility locations. Health tips will be stored in a small local database. I will test usability with a few travellers and collect their comments.

Scope:
The app covers one city and shows facilities from a manually prepared list. It does not include appointment booking or real-time doctor chat.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working app listing health facilities and tips for one city.
2. Usability feedback from a small group of testers.

Timeline:
Roughly 13 weeks for design, build, and testing.

Title:
A Telemedicine Platform with Social Sharing

Problem Statement:
People with minor health concerns often delay seeing a doctor and instead ask friends on social media, where the advice can be unreliable. A platform that connects users to verified doctors while keeping a familiar social feel could improve trust.

Objectives:
1. To build a web platform where patients can request video consultations.
2. To add a moderated community feed for general health questions.
3. To allow doctors to verify their accounts.

Methodology:
The platform will use React for the frontend and Node.js with a MySQL database for the backend. Video calls will use a third-party WebRTC service. The community feed will store posts and allow doctor replies. I will demonstrate the platform and gather feedback from a small set of test users.

Scope:
The prototype supports text consultations and one-to-one video. It will not handle prescriptions, payments, or insurance.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A functioning telemedicine web prototype with a community feed.
2. Feedback from test users on usefulness and trust.

Timeline:
14 weeks divided into design, development, and evaluation.

Title:
An Adaptive E-Learning System for Nursing Students

Problem Statement:
Nursing students revise large volumes of clinical material but most e-learning tools present the same content to everyone regardless of weak areas. A system that adapts question difficulty to each learner could make revision more efficient than a fixed quiz bank.

Objectives:
1. To build an e-learning platform that tracks performance per topic.
2. To implement a rule-based adaptive engine that adjusts question difficulty.
3. To evaluate learning outcomes against a non-adaptive version.

Methodology:
The platform will be built with Django and PostgreSQL. Questions are tagged by topic and difficulty. An adaptive engine raises or lowers difficulty based on recent accuracy using a simple mastery threshold. I will run a study with two groups of around twenty students each, comparing post-test scores between the adaptive and fixed versions.

Scope:
The system covers two nursing modules and multiple-choice questions only. It excludes simulation labs, video grading, and mobile apps.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working adaptive e-learning web application for two modules.
2. A comparison of post-test scores between adaptive and fixed groups.

Timeline:
15 weeks: 3 design, 8 development, 4 evaluation and write-up.

Title:
A QR-Based Micropayment System for Campus Vendors

Problem Statement:
Small campus vendors lose sales when students carry no cash, and existing payment apps charge fees that are high for very small purchases. A lightweight QR micropayment system aimed at sub-RM10 transactions could lower friction for both sides.

Objectives:
1. To build a wallet app where students top up and pay vendors by QR.
2. To implement a ledger that records and reconciles transactions.
3. To evaluate transaction speed and reconciliation accuracy.

Methodology:
The app will be built with React Native and a Spring Boot backend using MySQL. Payments use a signed QR token validated server-side; balances are updated in a double-entry ledger. I will simulate 500 transactions to measure average completion time and verify that no balances drift after reconciliation.

Scope:
The prototype uses a simulated top-up (no real bank integration) and targets in-campus vendors only. It excludes refunds, cross-bank settlement, and fraud scoring.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working QR wallet prototype with a reconciling ledger.
2. Measured transaction latency and reconciliation accuracy figures.

Timeline:
15 weeks across design, build, simulation, and evaluation.

Title:
Fraud Detection for Manufacturing Procurement Records

Problem Statement:
Manufacturing firms process thousands of supplier invoices, where duplicate or inflated entries cause financial leakage. Manual auditing catches only a fraction. A machine-learning classifier on procurement records could flag suspicious invoices for review.

Objectives:
1. To assemble and label a dataset of procurement transactions.
2. To train a classifier that flags potentially fraudulent invoices.
3. To evaluate it using precision, recall, and F1 against a rule-based baseline.

Methodology:
Using a public procurement dataset plus synthetic fraud injection, I will engineer features such as price deviation from supplier median and duplicate-invoice signals. I will train logistic regression and random forest models with 5-fold cross-validation and compare them to a threshold rule baseline, reporting precision, recall, and F1.

Scope:
The project handles structured invoice records only. It excludes scanned documents, real-time scoring, and ERP integration.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained fraud-flagging model with reported metrics.
2. A comparison showing improvement over the rule-based baseline.

Timeline:
15 weeks: data and features 4, modelling 6, evaluation and report 5.

Title:
A Recommendation Engine for a Public-Safety Equipment Store

Problem Statement:
Online stores selling public-safety equipment such as helmets and reflective gear carry many similar items, and buyers often cannot find the right product for their job role. A recommender that suggests items by role and past purchases could improve relevance over a plain search.

Objectives:
1. To build an e-commerce catalogue with role-tagged products.
2. To implement item-based collaborative filtering for recommendations.
3. To evaluate recommendation quality against a popularity baseline.

Methodology:
The store backend uses Node.js with MongoDB. I will generate a synthetic purchase dataset across user roles, then compute item-item similarity using cosine similarity for collaborative filtering. Offline evaluation will use precision@5 and recall@5 with a train/test split, comparing against a most-popular-items baseline.

Scope:
The project focuses on the recommendation logic and a basic catalogue UI. It excludes real payment, inventory management, and live A/B testing.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working recommender integrated into a sample storefront.
2. Precision@5 and recall@5 results versus the popularity baseline.

Timeline:
14 weeks across catalogue, recommender, and evaluation phases.

Title:
A Chatbot for Household Energy Saving Advice

Problem Statement:
Households want to lower electricity bills but rarely read long energy guides, and generic tips ignore their actual usage. A chatbot that answers questions and gives advice based on a user's appliance profile could make energy saving more actionable.

Objectives:
1. To build a conversational agent that answers energy-saving questions.
2. To estimate appliance-level consumption from user-entered usage.
3. To evaluate answer relevance and estimate accuracy.

Methodology:
The chatbot uses intent classification over a labelled set of energy questions, with responses drawn from a curated knowledge base. An estimator computes appliance kWh from wattage and usage hours entered by the user. I will test intent accuracy on a held-out set and check estimates against manufacturer figures, plus a small user survey on helpfulness.

Scope:
The chatbot covers common household appliances and English only. It excludes live smart-meter integration and multi-language support.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working energy-advice chatbot with consumption estimates.
2. Intent accuracy and estimate error figures plus survey feedback.

Timeline:
14 weeks: knowledge base 3, build 7, evaluation 4.

Title:
A Knowledge-Graph Search Tool for Small Business Records

Problem Statement:
Small businesses keep scattered records of customers, suppliers, and invoices across spreadsheets, making it hard to answer questions that span files, such as which suppliers a late-paying customer also deals with. A knowledge graph could connect these records for richer search than keyword lookup.

Objectives:
1. To extract entities and relationships from sample business records.
2. To build a knowledge graph and a search interface over it.
3. To evaluate query accuracy against keyword search.

Methodology:
I will parse CSV exports and use rule-based extraction to identify customers, suppliers, and invoices as nodes with linking edges, stored in Neo4j. A query interface translates a set of template questions into Cypher. I will create a test set of cross-record questions and compare answer correctness between the graph tool and a baseline keyword search.

Scope:
The tool handles three record types and English template queries only. It excludes free-text natural-language parsing and live accounting-software sync.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A knowledge-graph search prototype over sample business data.
2. Accuracy comparison on cross-record queries versus keyword search.

Timeline:
15 weeks across extraction, graph build, interface, and evaluation.

Title:
Semantic Segmentation of Crop and Weed Regions in Field Imagery

Problem Statement:
Precision-agriculture systems need to distinguish crops from weeds so herbicide is applied only where needed, but lighting variation and overlapping foliage make pixel-level separation difficult. Reliable segmentation on field images is the bottleneck for targeted spraying, and lightweight models are required to run on farm hardware.

Objectives:
1. To train a semantic segmentation model that labels crop, weed, and soil pixels.
2. To compare a U-Net baseline with a DeepLabV3+ encoder on accuracy and inference speed.
3. To assess robustness under varied lighting via augmentation.

Methodology:
I will use the public CWFID and Sugar Beets datasets, splitting 70/15/15 for train/validation/test. Models are U-Net and DeepLabV3+ (ResNet-50 backbone) trained with cross-entropy plus Dice loss, Adam optimiser, and augmentation for brightness, flips, and crops. Evaluation reports mean IoU, per-class IoU, and frames per second on a single GPU. A risk is class imbalance for weeds, mitigated by weighted loss.

Scope:
The work covers RGB field images and three classes only. It excludes multispectral input, real-time embedded deployment, and yield prediction.

Expected Outcomes:
1. Trained segmentation models with reported mean and per-class IoU.
2. An accuracy-versus-speed comparison guiding model choice for field use.

Timeline:
16 weeks: data prep 3, modelling 7, evaluation 4, write-up 2.

Title:
Real-Time Vehicle and Pedestrian Detection for Intersection Safety

Problem Statement:
Camera-based intersection monitoring can warn of near-collisions, but detectors must run in real time and stay accurate for small or partially occluded pedestrians. Off-the-shelf models trade speed for accuracy; the gap is a configuration that holds acceptable recall on vulnerable road users at usable frame rates.

Objectives:
1. To train an object detector for vehicles and pedestrians on traffic imagery.
2. To compare YOLOv8 variants against a Faster R-CNN baseline on accuracy and latency.
3. To analyse detection recall specifically for small/occluded pedestrians.

Methodology:
I will fine-tune YOLOv8-n and YOLOv8-s and a Faster R-CNN baseline on a subset of the BDD100K traffic dataset, with an 80/10/10 split. Evaluation reports mAP@0.5, mAP@0.5:0.95, per-class AP, and inference latency on a single GPU. A dedicated slice of small-object and occluded pedestrian instances is analysed separately. Risks include label noise, addressed by spot-checking annotations.

Scope:
The project uses public 2D camera datasets and two object classes. It excludes multi-camera tracking, depth sensing, and on-device deployment.

Expected Outcomes:
1. Trained detectors with reported mAP and latency across variants.
2. A focused analysis of recall on small and occluded pedestrians.

Timeline:
16 weeks across data, training, evaluation, and reporting.

Title:
Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis of Public Opinion on Sustainability Initiatives

Problem Statement:
Policymakers gauge reaction to sustainability programmes from social media, but overall sentiment hides which aspects—cost, convenience, or environmental benefit—drive opinion. Document-level sentiment is too coarse; the need is aspect-level analysis that attributes sentiment to specific concerns.

Objectives:
1. To build an aspect-based sentiment model over sustainability-related posts.
2. To compare a fine-tuned transformer with a lexicon-plus-SVM baseline.
3. To report per-aspect sentiment distributions for three initiative types.

Methodology:
I will collect English posts on sustainability topics and annotate a sample for three aspects with sentiment polarity. I will fine-tune a DistilBERT classifier for joint aspect-sentiment prediction and compare it to a VADER-lexicon-plus-SVM baseline, using stratified 5-fold cross-validation. Metrics are macro-F1 and per-aspect F1, with inter-annotator agreement reported via Cohen's kappa. Class imbalance is a known risk, handled by resampling.

Scope:
The study covers English text and three predefined aspects. It excludes sarcasm detection, multilingual posts, and image content.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An aspect-based sentiment model with macro-F1 and per-aspect F1 figures.
2. Per-aspect sentiment distributions across three sustainability initiative types.

Timeline:
16 weeks: collection and annotation 5, modelling 6, evaluation 3, write-up 2.

Title:
Learned Cardinality Estimation for Query Optimization in a Logistics Database

Problem Statement:
Query optimizers in logistics databases rely on histogram-based cardinality estimates that degrade on correlated columns like route, depot, and date, leading to poor join plans and slow shipment queries. Better cardinality estimates could cut execution time without rewriting the workload.

Objectives:
1. To build a learned cardinality estimator for multi-predicate logistics queries.
2. To compare its plan quality and runtime against the native PostgreSQL optimizer.
3. To measure estimation error across correlated-column queries.

Methodology:
Using a synthetic shipment schema and a generated query workload with known true cardinalities, I will train a regression model (gradient-boosted trees) on query features to predict cardinality, then feed estimates via plan hints. Evaluation compares q-error on a held-out query set and end-to-end latency against the default optimizer over repeated runs. A risk is overfitting to the synthetic workload, mitigated by a separate query template for testing.

Scope:
The project targets read-only analytical queries on one schema. It excludes write workloads, distributed databases, and optimizer source-code changes.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A learned estimator with reported q-error versus the native optimizer.
2. End-to-end latency comparison on the held-out query workload.

Timeline:
16 weeks across schema/workload, modelling, integration, and evaluation.

Title:
A Facial-Recognition Attendance System for Government Office Check-In

Problem Statement:
Government offices still log staff attendance by card or fingerprint, which are slow at peak hours and unhygienic. Facial recognition could speed check-in, but accuracy under varied lighting and the risk of spoofing with photos must be addressed before such a system is trustworthy.

Objectives:
1. To build a face-recognition attendance pipeline with enrolment and matching.
2. To evaluate recognition accuracy across lighting conditions.
3. To add and test a basic liveness check against photo spoofing.

Methodology:
The pipeline uses MTCNN for detection and a FaceNet embedding with cosine-distance matching against an enrolled gallery. I will collect a small consented dataset across three lighting conditions and report identification accuracy, false-accept and false-reject rates. A blink-based liveness check is tested against printed-photo and screen-replay attempts. A privacy risk is acknowledged, with embeddings stored rather than raw images.

Scope:
The system handles a closed set of enrolled staff and frontal faces. It excludes mask-wearing recognition, large-scale identification, and mobile deployment.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working attendance prototype with accuracy and error-rate figures.
2. Liveness-check results against photo and replay spoofing.

Timeline:

Title:
A Pipeline for Robust OCR of Handwritten Student Answer Scripts

Problem Statement:
Digitising handwritten exam scripts would speed feedback in education, but general OCR engines fail on cursive handwriting, mixed math notation, and noisy scans, and they offer no confidence signal to route uncertain text for human review. The specific gap is an end-to-end handwriting OCR pipeline that pairs strong recognition with calibrated confidence so low-certainty regions are flagged rather than silently mis-transcribed.

Objectives:
1. To build a segmentation-and-recognition OCR pipeline for handwritten answer scripts achieving line-level character error rate below 12%.
2. To add a confidence-calibration module that routes low-confidence lines to human review, measured by expected calibration error.
3. To benchmark the pipeline against Tesseract and a cloud OCR API on accuracy and review-routing precision.

Methodology:
I will use the IAM Handwriting and CVL datasets plus a small consented set of real scripts, split 70/15/15. Preprocessing applies deskew, binarisation, and line segmentation. Recognition uses a CRNN with CTC loss, then a TrOCR transformer for comparison, trained with Adam and early stopping. Confidence is calibrated via temperature scaling and evaluated by expected calibration error; routing precision is measured at a tuned threshold. Baselines are Tesseract LSTM and a commercial OCR API. Metrics are character and word error rate, ECE, and routing precision/recall, with 5-fold validation on the training split. Risks include handwriting-style overfit, mitigated by writer-disjoint splits.

Scope:
The pipeline targets English handwritten lines and digits with basic math symbols. It excludes full mathematical-formula parsing, multi-column layout reconstruction, and automated grading of answer content.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An OCR pipeline meeting the target character error rate with calibrated, review-routing confidence.
2. A benchmark report comparing CRNN and TrOCR against Tesseract and a cloud API on error rate, ECE, and routing precision.

Timeline:
16 weeks: data and preprocessing 3, recognition models 6, calibration and routing 3, benchmarking and write-up 4.

Title:
Anomaly Detection and Forecasting for Wireless Sensor Streams in Retail Stores

Problem Statement:
Retail chains deploy wireless sensors for temperature, foot traffic, and shelf occupancy, but raw streams are noisy, contain gaps from packet loss, and drift as stores change layout, so naive thresholds produce false alarms and miss slow failures. The gap is a streaming analytics pipeline that imputes gaps, detects anomalies online, and short-horizon forecasts occupancy while adapting to concept drift, with evaluation against labelled incidents rather than synthetic spikes only.

Objectives:
1. To build a streaming pipeline that imputes missing sensor readings and detects anomalies with F1 above a stated baseline.
2. To produce 30-minute foot-traffic forecasts and report error against seasonal-naive and ARIMA baselines.
3. To quantify robustness to concept drift using a drift-injection protocol.

Methodology:
I will use the public Intel Lab and a retail foot-traffic dataset, augmented with a small self-collected sensor deployment, splitting chronologically to avoid leakage. Gaps are imputed by Kalman smoothing; anomaly detection compares an LSTM autoencoder reconstruction-error method against isolation forest and a robust z-score baseline. Forecasting compares an LSTM and Prophet against seasonal-naive and ARIMA, reported via MAE and sMAPE. Drift robustness is tested by injecting distribution shifts and measuring detection-delay and false-alarm rate. Evaluation uses precision, recall, F1 on labelled anomalies with time-series cross-validation. A resource risk is on-device compute, addressed by edge-friendly model sizing.

Scope:
The pipeline covers three sensor types and per-store single-site streams. It excludes multi-store federation, camera-based sensing, and automated actuation.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A streaming pipeline with imputation, online anomaly detection, and forecasting, with metrics against named baselines.
2. A drift-robustness analysis reporting detection delay and false-alarm rate under injected shifts.

Timeline:
16 weeks: data and ingestion 3, imputation and anomaly models 5, forecasting 4, drift evaluation and write-up 4.

Title:

Scope:

Title:
Edge Computing for Real-Time Solar Inverter Fault Detection

Objectives:

Methodology:

Detection latency, uplink bandwidth, and F1 score will be measured and compared against a cloud-only pipeline running the same model unquantised, with model size and inference time reported.

Scope:
The project covers edge deployment, quantisation, and a latency-bandwidth-accuracy comparison for a few fault types on one edge node. It excludes physical inverter hardware, multi-node orchestration, and grid control actions.

Expected Outcomes:

Title:

Title:
A Big Data Analytics Pipeline for Urban Bus Delay Analysis

Methodology:
Historical and replayed GPS data will be ingested through Apache Kafka into Apache Spark, which joins live positions with scheduled timetables to compute delays per route and stop. Aggregated results are stored in Parquet on HDFS and queried for a dashboard built with Apache Superset. Pipeline throughput and processing latency will be measured at increasing data volumes, and delay hotspots validated against known congested corridors.

Scope:
The project covers ingestion, batch and micro-batch delay computation, and hotspot visualisation for one city's bus dataset. It excludes real-time passenger-facing predictions, fare data, and multi-modal transport.

Expected Outcomes:
