2. A throughput and latency evaluation across data volumes

Title:

Objectives:
1. Design a star-schema data warehouse consolidating electricity, water, and waste data with a target dimension
2. Build automated ETL that ingests meter and billing exports, validates them, and loads the warehouse weekly
3. Deliver an interactive BI dashboard with KPIs, trend drill-down, and target tracking, evaluated for task-completion time and SUS usability against the current manual spreadsheet process

Methodology:
Source extracts (CSV meter logs, parsed billing data) are cleaned and conformed by a Python ETL job orchestrated with Apache Airflow into a PostgreSQL star schema with fact tables for consumption and dimensions for site, meter, time, and target. A Power BI dashboard exposes per-building KPIs, normalised intensity (per m2 and per occupant), and variance-to-target with drill-down. Evaluation uses ten staff completing five reporting tasks under both the old spreadsheet method and the dashboard, measuring task-completion time, error count, and System Usability Scale scores, analysed with a paired comparison.

Scope:
The project delivers the warehouse, ETL, and dashboard for electricity, water, and waste at three campus buildings over two years of historical data. It explicitly excludes real-time sub-metering, predictive consumption forecasting, carbon-offset accounting, and integration with the finance ERP, which are noted as future work.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A documented star-schema warehouse with an automated, validated weekly ETL pipeline
2. An interactive sustainability dashboard plus a usability and efficiency evaluation showing measured improvement over the manual process

Weeks 1-3 requirements and KPI definition; weeks 4-8 warehouse and ETL; weeks 9-13 dashboard build; weeks 14-18 user evaluation; weeks 19-24 analysis and write-up.

Title:
Probabilistic Time-Series Forecasting of Warehouse Outbound Demand for Logistics Planning

Problem Statement:
Third-party logistics warehouses must staff and allocate space based on next-day outbound order volume, yet many still forecast with simple moving averages that ignore weekly seasonality, promotions, and holiday effects, leading to overtime or idle labour. Point forecasts alone also hide uncertainty, so planners cannot size safety buffers, and there is little comparison of modern probabilistic forecasters on real warehouse demand.

Objectives:
1. Build and compare point and probabilistic forecasters for daily warehouse outbound volume
2. Quantify forecast accuracy and calibration against established baselines using rolling-origin evaluation
3. Translate probabilistic forecasts into staffing-buffer recommendations and assess their cost trade-off

Methodology:
Two years of daily outbound order data plus calendar and promotion features will be modelled with SARIMA and Facebook Prophet as interpretable baselines and LightGBM quantile regression and a Temporal Fusion Transformer as the main models. Evaluation uses rolling-origin (walk-forward) cross-validation reporting MAE, RMSE, and MASE for point accuracy, and pinball loss with prediction-interval coverage for calibration, all benchmarked against a seasonal-naive baseline. Quantile forecasts are converted to staffing buffers, and a simple cost model compares under- and over-staffing against the current moving-average approach.

Scope:
The study forecasts aggregate daily outbound volume at one distribution centre using historical and calendar features, with a 14-day horizon. It excludes per-SKU forecasting, inbound and returns flows, live system integration, and real-time retraining, which are listed as future work. Data is anonymised and handled under the partner's data agreement.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A reproducible benchmark of four forecasters with point and probabilistic metrics under rolling-origin evaluation
2. A staffing-buffer recommendation method with a cost comparison against the incumbent baseline

Timeline:
Weeks 1-4 data acquisition and cleaning; weeks 5-9 baselines and feature engineering; weeks 10-15 main models and tuning; weeks 16-20 evaluation and cost analysis; weeks 21-24 write-up.

3. Reduce paper usage in the clinic

Methodology:
The system will be built with PHP and MySQL. Patients book appointments online and doctors view records on a dashboard. I will include a simple report showing estimated paper saved. Testing will be functional testing of each feature.

Scope:
The system handles appointments and basic patient records for a single small clinic. It does not include billing or pharmacy modules.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working appointment and records web system
2. Less paper used by the clinic

Timeline:
Five months from requirements to deployment.

Title:
Telemedicine Platform for Delivery Driver Health

Problem Statement:
Logistics and delivery drivers spend long hours on the road and rarely visit doctors. A telemedicine platform would let them consult a doctor by video without leaving their route, helping catch health issues early.

Objectives:
1. Develop a telemedicine web and mobile platform
2. Support video consultation and prescription notes
3. Tailor scheduling around driver shift times

Methodology:
The platform will use a React frontend and a Node.js backend with WebRTC for video calls. Drivers book a slot, join a video room, and receive notes afterward. Data is stored in MongoDB. Testing will involve functional tests and a small usability survey with a few drivers.

Scope:
The platform covers booking, video consultation, and notes for one logistics company's drivers. It does not handle insurance claims or lab results.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A functional telemedicine platform
2. Positive usability feedback from drivers

Timeline:
About five months including a pilot test.

Title:
An E-Learning Portal for Citizen Training on E-Government Services

Problem Statement:
Many citizens struggle to use online government services because they do not know how the portals work. There is no central place that teaches them step by step, leading to failed applications and crowded service counters.

Objectives:
1. Build an e-learning portal with structured courses on common e-government tasks
2. Provide interactive tutorials with quizzes and progress tracking
3. Measure whether users complete tasks more successfully after training

Methodology:
The portal will be built with React, Spring Boot, and PostgreSQL. Courses are organised into modules with video, text, and quizzes; progress and quiz scores are stored per user. I will compare task-completion success between a trained and an untrained group using a short simulated task. Functional testing and a usability questionnaire (SUS) will be conducted.

Scope:
The portal covers three e-government services (tax filing, license renewal, benefit application) for desktop and mobile web. Real government integration and payments are out of scope; tasks are simulated.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working e-learning portal with progress tracking
2. Higher task-completion rates and a measured SUS score

Timeline:
Phase 1 requirements (month 1), Phase 2 build (months 2-4), Phase 3 testing and evaluation (months 5-6).

Title:
A Campus Fintech Payment App for Students

Problem Statement:
Students on campus often carry cash for canteens, printing, and events, which is inconvenient and hard to track. Existing bank apps are not tailored to campus needs and have high friction for small payments.

Objectives:
1. Build a mobile wallet app for campus payments with QR transactions
2. Provide a spending dashboard and budgeting alerts for students
3. Evaluate transaction speed and user satisfaction against cash and a generic e-wallet

Methodology:
The app will be built with Flutter and a Spring Boot backend, using a simulated payment ledger in PostgreSQL. QR codes encode merchant and amount; transactions update balances atomically. I will benchmark average transaction completion time and run a usability test (SUS) with 15-20 students, comparing against cash baseline timings.

Scope:
The prototype covers wallet top-up (simulated), QR pay, history, and budgeting for one campus. Real bank settlement and refunds are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working campus wallet app with QR payments and budgeting
2. Reported transaction times and SUS scores versus baseline

Timeline:
Months 1-2 design, months 3-4 development, months 5-6 testing and evaluation.

Title:
Credit-Card Fraud Detection for Online Retail

Problem Statement:
Online retailers lose money to fraudulent card transactions, and rule-based filters miss new fraud patterns while flagging too many legitimate orders. A machine-learning approach could improve detection while keeping false positives low.

Objectives:
1. Train classifiers to detect fraudulent retail transactions
2. Compare logistic regression, random forest, and XGBoost
3. Optimise for precision-recall given heavy class imbalance

Methodology:
Using the public Kaggle credit-card fraud dataset, I will engineer features, handle imbalance with SMOTE, and train logistic regression, random forest, and XGBoost. Models are evaluated with 5-fold cross-validation reporting precision, recall, F1, and AUPRC, since accuracy is misleading on imbalanced data. The best model is wrapped in a small Flask scoring API.

Scope:
The project covers offline model training and a demo scoring endpoint on one public dataset. Real-time streaming and production deployment are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained fraud model with reported precision, recall, F1, and AUPRC
2. A comparison table across the three algorithms plus a demo API

Timeline:
Month 1 data and EDA, months 2-3 modelling, month 4 API, months 5-6 evaluation and write-up.

Title:
A Product Recommendation Engine for a Smart-City Marketplace

Problem Statement:
Smart-city marketplaces list many local services and products, but residents struggle to find relevant ones. Without personalised recommendations, useful local listings get buried and small vendors lose visibility.

Objectives:
1. Build a recommendation engine for a local-services marketplace
2. Compare collaborative filtering with a content-based approach
3. Evaluate recommendation quality with offline ranking metrics

Methodology:
I will use a public e-commerce ratings dataset to simulate marketplace interactions. Item-based collaborative filtering (cosine similarity) and a TF-IDF content-based model will be implemented in Python with scikit-learn and Surprise. Evaluation uses an 80/20 split reporting Precision@K, Recall@K, and NDCG. The best model is exposed through a Flask API used by a small React storefront demo.

Scope:
The work covers offline training and a demo storefront with one dataset. Real-time updates and a live vendor base are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. Two recommender models with Precision@K, Recall@K, and NDCG reported
2. A demo storefront showing personalised recommendations

Timeline:
Months 1-2 data and models, months 3-4 integration, months 5-6 evaluation.

Title:
A Tourism Chatbot for Local Attraction Planning

Problem Statement:
Tourists visiting a new city ask the same questions about attractions, opening hours, and routes, but official sites are hard to navigate. A conversational assistant could answer these in natural language and suggest a short itinerary.

Objectives:
1. Build a chatbot that answers tourism FAQs and suggests attractions
2. Use retrieval over a curated attraction knowledge base
3. Evaluate answer relevance and intent accuracy

Methodology:
The chatbot will use a retrieval-augmented approach: a curated dataset of attractions is embedded with sentence-transformers and stored in FAISS; user queries retrieve top passages that a template or small LLM uses to answer. Intent classification handles greetings, FAQs, and itinerary requests. Evaluation measures intent accuracy on a labelled test set and answer relevance rated by 10 users.

Scope:
The chatbot covers one city's attractions in English via a web widget. Live booking and multilingual support are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working tourism chatbot with retrieval-based answers
2. Reported intent accuracy and user relevance ratings

Timeline:
Month 1 data, months 2-4 build, months 5-6 evaluation.

Title:
Knowledge-Graph Search over Social-Media Posts

Problem Statement:
Keyword search on social media returns noisy results and misses relationships between people, topics, and events. Representing posts as a knowledge graph could enable richer queries such as which users discuss a topic together.

Objectives:
1. Build a knowledge graph from a social-media dataset
2. Extract entities and relations to populate the graph
3. Enable graph-based search and compare it with keyword search

Methodology:
Using a public Twitter-style dataset, I will extract entities with spaCy NER and simple relation rules, then load nodes and edges into Neo4j. A query interface translates user questions into Cypher for entity- and relation-based search. I will compare graph search against a baseline keyword search on a set of test queries, measuring Precision@K and qualitative relevance.

Scope:
The project uses one static public dataset in English and a fixed set of relation types. Real-time ingestion and sentiment are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A populated knowledge graph with a search interface
2. Precision@K comparison between graph and keyword search

Timeline:
Months 1-2 extraction, months 3-4 graph and queries, months 5-6 evaluation.

Title:
Automated Segmentation of Skin Lesions for Melanoma Screening

Problem Statement:
Accurate lesion boundary delineation is a bottleneck in automated melanoma screening; manual segmentation is slow and inconsistent between clinicians. Deep segmentation models can assist, but generalisation across skin tones and imaging conditions remains a challenge.

Objectives:
1. Train a U-Net-based model to segment skin lesions from dermoscopic images
2. Compare U-Net against U-Net++ and a DeepLabV3+ baseline
3. Assess robustness across lesion types using stratified evaluation

Methodology:
Using the ISIC 2018 dataset, images are preprocessed (resizing, hair removal, normalisation) and augmented (flips, rotation, colour jitter). U-Net, U-Net++, and DeepLabV3+ are trained with a combined Dice and binary cross-entropy loss, using a fixed train/val/test split and early stopping. Evaluation reports Dice, IoU, and Hausdorff distance, with results stratified by lesion category. A Grad-CAM-style overlay aids qualitative review.

Scope:
The work covers binary lesion-vs-skin segmentation on dermoscopic images only. Classification of malignancy and clinical deployment are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. Trained segmentation models with Dice, IoU, and Hausdorff metrics reported
2. A comparison establishing the best architecture with stratified robustness analysis

Timeline:
Month 1 data/preprocessing, months 2-3 training, month 4 ablation, months 5-6 evaluation and write-up.

Title:
Object Detection for Automated Reading of Financial Documents

Problem Statement:
Finance back-offices process scanned invoices and statements where key fields (totals, dates, tables) must be located before extraction. Generic OCR ignores layout, so robust detection of document regions is needed to reduce manual keying and errors.

Objectives:
1. Train an object detector to locate fields and tables in financial documents
2. Compare YOLOv8 against Faster R-CNN on detection accuracy and speed
3. Quantify the effect of detection quality on downstream field extraction

Methodology:
Using a labelled subset of public document datasets (e.g., FUNSD and an invoice set) annotated for field and table regions, I will train YOLOv8 and Faster R-CNN with transfer learning and augmentation. Detection is evaluated with mAP@0.5 and mAP@0.5:0.95 plus inference latency. Detected regions feed a Tesseract OCR step, and end-to-end field accuracy is reported to link detection to extraction.

Scope:
The project covers detection of a fixed set of field/table classes on English documents. Multilingual layouts and full document understanding are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. Two trained detectors with mAP and latency reported
2. End-to-end field-extraction accuracy showing detection's downstream impact

Timeline:
Month 1 annotation, months 2-3 training, month 4 OCR integration, months 5-6 evaluation.

Title:
Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis of Manufacturing Equipment Reviews

Problem Statement:
Manufacturers receive feedback on machinery through reviews and support tickets, but overall sentiment hides which aspect (reliability, cost, service) drives dissatisfaction. Aspect-level analysis would let engineers prioritise fixes, yet manual tagging does not scale.

Objectives:
1. Build an aspect-based sentiment model for equipment feedback
2. Compare a fine-tuned BERT model against a TF-IDF plus SVM baseline
3. Evaluate per-aspect sentiment accuracy and analyse errors

Methodology:
A dataset of industrial-equipment reviews will be labelled for aspect categories and polarity (a public review corpus adapted, plus manual annotation). I will fine-tune BERT-base for joint aspect-polarity classification and compare with a TF-IDF + linear SVM baseline. Models are evaluated with macro-F1 per aspect using stratified k-fold cross-validation, with a confusion-matrix-driven error analysis on misclassified aspects.

Scope:
The work covers a fixed set of five aspects on English text. Real-time ticket ingestion and multilingual reviews are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An aspect-based sentiment model with per-aspect macro-F1 reported
2. A baseline comparison plus an error analysis highlighting weak aspects

Timeline:
Month 1 annotation, months 2-3 modelling, month 4 baselines, months 5-6 evaluation.

Title:
Learned Cost Estimation for Query Optimization in a Public-Safety Database

Problem Statement:
Emergency-dispatch databases run repeated spatial and temporal queries where the optimizer's cardinality estimates are often wrong, causing slow plans during peak load. Better cost estimation could cut query latency when seconds matter.

Objectives:
1. Build a learned cardinality estimator for a public-safety workload
2. Compare it against the database's native estimator on plan quality
3. Measure end-to-end latency improvement on representative queries

Methodology:
Using a synthetic incident dataset generated to mimic dispatch records in PostgreSQL, I will collect a workload of join and range queries with true cardinalities. A gradient-boosted regressor and a small neural estimator are trained on query features to predict cardinalities, then injected via plan hints. Evaluation compares estimated vs true cardinality (q-error) and measures execution time against the native optimizer over a held-out query set, repeated for variance.

Scope:
The project targets single-node PostgreSQL with a fixed schema and read queries. Distributed databases and write-heavy workloads are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A learned estimator with q-error and latency comparisons against the native optimizer
2. Analysis of which query shapes benefit most

Timeline:
Month 1 data/workload, months 2-3 modelling, month 4 integration, months 5-6 benchmarking.

Title:
Facial-Recognition Attendance for Energy-Plant Shift Workers

Problem Statement:
Energy plants track shift attendance for safety compliance, but badge systems allow buddy-punching and manual logs are error-prone. A face-recognition system could give reliable, contactless attendance while respecting privacy constraints on-site.

Objectives:
1. Build a face-recognition attendance system for shift check-in
2. Compare a FaceNet embedding plus SVM approach with a Dlib ResNet baseline
3. Evaluate recognition accuracy and resilience to lighting and spoofing

Methodology:
Faces are detected with MTCNN, aligned, and embedded with FaceNet; an SVM classifies identities, compared against Dlib's ResNet embeddings. A small enrolled gallery plus a public face dataset provide training and impostor sets. Evaluation reports accuracy, false-accept and false-reject rates across lighting conditions, plus a basic blink/liveness check against photo spoofing. Attendance logs are written to a PostgreSQL backend with a simple dashboard.

Scope:
The system handles enrolment and check-in for up to 50 workers under indoor lighting. Mask-occluded recognition and large-scale deployment are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working attendance system with accuracy and FAR/FRR reported
2. A spoofing-resilience analysis comparing the two embedding methods

Timeline:
Month 1 setup, months 2-3 model, month 4 dashboard, months 5-6 evaluation.

Title:
A Lightweight OCR Pipeline for Receipt and Invoice Digitisation in Small Businesses

Problem Statement:
Small businesses key receipts and invoices by hand, which is slow and error-prone, while commercial OCR services are costly and raise data-privacy concerns. Open-source OCR struggles with crumpled receipts, varied layouts, and mixed fonts, so an accurate, offline, layout-aware pipeline tuned for this domain is needed.

Objectives:
1. Build an offline OCR pipeline that extracts vendor, date, line items, and total from receipts/invoices with >=90% field-level F1 on a held-out set
2. Compare Tesseract, EasyOCR, and a fine-tuned PaddleOCR detector-recogniser on accuracy and latency
3. Add a layout-aware post-processing step (LayoutLMv3-based field tagging) and quantify its lift over rule-based parsing

Methodology:
The pipeline runs detection, recognition, then field extraction. Using SROIE and CORD plus 300 manually annotated local receipts, images are deskewed, denoised, and binarised. I benchmark Tesseract, EasyOCR, and fine-tuned PaddleOCR for text recognition (CER/WER), then compare regex/rule-based field parsing against a fine-tuned LayoutLMv3 token classifier. Evaluation uses an 80/10/10 split with field-level precision/recall/F1, CER, and end-to-end latency on CPU, with paired bootstrap significance tests. Risks (small annotation set, font drift) are mitigated by augmentation and active-learning relabelling.

Scope:
Scope is English receipts/invoices, single-page, printed text, run offline on a laptop CPU. Handwriting, multi-currency tax logic, and ERP integration are explicitly excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An offline OCR pipeline meeting the >=90% field-F1 target with reported CER/WER and latency
2. A benchmarked comparison plus an ablation showing the layout-aware module's contribution

Timeline:
M1 data/annotation, M2-3 OCR benchmarking, M3-4 layout model, M5 ablation/significance, M6 packaging and write-up.

Title:
Edge Anomaly Detection for Wireless Soil-Sensor Networks in Precision Agriculture

Problem Statement:
Wireless soil-moisture and temperature sensors in fields produce noisy, gappy streams where faulty readings (drift, dropout, spikes) are easily mistaken for real field conditions, leading to wrong irrigation decisions. Cloud-only analytics add latency and bandwidth cost, so an on-edge method that detects anomalies and imputes gaps under tight compute budgets is needed.

Objectives:
1. Build an edge-deployable model that flags sensor anomalies with >=0.85 F1 and imputes short gaps within a fixed error bound
2. Compare an LSTM autoencoder, an Isolation Forest, and a seasonal-decomposition baseline on detection and imputation
3. Quantify accuracy-versus-resource trade-offs after INT8 quantisation on a Raspberry Pi class device

Methodology:
Using a public agricultural sensor dataset plus a labelled synthetic fault injector (drift/dropout/spike), streams are windowed and normalised. I train an LSTM autoencoder (reconstruction-error thresholding), Isolation Forest, and an STL-residual baseline, tuning thresholds on a validation split. Detection is scored with precision/recall/F1 and PR-AUC; imputation with RMSE/MAE against held-out true values. Models are quantised to INT8 and benchmarked on a Raspberry Pi for latency, memory, and energy, with results averaged over multiple runs and significance tested.

Scope:
Scope is univariate-per-channel soil moisture/temperature streams, short-gap imputation (<=6 samples), and single-node edge inference. Multi-hop routing optimisation and actuator control are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An edge anomaly/imputation model meeting the F1 and gap-error targets with full metric reporting
2. A trade-off study comparing three methods pre/post quantisation on real hardware

Timeline:
M1 data/fault model, M2-3 modelling, M4 quantisation/edge port, M5 hardware benchmarking, M6 evaluation and write-up.

Title:
Blockchain Smart Contracts for Finance

Problem Statement:
Finance is very important and many problems happen with money. Blockchain can fix this because it is secure and new technology.

Objectives:
1. Make a blockchain system
2. Use smart contracts
3. Help finance companies

Methodology:
I will use blockchain and smart contracts to do payments. I will research online and watch some tutorials to learn how it works.

This is for all finance companies and banks everywhere. It will be very secure and save a lot of money.

Title:
AR App for Factory

Problem Statement:
Factories are complicated and workers get confused. Augmented reality is cool and can show things on the phone screen to help.

Objectives:

I will make an app with augmented reality. The phone camera will look at the machine and show some info. I will use Unity maybe.

For all factories and all machines in manufacturing.

Title:
VR Training for Safety

Problem Statement:
Public safety is dangerous and people need training. Virtual reality is a good idea because you can practice without danger and it feels real.

Objectives:

2. Train people for safety

I will make a VR simulation where people can train. They wear a headset and practice. I will use some VR software to build it.

This will be used by firefighters, police, and everyone in public safety to train them properly.

Title:
A 2D Game to Teach Energy Saving Habits

Problem Statement:
Many households waste electricity because people do not understand how daily habits affect their power bills. A simple game could make energy-saving concepts easier to grasp, but most existing games are either too technical or not engaging for casual players.

Objectives:
1. Design a 2D game where players manage a household and try to lower energy usage.
2. Include levels that teach about appliances and standby power.
3. Test whether players learn anything after playing.

Methodology:
The game will be built in Unity using C#. Players control a small house and make choices about appliances, and a score shows their energy bill. I will design a few levels with increasing difficulty and add simple graphics. After building it, I will let some classmates play and ask them questions.

Scope:
The game focuses on home electricity only, not water or gas. It will have around five levels and run on Windows desktop.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A playable 2D energy-saving game.
2. Some feedback showing whether players found it useful.

Timeline:
Around four months from design to testing.

Title:
Serious Game for Teaching Small Business Bookkeeping

Problem Statement:
New small business owners often struggle with basic bookkeeping and cash-flow tracking, and accounting courses feel boring to them. A serious game might make learning these skills more approachable, though existing apps tend to be plain tutorials rather than interactive experiences.

Objectives:
1. Build a game where the player runs a small shop and records transactions.
2. Teach concepts like income, expenses, and profit through gameplay.
3. Evaluate if players understand bookkeeping better after playing.

Methodology:
I will develop the game using the Godot engine. The player manages a virtual shop, buys stock, sells items, and must keep a simple ledger. Wrong entries lower their score. I will create a short quiz before and after play to compare scores from a small group of testers.

Scope:
The game covers only basic single-entry bookkeeping for a retail shop, not tax or payroll. It will be a single-player desktop game.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working serious game on bookkeeping.
2. Pre- and post-test results from a small sample of players.

Timeline:
About five months including development and testing.

Title:
A Record-Keeping App for Small Farm Health and Productivity

Problem Statement:
Small-scale farmers often track livestock health and crop yields on paper, which gets lost or is hard to review. A simple informatics app could help them store and look back at records, but many farm apps are built for large operations and are too complex.

Objectives:
1. Build a mobile app to record animal health events and crop harvests.
2. Show simple summaries and reminders for vaccinations.
3. Get feedback from a few farmers on usefulness.

Methodology:
The app will be built with Flutter and store data locally with SQLite. Farmers enter records through forms, and the app shows monthly summaries and reminder notifications. I will interview two or three farmers to gather requirements and later show them the prototype.

Scope:
The app targets small farms with a handful of animals and crops. It works offline and does not include sensor or IoT integration.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working mobile record-keeping app.
2. Feedback from farmers about whether it fits their needs.

Timeline:
Roughly four to five months.

Title:
A Telemedicine Booking Platform for a Transport Company Clinic

Problem Statement:
Drivers in a transport company often miss in-person clinic visits because of their schedules, leading to delayed checkups. A basic telemedicine platform could let them consult a doctor remotely, but generic apps do not fit the company's shift-based workflow.

Objectives:
1. Build a web platform where drivers can book and join video consultations.
2. Let doctors view a short health note before each call.
3. Test usability with a small group of users.

Methodology:
The platform will use React for the frontend and Node.js with a MySQL database. Video calls will use a third-party API such as Jitsi. Drivers register, pick a slot, and join a call; doctors see basic notes. I will run a small usability test with a few volunteers acting as drivers and doctors.

Scope:
The platform covers booking and video consultation only. It will not handle prescriptions, payments, or medical record storage beyond simple notes.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working telemedicine booking and video platform.
2. Usability feedback from test sessions.

Timeline:
Around five months from design to testing.

Title:
An E-Learning Platform with Progress Tracking for Sustainability Education

Problem Statement:
Schools introducing sustainability topics lack a structured online platform that organises lessons and tracks student progress, often relying on scattered slides and videos. Existing learning management systems are general-purpose and not tailored to short, themed sustainability modules with simple progress feedback.

Objectives:
1. Develop a web-based e-learning platform hosting sustainability modules with quizzes.
2. Implement progress tracking and a basic recommendation of the next module based on quiz scores.
3. Evaluate usability and learning satisfaction with a pilot group of students.

Methodology:
The system will be built with React, Spring Boot, and PostgreSQL. Content is organised into modules and lessons, with quizzes scored automatically. A rule-based logic suggests the next module if a quiz is passed. I will deploy a pilot to around 20 students and collect data through the System Usability Scale and a short knowledge quiz before and after use.

Scope:
The platform focuses on delivering pre-authored sustainability modules to secondary-school students. It excludes live classes, video conferencing, and adaptive AI tutoring.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A deployed e-learning platform with quiz-based progress tracking.
2. Usability scores and pre/post knowledge results from the pilot.

Timeline:
Two semesters: requirements and design (month 1-2), development (month 3-5), pilot and evaluation (month 6-7).

Title:
A Mobile Payment App for Coordinating Logistics Cash-on-Delivery Settlements

Problem Statement:
Logistics couriers handling cash-on-delivery often reconcile collected cash manually at day's end, causing errors and delays in settling with merchants. There is a need for a lightweight payment and reconciliation app that records each delivery payment and produces a clear settlement summary for couriers and merchants.

Objectives:
1. Build a mobile app that records COD and digital payments per delivery.
2. Generate daily settlement summaries reconciling collected amounts against assigned deliveries.
3. Validate accuracy and usability through a simulated delivery scenario.

Methodology:
The app will be developed in Flutter with a Firebase backend for authentication and data sync. Couriers mark each delivery as paid by cash or e-wallet (via a sandbox gateway), and the backend aggregates totals into a settlement report. I will test it with a simulated dataset of deliveries and a small group of users role-playing couriers, checking reconciliation correctness and gathering usability feedback.

Scope:
The project covers payment recording and daily reconciliation for a single courier's route. It excludes real bank integration, route optimisation, and multi-currency support.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working payment and reconciliation mobile app.
2. Accuracy results and usability feedback from the simulation.

Timeline:
Design (month 1), build (month 2-4), testing and evaluation (month 5-6).

Title:
Anomaly-Based Fraud Detection for E-Government Subsidy Claims

Problem Statement:
Government subsidy programs receive large volumes of claims, and manual auditing catches only a fraction of fraudulent or duplicate submissions. A data-driven screening tool could flag suspicious claims for review, but agencies often lack labelled fraud data, so the approach must work with limited labels.

Objectives:
1. Build a pipeline that flags suspicious subsidy claims using anomaly detection.
2. Compare an unsupervised model against a supervised baseline on labelled samples.
3. Provide a dashboard listing flagged claims with explanation features.

Methodology:
Using a synthetic subsidy-claims dataset (since real data is restricted), I will engineer features such as claim frequency, amount deviation, and applicant duplication. I will apply Isolation Forest and compare it to a logistic regression baseline on the labelled subset, measuring precision, recall, and ROC-AUC. A simple Flask dashboard will display flagged claims and the top contributing features.

Scope:
The project focuses on tabular claim screening using one synthetic dataset. It excludes document image verification and live integration with government systems.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A fraud-screening pipeline with a comparison of anomaly and baseline models.
2. A dashboard showing flagged claims and contributing factors.

Timeline:
Two semesters: data and features (month 1-2), modelling (month 3-4), dashboard and evaluation (month 5-6).

Title:
A Course Recommendation Feature for an Online Education Marketplace

Problem Statement:
Learners browsing an online course marketplace face hundreds of options and often abandon their search without enrolling. A recommendation feature suggesting relevant courses from a learner's history could improve discovery, yet many small platforms only sort by popularity, ignoring individual interests.

Objectives:
1. Build a recommendation module suggesting courses based on user interaction history.
2. Compare collaborative filtering with a content-based approach.
3. Evaluate recommendation quality using offline metrics.

Methodology:
I will use a public education dataset of user-course interactions, or a simulated one if needed. Item-based collaborative filtering and a TF-IDF content-based model on course descriptions will be implemented in Python with scikit-learn and Surprise. The two will be compared using precision@k and recall@k on a held-out test split. The module will expose recommendations through a small Flask API.

Scope:
The work covers building and offline-evaluating the recommendation algorithms. It excludes a full marketplace UI, real-time updates, and A/B testing with live users.

Expected Outcomes:
1. Two recommendation models with a documented comparison.
2. Offline evaluation results reported as precision@k and recall@k.

Timeline:
Data prep (month 1), modelling (month 2-4), evaluation and API (month 5-6).

Title:
A Retail Customer-Support Chatbot for Order and Return Queries

Problem Statement:
Small online retailers receive repetitive customer questions about order status and return policies, overwhelming staff during busy periods. A chatbot handling common queries could reduce response time, but rule-only bots fail on varied phrasing while fully generative bots risk inaccurate answers about store policy.

Objectives:
1. Build a chatbot that answers order-status and return-policy questions.
2. Combine intent classification with retrieval from a store FAQ.
3. Evaluate intent accuracy and answer helpfulness.

Methodology:
The chatbot will use a fine-tuned intent classifier (DistilBERT) over a labelled set of customer messages, and a retrieval step that pulls policy answers from an FAQ using sentence-embedding similarity. Order-status intents call a mock order API. I will evaluate intent classification with accuracy and F1 on a test set, and rate answer helpfulness through a small user study with sample dialogues.

Scope:
The chatbot covers order status and returns for one demo store. It excludes payments, multilingual support, and open-domain chit-chat.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working chatbot with hybrid intent-plus-retrieval design.
2. Intent accuracy/F1 scores and user helpfulness ratings.

Timeline:
Data and intents (month 1-2), model and retrieval (month 3-4), evaluation (month 5-6).

Title:
A Knowledge-Graph-Based Search Tool for Smart City Open Data

Problem Statement:
City open-data portals store datasets, facilities, and services in separate tables, so residents struggle to find connected information such as which facilities relate to a given service area. Keyword search returns isolated records without showing relationships, making exploration tedious for non-technical users.

Objectives:
1. Build a knowledge graph linking city facilities, services, and locations.
2. Provide a search interface that returns connected results and related entities.
3. Compare result relevance against a plain keyword search.

Methodology:
I will model entities and relationships from a public city open-data set into a Neo4j graph. A search interface will accept queries, map them to graph entities, and return results plus linked neighbours via Cypher queries. To evaluate, I will prepare a set of test queries with expected relevant entities and compare precision and recall against a baseline keyword search over the same data.

Scope:
The project covers one city's facilities-and-services data and an English search interface. It excludes real-time data feeds, map visualisation, and natural-language question answering.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A knowledge graph and connected-search interface.
2. Relevance comparison between graph search and keyword search.

Timeline:
Modelling (month 1-2), graph build (month 3), interface (month 4-5), evaluation (month 6).

Title:
Semantic Segmentation of Tourist Landmarks for an Auto-Tagging Travel Gallery

Problem Statement:
Travel-photo apps tag whole images but rarely separate the landmark from sky, crowds, and clutter, which limits cropping, background blur, and landmark-area analytics. Tourism datasets are also dominated by clear daytime shots, so models often fail on occluded or low-light scenes. This project targets pixel-level segmentation of landmarks under such varied conditions.

Objectives:
1. Train a semantic segmentation model isolating landmark regions from background in tourist photos.
2. Quantify performance gains from data augmentation on occluded and low-light images.
3. Compare a lightweight model against a heavier baseline on accuracy and inference speed.

Methodology:
I will build a dataset from the ADE20K and Cityscapes landmark-relevant classes plus a small self-labelled tourist set. A U-Net with a MobileNetV3 encoder will be compared against DeepLabV3+ (ResNet-50). Training uses combined cross-entropy and Dice loss with augmentation (occlusion cutout, brightness jitter). Evaluation reports mean IoU, per-class IoU, and frames-per-second on a held-out test split with 5-fold cross-validation on the self-labelled subset.

Scope:
The work covers outdoor landmark segmentation in still images. It excludes video, indoor scenes, and on-device deployment beyond benchmarking inference speed.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained segmentation model with mIoU reported overall and on hard subsets.
2. An accuracy-versus-speed comparison of the two architectures.

Timeline:
Data and labelling (month 1-2), training (month 3-4), augmentation study and evaluation (month 5-6).

Title:
Detecting Prohibited-Content Objects in Social Media Images Under Class Imbalance

Problem Statement:
Social platforms must flag images containing items like weapons or alcohol logos, but these appear in a small fraction of uploads, creating severe class imbalance that hurts standard detectors. Many academic detection studies use balanced benchmarks that do not reflect this skew, so reported accuracy overstates real moderation performance.

Objectives:
1. Train an object detector for a small set of prohibited-item classes on imbalanced data.
2. Measure the effect of focal loss and oversampling on minority-class recall.
3. Compare detection quality against a one-stage baseline.

Methodology:
Using the OpenImages subset for the target classes, I will deliberately preserve the natural imbalance. A YOLOv8 model trained with focal loss and class-balanced sampling will be compared to a plain YOLOv8 baseline and a Faster R-CNN reference. Evaluation uses mAP@0.5, per-class average precision, and a precision-recall analysis focused on minority classes, with a fixed validation/test split and confidence-threshold tuning on validation only.

Scope:
The project handles four prohibited-item classes in static images. It excludes video moderation, text/audio content, and production deployment or moderation policy decisions.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained detector with per-class AP reported under imbalance.
2. A quantified comparison of imbalance-handling techniques versus baselines.

Timeline:
Data setup (month 1), baseline (month 2), imbalance experiments (month 3-4), evaluation (month 5-6).

Title:
Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis of Patient Reviews for Healthcare Service Quality

Problem Statement:
Hospital review platforms aggregate star ratings but hide which aspects, such as waiting time, staff attitude, or cleanliness, drive patient dissatisfaction. Overall-sentiment models lose this granularity, and general sentiment lexicons miss clinical phrasing, leaving administrators without actionable, aspect-level feedback.

Objectives:
1. Build an aspect-based sentiment model classifying patient-review sentences by aspect and polarity.
2. Compare a fine-tuned transformer against a lexicon-plus-SVM baseline.
3. Produce aspect-level sentiment summaries per facility.

Methodology:
I will assemble a corpus of English patient reviews and annotate sentences with aspect categories and polarity, computing inter-annotator agreement on a sample. A fine-tuned BERT model for joint aspect-polarity classification will be compared with a VADER-plus-TF-IDF-SVM baseline, evaluated with macro-F1 per aspect and overall accuracy under stratified 5-fold cross-validation. Outputs feed a summary view aggregating polarity by aspect per facility.

Scope:
The work covers English text reviews and four predefined aspects. It excludes non-English reviews, sarcasm-specific modelling, and integration with live hospital systems.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An aspect-based sentiment model with per-aspect F1 reported.
2. Per-facility aspect-sentiment summaries from the held-out data.

Timeline:
Annotation (month 1-2), modelling (month 3-4), evaluation and summaries (month 5-6).

Title:
Learning-Augmented Query Optimization for Analytical Finance Workloads

Problem Statement:
Analytical queries over financial transaction warehouses can run slowly when the optimizer mis-estimates the cost of join orders, since classic cardinality estimates degrade on skewed, correlated columns common in finance data. Improving join-order choices through learned cost estimates could cut query latency without changing the storage engine.

Objectives:
1. Build a learned cardinality estimator for join predicates on a finance-style schema.
2. Integrate its estimates into a join-order selection routine.
3. Measure end-to-end query latency against the default optimizer.

Methodology:
Using a TPC-H-derived schema scaled to mimic finance tables in PostgreSQL, I will generate a workload of analytical queries and collect true cardinalities to train a gradient-boosted regression estimator on query features. The learned estimates will drive a join-order search compared to PostgreSQL's native planner. Evaluation reports estimation error (q-error), chosen-plan latency, and total workload runtime across multiple data scales, with a held-out query set.

Scope:
The project targets read-only analytical join queries on one schema. It excludes write transactions, index tuning, and distributed execution.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A learned estimator with q-error and latency improvements reported.
2. A latency comparison against the native optimizer across data scales.

Timeline:
Workload setup (month 1-2), estimator (month 3-4), integration and evaluation (month 5-6).

Title:
Robust Facial-Recognition Attendance for Factory Floor Conditions

Problem Statement:
Factory attendance via badge scanning allows buddy-punching, while off-the-shelf face recognition struggles with hard hats, masks, poor lighting, and motion at shift changes. An attendance system must stay accurate under these conditions and resist simple photo spoofing, which generic demos rarely address.

Objectives:
1. Build a face-recognition attendance pipeline tolerant to partial occlusion and low light.
2. Add a basic liveness check to resist printed-photo spoofing.
3. Evaluate recognition and spoof-rejection accuracy under simulated factory conditions.

Methodology:
The pipeline uses RetinaFace for detection and ArcFace embeddings matched against an enrolled gallery. I will fine-tune the matching threshold and apply augmentation simulating masks, hard hats, and low light. A blink-and-texture liveness check filters printed photos. Evaluation uses a self-collected set of volunteers under varied conditions, reporting recognition accuracy, false-accept and false-reject rates, and spoof-rejection rate, with thresholds tuned only on a validation split.

Scope:
The system handles enrolled employees at a fixed entry camera. It excludes mask-only faces with no visible features, large-scale crowd recognition, and payroll integration.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An attendance pipeline with accuracy and error rates under occlusion and low light.
2. Spoof-rejection results for printed-photo attacks.

Timeline:
Pipeline (month 1-2), data collection (month 3), augmentation and liveness (month 4-5), evaluation (month 6).

Title:
A Robust OCR Pipeline for Degraded Public-Safety Incident Forms with Confidence-Aware Routing

Problem Statement:
Public-safety agencies digitise handwritten and printed incident forms that are frequently faxed, stamped, or photographed under poor lighting, where commercial OCR returns silent errors on critical fields like dates and case numbers. Existing benchmarks use clean scans, so reported accuracy does not transfer; agencies need both higher field-level accuracy on degraded inputs and a calibrated confidence signal that routes low-confidence fields to human review rather than failing silently.

Objectives:
1. Build an end-to-end OCR pipeline that extracts key fields from degraded incident forms with field-level accuracy reported by field type.
2. Add per-field confidence calibration so that low-confidence extractions are flagged for review at a controllable precision-recall trade-off.
3. Benchmark the pipeline against a commercial OCR API and an open baseline on a held-out degraded test set.

Methodology:
I will construct a dataset of synthetic and ~300 real incident forms, applying degradation augmentation (blur, JPEG artefacts, stamps, low contrast) with stratified train/validation/test splits. Detection uses a fine-tuned DBNet for text regions; recognition uses a fine-tuned TrOCR model, with a layout step mapping regions to fields. Confidence is calibrated via temperature scaling and evaluated with reliability diagrams and expected calibration error. The system is compared to a commercial API and Tesseract on field-level accuracy, character error rate, and the review-routing precision/recall curve, using 5-fold cross-validation on the real subset. Risks (limited real data, label noise) are mitigated with synthetic pretraining and double-annotation of a sample.

Scope:
The pipeline targets a fixed set of six fields on two English form templates. It explicitly excludes free-text narrative transcription, non-English forms, multi-page stitching, and live deployment into agency systems; those are noted as future work.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An OCR pipeline reporting per-field accuracy and CER on degraded forms, beating both baselines on the key fields.
2. A calibrated confidence mechanism with an ECE figure and a review-routing curve showing reviewer effort versus error caught.

Timeline:
Two semesters: dataset and degradation pipeline (month 1-2), detection/recognition training (month 3-4), calibration and routing (month 5), benchmarking and write-up (month 6-7).

Title:
Edge-Friendly Anomaly Detection for Wireless Sensor Networks Monitoring Solar Inverters

Problem Statement:
Solar farms instrument inverters with wireless sensor nodes, but intermittent links cause missing and out-of-order readings, and faults often appear as subtle multivariate drifts rather than single-sensor spikes. Threshold alarms miss these correlated anomalies and flood operators with false positives during transient gaps, while heavyweight deep models exceed the compute budget of gateway hardware. The need is an accurate yet lightweight detector that tolerates gappy, correlated sensor streams on edge gateways.

Objectives:
1. Build a multivariate anomaly detector for inverter sensor streams that handles missing and irregular samples.
2. Constrain the model to run within a defined latency and memory budget representative of an edge gateway.
3. Evaluate detection quality and resource cost against statistical and deep baselines.

Methodology:
I will use a public photovoltaic/inverter sensor dataset augmented with injected fault patterns (drift, stuck-at, intermittent dropouts) and simulated packet loss for realistic gaps. A masked-input temporal convolutional autoencoder will model normal multivariate behaviour, with reconstruction error plus a learned per-channel threshold flagging anomalies. It will be compared to an EWMA/Hotelling T-squared statistical baseline and an LSTM autoencoder. Evaluation reports precision, recall, F1, and point-adjusted F1 on labelled fault windows, plus detection latency, model size, and inference time measured on a Raspberry Pi to verify the edge budget. Time-based splits prevent leakage, and a sensitivity study covers loss rate and threshold choice; limited real-fault labels are mitigated with injected, documented fault types.

Scope:
The work targets anomaly detection on numeric inverter telemetry from one site's sensor layout. It excludes root-cause diagnosis, control actions, multi-site transfer, and custom radio-protocol design; gaps are simulated rather than collected from live radios.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An edge-runnable anomaly detector with F1 and point-adjusted F1 reported against both baselines.
2. A resource profile (size, latency, memory on Raspberry Pi) confirming it meets the stated edge budget.

Timeline:
Two semesters: data and fault injection (month 1-2), model and baselines (month 3-4), edge benchmarking (month 5), sensitivity study and write-up (month 6-7).

Title:
Machine Learning for Tourism

Problem Statement:
Tourism is very big and many people travel. Companies want to know things about tourists so they can do better business.

Objectives:
1. Make a machine learning thing for tourism.
2. Help tourism companies.

Methodology:
I will use Python and machine learning to classify the tourists. Some research will also be done online.

Scope:
This can be used by all hotels, airlines and travel agencies everywhere in the world.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A good system.
2. Happy tourists.

Title:
Deep Learning Computer Vision on Social Media

Problem Statement:
Social media has a lot of pictures. People post many photos every day and there should be a way to look at them with deep learning.

Objectives:
1. Use deep learning for images.
2. Apply it to social media.
3. Get results.

Methodology:
The project will use a neural network and computer vision. I will train a model on images and see what happens.

Scope:
All social media platforms like Instagram, Facebook, TikTok and others.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An image system.
2. Better social media.

Title:
NLP in Healthcare

Problem Statement:
Hospitals have many documents and text. Natural language processing can help with healthcare because there is a lot of text in medicine.

Objectives:
1. Build an NLP system.
2. Use it in healthcare.

Methodology:
I plan to use NLP techniques and Python libraries to process medical text and find useful information for doctors.

Scope:
It will work for all hospitals and clinics and all kinds of medical text.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working NLP tool.
2. Doctors save time.

Title:
A Recommender System for Personal Finance Products

Problem Statement:
Bank customers are often shown credit cards and savings plans that do not match their spending habits. There is a need for a system that suggests more relevant financial products based on a user's transaction history.

Objectives:
1. Collect a dataset of user profiles and financial products.
2. Build a recommender system that suggests products.
3. Test if the recommendations are useful.

Methodology:
The system will use collaborative filtering to match users with products. I will use Python and possibly the Surprise library. Recommendations will be ranked and shown in a simple web interface.

Scope:
The project focuses on recommending credit cards and savings accounts for retail banking customers. It will not handle loans or investments.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A recommender system prototype.
2. An evaluation showing recommendation quality.

Timeline:
About 12 weeks split between data work, building, and testing.

Title:
Speech Recognition for Factory Floor Commands

Problem Statement:
Workers in a manufacturing plant often have their hands occupied and cannot use keyboards. A speech recognition system could let them control machines or log data by voice, but factory noise makes recognition harder.

Objectives:
1. Record a small set of spoken factory commands.
2. Build a speech recognition model for those commands.
3. Measure accuracy in noisy conditions.

Methodology:
The project will use an existing speech toolkit such as Vosk or the Google Speech API to recognise a limited vocabulary of commands. Audio will be collected with some background noise added for testing.

Scope:
Only a fixed set of around 20 English commands will be supported. The system will run on a laptop and not be deployed on real machines.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A command recognition prototype.
2. An accuracy report under quiet and noisy conditions.

Timeline:
Roughly one semester, with data collection first then modelling.

Title:
Network Intrusion Detection for Public Safety Networks

Problem Statement:
Public safety agencies run networks that connect cameras, sensors and dispatch systems. These networks are targets for attacks, and operators need an automated way to flag suspicious traffic instead of inspecting logs by hand.

Objectives:
1. Use a public intrusion dataset to train a classifier.
2. Detect common attack types such as port scans and denial of service.
3. Report detection accuracy.

Methodology:
The project will use the NSL-KDD dataset and a Random Forest classifier to label traffic as normal or attack. Standard preprocessing and feature selection will be applied, and accuracy and false alarm rate will be reported.

Scope:
The work is offline analysis of a benchmark dataset. It will not be deployed on a live network or detect zero-day attacks.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained intrusion detection model.
2. A short evaluation of detection performance.

Timeline:
Around 12 weeks: dataset study, modelling, evaluation.

Title:
A Web Application Vulnerability Scanner for Energy Sector Portals

Problem Statement:
Energy companies expose customer portals and monitoring dashboards on the web. Small operators rarely run security tests, so common flaws such as SQL injection or cross-site scripting can go unnoticed until exploited.

Objectives:
1. Build a scanner that checks a target web app for common vulnerabilities.
2. Cover at least SQL injection and XSS.
3. Produce a readable report of findings.

Methodology:
The scanner will crawl pages, find input fields, and send test payloads to detect injection and scripting flaws. It will be written in Python and tested against a deliberately vulnerable app such as DVWA rather than real systems.

Scope:
The tool targets two vulnerability classes and is tested only on a local practice application. It is not a full penetration testing suite.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working scanner prototype.
2. A sample vulnerability report.

Timeline:
One semester, building then testing on DVWA.

Title:
Static and Dynamic Malware Analysis Toolkit for Small Businesses

Problem Statement:
Small businesses rarely employ security analysts, so suspicious files are often opened without inspection. A lightweight toolkit that combines basic static and behavioural analysis could give non-experts a first verdict before a file is run.

Objectives:
1. Extract static features such as imported APIs and entropy from Windows executables.
2. Run samples in a sandbox to capture behaviour like file and registry changes.
3. Train a classifier that labels a sample as likely benign or malicious and explain the verdict.

Methodology:
Static features will be parsed with the pefile library, and dynamic behaviour will be captured in a Cuckoo-style sandbox VM. A Random Forest classifier will be trained on a labelled subset of the EMBER dataset plus collected samples, evaluated with precision, recall and F1 against a signature-baseline.

Scope:
The toolkit targets Windows PE files only and runs all dynamic analysis inside an isolated VM. It excludes mobile malware, packed-sample unpacking, and live network sandboxing.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working analysis toolkit with a verdict report.
2. An evaluation comparing the classifier against signature detection.

Timeline:
14 weeks: weeks 1-3 setup, 4-8 feature pipelines, 9-11 classifier, 12-14 evaluation.

Title:
A Responsive Web Platform for Smallholder Crop Advisory

Problem Statement:
Smallholder farmers often lack timely advice on planting and pest control suited to their specific crop and region. Existing advice is scattered across leaflets and phone calls, and is hard to access on the low-end phones farmers actually own.

Objectives:
1. Build a responsive web platform where farmers register their crops and location.
2. Deliver crop-specific advisory content and a simple pest-report feature.
3. Let extension officers post seasonal updates that reach the right farmers.

Methodology:
The platform will be built with React and a Node.js/Express backend backed by PostgreSQL. The interface will be designed mobile-first and tested across small screen sizes. Advisory content will be entered by officers through an admin panel, and usability will be checked with a small group of test users.

Scope:
The project covers three sample crops and one region's advisory rules. It is not a marketplace and does not include payments, real-time IoT sensors, or native mobile apps.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A deployed responsive web platform.
2. A usability test report from sample farmers and officers.

Timeline:
13 weeks across design, build, content, and user testing.

Title:
A Progressive Web App for Real-Time Public Bus Tracking

Problem Statement:
Bus passengers in many cities cannot tell when the next bus will arrive, leading to long uncertain waits. A solution must work on weak connections and be installable without app-store friction, which suits a progressive web app.

Objectives:
1. Build a PWA that shows nearby bus stops and live vehicle positions on a map.
2. Provide estimated arrival times and offline access to recent schedules.
3. Send a notification when a chosen bus is approaching.

Methodology:
The PWA will be built with React and a service worker for offline caching and installability. Vehicle positions will be consumed from a GTFS-Realtime feed and shown on a Leaflet map. Arrival estimates will be derived from feed timestamps, and the app will be tested with Lighthouse for PWA and performance scores.

Scope:
The app covers one city's published GTFS feed and a handful of routes for the demo. It excludes ticketing, payment, and route-planning across multiple transport modes.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An installable PWA with live tracking and notifications.
2. A Lighthouse report on PWA, performance and offline behaviour.

Timeline:
13 weeks: feed integration, map UI, offline layer, then testing.

Title:
A Cross-Platform Mobile App for Household Carbon Tracking

Problem Statement:
Households want to reduce their environmental impact but have no easy way to see how daily choices like electricity use, travel and food add up. A single app available on both Android and iOS could make this tracking routine.

Objectives:
1. Build a cross-platform app where users log activities in a few taps.
2. Convert logged activities into estimated carbon figures using published factors.
3. Show weekly trends and suggest one or two reduction tips.

Methodology:
The app will be built with Flutter so a single codebase runs on Android and iOS. Activities will be mapped to emission factors from a public dataset such as the UK DEFRA tables, stored locally with SQLite and synced to a Firebase backend. Estimates and charts will be validated against worked examples.

Scope:
The app covers electricity, road travel and a short food category. It uses fixed published factors rather than live utility data, and excludes carbon-offset purchasing.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working cross-platform app on Android and iOS.
2. A short report on estimate accuracy and user feedback.

Timeline:
14 weeks split across design, build, factor integration, and testing.

Title:
An Android Native App for Last-Mile Delivery Proof and Routing

Problem Statement:
Small courier companies often track deliveries on paper, so proof of delivery is lost and drivers waste time planning routes. A native Android app could capture proof and order stops efficiently on the cheap devices drivers use.

Objectives:
1. Build a native Android app that lists a driver's assigned deliveries for the day.
2. Capture proof of delivery via photo and signature with a timestamp and GPS location.
3. Order the day's stops using a simple nearest-stop route and show them on a map.

Methodology:
The app will be written in Kotlin using Android Jetpack components and Room for local storage so it works with intermittent connectivity. Proof data will sync to a Firebase backend when online. Routing will use device GPS and the Google Maps SDK with a nearest-neighbour ordering of stops, tested with sample delivery lists.

Scope:
The project targets the driver-side Android app only. It excludes the dispatcher web console, payment handling, and advanced route optimisation beyond nearest-neighbour ordering.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working Android app with offline proof capture and basic routing.
2. A test report on sync reliability and routing on sample data.

Timeline:
13 weeks: UI, local storage, proof capture, routing, testing.

Title:
An IoT Sensor Network for Monitoring Public Building Comfort in E-Government Offices

Problem Statement:
Citizens visiting government offices often endure crowded, poorly ventilated waiting areas. Facility managers lack live data on occupancy and air quality, so they cannot react before conditions get uncomfortable. A low-cost sensor network could feed a simple dashboard.

Objectives:
1. Deploy sensor nodes measuring temperature, humidity and CO2 in sample rooms.
2. Collect readings centrally over a wireless protocol.
3. Show live and historical conditions on a dashboard with threshold alerts.

Methodology:
Each node uses an ESP32 with a DHT22 and an MH-Z19 CO2 sensor, publishing readings over MQTT to a Raspberry Pi broker. Data is stored in InfluxDB and visualised in Grafana with alert rules. The network will be tested in two rooms over several days to check reliability and reading stability.

Scope:
The prototype covers three sensor nodes in two rooms and three measured variables. It excludes actuation such as automatic HVAC control and city-wide deployment.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working multi-node sensor network with a live dashboard.
2. A reliability report on data delivery and sensor readings.

Timeline:
14 weeks: hardware setup, networking, storage/dashboard, field test.

Title:
A Smart Home Automation System for Study-Focused Environments in Student Housing

Problem Statement:
Students studying at home are easily disrupted by inconsistent lighting, noise and air quality, yet generic smart-home setups optimise for comfort or energy rather than focus. There is little work on automation that adapts a room specifically to support study sessions and breaks.

Objectives:
1. Build a smart-home controller that adjusts lighting and ventilation based on a study/break schedule and live sensor readings.
2. Detect study sessions automatically from desk occupancy and noise level rather than manual switching.
3. Evaluate whether the focus-aware mode improves self-reported concentration against a static baseline.

Methodology:
The system uses ESP32 nodes for a PIR occupancy sensor, sound-level and CO2 readings, with smart bulbs and a fan controlled over MQTT through Home Assistant. A rule engine plus a lightweight decision-tree classifier infers study versus break states. Evaluation runs a within-subject study with 8-10 students over two weeks, comparing focus-aware automation to a fixed schedule using session logs and a concentration questionnaire.

Scope:
The project covers one desk-based study room with lighting and ventilation control. It excludes heating control, voice assistants, and multi-room coordination. Privacy is handled by processing audio only as a decibel level, never recording.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working focus-aware automation prototype with documented rules.
2. A comparative evaluation of focus-aware versus static control with limitations discussed.

Timeline:
15 weeks: weeks 1-3 hardware, 4-7 automation logic, 8-10 classifier, 11-13 user study, 14-15 analysis and writing.

Title:
Edge Computing for On-Shelf Product Recognition in Convenience Retail

Problem Statement:
Convenience stores lose sales to empty shelves, but cloud-based shelf-monitoring cameras are costly in bandwidth and raise latency and privacy concerns. Running recognition on an edge device in-store could give near-real-time stock alerts without streaming video off-site.

Objectives:
1. Build an edge pipeline that detects gaps and recognises products on shelf images.
2. Quantise and deploy the model on a low-power edge device within a target latency.
3. Compare edge inference against a cloud baseline on accuracy, latency and bandwidth.

Methodology:
A YOLOv8-nano detector will be trained on the SKU110K shelf dataset plus a small store-specific set for gap detection. The model will be quantised with TensorRT and deployed on a Jetson Nano, processing periodic shelf snapshots locally and sending only alert events upstream. Evaluation reports mAP, per-frame latency, and monthly bandwidth versus a cloud GPU baseline running the same model.

Scope:
The system targets shelf-gap and coarse product-category detection on still snapshots for one store layout. It excludes fine SKU-level pricing, theft detection, and continuous video analytics.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A deployed edge recognition pipeline producing shelf-gap alerts.
2. A benchmark report comparing edge and cloud on accuracy, latency and bandwidth.

Timeline:
15 weeks: dataset and training, quantisation, edge deployment, benchmarking, write-up.

Title:
A Cloud-Native Microservices Backend for a Smart-City Incident Reporting Platform

Problem Statement:
Smart-city incident reporting must absorb uneven, bursty load as residents report potholes, outages and hazards, but monolithic backends scale poorly and a single fault can take the whole service down. A microservices design can isolate failures and scale hot paths independently.

Objectives:
1. Design and build the backend as independent services for reporting, geolocation lookup, notifications and analytics.
2. Deploy on Kubernetes with autoscaling and demonstrate graceful behaviour when one service fails.
3. Measure latency and throughput under load against a monolithic baseline.

Methodology:
Services will be written in Spring Boot, communicating via REST and an event queue (RabbitMQ), each with its own PostgreSQL schema. They are containerised and deployed to a local Kubernetes cluster (k3s) with horizontal pod autoscaling, an API gateway, and Prometheus/Grafana monitoring. Load tests with k6 will measure p95 latency and throughput, and a chaos test will kill one service to observe isolation. A single-process build serves as the baseline.

Scope:
The project delivers the backend services, deployment manifests and monitoring. It excludes the citizen mobile UI, production cloud billing, and a city-scale dataset, using synthetic generated traffic instead.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A deployed microservices backend with autoscaling and monitoring.
2. A performance and resilience report comparing microservices to a monolith.

Timeline:
16 weeks: service design, implementation, Kubernetes deployment, load and chaos testing, analysis.

Title:
A CI/CD Pipeline with Automated Quality Gates for Tourism Booking Web Apps

Problem Statement:
Tourism booking sites push frequent changes for promotions and seasonal content, and manual deployment leads to slow releases and avoidable production defects. A disciplined CI/CD pipeline with automated quality gates could shorten lead time while keeping releases safe.

Objectives:
1. Build a CI/CD pipeline that runs build, tests, security and quality checks automatically on each change.
2. Enforce quality gates that block merges failing coverage, linting or vulnerability thresholds.
3. Measure the effect on lead time, deployment frequency and change-failure rate using DORA metrics.

Methodology:
A sample tourism booking app will be placed under a GitHub Actions pipeline running unit and integration tests, SonarQube quality analysis, Trivy container scanning, and a staging deploy with smoke tests before promotion. Quality gates are enforced as required checks. Blue-green deployment to a container host enables quick rollback. A baseline period of manual releases is compared with the automated pipeline using the four DORA metrics over a set of scripted change scenarios.

Scope:
The work covers the pipeline, gates and deployment automation for one sample app. It excludes building new product features and uses scripted change scenarios rather than a live team.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working CI/CD pipeline with enforced quality gates and rollback.
2. A DORA-based comparison of manual versus automated delivery.

Timeline:
15 weeks: pipeline setup, gates, deployment automation, measurement, analysis.

Title:
A Big Data Analytics Pipeline for Detecting Trending Topics on Social Media

Problem Statement:
Social media produces high-volume, high-velocity text where topics surface and fade within hours. Batch analytics miss this window, so a streaming pipeline is needed to surface emerging topics in near real time while remaining cost-aware.

Objectives:
1. Build an ingestion-to-analytics pipeline that processes a high-rate stream of social posts.
2. Detect and rank trending topics in sliding time windows with deduplication of near-identical posts.
3. Evaluate throughput, end-to-end latency and detection quality against a batch baseline.

Methodology:
Posts are ingested through Kafka, processed by Spark Structured Streaming for tokenisation, windowed term-frequency and a burst-detection step, with results stored in Elasticsearch and shown in Kibana. The pipeline runs on a small multi-node cluster and is fed a replayed public Twitter/social dataset at controlled rates. Trending output is compared to a daily batch job, and detection is judged against labelled known events using precision and lead-time-to-detection.

Scope:
The project targets English text-only posts and topic trend detection. It excludes sentiment analysis, image content, and a production-scale cluster, using a bounded replayed dataset.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working streaming analytics pipeline with a trending-topics dashboard.
2. An evaluation of throughput, latency and detection quality versus batch.

Timeline:
16 weeks: cluster and ingestion, streaming logic, storage/dashboard, evaluation, write-up.

Title:
A Business Intelligence Dashboard for Reducing Outpatient Clinic Wait Times

Problem Statement:
Outpatient clinics struggle with long, uneven patient waits, yet managers usually see only end-of-month aggregate reports that hide where time is lost in the patient journey. Without a near-real-time, drill-down view linking arrival, triage, consultation and pharmacy stages, interventions are guesswork. This project builds a BI dashboard that turns operational data into stage-level, actionable bottleneck insight.

Objectives:
1. Model an analytics schema capturing each patient-journey stage with timestamps and resource attributes.
2. Build ETL that ingests appointment and queue logs into a star-schema warehouse refreshed on a fixed interval.
3. Deliver an interactive dashboard with stage-level wait KPIs, drill-down by clinic and provider, and a what-if staffing slider, evaluated for decision-usefulness with clinic staff.

Methodology:
A dimensional star schema will be built in PostgreSQL, populated by a Python/dbt ETL from a public hospital event-log dataset (MIMIC-derived where available) plus synthetically generated queue events validated against published distributions. Power BI (with a Metabase open-source alternative) will present wait-time, throughput and utilisation KPIs with role-level access. The what-if slider uses a queueing approximation (M/M/c) calibrated to historical service rates. Evaluation combines data-accuracy checks against source logs with a task-based usability study (SUS plus timed bottleneck-finding tasks) involving 6-8 clinic staff, comparing the dashboard to the existing monthly report.

Scope:
The project covers descriptive and diagnostic analytics for the outpatient journey of one clinic department, with the staffing what-if as the only prescriptive feature. It explicitly excludes clinical decision support, predictive no-show modelling, and EHR write-back. Patient identifiers are excluded; only de-identified operational fields are used.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A populated star-schema warehouse with documented, scheduled ETL.
2. An interactive BI dashboard with validated KPIs and a what-if staffing view.
3. An evaluation report with data-accuracy results and usability findings versus the current reporting baseline.

Timeline:
16 weeks: weeks 1-2 requirements and KPI definition, 3-5 schema and ETL, 6-9 dashboard build, 10-11 what-if model, 12-14 usability study, 15-16 analysis and write-up.

Title:
Probabilistic Time-Series Forecasting of Intraday Cash Demand at Bank Branch ATMs

Problem Statement:
Banks must pre-load ATMs with enough cash to avoid outages while not stranding idle capital. Demand is non-stationary, with weekly, payday and holiday effects, and single-point forecasts give no sense of stock-out risk. This project builds probabilistic intraday cash-demand forecasts that quantify uncertainty so replenishment decisions can target a chosen service level rather than a guessed buffer.

Objectives:
1. Construct a clean intraday withdrawal dataset with calendar, holiday and payday features per ATM.
2. Build and compare probabilistic forecasting models that output prediction intervals, not just point estimates.
3. Translate forecasts into replenishment quantities at target service levels and evaluate cost and stock-out trade-offs against current practice.

Methodology:
Using a public ATM withdrawal dataset (e.g. the NN5 / Kaggle ATM series) augmented with calendar features, three models are compared: SARIMAX as a statistical baseline, LightGBM with lag and calendar features, and a quantile-loss DeepAR/Temporal Fusion Transformer for direct interval forecasting. Models are tuned and validated with rolling-origin (walk-forward) cross-validation to respect temporal order. Point accuracy uses MASE and sMAPE; probabilistic quality uses pinball loss and empirical interval coverage. Forecasts feed a newsvendor-style replenishment rule, and resulting cash-on-hand cost and stock-out frequency are compared to a moving-average heuristic baseline. Risks (data gaps, holiday shifts, concept drift) and mitigations are documented.

Scope:
The project covers intraday and daily cash-demand forecasting and the derived replenishment quantity for a fixed set of ATMs in the dataset. It excludes cash-in-transit route optimisation, denomination-mix planning, and live integration with bank systems; all work is offline on historical data.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A reproducible forecasting pipeline with the three compared models and a feature store.
2. A benchmark report on point and probabilistic accuracy with rolling-origin validation.
3. A replenishment evaluation showing cost and stock-out trade-offs versus the current heuristic at chosen service levels.

Timeline:
16 weeks: weeks 1-2 data and features, 3-6 baseline and gradient-boosting models, 7-9 probabilistic deep model, 10-12 replenishment rule and back-test, 13-14 evaluation, 15-16 write-up.

Title:
A Telemedicine Platform with Integrated Payment for Online Consultations
