Title:
An Adaptive E-Learning System for Machine Operator Safety Training in Manufacturing

Problem Statement:
New machine operators in manufacturing plants are often trained with the same fixed slides regardless of their prior experience, leading to slow learning for some and overload for others. There is a need for an e-learning system that adapts content difficulty to each worker's quiz performance.

Objectives:
1. Build an e-learning platform delivering safety modules for machine operation
2. Implement a rule-based adaptation that adjusts module difficulty from quiz scores
3. Evaluate whether adaptive sequencing improves quiz outcomes compared with fixed sequencing

Methodology:
The system will be built with React and a Node.js/Express backend storing content and progress in PostgreSQL. Adaptation uses a threshold rule: scoring below 60% routes the learner to remedial content, above 85% unlocks advanced modules. Evaluation compares an adaptive group with a fixed-order control group of around 20 trainees using average post-test scores and a t-test.

Scope:
The system covers three safety topics for one machine type and runs on desktop browsers. It does not include VR content, certification, or HR integration.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working adaptive e-learning platform with three safety modules
2. A comparison report of adaptive versus fixed sequencing scores

14 weeks: requirements (2), content build (3), development (5), evaluation (3), writing (1).

Title:
A Mobile Fintech Payment App for Reporting and Funding Public Safety Repairs

Title:
Machine Learning Fraud Detection for Energy Billing Anomalies

Problem Statement:
Energy utilities lose revenue to meter tampering and billing fraud, which is hard to spot manually among thousands of accounts. A machine learning model trained on consumption patterns could flag suspicious accounts for inspection more efficiently than threshold rules alone.

Objectives:
1. Prepare a labelled dataset of normal and fraudulent energy consumption records
2. Train and compare classifiers to detect billing anomalies
3. Evaluate detection performance against a simple rule-based baseline

Methodology:
Using a public smart-meter consumption dataset, features such as average usage, variance, and sudden drops will be engineered. Logistic regression, random forest, and XGBoost will be trained with stratified cross-validation. Because fraud is rare, SMOTE will address class imbalance. Models are evaluated with precision, recall, F1, and ROC-AUC and compared to a fixed-threshold rule.

Scope:
The project focuses on residential electricity accounts using one public dataset. Real-time deployment and integration with utility systems are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained fraud-detection model with documented metrics
2. A comparison report showing improvement over the rule-based baseline

14 weeks across data prep, modelling, evaluation, and reporting.

Title:
A Hybrid Product Recommendation System for a Small Online Business

Problem Statement:

2. Generate personalised product suggestions from purchase history and item attributes
3. Evaluate recommendation quality on a public retail dataset

Methodology:
Item-based collaborative filtering will use cosine similarity on a user-item matrix, while content-based filtering uses TF-IDF over product descriptions; the two scores are combined with a weighted blend. The Online Retail dataset will be used. Evaluation uses precision@k and recall@k with a train/test split, compared against a popularity-based baseline.

Scope:
The system is a prototype web demo for one small shop's catalogue. Real-time A/B testing and live deployment are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working hybrid recommendation prototype
2. An evaluation report with precision@k and recall@k results

Timeline:
One semester: data prep, model build, evaluation, write-up.

Title:
A Conversational Agent to Answer Farmers' Crop and Pest Questions

For knowledge questions, a retrieval step searches a small indexed corpus of extension articles and returns the best-matching passage. Evaluation measures intent classification accuracy on a held-out test set and collects relevance ratings from a few users on sample answers.

Scope:

Title:
A Knowledge Graph Search System for Public Transport Route Information

Problem Statement:
Commuters searching for transport options often must combine information from separate timetables, route maps, and fare tables. A knowledge graph linking stops, routes, and fares could answer connected questions like "cheapest way from A to B" that keyword search handles poorly.

Objectives:
1. Build a knowledge graph from open public transport data linking stops, routes, and fares
2. Support natural-language-style queries over the graph
3. Compare answer accuracy and query time against a keyword search baseline

Methodology:
Open GTFS transport data will be modelled as a graph in Neo4j with stops, routes, and fare relationships. A query layer translates a set of question templates into Cypher queries. Evaluation runs a fixed set of test questions and measures answer correctness and response time versus a keyword search over the same flat data.

Scope:
The project uses one city's open transport dataset and a fixed set of question templates. Real-time arrivals and free-form natural language parsing are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:

2. A comparison report on accuracy and query time

One trimester: data modelling, graph build, query layer, evaluation.

Title:
Semantic Segmentation of Rooftop Solar Potential from Aerial Imagery for Urban Sustainability

Problem Statement:
City planners promoting rooftop solar lack quick estimates of usable roof area across neighbourhoods, and manual mapping does not scale. Automatically segmenting rooftops and obstructions from aerial imagery would let planners estimate solar potential at scale, but generic building footprints ignore chimneys, shading, and roof orientation that affect real capacity.

Objectives:
1. Train a semantic segmentation model to separate usable rooftop area from obstructions in aerial images
2. Convert segmented usable area into an estimated solar capacity figure per building
3. Evaluate segmentation against annotated ground truth and benchmark two architectures

Methodology:
Using the public Inria Aerial Image Labeling dataset plus a small manually annotated obstruction set, a U-Net and a DeepLabv3+ (ResNet-50 backbone) will be trained with data augmentation. Training uses a combined Dice and cross-entropy loss with 5-fold cross-validation. Segmentation is evaluated with IoU, Dice, and pixel accuracy; solar estimates are validated against published per-area capacity factors on a held-out set.

Scope:
The project covers rooftop and obstruction segmentation plus area-based capacity estimation for one urban region. Tilt from 3D models, financial return modelling, and live deployment are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained segmentation model with documented IoU/Dice scores and a U-Net vs DeepLabv3+ comparison
2. A per-building usable-area and estimated-capacity report for the study region

Timeline:
14 weeks: data and annotation (3), modelling (5), evaluation (3), capacity analysis and write-up (3).

Title:
Real-Time Pallet and Forklift Detection for Warehouse Logistics Safety

Problem Statement:
Warehouse near-misses between forklifts and workers are a recurring logistics safety problem, and existing camera systems only record footage without flagging risky proximity. An object detector that locates forklifts, pallets, and people in real time could trigger proximity warnings, but generic detectors miss the partial occlusion and motion blur common in warehouse aisles.

Objectives:
1. Build an annotated dataset of forklifts, pallets, and people from warehouse-style footage
2. Train and compare object detectors for these classes under occlusion
3. Implement and evaluate a proximity-warning rule using detected bounding boxes

Methodology:
Frames from public warehouse and forklift datasets will be annotated in YOLO format. YOLOv8 and Faster R-CNN will be trained with augmentation for blur and occlusion, with hyperparameters tuned on a validation split. Detection is evaluated with mAP@0.5 and per-class precision/recall; the proximity rule (bounding-box distance threshold) is evaluated on labelled near-miss clips for alert precision and recall.

Scope:
The project targets three object classes in indoor warehouse footage at near-real-time on a single GPU. Multi-camera tracking, 3D depth, and PLC integration are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained detector with mAP results and a YOLOv8 vs Faster R-CNN comparison
2. A proximity-warning module evaluated on labelled near-miss clips

Timeline:
14 weeks: annotation (3), training (4), proximity module (3), evaluation and writing (4).

Title:
Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis of Citizen Feedback on E-Government Services

Problem Statement:
E-government portals collect large volumes of free-text citizen feedback, but overall sentiment scores hide which specific aspects (e.g. login, response time, clarity) people complain about. Aspect-based sentiment analysis could pinpoint problem areas, yet generic sentiment models trained on product reviews transfer poorly to public-service language.

Objectives:

2. Fine-tune a transformer model for aspect-based sentiment classification
3. Compare performance against a lexicon-based and a BiLSTM baseline

Methodology:
A corpus of public-service feedback will be collected from open complaint portals and annotated for five service aspects with positive/negative/neutral labels. BERT-base will be fine-tuned for aspect-term sentiment classification using stratified train/validation/test splits. Evaluation uses macro-F1 and per-aspect accuracy, compared against a VADER lexicon baseline and a BiLSTM, with error analysis on misclassified aspects.

Scope:
The project covers English feedback and five predefined service aspects. Aspect extraction from scratch, multilingual feedback, and live portal integration are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An annotated aspect-sentiment dataset and a fine-tuned classifier
2. A comparison report with macro-F1 across BERT, BiLSTM, and lexicon baselines

Title:
A Learning-Based Cardinality Estimator for Query Optimization in an Education Analytics Database

Problem Statement:
Education analytics dashboards run multi-table joins over student, course, and activity data, where the database optimizer often mis-estimates row counts and picks slow plans. Improving cardinality estimation could reduce query latency, but classic histogram estimators ignore column correlations common in this schema.

Objectives:
1. Build a workload of representative analytic queries over an education-style schema
2. Train a learned cardinality estimator and integrate its estimates into plan selection
3. Evaluate query latency and estimation error against the default optimizer

Methodology:
Using a synthetic education dataset generated to match a realistic schema, a query workload with varied join and filter patterns will be created. A supervised model (gradient-boosted trees over query and column features) predicts join cardinalities, trained on executed-query statistics with cross-validation. Evaluation measures q-error of estimates and end-to-end latency of selected plans versus PostgreSQL's default estimator on a held-out workload.

Scope:
The project targets select-project-join queries on one fixed education schema in PostgreSQL. Updates, write workloads, and full optimizer replacement are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained cardinality estimator with documented q-error reduction
2. A latency comparison against the default optimizer on the test workload

Timeline:
14 weeks: workload design (3), model training (4), integration (3), evaluation (4).

Title:
A Liveness-Aware Facial Recognition Attendance System for Retail Staff

Problem Statement:
Retail chains using manual or card-based staff attendance face buddy-punching, where one worker clocks in for another. Facial recognition can stop this, but naive systems are fooled by a photo of a colleague, so liveness detection is needed for trustworthy retail attendance.

Objectives:
1. Build a facial recognition attendance pipeline for enrolled retail staff
2. Add a liveness-detection step to reject photo and screen spoofing
3. Evaluate recognition accuracy and spoof-rejection rate under store-like conditions

Methodology:
Face detection uses MTCNN and recognition uses FaceNet embeddings matched by cosine distance against an enrolled gallery. Liveness uses a blink/texture-based check evaluated on the public CASIA-FASD anti-spoofing dataset. Recognition is evaluated with identification accuracy and false-accept/false-reject rates on enrolled and impostor sets; liveness is measured by attack presentation classification error rate under varied lighting.

Scope:
The system handles single-person check-in for up to about 30 enrolled staff at one terminal. Mask-occluded recognition, payroll integration, and large-scale crowds are excluded.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working attendance prototype with logged check-ins
2. An evaluation report on recognition accuracy and spoof-rejection rate

Timeline:
14 weeks: pipeline build (4), liveness integration (3), evaluation (4), write-up (3).

Title:
A Robust OCR Pipeline for Extracting Structured Fields from Smart-City Permit Documents

Problem Statement:
Smart-city service desks process thousands of scanned permit and licence documents whose key fields (permit ID, address, dates) must be re-keyed by hand, a slow and error-prone bottleneck. Off-the-shelf OCR returns raw text but not structured fields, and accuracy collapses on noisy scans, stamps, and mixed printed/handwritten entries common in municipal paperwork. A pipeline that combines layout-aware OCR with field extraction and a confidence-based human-review gate is needed to make digitisation reliable.

Objectives:
1. Assemble and annotate a dataset of municipal permit scans with field-level bounding boxes and values
2. Build an OCR-plus-extraction pipeline that outputs structured key-value fields with per-field confidence
3. Evaluate end-to-end field accuracy and the precision/recall trade-off of the confidence-based review gate against a Tesseract+regex baseline

Methodology:
Around 1,000 permit scans (open municipal forms plus synthetically augmented noise) will be annotated for six fields. The pipeline uses a fine-tuned LayoutLMv3 model for layout-aware token classification over text from a high-accuracy OCR engine, with rule-based post-validation for dates and IDs. Training uses stratified splits with 5-fold cross-validation; augmentation simulates blur, skew, and stamps. Evaluation reports field-level precision/recall/F1 and exact-match accuracy, compared against a Tesseract+regex baseline; the confidence threshold for routing to human review is tuned on a validation set and reported as a precision-vs-review-load curve. Risks (limited handwriting data, class imbalance) are mitigated by augmentation and stratification.

Scope:
The project targets six predefined fields on English-language single-page municipal permits, producing structured JSON plus a review flag. Full handwriting recognition, multi-page table extraction, and production deployment to the city system are explicitly out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An annotated permit dataset and a reproducible OCR-plus-extraction pipeline with per-field confidence
2. An evaluation report with field-level F1, exact-match accuracy, baseline comparison, and a confidence-vs-review-load analysis

Timeline:
14 weeks: data collection and annotation (3), pipeline build (3), model fine-tuning (3), evaluation and review-gate tuning (3), write-up (2).

Title:
Anomaly Detection and Short-Term Forecasting of Visitor Density from Wireless Sensor Networks at Tourism Sites

Problem Statement:
Popular tourism sites suffer overcrowding that harms visitor safety and experience, yet managers react only after queues form because raw Wi-Fi and BLE sensor counts are noisy and hard to interpret. Existing dashboards show current counts but neither flag abnormal surges early nor forecast the next hour, so staff cannot pre-position resources. A pipeline that cleans wireless sensor streams, detects density anomalies, and forecasts short-term visitor load is needed for proactive crowd management.

Objectives:
1. Build a preprocessing pipeline that converts noisy Wi-Fi/BLE probe counts into a calibrated visitor-density time series per zone
2. Detect abnormal density surges and forecast visitor density 30 to 60 minutes ahead
3. Evaluate detection and forecasting accuracy against statistical baselines with cross-validation

Methodology:
Using a public Wi-Fi/BLE occupancy dataset (supplemented by simulated surge events for labels), probe counts are de-duplicated and aggregated into per-zone density series. Anomalies are detected with an LSTM autoencoder reconstruction-error threshold and benchmarked against seasonal-decomposition and isolation-forest baselines. Forecasting compares an LSTM and Temporal Convolutional Network against SARIMA and a naive seasonal baseline, evaluated with time-series cross-validation. Metrics are precision/recall/F1 and detection lead-time for anomalies, and MAE/RMSE/MAPE for forecasts; risks such as sparse labels and sensor dropout are handled by synthetic surge injection and gap interpolation.

Scope:
The project covers offline analysis of one multi-zone tourism venue's sensor logs, producing anomaly flags and 30-to-60-minute forecasts. Real-time streaming deployment, individual visitor tracking, and identity-level data are explicitly excluded for privacy and scope reasons.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A reproducible preprocessing-plus-modelling pipeline for sensor-based visitor density
2. An evaluation report comparing anomaly detection and forecasting models against baselines with lead-time and error metrics

Timeline:
14 weeks: data prep and calibration (3), anomaly model (3), forecasting model (3), evaluation against baselines (3), write-up (2).

Title:
Voice-Controlled Shopping Assistant for Retail Stores

Problem Statement:
Customers in retail stores sometimes find it hard to locate products or check prices, and staff are busy. A speech recognition system could let customers ask questions by voice. Existing kiosks mostly use touch screens, which can be slow and unhygienic.

Objectives:
1. Develop a speech recognition module that understands customer queries
2. Connect the module to a product database to answer questions
3. Evaluate how accurately the system understands spoken requests

Methodology:
The system will use an existing speech recognition library to convert speech to text, then match keywords to a product database. It will be developed in Python with a basic interface. Testing will involve volunteers speaking sample queries and checking the responses.

Scope:
The project covers a single retail store scenario with a fixed product list in English. It will not handle multiple languages or payment processing.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A voice assistant prototype that answers product questions
2. An accuracy report based on volunteer testing

Timeline:
Roughly two semesters: research and design first, then implementation and testing.

Title:
Network Intrusion Detection for Smart City Sensors

Problem Statement:
Smart cities rely on many connected sensors that can be targeted by attackers. Detecting unusual network traffic is important to keep services running. Many small deployments do not have any intrusion detection at all, leaving them exposed.

Objectives:
1. Build a machine learning model to detect abnormal network traffic
2. Train the model on a public intrusion dataset
3. Measure detection accuracy and false alarm rate

Methodology:
I will use the NSL-KDD dataset and train a classifier such as a decision tree or random forest to label traffic as normal or attack. Feature selection will be applied to reduce the number of inputs. The model will be evaluated using accuracy and false positive rate.

Scope:
The project focuses on offline detection using a public dataset for a smart city sensor context. Real-time deployment on live hardware is out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained intrusion detection model
2. A comparison of two classifiers on the dataset

Timeline:
Two semesters: data preparation and modelling, then evaluation and write-up.

Title:
Security Testing Tool for Tourism Booking Websites

Problem Statement:
Tourism booking websites handle personal and payment data, so they are attractive targets for attackers. Small tourism businesses often cannot afford professional security audits. A simple tool to check common web vulnerabilities could help them.

Objectives:
1. Develop a tool that scans web applications for common vulnerabilities
2. Cover issues such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting
3. Produce a report that lists the problems found

Methodology:
The tool will send test inputs to web forms and analyse the responses to detect signs of vulnerabilities. It will be built in Python and tested against a deliberately vulnerable practice website such as DVWA. Detected issues will be summarised in a report.

Scope:
The project targets a small set of common vulnerabilities on tourism booking sites. It will not test mobile apps or perform automated exploitation.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A vulnerability scanning tool prototype
2. A sample report from testing on a practice site

Timeline:
About two semesters, split between building the tool and testing it.

Title:
Static and Dynamic Analysis of Malware Spread Through Social Media Links

Problem Statement:
Social media platforms are increasingly used to spread malicious links and attachments that lead to malware infections. While antivirus tools catch known threats, many users still click unknown links. There is a need for a lightweight analysis pipeline that can flag suspicious files shared through social media before users open them.

Objectives:
1. Build a pipeline that performs static analysis of submitted files to extract features such as API calls and strings
2. Add a sandboxed dynamic analysis stage to observe runtime behaviour
3. Classify samples as benign or malicious and report the indicators found

Methodology:
Static analysis will use tools like PEfile and YARA rules to extract features from executables. Dynamic analysis will run samples in a Cuckoo-style sandbox to log behaviour. A simple classifier trained on a labelled malware dataset will combine the features. Evaluation will compare detection accuracy against the dataset labels.

Scope:
The project focuses on Windows PE files shared as links, using a public malware dataset. It will not analyse mobile malware or perform live social media monitoring.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working static-plus-dynamic analysis pipeline
2. An evaluation of classification accuracy with example reports

Timeline:
Semester one for static analysis and dataset setup; semester two for sandbox integration, classification and evaluation.

Title:
A Responsive Web Platform for Community Clinic Appointment Management

Problem Statement:
Small community clinics often manage appointments by phone or paper, which leads to double-bookings and long wait times. Patients have no easy way to see available slots. A responsive web platform accessible on phones and desktops could let patients book and clinics manage schedules more efficiently.

Objectives:
1. Develop a responsive web platform for patients to book and cancel appointments
2. Provide a clinic dashboard to manage schedules and view daily bookings
3. Evaluate usability with a small group of test users

Methodology:
The platform will be built with React on the front end and a Node.js and Express back end with a PostgreSQL database. Responsive design will use CSS media queries so it works on mobile and desktop. Usability will be assessed through task-based testing and a short questionnaire with around eight participants.

Scope:
The system covers appointment booking and basic schedule management for a single clinic. It will not include medical records, billing or insurance integration.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A deployed responsive appointment booking platform
2. A usability evaluation summarising feedback and task success rates

Timeline:
First semester for requirements and core booking features; second for the dashboard, responsiveness and user testing.

Title:
A Progressive Web App for Personal Budget Tracking

Problem Statement:
Many people struggle to track daily spending, and existing finance apps often require installation or constant internet access. A progressive web app (PWA) could offer an installable, offline-capable budget tracker that works across devices without app store distribution.

Objectives:
1. Build a PWA that lets users record income and expenses by category
2. Support offline use and installability through a service worker and manifest
3. Provide simple charts summarising monthly spending

Methodology:
The app will be developed with React and a service worker for offline caching, storing data locally with IndexedDB and syncing to a Firebase back end when online. Charts will be rendered using a charting library. Testing will confirm offline behaviour and verify that data syncs correctly when the connection returns.

Scope:
The project covers personal budget tracking with manual entry and basic charts. It will not include bank account integration or multi-currency support.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An installable, offline-capable budget tracking PWA
2. A test report covering offline use and data synchronisation

Timeline:
Semester one for core entry features and offline support; semester two for syncing, charts and testing.

Title:
A Cross-Platform Mobile App for Factory Maintenance Reporting

Problem Statement:
On factory floors, machine faults are often reported verbally or on paper, causing delays and lost records. Maintenance staff need a quick way to log issues with photos and track repair status. A cross-platform mobile app would let workers report problems from either Android or iOS devices.

Objectives:
1. Develop a cross-platform mobile app for reporting machine faults with photos
2. Allow maintenance staff to update and track the status of each report
3. Test the workflow with sample users acting as workers and technicians

Methodology:
The app will be built with Flutter so a single codebase runs on Android and iOS. Reports, photos and status updates will be stored through a Firebase back end. A role-based view will separate workers from technicians. Testing will follow scripted scenarios to confirm reports flow correctly from creation to resolution.

Scope:
The project covers fault reporting and status tracking for a single factory. It will not include predictive maintenance, IoT sensor data or spare-parts inventory.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working cross-platform fault reporting app
2. A test report showing the end-to-end reporting workflow

Timeline:
First semester for app design and reporting features; second for status tracking, roles and testing.

Title:
A Native Android App for Community Incident Reporting

Problem Statement:
Residents who witness public safety issues such as broken streetlights, flooding or suspicious activity often have no convenient way to report them to local authorities. Phone calls are slow and details are easily lost. A native Android app could let residents submit geotagged reports quickly.

Objectives:
1. Develop a native Android app for submitting incident reports with location and photos
2. Store reports so authorities can view them on a simple dashboard
3. Evaluate the app with a small group of residents for ease of use

Methodology:
The app will be built natively in Kotlin using Android Studio, with the device GPS for location tagging and the camera for photos. Reports will be sent to a back end with a REST API and stored in a database. A basic web dashboard will list reports. Usability testing will use task scenarios with around six participants.

Scope:
The project covers report submission and a viewing dashboard for one community. It will not include real-time dispatch, authority verification or push escalation.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A native Android incident reporting app with a viewing dashboard
2. A usability evaluation with participant feedback

Timeline:
Semester one for the reporting app and back end; semester two for the dashboard and user testing.

Title:
An IoT Sensor Network for Home Energy Monitoring

Problem Statement:
Households often do not know which appliances consume the most electricity, making it hard to reduce bills. Commercial energy monitors can be expensive. A low-cost IoT sensor network could measure consumption at several points and present the data to users in real time.

Objectives:
1. Build an IoT sensor network that measures electricity usage at multiple points
2. Send readings to a central server and store them over time
3. Display consumption trends through a simple dashboard

Methodology:
Sensors based on ESP32 microcontrollers with current sensors will measure usage and send readings over Wi-Fi using MQTT to a Raspberry Pi acting as a broker and server. Readings will be stored in a time-series database and shown on a web dashboard with charts. Testing will compare readings against a reference meter for a few appliances.

Scope:
The project covers monitoring of a small number of circuits in one home. It will not include automated appliance control or billing integration.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working IoT energy monitoring prototype with a dashboard
2. A short accuracy comparison against a reference meter

Timeline:
First semester for hardware and data collection; second for storage, dashboard and accuracy testing.

Title:
A Rule-Based Smart Home Automation Hub for Small Retail Shops

Problem Statement:
Small shops waste energy and staff time managing lighting, air-conditioning and signage manually, and off-the-shelf smart home hubs are tuned for residential use rather than business hours and footfall. There is a gap for an affordable, locally hosted automation hub that ties device control to opening hours and occupancy without relying on a paid cloud subscription.

Objectives:
1. Design and build an automation hub that controls lights, climate and signage based on schedules and occupancy
2. Implement a rule engine allowing shop owners to define triggers and actions through a web interface
3. Evaluate energy savings and usability against a baseline of manual control over a two-week trial

Methodology:
The hub will run on a Raspberry Pi using Home Assistant as the base, integrating Zigbee smart plugs and a PIR occupancy sensor via MQTT. A custom rule engine will let owners define if-then automations. Energy use will be logged with smart-plug meters and compared between an automated week and a manual baseline week. Usability will be assessed with a SUS questionnaire.

Scope:
The project targets a single small shop with up to ten controllable devices. It excludes integration with point-of-sale systems, voice assistants and outdoor devices.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working locally hosted automation hub with a rule-editing interface
2. An evaluation reporting measured energy savings and a usability score

Timeline:
Semester one for hardware integration and the rule engine; semester two for the interface, the two-week trial and evaluation.

Title:
Edge-Based Crop Disease Detection for Smallholder Farms

Problem Statement:
Smallholder farmers often lack reliable internet, so cloud-based crop disease detection apps are impractical in the field. Running inference on a low-power edge device would let farmers diagnose leaf diseases offline. The challenge is fitting an accurate model within the memory and latency limits of affordable edge hardware.

Objectives:
1. Train a leaf disease classifier and compress it to run on an edge device
2. Deploy the model on a Raspberry Pi for offline, on-device inference
3. Evaluate accuracy, inference latency and model size against a cloud baseline

Methodology:
A MobileNetV2 classifier will be trained on the PlantVillage dataset using transfer learning, then quantised and converted to TensorFlow Lite. The model will run on a Raspberry Pi 4 with a camera module. Evaluation will report top-1 accuracy, per-image latency and model size, and compare against the full-precision model. Test images will include field photos beyond the curated dataset to check robustness.

Scope:
The project covers a fixed set of crop and disease classes from PlantVillage, deployed on one edge device. It excludes pest detection, yield prediction and a multi-farm networked system.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A quantised on-device disease classifier running offline on a Raspberry Pi
2. An evaluation comparing accuracy, latency and size against the cloud baseline

Timeline:
Semester one for training and compression; semester two for deployment, field testing and evaluation.

Title:
A Cloud-Native Microservices Backend for Ride-Sharing Trip Management

Problem Statement:
Monolithic ride-sharing backends struggle to scale individual functions such as matching and payments independently, and a fault in one area can bring down the whole service. A cloud-native microservices architecture can isolate failures and scale services separately, but designing and evaluating such a system within a student project requires careful scoping.

Objectives:
1. Design a microservices backend separating trip matching, trip management and notifications
2. Containerise the services and orchestrate them with Kubernetes, exposing them through an API gateway
3. Evaluate scalability and fault isolation under simulated load

Methodology:
Services will be built in Spring Boot, each with its own database, communicating via REST and a message queue (RabbitMQ) for events. They will be containerised with Docker and deployed on a local Kubernetes cluster (minikube) behind an API gateway. Load testing with k6 will measure latency and throughput as replicas scale, and a service will be deliberately killed to demonstrate fault isolation.

Scope:
The project implements three core services with simulated riders and drivers. Real payment processing, a production mobile client and multi-region deployment are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A deployed microservices backend with three services on Kubernetes
2. A report on scalability under load and fault-isolation behaviour

Timeline:
Semester one for service design and containerisation; semester two for orchestration, load testing and evaluation.

Title:
A CI/CD Pipeline for Automated Carbon Footprint Reporting of Web Deployments

Problem Statement:
Development teams rarely know the carbon impact of their deployments, and existing CI/CD pipelines optimise for speed, not energy. Embedding a sustainability check into the pipeline could surface the estimated carbon cost of each build and deployment, nudging teams toward greener choices, but such tooling is not standard in typical setups.

Objectives:
1. Build a CI/CD pipeline that automatically builds, tests and deploys a sample web application
2. Add a stage that estimates the carbon footprint of the build and target infrastructure
3. Evaluate the pipeline by measuring estimate consistency and the overhead added to build time

Methodology:
The pipeline will use GitHub Actions to run build, test and deploy stages for a sample app deployed to a cloud instance. A custom stage will estimate carbon using region carbon-intensity data and resource usage via a tool such as the Cloud Carbon Footprint approach. Evaluation will compare reported estimates across repeated runs and measure the added pipeline time over a baseline without the stage.

Scope:
The project covers one sample application and one cloud region, focusing on estimation rather than precise measurement. It excludes full multi-cloud support and automated remediation.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working CI/CD pipeline with an integrated carbon-estimation stage
2. An evaluation of estimate consistency and added build overhead

Timeline:
Semester one for the base pipeline and sample app; semester two for the carbon stage and evaluation.

Title:
A Big Data Pipeline for Delivery Delay Prediction in Logistics

Problem Statement:
Logistics firms generate large volumes of shipment events but often analyse them in batch reports that arrive too late to act on. A streaming big data pipeline that ingests shipment events and predicts delivery delays in near real time could help dispatchers intervene earlier, yet building and evaluating such a pipeline within a student project requires a clear, bounded design.

Objectives:
1. Build a streaming pipeline that ingests shipment events and stores them for analysis
2. Train and serve a model that predicts whether a shipment will be delayed
3. Evaluate prediction quality and pipeline throughput on a public logistics dataset

Methodology:
Events from a public shipment dataset will be replayed into Apache Kafka, processed with Spark Structured Streaming, and stored in a data lake. A gradient-boosted model (XGBoost) trained on historical features will predict delays, served behind a small API and validated with time-based train/test splits. Evaluation will report precision, recall and ROC-AUC for delay prediction and measure events-per-second throughput.

Scope:
The project uses one public dataset replayed as a stream on a single multi-node local setup. Live carrier integration and route optimisation are out of scope.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working streaming pipeline with a deployed delay-prediction model
2. An evaluation of model metrics and pipeline throughput

Timeline:
Semester one for ingestion and storage; semester two for modelling, serving and evaluation.

Title:
An Interactive Business Intelligence Dashboard for Municipal Service Request Analytics in E-Government

Problem Statement:
Municipal "report-a-problem" portals collect thousands of service requests (potholes, waste, lighting), yet officials typically rely on static monthly spreadsheets that hide spatial and temporal patterns and offer no resolution-time benchmarking across departments. There is a measurable gap between the data captured and the actionable, drill-down analytics decision-makers need, with no open, reproducible BI reference built specifically on the standard Open311 request schema.

Objectives:
1. Design a dimensional data model and ETL process over an Open311 service-request dataset, achieving validated load of at least twelve months of records
2. Build an interactive dashboard with geospatial, temporal and department drill-downs plus SLA-breach and resolution-time KPIs
3. Evaluate decision-support effectiveness via task-based user testing (n=12 officials/proxies) measuring task completion time and SUS, benchmarked against a static-report baseline

Methodology:
A star schema (request fact; date, location, category, department dimensions) will be loaded via a Python ETL into PostgreSQL, with data-quality checks on completeness and duplicate detection. The dashboard will be built in Apache Superset, exposing choropleth maps, time-series, and cohort views with row-level filters. Evaluation uses a within-subjects A/B design comparing the dashboard against static reports across six analytical tasks, with paired t-tests on completion time and a SUS questionnaire; ETL correctness is checked against source-row reconciliation.

Scope:
Scope is one city's public Open311 dataset and a read-only analytical dashboard. Explicitly excluded: predictive routing of requests, write-back to the source system, real-time streaming ingestion, and citizen-facing mobile views.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A reproducible ETL plus dimensional warehouse and an interactive Superset dashboard with documented KPIs
2. A quantitative evaluation showing task-time and SUS differences versus the static-report baseline, with statistical significance reported

Timeline:
Weeks 1-4 requirements and data model; 5-9 ETL and KPI definition; 10-14 dashboard build; 15-20 user study and analysis; 21-24 write-up. Risk: dataset gaps mitigated by a secondary city dataset.

Title:
Probabilistic Short-Horizon Forecasting of Daily Student Engagement in a Virtual Learning Environment

Problem Statement:
Early-warning systems in education often flag at-risk students only after grades drop. Forecasting near-term engagement (daily VLE clicks) could enable earlier intervention, but most prior work reports point forecasts without uncertainty and evaluates on a single cohort, limiting trust and generalisability. A reproducible, uncertainty-aware forecast of short-horizon engagement on a public, multi-cohort dataset is missing.

Objectives:
1. Construct per-student daily engagement series from the OULAD dataset and define a 7-day-ahead forecasting task with leakage-free temporal splits
2. Compare classical (seasonal-naive, SARIMA, exponential smoothing) and ML/DL models (LightGBM, LSTM, and a probabilistic model producing prediction intervals)
3. Evaluate accuracy and calibration across cohorts, and quantify lead-time benefit for an at-risk-flagging downstream task

Methodology:
Using the Open University Learning Analytics Dataset, daily click series will be aggregated per student with calendar and assessment-proximity features. Models will be trained with rolling-origin cross-validation; the probabilistic model (quantile LightGBM and DeepAR-style) yields 7-day prediction intervals. Metrics: MASE and RMSE for accuracy, pinball loss and PICP for calibration, against a seasonal-naive baseline. Significance tested via the Diebold-Mariano test; cohorts held out to assess generalisation. Code and seeds released for reproducibility.

Scope:
Scope is forecasting daily aggregate engagement per student for 7-day horizons on OULAD. Excluded: intervention design, grade prediction, real-time deployment, and natural-language content of materials.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A reproducible benchmark comparing classical and probabilistic models with calibrated intervals across cohorts
2. Evidence on whether short-horizon engagement forecasts improve lead time for at-risk flagging versus the baseline

Timeline:
Weeks 1-3 data pipeline; 4-8 baselines and feature design; 9-14 ML/DL and probabilistic models; 15-19 cross-cohort evaluation and calibration; 20-24 downstream analysis and write-up. Risk: class imbalance mitigated by stratified cohort sampling.

Title:
Blockchain Smart Contracts for Small Business

Problem Statement:
Small businesses have many problems with payments and trust. Blockchain is a new technology that can fix this.

Objectives:
1. Make a blockchain system.
2. Use smart contracts.
3. Help small business.

Methodology:
I will use blockchain and smart contracts. Also some coding and research about how it works.

Scope:
For all small businesses everywhere. It will be very secure and good.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working blockchain.
2. Happy businesses.

Title:
AR App for Agriculture

Problem Statement:
Farmers do not have technology. Augmented reality can show them things on the phone which is helpful for the crops.

Objectives:
1. Build an AR app.
2. Make it for farmers.
3. Show plant information.

Methodology:
Use AR and a phone camera. I will download some tools and make the app point at plants.

Scope:
All kinds of farms and all plants. Anyone can use it.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An AR app.
2. Better farming.

Title:
VR Training Simulation for Transportation

Problem Statement:
Transportation training is dangerous and costs money. VR can make training safe and modern.

Objectives:
1. Create a VR simulation.
2. Train people.
3. Make it realistic.

Methodology:
I will use VR headsets and a game engine. There will be research and some testing later.

Scope:
For drivers, pilots, ships and trains. Everyone in transport can use it.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A VR training tool.
2. Safer transport workers.

Title:
A 2D Game to Teach Sustainability Habits

Problem Statement:
Many young people do not think about recycling and saving energy in daily life. A simple game could make learning these habits more fun than reading posters, but few free games target this in an engaging way.

Objectives:
1. Design a 2D game where players sort waste and manage a small eco-town.
2. Add levels that reward saving water and energy.
3. Test if players remember the lessons afterwards.

Methodology:
The game will be built in Unity with C# using free 2D sprites. Players collect points for correct recycling choices. I will run a small survey with classmates before and after playing to see if their knowledge improves.

Scope:
The game has three levels and runs on Windows desktop. It does not include multiplayer or mobile versions.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A playable 2D sustainability game.
2. Survey results showing whether knowledge increased.

Timeline:
About 12 weeks: design, build, then test.

Title:
Serious Game for Learning Warehouse Logistics

Problem Statement:
New warehouse staff take time to learn how to pick orders and arrange stock efficiently. Reading manuals is boring and real practice slows the warehouse down. A serious game might let them practise without real cost, but most training is still classroom based.

Objectives:
1. Build a game where players pick and pack orders against a timer.
2. Teach basic shelf layout and route planning rules.
3. Measure how player scores improve over several rounds.

Methodology:
The game will be made in Unity. The player moves around a virtual warehouse picking items from a list. Scores depend on time and correct routes. A few volunteers will play several rounds and I will record their scores to see if they get faster.

Scope:
One warehouse layout with about twenty item types. No real inventory integration and no mobile build.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working logistics training game.
2. Score data showing learning over rounds.

Timeline:
Roughly 13 weeks across design, development and testing.

Title:
A Health Record Portal for a Local Government Clinic

Problem Statement:
Small government clinics still keep patient visit records on paper, which makes it slow to find a patient's history and easy to lose files. A simple digital portal could store records and let staff search them, but many existing systems are too expensive for a small clinic.

Objectives:
1. Build a web portal to store patient visits and basic health data.
2. Let clinic staff search and update records by patient ID.
3. Add simple roles so only staff can see records.

Methodology:
The system will use a Spring Boot backend with a MySQL database and a React front end. Staff log in, add visits, and search by name or ID. I will test it with sample data and ask two clinic-style users to try the main tasks.

Scope:
Covers patient registration, visit notes and search. It does not include billing, lab integration or appointment scheduling.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working clinic record portal.
2. Feedback from test users on ease of use.

Timeline:
About 14 weeks for analysis, build and testing.

Title:
A Telemedicine Platform for Online Tutoring Health Checks

Problem Statement:
Students at residential learning centres sometimes feel unwell but cannot easily reach a doctor on campus. A basic telemedicine web app could let them book a video consultation and share symptoms, but current commercial tools are costly and not tailored to a campus setting.

Objectives:
1. Build a web app where students request a video consultation slot.
2. Let a nurse or doctor view submitted symptoms before the call.
3. Store a short record of each consultation.

Methodology:
The platform uses a React front end and a Node.js backend with PostgreSQL. Video calls use a free WebRTC library. Students fill a symptom form, pick a slot, and join a call. I will test the booking and call flow with a few classmates acting as patients and staff.

Scope:
Includes booking, symptom form, video call and a basic record. Excludes prescriptions, payment and integration with hospital systems.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working campus telemedicine prototype.
2. Notes on call quality and usability from test sessions.

Timeline:
Around 14 weeks: requirements, development, testing.

Title:
An E-Learning System for Retail Staff Onboarding

Problem Statement:
Retail chains hire many part-time staff who need quick training on products, point-of-sale steps and customer service. In-store training is inconsistent and depends on whoever is free that day. A structured e-learning system with short lessons and quizzes could standardise onboarding, but generic course platforms are not tailored to fast retail turnover.

Objectives:
1. Build a web-based e-learning system with modular lessons and quizzes for retail onboarding.
2. Track each trainee's progress and quiz scores on a dashboard.
3. Provide managers a report of who has completed required modules.

Methodology:
The system uses a Spring Boot backend, MySQL and a React front end. Content is organised into modules with text, images and multiple-choice quizzes. Progress and scores are stored per user. I will load sample retail content, run functional tests on the quiz and tracking logic, and gather usability feedback from five testers using a short questionnaire.

Scope:
Covers lesson delivery, quizzes, progress tracking and a manager report. Excludes video hosting, payment, and mobile native apps; it runs in the browser only.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working e-learning system with progress tracking.
2. Usability feedback and a summary of quiz completion rates.

Timeline:
14 weeks: requirements (2), design (2), development (7), testing and evaluation (3).

Title:
A Fintech Micro-Payment App for Smart City Parking

Problem Statement:
City drivers waste time looking for coins or queuing at parking machines, and councils struggle to track usage of street bays. A mobile micro-payment app that pays for parking by the minute could reduce friction, but many existing apps charge high fees and do not show live bay availability for a specific city zone.

Objectives:
1. Build a mobile app to start and stop parking sessions and pay per minute.
2. Show available bays in a chosen zone using sample sensor data.
3. Provide a simple admin view of revenue and occupancy.

Methodology:
The app is built with Flutter and a Spring Boot backend using MySQL. Payments are simulated through a sandbox payment gateway. Bay availability comes from a mock sensor feed. I will test session start/stop, payment calculation and the admin dashboard with functional test cases, and check timing accuracy against expected values.

Scope:
Covers session payment, zone availability display and an admin dashboard, using simulated payments and mock sensors. Excludes real bank integration, real-time hardware sensors and enforcement.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working parking micro-payment prototype.
2. Test results on payment accuracy and dashboard correctness.

Timeline:
14 weeks across analysis, build, integration and testing.

Title:
Fraud Detection for Online Tour Booking Transactions

Problem Statement:
Online tour booking sites face fraudulent transactions such as stolen-card bookings and fake refund claims, which cause chargebacks and damage trust. Manual review is slow and inconsistent. A machine-learning classifier could flag suspicious bookings, but tourism transaction patterns differ from generic e-commerce fraud studies.

Objectives:
1. Build a classifier that flags potentially fraudulent tour bookings.
2. Engineer features such as booking lead time, amount, and country mismatch.
3. Evaluate the model against a rule-based baseline using precision and recall.

Methodology:
Using a public credit-card or transaction fraud dataset adapted to booking fields, I will train logistic regression and random forest models in Python with scikit-learn. Class imbalance is handled with SMOTE. Models are compared with a simple threshold-rule baseline using precision, recall and F1 on a held-out test set. The best model is exposed through a small Flask API.

Scope:
Covers feature engineering, model training and evaluation on one dataset, plus a demo API. Excludes live payment integration and real-time streaming.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained fraud classifier with evaluation metrics.
2. A comparison report against the rule-based baseline.

Timeline:
14 weeks: data prep (3), modelling (5), evaluation (3), API and write-up (3).

Title:
A Product Recommendation Engine for a Social Media Marketplace

Problem Statement:
Social media marketplaces show users many listings but rarely tailor them, so users scroll past irrelevant products and sellers get fewer matches. A recommendation engine using past interactions could surface more relevant items, but social marketplace data mixes social signals with purchase intent, which generic recommenders ignore.

Objectives:
1. Build a recommendation engine using collaborative filtering on user-item interactions.
2. Add a content-based component using item categories and tags.
3. Evaluate recommendation quality with precision@k and compare the two approaches.

Methodology:
Using a public interactions dataset (e.g. an e-commerce ratings set), I will implement item-based collaborative filtering and a TF-IDF content-based model in Python. A hybrid combines both scores. Evaluation uses precision@k and recall@k on a held-out split, comparing collaborative, content and hybrid models. A small Flask demo returns top-N items for a user.

Scope:
Covers offline training and evaluation plus a demo endpoint. Excludes real social-graph data, live deployment and A/B testing.

Expected Outcomes:
1. Working collaborative, content-based and hybrid recommenders.
2. An evaluation comparing precision@k across the three approaches.

Timeline:
13 weeks: data and EDA (3), modelling (5), evaluation (3), demo and report (2).

Title:
A Conversational Agent for Hospital Appointment FAQs

Problem Statement:
Hospital front desks and phone lines are flooded with repetitive questions about visiting hours, appointment changes and document requirements. Staff spend time answering the same queries, and patients wait on hold. A chatbot could handle common FAQs, but it must avoid giving medical advice and instead route patients to the right service.

Objectives:
1. Build a chatbot that answers non-medical hospital FAQs.
2. Detect when a query needs a human and escalate it.
3. Evaluate intent accuracy on a labelled question set.

Methodology:
Intents are defined from a set of collected sample questions. I will train an intent classifier using sentence embeddings and a logistic regression head in Python, with retrieval of canned answers per intent. An escalation rule triggers when confidence is low or a medical keyword appears. Evaluation reports intent accuracy and escalation precision on a held-out labelled set.

Scope:
Covers FAQ intents, canned answers and escalation logic in a web widget. Excludes any diagnosis, live hospital system integration and voice input.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working FAQ chatbot with escalation.
2. Intent accuracy and escalation metrics on the test set.

Timeline:
14 weeks: data collection (3), model build (5), evaluation (3), integration and report (3).

Title:
A Knowledge-Graph Search Tool for Company Financial Filings

Problem Statement:
Analysts searching company filings use keyword search that misses relationships, for example which executives sit on which boards or which subsidiaries share owners. A knowledge graph could let users query these relationships, but building one from semi-structured filings and serving useful queries is non-trivial and rarely done for small filing sets.

Objectives:
1. Extract entities and relationships from a set of financial filings into a knowledge graph.
2. Provide a search interface that answers relationship queries.
3. Evaluate extraction accuracy against a hand-labelled sample.

Methodology:
Filings are parsed and named entities (companies, people, amounts) extracted using spaCy plus rule patterns. Relationships are stored in Neo4j. A query interface translates simple user questions into Cypher for common relationship patterns. I will hand-label a sample of filings to measure entity and relation extraction precision and recall, and demonstrate example queries.

Scope:
Covers extraction, graph building and a query demo over a fixed set of filings. Excludes real-time ingestion, full natural-language querying and trading recommendations.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A populated knowledge graph and search demo.
2. Precision and recall of entity and relation extraction.

Timeline:
14 weeks: parsing (3), extraction (4), graph and query (4), evaluation and report (3).

Title:
Defect Segmentation on Metal Surfaces for Manufacturing Quality Control

Problem Statement:
Manual visual inspection of metal parts misses small surface defects and is inconsistent across shifts. Existing classifiers only label whether a part is defective, not where the defect is, which limits root-cause analysis. Pixel-level segmentation would locate defects but requires models that work with limited annotated industrial images.

Objectives:
1. Train a segmentation model that produces pixel masks for surface defects on the NEU-Seg / Severstal steel dataset.
2. Compare a U-Net baseline against a DeepLabV3+ encoder on the same split.
3. Measure mean IoU and Dice per defect class and report failure cases.

Methodology:
Images are split 70/15/15 into train/validation/test with stratification by defect type. A U-Net with a ResNet-34 encoder serves as baseline; DeepLabV3+ is the comparison. Augmentation includes flips, brightness and elastic transforms to address limited data. Models train in PyTorch with Dice-plus-cross-entropy loss and early stopping. Evaluation uses mean IoU and Dice on the held-out test set, with qualitative review of worst masks.

Scope:
Covers segmentation of common steel surface defect classes on one public dataset. Excludes 3D defects, live camera integration and detection of new unseen defect types.

Expected Outcomes:
1. Trained U-Net and DeepLabV3+ segmentation models with per-class IoU/Dice.
2. An analysis of failure cases and augmentation effects.

Timeline:
14 weeks: data and pipeline (3), baseline (3), comparison model (4), evaluation (2), write-up (2).

Title:
Real-Time Object Detection for Public Safety CCTV Crowd Monitoring

Problem Statement:
Operators watching many CCTV feeds cannot reliably spot abandoned bags or sudden crowd density spikes in real time. Generic detectors are trained on everyday objects and underperform on overhead, low-resolution surveillance views, leaving a gap for a tuned detector that runs at usable frame rates.

Objectives:
1. Fine-tune an object detector to find people and unattended-bag candidates on surveillance-style footage.
2. Estimate crowd density from detections and flag threshold breaches.
3. Evaluate detection mAP and measure inference FPS on a single GPU.

Methodology:
A YOLOv8 model is fine-tuned on a subset of the MOT and a public abandoned-object dataset, resplit 80/10/10. Anchors and input resolution are tuned for small overhead objects. Density is computed per grid cell from person boxes. Evaluation reports mAP@0.5 and mAP@0.5:0.95 against the pretrained baseline, plus FPS on one GPU. A risk is class imbalance for the bag class, mitigated by oversampling and copy-paste augmentation.

Scope:
Covers person and abandoned-bag detection and density flagging on recorded clips. Excludes face identification, live multi-camera deployment and tracking across cameras.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A fine-tuned detector with mAP and FPS benchmarks versus baseline.
2. A density-alert demo on sample clips with a short error analysis.

Timeline:
14 weeks: data prep (3), fine-tuning (4), density logic (3), evaluation (2), report (2).

Title:
Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis of Public Reviews on Energy Providers

Problem Statement:
Energy companies receive thousands of online reviews mixing comments on billing, outages and customer service, but overall star ratings hide which aspect drives dissatisfaction. Document-level sentiment is too coarse, so a model that assigns sentiment per aspect is needed to guide service improvements, yet energy-domain aspect data is scarce.

Objectives:
1. Build an aspect-based sentiment model that classifies sentiment for billing, reliability and service aspects.
2. Compare a fine-tuned BERT model against a TF-IDF plus SVM baseline.
3. Evaluate macro-F1 per aspect on a held-out, manually labelled set.

Methodology:
Reviews are scraped or taken from a public utility-review dataset and a sample is hand-labelled per aspect. Aspects are detected with keyword seeds expanded by embeddings; sentiment per aspect is classified by fine-tuning DistilBERT, compared with a TF-IDF and linear SVM baseline. Data is split 70/15/15 with stratification. Evaluation reports macro-F1 and a confusion matrix per aspect, plus inter-annotator agreement on the labelled sample.

Scope:
Covers three predefined aspects on English reviews. Excludes multilingual reviews, sarcasm handling and live dashboard deployment.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An aspect-based sentiment model with per-aspect macro-F1.
2. A comparison of BERT versus the baseline and an error analysis.

Timeline:
14 weeks: data and labelling (4), baseline (2), BERT model (4), evaluation (2), write-up (2).

Title:
A Learned Index-Advisor for Query Optimization in a Small-Business Database

Problem Statement:
Small businesses run reporting queries on databases without a DBA, so missing or redundant indexes cause slow queries and bloated storage. Built-in advisors are tied to specific enterprise engines, leaving open-source MySQL users without guidance on which indexes to add for their actual query workload.

Objectives:
1. Build a tool that recommends indexes for a MySQL workload from query logs.
2. Estimate cost benefit of candidate indexes using EXPLAIN plans before and after.
3. Evaluate recommendations on a TPC-H-derived workload by measuring runtime improvement.

Methodology:
The tool parses the general query log to extract frequent predicates and join columns, generates candidate single- and multi-column indexes, and uses hypothetical-index EXPLAIN estimates to rank them. A greedy selection respects a storage budget. Evaluation runs a TPC-H-scaled schema and query mix, comparing total runtime and storage before and after applying recommendations, against MySQL's own default behaviour. Risks include misleading optimizer estimates, checked by re-measuring real runtimes.

Scope:
Covers single-table and simple join index recommendation for MySQL under a storage budget. Excludes partitioning, materialized views and write-heavy workload tuning.

Expected Outcomes:
1. An index-advisor tool with cost-benefit ranking.
2. Measured runtime and storage results on the TPC-H workload.

Timeline:
14 weeks: log parsing (3), candidate generation (3), selection (3), evaluation (3), report (2).

Title:
Facial Recognition Attendance for Farm Workers

Problem Statement:
Farms employing seasonal workers track attendance on paper, which is slow at shift start and open to buddy-punching where one person clocks in for another. A face-recognition attendance system could record presence automatically, but outdoor lighting and dust make recognition harder than in office settings.

Objectives:
1. Build a face-recognition attendance system that logs check-in and check-out.
2. Handle enrolment of new workers from a few photos.
3. Evaluate recognition accuracy under varied lighting on a small test set.

Methodology:
Faces are detected with MTCNN and embedded with a pretrained FaceNet model; identity is matched by nearest-neighbour over enrolled embeddings with a distance threshold. Attendance events are stored in a database with timestamps. I will collect a small dataset of volunteers under indoor and simulated outdoor lighting and report recognition accuracy, false-accept and false-reject rates. A liveness check is noted as future work, which is a limitation for anti-spoofing.

Scope:
Covers enrolment, recognition and attendance logging for a small set of workers. Excludes spoof detection, multi-camera setups and payroll integration.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A working attendance prototype with a logging dashboard.
2. Accuracy and error rates across lighting conditions.

Timeline:
14 weeks: setup (3), recognition pipeline (4), data collection (3), evaluation (2), report (2).

Title:
Robust OCR Pipeline for Freight Document Processing in Transportation Logistics

Problem Statement:
Freight forwarders manually key data from bills of lading and delivery orders that arrive as scanned images and phone photos, which is slow and error-prone, especially on skewed, low-contrast or stamped documents. General OCR engines transcribe text but do not reliably extract structured fields, and published work rarely targets noisy real-world freight forms, leaving a gap for a field-level extraction pipeline evaluated on transportation documents.

Objectives:
1. Build a pipeline that extracts key fields (consignee, container number, weight, date) from freight documents with measurable field-level accuracy.
2. Compare a Tesseract-plus-layout-rules baseline against a Donut transformer fine-tuned for document understanding.
3. Quantify robustness to skew and noise via controlled perturbation experiments and report a confidence-thresholded review rate.

Methodology:
A corpus is assembled from the public SROIE and FUNSD sets plus a hand-labelled set of freight forms, split 70/15/15 with stratification by form type. Preprocessing applies deskewing and adaptive thresholding. The baseline pairs Tesseract OCR with positional regex rules; the proposed model fine-tunes Donut end-to-end in PyTorch for key-value extraction. Field-level precision/recall/F1 and normalised edit distance are reported, with stratified results under synthetic skew, blur and JPEG-compression perturbations. Five-fold cross-validation on the freight subset estimates variance, and a confidence threshold routes low-certainty fields to human review. Risks (limited freight labels, container-code formats) are mitigated by augmentation and a checksum validator.

Scope:
Covers four field types on English single-page freight documents and the named perturbations. Excludes handwriting recognition, multi-page stitching and live ERP integration, which are documented as future work.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A field-extraction pipeline with per-field F1 and edit-distance metrics versus the baseline.
2. A robustness curve over perturbation levels and a recommended confidence threshold with its review-rate trade-off.

Timeline:
14 weeks: corpus and labelling (3), baseline (2), Donut fine-tuning (4), robustness and cross-validation (3), evaluation and write-up (2).

Title:
Anomaly Detection in Wireless Sensor Network Data for Building Sustainability Monitoring

Problem Statement:
Sustainability dashboards in buildings rely on wireless sensors for energy, temperature and CO2, but cheap sensors drift, drop packets and produce spikes that corrupt analytics and trigger false alerts. Simple threshold rules miss contextual anomalies (normal values at abnormal times) and cannot tell sensor faults from genuine events, so a context-aware detector evaluated on real sensor streams is needed before such data drives energy decisions.

Objectives:
1. Build an anomaly detector that flags point, contextual and collective anomalies in multivariate sensor streams.
2. Compare an LSTM-autoencoder against an isolation-forest and a seasonal-threshold baseline under matched conditions.
3. Evaluate precision, recall and detection latency on labelled anomalies and quantify robustness to missing data.

Methodology:
Public building-sensor datasets (e.g. Intel Berkeley Lab and a public smart-building set) are used, with anomalies partly labelled and partly injected (spikes, stuck-at, drift, dropouts) for ground truth. Features include lagged windows and time-of-day context; data is split chronologically 70/15/15 to avoid leakage. An LSTM-autoencoder flags points whose reconstruction error exceeds a validation-tuned threshold, compared against isolation forest and a seasonal-ETS threshold baseline. Metrics are precision, recall, F1 and mean detection latency, with results stratified by anomaly type and by missing-data rate (0-30%). Sensitivity to window length is tested, and the variance is estimated over multiple injection seeds. A risk is label scarcity, addressed by the injection protocol and reported separately from real labels.

Scope:
Covers offline detection on three sensor types with the named anomaly classes and missing-data rates. Excludes real-time streaming deployment, root-cause diagnosis and actuator control, listed as future work.

Expected Outcomes:
1. A trained detector with precision/recall/latency versus both baselines, stratified by anomaly type.
2. A robustness analysis across missing-data rates and a recommended operating threshold.

Timeline:
14 weeks: data and injection protocol (3), baselines (2), LSTM-autoencoder (4), robustness experiments (3), evaluation and write-up (2).
